title: Man to Man review – Tilda Swinton’s perfect pacing makes this multi-character monologue compelling | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Starting in Germany in the 1930s, there is a stinging topicality to Manfred Karge’s play addressing the renaissance of Nazi ideology
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Starting in Germany in the 1930s, there is a stinging topicality to Manfred Karge’s play addressing the renaissance of Nazi ideology
Content: Tilda Swinton – on a Bunny Christie set dotted with period East German technology – regularly transforms verbally and physically into other women and men.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTilda Swinton – on a Bunny Christie set dotted with period East German technology – regularly transforms verbally and physically into other women and men.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewMan to Man review – Tilda Swinton’s perfect pacing makes this multi-character monologue compellingRoyal Court theatre, LondonStarting in Germany in the 1930s, there is a stinging topicality to Manfred Karge’s play addressing the renaissance of Nazi ideologyMark LawsonFri 11 Sep 2026 19.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarly autumn London theatre has already featured two Oscar winners: Cate Blanchett in Electra / Persona and Mark Rylance in Tartuffe (Remixed). NowTilda Swintonmakes a trio. This shows the commendable dedication of some screen talent to theatre but also the box office need, in recessions, for famous faces. Unusually, there was a first night red carpet outside the Royal Court, leading a writer long associated with the venue to express “shock” to ushers at such Hollywood vulgarity.Swinton is reprising Manfred Karge’s Man to Man, which she first performed 39 years ago, in a production heading to Edinburgh, Berlin and New York. The piece is a multicharacter monologue starting in Germany in the 1930s.When her husband, Max, dies, Ella Gericke puts on his clothes and takes over his job as a crane operator. She seems to act from some combination of bereavement denial, cross-gender curiosity and proto-feminist belief in equal employment.Ella’s challenge as Max is to be a bloke unremarkable enough not to alert men or arouse women. The next worst thing that could happen is Germany calling up men to war with the resulting medicals and barrack rooms.In the most chilling moment, the workmates’ certainty of her masculinity becomes dangerous when the lads attempt debagging to seek evidence of circumcision that might then have led to death.With high hair and white body paint that may suggest disguise or scabies, Swinton strikingly resembles David Bowie’s avatar Aladdin Sane, an earlier project exploring androgyny. With a gruff laddishness as her base tone, Swinton – on a Bunny Christie set dotted with period East German technology including fridge and tape machine – regularly transforms verbally and physically into other women and men.View image in fullscreenTilda Swinton’s high hair and white body paint may suggest disguise or scabies.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWhen the play premiered, identity fluidity was largely a metaphor or aspiration rather than the reality it now is, giving the text another level. The framing has also changed politically. Man To Man had 26 scenes when premiered in Germany in 1982 and first performed by Swinton five years later.Karge’s new section, featuring the fall of the Berlin Wall, featured in a 2015 Edinburgh fringe revival the dramatist has now written a 28th, addressing the renaissance of Nazi ideology in Germany: “The war dead have risen / In the dark of night.” There is a stinging topicality in this coda being premiered just five days after the far-right AfD party topped the state polls in Saxony-Anhalt. The 88-year-old playwright’s continuing revisions emphase that the ghosts of 1930s Germany still walk almost a century on.Anthony Vivis’s 1980s English version, revised by director Stephen Unwin, conveys Karge’s knack for vivid imagery. A smoker’s yellow stained finger is able to write an endearment in after-sex sweat on Ella’s body; Hitler youth piss swastikas in the snow.The show at times resembles performance art – Swinton slept in a glass box as a living exhibit in a 1995 installation – but the performer’s verbal flexibility and perfect pacing make Man To Man compelling theatre. However incongruously at an historically radical venue, this truly is a red carpet event.At royalcourttheatre.com, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreTilda SwintonWest EndreviewsShareReuse this content

title: He was at his desk at the Pentagon on 9/11. As the chaos unfolded, he refused to leave | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: Matthew Klimow recalls the day a hijacked airliner crashed into the headquarters of the US defence department in Arlington, Virginia
Author: David Smith
Headline: Matthew Klimow recalls the day a hijacked airliner crashed into the headquarters of the US defence department in Arlington, Virginia
Content: The Pentagon after terrorists highjacked an airplane and crashed into the building on 9/11.Photograph: Greg Mathieson/Mai/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Pentagon after terrorists highjacked an airplane and crashed into the building on 9/11.Photograph: Greg Mathieson/Mai/Getty ImagesSeptember 11 2001He was at his desk at the Pentagon on 9/11. As the chaos unfolded, he refused to leaveMatthew Klimow recalls the day a hijacked airliner crashed into the headquarters of the US defence department in Arlington, VirginiaDavid Smithin WashingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 09.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“All day I had been a good soldier: stolid, resolute, unemotional, rational, and dispassionate,” writesMatthew Klimow, recalling the wave of emotion that overwhelmed him as he arrived home from the Pentagon on 11 September 2001. There was sadness for the lives lost. But there was another emotion, too: humiliation.“We, as a nation, had been humbled,” writes the retired army colonel, who remained at the Pentagon even after it was struck by a hijacked airliner, killing all 64 people onboard and 125 inside the building. “The fighting force of which I was part had been impotent, unable to protect our fellow citizens. The darkness I felt matched the darkness inside my house as I opened the door.”Klimow recalls the longest day of his career inAs the Pentagon Burned, a study in leadership and a first-person account of the chaos that unfolded at the headquarters of the US defence department in Arlington, Virginia, on the day that planes also hit New York and Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Donald Trump marked the 25th anniversary of the United States’ worst terrorist attack in a ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday.View image in fullscreenMatthew Klimow at Nato headquarters in Brussels in 2013. Klimow’s career spans more than half a century of military and diplomatic service.Photograph: Virginia Mayo/AFP/Getty ImagesKlimow’s book recalls how leaders at all levels suppressed their emotional shock to respond with calm determination and grace under pressure. But it also tells how the attacks revealed a tension between military protocol and the need for improvisation, and how coordination was plagued by erroneous intelligence, overlapping chains of command and communication gaps – including a critical half-hour whenDonald Rumsfeld, the US secretary of defense, was unreachable.Born and raised in Johnson City, New York, Klimow’s career spans more than half a century of military and diplomatic service. He entered the military academy at West Point in 1970 and graduated in 1974, commencing a 29-year army career that took him from commanding paratroopers in the 18th Airborne Corps toearning the Silver Starfor gallantry during the Gulf war.On the morning of September 11, Klimow was executive assistant to GenRichard Myers, vice-chair of the joint chiefs of staff. The chair, Gen Hugh Shelton, took off early for Hungary. The acting role fell to Myers, who would assume the position full-time on 1 October.Klimow was in his office by 5.15am. Since Myers’ confirmation hearings before the US Senate were imminent, he left for Capitol Hill around 8.45am, taking along his young aide-de-camp, Capt Chris Donahue. Klimow remained at his desk, his eyes drifting to a television monitor kept on mute.Suddenly, the screen filled with the horrific image of theWorld Trade Center’s north tower on fire. Speaking by phone from Monterey, Tennessee, Klimow, 74, says: “When I looked up, there was the newscast of the World Trade Center burning and I turned the volume up and I was just dumbfounded because it’s such a clear blue sky. I was in denial. I kept thinking it’s some freak accident, a small airplane maybe, and they were speculating the same thing on the newscast.”View image in fullscreenShocked crowds of observe the burning World Trade Center towers in New York City on September 11.Photograph: Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis/Getty ImagesThe secure “red switch” telephone began to bleep. On the other end wasGen Ralph Eberhart, commander of North American Aerospace Defense Command (Norad). “That set off alarm bells with me as soon as I heard his voice, which I knew. He asked for General Myers. I said he’s on Capitol Hill. And he said, ‘Colonel, it’s urgent. Get hold of him. Get him to a phone. I need to talk to him now.’”Klimow immediately called Donahue, and told him to barge into a senator’s office and retrieve Myers. The red switch rang again. This time Eberhart’s words were chilling: “We have several airplanes in the air on radar. An unknown number of them have been hijacked.”As Klimow frantically took notes, his secretary waved wildly: Shelton was calling on an unsecure line. Klimow found himself with the secure red switch handset pressed to his left ear, and the unsecure telephone to Shelton in his right. He began a frantic double-relay, feeding the developments to the towering, impatient four-star general across the ocean.Then, the ground shook. “All of a sudden, Mary Turner, our secretary, jumped up and said, ‘I think the building moved!’ Then there was absolute pandemonium outside our door. People were shouting, running down the corridor and I yelled, ‘Shut the door, Mary, I can’t hear!’”PanicIn his deep focus, Klimow had not heard the thunderous impact of Flight 77 slamming into the western facade of the Pentagon. Finally, aNational Military Command Center (NMCC)watchofficer broke into the red switch conference: the Pentagon had been hit.By chance the plane had smashed into a newly renovated wedge of the Pentagon, outfitted with state-of-the-art ballistic glass. This helped reduce the casualty count, but prevented the kinetic energy from escaping, channelling fireballs through the long corridors and hallways.View image in fullscreenFirst responders on scene, after an attack at the Pentagon on September 11, in Arlington, Virginia in this image provided and edited by FBI to conceal the identity of first responders.Photograph: Getty ImagesKlimow went to the river entrance to meet Myers, and the two men fought their way back up the stairs into the burning building. Two police officers tried to bar their entry. Myers and Klimow pushed past them and descended into the NMCC, a windowless cold war labyrinth.Early reports via the red switch incorrectly stated that American Airlines Flight 11 – which had already struck the World Trade Center – was confirmed hijacked, and heading toward Washington.Acritical friction pointexisted between Norad and the air national guard. Norad scrambled jets from Langley air force base, but initially lacked the rules of engagement (ROE) to shoot down civilian aircraft. Meanwhile, the Secret Service prompted the launch of fighters from Andrews air force base, outside the normal military chain of command. Those aircraft were operating under a more permissive “weapons free” rule of engagement.The Langley pilots initially flew east because an erroneous generic flight plan sent them that way, and they believed they were responding to the threat of a cruise missile attack from the sea. This lack of “situational awareness” delayed their arrival in Washington.Klimow, meanwhile, experienced a sudden dread when he turned around and realised Myers was gone. As the executive assistant, Klimow’s sole purpose was to remain at the acting chair’s side.“I panicked,” he confesses. “I tore out of there. I ran as fast as I could into the corridors of the Pentagon and I can’t tell you how eerie it was because there are 22,000 people who work in the Pentagon and the place was deserted, there was a film of smoke in the air and they didn’t turn off the fire alarm. There’s this blaring alarm with a recorded message to evacuate the building just echoing.“I ran to our office. It was absolutely deserted and I stood in the centre of our office thinking, where did he go? It struck me, he’s with Secretary Rumsfeld, which is the office above us, so I ran up the staircase and darted into the outer office. Gen Myers was coming out of Rumsfeld’s inner office and he shook his head and said, he’s not here.”HumiliationWhen Flight 77 struck, Rumsfeld’s immediate instinct was to run toward the fire, helping carry stretchers and rescue survivors. Klimow regards it as an act of personal bravery that nevertheless created a serious operational problem.View image in fullscreenMedical personnel and volunteers working the first medical triage area set up outside the Pentagon after a hijacked commercial airliner crashed into the south-west corner of the building.Photograph: Greg Mathieson/Mai/Getty Images“For 30 minutes, no one could get hold of the secretary of defense when our country is under attack,” Klimow says. “He eventually made his way into the NMCC and described the destruction outside and he was calm and cool, like everybody. But when he talked toVice-President [Dick] Cheney, I knew something was amiss, and it took me weeks later to figure out what had happened.“He was briefed by General Myers on Norad’s response and the rules of engagement, and the vice-president was talking to him about fighters coming out of Andrews air force base with different rules of engagement, but they were talking past each other. They didn’t realise they were talking about two different responses by the air force.”Klimow’s wife, Edie, a retired army nurse and major whom he met in Germany, had spent the day racked with anxiety. Their son, Daniel, in middle school, had been told by teachers that the Pentagon was under attack. “He had this vision of terrorists running through the hallways with machine guns,” Klimow says.It was after midnight when Klimow finally walked out of the smoking ruins of the Pentagon. Covered in grey soot and smelling of burning jet fuel, he drove home to Arlington, Virginia. The silence was broken by a sound he had never imagined hearing over the capital.“It was the eeriest thing. It was the sound of American jet fighters overhead. When I realised that my own neighbourhood, my own capital city and my own country had to be protected by a combat air patrol, it was humiliating to think that we had been so surprised by such a devastating attack.“The lights were off in the house and I thought Edie must be asleep, but I opened the door and she was there waiting for me. That’s when we had this big emotional embrace and knew that we would get up the next day and start working on a solution.”WisdomThe solution that Klimow and his colleagues began drafting on 12 September would eventually morph into the “war on terror”, a sprawling military campaign that would redefine the global order, not necessarily to the US’s advantage. Looking back from the vantage point of 2026, Klimow views those choices with sober realism.“Everything looks different with hindsight but, that cliche aside, we had little choice but to enter Afghanistan militarily and to make sure that the launching pad for what al-Qaida used to do to us was eliminated from Afghanistan.“Did we make wise decisions tactically or operationally? Sometimes yes, sometimes no, but strategically I don’t think in the days and weeks following 9/11 there was any doubt in most people’s mind that this required military action, not just diplomacy.”Diplomacy became Klimow’s own second act during afive-year spell as the US ambassador to Turkmenistan. It gave him a close perspective on the end of the US’s longest war: the 2021 withdrawal from Afghanistan after 20 years and the return to power of the Taliban.Amid the mayhem was a familiar face: Donahue, the captain whom he ordered to barge into a senator’s office on 9/11. Donahue rose to become a major general commanding the 82nd airborne division. On 30 August 2021, a night-vision photograph was beamed across the world, showing a solitary US soldier boarding the final C-17 transport plane out of Taliban-controlled Kabul airport. It was Donahue –the very last US soldier to leave Afghanistan.View image in fullscreenLt Gen Christopher Donahue on 2 June 2023 in Fayetteville, North Carolina.Photograph: Melissa Sue Gerrits/Getty Images“Talk about the irony of being there at the beginning and being there at the end,” Klimow muses.The days and weeks after 9/11 were arguably the last time the United States was truly united. The Iraq war, financial crisis, social media, rise of Donald Trump and Covid-19 pandemic have divided and redivided the nation. But 25 years later, Klimow refuses to despair.“There were seams that were ripping in our society in the 1960s, and I was witness to that. But we pulled things together,” he says. “It’s not the same situation, of course, but I have a firm belief that we go through cycles like this, and America’s principles, and our resilience, and our devotion to liberty and freedom are unshakable.“I’m still a big believer in the American dream and what we can do together, and the belief that we will continue to pull together, in ways that may be different from some of our historic past, but our resilience and the brilliance of our nation’s founding still make that possible.”Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001US politicsUS militaryWashington DCUS national securityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence | Movies | The Guardian
description: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killing
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killing
Content: ‘It’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen’ … Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen’ … Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceXan Brooksin VeniceRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killingFri 11 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a darkened rooftop in Tel Aviv, Israeli intelligence officers outline the details of their work. These men tell us how they helped develop an AI mapping tool that trawled for phone signals and recommended apartment buildings inGazato bomb. Indirectly, they admit, they are responsible for thousands of deaths, but they never spoke up because that wasn’t their place. “My role is technical,” says one. “I’m just a small cog,” says another.Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmRead moreNAZA – directed by the Israeli film-makers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham and produced by the Guardian – is a chilling documentary about a mass slaughter that was authorised at the highest levels of government. But it is also, primarily, about the process, the system, the little links in the killing chain. Szor and Abraham build their film around the accounts of 24 anonymised military and intelligence insiders.NAZA, we learn, is an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. The Israel Defense Forces prefer to target Hamas terrorists in their homes at night – and if they live with their family, or in heavily populated neighbourhoods, too bad. At one point, a source claims, approval was given to kill 500 NAZA for one Hamas member.I meet Szor and Abraham at the Venice film festival, where NAZA is competing for the Golden Lion award. The pair won an Oscar for their previous documentary, 2024’sNo Other Land(co-directed with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal), which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank. “No Other Land documented horrible crimes,” Abraham says. “But at the same time it gave people … I don’t want to say hope, but some light to latch on to. It’s not a coincidence that this film is all in the dark. We are in a very dark place right now.”double quotation markSome people talk because they feel the opposite of shame. They feel pride in their accomplishment and expertiseYuval AbrahamThe Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties. NAZA briefly shows us the rubble, grieving parents, dead children on the ground. Its main backdrop, though, is placid, normal Tel Aviv, just 44 miles to the north, where rush-hour traffic drifts dreamily on the street and the cinematheque is showing a Claude Lanzmann retrospective. Tellingly, the film was executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the director ofThe Zone of Interest. Glazer, says Szor, supported the structure and creative approach she and Abraham had adopted, that fostered the sense of a home that sits next door to hell.NAZA deliberately concerns itself with the system – the policy of mass surveillance, the industrial business of murder – more than the individual psychology of those involved. But presumably its sources must feel guilt and shame, otherwise they’d never have agreed to put their careers and liberty at risk.View image in fullscreen‘We are in a very dark place right now’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianAbraham is unconvinced. “Well, it depends which one,” he says. “There are many motivations for an individual to speak. Some people talk because they feel the opposite of shame. They feel pride in their accomplishment and expertise. Remember that these people serve in sensitive units. They are not often asked what they do. So there is an attraction to [our] curiosity that drives them to speak up.”The film uncovers a system that is fiendishly efficient. Its series of disconnects appears designed to distance the perpetrators from the crime. Many of these men work remotely from Tel Aviv. AI selects the target and a drone drops the bomb. Even the language feels purposely euphemistic and obfuscatory. NAZA translates as collateral damage, which in turn translates to human beings.“Sure, it’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen,” Abraham says. “There is some truth in that, I guess. But equally it should be said that intelligence officers know the most. They listen to the cellphones. They know the house they are bombing is full of children. They can hear babies crying. They still order another strike.”What is the status of these men now? Some discuss their work in the past tense. Others don’t, which suggests that they might still be at work, overseeing airstrikes each night. Abraham won’t say; he’s mindful of protecting his sources. “But you can imagine. We are dealing with 24 people, so there is a whole variety of statuses.”Documentary NAZA gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice film festival premiere – videoNAZA prompts obvious questions about the creatures of darkness we see on screen. But it prompts intriguing ones, too, about Szor and Abraham, a pair of dissident investigative journalists from the country’s middle class. In the furious, febrile climate of post-7 October Israel, their work is liable to make them pariahs, if not enemies of the state.Szor jokes that she just wields the camera and therefore keeps out of sight. “Nobody knows who I am, and I’m very happy about that. But some of my family – and some people I’m close to – don’t accept what I do. After the Oscars [last year] they were very ashamed, very angry. But this is a small price to pay.”Abraham, by contrast, is more vocal and visible. After No Other Land’s premiere at the 2024 Berlin film festival, his family home wastargetedby a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he says. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”double quotation markWhen we say we have to learn from the Holocaust, the way to do that is to think about patterns that can be seen in the presentYuval AbrahamEven so, he adds quickly, let’s keep things in perspective. “We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic. So yeah, it was scary for my mum. But she went and slept at my sister’s and her house is still there. For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons. Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”Rooftops at night are a good location, says Szor. They lend themselves to contemplation and help people speak more freely. One soldier recalls the “insane fun” of planning airstrikes. Another remembers visiting Holocaust sites as a boy and wondering how the German people could have acted as they did. “I still see the Nazis as evil,” he says. “But what does that mean I am?”After its Venice premiere, NAZA is greeted with a 25-minute ovation. Varietycallsit a “devastating exposé” of systematic mass slaughter. The Hollywood Reporterclaimsthat its “bombshell” revelations are likely to provoke outrage and disgust “on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu”(The Israeli military on Friday said it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary, and criticised the film’s use of anonymous testimonies, which it said “cannot be verified”. In its statement to the Guardian, the IDF said that it “makes unprecedented efforts to minimise harm to civilians” during its offensive in Gaza.)NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsRead moreAt the official press conference, the film-makers are asked about parallels between the Holocaust and the killing in Gaza. Abraham points out that this connection was made by one of the soldiers in the film. But he takes the man’s point. “When we say ‘never again’ and that we have to learn from what happened in the Holocaust, the way to do that is to think about patterns that can be seen and observed in the present. I’m not saying [the situation is Gaza] is the same or identical. I don’t think it is. But what we should be doing is recognising these similar patterns of dehumanisation and killing.”Who are these men who we can barely see on the screen? The polite data analysts. The soft-spoken officers. Almost all, it turns out, are products of Tel Aviv’s middle class: intelligent, educated and liberal, at least up to a point. Or to put it more bluntly, these are Szor and Abraham’s people. They come from the same neighbourhoods, share similar interests and probably have friends in common. It’s the ultimate paranoid horror trope: the call that comes from inside the house. It shows the extent of the rot and the film-makers’ own proximity to it.NAZA asks how these men helped kill tens of thousands of civilians. That’s somehow simpler and less frightening than asking why. Abraham shakes his head. “And I have to say I don’t have a clear answer as to why so many people took part in this. And why so few people – in fact, I don’t know of any – refused in real time to do it. It’s scary what that says about the state of Israel. When people talk about genocide, they often speak about it as something that spreads across society, this general atmosphere that normalises death. When everyone else is doing it, it’s easier not to ask questions.”Additional reporting by Lorenzo Tondo in JerusalemExplore more on these topicsFilmNAZAVenice film festivalFestivalsGazaPalestineNo Other LandinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Faith review – intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitor | Movies | The Guardian
description: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut drama
Content: Alpha-grade casting … James McAvoy and Erin Doherty in Faith.Photograph: Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenAlpha-grade casting … James McAvoy and Erin Doherty in Faith.Photograph: Toronto film festivalMoviesReviewFaith review – intense performances power startling and unsettling tale of mysterious suitorToronto film festival:Erin Doherty plays a happily single mother in a downbeat town courted by an enigmatic James McAvoy in this expertly taut dramaPeter BradshawFri 11 Sep 2026 16.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleErin Doherty andJames McAvoyboth bring their A-game in this startling, involving movie from British writer-director Paul Andrew Williams, whose productivity and creativity continue to be an industry tonic. It’s an eerie mystery drama that Doherty and McAvoy perform with ferocious commitment. There’s something of Atom Egoyan or even M Night Shyamalan here … and I even found myself wondering if Williams intended us to think of Shakespeare’s Hamlet and Laertes’ lines about his father, Polonius: “… to his good friends thus wide I’ll ope my arms / And like the kind life-rend’ring pelican, / Repast them with my blood.”We are in a downbeat British town, perhaps somewhere in the London estuary, a place to which a candy factory provides employment. Mina (played by Doherty) is a smart, capable single mum to 9-year-old Jamie (Smylie Bradwell); she works on the production line in cap and hairnet like all the others: much liked by everyone there. She is not fussed by the absence of Jamie’s dad and is perfectly content with hanging out with her friends and her sister (Liv Hill).One night at a raucous pub quiz, for which she has had to hire a local girl as a babysitter to look after Jamie back at home, Mina finds herself drawn to an enigmatic, self-possessed guy standing by the bar, smiling benignly and drinking something non-alcoholic: this is Michael, played by McAvoy. With easy confidence and a quiet kind of authority, he chats to Mina and she can’t quite read this handsome man or read his intentions. Is he flirting or what? McAvoy’s Scottish accent also blurs the class distinction that may or may not exist between them. After walking her home, charming her and even love-bombing her with devastating compliments, Michael is the perfect gentleman and says he won’t come in. Later, Mina is even more fascinated to learn that Michael volunteers at a local food bank. But how does he earn a living?Mina’s suspicious sister notes how well-spoken he is; she has perhaps picked up on something that the audience might also have noticed, that Michael has something secretive and supercilious about him. She wonders if he is or was a teacher, or if this food bank is some sort of court-ordered community service. But Mina won’t hear of any disparagement of this obviously remarkable man who is paying her the kind of attention she hasn’t had in a very long time. Michael comes round to their house and is a huge hit with Jamie; he asks Jamie if he likes computer games and goes upstairs with him to Jamie’s bedroom to play Super Mario Kart, while Mina, glowing at Michael’s quasi-paternal instincts, stays downstairs to chat with her sister.Williams shrewdly controls the film’s growing, complex mood: a cocktail of dread, fascination and something else, as if Mina has been made a party to some occult conspiracy that Michael isn’t in any hurry to reveal. He already seems to know something about Mina’s babysitter that Mina herself hasn’t suspected. The film’s central dramatic events then kick the mood up into a higher gear. Mina is passionate, bewildered and Michael assumes the priestly air of someone who has seen it all before and who is either here to help or is some kind of vampiric outsider. The problem seemed initially to be that he was too good to be true. Clearly that isn’t the issue.Williams’s alpha-grade cast present this tale of mystery with intelligence and focus and Williams shoots his principals often in looming closeup, as if the drama’s strange secret could be read in the faces themselves.Faith screened at theToronto film festival.Explore more on these topicsFilmToronto film festivalDrama filmsThrillersJames McAvoyFestivalsToronto film festival 2026reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Wake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the world  | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Donald Trump and King Charles inspecting a guard of honour at Windsor Castle, September 2025.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and King Charles inspecting a guard of honour at Windsor Castle, September 2025.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpWake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the worldSimon JenkinsThe US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t waitFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTShareIf Americans vote for a Republican majority in both houses of Congress in November, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” But they must not spend it in Canada or China or anywhere else outside the US.So said Donald Trumpin Texas on Wednesday in advance of the forthcoming midterm elections. He further told voters to “Pretend that I’m on the ballot”. It was a climactic moment in an almost two-hour rant.Trump does not have the requiredtrillion dollarsin his pocket, and it would be illegal to disperse such a sum without congressional approval. In any case, JD Vance now appears to haverowed backon the promise.Observers from abroad must beware: it is unwise to subject Trump’s populism to the discipline of truth. Trump also said Americans should thank him for attacking Iran since that country was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”, which it intended to use against them. It was the old Saddam Hussein gambit.The problem is that almost every one ofTrump’s speechesrefers back to himself, as if he and the United States were synonymous. He claimed to have won the presidency three times. He says: “If we hadn’t won the last election, I’m not sure that our country right now would even exist.” He added that the arena where he was speaking was packed, with crowds outside clamouring to get in. Pictures show ithalf empty.Anyone watching can see why there has been much medical debate over whether Trump is exhibiting signs ofnarcissism disorder. Key symptoms are mendacity and inconsistency. In 2021 members of the House of Representatives called for the constitution’s25th amendment, by which a president can be declared unfit for office, to be invoked over the Capitol Hill riot. But that has a high constitutional threshold, requiring a majority of his sycophantic cabinet to declare him unfit.As for more conventional checks on a wayward president, they have proved extraordinarily weak. A Congress over which Trump exerts a populist terrorism has been reluctant to use its powers to call him to account. He has flagrantly declared wars without congressional authority, abusedexecutive ordersas “emergencies” and frozen federal spending to halt the “advance [of] Marxist equity”. He has even tried toredefine US citizenship, which is unconstitutional.Very gradually some institutions supposed to hold the White House in check are finding muscle. Judges haveblockedattempts to limit birthright citizenship. Trump’s blanket firing of public officials is beinglegally challenged, although the supreme court has often sided with him. Even the Senate Republican leader,John Thune, has balked at Trump’s proposedSave America Act– which would require anyone voting to show documentary proof of US citizenship. Its outrageous gerrymandering would shrink Democrat votes and aid Republicans. It is an echo of the Jim Crow laws of the post-civil war south.Where this president leaves the US’s longstanding allies overseas is less clear. Visitors to the British embassy in Washington are traditionally warned that “we disagree with America about almost everything, but remain the closest of friends”. Britain distanced itself from war in Vietnam but joined the US, inexplicably, in Iraq. But nothing has come near Trump’s sustained abuse of Britain in the past year on everything from defence spending to wind turbines. He sees the UK as “weak” and “on the edge of disaster”. It was “once” the US’s greatest ally. But by implication, is no more.This opens the central weakness in Anglo-American relations that Trump has made explicit. This is the assumption that the US would honour the principle of collective defence and go to war with Russia, in the event that Russia declared war on Europe. This held during the cold war, with the US’s guarantee of Europe’s security taken as axiomatic.Since the end of the cold war, that guarantee has become ever more flimsy. Despite events in Ukraine, it has longseemed implausible that Russia would declare nuclear waron the west, let alone on America itself. It is therefore equally implausible that the US could threaten Russia with nuclear retaliation.At which point a central essence of the Nato alliance starts to crumble. European governments have seen a president ready to annex foreign countries, invade others, disrupt world trade with aggressive tariffsand defy international law. Can such a wayward and egocentric man, devoid of domestic constraints, really be relied on to exercise extreme caution and dependability in circumstances where nuclear weapons are at issue – whether or not the end of the cold war has diminished the threat of east-west confrontation?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn other words, nations should start looking realistically at the defence of their own continent and their own borders. There is no new world order any longer. That balloon has been punctured.Friends of the US have always relied on its constitution to hold autocratic presidents to the straight and narrow. But not since Andrew Jackson in the 1830s has there been one who flouts law and convention as brazenly as Trump. Over the next two years his nation’s political institutions are to be sorely tested. But then he will be gone. Perhaps only then will Britain learn his legacy.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsUS foreign policyDefence policyUS national securityUS midterm elections 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: From ‘Ozempic breath’ to hair loss: sorting the science from the hype about weight loss jabs | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Do you gain weight once you stop using them? Do they make your face saggy? Can they improve your mental health? Experts explain whether 13 common beliefs about GLP-1s are true or false
Author: Isabelle Aron
Headline: Do you gain weight once you stop using them? Do they make your face saggy? Can they improve your mental health? Experts explain whether 13 common beliefs about GLP-1s are true or false
Content: Is it all just a lot of hot air?Illustration: Matt Chase/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIs it all just a lot of hot air?Illustration: Matt Chase/The GuardianLife and styleFrom ‘Ozempic breath’ to hair loss: sorting the science from the hype about weight loss jabsDo you gain weight once you stop using them? Do they make your face saggy? Can they improve your mental health? Experts explain whether 13 common beliefs about GLP-1s are true or falseIsabelle AronFri 11 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey suppress your appetite so you never feel hungryFALSE“GLP-1 medications mimic Glucagon-like peptide-1 – one of the hormones involved in appetite regulation. It doesn’t completely suppress hunger, but it is powerful,” says Dr Federica Amati, nutrition lead at Imperial College School of Medicine and author of The Appetite Reset. “The medicine is about 1,000 times stronger than what we naturally produce from our gut,” she explains. As food passes through the gut, cells called L-cells sense the nutrients, which sparks the production of the GLP-1 hormone. Without the drugs, these bursts of GLP-1 production last a few minutes. “It’s a bit like a sparkler. In comparison, the drugs are like a bonfire that roars for a week,” says Amati. Because the GLP-1 hormone stays in your body for longer if you are on the drugs, you feel fuller faster and your appetite gets suppressed, but you will eventually get hungry.They can cause gastrointestinal issuesTRUE“Nausea, constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and vomiting are well-recognised side-effects,” says Dr Adrian Brown, associate professor and specialist dietitian at University College London. “They tend to occur during dose escalation, and most symptoms improve over time.” Eating smaller meals, staying hydrated and limiting fatty foods can help.“One of the best ways to prevent these side-effects is to prepare your gut, liver and pancreas before you start taking the medications,” says Amati. “If you go into treatment with existing reflux or constipation, it’s only going to get worse.” She advises eating more plants and gradually upping your fibre intake. Once taking the drugs, never push past the point of fullness. “The gastric emptying is so slow that you need to stop straight away.”They make you forget to drink waterPARTLY TRUEThe drugs themselves don’t make you want to drink less, but people can experience this as a side-effect. This is partly because we get a lot of water from food, especially fruits and vegetables. “These drugs massively reduce the amount that you eat – up to 40% reduction in calories,” says Amati. You may also drink less if you’re experiencing nausea, constipation or reflux. “It’s important that you do drink, because dehydration is one of the key reasons why reflux and constipation may be worse,” she says. As well as drinking water, she recommends having hydrating foods and smoothies, especially on the day you take the drugs (typically, the injections are used once a week, while the pills are taken daily), when you can have the most appetite suppression.They can make you deficient in nutrientsTRUETaking GLP-1 medication can “substantially reduce food intake, and that creates the potential for nutrient deficiencies if the quality of a person’s diet is poor,” says Brown, who has researched this area. He found that some people on these drugs may not get enough vitamin D, vitamin B12, iron, calcium and protein.“If your diet was relatively healthy to begin with, that’s fine because you’re just eating less. But this is not true for many people,” says Giles Yeo, professor of molecular neuroendocrinology at the University of Cambridge and an obesity expert. “For those whose diets were not great to begin with, there’s a danger of going into malnutrition. You can’t just inject yourself and hope for the best. You have to think about your diet and exercise.”Once you come off them you gain weight againPARTLY TRUE“Obesity is a chronic, relapsing, progressive condition. When medications for obesity are stopped, a person’s body will attempt to regain the weight,” says Brown. “Studies have shown that people can regain about 60% of the weight lost following stopping the medication.”In fact, one studyfrom the University of Oxfordfound that people who stop taking GLP-1 medication will return to their original weight within two years. “For a lot of people, these are likely to be long-term or for ever drugs,” says Yeo. “Your appetite is only suppressed when you’re on them. If you stop, your hormonal levels will go back to what they were. You’ll feel as hungry as before, which means the weight will come back.”While the idea of taking medication for ever might sound scary, Yeo points out that many people take medication for high blood pressure and statins, used for lowering cholesterol, for life. “I think the same is going to be true for these drugs,” he says.They make you lose muscle and you need to eat more protein while taking themTRUE“Whenever people lose weight, they don’t just lose fat, they also lose muscle. The key point is whether we can minimise it,” says Brown. “Current evidence suggests that up to 40% of the weight lost with GLP-1 medicine may come from lean mass [bone, muscle and connective tissue] rather than fat alone.”This is why it’s important to prioritise protein-rich foods and resistance training when taking GLP-1s. “It’s not negotiable – you have to do it if you want to preserve lean mass,” says Amati. “If you have excess fat mass and you engage in resistance training, you will lose fat first because that’s the stored energy source.” She recommends resistance training three times a week, including high-quality protein in every meal, and eating that first.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Matt Chase/The GuardianNot everyone responds to them in the same wayTRUE“These drugs don’t work for everybody – they’re not a magic bullet,” says Amati. “The data shows that 5-20% of people lose less than 5% of their body weight, so they’re classed as non-responders. If you’re someone who doesn’t have a very sensitive GLP-1 receptor, GLP-1 medications won’t have the desired effect.” While we don’t yet know why this is, Yeo says that it’s only a matter of time before we do.Anyoneshould use themto lose weightFALSEGLP-1 drugs were originally developed for people with type 2 diabetes. Now, they’re also licensed for people with obesity, or people who are overweight and have weight-related health problems. Despite this, many people are using GLP-1s for aesthetic reasons because they’ve become so easily accessible.“I see a lot of people accessing them to lose weight before a wedding or a holiday,” says Amati. “These drugs are not designed for that.” People taking GLP-1s in this way could end up with a worse body composition, she explains. “It’s much easier to regain fat than muscle, so you could find yourself with increased fat mass compared to before you started. Losing lean mass is not helpful for longevity.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey couldimprove your mentalhealthPARTLY TRUEWhen it comes to how GLP-1s impact anxiety and depression, Michael Browning, professor of psychiatry at the University of Oxford, says, “The evidence that they’re beneficial is pretty thin, and some studies are ongoing.”Things are more promising for addiction, particularly with alcohol, where there have been some randomised controlled trials. One of these showed that taking semaglutide (the GLP-1 agonist in Wegovy and Ozempic)reduced the number of heavy drinking daysfor participants. For other addictions, such as nicotine and other drugs, more research is needed. “There’s work in animals that suggests they might reduce nicotine dependence, but the evidence is not there in humans,” says Browning.They cause bad breath and smelly burpsMORE RESEARCH NEEDEDIs “Ozempic breath” a thing? “There is a lot of anecdotal evidence, but not any epidemiological studies,” says Dr Praveen Sharma, an associate professor at the University of Birmingham’s School of Dentistry.While there’s no hard evidence yet, it could be side-effects like vomiting and dehydration that lead to a dry mouth, he says. Saliva “keeps the mouth hydrated and the bacteria level low”, so having a dry mouth can mean “you get a proliferation of bacteria, which can result in bad breath”.As for burps? Dr Lindsey Ann Edwards, senior lecturer in microbiology at King’s College London, says that by slowing gastric emptying, GLP-1 medication can “cause food to remain in the stomach and upper gastrointestinal tract for longer, creating more opportunity for the gut microbiome to ferment partially digested food. This microbial fermentation can generate gases which may contribute to unpleasant-smelling or “sulphur” burps.They can make your hair fall outTRUEYour body goes through a stress response when you take GLP-1 drugs, says consultant dermatologist Dr Angela Tewari. “That puts stress on the hair, and you can experience telogen effluvium, which is stress response hair loss. It puts your hair into a shedding phase,” she says.The good news is that this kind of hair loss is reversible. As your body gets used to the medication, this side-effect will ease off, although the pace at which your hair grows back will vary. “It can be an inch a month for some people. Generally, how fast your hair grows is a genetic thing,” says Tewari, who recommends taking the lowest possible dose of GLP-1s and eating food rich in protein, zinc, iron and vitamin C to encourage a healthy scalp.Your facemay get saggy and gauntTRUEYou may take GLP-1s to change your body, but what do the drugs do to your face? Under your skin, you have a “support system”, explains Tewari. “There’s your collagen, and under that you have a fat layer and a muscle layer. That all makes the skin look plumper.” When you lose the fat layer quickly, the top layer of your skin is still expanded, as it has stretched over time to support the other layers. This means your skin will sag as there is less support underneath, so it can look wrinkled and dull. To counter this, many people end up spending money on injectables, says Tewari. “I wouldn’t jump into any procedures straight away. Allow your body to settle into its new look before you do anything,” she says.Weight loss isn’t the only health benefitMORE RESEARCH NEEDEDAs more people take GLP-1s, researchers are looking at the benefits beyond weight loss. One study found that people on GLP-1s were30% less likely to develop breast cancer. Another found that patients with breast, lung, bowel or liver cancer who took them were up to 50%less likely to have their cancer spread.“What’s challenging is disentangling the direct impact of these drugs and the secondary impact of losing weight,” says Dr Simon Cork, associate professor of physiology at Anglia Ruskin University’s School of Medicine. “Obesity increases your risk of at least 13 types of cancer. By reducing your weight, the likelihood of you developing cancer will also be reduced.”Cork has researched GLP-1s and cardiovascular disease, and found that “the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with obesity taking GLP-1 was reduced by about 14%”. More research is needed, but if there are “weight-independent effects of these drugs”, Cork says the difficulty will be in trying to separate those benefits from weight loss, as some patients won’t need to lose weight.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleWeight-loss drugsObesityDiabetesDrugsHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK given record £36m donation by British crypto billionaire | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Ben Delo was convicted in US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls but pardoned by Trump
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Ben Delo was convicted in US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls but pardoned by Trump
Content: Ben Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationView image in fullscreenBen Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationReform UKReform UK given record £36m donation by British crypto billionaireBen Delo was convicted in US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls but pardoned by TrumpRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 11 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been given a record £36m donation by Ben Delo, a British cryptocurrency billionaire convicted in the US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls.The businessman, who has moved back to the UK from Hong Kong, is now the biggest UK political donor by far, dwarfing the £15m contribution to Reform UK from Thailand-based Christopher Harborne.The huge donation will be a boost for party leader Nigel Farage at a time when he is facing a police investigation into overseas funding for Reform, plus a standards inquiry into a £5m undeclared personal gift from Harborne.It had been thought Delo could be caught by the overseas cap requiring donors to have been resident in the UK for 12 months before giving more than £100,000 butReform insisted earlier this month that they were confident Delo would not have to take back any cash.Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned byDonald Trump. He has previously given Reform £8m since the start of the year.His gifts show the rise of Reform’s mega-donors, which Labour has been considering clamping down on.Keir Starmer shied away from the idea of a cap on all donations and Andy Burnham also recently backed away from supporting a cap. However, more recently the government said it was looking at ways of dealing with mega-donations to make sure a few figures are not having an excessive influence in politics.On Friday night, Stella Creasy, the Labour MP pushing for a cap, said: “The government has admitted UK mega-donors are a problem – donations like this show why we must act and the good news is it’s not too late to do something about them.“We can still stop these people from distorting the next election by confirming what the cap should be on UK donations in the representation of the people bill in the Lords.Met police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UKRead more“This donation tonight – more for Reform on one day than the entire amount spent by Labour in the general election – shows that cannot come too soon to protect British democracy.”Many more Labour MPs were also horrified by the prospect of such a huge cash injection for Reform ahead of the next election.Delo’s donation was revealed in the Telegraph, which was given the information by Reform after the party was approached by the Sunday Times earlier on Friday.Farage said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo has shown such confidence in Reform. Ben knows that we are the only party that can turn the country around and reverse Britain’s decline.”In a Telegraph article in April, Delo explained his motivation for turning to Reform, saying England was his home and that “the biggest obstacle to national recovery is the entrenched self-deception of our elites”.“Their regime of nonsense now poses such a grave threat to the UK that, for the first time in my life, I’ve become politically active,” he wrote.He said that as a person on the autism spectrum, he did not like it that “the official culture of government now forces everyone to be chronically dishonest”, citing expression of views on transgender people.In his Telegraph article, he wrote: “I helped build one of the world’s first major crypto trading platforms, fell foul of US regulators, accepted a plea bargain and a civil fine for a regulatory failing that isn’t even a crime in the UK, but then ended up being pardoned by Donald Trump, the US president, anyway.”Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum and public life, as well as non-affiliated groups and individuals, from a political base near Westminster Abbey.AGuardian investigationinto Delo’s political base found he had given support in kind to Rupert Lowe, the anti-migration MPchallenging Farage from the right, while also connecting with more mainstream figures including the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, and the former Tory cabinet minister Michael Gove.Delo’s lawyers previously told the Guardian that he provided space for those with diverse views to express them, and financial support to a broad range of organisations, many of which had conflicting views. This did not mean he endorsed the opinions of each, they said.Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingThe super-richCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: MPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and Wales | Assisted dying | The Guardian
description: Bill’s failure in Commons sparks anger among its supporters after Lords blocked earlier legislation
Author: Peter Walker
Headline: Bill’s failure in Commons sparks anger among its supporters after Lords blocked earlier legislation
Content: Campaigners for and against the proposed change in the law outside the Palace of Westminster on Friday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCampaigners for and against the proposed change in the law outside the Palace of Westminster on Friday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesAssisted dyingMPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and WalesBill’s failure in Commons sparks anger among its supporters after Lords blocked earlier legislationPeter WalkerSenior political correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 12.53 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA renewed attempt to legalise assisted dying has been voted down by MPs in a decision that is likely to scupper the idea for a political generation, sparking anger among supporters after an earlier bill was blocked by the Lords.A private member’s bill put forward by Labour’s Lauren Edwards, which would have permitted assisted dying inEnglandand Wales in certain limited circumstances, was defeated by 286 to 270 at second reading, the first chance MPs have to vote on a measure.After the decision some MPs cheered and hugged in the Commons chamber, while anti-assisted dying activists celebrated in Parliament Square. But supporters of the measure said a public which, according to polling, generally supports the idea would be baffled by the inability of politicians to enact it.An earlier private member’s bill to permit assisted dying, spearheaded by another Labour MP, Kim Leadbeater, was approved by MPs in the last parliamentary session but ran out of parliamentary time in April after a handful of peersthwarted it in the Lords, tabling hundreds of amendments.In a statement after the vote, Edwards said voters wanted change and “will not understand why that couldn’t happen because a minority in the House of Lords used procedural devices to block it and MPs balked at insisting that they do their job”.She added: “Assisted dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough. Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again, as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand.”Leadbeater said she felt “really sad”, adding: “I feel really disappointed – not for me but for the many people who’ve campaigned on this issue long before I came along and the terminally ill people who are quite simply asking for choice, asking for compassion, asking for dignity in their dying days.”A number of MPs and peers were “deeply upset” at events and would attempt to bring the issue back, she predicted, while saying she did not know when this would be.In another statement after the vote, threeLabourMPs who voted against the plan, Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato, insisted their decision was purely based on practicalities.They said: “MPs have voted against this bill because it wasn’t an abstract debate but a decision about a real bill that was unsafe and unworkable. But this is not a moment for celebration. We understand the deep concerns of so many people across the country who have campaigned hard for a change in the law.“But the truth is none of the relevant royal medical colleges, professional groups or experts will attest to the safety or workability of this bill.”Much of the other reaction was split along more entrenched lines, with John Sherrington, the Catholic archbishop of Liverpool, thanking MPs for the vote.In contrast, Andrew Copson, the chief executive of Humanists UK, said: “This vote provides not one extra penny for palliative care or disability support. On the contrary, it makes it less likely. And terminally ill people will still suffer, travel to Switzerland, and take their own lives in increasing numbers, while today’s inequalities continue.”Friday’s debate before the vote saw some emotionally charged speeches, including from Dalton,who needs lifelong treament for terminal metastatic breast cancer. She argued that the bill did not adequately protect people with treatable depression who also had a terminal illness.Another Labour MP, Claire Hazelgrove, who supported the bill, said her mother chose to end her life aged 61 while suffering a late-stage terminal illness. Hazelgrove said: “She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated. I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”4:36MPs recount personal experiences as they debate assisted dying bill – videoWith many of the arguments for and against the bill being repeats of those made when Leadbeater’s version was approved, the defeat appeared to be a product in part of less motivation among supporters of the plan.Leadbeater’s bill was backed by 330 votes to 275 on its second reading, and by 313 to 291 at the third reading. Friday’s result thus saw the totals for both sides falling, but with a greater drop-off among supporters.Some MPs had said they were lobbied notably less by pro-assisted dying campaigners this time than with Leadbeater’s bill.There was also a more sceptical view of the issue from Andy Burnham’s Downing Street than there had been under Keir Starmer.With Burnham and his ministers staying officially neutral in what was seen as a matter of conscience, the prime minister announced hewould not voteon the bill – his predecessor voted in favour – andsaidhe believed the debate on assisted dying should be paused until social care was improved.Another factor was the possibility of using the Parliament Act to force the bill through the Lords if peers tried to stop it again, under provisions that prevent the upper house from indefinitely blocking measures backed by MPs. This ideahad brought concernsfrom some MPs.Closing Friday’s debate, the health minister Alison McGovern said the government would enact the plan if it became law, but reiterated concerns about social care. She said: “In my opinion, social care has been ignored for far too long, both the 1.5 million people, mainly women, who work in it, and the families who need it, and we heard that across the house today.”Explore more on these topicsAssisted dyingEnglandWalesHouse of CommonsLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Military aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outage  | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Meltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report says
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Meltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report says
Content: Passengers at Heathrow airport in west London during the disruption on Tuesday.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers at Heathrow airport in west London during the disruption on Tuesday.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAAir transportMilitary aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outageMeltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report saysRaphael BoydFri 11 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours.According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours.The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”.The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident.The outage is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical problem led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that episode, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented.Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”.Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”.O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.”The delays led to someaircraft full of passengers being stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany.Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers affected were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”.The Ministry of Defence has said there was no wrongdoing on the part of the military.A spokesperson from the MoD said: “We do not believe there’s any indication of an error on the part of the military. This is subject to the live Nats investigation, so it’d be inappropriate for us to comment further while that’s ongoing.”Explore more on these topicsAir transportAirline industryTransportFlightsMilitarynewsShareReuse this content

title: UK lawmakers urge Burnham to back ban on superintelligent AI after chilling warnings | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Letter from 70 MPs and peers follows Anthropic employee’s claim new technology could wipe out humans
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Letter from 70 MPs and peers follows Anthropic employee’s claim new technology could wipe out humans
Content: OpenAI and Anthropic were ‘gambling with our lives’, one AI researcher said this week after quitting his job at Anthropic.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenOpenAI and Anthropic were ‘gambling with our lives’, one AI researcher said this week after quitting his job at Anthropic.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)UK lawmakers urge Burnham to back ban on superintelligent AI after chilling warningsLetter from 70 MPs and peers follows Anthropic employee’s claim new technology could wipe out humansAI could kill all humans in next decade, warn experts: but how seriously should we take them?Robert BoothUK technology editorFri 11 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 70 MPs and peers have urged Andy Burnham to back a ban on the creation of artificial superintelligence (ASI) and lead an international movement to stop the technology after a week ofwarningsfrom experts of a 10% chance it could kill all humans.Fifteen former government ministers, along with the former head of the civil service Robin Butler, senior Labour MPs including John McDonnell and leading Conservatives, Liberal Democrat and Scottish National party MPs have written to the prime minister. They urged him to throw the government’s weight behind a bill, tabled in the Commons on Tuesday, that would prohibit ASI – an as-yet-nonexistent AI that would outcompete human capabilities in most domains.They have escalated their campaign to Downing Street afterconcerning statements from current and former AI insiders. Evan Hubinger, a senior employee at Anthropic, said he believed there was a greater than 10% chance the technology could wipe out humanity, and Jacob Coxon, a 28-year-old researcher at Anthropic, who previously worked at OpenAI, quit on Tuesday with a warning that went viral, claiming “neither company was acting responsibly”, they were “gambling with our lives” and were locked in a race for AI supremacy.Alex Sobel, the Labour MP behind the bill, said he and other signatories – ranging from the children’s TV presenter Floella Benjamin to the former Conservative environment minister Zac Goldsmith and former Northern Ireland first minister Arlene Foster – want Burnham to foster “a clear framework where superintelligent AI cannot be created”. He added: “AI companies have made it clear that they will develop agents without constraint. They’re trying to develop superintelligence, while openly admitting there is a significant risk of human extinction.”The bill mirrors legislation banning ASI promoted in Washington DC by Bernie Sanders, who this week said: “You’ve got to be a moron not to say slow it down.” It is backed by the Nobel prize-winning nuclear proliferation campaigner Beatrice Fihn and the leading Berkeley AI professor Stuart Russell, as well as Control AI, a transatlantic lobby group funded by the billionaire Skype co-founder and self-described “anti-extinctionist” Jaan Tallinn.A ban on ASI in the UK, but not in the US or China where the frontier models are being created, risks having little impact. But the parliamentarians’ bill aims to pave the way to an international agreement. They call on Burnham to use next year’s UK presidency of the G20 to create “a coalition of the willing to tackle this national and international security threat”.A government spokesperson said: “While we do not consider the measures proposed in the bill to be the right approach, we are exploring whether additional targeted interventions may be needed in future to address the most significant AI-related national security risks.”Others have played down the risk, saying that ASI remains only theoretical and that guardrails could work to prevent the worst outcomes. Experts warn that these could include catastrophic cyber-attacks, novel biohazards and AIs in control of autonomous weaponry. This week’s wave of concern follows aspate of more minor but still worrying incidentsinvolving unexpected misbehaviour by AI agents under training by OpenAI and Anthropic in which they broke out of training environments, secretly conspired and hacked into other systems.Elon Musk, who runs xAI as part of his SpaceX empire, suggested without evidence that this week’s warnings of catastrophic risk were part of a “psyop” that “has been prepared for a long time”. The world’s richest man gave a different read on the state of AI, claiming: “AI+robots will more than double the global economy in less than 10 years.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic revealed another incident of a rogue AI this week andsaidcriminals, state-sponsored groups, spyware vendors, scientists and propagandists had attempted to use its AI models to design missiles and bombs, create deadly pathogens and surveil dissidents. At its main rival, OpenAI, Paul Christiano, an AI adviser to the US government, joined the lab’s non-profit foundation and immediatelywarnedthe company was not on track to reduce the risk of “catastrophic” loss of control to an acceptable level.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Andy BurnhamOpenAIAnthropicShareReuse this content

title: Man sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’  | Employment tribunals | The Guardian
description: UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity
Content: Dayne Oram takes part in a rally outside the Rockstar Games tribunal in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenDayne Oram takes part in a rally outside the Rockstar Games tribunal in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAEmployment tribunalsMan sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activityPatrick GreenfieldFri 11 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA worker fired by the makers ofGrand Theft Autohas said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working.Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal inGlasgowexamining whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 employees for trade union activity on Friday that he thought the company started keeping an eye on a group of workers after the petition was sent to leadership in 2023.Rockstar, which disputes the claims, says Oram and his colleagues were dismissed for gross misconduct after confidential company information was shared, not because of trade union membership or activity.The workers had been helping to make Grand Theft Auto VI, which is set for release on 19 November and will probably be among the biggest launches in gaming history. The production for the game, which has reportedly generated more than $3bn (£2.27bn) in preorders, is led from the company’s Edinburgh office Rockstar North.View image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto 6 is set for release in November.Illustration: Rockstar GamesMuch of the case relies on what was shared in a Discord forum, used by about 300 Rockstar employees to discuss the company. Oram was involved in setting up the forum and helped moderate it, which is where Rockstar says sensitive information was shared and discussed.Oram told the tribunal that discussions on the forum could “get a bit out of hand”. Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar at the tribunal, read Oram the forum rules requiring workers to remain “professional and constructive” when posting. Cordrey suggested that the rules had been “routinely broken”.Cordrey read out a number of Discord posts where he suggested employees were making disparaging remarks about the company and management, including messages in which one was called “cowardly corporate fucks” and another was called a “cunt”.Oram told the tribunal that he would probably “remake” some of the moderation decisions if he had the chance to do so again, but said moderators did not want to “over-police” the channel.Oram also said he believed there was a connection between the list of names who signed the 2023 petition about remote working and the eventual firings in 2025. But Cordrey questioned whether this was really the case when 141 of 154 people who signed it were not fired.View image in fullscreenRockstar Games’ Edinburgh office.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA“It was maybe the start of them keeping an eye on things,” Oram told the tribunal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe case is expected to last about six weeks, with testimony from Rockstar Games witnesses set for October. Thecompany remains in talks with current workers, who hope official union recognition can be secured before the release of GTA VI.In total, 34 Rockstar workers were fired last year, including three in Canada who are not taking part in the tribunal. Of the 31 who were based inScotland, 23 are involved in the case and are being represented by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain.A spokesperson for Rockstar Games said: “Rockstar Games’ position has been clear and consistent throughout.“Individuals across the UK and Canada were dismissed for gross misconduct following the sharing of confidential company information, not because of alleged trade union membership or activity.
