We reject the claims and will defend them vigorously before the tribunal,” the said.The tribunal in Glasgow continues before the judge Lucy Wiseman.Explore more on these topicsEmployment tribunalsGrand Theft AutoGlasgowScotlandWork & careersnewsShareReuse this content

Content: Sam Altman speaks during a discussion with Howard Lutnick at a summit, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersView image in fullscreenSam Altman speaks during a discussion with Howard Lutnick at a summit, in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, on 2 September 2026.Photograph: Jonathan Drake/ReutersOpenAIAI agents OpenAI was testing uploaded malicious software to another service, say researchersTwo months before hacking Hugging Face, malicious packages authored by internal OpenAI agents were uploaded to RubyGemsReutersFri 11 Sep 2026 19.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI agents being ⁠tested by OpenAI uploaded hundreds of malicious packages to software service RubyGems ⁠in May,two ⁠months ​before they hackedopen-source platform Hugging Face, a group of AI ⁠researchers said on Friday.“On May 11th, 2026, hundreds of malicious packages were uploaded ⁠to RubyGems by AI agents. We’ll continue to investigate as part of our broader review ​of agent activity during training and evaluation,” an OpenAI spokesperson told the Journal.OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. ⁠RubyGems could not immediately be reached.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe incident ​preceded ​OpenAI agents’ July hack ​of Hugging Face, in which a ​swarm of ‌roughly 700 ​AI ​agents created by OpenAI carried out the attack and in many cases tried to cover their tracks.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back
Content: Ireland’s government is said to be anxious about Donald Trump’s meeting with Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence.Composite: ReutersView image in fullscreenIreland’s government is said to be anxious about Donald Trump’s meeting with Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence.Composite: ReutersIrelandIreland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet TrumpMany are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds backRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCatherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath.Trump is to fly into Dublin on Saturday morning for a two-day visit centred on golf. But before making it to his beloved greens, protocol obliges him to meet a woman who has given every impression of loathing him.A courtesy call to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence and workplace in the city’s Phoenix Park, has left the government anxious and the media reaching for popcorn. “What could possibly go wrong?” headlines ask.Many inIrelandare rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy.The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had no concerns “at all” about the encounter, but one senior official said the government was on tenterhooks. “We need to get him [Trump] in the Áras, then out of the Áras. We’ll breathe easier after,” they said.View image in fullscreenAs MP, Connolly protested Trump’s 2019 visit to Ireland and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues.Photograph: Niall Carson/PABeforewinning the Irish presidency– a ceremonial post – last year, Connolly was an independent leftwing member of parliament for Galway who protested against Trump’s2019 visitand more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. “If we are going to act as an independent sovereign state, a neutral republic, we must use our voice to speak to power and the abuse of power by president Trump,” she said.Asked in March about the criticism, Trump replied: “He’s lucky I exist.”Trump is now to meet Connolly – and Martin in a separate meeting – before heading to his golf resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.Heavy security around the Phoenix Park and Doonbeg will insulate the US president from protests, including a “No welcome for Trump” demonstration that is expected to draw thousands to central Dublin on Saturday afternoon.View image in fullscreenGarda officers patrol the beach at the Irish Open in Doonbeg before Donald Trump’s expected arrival at the weekend.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PASome hope Connolly will speak for them when she meets Trump behind closed doors. “She should speak truth to power,”Rosie O’Donnell, the US comedian who moved to Ireland after Trump won a second term, told the Irish Independent. “I don’t think she should drop what she believes in to be polite to a madman. He is like a mad king that has destroyed the country.”Leftwing parties that supported Connolly’s presidential run urged the former barrister to “find a way” to convey criticism without causing a diplomatic storm. Trump has expressed affection for the emerald isle but also wants American tech and pharmaceutical firms to move jobs and taxes from Ireland to the US, a scenario that could devastate Irish state finances.During her election campaign, Connolly promised to heed constraints of the office, which is largely symbolic and has no responsibility for foreign policy. She also said that if asked, she would meet Trump.“That implies that it’s not to meet him in order to berate him,” saidBobby McDonagh, an former Irish ambassador to the UK and EU. “She’ll have an opportunity to have a chat with President Trump and make some gentle points reflective of Irish values. I expect it to go smoothly.”Connolly could emulate Martin, who discreetly rebutted some of Trump’s opinions during a visit to the White House, said McDonagh. “He had the emotional intelligence and experience to do it in a way that didn’t provoke any reaction.”The six-time major champion golferRory McIlroysaid he and other competitors at Doonbeg would focus on the game, not politics. “It’s going to be different with him being here but we’re here to play a golf tournament and it’s a good golf course so we’ll keep our heads down and play,” McIlroy said.Explore more on these topicsIrelandDonald TrumpEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘World’s most profitable football business’: Abramovich’s frozen Chelsea cash earns £175m | Roman Abramovich | The Guardian
description: Proceeds are in a UK account amid a dispute about how the money should be used and a separate criminal investigation
Author: Rob Davies
Headline: Proceeds are in a UK account amid a dispute about how the money should be used and a separate criminal investigation
Content: Roman Abramovich was hit with sanctions and the proceeds from the sale of Chelsea FC were locked in a UK bank account.Photograph: Paul Marriott/AlamyView image in fullscreenRoman Abramovich was hit with sanctions and the proceeds from the sale of Chelsea FC were locked in a UK bank account.Photograph: Paul Marriott/AlamyRoman Abramovich‘World’s most profitable football business’: Abramovich’s frozen Chelsea cash earns £175mProceeds are in a UK account amid a dispute about how the money should be used and a separate criminal investigationRob DaviesFri 11 Sep 2026 13.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFunds from Roman Abramovich’s sale of Chelsea FC have earned at least £175m in interest while locked in a UK bank account, new accounts show, leading one analyst to describe the company housing the frozen cash as “the most profitable football business in the world”.Accounts for Fordstam, the company through which the billionaire Russian oligarch ownedChelsea, show that the proceeds of the salecompleted in May 2022have risen from £2.3bn to nearly £2.5bn.Abramovich, who washit with UK sanctions in 2022over his ties to Vladimir Putin, has previously pledged to donate the money to victims of the war in Ukraine. However, the funds have yet to be released, amid an ongoing legal dispute with the British government about how the money should be used.The picture is further complicated by a separate criminalinvestigation by the Jersey authoritiesinto the original source of the oil tycoon’s wealth.There is also uncertainty about whether £1.4bn in loans – part of a vastnetwork of offshore companiesthat the oligarch used to fund Chelsea’s success – will be deducted from the final sum available for donation.In the meantime, the money, an initial £2.35bn, has been accruing interest rapidly, earning £114m in 2024 and nearly £63m the year before that. The total is likely to have risen significantly because another two years have elapsed since June 2024, the latest date covered by the accounts.Stefan Borson, a football finance expert who is head of sport at the law firm McCarthy Denning, said: “With the interest received, this now appears to be the most profitable football-related business in the world,” a tongue-in-cheek reference to the lack of profitability among high-spending football clubs.“It sheds no further insight as to what progress (or otherwise) has been made in distributing the proceeds of the sale.”The £2.5bn proceeds remain frozen in a Barclays bank account owing to a dispute with the UK government, whichpledged to take legal actionafter Abramovich missed a March 2026 deadline to free up the funds.The government wants the money to be earmarked for Ukraine but, according to reports, Abramovich is prepared to defy ministers by giving it to a foundation with a more global outlook.A government spokesperson said: “We have been clear from the start that the proceeds of the sale ofChelseaFC must be used for humanitarian causes in Ukraine. Roman Abramovich has yet to fulfil the commitment made at the time of the sale. The government is taking further steps to ensure that promise is kept, including continuing preparations for potential legal action if necessary.“Our absolute priority remains ensuring the funds reach the most vulnerable in Ukraine who have endured over four years of relentless suffering.”It is also unclear whether the donation will be reduced by any demand from Abramovich that Fordstam repays £1.4bn in loans extended by his Camberley International Investment vehicle, based in Jersey.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s always been vague as to whether Abramovich was going to donate the whole sale proceeds to the Ukraine relief fund or just the profits,” said a football finance expert, Kieran Maguire.“The sum due to his offshore company is still in the accounts which suggests the latter.”The future of the loan is further complicated by two factors.As long as Abramovich is under sanctions, the money cannot legally be repaid to him without a licence from the Office for Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI), part of the Treasury.At the same time, prosecutors in Jersey are investigating whether the proceeds of the Chelsea sale amount to the proceeds of crime, as part of a corruption and money-laundering investigation. The inquiry is looking at the source of much of Abramovich’s wealth, including the sale of his oil and gas company Sibneft, which the Russian government acquired for $13bn in 2005.The Guardian approached lawyers for Roman Abramovich for comment.Explore more on these topicsRoman AbramovichChelseaRussiaFinancesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfold | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: The world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home
Author: David Smith
Headline: The world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at home
Content: ‘The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.’Illustration: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreen‘The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.’Illustration: Guardian DesignSeptember 11 2001Mistakes, mistrust and misdirection: 25 years after 9/11, its dark legacy continues to unfoldThe world’s most powerful country responded to the worst terrorist attack in its history by inflicting terror of its own – around the world, and at homeDavid Smithin WashingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.38 EDTShareAs clear as that cloudlessSeptembermorning,Jenna Jacobs McPartlandremembers the moment everything changed. “I was cleaning the bathroom and watching the Today show in the background and nine months pregnant,” the 52-year-old recalls by phone. “I think they were showing ‘Today throws a wedding’ when the news broke in.”A plane had hit the north tower of the World Trade Center in New York. McPartland did not know that her husband, Ariel Jacobs, was attending a conference at itsWindows on the World restaurant.“I called his office to say, ‘Hey, turn on the TV. Do you guys know what’s going on?’ His assistant said, ‘Oh my God, Jenna, he’s there.’ The whole world disappeared and there was this sort of hollow collapsing feeling.”Ariel Jacobs did not live to see his son, Gabriel,born six days after September 11, 2001. McPartland, then living in Briarcliff Manor, New York,would marry twice more, set up a grief support charity,and become a chef and restaurateur. Each 9/11 anniversary, she has a picnic at the cemetery where a few pieces of bone from her late husband are buried.Speaking fromFairfield, Connecticut, McPartland says: “Ari was an incredibly joyful person who cherished his life. I made a conscious choice to honour him by living as joyfully as I can. It’s not always easy. I still cry pretty frequently. If there’s a movie with a building getting blown up, or if I’m reading a book and they casually mention ‘post-9/11 this’ or whatever, it catches me off guard. The grief finds a place to live in the heart,and you visit it.”View image in fullscreenView of smoke from the collapse of the World Trade Center’s South Tower, in the wake of the September 11 terrorist attacks, as seen from Exchange Place, Jersey City, New Jersey, September 11, 2001.Photograph: Michael J Powell/Getty ImagesMcPartland and other victims’ families have learned to live with that grief over the past 25 years. But America writ large has struggled to carry the weight of the worst terrorist attack in its history. The world’s most powerful nation responded by inflicting terror of its own, betraying its history as a safe harbour for immigrants,and pitting Americans against one another. The initial heroism, goodwill and unity of 9/11 gave way to discord at home and diminished moral authority abroad.McPartland adds: “It makes me incredibly sad and bordering on angry that the death of my husband has been invoked to cause more violence. It is the othering of people that got him killed in the first place and, when we Americans fail to learn that lesson and choose collectively as a nation to other people, whether it’s immigrants or other nations, that is a deepening of that tragedy that is sickening and unfathomable to me.”Unspeakable lossOn September 10, 2001George W Bushtravelled to Florida to push education reform legislation. AOL was seeking a big stake in AT&T’s cable unit.Promising tennis player Lleyton Hewitt, 20, had just swept Pete Sampras aside to win the US Open.America seemed unassailable. It had won the cold war and enjoyed a relatively peaceful 1990s as “the indispensable nation”, in secretary of stateMadeleine Albright’sframing. From fiscal years 1998 to 2001, the federal government recorded four consecutive budget surpluses.But what had been dubbed “the American century” came to an apocalyptic endon the next morning. Nearly 3,000 people were killed as 19 al-Qaida hijackers seized control of four airliners, slamming two of the planes into the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth into a field in western Pennsylvania.Among the most wrenching images were office workers leaping to their deaths from the burning twin towers. On the wall of thenational September 11 museumin New York is a quotation from James Gilroy, a resident of lower Manhattan: “She had a business suit on, her hair was all askew … This woman stood there for what seemed like minutes, then she held down her skirt and then jumped off the ledge … I thought, how human, how modest, to hold down her skirt before she jumped.”Unthinkably, both of the 110-storey towers collapsed, unleashing giant clouds of ash and dust on the streets of lower Manhattan as fragments of paper fluttered down like confetti.David Blight, a historian who advised the museum, which opened in 2014, said: “It’s the most visual event in history–so photographed, so much footage, so many documentaries. It is so shocking, so horrifying that you can’t watch it without a certain weeping. One of the things that should never stop about 9/11 is the essential grief of it. There is a sheer sense of unspeakable loss.”At first the loss brought out America’s better angels. Firefighters and first responders displayed inspiring courage. Ordinary citizens queued to donate blood. The nation came together as rarely before and received global sympathy, with Russia pledging support, Iran holding candlelight vigils and Nato invoking Article 5 for the first and only time in its history. Bush visited Ground Zero in New York and,wielding a megaphone, declared that “the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon.”View image in fullscreenAs rescue efforts continue in the rubble of the World Trade Center, George Bush raises a US flag while standing in front of the World Trade Center with firefighter Bob Beckwith during a tour of the devastation on 14 September 2001.Photograph: Doug Mills/APThey did. The US invaded Afghanistan to destroy al-Qaida and topple its Taliban protectors, a war that would drag on for a record 20 years only forthe Taliban to return. Bush then attacked Iraqon the false premisethat Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction, at a cost of hundreds of thousands of lives.The global war on terror expanded into a sprawling enterprise of military intervention, intelligence operations, detention and interrogation. Some suspects were tortured, including through waterboarding at CIA “black sites”.A quarter of a century later, 100 million Americansare too young to remember 9/11and only from this vantage point, perhaps, can the consequences be seen clearly.Historians and policy experts interviewed by the Guardian suggest that the reaction to 9/11 was a profound strategic miscalculation that distracted the US from the rise of China and sowed the seeds of its own decline.Hunting for enemies“9/11 is when things began to go wrong for the United States,” suggestedBill Galston, a former policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The United States was at the apogee of its post-cold war power on September 10 and then, through a series of missteps and misjudgments on both the foreign and domestic front, we have thrown away a great deal of not only our power but our credibility.“In my judgment, 9/11 set off a quarter-century of misgovernment in the United States and we’ll pay the price for that for a very long time.”Did Osama Bin Laden, the al-Qaida leader who masterminded the attacks, win after all? If the metric of victory is measured by Bin Laden’s immediate, messianic desire to establish a global caliphate and expel all western presence from the Middle East, he evidently failed. Al-Qaida was eventually hunted to near-extinction andBin Laden himself killedin a Pakistani compound in 2011.But if the terrorist’s success is measured by the magnitude of the self-inflicted wounds they provoke from their target, Bin Laden’s legacy is a slow, autoimmune decay within the US,it may have exceeded his darkest fantasies.Ben Rhodes, a former deputy national security adviser under Barack Obama, said: “Bin Laden in some ways failed in his intentions. He wanted the United States out of the Middle East. He wanted to topple certain governments in the Middle East. But in other ways 9/11 is the most successful terrorist attack in history insofar as it prompted such an overreach from the United States that we hastened our own decline, division and betrayal of our own story.”Like countless others, the course of Rhodes’ life was changed by 9/11. He was 23 and working on a city council election campaign at a polling site on the Brooklyn waterfront. He saw the second plane hit the twin towers and watched the rest of the carnage unfold. The event spurred him to move to Washington,and get involved in foreign policy.He regards the cost of 25 years of “forever wars” as incalculable. They placed a huge burden on the Americans who fought them and had to deal with problems ranging from war wounds tothe opioids crisis. They also contributed to the destruction of the rules-based order, paving the way for Russia’s Vladimir Putin and others to reject the rules and use the language of counter-terrorism to justify stringent crackdowns.Then, there is the domestic sphere. Rhodes says the typicalFox Newsviewer during the Bush years was promised great victories over foreign enemies. “When nations don’t keep those types of promises, when you unleash that kind of nationalism and xenophobia and you don’t succeed on the battlefield, history tells you that people start to look for enemies within to blame,” he explained.“My experience in the Obama years is very much that ‘the other’ that had been constructed around terrorists morphed into the Black president or the immigrants crossing the southern border or LGBT people. The segments were the same but the enemy had changed to an enemy within.”Living with the legacyDonald Trump launched his first bid for the presidency, a decade ago, against the backdrop of this search for blame. Promotingthe lie that Obama is a Muslim, demonising immigrants, and promising to build a border wall, he cut through by railing – in a clear break from Bush and Republican orthodoxy – against political elites for waging forever wars that he claimed he would stop (he has called the invasion of Iraq “the single worst decision ever made” in US history).“You’d never have Donald Trump as president without 9/11 because he basically stepped into that slipstream of othering people and captured the ugly xenophobia and nationalism that had been unleashed and the anger that people, particularly on the right, felt at being gaslit by the Bush administration for eight years,” said Rhodes.“It’s no coincidence that Trump’s ascent was marked by the destruction of Jeb Bush, who symbolised all those broken promises.”Now, Rhodes argues, the war on terror has come home. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents are “basically running counter-insurgency strategies in American cities, with the same military equipment that we used to fight wars now in the hands of law enforcement”, he said.“Some of the same people have signed up to do it,and the same surveillance technologies that we use against terrorists abroad are now used against Americans. We are now living in the theatre of the war on terror and it’s obviously a source of growing discomfort to many Americans.”View image in fullscreenResidents and protesters clash with federal agents in the East Side neighborhood on  14 October 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. Donald Trumps’s administration continued to enforce immigration laws in Chicago and the surrounding suburbs during their ‘Operation Midway Blitz’.Photograph: Joshua Lott/The Washington Post/Getty ImagesAs the US overextended itself abroad, the machinery of endless war also boomeranged back on to the domestic front,eroding civil libertiesand legal norms it claimed to defend. ThePatriot Act, which dispensed with rules that prevented the state monitoring US citizens without “probable cause”, was passed just 45 days after the attacks, radically expanding the powers of law enforcement agencies.Jameel Jaffer, who moved to New York just weeks after the attacks before spending 14 years litigating national-security cases for the American Civil Liberties Union, saw the transition from the ground level. His early volunteer work involved visiting immigration detention centres in New York and New Jersey, where hundreds of immigrants had been rounded up in the panic after September 11.Over the next decade and a half, Jaffer litigated major constitutional battles involving warrantless wiretapping, secret detention and targeted killings. He watched as the National Security Agency developed an enormous surveillance apparatus, much of which becamepublic through reportingand, later,Edward Snowden’s disclosures.Jaffer, now executive director of theKnight First Amendment Instituteat Columbia University, argues that many of the surveillance authorities created after 9/11 remain in place or have become even more sweeping. “So much of what’s going on now is traceable to the institutions and authorities that were created after 9/11 and that the courts failed to limit,” he said. “The use of the material support laws toprosecute anti-ICE protesters in Texas. The use of the Espionage Act to threaten and intimidate journalists who are writing about issues that the public needs to know about.“Even the arrests and detentions and threatened deportation of students for protesting on university campuses: that policy is built on deference that the courts extended to the executive branch 25 years after 9/11. We are absolutely living with the legacy of these decisions made and policies instituted in the years after 9/11.”A new eraGuantánamo Bay, where 780 men and boys have been imprisoned since 9/11, became one of the most visible symbols of the era. The Iraq war produced theAbu Ghraib scandal, in which US personnel and contractors subjected detainees to abuse, humiliation and torture.Obamatried, and failed, to shut down Guantánamo. Trump has sincefaced intense criticismfor sending immigrants to the prison.Jeremy Varon,a history professor at the New School in New York and leading member of Witness Against Torture, a group seeking to close Guantánamo, said: “The United States committed to a programme and policy of torture, violating international law and its own laws, and an element of gratuitous cruelty and even sadism became operationally part of the war on terror.“People equated national strength and security with the ability to inflict harm on vulnerable others. The more violence we dish out, the stronger and the better and the safer we somehow are and a lot of that violence boomeranged and made new enemies.“But beyond those it victimised, it destroyed any pretence that we’re a constitutional order that obeys the rule of law, that honours national treaties. It inaugurated an era of executive power operating with utter impunity and immunity. The lawlessness of Trump is an utterly predictable consequence of the contempt for the rule of law, oversight, checks and balances that the Bush administration displayed.”For Varon, there is a clear connection between the brutal methods of the global war on terror and the excesses of ICE under Trump. He points to notorious detention centres in Texas and New Jersey where inmates routinely suffer medical neglect, and recent reports of harrowing deportation flights where migrantsare flown to Africa in shackles.“People report living in fear and filth and squalor without access to basic hygiene, to attorneys,” he said.“Families are broken up and there’s a level of the willful infliction of suffering that is staggering and wouldn’t seem to be even a necessary part of the broad immigration strategy.“Again there’s this sick need that collectivities feel they have to dominate those that they perceive as lesser. Muslims and Arabs were the great community under suspicion and that’s been replaced to a large extent by brown-skinned migrants from other parts of the world. When you have a rhetoric that demonises people as criminal and subhuman, it invites their mistreatment.”A different pathThe collateral of this 25-year trajectory has been the evisceration of trust in US public institutions. Varon argues that this environment birthed a “post-truth condition” where empirical reality was abandoned andconspiracy theories thrive.The official September 11 narrative was challengedby the “truther” movement, which suggested the attacks were an “inside job” orchestrated by the US government. The Bush administration’s false claims about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction laid the groundwork for Trump’s cynical style, which relies on the public believing that everyone is lying so they might as well vote for ademagogue who is honest about it.Only last week it was reported that Trump has ordered the Department of Homeland Security, created in the aftermath of 9/11,to burnish his false claims of election fraudby embarking on a weeks-long search for non-citizens on US voter rolls, a move seen by watchdogs as an intimidation effort ahead of November’s midterm elections.The president will attend a commemorationat the Pentagon on Fridaywhile JD Vance will be at the national 9/11 memorial in New York.Once again crowds will pause to remember the workers desperately waving clothes, sheets and tablecloths from the doomed towers, the firefighters who climbed staircases and never returned, the airline passengers who stormed the cockpit to stopUnited Airlines Flight 93reaching its target in Washington.But will they weigh what came next, what it cost the US in blood and treasure and what might have happened if the country had chosen a different path?“Consider what we didn’t do,” said Rhodes. “I sometimes am haunted by this. The trillions of dollars spent on a forever war: what could that have been spent on? Climate change, universal healthcare, public education. There’s a real opportunity cost to how we chose to spend our time and resources.“If you came down to Earth from another planet and you had to make sense of the fact that the United States spent several trillion dollars chasing a relatively small number of terrorists around a few countries, toppling governments and then fighting insurgencies, when it has huge problems with deindustrialisation, with its education system, with the onset of climate change, you would think this is a country that has gone insane.”

title: ‘I think of him every year’: remembering those lost in 9/11, 25 years later | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: Guardian readers share stories of the friends, colleagues and mentors whose lives they continue to honor decades after the attacks
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Guardian readers share stories of the friends, colleagues and mentors whose lives they continue to honor decades after the attacks
Content: ‘This past Christmas, I was back in NYC for the first time in 15 years. I made a visit to the memorial and found his name on the plaque and silently thanked him for his welcoming smile and his service.’Photograph: Stephanie Keith/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘This past Christmas, I was back in NYC for the first time in 15 years. I made a visit to the memorial and found his name on the plaque and silently thanked him for his welcoming smile and his service.’Photograph: Stephanie Keith/Getty ImagesSeptember 11 2001‘I think of him every year’: remembering those lost in 9/11, 25 years laterGuardian readers share stories of the friends, colleagues and mentors whose lives they continue to honor decades after the attacksMarina DunbarFri 11 Sep 2026 07.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe September 11, 2001 attacks killed 2,977 people, resulting in the largest loss of life caused by a foreign attack on American soil. Twenty-five years later, Guardian readers who lost friends and loved ones are continuing to honor their memories through stories about their lives, relationships and the moments they shared.Christopher Allen, 69, a retired estate manager from Niantic, Connecticut, remembers Jeremy “Caz” Carrington.Allen said he and his wife, Kim, met Carrington at the now-closed Santa Fe Junction bar and restaurant in East Hampton,New York. The men bonded as fellow British expatriates, talking about soccer, darts and London.“He was a portly sort of guy but moved quick, thought even quicker and was generally the life and soul of the party,” Allen said. Carrington worked for Cantor Fitzgerald, a firm which lost more people on 9/11 than any other organization.Six months after the attacks, Allen attended a celebration of Carrington’s life in East Hampton. Family members came from the UK, and friends and relatives shared stories about him.“The Celebration of Life service was not traditional or mournful; it was hilarious,” Allen said. “He really did live life to the fullest and we were all very grateful to have known him.”At the gathering, Allen met Carrington’s mother, Kate, and discovered she had been his primary school teacher years earlier, when he knew her as Miss Ross. They stayed in touch, exchanging jokes and gardening ideas until her death. In Allen’s words, he is in awe that such “a wonderful friendship started from such a horrific tragedy.”For Cheryl Ann of Santa Monica, California, the person she lost was a friend named Caroline, whom she described as a successful Disney executive and a mentor.Cheryl, who had pursued photography after moving from New Jersey to Los Angeles, said Caroline admired her work and treated her as an equal while she was working as an executive assistant.“We became personal friends and she invited me into her home and her life,” Cheryl said. “With genuine enthusiasm she offered to mentor me.”On September 11, Cheryl woke to messages telling her to turn on CNN. She had friends, godchildren, business associates and other loved ones in the region and feared for people she could not reach by phone.“I didn’t sleep; I could barely eat; life as I knew it was over,” she said.Later, Cheryl saw her friend Caroline’s name on a passenger list shown on the news. She initially hoped it was someone else with the same name, but a mutual friend confirmed it was the Caroline they knew.“It annihilated me. I don’t know any other way to express the depth of the pain of the loss. She had a beautiful light that lit up any room she entered,” Cheryl said. “She literally glowed, as beautiful on the outside as on the inside.”Steve S, whose name was changed for privacy, remembers John P Sammartino as one of his best friends.The two met at university, Steve said, and Sammartino later served as best man at his wedding. Though their careers caused them to drift apart, they continued getting together to watch football matches and make homemade beer with college friends.Steve was involved in computer-related cleanup work at the Pentagon after the attacks. Late on 12 September, he said, his then-wife called to tell him Sammartino had been on the plane that crashed into the Pentagon.“I was crushed,” Steve said. “From feeling lucky that I wasn’t directly affected to being involved changed my outlook on 9/11.”Years later, Steve continues to visit his friend’s grave. Sammartino had been an electrical engineer, and Steve sometimes thinks about the advances his friend never saw. “He’d get a kick out of modern cellphone technology,” he said.Alison K, whose name was also changed for privacy, is a 47-year-old artist who said that her life was changed by a man she never actually spoke to. In 2000, she moved to New York City to pursue a master’s degree. On her way to class, she would pass a small fire station where “there was often a firefighter out front washing down a truck, chatting with his co-workers. He had a big bushy moustache and his arms were covered with tattoos.”The two would exchange smiles and waves, and his friendly demeanor helped bring her comfort as a young student in a strange new city. Weeks after the attacks, classes resumed and she passed by the fire station again, where she saw a paper taped to the station door.“It was my fireman, whose name had been Manny Mojica, and who was killed when responding to the tower emergency,” she said. “I think of him every year, and this past Christmas I was back in NYC for the first time in 15 years. I made a visit to the memorial and found his name on the plaque and silently thanked him for his welcoming smile and his service.”Songwriter Larry Dvoskin remembers Patrick “Paddy” Brown, a friend from Jivamukti Yoga classes who was a former marine and a captain with the New York City fire department’s Ladder 3 company.View image in fullscreenPatrick Paddy Brown, a former Marine and captain of the New York City fire department.Photograph: Courtesy Larry Dvoskin“He was truly a ‘man’s man’ long before the current craze of the manosphere,” Dvoskin said. “Instead, he was thoughtful, humble, and I found it humorous seeing him in spandex tights in my yoga classes.”Dvoskin said that at Brown’s funeral at St Patrick’s cathedral, he heard an account of Brown heading toward the second tower as it burned. Firefighters leaving the building warned him not to enter because it was too dangerous.Brown replied: “Are you fucking crazy? It’s my job to go in there!”Brown and his team then entered the building.“Those were the last words he is remembered by,” Dvoskin said. “‘It’s my job to go in there.’”Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001New YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The future scares me’: why unemployment has become biggest election issue for young New Zealand voters | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: As mainstream parties vie for votes with promises of jobs and economic growth, young people may take more convincing
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: As mainstream parties vie for votes with promises of jobs and economic growth, young people may take more convincing
Content: Luta has been unemployed for seven months and is desperate to find work. She plans to vote for the Green party in November’s general election.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLuta has been unemployed for seven months and is desperate to find work. She plans to vote for the Green party in November’s general election.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianNew Zealand‘The future scares me’: why unemployment has become biggest election issue for young New Zealand votersAs mainstream parties vie for votes with promises of jobs and economic growth, young people may take more convincingEva Corlettin WellingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 19.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 20.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThirty minutes north of New Zealand’s capital, raucous laughter is tumbling out of a nondescript building in Naenae – an economically deprived suburb in Lower Hutt – into the car park of a tiny shopping strip.Inside, 10 students aged between 15 and 24 are trying to better their chances of finding a job, with help from Youth Inspire, a not-for-profit that assists hundreds of young people each year into training, education or work.They have been working on CVs, learning to drive, and today are roleplaying challenging moments in a workplace. There is a lightness and camaraderie in the room that belies their day-to-day reality – one shaped by a desperate and lonely search for work that is not there.Line graph on New Zealand’s underutilisation rate among 15-24-year-olds“It’s really heartbreaking and it breaks my confidence,” says Luta Matagi, 23, who has spent seven months looking for work. “I may not have degrees but I am a hard worker. We are all hard workers in here.”These students are a handful of the 180,000 young New Zealanders either unemployed or underemployed in the past quarter. Nearly four in 10 (37%) of 15-24-year-olds are in this group, categorised by government as the “underutilised” – the worst rate in 30 years, according to Stats NZ.As New Zealand prepares for its general election in November, unemployment is a key issue. For voters aged 18-34, unemployment ranks as the second most pressing concern, behind the cost of living, according to a recent Ipsos poll.View image in fullscreenLuta Matagi, 23, says she is a ‘hard worker’ but has lost count of the number of jobs she has applied for.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianMichael, 20, joined Youth Inspire to upskill, after finding “nothing out there” when it came to electrical apprenticeships. He is not alone. Apprenticeship numbers have slid 32% since 2022 to a 15-year low in 2025, government figures show.Michael says he has applied for at least 40 entry-level jobs in the past two years. He has not had a single interview. “It’s isolating searching for jobs alone,” he says.Matagi can’t count how many jobs she has applied for, “just to get rejected from all of them”.Young people routinely bear the brunt of an economic downturn, says Shamubeel Eaqub, chief economist at Simplicity, which provides fund management for New Zealand’s national saving scheme. “When there are only a few vacancies, then the people in the front of the queue are the ones who have got the most experience and the most to offer.”Line graph on New Zealand’s unemployment rate among 15-24-year-oldsThe effect can be scarring both for their career and their mental health, Eaqub says. “By the time the economy recovers, you’re going to be competing with the next cohort of young people who are now into the workforce.”The government has promised to grow the economy to increase jobs for young people. At the same time it is toughening jobseeker benefit criteria for some of that cohort.Matagi, like most of her peers, is on the jobseeker benefit. If she doesn’t find work soon, she will have to sell her car, which could further hinder her ability to get a job. She says the government is “so misguided” and not supporting young people enough. Its policy preventing 18-19 year olds whose parents earn a combined income of $65,529 (US$38,412) or more from accessing the benefit from November will place further strain on them and their families, she says.“It’s so sad to say, but the future scares me.”View image in fullscreenYoung people who are looking for work attend a Youth Inspire workshop in Lower Hutt, Wellington.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianZainab Ali, the organisation’s chief executive, sees the pressures on young people growing. “I used to notice pies and cans of [the drink] V being stolen from the shops near Youth Inspire, now what I am catching is bread, milk and eggs. They are the basics. That change tells you it is getting harder out there.”About 500 people are on the Youth Inspire waitlist. Ali says the hundreds that have already been through their doors are incredibly motivated.“They are struggling and still going,” she says. “And I would challenge anyone that thinks young people are lazy or not willing to work that we have the evidence to show that is not the case.”‘Young people need to see some hope’View image in fullscreenZainab Ali, chief executive of Youth Inspire, says young people are eager to work.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianNew Zealand’s economy has been battered by recession and stagnation that arrived in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic. Rising inflation piled pressure on businesses and drove households to rein in spending. Company liquidations rose 14% in the past year, and nearly 3,000 hospitality businesses ceased trading, credit bureau Centrix reported in September. There are, however, some flickers of improvement. Rating agency Moody’s said in September it expected 1.6% GDP growth in 2026.Ali says entry-level jobs have disappeared, retail shops are not hiring and the availability of full-time work is slim. “We used to count full-time work as the benchmark – that’s not the case now. Casual is most prevalent, but generally it is fixed-term or short-term work.”Labour’s spokesperson for finance and economy, Barbara Edmonds, says the national unemployment rate – currently at an 11-year high of 5.6% – is “a damning verdict” on incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon’s economic management.“Our young people need to see some hope … they want to see that there are jobs available for them.”Edmonds says Labour would aim to turn around unemployment figures by backing trades and apprenticeships, guaranteeing graduate nurses a job, and introducing a “Future fund” – a policy to invest in innovative businesses and infrastructure to create jobs.But the National party’s minister for social development and employment, Louise Upston, blames high unemployment on the previous Labour government’s “reckless fiscal and economic management”.“It takes time to right the ship,” she says in a statement, adding her government is committed to growing the economy to boost job creation.View image in fullscreenThe Taitā railway station in Lower Hutt.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianResponding to criticism over her policy to limit access to benefits for 18-19 year-olds, Upston says young people should be in education, training or employment and “it’s a common-sense expectation that it’s their parents who will support them, not the taxpayer”, if they cannot do one of these things.As the mainstream parties vie for votes with promises of jobs and economic growth, young people may take more convincing.Recent pollingshowssupport for Labour and National slipping awayin favour of the minor parties, with younger women showing the highest support for left-leaning minor parties and younger men showing the highest support for minor rightwing and centrist parties.Voter turnout for younger, and poorer, people has historically been low but Ali says she is noticing “a huge trend” in the community of families who have never voted and are enrolling for the election because of concern for their children. “That gives me heart,” she says.View image in fullscreenMichael, 20, says he has applied for about 40 jobs since leaving school.Photograph: Josie Mossman/The GuardianMatagi and Michael say they will vote for the minor Green party. Matagi feels the party’s MPs “see our point of view”. Michael, meanwhile, believes “they look out for the underdog”.The pair feel this election could be the difference between a career-less future and a path to a new life. “There is not much hope,” Michael says, “unless we get a new government.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandNew Zealand election 2026New Zealand politicsUnemploymentYoung peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘They’re lifesavers’: the Birmingham clinic giving hope to traumatised asylum seekers | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: MSF-run centre offering intensive psychological care has received more than 350 referrals since opening last year
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: MSF-run centre offering intensive psychological care has received more than 350 referrals since opening last year
Content: ‘Azad’, who has received treatment at the centre, came to the UK on a small boat after fleeing persecution in Iran.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Azad’, who has received treatment at the centre, came to the UK on a small boat after fleeing persecution in Iran.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianImmigration and asylum‘They’re lifesavers’: the Birmingham clinic giving hope to traumatised asylum seekersMSF-run centre offering intensive psychological care has received more than 350 referrals since opening last yearNeha GohilMidlands correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 15.30 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAzad*, an asylum seeker from Iran, recounts his story in a gentle and mild manner, seated in the stillness of a therapy room at a trauma clinic inBirmingham.The centre, which opened its doors in July last year to address the “unmet mental healthcare needs of those seeking sanctuary”, is run by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), or Doctors Without Borders. It provides specialised trauma-focused psychological care for refugees and asylum seekers in the city and surrounding areas.It has so far received more than 350 referrals from the NHS and refugee organisations, and held 521 consultations for patients – many of whom have survived conflict, persecution, torture and other forms of violence and exploitation in their home countries or on their migration journey.Data MSF shared with the Guardian by MSF shows that of 150 case files reviewed by MSF, 88% documented experiences of violence and one in three detailed suicidal thoughts at the moment they came to MSF.Azad, who arrived in the UK on a small boat , was approached by MSF at the hotel he was being accommodated in Birmingham. He had known for a long time that he needed help, he said, but had nowhere to turn. “It was the only person who didn’t see me as a number, listened like I’m a human,” he said.Azad’s journey to the UK had begun several years earlier, when the Iranian authorities cracked down on protests that had swept across the country in late 2022 against the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini in police custody. She had been arrested for allegedly violating rules requiring women to wear the headscarf.View image in fullscreenAn MSF therapist demonstrates a ‘lifeline’ in which a flower represents a happy time, a stone a traumatic experience and a candle a loss.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAzad, a Kurdish-Iranian civil engineer, took part in the demonstrations and said he had witnessed people being shot and others blinded. After authorities spotted him spraying graffiti, his father urged him to flee the country, fearing for his safety. The authorities later ransacked his family home, he said.Azad travelled to Germany, where he applied for asylum but was rejected – a decision he said was driven by a “racist” interviewer and delays that prevented an appeal hearing. The decision left him feeling hopeless. “There were times that I was feeling I have nothing to live for,” he said as he recalled an attempt to take his own life.The UK was his last and only option, he said. When he arrived, he alleged border officials had sworn at him. MSF staff said the mental health struggles of their patients had been further compounded by the rise in “hostility and anti-migrant sentiment in the UK”.Some of their clients had to be moved from hotels far-right protesters routinely targeted. Others described being physically assaulted.A clinical psychologist at the clinic, who did not want to be named, said: “What they are routinely sharing with us is a lot of fear around the environment in the UK. Attitudes towards migrants becoming more and feeling more hostile.“And that’s a combination of policy but also the general kind of narrative and rhetoric within the UK.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe charity said it was important for MSF to provide such intensive psychological treatment in the countries where refugees and asylum seekers hoped to settle.“If you open a wound and you cannot heal it, the wound will get worse,” said Fouzia Bara, head of MSF’s migration taskforce. “Birmingham is the safe place where we can start the healing process. This is why we are providing highly intensive care because unfortunately the journey of migration, it’s a journey of violence.”Azad, who has been diagnosed with complex post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and is nearing the end of his treatment, described the transformative impact the support has had on his life.“They are lifesavers. I had nothing, there was no life in me. But they showed me, no, you can have a life,” he said.*Name has been changedIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumMental healthCounselling and therapyRefugeesHealthPost-traumatic stress disorderMigrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A tragic day’: campaigners react as MPs say no to legalising assisted dying | Assisted dying | The Guardian
description: Opponents say proposed law change for England and Wales was ‘unsafe and unworkable’ after bill is narrowly defeated
Author: Alexandra Topping
Headline: Opponents say proposed law change for England and Wales was ‘unsafe and unworkable’ after bill is narrowly defeated
Content: Distressed pro-assisted dying campaigners react at Parliament Square in London after MPs voted by 286 votes to 270 against the bill.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenDistressed pro-assisted dying campaigners react at Parliament Square in London after MPs voted by 286 votes to 270 against the bill.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAAssisted dying‘A tragic day’: campaigners react as MPs say no to legalising assisted dyingOpponents say proposed law change for England and Wales was ‘unsafe and unworkable’ after bill is narrowly defeatedAlexandra ToppingPolitical correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs it became clear that MPs hadvoted against the assisted dying bill, campaigners who had fought for a change in the law looked broken. Standing outside the Houses of Parliament, many wearing pink caps and T-shirts with slogans such as “Give me choice over my death”, they held on to each other for comfort. Some were in tears, others stood in shocked silence.MP Lauren Edwards, who sponsored the bill that would have allowed terminally ill adults inEnglandand Wales with six months or less to live to seek medical assistance to end their lives, said its failure to pass was disappointing “for the many thousands of terminally ill people and their loved ones who were given hope when the Commons voted for this bill last year”.“It is all the more heartbreaking for them because support for choice at the end of life is still as strong in parliament as it was before,” she said. “The objections raised today were not about the principle of assisted dying but about parliamentary process.”Longtime assisted dying campaigner Esther Rantzen, who has terminal cancer and said she no longer had the strength to join supporters in Parliament Square, told the BBC: “I am sure a change in the law will come. I am deeply sad that it won’t come soon enough for many of the people who need it, it’s a tragic day.”Her daughter Rebecca Wilcox said she was devastated about the failure of the bill, a near-identical version of one which passed through the Commons but wasblocked in the Lords, after being talked out of time by a handful of peers. “I don’t think it’s a vandalism of democracy, I think it’s a demolition of democracy,” she said.As it was declared in the Commons that the bill had been defeated by 286 votes to 270, there were some cheers, some gasps and then a brief moment of silence as MPs processed what they had just heard.Among those who had opposed the bill there was relief, but little celebration. In a joint statement, the Labour MPs Ashley Dalton, Meg Hillier and Jess Asato called it “unsafe and unworkable”, but they understood “the deep concerns of so many people” who had campaigned for a change in the law.4:36MPs recount personal experiences as they debate assisted dying bill – videoDalton played a critical role in the highly emotive debate that preceded the vote. About 70 MPs had put their names forward to speak and the chamber was almost full.The former minister, who is undergoing chemotherapy to manage incurable stage 4 breast cancer, revealed that she had received a terminal diagnosis ahead of the second reading of the bill, but had kept it to herself.“When you hear those words, depression, anxiety, grief, fear, shame, and guilt come in bounds. Suicide risk is highest immediately after diagnosis, and it usually falls quickly within three to six months,” she said, arguing that the bill made no provision to support that moment of transition.“My days may be numbered,” she said. “But that doesn’t mean that I want this chamber to rush through bad law just so I might have a chance to see it or use it.”Claire Hazelgrove, the Labour MP for Filton and Bradley Stoke and a supporter of the bill, spoke movingly about her mother, who died last October after living with a rare blood cancer.She had “loved life and laughter”, but at the end of her life she was in excruciating pain.“She had access to good palliative care, but what we learned, the hardest of ways, is that not all pain can be palliated,” said Hazelgrove. “I will never forget seeing her writhing and screaming in pain at points for weeks.”There were interventions from medical professionals on the green benches too. Glasgow South West MP Zubir Ahmed, a transplant surgeon and formerLabourhealth minister, said the social and palliative care system was not ready.“When I am asked to prognosticate as to whether someone has six months to live or not, I am as often wrong as I am right,” he told the Commons.After it became clear the bill had been defeated, many said it had to be a catalyst for change.“As a society we must not lose focus on the urgent need to fix the hospice funding crisis,” said Toby Porter, CEO of Hospice UK. “Opponents and supporters of the bill must now channel their energy and passion into fixing it, to ensure everyone can get the end of life care they need.”Explore more on these topicsAssisted dyingHouse of CommonsEnglandWalesHospicesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I tested 40 lunch boxes – here are the best in the UK for leaks, looks and sustainability | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Tired of squashed sarnies and spilt dressing? From stainless steel to insulated to plastic-free, here are the lunch boxes for kids and adults we rate the most
Author: Zoë Phillimore
Headline: Tired of squashed sarnies and spilt dressing? From stainless steel to insulated to plastic-free, here are the lunch boxes for kids and adults we rate the most
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleReviewI tested 40 lunch boxes – here are the best in the UK for leaks, looks and sustainabilityTired of squashed sarnies and spilt dressing? From stainless steel to insulated to plastic-free, here are the lunch boxes for kids and adults we rate the mostThe best water bottlesZoë PhillimoreFri 11 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf packed lunches are a high-stakes game in your household (as they are in mine), the right lunch box is crucial. There’s nothing worse than opening the lunch you’ve been looking forward to since 8am to find yoghurt has leaked on to your sandwich and your cucumbers have dried out.A lunch box may look like a simple bit of kit, but keeping food contained from kitchen to school dinner hall or workplace desk is a surprisingly demanding job. And the humble lunch box has come a long way from the simple plastic tubs that used to contain our clingfilm-wrapped, squashed sandwiches at school. Today, you can find bento boxes with multiple compartments, stainless steel containers, silicone pouches and leakproof designs promising to keep everything from yoghurt to salad dressing safely contained.But more choice doesn’t necessarily make it easier to choose one. If you’re trying to cut down on single-use packaging, a good lunch box should be durable enough to last, practical enough to use every day and, crucially, capable of keeping its contents where they belong. I tested 40 to find the best lunch boxes for packed lunches at all ages.At a glanceBest lunch box for adults overallBlack+BlumLunch box Original£23.95 at Black+BlumBest lunch box for kids overallMunchkinKids’ bento lunch box£22.99 at John LewisBest budget lunch boxBrabantiaMake & Take lunch box bento£15.95 at AmazonBest lunch box for sandwich loversStanleyLegendary Classic Useful box£40 at SelfridgesBest stainless steel lunch boxBlack+BlumStainless steel lunch box£33.95 at Black+BlumBest insulated lunch boxThermosIcon Series food flask£19.50 at John LewisWhy you should trust meI’ve spent the past six years testing products for articles like this one. That’s meant sorting the wheat from the chaff in various situations, whether setting up seven side-by-side trampolines in the garden (my kidslovedthat commission) or filling my house withflowersto the point my delivery drivers worried there was something gravely wrong with me. So I’m well versed in assessing products.As luck would have it, my lifestyle also requires the frequent use of lunch boxes. I have three primary-school-age children, so I am often found in the kitchen at 7.30am, cramming lunch boxes full of healthy delights that will doubtless be discarded in the school dining hall. I’ve suffered the thrills (few) and spills (many) of several different lunch box formats, so I was eager to find ones that actually keep things in place and still appealing by 1pm.How I testedView image in fullscreenDress rehearsal: testing whether a caesar salad stays where it should.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianI started testing the lunch boxes (40 in total) with my kids at the end of the school year. By this point, I was at a low ebb of patience with packed lunches, so if I was wowed by a lunch box, I knew I was on to a good thing. But lunch boxes aren’t just for kids, so I also packed my own lunches for days out to the beach, the park or just a nearby bench to get away from my desk.My kids dutifully and unwittingly tested the lunch boxes to their absolute limits. They were crammed into school bags, chucked across playgrounds (and I meanchucked), and left on school playing fields over the weekend. If you haven’t had to fish three lunch boxes out of the mouldy lost property on a Monday morning, are you even living?I took a slightly more scientific and mildly less chaotic approach at home. I filled the lunch boxes with water and shook them hard, checking for drips. I then left them on their sides for 30 minutes to see if any water found its way out.Of course,yoghurt, salad dressings andhummusdon’t act in exactly the same way as water. I also made a range of lunches to see how they stood up to the pressure. Could I squeeze in a bag of Walkers? Did my salad end up tasting faintly of metal? Did dressing survive the walk to my favourite bench down the road?No one wants to lug around a lunch box that weighs the same as a small baby, so I also weighed all the lunch boxes when they were empty. I looked at how practical the compartment sizes were – it may be delightful to see lots of little boxes, but do they work in the real world? And I spent a lot of time at the kitchen sink, washing up lunch boxes to assess how easy they were to clean.Lastly, as this is the Guardian, sustainability was an important factor. I investigated the materials the lunch boxes were made from, how durable they seemed (this is where the chucking became key), how easily I could find replacement parts, and how recyclable they were at the end of their life. A manufacturer’s warranty or stated lifespan was welcome, too.After testing I donated all the lunchboxes tothe Salvation Army, which sells secondhand items to raise funds for its work.The best lunch boxesView image in fullscreenBox clever: did the test subjects stack up?Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianBest lunch box for adults overall:Black+Blum lunch box OriginalBlack+BlumLunch box Originalfrom£23.95£23.95 at Black+Blum£24 at SelfridgesWhat we loveFlexible option; good selection of compartmentsWhat we don’t loveToo big to slip into a small bagView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£23.95 at Black+Blum£24 at SelfridgesBlack+Blum is best known for its stainless steel lunch boxes (more on that later), but this plastic lunch box will turn heads. It comprises a 1l clip-top main box, an inner dish with a lid fitting a stainless steel fork, a sauce pot and a “garnish area”. It also has a vacuum seal and alifetime guarantee (with limitations). Black+Blum sells the lid separately if you ever lose it or the seal goes.Why we love itHowever fancy you go with your packed lunch, this lunch box is probably up to the job. Did I mention the “garnish area”? I whacked in a trusty chicken caesar salad for my walk to the park bench, and found I was able to keep most vital components separate until I wanted to mix them. Chicken, parmesan and croutons in the inner dish, salad leaves in the main compartment and dressing in the sauce pot. I liked that I could clip the fork on the outside of the box if I didn’t take the inner dish with me – although storing cutlery on the outside of the box does slightly give me the ick.This lunch box definitely feels more grownup – I wouldn’t trust my kids to bring all the components back from school, and they’d probably find it boring. But as an adult, I loved it. The clips are robust and won’t prise open when they shouldn’t, and the vacuum seal keeps everything fresh. I also found it easy enough to open. The sauce-pot lid screws firmly shut and is fairly leakproof, except during vigorous shaking. The inner-dish lid just fits on with no seal, so this won’t lock in anything too saucy. Washing it didn’t fill me with deep joy, due to the many components, but it lacks any nooks and crannies.It’s a shame that …while it says it’s dishwasher and microwave safe, the lid isn’t. Also, it’s pretty bulky.Material:BPA- and BPS-free polypropylene, Tritan and siliconeCapacity:1lWeight empty:510gDimensions:20 x 20 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe?Yes (but not lid)Microwave safe?Yes (but not lid)Freezer safe?YesNumber of compartments:4Black+BlumLunch box Originalfrom£23.95£23.95 at Black+Blum£24 at SelfridgesWhat we loveFlexible option; good selection of compartmentsWhat we don’t loveToo big to slip into a small bagBest lunch box for kids overall:Munchkin Kids’ bento lunch boxMunchkinKids’ bento lunch boxfrom£22.99£22.99 at John Lewis£22.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePerfectly balanced and sized for kidsWhat we don’t loveA lot of plastic; could be easier to washView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£22.99 at John Lewis£22.99 at AmazonA versatile little box with everything kids should need for lunch: plenty of compartments, cutlery and an easy-to-open clip. This colourful lunch box also feels seemingly indestructible, surviving a school day and a night in lost property.Why we love itMy mini testers were drawn to these boxes in tropical colourways. Inside, there’s a moulded plastic inner tray with five compartments. The lid has a removable silicone inner, which also has nodules you can snap the stainless steel fork and spoon into. That’s right – there’s a spoon and fork included, which is great for primary-age children. All the compartments are a decent size for smaller appetites. I could just about fit a sandwich in the main compartment and empty a packet of pretzels into one of the long, thin compartments.As the silicone seal encloses each compartment separately, you can chuck a pasta salad in one compartment, and it won’t filter into the yoghurt in the neighbouring area – not the case on many kids’ lunch boxes I tested. My kids seemed to find the bento format exciting, and anything that focuses them on actually eating in the school lunch hall is a big tick for me – the box came home empty.It’s a shame that …it’s a hefty bit of plastic, and there’s no way to buy spare parts – my kids lost the spoon. While it’s dishwasher safe, it takes up a huge amount of space in there, and as the bottom compartment doesn’t lift out, hand washing is a bit more annoying.Material:plastic and siliconeCapacity:500mlWeight empty:740gDimensions:23 x 20 x 7cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe?YesMicrowave safe?NoFreezer safe?NoNumber of compartments:5MunchkinKids’ bento lunch boxfrom£22.99£22.99 at John Lewis£22.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePerfectly balanced and sized for kidsWhat we don’t loveA lot of plastic; could be easier to washBest budget lunch box:Brabantia Make & Take lunch box bentoBrabantiaMake & Take lunch box bentofrom£15.95£15.95 at John Lewis£15.95 at AmazonWhat we lovePlenty of space to pack a hearty lunchWhat we don’t loveIt takes up a lot of real estate in your bagView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£15.95 at John Lewis£15.95 at AmazonThis is a practical – if large – lunch box. Inside the main compartment are two smaller boxes, one of which has a lid. There’s also a lift-out divider, which means you can lift everything out in one go if you want. Two clip fastenings and a seal around the lid of the main box keep things secure. All in all, it’s functional if not super sexy (and how sexy do you expect a lunch box to be?).Why we love itI was impressed with the number of useful compartments in this lunch box. They’re all large enough to be genuinely useful – you’ll easily fit a side salad or a decent portion of fruit in one of the smaller boxes. Some compartments in other lunch boxes seemed only suitable for a mouse’s lunch. With the divider in place and the boxes in situ, there is still enough space in there to fit a sandwich. It’s a shame that the divider isn’t adjustable, though, which would make it more flexible. But its rigidity does make it easy to take out everything in one go.This lunch box is easy to clean, and you can stick the whole thing in the dishwasher. It feels robust and rigid, and the opaque colour means it didn’t pick up any unsightly discoloration in testing. Brabantia offers a five-year guarantee as well as spare parts – the seal on the main lid and the container with lid can be boughtseparately on Brabantia’s website.It’s a shame that …it’s so big. You might need to carry a separate tote to take it to and from work. It’s great for picnics, though.Material:BPA-free plastic, silicone sealCapacity:2lWeight empty:400gDimensions:26 x 17 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe?YesMicrowave safe?YesFreezer safe?YesNumber of compartments:3BrabantiaMake & Take lunch box bentofrom£15.95£15.95 at John Lewis£15.95 at AmazonWhat we lovePlenty of space to pack a hearty lunchWhat we don’t loveIt takes up a lot of real estate in your bagBest lunch box for sandwich lovers:Stanley Legendary Classic Useful boxStanleyLegendary Classic Useful boxfrom£40£40 at Selfridges£40 at JD SportsWhat we loveSimple and functional design; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveThe price is steep; not watertightView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£40 at Selfridges£40 at JD SportsStanley is a big force in thewater bottlemarket, and its lunch box kept following me around the internet when I was researching this article. It’s a satisfying functional stainless-steel design with two flip latches to hold the lid on. The inside is pretty capacious, with no frills.Why we love itIt’s surprisingly hard to find a lunch box that will properly fit a sandwich without a hint of squashing: I really hate finding my sandwich crushed and sad at lunchtime. The Stanley Legendary was up to the job – with extra room for a packet of crisps and a piece of fruit. You could even fit a baguette sandwich in here with room to spare. Satisfyingly old-school. With a capacity of 1.18l, this box is slightly larger than the Black+Blum lunch box above. There’s only one compartment, though, so if you’re taking a range of dishes, everything will need to be premixed. And there’s no seal on this lunch box, so things are prone to leaking.It looks great and feels well made – it’s rigid and would survive being dropped. In fact, at 480g, it feels incredibly robust. The mechanisms are simple, and with no seal to give way, this lunch box feels as if it would last and last. It’s easy to wash, too: dishwasher safe and with no bits and bobs to scrub (or lose).It’s a shame that …it’s quite pricey for a single-compartment lunch box, and it’s definitely not leakproof – but it is a great pick for sandwich lovers.Material:stainless steelCapacity:1.18lWeight empty:480gDimensions:25 x 16 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe?YesMicrowave safe?NoFreezer safe?NoNumber of compartments:1StanleyLegendary Classic Useful boxfrom£40£40 at Selfridges£40 at JD SportsWhat we loveSimple and functional design; easy to cleanWhat we don’t loveThe price is steep; not watertightBest stainless steel lunch box:Black+Blum stainless steel lunch boxBlack+BlumStainless steel lunch boxfrom£33.95£33.95 at Black+Blum£33.95 at John LewisWhat we loveSuper-fresh food; functional designWhat we don’t loveIt’s quite spennyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£33.95 at Black+Blum£33.95 at John LewisThis large stainless steel lunch box has a capacity of 1l, just slightly smaller than the Stanley lunch box above. Unlike the Stanley, there’s a strong vacuum seal here, meaning it’s leakproof and will keep your lunch fresh. Inside is an adjustable divider, and on the outside, a coloured silicone band holds the metal fork and keeps the lid shut tight.Why we love itThis lunch box was the perfect size for me, whether I was packing a salad or a sandwich. It’s a bit of a squeeze, but it can fit a sandwich as well as something on the other side of the divider. It can also fit a decent-size salad and keep it satisfyingly fresh thanks to that super-strong vacuum seal. It’s so tight, in fact, that you need to lift the valve before opening the box. In return, it’s totally leakproof. There’s no salad dressing pot provided, but you can be confident that a predressed salad won’t leak.It’s safe to put the box in the freezer, ovenor dishwasher (after removing the lid and silicone band). I liked being able to batch-cook a lasagne or macaroni cheese directly in the box before chucking it in the freezer for later. It comes with a lifetime guarantee, and you canbuy spare parts on the websiteif you lose something.It’s a shame that …the lid goes on so tightly that those with dexterity problems – and kids – might find it difficult to open.Material:stainless steelCapacity:1lWeight empty:460gDimensions:20 x 14 x 6cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe?Yes (except the lid)Microwave safe?NoFreezer safe?YesNumber of compartments:2Black+BlumStainless steel lunch boxfrom£33.95£33.95 at Black+Blum£33.95 at John LewisWhat we loveSuper-fresh food; functional designWhat we don’t loveIt’s quite spennyBest insulated lunch box:Thermos Icon Series food flaskThermosIcon Series food flaskfrom£19.50£19.50 at John Lewis£19.50 at ArgosWhat we loveGreat for keeping soup, porridge et al hotWhat we don’t loveIt’s fairly heavy and bulkyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£19.50 at John Lewis£19.50 at ArgosIf you want to take a hot lunch on the go without access to a microwave, an insulated lunch box is a practical answer. This Thermos one has a decent 710ml capacity, which is enough for soup, pasta or noodles – even for bigger appetites. There’s also a lid that can double as a very small bowl if you’re in a bind, and a folding spoon that can be stowed in the lid.Why we love itThis food flask is vacuum insulated, meaning there’s no air between the two metal walls of the container and very little material for the heat from your food to escape through. The result is that your food stays warm until lunchtime. Thermos advises filling the flask with hot water to warm it before putting food into it, which worked well for me – my testers said their pasta was still hot at lunchtime.I also liked that there’s a spoon inside the lid. Often schools won’t allow you to use their cutlery if you have a packed lunch, and I’ve also had to scramble around to find cutlery during my own lunch break at work. This also meant I could take the flask to a park bench without worrying about forgetting cutlery (it has happened). The brand also sellsspare parts, including the seal and stopper.It’s a shame that …it’s quite heavy, and the inner lid may be tricky for kids to open.Material:stainless steel plus BPA-free plastic stopper and silicone sealCapacity:710mlWeight empty:510gDimensions:10 x 10 x 19cm (WDH)Dishwasher safe?YesMicrowave safe?NoFreezer safe?NoNumber of compartments:1ThermosIcon Series food flaskfrom£19.50£19.50 at John Lewis£19.50 at ArgosWhat we loveGreat for keeping soup, porridge et al hotWhat we don’t loveIt’s fairly heavy and bulkyThe best of the restView image in fullscreen‘Robust, leakproof and great for kids’: the Elephant Box Click and Seal small lunch box.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianElephant Box Click and Seal small lunch boxElephant BoxClick and Seal small lunch box£26£26 at Elephant BoxWhat we loveGenuinely leakproof; great sustainability credentialsWhat we don’t loveIt’s pretty small for the priceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£26 at Elephant BoxBest for:a plastic-free lunch boxThis Elephant Box lunch box is extremely robust – great for kids, adventurous types, or just surviving the office’s fridge Tetris. If that’s not enough, the bright green elasticated strap is great for sliding in cutlery (not included). It’s a little on the small side, though, and the inner divider isn’t leakproof, so it won’t keep wet and dry stuff separate.Elephant Box offers a 15-year guarantee on this lunch box, as well as a repair service andspare partsseparately. The main compartment is big enough to hold a sandwich in the top. However, the bottom layer isn’t big enough to fit a packet of crisps or juice carton.If your food container cupboard is a hellscape like mine, it’s also a mercy that these boxes are designed to be stackable. A screw-top compartment with a transparent lid is designed for dry goods such as nuts, seeds, fruit and granola, and underneath, a screw-lid sealed bowl has enough capacity for even the biggest morning feasts.If you want to avoid those expensive Pret breakfast runs, this is a decent solution. I liked that I could keep my dry and wet foods separate until I wanted to combine them. Initially, I was concerned that the upper compartment wouldn’t be secure, but despite there being no seal, the lid stayed put during testing. The capacious bowl beneath fits a generous serving of overnight oats. And the real selling point of this bowl is that you can keep the dry food crunchy and unsquashed. This meant I could keep fresh raspberries intact or clusters of granola crunchy until I was ready for them.
