It comes with a five-year guarantee, and spare parts, including the silicone seal, areavailable separately.It didn’t make the final cut because …it doesn’t offer the same versatility as other lunch boxes here.Material:BPA-free plastic;capacity:500ml;weight empty:510g;dimensions:11 x 11 x 11cm (WDH);dishwasher safe?Yes;microwave safe?Yes;freezer safe?Yes;number of compartments:2BrabantiaMake & Take breakfast bowlfrom£9.95£10.95 at John Lewis£9.95 at AmazonWhat we loveLeakproof, light and inexpensiveWhat we don’t loveIt’s specific, so won’t suit everyonePick Plates Pick snack boxPick PlatesPick snack boxfrom£12.99£12.99 at Regn£13.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressively robust – will outlive childhoodWhat we don’t loveIt’s too small for older kids and adultsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Zoë Phillimore/The Guardian£12.99 at Regn£13.99 at AmazonBest for:kids’ (and adults’) snacksThis cute box of tricks is the solution I wish I had when my kids were younger. It’s for slinging at them on the back seat of the car or in the pram when you’re out and about. There are four small compartments inside, which are the perfect portion size for smaller appetites.The whole thing is made from silicone, including the valve. Remove this valve (the star on the lid) and compress the box slightly to squeeze out excess air, then reinsert it to seal it and keep everything a bit fresher. You can also remove the valve if you want to microwave the contents with the lid on. The whole thing feels pretty childproof – it’s soft and literally bounces if you drop it. Most importantly, it doesn’t leak, even when dropped from a height.It didn’t make the final cut because …the compartments are small, so they lack versatility for bigger appetites.Material:silicone;capacity:500ml;weight empty:298g;dimensions:14 x 14 x 6cm (WDH);dishwasher safe?Yes;microwave safe?Yes;freezer safe?Yes;number of compartments:4Pick PlatesPick snack boxfrom£12.99£12.99 at Regn£13.99 at AmazonWhat we loveImpressively robust – will outlive childhoodWhat we don’t loveIt’s too small for older kids and adultsWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenKeep it clean: regular washing helps lunch boxes last longer.Photograph: Zoë Phillimore/The GuardianWhat makes a lunch box leakproof?A continuous, tight seal around the container gives you the best chance of a leakproof lunch box. This is usually a silicone strip that fits snugly around the inside of the lid. The lid should also compress evenly around the whole box to seal it shut. A clip closure can also help keep the seal locked down when the lunch box is being jostled around in a school bag or during a work commute. Just keep the seal free of grease or crumbs – any residue will affect how well it works.Which material is best for a lunch box?There’s no definitive answer – sorry.Stainless steelis durable and doesn’t retain smells or stains. On the downside, however, it can dent, is heavy and usually can’t go in the microwave.Plasticis better if you want something lightweight that’s more likely to be freezer and microwave safe. However, it often holds on to smells and stains and can become brittle over time. You may also be keen to avoid it for environmental reasons.Siliconeis more unusual as a material for the whole lunch box, but not unheard of. Silicone lunch boxes are flexible and durable, but noticeably heavier than plastic and can retain grease – so cleaning them can be a real pain.Glasslunch boxes are great for food storage, as glass doesn’t retain stains or odours and is relatively easy to clean. It can also often go in the oven, microwave and dishwasher. But again, they’re heavier and less robust, and you may not want your kid to be slinging around glass at school.Howto look afteryour lunch boxTo keep your lunch box in tip-top shape for as long as possible, it’s imperative to wash it as soon as you can after eating. Salty or acidic food can be particularly damaging to a food container if it’s left to sit. Use a non-abrasive detergent and try to avoid scourers, as these can damage the finish. For hand washing, use washing-up liquid and warm water. If your lunch box has a removable silicone seal, take it off and wash it thoroughly from time to time. After you’ve washed everything, leave it to air-dry fully. Don’t reassemble a lunch box that’s not completely dry: trapped moisture creates conditions for mould, mildew and unpleasant smells.Check whether your lunch box is dishwasher, freezer, oven and microwave safe, and always follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Don’t put metal containers in the microwave – no good will come of that.Is a more expensive lunch box worth it?A pricey lunch box isn’t automatically better than a cheap one. Look at the construction and durability. If you want to invest in a genuinely good lunch box, look for a good seal, tougher materials, replacement parts and a decent warranty. A £30-£40 stainless steel lunch box that remains leakproof for years and has replacement seals available may be better value than a £10 box that needs replacing every year.It’s probably not worth forking out for a super fancy lunch box with loads of compartments or clever features if they don’t actually solve a problem you have.For more:The best water bottles – testedThe best travel mugs for taking hot drinks on the goThe best backpacks for work, travel and wild adventureBrilliant buys to supercharge school, work and everything in betweenZoë Phillimore is a journalist with 20 years of experience. She’s put many things to the test, from mattresses to makeup. She has become the go-to personfriends and family consult with before making any purchase, earning her the nickname “Zoogle”. Aside from this, Zoë loves travel, being outside – especially on the beach – and reading. She has three children, who seemingly require endless packed lunches and have an unending talent for breaking or losing lunch boxesExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThe FilterFoodHomesParents and parentingFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gore, gimps and a potty-mouthed magpie: welcome to the Lisbon horror festival where nightmares are a dream | Horror films | The Guardian
description: MotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares. Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grail
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: MotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares. Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grail
Content: ‘Massacred by the punters within 20 minutes’ … MotelX celebrates their 20th edition with a bloody good birthday cake.Photograph: Bruna BuniottoView image in fullscreen‘Massacred by the punters within 20 minutes’ … MotelX celebrates their 20th edition with a bloody good birthday cake.Photograph: Bruna BuniottoHorror filmsGore, gimps and a potty-mouthed magpie: welcome to the Lisbon horror festival where nightmares are a dreamMotelX – Portugal’s only film festival dedicated to horror – hopes to inspire local film-makers by showcasing world-class scares. Now in its 20th edition, its directors say truly nerve-shredding cinema is its holy grailPhil HoadFri 11 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf horror happens in the dark, the midnight movie showing was once the perfect way of gauging the genre’s health. But those days may be over. “When we were a film club, our first ever cinema screening was Takashi Miike’s Ichi the Killer in 2003, and it was full,” says Pedro Souto, co-director of Lisbon’s horror-centricMotelX festival. “But you don’t have that many people at midnight any more. I don’t know why.” He’s right: the midnight slot I attend – of the gore-bathed Indonesian kung fu flick Ikatan Darah – is only half full. Only a few appreciative chuckles when meat-cleavers plunge into craniums suggest the old midnight spirit still lives.No need to panic, though: horror has simply embraced the light. With the genre exploding in the 2010s and 2020s, and blockbusting grosses this year for the likes ofObsessionandBackrooms, MotelX is able to gorge itself on this cultural jugular. Now in its 20th edition, the festival has expanded to 11 days, with more than 170 films from 40 countries. Flashy branding – a howling gimp and the signature X, both in inflatable PVC – is dotted on around city billboards. At the opening ceremony, a gigantic birthday cake – the self-same gimp emerging from a lake of gelatine “blood” – is massacred by the punters within 20 minutes. Crowds seem abundant at most screenings, dominated by a heatwave look (dark singlets, shorts and sweaty tattoos) best described as “goth Decathlon”.View image in fullscreenEmbracing the light … horror fans at MotelX.Photograph: Bruna BuniottoMotelX, the only purely horror festival inPortugal, grew out of a private film club catering to the country’s emerging love affair with the dark stuff in the 1990s. “Living in the suburbs, there was nothing much to do other than go to the movies,” says the festival’s other co-director, João Monteiro, sitting with Souto in the São Jorge cinema, the coffee-toned modernist palace where most screenings take place. “As well as the cinema, there were video clubs, so we spent the whole time renting horror movies like the seventh Friday the 13th. It was our initiation, like when kids in tribes become adults.”He puts it this way because Portugal had virtually no tradition of horror cinema; it was frowned on by the Estado Novo regime, so there was no domestic output. “You could only do comedies, or films with a nationalistic take, all about Lisbon basically,” says Monteiro. Their research efforts only turned up about 25 films between 1910 and MotelX’s inaugural year in 2007 that could qualify as horror – where in neighbouring Spain, there was a mini-boom in the late Franco years. Foreign imports – Hammer films and the oddgiallo– were often heavily censored.View image in fullscreenA gem in the rough … ultra-grim Iranian horror Poultry FarmMotelX is hoping to help fill that void, through its award for the best unproduced screenplay and by showcasing Portuguese work (the majority of which is still in the shorts category). And then there is the job of irrigating the local scene with horror cuts from around the world. This year, there’s at least one gem in the rough: Mohammad Reza Ardalan’s Poultry Farm, an ultra-grim Iranian film that Souto and Monteiro knew nothing about when they were offered it by a sales agent they had previously worked with. It turned out to be a richly characterised slow-burner about a young Iraqi-Kurd recruit working the chicken sheds at a farm, where secrets are lodged as obdurately as the rocks they prise from the ground. With its roots in Iranian social realism, it patrols the frontiers of noir and horror with great effectiveness, as it scrutinises this quasi-feudal society and the immigrants at its mercy.US horror-comedy Drag was a fun opening film: an antidote to the sprinting-zombie movie in which an inept burglar (Lizzy Caplan) puts her back out helping herself to “rich people’s shampoo” and must be painstakingly hauled from the crime scene. With its knowing placement of excruciatingly painful obstacles, the film plays like a Wile E Coyote cartoon – until the sinister owner, John Stamos’s abstract-expressionist artist, turns up prematurely to dose us with musings on the male gaze.View image in fullscreen‘I now know the Portuguese for werewolf if I’m ever caught here on a full moon’ … 1968 Estonian witch-panic classic LibahuntThe artists are the guests in Corrin Evans’s 1990s-set Corpus, in which a grungy photographer/small town dealer is invited to a party at an upstate New York mansion by his it-boy model ex-boyfriend. With her interminable hangout scenes, Evans – who was previously an intimacy coordinator for MaXXXine – is clearly besotted with the decade’s club scene. But she only moves past self-conscious hipsterdom and finds a natural rhythm during the film’s carnal second half, when sexual onlookers and objects fuse to suggest something intriguing about the nature of desire.There were no English-language subtitles at the Cinemateca Portuguesa for 1968 Estonian witch-panic classic Libahunt (Werewolf). But no matter: the cinematography’s incantatory flair spoke for itself, and I now know the Portuguese for werewolf (lobisomem), if I’m ever caught here on a full moon. Such pagan dalliances are becoming played-out in modern horror, but the Basque-language portmanteau Gaua (Night) is a lush example with rich production design. Indulging the occultist audience with a full-on flying pandemonium to finish, it exists somewhere adjacent to the Robert Eggers-Ari Aster coven.View image in fullscreenThe Robert Eggers-Ari Aster coven … lush Basque-language occult drama GauaPhotograph: Album/AlamyThe Virgin of the Quarry Lake, Laura Casabé’s impressive, febrile, supernatural coming-of-age tale, is almost as damning about Argentina as Poultry Farm is about rural Iran. Taking place in 2001, in a Buenos Aires of blackouts and standpipes, Dolores Oliverio is moping, petulant and ruthless, fending off a worldly rival for her childhood sweetheart. You could pretend The Fox, directed by Dario Russo, is trying to say something equally profound about small town Australia. But as it cheerfully admits, there is nothing whatsoever to be learned – or maybe just a little, about daft human desire – from this droll cautionary relationship fable. Jilted hunter Nick (Jai Courtney), eager to bring his cheating partner (Emily Browning) to heel, ignores the Antichrist rule: never trust the weird talking fox (voiced here by Olivia Colman). Not that Sam Neill’s potty-mouthed magpie is much better.My only complaint is not encountering anything truly frightening (though I only catch a three-day sliver of the festival). Souto says finding such nerve-shredders is MotelX’s holy grail. But Monteiro counters that, now Portugal is growing into the macabre, such work has become tougher: “I think we become adults today. We don’t fear horror films. We have no nightmares. I’m trying to find films that can still make me feel as I did in the beginning, like when I first saw Alien. Because right now, it’s impossible.”MotelXruns until 13 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsPortugalFestivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mossy catwalks, mycelial designs and Monty Don: the growth of gardener style | Gardens | The Guardian
description: Aspirational clobber, hot horticulturists and a TikTok content rise suggest gardening has never been cooler
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Aspirational clobber, hot horticulturists and a TikTok content rise suggest gardening has never been cooler
Content: Monty Don is to front a campaign for New Balance, which is launching a pair of trainers alongside the jewellery designer Bleue Wickham-Burnham.Photograph: New BalanceView image in fullscreenMonty Don is to front a campaign for New Balance, which is launching a pair of trainers alongside the jewellery designer Bleue Wickham-Burnham.Photograph: New BalanceGardensMossy catwalks, mycelial designs and Monty Don: the growth of gardener styleAspirational clobber, hot horticulturists and a TikTok content rise suggest gardening has never been coolerEllie Violet BramleyFri 11 Sep 2026 10.07 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou could argue that photosynthesis, soil bacteria, chlorophyll and germination, by their nature, never go out of style. But somehow, as the news broke this week thatMonty Don would step down from Gardeners’ Worldafter 23 years behind the shovel, gardening is having a moment in the sun.On Saturday, New Balance will launch a pair of trainers alongside the jewellery designer Bleue Wickham-Burnham in a campaign fronted by Don himself, photographed shrinking into a bush with a pair of the trainers around his neck. In high fashion of late, the gardener Charlie McCormick became the face of JW Anderson’s spring 2027 campaign, and Alfie Nickerson, who grows flowers biodynamically in Norfolk for his brand Burnt Fen Flowers, has recently been plucked by Jimmy Choo for its autumn campaign, Wild Rose. Catwalks have been mossy, designs have been mycelial.In more everyday settings, a pair of beige hemp gardening clogs havebecome the kind of thing twenty-somethings Lime bike across London to bag. Gardener style – cords, gilets, Blundstones and barn jackets – is now as familiar on concrete as compost. Don might have been wearing a chore jacket – arguably not a gardener’s staple, despite its factory origins – on the telly for more than a decade, but they are now omnipresent in cafes, ad agenciesand other places far from an allotment.Online, gardeners are finding new audiences, in some cases for reasons besides their knowledge of gerberas: i-D magazine has hailed anew gen of “hot gardeners”as part of the catalyst for a 50% increase in gardening content on TikTok this year, alongside actual interest in it.View image in fullscreenMonty Don posing in the Royal Horticultural Society and BBC Radio 2 Dog Garden at the RHS Chelsea flower show in 2025.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyFancy gardening tools and clobber are aspirational: a site calledGardenheirhas made a name for itself selling hand-forged tools,£275 two-gallon watering cansand various itemsin collaborationwith the French workwear brand Le Laboureur that seem more likely destined for a small-plates restaurant than a vegetable patch.Niwaki is another site for very fancy gardening gear. According to Jake Hobson, its founder, the popularity of gardening togs is as much about the mindset it offers as practicality. “They communicate a particular attitude. They’re comfortable and loose-fitting, but they also suggest that you’re ready for action,” he says.Niwaki has intentionally pushed its products to new, non-gardening markets. “We sell a lot from Chiltern Street to customers who may or may not have a garden, and who may or may not even wear it in the garden,” he says, drawing a parallel with the broader rise in the appeal of workwear.View image in fullscreenNiwaki’s limited-edition camo range.Photograph: NiwakiHe delights in seeing Niwaki’s gardening gear worn outside the garden, such as one of their hard-wearing canvas tool bags, designed “especially for the travelling pruner”, being worn to the airport. Or the brand’s Tobizubon, which he describes as “the very, very balloon-shaped Japanese gardening trousers” and which are “incredibly popular in France. I’ve seen some amazing people wearing them in Paris, often with boots or funky shoes, and sometimes with a smart jacket on top.”As with all things gardening, it hasn’t happened in a rush. Matt Collins, the head gardener at the Garden Museum, in central London, thinks it has grown in tandem with an exaltation of the position of professional gardeners more generally, and an overdue understanding that it’s creative, worthy work. “For a long time, it was seen as quite a kind of lower-status [job] … gardeners are cool, gardeners do important work.”According to Selina Ozanne, the head gardener at The Exchange, in Erith, south-east London, “gardening is often romanticised. It has charm, as well as aesthetic appeal.” Plus she thinks it “holds a lot of nostalgia for people. It’s often a hobby associated with parents or grandparents.”Gardeners, both professional and amateur, are more visible now, says Collins. And not just on social media. “Galleries and museum spaces and communal spaces are investing more and more in gardens.” Plus, non-gardeners are doing more gardening in public. “People who don’t have the privilege of a garden of their own … are finding other places to garden,” in parks and local community gardens, says Collins.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe timing is key. With climate a central topic, people who are caring for our planet seem like logical recipients of adoration. Plus, as AI expertsthis week warnedof the high likelihood of extinction by AI, the calming, eternal nature of gardening feels even more appealing. “There’s definitely a feeling that gardening is one of those crafts that can’t fully be automated,” says Collins. “Watering schedules can be automated, seed-sowing even, maybe, but the act of observing and engaging in gardens remains quite human.”View image in fullscreenMonty Don fronts the New Balance campaign.Photograph: New BalanceFor younger people, there is arguably a more specific appeal. Ozanne, of the “Nokia 3310 generation”, spent her childhood “heavily outdoors, building dens and climbing trees”. For the current generation, she thinks gardening “holds a sense of intrigue and presents escapism from a chronically online society”.Collins points out a few thorns. Where fashion might sell a glamorous ideal of gardening, all forms of it involve muck, and not just some photogenic mud. Public gardening in particular, he says, “can be really difficult”. There can, he says, be “dog shit, human shit, sometimes, and grimy waste bags”. For Ozanne, who wears brands like Gramicci and Toast – repaired over and over again – the work makes her want to dress up. “I knew early on that if I was going to be out in public, picking up litter and dodging all manner of nasty things, that I wanted to look good doing it.”But, says Collins, the glorification of the gardener isn’t necessarily translating to “their pay grade and how their actual value has been translated into [the] real world”. Gardening isn’t, according to Ozanne, “a career that’s accessible to everybody – both physically and financially”.Explore more on these topicsGardensTikTokSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Somewhere to be themselves, and be kind’: the Filipino folk-popper creating a hand-drawn world for gen Z to escape to | Music | The Guardian
description: What started as a school project about plucky fictional kids in animal masks sparked an obsessive fanbase and a major label deal. Now the Icelandic-Filipino artist behind it all is ready to reveal themself
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: What started as a school project about plucky fictional kids in animal masks sparked an obsessive fanbase and a major label deal. Now the Icelandic-Filipino artist behind it all is ready to reveal themself
Content: ‘We are huge nerds!’ … Yaelokre.Photograph: Olivia BrytzView image in fullscreen‘We are huge nerds!’ … Yaelokre.Photograph: Olivia BrytzMusicInterview‘Somewhere to be themselves, and be kind’: the Filipino folk-popper creating a hand-drawn world for gen Z to escape toHannah J DaviesWhat started as a school project about plucky fictional kids in animal masks sparked an obsessive fanbase and a major label deal. Now the artist behind it all – known as Yaelokre – is ready to reveal themselfFri 11 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarpy Hare by Yaelokre is the kind of song you might expect to have gone viral in the 1520s, not the 2020s. Backed by guitalele (that’s a guitar/ukulele hybrid), the lullaby begins with the line “Harpy Hare, where have you buried all your children?” performed by fictional kids from the equally fictional world of Meadowlark who are depicted in fey illustrations wearing animal masks. But two years ago it became an unlikely TikTok hit, reaching No 1 on Spotify’s Global Viral Songs chart.That was in summer 2024, when the world of Meadowlark was a bit more DIY. Not only was its creator still making tracks and illustrations from their “diary turned storybook” in their bedroom, there was no Reddit community around them yet and only the faintest of whispers about Yaelokre online. These days, Keath Ósk, the Icelandic-Filipino artist behind the project, has almost three million monthly Spotify listeners; last year they played a sell-out UK and Ireland tour, and they have just released their first album under their own name, delighting a following of gen Z and queer listeners who write fan fiction about Ósk’s world and cosplay as their hand-drawn characters, prompting questions on Reddit such as: “My costume has bells [on it], should I remove them for the concert?”Meadowlark’s kids transmit messages of bravery and courage and celebrate childlike wonder in a world determined to stamp it out. Ósk’s folkloric storytelling has created a deeply parasocial fandom, attracting followers who find solace in this outsider world, and some who find LGBTQ+ and neurodivergent readings in Ósk’s music. One mother wrote online that their 10-year-old child had “found her people” at one of Yaelokre’s live shows after being bullied.Keath Ósk: Harpy Hare – videoThe project started as a kind of escapism for Ósk, they say when we meet in a London cafe for their first proper interview. They don’t share their gender or age but appear to be in their early 20s, wide-eyed, playful, clad entirely in earthy shades of beige, with a messy bleach-blonde mop; they have a surprisingly plummy British accent for a recent transplant to London. “I wanted to be an illustrator for children but I was also enjoying the media my dad was sharing with me – video games like Skyrim and fantasy books. We are huge nerds!” Ósk used to sign their illustrations as Yaelokre, a portmanteau of yellow and ochre. They would also practise voice acting: “My mum would catch me talking to myself and be like, ‘Are you doing alright?!’” – which led them to fuse their love of fables with another passion, music.Ósk grew up predominantly in the Philippines, on Luzon island, occasionally venturing to Iceland to visit their father’s family. They miss Filipino food, they explain, even if as a culture “we’ve absolutely botched spaghetti – we love making it sweet”. Singing is a big part of Filipino culture, and the nation’s love of enthusiastic home karaoke sessions is well documented. “It’s huge there,” says Ósk. “You’d know your neighbour was having a birthday party because you could hear their auntie screaming their lungs out.” Perhaps less known, at least in the west, are the regional singing contests that offer entertainment and a way out of grinding poverty for some. Ósk’s mother would enter such contests “when she needed extra money, to buy milk for me as a baby. I’m not ashamed of saying that I grew up really, really poor.” The culture of people singing competitively for money is, says Ósk, “such a wonderful and also a sad thing”.View image in fullscreenPart of the lore … illustration of The Lark by Yaelokre.Photograph: PR HANDOUTTheir own foray into music happened organically, they explain, as the Meadowlark concept expanded dramatically from a school project about a friendship between a hare, a goat, a tree and a baby moose. They contemplated writing a book about them, but deterred by the need to “build a whole plot” around the characters, they turned to music instead, creating a theatrical sound world that spun its own myths. It didn’t take long from Ósk putting music online to blowing up on TikTok and signing – as Yaelokre – with Atlantic Records in early 2025.They moved to London earlier this year, where they rerecorded 11 original tracks for their debut album, Foreword, giving their sound a bolder update: sometimes belting karaoke-style, or channelling the Filipino rapper Gloc-9 on the scatter-gun delivery of And the Hound. There’s also a cover of Bonnie Tyler’s Holding Out for a Hero: in their hands, it sounds more like an epic poem than an 80s power ballad. Ósk also sings in Tagalog. “I want to be able to represent where I came from,” they say. “I’m so patriotic. When people ask about my gender, I just go, I’m Filipino …” Ósk doesn’t see the shift in sound as a contradiction: “I have so many layers and [Yaelokre] is not my only world. I have my own history and truth outside it. A lot of my young audience are going to grow up with Yaelokre. I grew up with Pinoy hip-hop!”View image in fullscreen‘I have so many layers’ … Yaelokre.Photograph: (awaiting credit)Where’s her Pulitzer already? Joanna Newsom’s 20 best songs – ranked!Read moreThey’re clear that this isn’t the end of Yaelokre and its animal mask-wearing child mascots; they’re working on new music involving the characters soon. But there have been challenges along the way, and perhaps Ósk is happy putting some distance between themself and their creations. Earlier this year, they removed two characters from Meadowlark lore after they were sexualised by some members of the fanbase. Some fans have seen it as a sign that Ósk is angry with them, but they say there’s no rage. “I want to be able to filter as much as possible so that the community is safe, but I’m not angry. I think people are still learning. My one rule is please don’t sexualise any of my characters, because they represent me.”Ósk wants to keep the fandom as wholesome as possible, even staging sustainable clothing swaps at live shows, to help cherish a sense of wonder. “There’s a space for people to learn and to be themselves and to be kind,” they say, “and to have a community where they don’t feel like they’re alone in this world.” Is this a world they would have benefited from growing up? “Most definitely. Making this story is what I could call my moral compass. It’s less about getting into playlists or winning awards and more about reaching the kids who didn’t grow up with these principles – I want to be able to share my wisdom and what I’ve learned.”Foreword is out now on Atlantic Records. Keath Ósk tours Europe and the UK from 7 October and North America from 9 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusicFolk musicPop and rockinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning | Premier League | The Guardian
description: English top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighter
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: English top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighter
Content: Chelsea's Cole Palmer, Liverpool's Bradley Barcola, Arsenal's Kai Havertz.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChelsea's Cole Palmer, Liverpool's Bradley Barcola, Arsenal's Kai Havertz.Composite: Getty ImagesPremier LeagueBallon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turningEnglish top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighterJacob SteinbergFri 11 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePremier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players onthis year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.The trio givingArsenala presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.Men’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years?Read moreIt was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.View image in fullscreenAnthony Gordon has said Spanish football demands a ‘different level of tactical and technical intelligence’.Photograph: Newhouse Media/MB Media/Getty ImagesNow comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.Graphic showing Premier League games have been more end-to-end early in 2026‑27There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up.Manchester Citymay soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals –Arsenal taking on Chelseaat the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHavertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard,Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.View image in fullscreenFlorian Wirtz has struggled to adapt to the pace of the Premier League.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoThis matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenalbut stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool afterhis arrival from PSG.Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beatChelsea. It felt refreshing.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBallon d'OrArsenalChelseaLiverpoolManchester CityLa LigafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurt | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: England reached the World Cup semi-finals although the midfielder did not play a minute but he is key to Manchester United’s hopes in the derby
Author: David Hytner
Headline: England reached the World Cup semi-finals although the midfielder did not play a minute but he is key to Manchester United’s hopes in the derby
Content: Kobbie Mainoo’s statistics this season show a player just as adept on the ball as off.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo’s statistics this season show a player just as adept on the ball as off.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoManchester UnitedKobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurtEngland reached World Cup semis yet midfielder did not play a minute. But he is key to Manchester United in derbyDavid HytnerFri 11 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a sight the England press pack became increasingly used to seeing after the team’s World Cup matches over the summer. Kobbie Mainoo was invariably the first to leave the dressing room, walk through the mixed zone – eyes dead ahead, features impassive – and board the bus.It was as if he could not get out of the stadiums quick enough andthe further England progressedthe more pronounced it started to feel. There was a real gap between Mainoo and the next England player to depart the stadiumin the knockout rounds. The Manchester United midfielder is inscrutable, even in the heat of battle. It is part of his enviably unflappable temperament. It was no great leap to imagine what lay behind the mask – tremendous frustration as Thomas Tuchel kept on leaving him out.Sesko soars as Manchester United surge past Sabah on Champions League returnRead moreMainoo did not play a single minute at the tournament. He was an unused substitute all the way to the semi-final exit against Argentina, and when everyone expected to see him in thethird-place playoff against Francehe did not make the bench. The Football Association said before the game he had picked up an unspecified injury.For Mainoo it was a lost summer and yet it was physically and mentally draining all the same, what with the training and travel; the demand to stay focused as he waited and waited. Like every player who was part of a squad that reached the final weekend of the World Cup, he reported late for pre-season training with his club. Mainoo played the last half hour of United’s final friendly against Milan and that was it. On the opening weekend of the season, he was fit enough only to be a substitute at Hull, coming on with 23 minutes to goand United 2-0 down, en route to a damaging defeat.There has been a spotlight on Mainoo, with some fans wondering how he would react to the suffocation of his World Cup dream; his treatment by Tuchel, who preferred Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice in the deeper midfield positions and, also, at various times, Reece James, Jude Bellingham, Jordan Henderson, Morgan Rogers and Nico O’Reilly. Nobody should have worried. Mainoo is made of stern stuff. United regeared their midfield to the tune of £155m during the transfer window, adding Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. Baleba has not yet played because of injury, but as United prepare for Sunday’s derby at Old Trafford, it is Mainoo who has reasserted himself.The 21-year-old has been outstanding in each of United’s matches since the opener at Hull – against Ipswich, Everton and then Sabah in the Champions League on Thursday night. The question for Michael Carrick in the derby will be Mainoo and who in front of the back four.View image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo in action against Sabah in United’s 4-0 Champions League win.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoThere is a reason why the United support have adapted the lyrics to Billy Ocean’s Love Really Hurts Without You to declare that their team cannot play without Mainoo. A couple of statistics. In the past three games, he has attempted 211 passes and completed 201, which represents extraordinary security on the ball – particularly given the frequency with which he has it. Also, the degree of risk inherent to so much of what he does.Then there is the number that shows he made a game‑high 15 defensive contributions against Ipswich and Everton. He is improving out of possession. As much as anything, though, it is the quickness of the feet, the hip-shaking feints and changes of direction; how he simultaneously keeps his opponents on their heels and recalibrates United’s angles of attack.Mainoo, of course, has already made his big comeback this year. Ruben Amorim could not fit him into his 3-4-2-1 system; the Portuguese did not trust him defensively. But even so, it continues to feel absurd that Amorim did not give him a single start in the Premier League last season. Mainoo’s first in the competition camein January against Cityat Old Trafford after Carrick had taken over.It was the first match of Carrick’s second spell as the club’s manager and nobody really knew how it would go. “The players … maybe myself [as well], the coaches, obviously you guys in the media,” Carrick says. Everything came together in spectacular fashion, United winning 2-0, Mainoo straight back into the groove that had helped him win over Amorim’s predecessor, Erik ten Hag.If it was an ignition point for Carrick, it was the same for Mainoo, whose form for the remainder of the season helped to drive United to a third-place finish and convince Tuchel to take him to the World Cup. As an aside, Mainoo v Anderson, who completed a £116m move from Nottingham Forest to City in July, will be box office. Anderson was a target for United before City blew them away with their offer. He called City “the kings of Manchester” on the day he signed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited’s dominance of the derby in January was almost total and a key takeaway was the slick first-time football they played. Remember the passing sequence when Rayan Cherki was triangulated by Matheus Cunha, Luke Shaw and Bruno Fernandes? The click was immediate for Carrick. This is the type of stuff that he wants; what he needs to see more of against City as he hopes to locate a bit of early-season momentum.View image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo had a delayed start to the league season because of his involvement with England at the World Cup.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPACarrick knows a deep-sitting tempo-setter when he sees one, the player of the pass before the pass, and he doubled down on this sort of technician with his summer reboot, especially in Tielemans. It was also noticeable that when the luckless Mason Mount, who is back from his latest injury, came on for Tielemans against Sabah, he did so in a deeper midfield role. Carrick’s idea is to play through the middle. It is about balls to feet, timing, distances.“It was nice to get Mason on in the second half and Andrey Santos [for Mainoo] and keep seeing the same things,” Carrick says. “It’s the combinations and connections. Taking the ball and playing close together at times. We have the technical ability for the boys to take the ball in the middle of the pitch. A lot of it is on wavelength and understanding … where each of them want the ball, which we are developing. It’s probably something that we’ve done a bit more of this season.”Carrick is expected to start Tielemans alongside Mainoo with Fernandes as the third midfielder. They will be up against Anderson, Enzo Fernández and Cherki. It is a mouthwatering showdown. It will be where the derby is won or lost.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: England not picking a spinner feels like going out for a walk without an umbrella | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Dan Lawrence took two wickets in the end but the lack of a specialist was keenly felt on a day when Pakistan dug in against an all-pace attack
Author: Andy Bull
Headline: Dan Lawrence took two wickets in the end but the lack of a specialist was keenly felt on a day when Pakistan dug in against an all-pace attack
Content: Dan Lawrence bowling for England on day three of the third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston.Photograph: Colorsport/Barry Mitchell/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDan Lawrence bowling for England on day three of the third Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston.Photograph: Colorsport/Barry Mitchell/ShutterstockEngland v Pakistan 2026AnalysisEngland not picking a spinner feels like going out for a walk without an umbrellaAndy Bullat EdgbastonDan Lawrence took two wickets in the end but the lack of a specialist was keenly felt on a day when Pakistan dug in against an all-pace attackFri 11 Sep 2026 14.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTShareAt half past two in the afternoon the fans struck up a conga in the Hollies Stand. Fifteen Fred Flintstones, 11 Oompa Loompas with one Willy Wonka, five cardinals with an inflatable doll, four centurions, three six-foot bottles of tequila, two Dave Bedfords, one Geri Halliwell, one Donald Trump, and a Dolly Parton bringing up the rear. Out in the middle, England’s four fast bowlers were flogging an endless succession of back-of-length balls at the Pakistani middle order, who blocked and ducked and slashed and cut.It was round about this moment that the Pakistanis could, perhaps, have been forgiven for asking whether English cricket was quite the force we’ve all been led to believe these last few weeks.Razaullah lights up for Pakistan to slow down England’s victory march in third TestRead moreFor the first time in this series, the Pakistan batters stuck to the task. England had to confront the problem of trying to work out what to do when the opposition aren’t gifting them wickets all in a tumble. It had been a while. The last time they had to bowl even a 51st over in a single innings was at the tail end of the match against New Zealand at Trent Bridge, 75 days ago, when Ben Stokes was still captain. Ollie Robinson hasn’t had to bowl as many as the 21 overs he delivered in this innings since Sussex played Leicestershire in May.This is the era of quick cricket. Only the optimists buy advance tickets for the fourth day’s play these days. There have been seven two-day Tests in the last decade. There were only six in the entirety of the 20th century. Ten of the 20 shortest Tests that had a winner have been played in the last five years, five of them in the last 12 months. Old batters blame young batters, young batters blame groundstaff, groundstaff blame administrators, fast bowlers ask why they don’t get the credit, and spin bowlers whether they’ll get a bowl at all.In a match that moves at that sort of speed you can get away without picking a spinner. But it still feels a little like going out for a long autumn walk without an umbrella: you’re fine all the way up to the point when you find you’re very much not. England, of course, have equipped themselves with Dan Lawrence, who has taken nine wickets at 71 runs each for Surrey in the championship this year, and whose bowling is habitually described as being better than it looks. It could hardly be worse, given that he runs up like a man who’s trodden barefoot on his kids’ Lego set in the black of the night.Lawrence’s success in this role seems largely to depend on his never actually having to perform it. In three Tests, he’s been asked to bowl all of 9.4 overs, half of them in a desperate attempt to buy a wicket off the tail at the butt end of Friday’s play. Until Lawrence had Azan Awais caught down the leg-side with a delivery that just grazed the outside edge of his bat, this was going to go down as the first three-Test series in this country for 50 years in which an English spinner hadn’t taken a wicket.Joe Root promptly yanked Lawrence out of the attack regardless. He preferred to return to his four quicks, even though three of them were going at more than four an over. The rhythm felt off, England had no way to change the tempo of the day’s play, or tax the batsmen’s techniques in new ways, to try their patience, or test their ability against anything that gave them time to think. Test cricket’s supposed to be a game played in chords. England spent the day hammering away at the one single note over and over.Steve Smith said back during the last Ashes that he wasn’t sure whether there was any value in picking a spinner, and if even Nathan Lyon’s struggling to justify his place in the team you have to wonder what hope there is for England’s spinners. There are more of them out there than the Test selectors seem to believe, Jack Leach is still whirring away for Somerset, and has 31 wickets at 18 each this season, Yorkshiremen will tell you Dom Bess is bowling better than ever, and has 32 at 29, Mason Crane has 30 at 34 for Glamorgan, Liam Patterson-White 35 at 26 for Nottinghamshire.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter picking, and sticking, with Shoaib Bashir for two years the selectors now seem to have decided that unless a man can bowl like Graeme Swann they’re better off picking someone who can bat like Lawrence. You can get away with this if you have Viv Richards at No 3 and a battalion of the finest fastest bowlers ever to play the game jostling for the spots in the tail. But Pakistan’s batting was a vital reminder that England will need to find a better solution before their next Test.Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Liam Farrell leads from front as Wigan crush Catalans to secure League Leaders’ Shield | Super League | The Guardian
description: Liam Farrell scored in his first match since announcing he would retire at the end of the season as Wigan routed Catalans to claim the League Leaders’ Shield
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Liam Farrell scored in his first match since announcing he would retire at the end of the season as Wigan routed Catalans to claim the League Leaders’ Shield
Content: Liam Farrell with the League Leaders’ Shield after Wigan’s victory over Catalans.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAView image in fullscreenLiam Farrell with the League Leaders’ Shield after Wigan’s victory over Catalans.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PASuper LeagueLiam Farrell leads from front as Wigan crush Catalans to secure League Leaders’ ShieldWigan 50-12 CatalansCaptain scores one try and sets up anotherAaron Bowerat the Brick Community StadiumFri 11 Sep 2026 17.58 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePerhaps the biggest compliment you could pay this Wigan side is that they managed to make a night billed “Frantic Friday” by the broadcasters feel as tense as a pre-season friendly.The drama was, in the end, nowhere to be seen in front of almost 20,000 Wigan supporters. Incredibly, this was not even a flawless display from the home side despite the fact they scored 50 points to saunter their way towards leg two of what appears increasingly likely to be a domestic treble. But that is the standard they are operating at right now: just too good for everyone else.Table-topping Wigan hit ominous form at season’s sharp end in pursuit of trebleRead moreIn reality, the job was done last weekend when they dismantled Leeds at Headingley to usurp Rhinos at theSuper Leaguesummit. Catalans, who have been dreadful this year, were never really going to cause one of the biggest upsets we would have seen for some time. And Wigan strolled to the League Leaders’ Shield with minimal fuss.By half-time, they were 24-6 ahead and it was merely a matter of how many they would score thereafter. Wigan’s cause for top spot was aided even further by Leeds inexplicably slipping up at home to Hull – meaning that even the team considered to be their closest rivals are faltering at precisely the wrong moment.Meanwhile, Matt Peet’s side are getting better every week, with this their 15th consecutive league victory. Two more and they will have the treble, with the lowest-ranked winner of next week’s elimination playoff games having the daunting task of coming to Wigan and trying to halt this juggernaut. Good luck with that. The League Leaders’ Shield is derided in some quarters as less important than other trophies, but Wigan pride themselves on it. To be the most consistent team throughout the year matters in these parts.“This trophy more than the others represents the club, the consistency,” Peet said. “For every Billy Boston there’s all of us, and that’s what makes the club a great place.”A word for Peet too, who has now won nine major trophies in just five seasons at Wigan. If they win the Grand Final, he will be the most successful coach in Super League history with 10 trophies: but the evidence is fairly heavy that he is already the greatest coach this competition has seen.His side made light work of Catalans and the occasion. It was all fairly low key as Wigan ran in four tries to Dragons’ one in the first half, with the highlight their captain, Liam Farrell, going through to score in the week he announced he would be retiring at the end of the season.As news filtered across the Pennines that Leeds were losing at home, the job appeared done by the break with Wigan 18 points ahead. But champion teams do not let up; and the hosts continued to pile on the points in the second half with Austin Daniel and Jai Field next to add their names to the list of try scorers.View image in fullscreenAdam Keighran goes over for a late try to add to his seven successful conversions for Wigan.Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PAPeet could afford to take off Field and Bevan French in the final quarter, with an extended break over the next fortnight for all of Wigan’s stars before their playoff semi-final. But Wigan continued to score points, with Zach Eckersley, Adam Keighran and Liam Marshall all crossing in a dominant final quarter.The trophy lift followed shortly after full time and it was delivered by Farrell with only a fraction of the emotion he and his teammates will produce if they are lucky enough to do it again next month. The strains of Tina Turner’s hit The Best played out as leg two of a possible treble was completed in style – and few would argue against Wigan being exactly that right now.Explore more on these topicsSuper LeagueWigan WarriorsCatalans DragonsRugby leaguematch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000m | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen provided the highlight on the first evening of the inaugural Ultimate Championships by storming to victory in the men’s 5,000m
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen provided the highlight on the first evening of the inaugural Ultimate Championships by storming to victory in the men’s 5,000m
Content: Jakob Ingebrigtsen wins the men's 5,000 metres ahead of his rival Cole Hocker.Photograph: Tamas Vasvari/EPAView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen wins the men's 5,000 metres ahead of his rival Cole Hocker.Photograph: Tamas Vasvari/EPAAthleticsJakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000mNorwegian leaves rival Hocker trailing to claim $150,000Briton Jazmin Sawyers second in the women’s long jumpSean Inglein BudapestFri 11 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a scene that has become gloriously familiar down the years. Jakob Ingebrigtsen leaving the world’s best athletes gasping in his slipstream, holding one imperious finger in the air, revelling in his athletic genius. But this victory over 5,000m at the inaugural Ultimate Championships carried extra sweetness – and spice.The sweetness? That came from winning a mammoth first prize of $150,000 after an achilles injury he feared might derail his career. And the spice? Well, that was provided by the way Ingebrigtsen utterly obliterated his great American rival Cole Hocker, a man he had branded a “coward” just a week ago.Brave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and fieldRead moreIngebrigtsen has never been shy of venturing an opinion, and he was aggrieved when Hocker insisted on having his own pacemaker for the 1500m Diamond League final – and then refused to follow him. That led to a high-profile war of words, and a rematch that was the talk of Budapest.And, my, did it live up to the hype. The pace was quick, but the Norwegian was so confident he had time to look around twice on the final lap before launching a devastating final kick to win in 12min 59.24sec, with Hocker, the reigning 5,000m world champion, nearly a second back.“I was predicted number 12 by WorldAthleticscan you imagine?” said a bemused Ingebrigtsen, who is the Olympic champion at this distance after all.Ingebrigtsen was then asked whether it was not only sweet to beat Hocker but … yet before the questioner had finished formulating his sentence, the Norwegian replied “but to crush him” before smiling.His time over the final lap was a rapid 54.39sec, while over the last 100m it was 12.6 – which was particularly impressive given he was only able to step up his comeback from injury in July.“Being injured I was fearing the worst outcome and did not know if I would be able to run at all, especially at this level,” he said. “This is amazing, I am extremely happy.“I had a big hiccup in early May, with the flu, where I was not able to train properly. So I really started training in July but you can’t fake fitness. Fitness is very honest in terms of training. The guy that puts in the best amount of work for the longest period of time is usually the best runner.“But I’ve gained quite a lot from the last couple of races that I’ve done. I felt stronger, stronger, smoother, smoother, and that gave me a lot of hope.”Ingebrigtsen, though, was non-committal over whether he will race in Sunday’s 1500m against Josh Kerr. “I’ve been drinking a lot of coffee until now, so get a good night’s sleep and see how I feel tomorrow.”There was British success too on the first night of the Ultimate Championships with Jazmin Sawyers coming second to the Italian Larissa Iapichino in the women’s jump with a final leap of 6.78m. That capped a fine season for Sawyers, who also won Commonwealth gold and European silver, and it also made her $75,000 (£55,000) richer.“It’s an incredible amount of money,” admitted Sawyers. “Prize money like this just means a big sigh of relief … I will buy something – I’m going to upgrade my sewing machine.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was also a bronze for the British 4x100m mixed relay team behind the USA and Jamaica, much to the delight of Success Eduan, who anchored the British team.At some point next week, Eduan will deliver the four babies she requires to complete her BSc in midwifery. But she said that her share of the $25,000 prize – around £4,730 – would help her start paying off her student debts.View image in fullscreenJazmin Sawyers’ season of success continued.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA“I’m finishing hopefully next week,” she said. “I still have one more placement. I’ve got four more left to deliver, I arrive in Manchester on Monday afternoon, and I have a Monday night shift that day. Three nights, so I finish on Thursday morning.”There are still two days left at these Ultimate Championships, but this was an encouraging start. It was faster paced than the recent European championships. It also looked the part with a black infield and bright lights. There were plenty of impressive performances too, with Mondo Duplantis’s 6.25m leap to win the pole vault one of the standouts.Keely Hodgkinson also made an impressive return in his first run back to win her semi-final in 1:57.57 before delivering her trademark clap. She will face her two main rivals Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol in Saturday’s final.On the downside, it was cold. Cold enough, in fact, that the Ukrainian high jumper Yaroslava Mahuchikh wore sleeping bags between her jumps. Not that it unduly bothered her as she took victory in 1.99m.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Solheim Cup: USA fightback sparks hope of away win after Europe’s fast start | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: After a morning session that ended 2-2 in the Solheim Cup, USA clawed Europe back to 4-4 after sinking early on in the fourballs
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: After a morning session that ended 2-2 in the Solheim Cup, USA clawed Europe back to 4-4 after sinking early on in the fourballs
Content: Carlota Ciganda gives it the celebration her all after holing a putt on the 18th to earn a half point for Europe.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenCarlota Ciganda gives it the celebration her all after holing a putt on the 18th to earn a half point for Europe.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APSolheim CupSolheim Cup: USA fightback sparks hope of away win after Europe’s fast startScores level at 4-4 after day oneEurope fail to make advantage pay in fourballsEwan Murrayat Bernardus GolfFri 11 Sep 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rain poured and the United States roared. Hope had cascaded through the European contingent at thisSolheim Cupduring Friday afternoon until the sort of fightback that endorsed the sense that, come Sunday evening, the US will have won this trophy in a foreign land for the first time since 2015. This compelling day concluded with the scores level at 4-4. For Europe, it had promised to be so much better.Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe 4-4 USA after day one drama in fourballs – as it happenedRead moreAfter a morning session that closed all square at 2-2, Europe surged ahead in three fourball matches. This felt like validation for Anna Nordqvist, the home captain. She had opted not to deploy any of the four players who returned two foursomes points – Maja Stark, Linn Grant, Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit – after lunch.Heads turned, especially in respect of Maguire. She was controversially lightly raced as Europe lost in the 2024 Solheim Cup. Victory for Maguire and Henseleit over Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan meant the Irishwoman became statistically the most successful European Solheim Cup player of all time. Maguire had cause to wonder why she was left on the sidelines; especially as Céline Boutier and Nanna Koerstz Madsen, who visibly toiled in the foursomes, slumped to a second defeat out of two. Megan Khang and Alison Lee cantered to a 5&3 fourball success in the one straightforward clash of the afternoon.As the heavens opened and competitors turned for home, the US discovered pulses elsewhere. Blue started to be wiped from scoreboards. The sun was out again by the time Yealimi Noh produced the shot of the day, from a fairway bunker on the 17th. Noh could not even see the green from the sand trap yet played a glorious iron to five feet. As Noh converted from there, a three-up lead for Charley Hull and Lottie Woad after 11 holes had been cancelled out. Noh had made birdie at four holes from a run of six.On the final green, Noh stood over a putt to complete the turnaround and win the match. Woad had been visibly distracted by music coming from the spectator village while over her attempt at a three. Noh, in fairness, had the same backdrop. The American’s attempt was tame yet a halved match represented a blow to Europe given early dominance. Noh’s partner Angel Yin was in floods of tears afterwards; her Solheim Cup involvement had been in serious doubt due to illness.View image in fullscreenUSA’s Nelly Korda (left) and Lauren Coughlin beat Charley Hull and Lottie Woad 4&3.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APCarlota Ciganda and Julia López Ramírez were two holes to the good over Nelly Korda and Lauren Coughlin at the turn. Korda looked horrendously out of sorts. By the 16th tee, the US were one up. Europe won that hole in what suddenly looked such a crucial match. Mind games applied on the 17th, where Europe opted not to concede either one of two tap‑in American putts for a half. López found sand at the last, with Ciganda even more wayward. Ciganda struck lucky not only there but with a wild second. And still, she rescued half a point with the day’s last act. Korda and company were rightly irked.Europe’s star turns in the afternoon were debutants. Chemistry was obvious between Mimi Rhodes and the huge-hitting Nastasia Nadaud, who closed out their success over Allisen Corpuz and Auston Kim on the penultimate green.Hull and Woad were comfortably beaten by Korda and Corpuz in the morning. Alison Lee and Coughlin took match two over Boutier and Koerstz Madsen. Henseleit and Maguire defeated Andrea Lee and Duncan for Europe’s first point of the event. Stark and Grant ended the morning session by swatting aside Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.The Solheim Cup involves a more sedate backdrop than its male equivalent and is all the better for that. The last Ryder Cup staging at Bethpage regressed into a moronic mess. In this rural corner of the Netherlands, nobody missed the yobbish element.Nordqvist revealed team Europe had sought out a group of colourfully dressed fans who typically appear front and centre at Ryder Cups. The self-proclaimed “guardians of the cup” were invited to the Netherlands but, according to a Solheim Cup official, still had to pay for their tickets.“I don’t think I’ve ever seen as many European supporters,” said Nordqvist. “I know it’s just so amazing to play in an atmosphere like that. We have recruited the team from the Ryder Cup and they have been teaching everyone all these amazing songs. So it has been really cool to be on the first tee today.”Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Benn and Garcia turn past scandals into a $30m Las Vegas world title payday | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Fight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championship
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Fight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championship
Content: Ryan Garcia (left) and Conor Benn fight for the WBC welterweight world championship on Saturday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Ian Maule/APView image in fullscreenRyan Garcia (left) and Conor Benn fight for the WBC welterweight world championship on Saturday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Ian Maule/APBoxingBenn and Garcia turn past scandals into a $30m Las Vegas world title paydayFight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championshipBryan Armen GrahamFri 11 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour years ago Conor Benn’s career was thrown into limbo after two positive drug tests scuppered his blockbuster fight with Chris Eubank Jr. Two years ago Ryan Garcia was serving a one-year suspension after testing positive for ostarine at the time of his greatest victory.On Saturday night they will each be rewarded with an eight-figure payday when they meet at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas for Garcia’s WBC welterweight championship. The purses have not been disclosed, although reports have put the combined pot at around $30m (£22m) with each fighter expected to haul in roughly $15m.Their routes to one of boxing’s biggest stages on Mexican Independence Day weekend have been different, as were the cases against them and their eventual outcomes. Both men insist they are not drug cheats, with Bennhaving ultimately been clearedby the National Anti-Doping Panel. But their collision course offers a striking reminder of a sport in which scandal can derail a career without necessarily compromising the value of the fighter involved in it.Garcia (25-2, 20 KOs), the 28-year-old from Victorville, California, one of boxing’s first Gen-Z superstars, tested positive for the performance-enhancing anabolic agent ostarineon the day beforeand theday afterhis surprise win over Devin Haney in April 2024. His majority-decision victory wasoverturned to a no-contest, he was suspended for a year and his team blamed contaminated supplements.Benn (25-1, 14 KOs) went through a longer and considerably more complicated ordeal. Two positive tests for the female fertility drug clomifene, a banned substance that can boost testosterone by 50%, emerged before the Londoner’s proposed fight with Eubank in October 2022, launching a regulatory battle that prevented him from fighting in Britain for two years. Benn maintained his innocence throughout.Three years later, here they are. Garcia will make the first defense of the WBC title he won by dropping and outpointing Mario Barrios in February. For the 29-year-old Benn, it is a first world title shot and a chance to follow in the footsteps of his father, Nigel, who captured the WBC super-middleweight title more than three decades ago.View image in fullscreenConor Benn’s most recent fight was at a 150lb limit in April rather than the 147lb welterweight limit he has to make now.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAThat Saturday’s fight was made at all speaks volumes about professional boxing’s peculiar moral ecosystem, where there is no single governing authority, universal anti-doping system or commissioner capable of imposing consistent sanctions across jurisdictions. Much of the power instead rests with promoters, broadcasters and sanctioning bodies whose financial interests are rarely served by keeping valuable fighters out of the ring.Dismissed by critics for his good looks, luxury-brand endorsements and huge social-media reach – upwards of 13.1m Instagram followers with 9m more on TikTok – Garcia has amassed a massive following while oscillating between elite performances and episodes of extraordinary self-sabotage. His return from suspension brought an immediate world title shot – and a flatunanimous-decision loss to Rolando Romeroin May 2025 – only for him to rebound against Barrios nine months later and win his first recognized world championship.Benn’s journey has been different but hardly quieter. After eventually returning to fight in Britain, he lost to Eubank in April 2025before avenging the defeatseven months later. Those fights restored his commercial momentum but did considerably less to establish him as a leading welterweight challenger.Benn has not fought at the division’s 147lb limit for four‑and‑a‑half years, having recently campaigned at middleweight before coming down to 150lb to face Regis Prograis in April. Getting back down to welterweight may be the biggest gamble of all. “People say: ‘Oh, you can’t go up to this weight and then go back down.’ All right, cool. Well, just watch me do it,” Benn said at Thursday’s final press conference. “Discipline prevails, and I will make the weight.”Garcia remains skeptical, suggesting the effects of the cut could leave Benn vulnerable once the punches start landing. “Even if he makes the weight, your brain can’t rehydrate fast enough,” Garcia said. “Them punches going to do some real damage.”There is, beneath all the uncomfortable baggage, an intriguing fight between two men who certainly talk a good game. Garcia expects Benn to come forward and “try to resort to some dirty tactics”. Benn’s description of his approach sounded remarkably similar: “Tenacity, ferocity, spite, experience. I’m here to come and really set the tone from the first round.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTherein lies the danger for the challenger. Garcia is the more naturally gifted boxer, with exceptional hand speed and a vicious left hook that is most dangerous against opponents coming forward. Benn’s best route to victory may require him to walk directly toward Garcia’s best weapon.Garcia has shown he can be vulnerable when forced backwards, but Benn does not possess the timing or precision of Gervonta Davis, who handed Garcia his first professional setback with awithering seventh-round body shot in 2023. Benn, meanwhile, insists that virtually every apparent disadvantage works in his favor because it leaves Garcia carrying the expectations.View image in fullscreenRyan Garcia has argued this week that Conor Benn is not in the title fight on merit but because of his famous boxing father.Photograph: Ringo HW Chiu/AP“The pressure’s on Ryan completely,” Benn said. “No one’s given me a chance in this fight. Twenty amateur fights, just not made 147 for four-and-a-half years, the weight problem, the this, the that. No one’s given me a chance.”There is also something more personal at stake for Benn, who has spent years carrying the advantages and burdens of his surname, including Garcia’s repeated contention this week that he would never have reached this position without it. There is a certain irony in Garcia attacking Benn as a nepo baby: Garcia has been a child of boxing privilege in his own right, enjoying nearly every advantage the industry can confer, never more than during his microwaved redemption. “It’s just a blessing to be in this position, to be headlining in Vegas, to be fighting on a mega show and put the Benn name back up in bright lights,” Benn said.For all the talk of legacy, Saturday also offers a revealing snapshot of boxing in 2026. Two men once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests will instead fight for a world championship and another handsome payday. Few sports are better at turning yesterday’s scandal into tomorrow’s main event.Explore more on these topicsBoxingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Welcome to the Madring, a new, brutal and unforgiving F1 challenge for Spanish Grand Prix | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: New hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunities
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: New hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunities
Content: Spectators watch on opposite La Monumental corner at the Madring circuit.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenSpectators watch on opposite La Monumental corner at the Madring circuit.Photograph: David Davies/PAFormula One 2026Welcome to the Madring, a new, brutal and unforgiving F1 challenge for Spanish Grand PrixNew hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunitiesGiles Richardsat the MadringFri 11 Sep 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Madrid’s Puerta del Sol this week,Formula Onefans were not shy in calling on the gods to look kindly on their favoured drivers on a newly built circuit that appears punishingly unforgiving.Legend has it that rubbing the paws or backside of the bear in the famous El Oso y el Madroño statue at the square’s heart confers good luck. The drivers may well need it. Day one of action at the Madring track began with F2’s Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak careening into the barriers and his car catching fire, leaving the onlookingGeorge Russellshocked before the F1 drivers took to the wheel.View image in fullscreenThe Art Racing car of Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak is removed on a lorry.Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty ImagesDespite fears the Madring would not be ready, it is done and dusted. What sort of racing it will present for the Spanish Grand Prix is now the question.
