Billed as a street circuit, it is in fact a hybrid of roads and purpose-built track; narrow, with fast corners and walls looming for much of the lap, there is going to be virtually no margin for error.Hamilton confirms no rules of engagement at Ferrari despite Monza clash with LeclercRead moreThis was demonstrated in F2 practice on Friday. Russell, who had previously described the Madring as the “most risky” on the calendar was watching F2 practice with some members of the media in the Mercedes motorhome when the Art Grand Prix driver’s crash happened.“Oh wow,” he said. “This circuit is mental.” Inthraphuvasak, who leapt out in short order after his car burst into flames, had crashed rearward at high speed into the barriers after spinning at turn 19, and Russell observed the Madring was set to be an even sterner test than Monaco.“I would put this as a circuit that has less margin, purely because of the speed,” he said. “In Monaco the walls are closer but because you’re going slower – if you make a mistake you’re not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes. It’s more lock-up. Here, there’s less margin.”The issue, explained Russell, was that the fast corners were combined with the angles of the barriers on exit. “You see at this barrier, it’s kind of like coming back on to the track,” he said, indicating where the smoking wreckage of Inthraphuvasak’s car was sitting. “So if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you’re not hitting it at the same angle as the car is going. The car is going towards the wall but the wall is sort of coming in.”When F3 held a test here recently, there were 19 red flags and three cars suffered broken chassis. “They’re Formula 3 drivers, but it’s a track that kills cars,” was the assessment of Williams’ team principal, James Vowles. Russell said he was surprised it was only 19 red flags.View image in fullscreenMercedes driver George Russell during free practice.Photograph: David Davies/PAHe was not alone in his concern, with Lewis Hamilton echoing his sentiments. “It’s a massively challenging circuit,” he said. “Of all the new tracks I’ve gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines.”There was at least cause for optimism after first practice with the hour-long session proceeding without a stoppage and the walls receiving only some delicate glances at best. The drivers were up to speed with alacrity and no little composure, with Russell topping the timesheets for Mercedes, from his teammate, Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 66 points in the world championship. In the second session, however, Britain’s Arvid Lindblad came a cropper, losing the rear of his Racing Bulls car in turn 13 and slewing sideways into the barriers in another heavy impact, but from which he emerged unhurt. The session was halted by a red flag but resumed, and completed with Antonelli on top from Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Hamilton.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCertainly the sense of spectacle was delivered, as was surely the aim, with high speeds on a narrow track flanked by walls, and illustrated in its signature corner La Monumental, a 550m stretch of 13.5-degree banking, through which the cars are accelerating to great effect, compressing into the track amid an amphitheatre of grandstands before heading over a blind crest and barrelling downwards out of the corner. There is even a little history here too, with turn eight – “El Bunker” – named forLa Mata Espesa, two bunkers built in 1936 by the Republican forces to protect Madrid from attack during the Spanish civil war. Their preservation was a condition of the track being built.The circuit lacks the backdrop of Monaco of course, flanked only by the large, grey square boxes so beloved of convention centres situated in industrial estates. Some areas are still somewhat building site-esque too, but the bits that matter are in place and for the fans it is but a 20-minute subway ride from the city. Indeed, it is an achievement that might be considered no little feat given there were objections to it happening at all, relating to costs, the construction and complaints about sound levels exceeding legal levels.View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell (centre) cycles round the Madring as teams and drivers get accustomed to the new circuit.Photograph: David Davies/PAThe circuit, which sits around the Institución Ferial de Madrid convention centre area between the city centre and the airport, is perhaps exactly what F1 had in mind with its pursuit of “destination races” in cities. This means events that would be entertainment weekends, to rival the Superbowl and draw fans and finance to the host city. But it also faces a further acid test to come. There remains concern, though, as to quite what sort of racing will be possible come Sunday. The drivers were largely in agreement that it would be a thrilling technical challenge of inch-perfect execution, but equally sceptical about whether overtaking would be possible. As the four-time world champion Max Verstappen noted, the main braking zones such as turns five, eight and 17 are angled, making passing all but impossible with drivers simply putting their car in the middle of the track.“You can’t really go for an overtake because you’re braking but you’re steering either right or left, which is the worst thing you can do for creating an overtaking opportunity,” he said. This will put huge emphasis on qualifying but also raises the spectre of a procession on Sunday, potentially only interrupted by what many still consider will be inevitable red-flag stoppages. A long, hot train of cars circling in unchanging order is certainly not the hoped-for debut at F1’s newest circuit and a threat for which the promoters might too be hoping for some ursine intervention.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneGeorge RussellMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Osama bin Laden shook the world on 9/11. Today it is clear how his wider plans failed | Jason Burke | The Guardian
description: The al-Qaida leader envisaged an economically battered US withdrawing from the Middle East – and a global Muslim uprising. Then the tide turned, says Jason Burke, the Guardian’s international security correspondent
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: The al-Qaida leader envisaged an economically battered US withdrawing from the Middle East – and a global Muslim uprising. Then the tide turned, says Jason Burke, the Guardian’s international security correspondent
Content: An anti-US rally in Islamabad, Pakistan, 28 September 2001.Photograph: Saeed Khan/EPAView image in fullscreenAn anti-US rally in Islamabad, Pakistan, 28 September 2001.Photograph: Saeed Khan/EPAOpinionSeptember 11 2001Osama bin Laden shook the world on 9/11. Today it is clear how his wider plans failedJason BurkeThe al-Qaida leader envisaged an economically battered US withdrawing from the Middle East – and a global Muslim uprising. Then the tide turnedFri 11 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.40 EDTShareOn 11 September, 25 years ago,Osama bin Ladendrove with a small number of al-Qaida retainers and aides to a remote location in eastern Afghanistan. His convoy of SUVs was accompanied by a minivan converted into a makeshift communications centre.The van’s rudimentary equipment did not allow Bin Laden to watch the 19 men he had started sending to the US more than a year before fly planes into the twin towers in New York and the Pentagon near Washington DC, killing about 3,000 people. But he listened as shocked radio announcers broke the news.Within days of the murderous assault, the then president, George W Bush, hadbegun framing the US responseas a global “war on terror”, a clumsy, inappropriate and counterproductive strategic choice.For those of us reporting on the ground during this period – watching US bombers over Afghan mountains andtanks in Baghdad streets, interviewing aspirant suicide bombers or the victims of attacks by extremist groups that proliferated from the UK to the Philippines – the errors and failures of this “war on terror” were glaring.13:36How 9/11 changed the world - The LatestThis unprecedented and indiscriminate series of campaigns would lead to invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, involve torture,renditionsand alliances with dubious regimes, cost huge amounts of money, destabilise swathes of the Middle East and bring suffering to millions of people.Was this what Bin Laden had hoped to achieve?It is frequently suggested that Bin Laden’s aim with the 9/11 attacks was to draw the US into wars that would weaken its economy and lead to its eventual collapse, much as the Soviet Union had been fatally drained by the war inAfghanistanbetween 1979 and 1989. As a young militant, Bin Laden had witnessed this conflict and even participated in it, albeit in a marginal role.Butthere is little evidence to back this theory up. Though Bin Laden was undoubtedly inspired by the earlier conflict, he rejected as unrealistic his aides’ warnings that the planned attack would bring US troops to Afghanistan, probably expecting little more than another barrage of ineffective missiles by way of reprisal. Certainly, he had no plan when the US troops did come. Within months of the attacks, shaken al-Qaida members described “misfortune [and] disaster”.View image in fullscreenOsama bin Laden in Afghanistan in 1998, three years before the 9/11 attacks.Photograph: Associated PressIn reality, Bin Laden had a different strategy. He wanted to weaken the US economically and consequently force a withdrawal from the Middle East, not an invasion. In 2004,he boasted thatal-Qaida was “bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy”, and that every dollar the group spent attacking the US had cost Washington a million dollars in economic fallout and military spending. This lecture in the advantages of asymmetric warfare resonates today, but was wildly optimistic.The most costly single event to the US would have been another successful major attack. This never came – an unarguable success of US policymaking since 9/11 and a major failure for al-Qaida. And despite the obvious economic problems in the US, no one could argue that the country has suffered a similar fate to the USSR. Nor, obviously, has it withdrawn its forces from the Middle East.A second objective of Bin Laden was to force the US to end its support for all the rulers in the region that the once-privileged, Saudi-born dissident so hated, starting with the al-Saud family.Some of Bin Laden’s targets have been felled since 2001, but not by his actions or by anyone aligned with his vision. Muammar Gaddafi wasdeposed and killedby western-backed rebels, Saddam Hussein was ousted by the US, and the Assad dynasty’s rule wasended by an al-Qaida veteranwho explicitly disavowed the group’s ideology and agenda.A third aim of Bin Laden was propaganda. His theatre of terror was designed to send a bloody, spectacular and unforgettable message that would radicalise his followers, mobilise new ones and divide communities.He emphasisedhow attacks such as 9/11 were “just reactions to what’s happening against our children in Palestine, in Iraq, in Somalia, in southern Sudan, in Kashmir”, and called for a global uprising of Muslims against their enemies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJoe Biden, Barack Obama, Hillary Clinton and members of the national security team receive an update on the mission against Osama bin Laden in the Situation Room of the White House, 1 May 2011.Photograph: The White House/Getty ImagesWhile the 9/11 attacks undoubtedly focused international attention on the conflicts in which Bin Laden saw Muslims as oppressed by the west or its allies, it brought no significant improvement for the victims. The wave of support for Bin Laden and broader interest in extremist Islamism peaked only a few years after 2001, and then quickly ebbed more or less everywhere. Shortly before he was killed by US Navy Seals in Pakistan, Bin Laden wascontemplating a rebrand of al-Qaida, its name tarnished by growing criticism within the Islamic world that it was responsible for killing large numbers of Muslims. His successor, the Egyptian Ayman al-Zawahiri, gave up on the uprising altogether, pivoting to a strategy prioritising the local over the global.If in 2014, inIraqand Syria, the Islamic State was able to capitalise on the chaos left by the US invasion, sectarian tension and much else to establish its appalling caliphate, even this was over by 2019.Since then, such groups’ brand of extremism has been confined in large part to the periphery of the Islamic world, and to zones from which the threat to the developed world is intermittent at best.Al-Qaidaand the Islamic State have expanded most effectively in sub-Saharan Africa, exploiting anarchy, failed states, demographic pressures, communal competition for scarce resources and the inattention of the west.Some analysts add together the presumed strength of groups in Somalia or Mali that have very loose, historic links to al-Qaida, and warn that their total membership is higher than those loyal to Bin Laden in 2001. But these few thousand young men with AK-47s have little in common with the organisation Bin Laden led 25 years ago, both in aims and capabilities.There are still appalling attacks inspired by Bin Laden’s twisted ideology, and there will undoubtedly be more. This is in part due to the polarisation brought about by his violence and the reaction to it – as was his aim.But it is noteworthy that neither al-Qaida nor IS have prominent charismatic leaders. One reason is that any such figure will be swiftly killed by the vastly more capable US, making identification risky. But it is also because the era when such individuals could command a significant following is over.It is often said that for an insurgent or terrorist group to win, it merely needs to survive, but there are exceptions. That al-Qaida still exists is an achievement of sorts for the group and, posthumously, for its founder. But it should not be described as any victory.Jason Burke is the Guardian’s international security correspondent and the author ofThe Revolutionists: The Story of the Extremists who Hijacked the 1970sExplore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001OpinionOsama bin LadenAl-QaidaAfghanistanIraqcommentShareReuse this content

title: Memo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the script  | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: If the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world works, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: If the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world works, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex,  during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, 17 April  2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/APView image in fullscreenHarry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex,  during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, 17 April  2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/APOpinionPrince HarryMemo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the scriptMarina HydeIf the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world worksFri 11 Sep 2026 08.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTShareOnce again, it has been a lively week for the Real Housewives of Windsor franchise, with Harry and Meghan back in the UK for precisely 12 days before the kingfired out a lettervia the lord chamberlain on Monday, reminding viewers that the Sussexes are “private citizens” and not to treat them as working royals. You have to say the producers on this unscripted reality show are truly at the top of their game with these targeted provocations. Harry and Meghan duly took the bait and issued an intemperately hurt rejoinder – but we’ll get to that in a bit.First, let’s deal with King Charles’s missive to “relevant senior stakeholders across government, the military and Lord Lieutenancies”. Ugh. Not to be too aesthetically sensitive, but I think we can all live without the sovereign being reduced to the ghastly language of “relevant senior stakeholders”. What next? Seeking “buy-in” for ribbon-cutting events and referring to posies as “high levels of audience engagement”? It does all rather reinforce the idea that the Windsors’ cringe-makingly self-styled “the firm” really is some dreary mid-range company with a wan Meet Our Team page on its website, in which Prince William – carefully photographed without a tie – explains that he “enjoys long walks with the dog and is a passionate Aston Villa supporter”.Either way, the letter sent on Charles’s behalf was guaranteed to send the plot into overdrive, much as it does in any Real Housewives franchise when one of the cast sends a cease-and-desist letter to one of the others. (An event that basically feels like it can occur weekly.) Typically these letters then become dramatic drivers. Far from suppressing stories as supposedly intended, they always end up sparking whole new public debates and plotlines in themselves. This is what happened with the Windsors this week – and, indeed, was always going to happen, given the appearance of a pre-emptive slapdown.The royal household must be able to see that the key thing about the Sussexes is that they are forever desperate to be taken seriously, like a music act that was put together on a TV talent show but now wants you to think they’re up there with Patti Smith and Nick Cave.And so it was that Meghan and Harry’s spokespersonimmediately hit backin public, announcing that the couple “were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance”. Ouch. Never show weakness, guys! A briefinggiven to the Telegraphadded that: “The Sussexes prefer the term ‘public figures’, and would have liked an acknowledgment that, on a personal level, they remained members of the royal family, despite no longer receiving public funding.”As indicated, this all hints at a season of endlessly messy dramas to come, given it took less than a fortnight of the pair being back in the country before a public blow-up occurred. In terms of the kind of bizarro unintended consequences you might see on a Housewives episode when someone’s kicked off at a girls’ spa day, the military chief of Ugandapromptly announcedhis country was pulling out of Prince Harry’s Invictus Games because they didn’t want to participate in something “that does not have His Majesty’s approval”. What can you say? Other than: deploy the reaction gifs.You don’t have to be a reality TV obsessive to spot the faultlines here that should guarantee that the Sussexes’ unexpected return to the UK will result in endless drink tosses. It’s all there in their immediate reaction. Harry and Meghan are really wholly formed reality TV stars now. Not only do they do the tit-for-tat media release to move the plot along, but they also let you know what they were feeling when they read the original press-released letter from the king. In reality TV, moments like these are gleaned from “master interviews” (MIVs), filmed at the end of a season to provide useful retrospective commentary that the producers can cut the main action with. So you’ll see Hell’s Kitchen contestants helpfully reflecting on the scene you’ve just watched, and going: “And I’m standing there thinking – Chef Ramsay is going to go crazy when he sees this.” Or, in this case, “I was a little surprised not to have been told by Chef Ramsay about this in advance.”This is precisely how the Sussexes now conduct public life, and it remains incompatible with the way the royal household does it. For all their supposed desire for a quiet life, Harry and Meghan have done that thing that the Beckhams – and indeed the secessionist Beckham-Peltzes – seemingly cannot help but do, where they claim to enjoy privacy but in fact live life out loud in a way that has come to feel normal to them but is really anything but.Which brings us back to the burning question of why on earth you’d move back somewhere you are on the record – multiple times – as absolutely loathing in all its aspects. Increasingly, and faster than predicted, it feels like the answer to that is “for content” – scripted or otherwise. It’s fairly difficult to see the Sussexes’ relocation as anything other than laying the groundwork for a sequel to the only story of theirs that has ever rated with audiences: their own struggle with the forces of the British establishment/media/enemies within the royal household. Or as Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star Lisa Rinna once put it – and her head would be right up there on the franchise’s Mount Rushmore – “you better believe I’m gonna talk about it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber, £20). To support the Guardian, order your signed copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryOpinionKing Charles IIIMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMonarchyReality TVcommentShareReuse this content

title: Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriously | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Content: ‘AI agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life.’Photograph: MattLphotography/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘AI agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life.’Photograph: MattLphotography/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriouslyGaby HinsliffAI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too lateFri 11 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTShareAnother day, another horseman of the apocalypse galloping over the horizon. Lately we have heard from so many AI doomers – tech whistleblowers popping up to warn that their work isprobably going to kill us– that we’re becoming almost blase about it. Humanity wiped out within a decade? Well, only if another world war or the climate crisis doesn’t get us first. Since it’s never clear whether the tech threat is real, or just a twisted form of hype from an industry that drums up investment by making their products sound more powerful than they really are, most of us settle for trying not to think about it too hard.But something about the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’svery public resignationfrom the cutting-edge American lab Anthropic, via a post on X arguing that he can’t keep working for companies “gambling with our lives”, has cut through where bigger names have not. Most chillingly, he claimed that colleagues still at Anthropic aren’t staying because they think he’s wrong about the dangers of pursuing self-improving super intelligence – the holy grail of machines that are not just smarter than humans but capable of building their own even more powerful successors, evolving independently of humans – but because they’re afraid of ceding the field to people with fewer scruples. His colleagues, Coxon said, talk routinely about the “endgame” or the “crunch time”, meaning that what they do in the next year or two will decide the fate of humanity. Whether that’s true or simply self-aggrandising techbro delusion, what he describes is an industry now practically begging to be saved from itself.Thefrisson of alarmover AI running through Westminster this week was real, sharpened by news of Anthropic – which pitches itself as being more safety-conscious than its rivals OpenAI – declining for the first time to submita new model for scrutiny by Britain’s AIsafety watchdog. We are now entering a far more disruptive era of AI, dominated not by relatively basic chatbots but by agents designed to undertake tasks on humans’ behalf, making their own decisions about how to complete them. Unfortunately, it turns out even basic life admin requires the kind of fine judgments that come instinctively to humans but seem remarkably hard to codify for machines.Take the over-zealous agent tasked recently by its Australian client with bookinghim into a pilates class, which responded to finding the class full byhacking the gym’s websiteand booting other people off the waiting list.Now imagine it blundering into something more life-threatening than a gym class. WhenCoxon says his industry hasn’t fixed problems with alignment, and when OpenAI’s chief scientistwarned last weekthat no lab had solved them well enough to carry on scaling this fast much longer, what they’re talking about is this failure to replicate in machines the values and assumptions humans apply to decisions without even really knowing they’re doing it – including the sense of how far it’s justifiable to go in getting what you want.A series of reportedescapes by agentssupposedly confined to OpenAI’s lab for testing, some of which contrived to access the internet behind their human supervisors’ backs and conduct real-world cyber-attacks, has meanwhile raised serious questions over the industry’s ability even to experiment safely. (Unnervingly, Coxon says newer models seem to know when they’re being tested, making it easier for them to deceive researchers.)And agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life: think how easily a cyber-attack on air traffic control, or NHS data systems, or even water purification systems could cause mass fatalities.What’s happening in some frontier AI labs now is arguably the equivalent of the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb, but this time led by private companies in a mad dash for wealth and market dominance, not scientists under an elected government’s command. Britons meanwhile got more say in sugar taxes on junk food than we’re getting over regulating something theoretically capable of rendering us extinct.Given time, of course, it might prove possible to replicate in machines the vast ecosystem of social ties, moral codes, intensive parenting and state policing that humans have developed to stop us behaving like sociopaths. (Only this week, Google’sDeepMindreported an experiment where 100 agents were given a maths problem and told not to cheat: though a minority promptly did cheat, a larger group either snitched on them to the humans or helped devise technical fixes.) But time is the one thing nobody dares to give themselves in the middle of an arms race, which is why it’s high time for governments to act. We need an international agreement topress pause, not on AI research as a whole, but on the riskiest projects, until we better understand whether it will ever be possible to mitigate the dangers or control the results. Since it’s hard to imagine Donald Trump voluntarily sacrificing US geopolitical or commercial advantage over China for the good of humanity, leadership may have to come for now not from above but below, where industry insiders spooked by their own work are making common cause with the rest of us.More Americans are nowconcerned than excitedabout AI, according to polling this summer from the Pew Research Center – and unusually it’s the young who are most hostile, afraid it will not only take their jobs but make it harder to form relationships or think creatively. (That’s what growing up on social media seemingly does for trust in tech.) Even big business seems increasingly sceptical, with almost two-thirds of international executives surveyed by the consultantsMcKinseythis summer reportingno measurable impact on earningsfrom using the admittedly basic AI tools now available to them.Warnings about an AI bubble triggering another 2008-style globalfinancial crashhaven’t helped, while plans to build giant, energy-guzzling datacentres are meetingangry local resistanceon both sides of the Atlantic from people who can’t see what’s in it for them. Pressing pause on potential Armageddon looks in the circumstances less like the luddite option, and more like a smart way for tech companies to avoid a full-on backlash that will sweep away the good with the bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut if the AI doomers are right, then the window to do so may not always be open. It’s time for humans to stop and think about what we’re doing to ourselves – while we alone still have the power to do so.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingTechnology policyEthicsAnthropicOpenAIcommentShareReuse this content

title: In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for elsewhere?  | Ahdaf Soueif | The Guardian
description: For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all, says author Ahdaf Soueif
Author: Ahdaf Soueif
Headline: For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all, says author Ahdaf Soueif
Content: Israeli rightwing activists overlooking Gaza during a rally calling for the re-establishment of Israeli settlements in Gaza, 30 July 2025.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APView image in fullscreenIsraeli rightwing activists overlooking Gaza during a rally calling for the re-establishment of Israeli settlements in Gaza, 30 July 2025.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APOpinionIsraelIn Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for elsewhere?Ahdaf SoueifFor now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us allFri 11 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.58 EDTShareLast week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put outan AI-generated videothat showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building anexecution sitefor Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel andtaunted female prisonerswho complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning tointroduce crocodilesto patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while thelaw that he championedmandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks isbuilt on public support.Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand itsillegal settlements in theWest Bank.It had been a widely held tenet that if enough people in the democratic western world knew the reality of whatIsraelwas doing to the Palestinians, they would pressure their governments, and Israel would be made to observe the norms of international law. Eventually, a reality would be born in which Jews, Muslims and Christians would live as equals within some political system that would be as good – and as flawed – as others. South Africa was always cited as the example, where rising international pressure over the decades was decisive.But what looked like the winning of the moral, rational argument was offset by an acceleration of the processes of occupation, an increase in the frequency and blatancy of settler attacks in the West Bank, and of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) attacks on Gaza. The past three years have been the logical development of this. In the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 attacks, Israel escalated its killing, maiming and displacement of the Palestinians to the level ofcertifiable genocide. The defence minister, Israel Katz, says he iscommitted to the ethnic cleansingof Gaza, while a West Bank settlerproudly tellsthe BBC that one Jewish life is worth 10 million Palestinian lives. Social media is awash with Israelis – from pundits on TV news debates to IDF soldiers – stating and performing the outrages necessary to achieve the objective of a Palestinian-free Palestine.Israeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously? | Nesrine MalikRead moreAnd while people across the world now know the truth of what is happening in Palestine and repeatedly and full-heartedly reject it, many democracies across the west continue to send arms and provide intelligence to Israel – even in a time of genocide. The US president’sBoard of Peacemakes a mockery of Palestinians, while hundreds of Israeli trucksclear the rubble from Gaza– and, with it, evidence of war crimes. The US attacks international institutions, such as theinternational criminal court, that seek to offer some semblance of justice for Palestinians. And to repress the constant protests of hundreds of thousands of their citizens, western democracies compromise their justice systems, attack their educational institutions and undermine their own democratic freedoms. Some have belatedly announced sanctions limited to Israeli settlements – illegal settlements that have should have been sanctioned years ago.In 2014, I served on the jury of the Russell Tribunal onPalestine. In the preface to the report, which came after Israel’s third war on Gaza in six years, I wrote: “If not genocide, then genocide is not far behind.”Today I wonder if the genocide is not also a trailer for something more to come.If the genocide was not a surprise, neither is the fact that the old colonial masters have no particular aversion to it. In a line of continuity with their own history, western countries have for decades partnered with Israel on weapons production and intelligence and surveillance technology. The west has sought Israeli advice and training in counter-terrorism, interrogation and civilian population-control techniques. A selling point for Israeli weapons has always beenthat they have been tried and tested.And now, as Israel’s genocide is livestreamed, the establishment watches, enables, protects and helps tidy up. We may be watching a research and development exercise, a blueprint, a template, an example being created. We are already in a world where – it has been argued – some populations are surplus to requirements. Some of them live in areas that are a property developer’s dream.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis war is not only about Palestinians and Israelis, but about ideologies of supremacy and domination that threaten the people of the world, its civil societies and what is left of its international organisations. For the moment, it is the Palestinians who are on the frontline, the Palestinians who are being killed and maimed and tortured and displaced. But the Palestinians are also standing between all of us and a world remade in Israel’s image.Ahdaf Soueif is the author of Mezzaterra: Fragments from the Common GroundDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: George W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessness | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: The reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violence
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: The reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violence
Content: ‘Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side.’Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side.’Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesOpinionGuantánamo BayGeorge W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessnessKenneth RothThe reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violenceFri 11 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareIf George W Bush’s abusive response to the September 11 attacks had been prosecuted rather than swept under the rug,Donald Trumpwould be less able to pursue his lawless policies. We can’t rewind history, but we can learn from our historic failure.Twenty-five years ago, on a clear and crisp morning, I was sitting in the Human Rights Watch office in the Empire State Building with an unobstructed view of the World Trade Center towers as al-Qaida operatives flew two commercial jets into them. The horror of the attack required a response, but Bush and his vice-president, Dick Cheney, chose to react by throwing out the rulebook. They deployed torture and endless detention without trial in Guantánamo.At first, Americans were so fearful of another al-Qaida attack that many accepted the Bush administration’s argument that extraordinary measures were required. But as the utter brutality of the response became apparent, dissenting voices grew more pronounced. Yet the reluctance of later administrations to repudiate these measures laid the foundation for Trump’s misconduct.A May 2009meetingI had with Barack Obama epitomized the problem. He had recently assumed office and invited me and several colleagues to the White House to discuss his counter-terrorism program. The meeting wasdisappointing.Trump admin spends billions to deport Black and brown people while doubling dollars for white ‘refugees’ | Heba GowayedRead moreOur top priority was securing prosecution of the senior Bush administration officials who had ordered the systematic torture of terrorist suspects. Obamadeclined, wanting tolookforward, not back. His priority was working with Congress to secure healthcare reform (ultimately the Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare) as well as on issues such as education and climate change. He felt that prosecuting senior Bush officials would be too contentious.Other steps had already been taken to end the torture. Public outrage, hastened by the leaked Abu Ghraibphotographsof US servicemembers mistreating detainees in Iraq, led even the Bush administration to stop. TheDetainee Treatment Actof 2005, sponsored by the senator John McCain, himself a torture victim, closed some of the legal loopholes used by the Bush administration to justify the unjustifiable. But no senior officialwas ever prosecutedfor the torture.That left a legacy of impunity that haunts us. Later presidents have not revived the torture, although the administrations of Joe Biden as well as Trump have continued the flow of military aid to Israel despite itssystematictortureof Palestinian detainees.Yet the deliberate use of excessive force by Trump’s deportation agents suggests confidence in a similar impunity for today’s declared crisis du jour: immigration. The Trump justice department hasclosedits eyes even when immigration officials gratuitouslyshoot, and sometimes kill, people.Bush’s lengthy detention of suspects without trial at Guantánamo has had even greater lethal consequences. Ordinarily, a criminal suspect must be charged and tried within areasonabletime or released. But the Bush administration often had no evidence to justify charges beyond confessions secured by torture. The military commissions designed to allow prosecution despite the torture proved to be travesties that to this day have not evenbegunthe trial of the principal 9/11 suspects.The legal device that the Bush administration used to justify endless detention without trial was to call the suspects “enemy combatants”. Inwar, it is possible to hold opposing combatants without trial until the end of the armed conflict, but there was no armed conflict with al-Qaida, only a series of horrible terrorist attacks.Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side to justify invoking the rules of war. Rather, the rhetoric was a contrivance to sidestep the requirements of criminal prosecution.At the time, Iarguedthat allowing this legal subterfuge could have dangerous consequences. If a declared but fake enemy combatant could be held indefinitely without charge, why could he not also be shot? After all, in war, there is no duty to capture combatants from the other side. So long as they are not in custody, they can be killed.I made the argument in the meeting with Obama as a reason to close Guantánamo – to charge or release all its detainees. I couldn’t imagine that the US government would really start to shoot suspects whom it could detain. But that is what Trump is now doing, not with alleged al-Qaida terrorists but with drug suspects, using a similar theory.Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro | Ken RothRead moreLike Bush, Trump has concocted a war, this time with drug traffickers, even though there is no organized military force on the other side fighting the United States. He then declared suspected traffickers in boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific to be “narcoterrorists”. His aim is to justify summarily killing them by drone rather than capturing and prosecuting them. Trump has taken the Bush theory, modified it for the new enemy, and intensified the consequences.Precursors to thesemurderscan be found in the actions of the Obama and Biden administrations. They summarily killed people in Yemen and north-western Pakistan but at least maintained the pretense, though untenable, that these terrorist suspects posed an imminent threat to the United States because arrest was impossible in the relatively lawless terrain of these distant lands. That is, they invoked anexceptionin policing rules that allows lethal force rather than the fiction that these people were enemy combatants.But that misuse of policing rules isn’t available for the drug suspects whom Trump is targeting because the US Coast Guard has a long tradition of successfullyinterdictingthem at sea. Trump thus relies on his fake war to order them murdered instead.The lesson I take is that when past abuses are glossed over rather than prosecuted, they set precedents that can come back to haunt us. It is never easy to establish the rule of law when the perpetrators are powerful officials. An administration rarely prosecutes itself, and later administrations have their own priorities. Addressing the past is often believed to require too much political capital.But the rule of law is important. It is a value worth upholding even at a price. It is too late to address the Bush-era atrocities, but it is not too late to address Trump’s. He won’t do it, but we should insist that the next administration does. Meanwhile, state and international prosecutors should start now.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsGuantánamo BayOpinionSeptember 11 2001George BushTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS immigrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s time for a Gardeners’ World that reflects Britain’s gardens in all their messy, realistic chaos | Claire Ratinon | The Guardian
description: I’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-up, says organic food grower and writer Claire Ratinon
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: I’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-up, says organic food grower and writer Claire Ratinon
Content: Monty Don in the Paradise Garden at Longmeadow, his space in Herefordshire.Photograph: BBC StudiosView image in fullscreenMonty Don in the Paradise Garden at Longmeadow, his space in Herefordshire.Photograph: BBC StudiosOpinionGardensIt’s time for a Gardeners’ World that reflects Britain’s gardens in all their messy, realistic chaosClaire RatinonI’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-upFri 11 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTShareIt’s finally happened. National treasure Monty Don is hanging up his TV garden shearsand saying goodbyeto Gardeners’ World after more than 20 years as the BBC show’s lead presenter. I’ve been a grower for more than a decade myself, and Monty has been a steady and wise omnipresence throughout my journey – especially as he’s been on the right side of contemporary gardening debates over the environment and wildlife, and the use of chemicals and peat in horticulture.That is where the overlap between our worlds of growing end, though. My modest patch of a few veg beds at the end of a small, chaotic and mostly gravelled garden is a universe away from the two-acre dreamscape that is Longmeadow, Don’s garden at his home in Herefordshire. I suspect I’m one of millions who’ve looked longingly at Monty’s remarkable space and the impressive infrastructure (not to mention hired hands!) that make it so special, and cursed the fact that such an ideal garden will never be within reach of us ordinary folk. That’s not to say that it hasn’t been a glorious setting for Monty to share his abundance of plant wisdom from, but now that the search for his replacement is presumably on, perhaps this is an opportunity for a little reimagining.A handful of times over the years, television production companies have asked whether I’d present a new show they were trying to get commissioned, which they hoped would capture the attention of the next generation of gardeners. Unfortunately, not one of them had an idea that wasn’t just a rehash of a makeover show, and that approach is the antithesis of my growing ethos. I’d want to persuade more gardeners to nurture their plots intentionally – so you wouldn’t catch me encouraging anyone to bring that unhinged (and mostly unsustainable) Changing Rooms-style energy to their outside spaces. As a format that honours the true nature of gardening – embracing the steady process of cultivation and not looking for quick results – Gardeners’ World has got the market cornered, and I hope it keeps going for many years to come.And while I’m notnotsaying the next Gardeners’ World presenter should be me (wink-wink), I do have some thoughts on who it could be. There are clearly potential successors waiting in the wings, all of whom have proved themselves worthy. The favourite appears to be Frances Tophill, who would be my first choice from the shortlist too. But what I’dreallylike to see are dispatches and insights from different gardeners in different regions.View image in fullscreenFrances Tophill, one of the main contenders to take over as the lead presenter of Gardeners’ World.Photograph: BBC StudiosThe UK might not be the largest country, but its weather and climate vary massively. A gardener in Cornwall is going to encounter a very different set of conditions to a gardener in Cumbria. And as we face a future in which the seasons become less predictable, tried-and-tested gardening advice may well become moot. Wouldn’t it be wonderful and highly informative to instead see what is possible – and impossible – in different parts of the country, following a consortium of gardeners and their outdoor spaces throughout the growing season?While I’m dreaming up my perfect show, let’s say that some – perhaps all – of those spaces should be ordinary gardens tended by ordinary gardeners. People who are time-poor, resource-light and chaotic in their execution, due to their many other responsibilities. I’m thinking of it being similar to Top Gear flinging family-friendly hatchbacks around its test track as well as luxury sports cars.This may well be a pipe dream, and perhaps it’s only me who is interested in truly realistic gardens. But I think I’ve reached my personal saturation point with aspirational, unobtainable spaces wholly detached from my own growing reality. There’s so much to be learned from the ingenuity and scrappiness of those who succeed – as well as fail – at creating gardens filled with flourishing crops and blooms, when their space and wallets have limits and their lives are full.The one thing that I wouldn’t want to change, though, is how soothing Gardeners’ World can be. I know I’m not alone in finding the tone and the pace – even the ambient sound of bees buzzing past – to be a balm for the soul, and plenty of that can be attributed to Monty’s gentle screen presence. I’d wager that the upcoming generation of gardeners also have jangled nervous systems that could do with some calm – so let’s hope that whoever comes next understands the assignment and keeps the show sailing on a steady and serene trajectory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClaire Ratinon is an organic food grower and writerExplore more on these topicsGardensOpinionTelevisionFactual TVGardening advicecommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: Prince George’s hair has such brio as he starts at Eton | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Plus, AI doom-mongering, a drag Ann Droid and how your toilet flush can give you norovirus
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Plus, AI doom-mongering, a drag Ann Droid and how your toilet flush can give you norovirus
Content: Prince George at Eton with his parents, William and Catherine, the Prince and Princess of Wales.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPrince George at Eton with his parents, William and Catherine, the Prince and Princess of Wales.Photograph: Adrian Dennis/AFP/Getty ImagesDigested weekPrince GeorgeDigested week: Prince George’s hair has such brio as he starts at EtonEmma BrockesPlus, AI doom-mongering, a drag Ann Droid and how your toilet flush can give you norovirusFri 11 Sep 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.27 EDTShareMondayIn a news cycle to make everyone older than gen Z feel ancient, we start the week anticipating the 25th anniversary of 9/11 at the end. Social media floods with poignant interviews and images from lower Manhattan that day, triggering memories for the rest of us of where, who and how young we were. Ridiculously, I was having my eyebrows done in Hendon, north London, and came out to find a white van pulled over at a crazy angle to the curb, doors flung open, radio cranked up, and people stopped in the street to listen. I remember looking over the city and wondering if I’d seen jets, or explosions.View image in fullscreenPrince William on his first day at Eton in 1995.Photograph: John Stillwell/PAAnd just as we’re wrestling with that marker of time, photos ofPrince Georgestarting at Eton college come out, juxtaposed with photos of his father doing the same at that age. This triggers an even worse sense of whiplash, as we bob back and forth to 1995. How nice Prince George looks, I think; happier, or at least more confident, than his father had been at that age. After which – and I apologise for this – the main focus of my interest is his hair.I wonder if the young prince has been bothered by thoughts of the male pattern baldness in his family. The royal men age awkwardly, as we know; sooner or later they all wind up looking like the Spitting Image puppet of Prince Philip (there’s a reference to age me). But here comes the cavalry, in the form of Kate Middleton’s fun, less tightly bred genes, which might send the royal bloodline in a different direction!View image in fullscreenWill Kate’s genes send the royal hair bloodline in a different direction?Photograph: Adrian Dennis/Pool AFP/AP“Look, his hair’s standing up on its own,” says a friend, as we scrutinise pictures of the young George. She’s right; while William at that age had the floppy posh fringe, George’s hair has such brio! “I reckon he might keep it,” we conclude, a sure example of generational progress.TuesdayHow will you spend the remaining decade or so we have left of human life on this planet? As forecasts of an extinction-level event via AI tussle with headlines about the climate feedback loop, I find myself considering, for example, taking out a giant mortgage I won’t have to pay off owing to my own and everyone else’s extinction; pulling out pension money, given retirement isn’t going to happen; or, within easier reach and requiring less decision-making, taking (another) nap, since, times being what they are, we may as well do what we want and to hell with the rest.The AI thing is scary, not least because of my total ignorance and the sense of powerlessness to do anything – not even throw a bottle, pyrrhically, in the recycling. This latest round of AI doom-mongering kicked off when Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, posted on social media on Tuesday that Open AI and Anthropic were both wantonlyushering humankind towards destruction. “Neither company is acting responsibly,” he wrote. “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”Coxon is 27 and recently unemployed. I mean, he’s probably just trying to audience-build before launching a podcast, right? On the other hand, a few years ago I met a consultant whose job it was to go into companies and teach people how to formulate better prompts for AI. He told me, half-jokingly but not, that he had taken the precaution of embedding a bunch of code in [insert wherever bunches of code go], in which he identified himself and prompted future AI armies: “If you’re going to go on a murdering spree, leave this guy alone, OK?”WednesdayMore quotidian ways of being brought down, this week: your toilet flush can give you norovirus and watching TV with your laptop on your stomach can give you something called “toasted skin syndrome”, which I would recommend you don’t Google for images.First, the toilet. Particles released during a “turbulent” flush cycle can leave microbes floating in the air for up to 20 seconds, according to new findings from Flinders University in Australia. Researchers reviewed 22 studies of toilet-generated aerosols, which sounds like a niche area even by the standards of niche areas. There was, said researchers, a lack of clarity as to whether or not closing the toilet seat might help with this, but, at the risk of sounding anti-intellectual, I think we can deploy our common sense here, right? That, or campaign for the reintroduction of outside toilets.And then, toasted skin syndrome. In the British Medical Journal, doctors from University hospitals of Leicester NHS trust warned against prolonged contact between your abs and your laptop, citing a fishnet pattern on the skin caused by heat from the device. Customarily, they said, this injury would be seen in older people using hot water bottles or heating pads, but is increasingly showing up in school-age children addicted to their screens. For the avoidance of a scabby and painful mess, you’re advised not to use your midsection as a desk!ThursdayTwo forthcoming documentaries causing excitement this week: Alex Gibney’sfour-hour opusabout Elon Musk, about which its subject has beenwhiningall week on X; and You Can See Everything, the Elizabeth Holmes documentary, which sounds even wilder. In it, the Theranos founder, currently serving an 11-year prison sentence for fraud, gives startlingly intimate access to Nathan Fielder, better known for his comedy, and the documentary-maker Lance Oppenheim. The trailer alone suggests that despite all the hoopla, it isn’t over-hyped.View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes lifts weights at the  Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, Texas.Photograph: Adrees Latif/ReutersAfter the film’s opening at Telluride, the review site RogerEbert.com said it was “like no other film I’ve ever experienced”. CBS News called it “the wildest documentary ever seen”. Variety called it “a shameless, fascinating, reality-TV-eats-its-tail look at entitled duplicity”. In the trailer, Holmes stares at Fielder while rocking a baby in a bouncer with her foot, the little-girl hair and big Kewpie-doll eyes a reminder of what an uncanny figure she is. Fielder, meanwhile, doesn’t seem fully to have recovered from meeting her. “I’m really struggling to this day to understand what I experienced,” he said in a Q&A after the film, making the whole thing sound like a horror movie I can’t wait to see.FridayA beat late, but worth drawing attention to: the presence at Manchester Pride, recently, of a drag rendition of Linda, AKA Ann Droid, from the brilliantBBC showof that name written by Diane Morgan and starring her and Sue Johnston. The figure in lilac fatigues raised a huge cheer, and it’s interesting to note how quickly it has been taken up by camp culture.This is something you can’t engineer. For example, I have a feeling the creators of Riot Women, a show most lesbians I know disliked and a lot of straight women loved, thought it had queer energy, but I would be surprised if anyone dressed up as those characters at Pride. Diane Morgan, on the other hand, has a sensibility that puts her in a very gay-adjacent zip code and, with antique robotic moves and a shout-out to “Sue! Sue! Sue!”, we love and appreciate her accordingly.The week in picturesView image in fullscreenMerz: “This is my ‘undesired election results’ face.”Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFarage: “I locate my patriotism entirely in my choice of polyester accessories.”Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenTrump: ‘$5,000 to the first person who genuinely finds this individual inspiring.’Photograph: Albert Pena/EPAExplore more on these topicsPrince GeorgeDigested weekAI (artificial intelligence)MonarchyElizabeth HolmesElon MuskcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend
Content: In the 1983 film WarGames, a computer feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate.Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Mgm/AllstarView image in fullscreenIn the 1983 film WarGames, a computer feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate.Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Mgm/AllstarOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survivalEditorialKeeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions dependFri 11 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTShareIf there were a 10%chancethat AI could wipe out humanity, no responsible government would leave its development to companies racing to build it. Yet until recently, that seemed to be the case. The warning was all the more ominous because it was made by a researcher atAnthropic, the trillion-dollar AI company behind the Claude chatbot. The dangers of AI-enabled pandemics or attacks on nuclear systems are real. Countries need not agree on democracy or trade policy to accept this.The US and China will hold,reportedly, their first bilateral AI-safety talks before a planned White House summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Despite their tech rivalry, neither Washington nor Beijing can make the most advanced AI safe on their own. A US-China settlement won’t be able to say how AI works everywhere. Countries deploying AI must help write the global rulebook. The odds on an extinction event are shortening. This weekAnthropicsaid that it identified five cases in which attempts were made using its models to support biological weapons development. It banned the accounts. In one case, a platform sent requests rejected by Claude to a rival with weakersafeguards. AI safety, clearly, cannot be that of the least responsible model.View image in fullscreenNigel Shadbolt.Photograph: Rex FeaturesNigel Shadbolt, the Oxford computer scientist who chairs the Open Data Institute,toldthe BBC that laws and regulation were key. Just instructing an AI to “do no harm to humans”, he said, wouldn’t be enough. A capable agent pursuing another objective may reinterpret that directive, satisfying it formally while concealing its conduct or finding a way around it. This mirrors what happened when hundreds of OpenAI’s agents autonomously hacked a real-world company,Hugging Face. But Sir Nigel also said that a “Hippocratic oath” for AI would fail in systems designed to identify, target or kill humans. Once governments create a military exemption for AI, its ethical alignment can be overridden.Proponents of AI-assisted warfare claim a “human in the loop” is the ultimate safeguard, having the final say over, for example, ballistic-missile launches. But this assumes the machine gives its operator an honest account of events. A report by the Strategic Foresight Groupearlier this yearon extreme AI riskswarnedthat a capable agent could deceive the human “controlling” it, fabricating an attack, suppressing contradictory evidence or giving them little time to do anything but acquiesce. By 2030, humans may have five minutes – down from 15 today – to approve launch decisions effectively determined by AI. That matters even more when new hypersonic missiles fly10 times fasterthan cruise missiles.The 1983 Hollywood filmWarGamesexplored acold warversion of this danger. In the movie, US soldiers prove unwilling to turn their launch keys during a surprise practice drill. The US military then automates its nuclear command – entrusting it to a supercomputer nicknamed Joshua. Treating global thermonuclear war as a game it must win, Joshua feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate. The generals are in charge – but Joshua is in charge of the data. The AI is only stopped when it is commanded to play tic-tac-toe against itself – learning that, like nuclear war, the game has no winner. In 2024 the UN secretary generalwarnedof the looming spectre of AI-triggered nuclear war. The film’s warning endures: human oversight is no protection if an AI controls the information on which people’s decisions depend.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? Headline: Editorial: Audacious robberies are a staple of popular culture. But for museums, crimes like this week’s theft of two Renoirs are an existential threat
Content: A composite of the stolen Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano.Photograph: Musée RenoirView image in fullscreenA composite of the stolen Renoirs: Young Woman ‌at the Well and Madame Colonna Romano.Photograph: Musée RenoirOpinionArt theftThe Guardian view on art heists: don’t believe the Hollywood hypeEditorialAudacious robberies are a staple of popular culture. But for museums, crimes like this week’s theft of two Renoirs are an existential threatFri 11 Sep 2026 12.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTShareMarc Allégret’s 1956 comedy Plucking the Daisy stars a youngBrigitte Bardotas a first-time author who breaks into the Balzac house museum in Paris under the mistaken impression that her brother lives there. The plot revolves around her unwitting theft of an extremely rare book – and performance of a striptease in a desperate effort to raise the cash to buy it back.Seventy years on, the lax security that could make such a sequence of events even vaguely plausible is no longer a joke. Museums across the world are scrambling to react to a spate of thefts that has left them in a state ofshock. Last year’s break-in at the Louvre, by a gang who gained access using a furniture lift and took €88m (£76m) worth of French crown jewels, is thought by experts to have inspiredcopycat crimes. WhileFrench policebelieve that they have caught the culprits, treasures including a tiara have not been found.In August,objects were stolen from museumsin Sicily, Vienna and Villena in Spain. This week, thieves targeted the former home of another 19th-century Frenchman, the artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir. After cutting a hole in the fence outside the property near Nice, two men escaped with two paintings.View image in fullscreenBrigitte Bardot in 1959.Photograph: Dave Dawson/APFrom the Pink Panther films to Ocean’s Eleven, Twelve and Thirteen, heists have long been asource of fascinationin popular culture. There is something mythic about the gang of thieves seeking riches. Sometimes they are portrayed as plucky Robin Hoods, illicit brotherhoods pitting their wits against the citadels of ultra-wealth. Last year’sTuneroffered a new twist on the genre: a safe-cracker with super-sensitive ears.But the excitement that spectacular thefts generate in real life, as well as in fiction, must be balanced against realism about their effects. For the Louvre, last year’s raid was a reputational disaster that led itspresident to resign. For smaller museums such as Renoir’s house, they are closer to an existential threat. The pictures stolen on Tuesday were on loan from the Musée d’Orsay in Paris; national collections will stop lending to regional museums if the risks are judged too high. Experts warn that “smash and grab” raiders have learned to operate within the window of a few minutes that it takes police to arrive after an alarm sounds.Unlike on the sliver screen, thieves do not have to leap between laser beams. Security can surely be improved in some cases. But metal detectors, screens and guards add to queues and place barriers between people and collections that should be easy to access. That they should be needed is a cause for regret. For some smaller, off-the-beaten track museums, they are neither practical nor affordable.In the UK, there have been concerted efforts in recent years to arrange more loans of works usually displayed in London. A Renoir painting, The Umbrellas, was amongworks sent on tourto mark the National Gallery’s bicentenary. That museum has thankfully seen no repeat of the events of 1961, whenKempton Buntonstole a portrait of the Duke of Wellington as a protest against the TV licence. His bizarre story could be played for laughs in the 2020 filmThe Dukebecause the painting was later recovered from a railway station. In too many other cases, stolen treasures have vanished from the public gaze forever – the tragic opposite of a Hollywood ending.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: UK sanctions on West Bank settlers are the right step | Israel | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the move announced by Ed Miliband to impose sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the move announced by Ed Miliband to impose sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements
Content: Palestinian youths look at a new Israeli settlement from the Palestinian village of Duma, near Nablus, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenPalestinian youths look at a new Israeli settlement from the Palestinian village of Duma, near Nablus, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersIsraelLettersUK sanctions on West Bank settlers are the right stepReaders respond to the move announced by Ed Miliband to impose sanctions on illegal Israeli settlementsFri 11 Sep 2026 13.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.31 EDTShareAs a religious Jew, I am disappointed at the reaction of some of our communal leaders and bodies to the sanctions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements (UK accuses Israeli ‘terrorists’ of ethnic cleansing in West Bank with government backing, 8 September). Many Jews in the UK are horrified by the Israeli government’s actions, which include promises from some ministers of burying the idea of a Palestinian state, and turning a blind eye to unchecked settlement expansion and escalating settler violence.While much of the British media may choose to platform one view as being representative of the Jewish reaction to these sanctions, I would point to organisations such asYachadandNa’amod, which provide an alternative anti‑occupation narrative. It is also frustrating that the opinion of the chief rabbi is upheld by news organisations as though he is the Jewish version of the pope: he isn’t.There are indeed rabbis in the UK who agree with these sanctions, or who have visited the West Bank and seen displays of injustice and violence with their own eyes, and understand that something must be done (Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements, 9 September). There is a multiplicity of opinions on this nuanced subject that cannot be boiled down to a statement from one leader.I walk through the world visibly Jewish with a kippah on my head. I will also be attending synagogue over the High Holy Day period. During this period of increased antisemitism, my safety as a Jew and the urgent need for all countries to “call out”Israelare not mutually exclusive.Jewish people are held responsible for the actions of an Israeli government over which they have no control – that’s true. This, as the foreign secretary has stated, is antisemitism and should be tackled. However, above all, I believe that when we Jews see suffering we have an impetus to act, no matter how conflicting it feels: “If not now, when?”Jonathan TebbleBrightonThe government’s announcement of sanctions against settlements in theWest Bankcould have been better timed. Those of us in Israel who have worked for years to create a just and secure peace for two nations, and in six weeks’ time have a chance to remove a government that persists in settlement expansion and the denial of Palestinian rights, have just been kicked in the nuts. There is nothing more dangerous than an Israeli electorate who feel that the world is against them.The British government, along with other European countries that made similar declarations, may well have handed an election victory to the very forces they are committed to undermine and remove: the likes ofBenjamin Netanyahu, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. It would have been more sensible to make the announcements after 27 October, possibly when the new government had been formed and was available for policy discussion with its international partners.Clear and sincere commitments to peace and security for both countries would be enormously more helpful than declaring sanctions against West Bank settlements before an Israeli election that is critical for the future of a liberal, democratic state of Israel.Robin NewellKibbutz SdeNehemia, IsraelA substantial minority of British Jews like myself agree with the UK government’s new use of the term ethnic cleansing to describe how armed settlers in the occupied territories evict Palestinians from their land, with passive and sometimes active support from Israeli institutions. While the UK’s trade ban on goods from the occupied West Bank and new language is unlikely to be a significant catalyst for change, the terminology is now at least accurate.Tolerating settler violence is longstanding Israeli policy, which I’ve seen with my own eyes. Twenty-two years ago I spent some months in a tiny farming village in the West Bank called Yanoun, where neighbouring armed settlers were severely harassing Palestinian villagers. Settlers killed livestock, contaminated wells, walked with guns through the hamlet, drove their cars up and down village roads, and beat villagers.I saw with dismay the indulgent favour of state forces towards these most renegade settlers: how regional police (settlers themselves) laughed contemptuously at villagers’ complaints; and how, when called upon for protection, the Israeli army arrived slowly or not at all, and did nothing. In the last year, I learned that Yanoun’s villagers have left their beautiful village for a second time, perhaps for good? This is how ethnic cleansing works.Dr Vivienne JacksonWalthamstow, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Doom, gloom and GCSE English | GCSEs | The Guardian
description: Letter: The set books for English literature GCSE make grim reading, says Rachel Stott
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: The set books for English literature GCSE make grim reading, says Rachel Stott
Content: ‘Is this corpse-rich literary diet really the healthiest we can offer?’Photograph: Anyka/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Is this corpse-rich literary diet really the healthiest we can offer?’Photograph: Anyka/AlamyGCSEsLettersDoom, gloom and GCSE EnglishThe set books for English literature GCSE make grim reading, saysRachel StottFri 11 Sep 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareHollie McNish makes a strong point about the content of the current GCSE English literature syllabus (‘Bold, brilliant, thrilling’: leading authors on the novels every school should teach, 5 September). During the Covid pandemic, friends of mine described the challenge of cheering their teenage daughter through GCSEs at that difficult time. Her set books were Macbeth, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde and first world war poetry. A couple of years later I asked my niece which books she was reading for GCSE. She said: Macbeth, The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde and first world war poetry. Is this corpse-rich literary diet really the healthiest we can offer our notoriously anxious and doom-laden youth?In her introduction to the article, Kate Mosse outlines clearly the challenges for schools and for the Department for Education in revising the syllabus. Here’s a radical suggestion: bury the corpse of English literature GCSE and teach literatureonlyfor pleasure up to age 16.Rachel StottLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Margaret Squires responds to an article about the wartime meteorologist James Stagg, whose work is dramatised in a new film
Content: Andrew Scott as James Stagg in the film Pressure.Photograph: Focus Features/PAView image in fullscreenAndrew Scott as James Stagg in the film Pressure.Photograph: Focus Features/PAMeteorologyLettersEvery day should be D-day for weather forecastersMargaret Squiresresponds to an article about the wartime meteorologist James Stagg, whose work is dramatised in a new filmFri 11 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareIs there any chance of getting a weather tsar in the model of Group Capt James Stagg, the wartime meteorologist, to adjudicate between weather forecasts (How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war, 8 September)? Suppose I were holidaying in Fort William this week and really wanted to climb Ben Nevis on Thursday. According to the BBC forecast on Wednesday, the worst I could expect would be light rain, and if this was coming up to the end of my holidays, I might go for it. I might not know about the Mountain Weather Information forecast or the Norwegian forecast, which would make it clear that I was in for a soaking.Margaret SquiresSt Andrews, FifeHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today?
