title: Enjoy Łódź – but don’t omit its tragic past | Holocaust | The Guardian
description: Letter: Dr Richard Bradbury responds to a travel article about the Polish city, home to one of the largest Jewish ghettos during Nazi occupation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Dr Richard Bradbury responds to a travel article about the Polish city, home to one of the largest Jewish ghettos during Nazi occupation
Content: The Jewish memorial at Radegast station, Łódź. Approximately 200,000 Jews from the city were murdered during the second world war.Photograph: piccaya/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Jewish memorial at Radegast station, Łódź. Approximately 200,000 Jews from the city were murdered during the second world war.Photograph: piccaya/Getty ImagesHolocaustLettersEnjoy Łódź – but don’t omit its tragic pastDr Richard Bradburyresponds to a travel article about the Polish city, home to one of the largest Jewish ghettos during Nazi occupationFri 11 Sep 2026 13.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareI was shocked to read your travel article detailing the delights of Łódź without a single mention of the city’s past as the site of one of the largest ghettos during the second world war (A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories, 5 September).The article says: “I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. ‘It was not too badly damaged,’ she says. ‘Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.’” I wonder how the surviving family members of the perhaps 200,000 people who died after being herded into the ghetto, often to work as slaves for the Nazi war effort, would feel about that.Łódź is indeed a wonderful city, and I have watched its transformation since I worked there in the late 1980s. Your article highlights the many great pleasures of the city today, as I too experienced on my most recent visit in July. But as so many have said in the past, if we ignore history, all too often we repeat it.Dr Richard BradburyExton, DevonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Content: Houthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAYemenIran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping routeRampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exportsWhy the rapid Houthi advance matters and what’s at stakePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 11 Sep 2026 11.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, includingthe loss of the port city of Mochaon Thursday.Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.Houthi advance mapSaudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude sinceIranhas been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments.Oilprices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and theHouthishave been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.View image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIn a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.View image in fullscreenPerim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph.Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./APThe Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.Map of Houthi-controlled areas of YemenThe US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.View image in fullscreenA view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesOn her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisUS-Israel war on IranIranOilSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country
Content: Questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration.Photograph: Wdnet Studio/AlamyView image in fullscreenQuestions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration.Photograph: Wdnet Studio/AlamySweden‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policySweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU countryLisa O’Carrollin StockholmFri 11 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain afterBrexit, before the deadline of December 2021.But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since.In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”.“I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.”Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden,considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics, was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said.Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve.He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 inSweden– deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration.In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%. France deported 450, Spain 250 and Germany 160, while Italy deported just 15 Britons in that period.Different countries collate data in different ways, but Eurostat data suggests the Netherlands is another outlier, with 2,270 Britons deported in the same period.Data shows 2,100 removal orders were also issued in Sweden, though it is not clear how many of these resulted in voluntary departures or progressed to deportations.View image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, 78, walks her dog just hours before she is due to be ‘removed’ from Sweden after 22 years.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollPeople served with removal orders includeJoyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, andGeorge Mason, a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit.John Sellers, a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January.The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit.“The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017.Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected byits apparent lurch to the rightmore broadly, servingdeportations on childrenand evena 95-year-old Iraqi womanwho had lived in Sweden for 20 years.“The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelinwrote this weekahead of the general election on Sunday.British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals.View image in fullscreenGeorge Mason, 74, seen here with his daughter Michelle, has been served with a removal notice.Photograph: The Mason family“The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, whichrecently revealed the pressure applied to Swedenby the European Commission.Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace[George]Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].”Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same.Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party,has promised new lawsif his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.”The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders.The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes.Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged.David Milstead,who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily.A spokesperson for theEuropean Commissionsaid: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.”This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”.View image in fullscreen‘Some of these cases are just stupid,’ said Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party.Photograph: Centerpartie, SwedenIn other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion.Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”.While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA.Inthe case of “CG”,the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland.“In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said.“While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.”The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles.Explore more on these topicsSwedenBrexitEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionMigrationImmigration and asylumEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis | Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) | The Guardian
description: Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt
Content: The AfD’s parliamentary group leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, referred to the MPs under criminal investigation as ‘the bad guys’.Photograph: Karina Hessland/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe AfD’s parliamentary group leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, referred to the MPs under criminal investigation as ‘the bad guys’.Photograph: Karina Hessland/ReutersAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-NazisFar-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-AnhaltWhy is the AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next?Kate Connollyin BerlinFri 11 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historicwin in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks.View image in fullscreenThe AfD’s newly elected members of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament.Photograph: Karina Hessland/ReutersGerman media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations.The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge.An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate.His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”.Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington.Russian president Vladimir Putin initially said he would not comment on the AfD victory, but speaking to reporters during a visit to India for the BRICS summit later blamed “western globalists”.“I think that everything happening inEuroperight now is basically ‌the result of system errors by the so-called West … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics,” Putin said.The AfD has promised to curb migration and restore ties with Moscow.Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund at the AfD election party after polls closed last Sunday.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersSiegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms inGermanyto the party’s planned deportation offensive.In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.”The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”.“This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said.Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority.Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.Explore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: North Sea gasfield decision likely delayed until after Holborn and St Pancras byelection | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: Greens accuse Labour of hiding position to avoid criticism before contest, in which Zack Polanski is standing
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Greens accuse Labour of hiding position to avoid criticism before contest, in which Zack Polanski is standing
Content: Climate activists in Scotland protest against the Jackdaw and Rosebank gasfields.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenClimate activists in Scotland protest against the Jackdaw and Rosebank gasfields.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianFossil fuelsNorth Sea gasfield decision likely delayed until after Holborn and St Pancras byelectionGreens accuse Labour of hiding position to avoid criticism before contest, in which Zack Polanski is standingRowena MasonandKiran StaceyFri 11 Sep 2026 11.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA decision on approving the controversial Jackdaw gasfield in the North Sea is to be delayed until later this autumn, with the Greens accusing Labour of hiding their position before the crucialHolborn and St Pancras byelection.Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, had been poised to give her recommendation toapprove the Jackdaw field off the coast of Aberdeen next week.However, multiple Whitehall sources say the decision is not expected to be made in the remaining few days before the House of Commons goes into recess on Tuesday for party conference season.The delay means the announcement is unlikely to come before Holborn and St Pancras constituents vote in a high-profile byelection on 8 October, in which the Green party leader Zack Polanski is the candidate vying against Labour’sSagal Abdi-Waliin Keir Starmer’s former seat.Polanski has criticised the government over signals that it will press ahead with Jackdaw despite the hottest ever summer caused by the climate crisis.After his selection, Polanski saidLabourhas “started the campaign with an act of dishonesty and betrayal”.“They are clearly going to allow new drilling in the North Sea but want to keep it under wraps during a byelection where they know the public want tougher action on climate, not backsliding.“Labour talks about change, but this is change for the worse. We have a climate crisis but Labour is taking the side of fossil fuel corporations, and the voters have a clear choice in this byelection between action on climate change or shortsighted rowing backwards.”The delay also means Andy Burnham could avoid controversy over Jackdaw at the Labour party conference in Liverpool at the end of the month.Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, said delays in approving Jackdaw would mean it takes longer to increase UK domestic production in the North Sea.In a letter to the prime minister published on social media, Bowie asked Burnham to confirm “suggestions that you are about to delay the decision on the Jackdaw gasfield until after the conference recess and Holborn and St Pancras byelection”.He added: “If this is the case, it would be nothing short of you placing the interests of the Labour party before the interests of Great Britain.”A separate decision is also pending on the Rosebank oilfield project.Environmental campaigners have called for both projects to be abandoned, while the US president, Donald Trump, hasurged the prime ministerto open them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLabour’s manifesto committed to a ban on new drilling licences in the North Sea, but the companies behind Jackdaw and Rosebank are seeking environmental approval for existing licences.Last week, a spokesperson for the energy department said: “The North Sea remains a vital national asset, supporting jobs, growth and the UK’s energy security. We are clear that oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come, alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.”The companies resubmitted their applications for environmental approval earlier this year. Granting those permits would not violate Labour’s manifesto commitment not to issue new oil or gas licences, but many of the party’s MPs are opposed to the projects entirely.Under the process, the energy secretary gives her recommendation to the North Sea Transition Authority, which then later issues a formal approval.Consultations on Jackdaw and Rosebank, which the industry says will provide 10% of the UK’s oil and gas output at their peak, closed last month, and Fahnbulleh has since been considering her response.Campaigners say the fieldswould produceas much as £336bn worth of damage to the economy as a result of the carbon pollution from the oil and gas produced.Both fields have licences to operate, but environmental approval was rescinded after a judge ruled the companies running them – Shell and the Norwegian firm Equinor – needed to account for the carbon emissions that would be created by burning the oil and gas they produce.Explore more on these topicsFossil fuelsHolborn and St Pancras byelectionZack PolanskiLabourEnergyGasEnvironment policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Northern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next year | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform
Content: A law passed last year aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers, but campaigners said it did not got far enough.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyView image in fullscreenA law passed last year aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers, but campaigners said it did not got far enough.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyNorthern IrelandNorthern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next yearDUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniformRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchools inNorthern Irelandmust give girls the choice to wear trousers as part of their uniforms as well as for PE and games, according to revised guidelines.From next year schools would no longer be able to prohibit female pupils from wearing trousers, Paul Givan, the country’s education minister, said on Friday. “Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me,” hetold the BBC.A law passed last year that was aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers.However, campaigners said the change did not go far enough and put pressure on Givan, a Democratic Unionist party member of the Northern Ireland assembly (MLA) whosaid his own daughters wore skirts to school, to revise the guidelines.Givan said he had to strike a balance between schools’ autonomy and the level of prescription in departmental guidelines. “I have listened carefully over recent months to young people and the message is clear: girls want the choice to wear trousers as part of their school uniform.”The revised guidelines would not go into immediate effect to give schools time to update their policies, said Givan.Other parties welcomed the change but accused the education minister of dragging his feet.“I’m glad that it appears the minister has seen fit to U-turn on his decision not to ensure that all girls have the right to wear trousers as part of their school uniform,” said Nick Mathison, an Alliance MLA and chair of the Stormont assembly education committee.“I want to thank all of the young campaigners who have been bravely raising their voices about this, and whose dedication will lead to seeing this wrong righted. The fact that in 2026 young girls and women had to campaign for this at all will not be forgotten.”Substantial sums of public money were spent on drafting legislation to fix the minister’s error of judgment, Mathison added.A girl’s right to wear trousers should not have been controversial, said Cathy Mason, a Sinn Féin MLA. “It should not have required further legislation from the education committee to force movement on something so basic.”Cara Hunter, a Social Democratic and Labour party MLA, said young people who challenged the existing rules and refused to let the issue disappear deserved credit for the change. “The department must now deliver. This cannot be a right that exists on paper but becomes an argument at the school gate,” she said.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandSchoolsEducation policyPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsChildrenNorthern Irish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: One in nine migratory birds threatened with extinction, global report says | Birds | The Guardian
description: Findings on decline of species such as Arctic tern and turtle dove published alongside flyways pledge at Kenya summit
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: Findings on decline of species such as Arctic tern and turtle dove published alongside flyways pledge at Kenya summit
Content: Arctic terns on the Isle of May, Scotland. The report  also highlights how conservation action, often across national boundaries, is reviving some species.Photograph: Travel/AlamyView image in fullscreenArctic terns on the Isle of May, Scotland. The report  also highlights how conservation action, often across national boundaries, is reviving some species.Photograph: Travel/AlamyBirdsOne in nine migratory birds threatened with extinction, global report saysFindings on decline of species such as Arctic tern and turtle dove published alongside flyways pledge at Kenya summitPatrick BarkhamFri 11 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne in nine migratory birds are threatened with extinction and 45% of migratory species such as cuckoos, turtle doves and Arctic terns are in decline, according to a global report.The migratoryslender-billed curlewwas officially declared extinct last year, the first global bird extinction in mainland Eurasia and Africa in recent centuries. Worldwide, seven migratory bird species have been confirmed or are suspected to have become extinct over the last 150 years.The threats to migratory birds, which are overwhelmingly caused by humans and include the intensification of farming, unsustainable hunting, pollution, invasive species and global heating, were revealed in theState of the World’s Birds report.View image in fullscreenEuropean turtle doves perch on a branch in Bursa, Turkey.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesSeabirds and shorebirds, which depend upon marine habitats and coastal wetlands, are faring particularly badly, according to the analysis, which is produced every four years by BirdLife International.Bird migration is changing. What does this reveal about our planet? – visualisedRead moreStuart Butchart, the chief scientist atBirdLife International, said: “Migratory birds are sentinels, and their declines reveal growing pressure on the natural systems that sustain us. But the science is equally clear: conservation works, with coordinated action preventing extinctions and helping populations recover. The solutions exist: what is needed now is their implementation at flyway scale.”The report was published at theGlobal Flywayssummit in Nairobi, Kenya, where governments, scientists, conservation NGOs and financial institutions signed a commitment to increase efforts to protect migratory birds along their flyways, the routes taken by billions of migratory birds moving between continents and seasons.The Nairobi Flyways Declaration comes with three development banks integrating flyway conservation into their lending frameworks, providing $6bn (£4.4bn) for habitat protection and restoration along migratory routes.View image in fullscreenA murmuration of red knots and other birds at RSPB Snettisham in Norfolk.Photograph: Paul Bradley/AlamyThreats to migratory birds include persecution, with an estimated 13.1 million to 42.7 million migratory birds illegally killed or taken every year in Europe, the Mediterranean, the Caucasus and the Arabian peninsula. Many of these are songbirds caught in mist nets or on “lime sticks” for human consumption.Invasive species, such as rodents sometimes accidentally introduced on to small islands where seabirds breed, also threaten migratory birds.Loss or damage to natural habitats is another prime cause. According to the report, scientific monitoring over the past decade has found that more than half (58%) of 1,099 key biodiversity areas for migratory birds are in poor or very poor condition.But the report highlights how conservation action, often across national boundaries, is reviving some species.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA blue petrel.Photograph: JJ Harrison/UC Davis/PAThe eradication of non-native rabbits, cats, rodents and the weka bird from Australia’s Macquarie Island, an important site for breeding seabirds, has led to a resurgence in populations of migratory seabirds including the blue petrel, grey petrel, white-headed petrel and the Antarctic prion.In China, an ambitious countrywide programme to remove smooth cordgrass, a North American grass introduced in 1979 to stabilise coastal mudflats for development, has restored 37,553 hectares (92,756 acres) – half the total area – in its first year, opening up vital food-rich mudflats to shorebirds again.In Britain, the restoration of wetlands on agricultural land threatened by coastal erosion at Wallasea Island, Essex, has led to peaks of more than 32,000 waterbirds returning to the site, including 11,270 red knots.View image in fullscreenDark-bellied brent geese in flight at Wallasea Island.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/AlamyOutlined at the summit were plans by the Asian Development Bank to mobilise $3bn over the next decade to protect at least 50 priority wetlands across the east Asian-Australasian flyway, with the funds also supporting nearly 200 million people who depend on these ecosystems. The Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean is mobilising $3bn-$5bn up to 2050 to safeguard more than 30 landscapes and seascapes. Several billion dollars has also been pledged by the World Bank and BirdLife to support flyways across Africa, Europe and Asia used by more than 2 billion migratory birds.Princess Takamado of Japan, the honorary president of BirdLife International, said: “Migratory birds do not recognise borders. They connect Asia to Africa, the Arctic to the tropics. The Nairobi Flyways Declaration acknowledges this reality – that it needs international cooperation and coordination to keep migratory birds safe. I am excited and proud to see that the scientific community, conservation organisations and the financial sector are uniting to make this happen. We stand at an important turning point. We have been waiting for this moment for a long time.”Martin Harper, the chief executive of BirdLife International, also called the Nairobi Declaration a turning point but said governments, businesses and civil society needed to play their part. “Development banks are rising to the challenge. The BirdLife Partnerhip is prepared to act. We now need others to step up to reverse the declines and save the wonder of migration.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsAnimalsConservationWildlifeEndangered speciesBiodiversityWetlandsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Fresh from the roof’: the supermarket growing salad a few metres above the tills | Germany | The Guardian
description: Customers seeking greens at one Berlin outlet are dealing with some very local supply chains indeed
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Customers seeking greens at one Berlin outlet are dealing with some very local supply chains indeed
Content: Lettuce grown at the Felix Thomas REWE supermarket in Lankwitz, Berlin. Photograph: Christoph GroßeCustomers seeking greens at one Berlin outlet are dealing with some very local supply chains indeedByHannah Docter-LoebFri 11 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWalking into the Felix Thomas REWE supermarket in Lankwitz, Berlin, customers are immediately presented with a choice of greens: romaine, rocket, iceberg. But last month, a new option joined the selection: Lankwitz loose-leaf lettuce. A combination of head lettuce, romaine lettuce, Lollo Rosso, and dark green easy leaf lettuce, its yellow packaging makes it stand out in a row of green. But it’s not just the flashy packaging that makes it distinct. Unlike its neighbouring lettuces, which come from regional farms or all the way from Italy, these greens were grown just a few metres away – or rather, a few metres up. “Frisch Vom REWE Dach” or “Fresh from the REWE roof”, the bags read.Rooftop farms are nothing new: in cities such asParis,Hong Kong,CopenhagenandNew York, similar farms supply food to adjacent food retailers or even restaurants. This model has the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from transportation (and its associated costs), minimise the urban heat effect, make use of dead space and perhaps even improve the relationship between buyers and their food.Germany is also no stranger to rooftop farms. In 2021, REWE and ECF – a Berlin-based agricultural technology company – opened their first green farming market on top of a store in Wiesbaden-Erbenheim, selling basil below. But at 2,760 sq metres, the Lankwitz REWE is now Germany’s largest rooftop farm.View image in fullscreenThe Felix Thomas REWE supermarket was clearly designed with the farm in mind.Photograph: Christoph GroßeREWE provides the space, location, and distribution channels to sell, and ECF designed and manages the greenhouse. The Lankwitz lettuce has become a selling point of sorts: store manager Felix Thomas says one customer travelled more than 50km just to get their hands on a bag. And the integration of the farm into REWE’s market and corresponding supply chain is novel, says ECF CEO and founder Nicolas Leschke.The supermarket was clearly designed with the farm in mind: skylights throughout the store offer a window into what’s growing above. “The cool thing about producing locally and on a building is you can create synergy within the building,” Leschke said. The greenhouse is heated through the waste heat of cooling aggregates downstairs, and rainwater is the primary source of water for the greenhouse and plant production. Some of the greenhouse is also powered by sustainable energy – primarily solar.The operation is meant to be year-round. The farm makes use ofhydroponic technologies: the lettuce varieties are grown with very little soil. The whole growing process takes a little over three weeks. Once cut, the greens go straight downstairs to be packaged and sold, both on site and in other stores in the city and region.View image in fullscreenThe farm makes use ofhydroponic technologies: the lettuce varieties are grown with very little soil, and the whole growing process takes a little over three weeks.Photograph: Christoph Große“We don’t even have an extra truck on the road that usually is necessary to transport the goods from the producer to the central distribution,” Leschke said.Prajal Pradhan, an associate professor at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, who recently published a study onurban agriculturein Europe, sees REWE’s latest rooftop as a step in the right direction.“There is a disconnection between producers and consumers,” he said. “This is a way to go forward, because you can provide fresh vegetables to urban consumers on site.”However, he stresses, it should not be an alternative to having a personal or community rooftop garden. He says urban agriculture should be inclusive and find ways to include the whole community, a sentiment echoed by study co-author Stepan Svintsov, a remote sensing expert based in Berlin.“Getting people together from a dense city and sharing agricultural knowledge among them helps bring the community together,” Svintsov said. REWE currently offers tours to see the facility from outside, but no one can enter the production rooms.There is a large potential for rooftop farms and the like inEurope. Pradhan, Svintsov and their colleagues’ review looks at the biophysical viability for urban agriculture in European cities: seeing how urban rooftop and ground-based areas are well suited for cultivating vegetables. They found that urban agriculture in European cities could produce up to 20m tonnes of vegetables annually. This translates to about 28% of the continent’s vegetable demand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSkylights throughout the store offer a window into what’s growing above.Photograph: Christoph GroßePradhan also previously co-authoreda studythat showed how a large share of Berlin’s vegetable consumption could be produced within the city. “This [supermarket] could also be an inspiration for other people to do something together,” says Pradhan.Leschke’s ambitions are bigger than just Berlin. He hopes to build at least 20 supermarket rooftop farms over the next 10 years, and ideally at least one in every REWE region in the next five years.“If we can produce in Germany year-round, we should,” he said, emphasising the importance of becoming independent of global supply chains.But for now, that does not seem to be on customers’ minds. At the salad display, a customer eyes the selection, opting for two bags of the Lankwitz lettuce. Another makes a beeline for the local variety. As she explains, she’s making a salad of tomato and mozzarella later, and she likes the idea of using the greenhouse greens. After all, it’s fresh from the roof.View image in fullscreenThe rooftop greenhouse at the Felix Thomas REWE supermarket in Lankwitz, Berlin.Photograph: Christoph GroßeExplore more on these topicsThe alternativesGermanyEuropeFoodFood sciencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: They drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save lives | Tornadoes | The Guardian
description: Tornadoes kill hundreds each decade in the US. These researchers are investigating why some storms produce twisters – despite the fatal risks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tornadoes kill hundreds each decade in the US. These researchers are investigating why some storms produce twisters – despite the fatal risks
Content: View of a tornado research vehicle through the windshield of the photographer’s rental car after a 14-hour unsuccessful tornado chase across multiple states in southern Iowa, on 10 June 2026.Photograph: Cheney OrrView image in fullscreenView of a tornado research vehicle through the windshield of the photographer’s rental car after a 14-hour unsuccessful tornado chase across multiple states in southern Iowa, on 10 June 2026.Photograph: Cheney OrrTornadoesThey drive toward tornadoes. We went with them to see how their work could save livesTornadoes kill hundreds each decade in the US. These researchers are investigating why some storms produce twisters – despite the fatal risksMasha HamiltonFri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 14.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a narrow road in southern Iowa, my phone shrieked.Tornadowarning. Take shelter now in a basement or an interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building.Again, the alert sounded. Then again. As if shelter were a choice.I peered through a peephole of scratched glass, wedged into the lead storm-chasing truck with tornado researchers Josh Wurman and Karen Kosiba.On either side of us, only fields. No houses. No basements. No sturdy buildings. The dark belly of a storm dragged across a horizon gone an eerie green.For tornado chasers, it was a near perfect sky.My son Cheney, a photojournalist, was somewhere behind us in a rental car alongside two other research vehicles. The convoy was strung out across miles of highway. He had been tracking my location, but now I had lost cell service.I couldn’t reach him. I kept dialing. No answer.When a call finally went through, Cheney told me the wind was driving the rain so hard the road had disappeared.“I’m scared,” he said.Blinded, he had turned one way, then the other. Finally, he stopped. Either direction, he feared, could put him in a tornado’s path.Cheney was no stranger to danger. He has covered Ukraine during wartime, spent a New Year’s Eve alone in a car reporting on Chicago homicides, and crisscrossed the country documenting violent weather, including the devastating 2021 tornado in Mayfield, Kentucky.I hadn’t heard him express fear since childhood.Then he said it again. “I’m scared. I don’t know what to do.”About 1,200 tornadoes strike the United States every year. Between 2020 and 2025, they killed roughly 410 people, injured nearly 3,800 and caused about $8.5bn in reported property damage.The tornado map is changing too. A 2024 study found 25% fewer moderate-or-stronger tornadoes in the western US and 12% more in the east, where mobile homes are more prevalent, basements to get to safety are scarcer, and twisters more likely to strike at night.View image in fullscreenLeft to right: Josh Wurman and Karen Kosiba observe iridescent clouds, showing bands of pastel colors along their edges, in Washburn, North Dakota, on 9 June 2026.Photograph: Cheney OrrSometimes the change from ordinary to deadly takes only minutes. Several months earlier, physician Jason Persoff had told me about chasing near Joplin, Missouri, in May 2011. A little after 5pm, he and his partner began looking for hotel rooms, figuring they were done for the day.“Suddenly, it was as if someone vomited on the radar,” Persoff remembered. “It was incredible.”A violent tornado seemed to emerge from the sky almost fully formed. Its sound lodged deep in Persoff’s body. “I felt irrational fear,” he said. “Like a primal warning.”They pulled over to help stranded truckers as police arrived. Persoff told one officer he was a physician.“I hope you don’t work at St John’s,” the officer told him. “That hospital’s been destroyed.”“That’s still one of the most terrifying things I’ve ever heard,” Persoff said.More than 150 people were killed in that tornado.Wurman, whose team I traveled with, is among the researchers trying to understand why some storms produce tornadoes while others do not, and what tornado winds do close to the ground – knowledge that could improve warnings and help engineers design buildings to withstand them.But the systems built to study and forecast tornadoes are under strain.View image in fullscreenA team of storm chasers  follows tornadoes on Highway 11 near Wakita, Oklahoma, on 10 May 2010.Photograph: Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service/Getty ImagesIn the first four months of 2025, the National Weather Service lost roughly 13% of its workforce – more than 560 employees – to firings, retirements, resignations and attrition.By the 2026 storm season, the agency was hiring again, but staffing gaps remained, and some stations were unable to maintain the twice-daily weather-balloon launches on which forecasters and researchers rely.Scientists I spoke with said they had lost confidence in forecast guidance. Chris Weiss of Texas Tech, who led a parallel chase team with the National Severe Storms Laboratory, was blunt: “I don’t remember when a suite of models has performed as poorly as this year.”Frustrated by the blurred, distant view from fixed-site radar, Wurman invented the Doppler on Wheels – mobile radar laboratories known as DOWs – three decades ago. Filling one with diesel costs about $1,000, and that is the inexpensive part: the greater investment lies in the trucks, trained graduate students and experienced crews that take years to build.But funding has become more uncertain. By the end of this field season, neither Wurman’s team nor Weiss’s could count on support for the next one.Cessily Skinner, whose family has lost two homes to tornadoes in west-central Georgia, closely monitors every approaching storm. Now the cuts give her another reason to fear: “As someone who lived through a storm with all the data in place,” she said, “it’s terrifying to think, ‘OK, so now we reallyareguessing.’”View image in fullscreenPeople react as they see the wreckage of their home in the aftermath of a tornado, after a volatile storm system tore through the US south and midwest in Glenallen, Missouri, on 5 April 2023.Photograph: Cheney Orr/ReutersWith Cheney still on the line, a team member plotted his location against the storm. The radar could see what he could not. A tornado we were tracking was east of him and moving east. Cheney should be safe, she said, as long as he stayed put and waited it out.I repeated this to him.As we spoke, the rain loosened. The sky lifted. The road reappeared. Cheney pressed the gas and began closing the distance between us.The second radar truck arrived first. Fifteen long minutes later, Cheney’s rental car came into view.Relief and disappointment arrived together. The convoy was whole again. But the day had yielded none of the data the scientists had come for.Several tornadoes touched down across the region that afternoon. None crossed the roads where our instruments were waiting.The storms left behind a sky ribboned with dark clouds. Some team members stood outside the trucks and applauded its beauty, lifting their phones for photographs. Wurman and Kosiba were not among them. They were already studying the models, deciding where the team should spend the night to be best positioned for morning.Tornadoes offer enough spectacle to draw film-makers, thrill-seekers, and carloads of chasers with cameras. But scientists who chase for data need more than drama. They need geometry: an open horizon, a road in and a road out, a storm that forms where the instruments can reach it.Even when everything lines up, a mobile radar crew can spend weeks following one promising storm after another, only to watch each weaken and dissolve before the instruments capture the measurements they came for.Why do they keep doing it?For data analyst Paul Robinson, the pull started with an image on television: Dorothy clutching Toto, calling for Auntie Em as a black twister writhed in the distance.View image in fullscreenPaul Robinson stands in the doorway of a Doppler on Wheels (DOW) vehicle while taking a short break in a Walmart parking lot during a multistate tornado chase in rural Illinois.Photograph: Cheney Orr“The Wizard of Oz is still my favorite movie tornado,” he said. “For me, it captures the feeling.” Growing up in West Virginia, he began keeping a notebook, recording the weather whenever it turned severe.But 31 May 1985, turned that interest into purpose.Everyone on this team seems to carry a storm they cannot forget. Robinson’s was not a single tornado but an outbreak: 43 twisters tearing across Ohio, Pennsylvania, New York and Ontario, killing 89 people.“That convinced me that maybe I could do some good by going into tornado research,” Robinson said.Research scientist Trevor White’s defining storm came later, on 24 May 2016, near Dodge City, Kansas.“Every chaser and their mother came out,” he recalled. “We were on it from the time it was a small cumulus cloud. I had never seen a storm that could effortlessly produce tornadoes. I counted three on the ground at the same time.”In two hours, a dozen tornadoes formed beneath the supercell. It was nearly perfect in the way that mattered most: no one died, and the tornadoes remained mostly over open country.But even experienced researchers cannot always remain beyond a tornado’s reach.In 2013, veteran tornado researcher Tim Samaras was killed near El Reno, Oklahoma, along with his son Paul and colleague Carl Young. Samaras was Wurman’s friend. Wurman’s team was tracking the same tornado that day.Asked by a reporter whether the deaths made him reconsider his work, Wurman noted that covering extreme weather “isn’t dangerous statistically”. Samaras, he said, was among the most responsible chasers he knew. Wurman would not speculate about what had gone wrong but said his own team would review its procedures.Wurman and his colleagues then returned to the data, reconstructing the motion of the nearly impossible-to-see subvortex that had overtaken Samaras and his team.He pursues the sky at its most theatrical without surrendering to drama himself. He would rather leave a question open than force an answer the data cannot support.“I wish this research were more of a eureka thing,” Wurman said, “but it’s not. We can’t do laboratory-type experiments. We can’t put 10,000 patients into a study. Meteorology is horrible that way. We’re trying to understand what’s special about the circumstances where tornadoes form and what it looks like when they do. But we can’t control the environment.”“Every time we’re in a disaster area, I carry with me the trauma of people who survive it,” White told me. “I don’t know if we can do anything to ease the impact of that experience, but I’ll never stop searching. The only thing worse than a human tragedy is a human tragedy where you can’t learn anything.”View image in fullscreenA woman inspects her wrecked bedroom in the aftermath of a tornado in Wynne, Arkansas, on 1 April 2023.Photograph: Cheney Orr/ReutersA mile outside Good Hope, Illinois, the deployment order came. Our truck slid to a halt on the shoulder of a two-lane road slick with rain.Robinson jumped out to unleash the radar dish. It began sweeping the sky, each rotation shuddering through the vehicle.Back in the driver’s seat, he talked to himself – “c’mon, c’mon” – as he worked the controls to lower a stabilizing pad into the mud, trying to keep the vehicle’s right side from sinking. He kept the left wheels on the pavement, he told me later, in case we needed to move fast toward – or away from – a tornado.In the back, White balanced one keyboard on his lap and kept several others within reach. Four screens glowed in front of him.“Frustrating,” Robinson murmured. “We’re getting data, but I want to see it; I want to see the fury.”The horizon closed around us. From the front passenger seat, I watched a low shelf of black clouds over the cornfields, its ragged underside reaching down in unfinished gestures.The walkie-talkie crackled, then Wurman’s voice came through. “What do you see?”No one answered immediately. White and Robinson studied the screens and conferred quietly in technical shorthand. They were looking for a hook curling in the rain, a couplet tightening in the wind field, some sign that the atmosphere had made up its mind.The clouds kept darkening. The dish kept turning. The truck kept shuddering. Robinson waited through one scan, then another, watching new data appear on the screens over White’s shoulder.Finally he spoke, his voice tight. “It’s falling apart, isn’t it?”After a few more minutes, Wurman confirmed he saw the same. He called out a new waypoint and then we were speeding again down a country road, pursuing the uneasy hope at the center of this work: a storm dangerous enough to teach but merciful enough to spare.When things align, the value of a single intercept can endure for years. On 18 May 2013, the team captured data from an EF4 tornado near Rozel, Kansas. It remained on the ground for about 30 minutes, long enough for the researchers to hold position and gather unusually rich measurements.“That gave us a chance to dig in deep,” Kosiba said. “And that data is still being used by engineers today. That’s why you have to keep going out, even with the misses. We’re in it for the long haul.”A 2024 study co-authored by Wurman and Kosiba analyzed mobile-radar wind profiles from 36 tornadoes. Those findings helped shape new national standards for designing buildings to withstand tornado winds, showing the potential impact of readings collected in the path of storms.This is the scale on which science advances: one measurement clarifying another, a dataset enduring long after the tornado itself disappears.Behind every chase is a life forced to accommodate the forecast. We had driven 2,000 miles in three days, from dawn until after dark, crossing and recrossing North Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Illinois. Wurman’s team had gone weeks without the intercept they needed. Weiss’s team had endured an equally disappointing season.“We put in the same effort for fewer results,” Weiss told me. “We have lives and families, and we’re making a lot of sacrifices. So when it doesn’t work out, it eats at you.”White has a soft spot for hummingbirds. He keeps several feeders at home, and goes to great lengths to find someone to refill them when he’s gone. His absence is measured out in sugar water. He carries a small stuffed hummingbird on the road.“I told my wife a week ago we’d be home tomorrow. Instead, we are still out here, and there’s no end in sight,” he said. “But there’s something fundamental about this research that draws me in. The best version of me is the version that does this work.”View image in fullscreenA support scientist drives the tornado scout vehicle as they chase a supercell thunderstorm on 9 May 2017 in Lamb county, Texas.Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty ImagesBefore this trip, I had imagined storm chasing as a form of appetite, the desire to see the most violent thing the sky could make. I hadn’t understood its strange rhythm: tedious hours beneath empty skies, then sudden races down country roads, decisions pressed into seconds, and moments of stark fear.The work demands patience when nothing happens and clear judgment when everything happens at once. Inside the truck, it looked less like appetite and more like devotion: painstaking, deliberate, largely invisible.In a culture that rewards quick verdicts and emphatic claims, these scientists let the sky contradict them. They reverse direction and answer to evidence rather than personal conviction. That discipline feels radical.Years from now, the data they gather may become a stronger roof, an earlier warning, hospital walls that hold. The researchers may never know whose lives their persistence reaches.That last night with Wurman’s team, I wrote three lines in my notebook:We went storm chasing.Nothing happened.We learned a lot.Explore more on these topicsTornadoesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Curse of the Nile’s gold: how Sudan is losing its fertile fields and ability to produce food | Global development | The Guardian
description: An artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and society
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and society
Content: Sudanese Rapid Support Forces (RSF) display gold bars seized from a plane that landed at Khartoum airport in an investigation into possible smuggling.Photograph: Mohamed Nureldin Abdallah/ReutersView image in fullscreenSudanese Rapid Support Forces (RSF) display gold bars seized from a plane that landed at Khartoum airport in an investigation into possible smuggling.Photograph: Mohamed Nureldin Abdallah/ReutersGlobal developmentCurse of the Nile’s gold: how Sudan is losing its fertile fields and ability to produce foodAn artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and societySupported byAbout this contentSamira Hassan Khalifa in Abu HamadFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Abu Hamad, on the banks of the Nile, verdant orchards, gardens and fields once produced a bounty of dates, citrus fruits, winter grains and cereals for the towns and cities of easternSudan, including Khartoum and Port Sudan.Today, the land looks drastically different. Trees have been cut down, agricultural areas cleared, and farms have been replaced by shops and commercial sites. Dotted around the town and its outskirts, more than 700 mounds of grey waste are poisoning the soil, water and air. The mounds are the toxic remnants of artisanal gold mining, a practice that began in about 2008 and has intensified over the past six years.In 2024, artisanal operations accounted formore than 90% of Sudan’s gold production. And Abu Hamad in River Nile state has become one of thelargest gold-mining and trade towns in the country.Desperate for income, locals process tailings, the byproduct of artisanal mining, whichcontains about 70% of goldand is extracted using chemicals such as cyanide, mercury or thiourea, a compound that was initially thought to be relatively safe.The creeping toxicity has decimated the agricultural foundation of Abu Hamad, transforming the town’s tranquil way of life into a daily battle against pollution and disease. Flood waters carrying runoff from mining sites have caused massive spikes in soil salinity, leading to a catastrophic decline in food production. Mohamed Fathi al-Rahman al-Khalifa, a local farmer, has watched the soil turn hostile.View image in fullscreenA gold milling station in Abu HamedPhotograph: Ayin“When the trees were still very young, the first harvest produced nearly four truckloads of oranges. Today, production does not exceed half a truckload,” Al-Khalifa says, highlighting the unnatural stunting of his orchards.The agricultural collapse across all major staples is staggering, say farmers. A single acre (0.4 hectares) of wheat that historically yielded between 40 and 60 sacks now produces 12 to 18 sacks.Similarly, fava bean yields have plummeted from an average of 40 to 50 sacks perfeddan(a unit of land equivalent to about an acre, 0.4 hectares) to just three or four, according to local farmers. Even fully mature orange groves that should easily produce 10 truckloads of fruit now yield less than half a truckload, they say, with much of the harvest arriving misshapen and thick-peeled.Al-Khalifa warns of a looming catastrophe that extends far beyond the borders of River Nile state. “Food security is no longer merely a local issue affecting Abu Hamad. It has become a national issue that concerns Sudan as a whole.View image in fullscreenA defector from the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) arrives after surrendering to the Sudanese military in the west of Omdurman last month.Photograph: AFP/Getty Images“Sudan possesses enormous agricultural potential and is crossed by the Nile River, [meaning] agricultural products should be abundant and affordable, yet the reality is quite different. Today, we see rising prices for vegetables and farm products across different states and cities,” he says.The tragedy of Abu Hamad is not isolated. It is deeply entangled in Sudan’s war, now in its fourth year. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) rely heavily on the gold sector. Since the war started in April 2023, both sides have been involved in controlling mining, says researcher Suliman Baldo of the thinktank Sudan Transparency and Policy Tracker.Last year, the mining sector generated approximately $1.8bn (£1.3bn) in revenue from production and exports,producing roughly 75 tonnesof gold over the year and exceeding the SAF-controlled government’s target by13%.This gold accounted for58% of Sudan’s total export valuein the SAF-controlled areas. The actual profit margin, however, may prove much higher, given the high level ofgold smuggling across the border into Egypt. Production and trade levels among theRSF-controlled minesremain undocumented.For the most part, Sudan’s war has allowed mining operations and gold trading to take place unabated and unregulated. According to Mubarak al-Fadil al-Mahdi, the head of the Umma party, a former investment minister and a businessman with ties to the gold sector, there is very little incentive for the warring parties to stop these practices.“This is one of the Sudanese army’s most important incentives to perpetuate the war and prevent it from ending so that it can benefit from the corruption of these funds,” al-Mahdi says. “These funds are not subject to any oversight and are solely managed by the army commander and the governor of the central bank.”The devastating impact of this unregulated mining is equally visible in the region’s pastures. Abu al-Qasim al-Khazin, a livestock herder from the Al-Sharik locality within the district of Abu Hamad, paints a grim picture of the toll the chemical runoff is taking on local fauna.View image in fullscreenAbu al-Qasim al-Khazin, a livestock herder in Abu Hamed.Photograph: Ayin“We have seen numerous cases of animals born completely without hair [and] extremely unusual cases in which animals were born without eyes,” Al-Khazin explains.The toxins affect more than just physical development. “In some cases, the animals appeared to have completely lost their normal behaviour – some people described their condition as resembling madness.”The environmental disaster has inevitably become a public health emergency.Analysis in 2022revealed that 20% of drinking water samples contained mercury.A local doctor and medical activist, who asked to remain anonymous for security reasons, says that health issues previously rare in the area are now everyday realities. “Among these concerns is the rising rate of miscarriages among pregnant women, as well as cases of congenital abnormalities in foetuses,” they say.The strain on local healthcare is immense, with the dialysis centre in Abu Hamad now serving close to 100 patients – far beyond its original intended capacity – after a rise in kidney failure.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe danger peaks during the rainy season, when the lethal grey mounds are disturbed. “During the rainy season two years ago, we witnessed mining waste and tailings being washed away by flood waters and carried into residential neighbourhoods,” the doctor says.Hashim Abdelazim al-Mahi, an engineer and local environmental activist, has tracked the devastatingreality of the pollution. He points to the introduction of thiourea, as an alternative to cyanide in the gold extraction process.“When thiourea was first introduced into Sudan [in 2017] it was promoted as an environmentally friendly material. However, reality has shown otherwise,” Abdelazim says.According to recent local medical records, approximately one out of every 50 children is born with some form of serious congenital abnormality, including cleft lip conditions and complex cases such as skull deformities.View image in fullscreenMoahmed Ahmed Abdelaziz, the headteacher of the Northern Boy’s School.Photograph: AyinDespite the risks, Abdelazim is not demanding a complete end to the industry but rather an end to the negligence. “Of course [gold] mining will continue. We cannot expect the industry to stop completely,” he says. “Mining should not stop, but the state must stop these harmful practices linked to the industry and address them seriously; human health should remain a priority for the state and should never be compromised or bargained away.”As the land dies, the social fabric of Abu Hamad is unravelling. Driven by soaring poverty and the allure of quick profits, young men are abandoning their education to enter high-risk mining operations.Mohamed Ahmed Abdelaziz, the headteacher of the Northern Boys’ School in Ghariya, has watched his classrooms empty. Primary school classes have dropped from 75 pupils to 20, and secondary classes show identical attrition. “A student may see someone working in mining who has bought a vehicle or earned a substantial income within a short period and begin to ask himself, ‘Why should I continue studying?’” he says.The long-term consequences of this shift in community priorities is deeply troubling to the veteran educator. “If large numbers of students continue to abandon their studies, society will lose the teachers, doctors, engineers, university professors and other professionals it needs for development.”For the young men in the pits, survival, not greed, drives their decision. Al-Daw Adam Jibril Mohammed, a high-achieving student, dropped out of university when he could no longer afford the tuition.View image in fullscreenA group of young artisanal miners in Abu Hamed.Photograph: Ayin“I felt that education required many years of study, while mining offered immediate and direct financial returns,” Adam says. However, the reality of the work is gruelling and far from a guaranteed payday. “A person may work an entire day and find nothing whatsoever; income from mining is uncertain and depends largely on luck.”In July, the prime minister, Kamil Idris, who is part of the army-controlled government, ordered theimmediate removal of all gold-processing millsfrom residential and military areas. The directive will also introduce mandatory ID cards for miners and increased security in mining regions. In 2024, authorities also tried toban the use of mixers such as mercury and cyanidein Wadi Halfa, Northern state, and South Kordofan state. But these piecemeal efforts have proved too little, too late.In Abu Hamad, the contaminated mounds of toxic soil and gravel remain exposed and untreated. As the rainy season approaches, the risk of these toxins seeping into the Nile River increases.While the war rages on, the residents of Abu Hamad must navigate a landscape permanently altered by human greed. Until state authorities intervene to regulate the informal sector and enforce safe processing methods, the grey mounds will continue to multiply. For the farmers, herders, doctors and children of Abu Hamad, the gold rush has yielded little wealth – only a slow, relentless poison.This story by independent Sudanese outlet Ayin Network is supported by the Impact Reporting programme of the Institute for War & Peace Reporting (iwpr.net)Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSudanGlobal healthPollutionMining (Environment)Food securityMining (Business)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Mail on Sunday ends up funding state school scholarship via payout to MP  | University of Derby | The Guardian
description: Labour’s Catherine Atkinson says she will give students £5,000 paid to her by paper that falsely accused her of concealing private school education
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Labour’s Catherine Atkinson says she will give students £5,000 paid to her by paper that falsely accused her of concealing private school education
Content: Catherine Atkinson said she would fund scholarships for local law students at the University of Derby who – like her – attended state schools.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenCatherine Atkinson said she would fund scholarships for local law students at the University of Derby who – like her – attended state schools.Photograph: House of CommonsUniversity of DerbyMail on Sunday ends up funding state school scholarship via payout to MPLabour’s Catherine Atkinson says she will give students £5,000 paid to her by  paper that falsely accused her of concealing private school educationRichard AdamsEducation editorFri 11 Sep 2026 12.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA new scholarship supporting state-educated students will be inadvertently funded by theMail on Sunday(MoS), using a payout it made after being threatened with legal action by the Labour MP Catherine Atkinson.The Derby North MP says she will use the proceeds of about £5,000 from the newspaper to fund scholarships for local law students at theUniversity of Derbywho – like her – attended state schools.In early July the MoS said Atkinson attended a private school and accused her of concealing it from her biographical entry in Who’s Who.Cambridge college urged to drop ‘immoral’ private school recruitment driveRead moreDespite Atkinson correcting the journalists who contacted her, the MoS published an article making the false claim, accompanied by a large photograph of the MP.
