The newspaperlater apologisedand paid damages and legal costs after the former lawyer responded firmly that she had attended state schools.“I am grateful for the state-school education that helped me build a 17-year career as a barrister,” said Atkinson, who attended Sacred Heart high school, a Catholic comprehensive in Hammersmith, west London.“The claim that I had concealed a private education from my constituents was false. I am using the money from this settlement to support students from Derby’s state schools in beginning their own careers in law.“Strengthening our justice system means taking seriously who gets the opportunity to work in it. When financial barriers keep capable people out of the profession, the public loses the benefit of their talent.“The legal profession has a shared responsibility to help remove those barriers. We should be looking for future lawyers in every school and supporting those who need help to get started.“There are students in Derby today who could spend their careers defending the rights of others. They deserve the opportunity to build that future.”Atkinson was elected at the 2024 general election as MP for Derby North, where the University of Derby’s law school is situated.At least £5,000 from the settlement after expenses will go towards the Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award, providing a £500 award each year for at least 10 years. The award will be open to first-year law students who were educated at a state school within the city of Derby.Prof Kathryn Mitchell, the university’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed Atkinson’s support.Mitchell said: “At the University of Derby we firmly believe in the transformative nature of education and, as a champion of social mobility and inclusion, aim to create opportunities for all across our region and beyond, regardless of age, background or location.“We want talented students from Derby’s state comprehensive schools to have every opportunity to pursue a career in law.“The Catherine Atkinson future lawyers award will provide financial support as recipients begin their degrees. We welcome Catherine’s commitment to social mobility and her investment in local students over the next 10 years.”DMG Media, which owns AssociatedNewspapersand the MoS, was contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsUniversity of DerbyDerbyStudentsMail on SundayDaily Mail & General TrustSchoolsLawnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK man admits using online network for sexual crimes against unconscious woman | Crime | The Guardian
description: Darren Conway pleads guilty to voyeurism and encouraging a husband to abuse his wife
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Darren Conway pleads guilty to voyeurism and encouraging a husband to abuse his wife
Content: Darren Conway ‘put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes’, police said.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PAView image in fullscreenDarren Conway ‘put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes’, police said.Photograph: Metropolitan police/PACrimeUK man admits using online network for sexual crimes against unconscious womanDarren Conway pleads guilty to voyeurism and encouraging a husband to abuse his wifeKevin RawlinsonFri 11 Sep 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has admitted using an online sexual abuse network to commit a host of sexual crimes, along with another man, against the latter’s unconscious wife.Darren Conway, 52, pleaded guilty to 11 charges at Wood Green crown court. They included voyeurism, possession of extreme pornography and encouraging the other man to sexually abuse his wife on Conway’s behalf.“Conway’s actions were shocking,” said Scotland Yard’s Commander Andy Day. “By encouraging others to engage in sexual offending against victims who were unconscious, asleep, or otherwise stupefied, he has put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes – all for his own sexual gratification.”Day said it was a case of “drug-facilitated sexual offending” that could have a “lasting and devastating impacts on its victims”.Conway solicited naked images of sleeping women on at least 10 occasions between 2023 and 2026, according to the indictment. While most of the charges to which he pleaded guilty on Friday related to the wife of the man with whom he was in contact, police fear there are many more victims. Officers said they were still working to identify others in footage found on Conway’s devices – adding that, “while much of the offending is believed to have taken place in the UK, it is also possible that some victims are based overseas”.The prosecutor Alexander Agbamu said: “The indictment reflects the defendant’s involvement in an online forum which connects others who are involved in organised sexual offending and domestic abuse.” The Metropolitan police said the forum was uncovered in October 2025 in the wake of the Gisèle Pelicot case in France. Its discovery precipitated the establishment of a national coordination group led by the National Crime Agency.Scotland Yard said Conway was arrested on 30 July after being identified as one of the groupchat members. Messages officers found on his devices showed he had been encouraging fellow members to “engage in drug-facilitated sexual offending, alongside images and videos of a sexual nature”, the Met police said.Police discovered Conway had urged the other man to remove his wife’s clothing and underwear, and to commit sexual offences against her. “He later requested that the other member share images while they sexually assaulted her … The women were unaware that he was viewing them and unable to provide consent.”Tracy Easton, the chief crown prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service in south London said: “Darren Conway committed vile acts against women in their own homes, a place where they should have been safe. Organised drug-facilitated sexual assault is abhorrent and we are determined to work with policing to bring offenders to justice. I hope this guilty plea gives confidence to anyone who believes they may have been subjected to similar abuse to come forward.”The judge John Dodd KC told Conway he would be sentenced on 30 October.Explore more on these topicsCrimeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: RNLI reports ‘significant’ donations boost after being targeted by far right over small boats | RNLI | The Guardian
description: Charity condemns ‘disgraceful’ intimidation and insists it will continue core purpose of saving lives at sea
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Charity condemns ‘disgraceful’ intimidation and insists it will continue core purpose of saving lives at sea
Content: Police officers outside the Royal National Lifeboat Institute building in Poole, Dorset, on Tuesday amid a far-right protest.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreenPolice officers outside the Royal National Lifeboat Institute building in Poole, Dorset, on Tuesday amid a far-right protest.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PARNLIRNLI reports ‘significant’ donations boost after being targeted by far right over small boatsCharity condemns ‘disgraceful’ intimidation and insists it will continue core purpose of saving lives at seaCaroline DaviesFri 11 Sep 2026 08.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) has had a “significant” boost in donations since becoming a target of far-right agitators protesting over small boat crossings.The charity’s staff and volunteers have been subjected to “online and physical abuse” after involvement in a rescue on Sunday in which a dinghy carrying asylum seekers was brought into Portsmouth.RNLI vice-president Sir Robin Knox-Johnston condemned the intimidation as “frankly quite disgraceful”, amid calls by far-right protesters for people to stop donating.An RNLI spokesperson said:‘We’ve seen a significant increase in the number of donations we have received this week, and we’ve welcomed a number of new supporters to our charity.“As always, we’re so grateful for the support we receive from our amazing supporters, without them we would not be able to deliver our vital lifesaving service. Sadly, we have also been contacted by a number of supporters and members of the public who have informed us that they wish to withdraw their support in recent days.“Everyone at the RNLI remains focused on our core purpose of saving lives at sea.”The charity has increased security measures and said it would continue to rescue those in danger in the Channel.After lifeboats took 120 asylum seekers intercepted off the Isle of Wight to Eastney in Langstone Harbour on Sunday, some crew members were targeted by protesters, with their photos and names shared in posts on social media.OnWednesday evening, dozens of Dorset policeofficers were posted outside the charity’s headquarters in Poole as about 50 people gathered to protest against the RNLI’s involvement.Hampshire police have been patrolling RNLI sites, while the Sussex force was investigating “offensive and threatening” remarks made on social media.On Friday, Poole Old Lifeboat Museum said it had made the decision to close after several incidents of “protesters verbally assaulting our volunteers”,the BBC reported.Knox-Johnston said of the charity being targeted: “Like many supporters of the RNLI, I am very angry about it because they are picking on the wrong people.“These are volunteers who risk their lives to go out and save anyone at sea” Knox-Johnson, the first solo sailor to circumnavigate the world non-stop, told BBC Radio Solent. “What people don’t seem to understand is the RNLI don’t go out looking for people – they only go out when specifically asked by the coastguard, whose job is safety of life at sea – regardless of nationality.“They are doing their job, they are saying there are people whose lives are in danger – RNLI please can you send a boat and remove the risk.“If you want this to stop the government have got to stop it, but picking on RNLI crews who are doing the job they are trained to do is frankly quite disgraceful.”The RNLI has advised volunteers that they should consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing if they feel this might put them at risk. They have also been advised that they should feel empowered to close RNLI shops or lifeboat stations if they feel in danger.Volunteers have been asked to challenge people near lifeboat stations if they do not have ID, but advised not to engage with members of the public and asked to explain the RNLI’s actions.The charityemphasised earlier this weekthat responding to small boats was only a tiny percentage of its work and updated its webpage explaining its work in the Channel. It described rumours that the RNLI housed asylum seekers on its premises, or that there were RNLI missions to move migrants to secret locations as “completely baseless and untrue”.RNLI lifeboats launched 9,058 times in 2025 but only 109 of those call-outs were to small boats in the Channel, representing 1.2% of its rescue work. Almost 95% of those who crossed the Channel in small boats last year were picked up by the UK Border Force, it said.Explore more on these topicsRNLIThe far rightCharitiesVoluntary sectorProtestImmigration and asylumFar rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOs | Immigration and asylum | The Guardian
description: Rights groups say those missing after being deported under one in, one out deal include dozens of age-disputed children
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: Rights groups say those missing after being deported under one in, one out deal include dozens of age-disputed children
Content: About 1,400 people who arrived in the UK on small boats have been returned to France since September 2025.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAbout 1,400 people who arrived in the UK on small boats have been returned to France since September 2025.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesImmigration and asylumHundreds of asylum seekers removed from UK to France have disappeared, say NGOsRights groups say those missing after being deported under one in, one out deal include dozens of age-disputed childrenUK politics live – latest updatesDiane TaylorFri 11 Sep 2026 07.33 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of asylum seekers including at least 41 age-disputed children who were removed toFranceunder the “one in, one out” deal have disappeared, human rights organisations have said.The pilot scheme was hailed as “groundbreaking” by the former prime minister Keir Starmer when he and the French president, Emmanuel Macron,announced itin July 2025. Under a treaty drawn up for this agreement, it forcibly returns small-boat asylum seekers to France in exchange for others brought legally to the UK from France.‘I would rather die than return to France’: the brutal reality of the UK’s one in, one out schemeRead moreThe deal isdue to expire on 1 Octoberand at the moment it is not known what, if anything, will replace it.The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, is reportedly pushing for the deal to be extended and scaled up, and the French government has indicated it wants the scheme to be expanded Europe-wide rather than France having to accept small-boat returnees alone.One French politician told the Guardian that so far France’s overtures to other countries to take back a share of small-boat asylum seekers had received a negative response.View image in fullscreenA refugee folding a blanket at a makeshift camp on the outskirts of Calais.Photograph: Kiran Ridley/Getty ImagesAbout 1,400 small-boat arrivals have been returned to France since September 2025, just 4% of 32,000 who have crossed the Channel since the deal was signed. These figures do not include the significant minority who have come back to the UK a second time, some of whom are now living under the radar here. The UK and Franceamended the treatyto allow for people returning to the UK in lorries to be sent back to France a second time.At a meeting in parliament this week chaired by Mike German, a general rapporteur on asylum and migration policy for the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe, and Alex Sobel, the new chair of parliament’s joint committee on human rights, parliamentarians were told about the disappearances and other concerns about the scheme by NGO representatives working on the ground.Maddie Harris, the director of the Humans For Rights Network, said several NGOs had between them compiled a list of at least 41 age-disputed children and young people whom they claimed had been unlawfully returned to France. It is unlawful to detain lone children in adult immigration detention centres, and they are excluded from the one in, one out treaty.TheHome Officedisputed this and told the Guardian: “This is categorically untrue. Nobody has been returned to France where their age is in dispute.“Every detained person is advised of their right to legal representation and how they can obtain such representation within 24 hours of arrival at an immigration removal centre. Age assessments are carried out to maintain the integrity of our border, while ensuring those genuinely under 18 receive the appropriate support.”View image in fullscreenA screengrab from video issued by the Home Office shows Border Force officers processing small-boat migrants, including biometric and security checks, before their relocation to an immigration removal centre to await their return to France.Photograph: Home Office/PAHowever, the prisons and detention Independent Monitoring Boards have reported that almost a hundred childrenhad been identified as unlawfully detained as adultsfor the scheme. The IMBs’ interim chair, Jane Leech, attended the meeting and raised concerns that some people were being unlawfully detained for the scheme because the Home Office was “detaining more people than they can remove”.French politicians have told the Guardian that only 200 people forcibly returned to France were still in contact with the authorities there, with hundreds of others having gone underground in countries across Europe.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian has interviewed dozens of returnees who are no longer in contact with the French authorities and are living underground in Europe. They say they have disappeared due to hostility from the French authorities, pressure to return to their home countries where they believe they will be unsafe, or the threat of being forced back to other European countries such as Bulgaria that they passed through on their journeys.Home Office sources said that what happened to people once they were returned to France was a matter for the French authorities. France’s interior ministry declined to comment on the disappearances.View image in fullscreenBorder Force officers processing small-boat arrivals detained under the one in, one out deal at the Manston immigration centre in Kent.Photograph: Home Office/PAHarris said the forced return of lone children to France was “shameful”. She said: “We support many children detained under this scheme and attempt to secure their release. However, at least 41 children have been removed from the UK to France and their whereabouts is currently unknown. The vast majority of these children have experienced acute violence and exploitation and are now without protection somewhere in Europe.”Nihal Osman, a programme coordinator for Médecins Sans Frontières, told the parliamentary meeting that asylum seekers were returned to France from the UK in a “deeply concerning” condition, with many displaying severe psychological symptoms such as flashbacks, acute anxiety, self-harm, suicidal thoughts and psychological breakdown.“What we are witnessing is the accumulation of trauma on trauma,” she said.Sobel said he was “deeply concerned” about the ongoing securitisation of the French border to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel to the UK. “The French police are doing things it would be unacceptable for British police to do,” he said.Explore more on these topicsImmigration and asylumHome OfficeFranceEuropeHuman rightsChildrenChild protectionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Republican senator fires aide who used Nazi soldiers as Facebook profile picture | Republicans | The Guardian
description: Washington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on Spotify
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Washington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on Spotify
Content: Jon Husted, whose Senate race is on a knife-edge, in Dallas on Wednesday. The Husted campaign did not say whether Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his hiring.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Husted, whose Senate race is on a knife-edge, in Dallas on Wednesday. The Husted campaign did not say whether Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his hiring.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesRepublicansRepublican senator fires aide who used Nazi soldiers as Facebook profile pictureWashington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on SpotifyRobert Taitin WashingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Republican senator forOhio, Jon Husted, has fired an aide who was discovered to have used a photo of Nazi SS soldiers as his Facebook profile photo.Stephen Woytek was appointed as Husted’s political director last month in the senator’s knife-edge re-election contest against former Democrat senator Sherrod Brown.According to the Washington Post, Husted had decided to “part ways” with Woytek, 25, after learning that his Facebook profile showed he followed a military re-enactment group called LAH Living History Unit, which portrays the 1st SS Panzer division.The group’s website says its members dress up as the Leibstandarte, a Waffen-SS armored division that began as Adolf Hitler’s bodyguards. LAH says the Leibstandarte “came to symbolize the highest dedication to duty and individual as well as collective loyalty”. The group claims to be “non-political” and insists is disavows “political and religious persecution” that happened the second world war.A Spotify playlist recently created by an account bearing Woytek’s name hailed the former racist white-minority regime of Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe, seen as a symbol of white supremacy by some racist groups.In a statement, a spokesperson for Husted said the campaign had ended its relationship with Woytek.“While he denies negative intent, his social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” the spokesperson said. “Senator Husted demands better of those who represent him. Upon learning about the social media posts today, Senator Husted made the immediate decision to part ways.”The campaign did not respond to the Post’s questions about whether and how Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his appointment, the newspaper reported.Woytek’s departure follows a series of damaging episodes in which young Republicans groups have been discovered expressing pro-Nazi sympathies in group chats and internet forums. And in Georgia, Republican congressman Mike Collins’s campaign for Senate has been shaken by controversies involving his staff’s online activity. This summer, Collins replaced top aide, Kip Talley, after Slaterevealedhe had been part of a group chat with white supremacists.Woytek, who serves in the national guard and was a graduate of the Citadel, a military academy based in Charleston, South Carolina, issued a statement of regret, saying he wished he had “exercised better judgment when posting about my activities online”.“I want to be unequivocal: I reject the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented. I believe it is important to educate our younger generations, which is why I participate in historical reenactments,” he said.LAH shared a photo on a Flickr account that showed Woytek in 2018 – when he was 16 – wearing an SS uniform and marching in an area adorned with Nazi flags. Woytek follows several suppliers of SS uniforms on his Facebook page.On a Quora account bearing his name, Woytek also answered a question on whether anything good had occurred under Hitler, writing in 2017 “that Hitler started an anti-smoking campaign”.More recently, he created a public playlist of pro-Rhodesia songs on Spotify called “Tales from Rhodesia”, which is captioned: “Homesick for a place that no longer exists.” One of the songs uses a slur to refer to African troops.The former British colony’s white minority government fought a long war against guerrilla groups after issuing a unilateral declaration of independence in 1965. The country was officially recognized as Zimbabwe under black majority rule in 1980, a year after the minority government accepted its rule was unsustainable and entered peace negotiations.Rhodesia has been used by white supremacists as a symbol of the supposed superiority of white rule.Explore more on these topicsRepublicansUS politicsOhionewsShareReuse this content

title: One giant step: first known adult T rex footprints found in North Dakota | North Dakota | The Guardian
description: The 23ft-long trackway, consisting of four three-toed footprints, two left and two right, date from 66.5m years ago
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: The 23ft-long trackway, consisting of four three-toed footprints, two left and two right, date from 66.5m years ago
Content: The adult Tyrannosaurus rex track, in North Dakota.Composite: Denver Museum of Nature and ScienceView image in fullscreenThe adult Tyrannosaurus rex track, in North Dakota.Composite: Denver Museum of Nature and ScienceNorth DakotaOne giant step: first known adult T rex footprints found in North DakotaThe 23ft-long trackway, consisting of four three-toed footprints, two left and two right, date from 66.5m years agoOliver MilmanFri 11 Sep 2026 10.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first known series of footprints from an adult Tyrannosaurus rex has been found inNorth Dakotaby a team of scientists.The 23ft-long trackway – consisting of four three-toed footprints, two left and two right – was first identified in the south-west of the state, in the dinosaur fossil area known as Hell Creek Formation, last year by researchers from the Denver Museum of Nature and Science in Colorado and Liverpool John Moores University in the UK.The findings, which havenow been published in a scientific journal, date from 66.5m years ago and are the first of their kind to be found and identified. While isolated footprints and juvenile, or related species, tracks have been found before, this is the first known series of footprints left by a wandering T rex.“Bones tell us an enormous amount about these animals, but footprints capture a moment of behavior,” said Tyler Lyson, senior curator of vertebrate paleontology at the Denver museum.“With a trackway, we can actually follow an animal as it moved across the landscape. That is incredibly rare for T rex.”Each of the footprints is about 3ft (0.91m) long, with a stride of about 13ft (3.96m). The research team used high-resolution 3D surface scanning to document each footprint and create physical 3D reproductions. From this work, researchers were able to make a rough estimate that the animal was walking about 3.5-4.5mph – about the same as a brisk human walking pace.The T rex, the most famous of all dinosaurs, lived about 66-68m years ago during the Cretaceous period, according to the known fossil record. The creatures, which stood 12-13ft tall, were among the last non-avian dinosaurs to walk the Earth before a mass extinction event wiped them out.Three of the discovered footprints are set to be recovered by helicopter later this year and transported to the museum in Denver. The findings are a particular joy for the Colorado schoolteacher who stumbled upon the site.“As a teacher, I’m always telling my students that science starts with curiosity, passion and careful observation,” said Kent Hups, who is a longtime museum volunteer and also co-authored the paper. “I never imagined that could lead me to a discovery like this.”Explore more on these topicsNorth DakotaDinosaursnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ileana Cotrubas obituary | Opera | The Guardian
description: Soprano whose strength lay in her ability to invest her characterisations with dramatic force
Author: Barry Millington
Headline: Soprano whose strength lay in her ability to invest her characterisations with dramatic force
Content: Ileana Cotrubas as Adina and Jose Carreras as Nemorino in L’Elisir d’Amore at Covent Garden, 1976.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyView image in fullscreenIleana Cotrubas as Adina and Jose Carreras as Nemorino in L’Elisir d’Amore at Covent Garden, 1976.Photograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyOperaObituaryIleana Cotrubas obituarySoprano whose strength lay in her ability to invest her characterisations with dramatic forceBarry MillingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 15.50 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Romanian soprano Ileana Cotrubas, who has died aged 87, was admired internationally, not least in Great Britain, where she lived at the start of her career, and Vienna, where she and her husband later made their home. What lent her lyric soprano voice, which may have lacked the voluptuousness and amplitude of other celebrated singers, its distinctive nature was its tightly focused tonal quality (occasionally criticised as plangent), combining inner strength with a touching vulnerability. She was also an excellent actor (her exemplar was Maria Callas), her stage portrayals tellingly incarnating the often wounded women she played.Outstanding among these was her Violetta in La Traviata, which encompassed the character’s frailty, her zest for life, her exuberance and her inescapably tragic situation, in performances that were throbbing with passion and almost unbearably intense. The cumulative sweep of the phrases in her dazzling rendition ofSempre Libera, as captured in a celebrated Deutsche Grammophon recording with Carlos Kleiber, and the profoundly poignantDite alla Giovine, in which she bids farewell to the past and to life, demonstrate perfectly the qualities for which Cotrubas is remembered.It was with Debussy’s equally frail Mélisande that she made her Glyndebourne debut in Pelléas et Mélisande in 1969, returning the following year in the title role of La Calisto, as well as Pamina in The Magic Flute, and Mélisande once again. She appeared in subsequent years as Susanna in The Marriage of Figaro and Tytania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream. From 1971, when she made her Covent Garden debut, she also became a regular there, undertaking roles such as Violetta, Adina (L’Elisir d’Amore), Norina (Don Pasquale), Amina (La Sonnambula), Gilda (Rigoletto) and Antonia (Tales of Hoffmann). Her casting, for her Royal Opera debut, as Tatyana inPeter Hall’s new production of Eugene Onegin, came, she later said, as a complete surprise to her. She assumed that Hall must have agreed with her assertion that a lyric soprano suited the role better than the usual spinto. The conductor (and music director),Georg Solti, however, had to be persuaded and auditioned her twice; she was then coached by Mark Elder, who was working at the time as a répétiteur at Covent Garden.Also in 1971, during the second year of an initial residency at the Vienna State Opera, another breakthrough in her career occurred when she appeared (alongsideNicolai Geddaas Alfredo, under the baton of Josef Krips) as Violetta in a special Christmas Day performance of La Traviata. Despite her qualms about accepting the role, something of a departure for her, she proved a resounding success, and went on to become a company favourite (from 1981 Kammersängerin), undertaking 109 performances until her final one, as Mimì in La Bohème, in 1990.Mimì also provided a memorable vehicle for her La Scala debut in 1975. The scheduled soprano,Mirella Freni, had fallen ill and Cotrubas, recommended by the Rodolfo,Luciano Pavarotti, was flown out from London, arriving at the last minute and going on with no rehearsal. She was received with vociferous enthusiasm by the Milanese audience.Born in Galati in eastern Romania, Ileana was the daughter of Vasile Cotrubas, a civil servant in the ministry of agriculture; both he and Ileana’s mother, Maria, were keen amateur opera singers. She studied in Bucharest and made her debut there in 1964 as Yniold in Pelléas et Mélisande. In the audience on that occasion was the celebrated pedagogue Nadia Boulanger, who complimented her on her excellent French. That attribute was to stand her in good stead in a number of the key roles she was to undertake.After further study in Vienna, she sang with the FrankfurtOpera(1968–71), also making several appearances at the Salzburg festival in those years. In addition to her Glyndebourne and Covent Garden performances of the 1970s she made her debut at the Paris Opéra as Manon in 1974. International acclaim followed in a repertory that was selective rather than extensive, centred on the lighter roles that exploited her particular talent to optimal effect, among them Mimì, in which she successfully deployed her acting skills to characterise the seamstress’s appealing nature and vulnerability.View image in fullscreenCotrubas with Placido Domingo and, left, Cornell MacNeil in La Traviata, Metropolitan Opera, 1981.Photograph: Jack Mitchell/Getty ImagesHer substantial recorded legacy also includes Charpentier’sLouise, in which she limns the title role with subtle, delicate touches, while managing to hint at a certain artfulness; Lauretta in Gianni Schicchi, where she delivers her famous ariaO Mio Babbino Caroas the piteous plea of the adored but dejected child she is; a charming but also vibrant Micaela inCarmen; a warm, intelligent Susanna; and a Léila (The Pearl Fishers) that demonstrates her superb artistry as well as, once again, her impeccable French diction.Looking back at her career on her retirement, Cotrubas reflected how she had “flirted” with a handful of heavier roles such as Elisabetta di Valois (Don Carlos), Amelia (Simon Boccanegra) and Desdemona, which she admitted did not ideally suit her voice even if she “just managed it” on account of her acting skills. Strauss’s Four Last Songs, demanding at least a measure of vocal opulence, similarly failed to show her at her best. Her considerable strengths lay rather in her ability to shape phrases, to spin a legato line and above all to invest her characterisations with psychological acuity and compelling dramatic force.An avowed traditionalist, she earned a reputation for speaking out against what she regarded as the excesses of directorial intervention. More than once she walked out of productions where she felt her insights were more authentic than those of the director (“I didn’t even need to transform myself into Tatyana, because I was Tatyana,” she said of her approach to the role). In fact she had no complaints about Hall in that regard: along with Jean-Pierre Ponnelle, Otto Schenk andJohn Schlesinger, he was among her most esteemed directorial colleagues.Those who gave offence were named and shamed in two books she wrote in conjunction with her husband, Manfred Ramin, a German conductor and critic: the first an autobiography (1998) entitled Opernwahrheiten (Opera Truths), the second a polemic, Die Manipulierte Oper (The Manipulated Opera, 2017), which addressed the wider operatic scene – unprepared, time-beating conductors who were complicit with wilful directors were also excoriated – in heavily satirical style.Ramin, whom she married in 1972, survives her.Ileana Cotrubas, soprano, born 9 June 1939; died 20 August 2026View image in fullscreenCotrubas’s parents were keen amateur opera singers.Photograph: Marcello Mencarini/AlamyExplore more on these topicsOperaobituariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Just worry upon worry’: Europe faces a bleak winter as supply shock pushes factories to the brink | Manufacturing sector | The Guardian
description: From Shropshire to Hamburg, depleting reserves and spiralling costs are spawning a continent-wide energy crisis
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: From Shropshire to Hamburg, depleting reserves and spiralling costs are spawning a continent-wide energy crisis
Content: Soaring energy bills are a grim prospect for many industrial businesses across Europe already stretched as a result of global unrest and earlier energy shocks.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSoaring energy bills are a grim prospect for many industrial businesses across Europe already stretched as a result of global unrest and earlier energy shocks.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesManufacturing sector‘Just worry upon worry’: Europe faces a bleak winter as supply shock pushes factories to the brinkFrom Shropshire to Hamburg, depleting reserves and spiralling costs are spawning a continent-wide energy crisisAlex DanielandLisa O’CarrollFri 11 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBridgnorth Aluminium has faced down Brexit, Covid and repeated energy shocks in recent years. But this winter is bringing extra “stress and pressure”, says its head of sales, Adrian Musgrave.Musgrave’s company makes rolled aluminium, used in packaging, construction and the manufacture of items such as cars and batteries. Like many stretched industrial businesses acrossEurope, Bridgnorth Aluminium faces a looming threat of soaring energy bills, which Musgrave describes as “just worry upon worry”.The cost of natural gas has doubled in the past two months, caused by renewed fighting between the US and Iran, reaching a three-year high in the UK and the EU this week. More price rises are likely in the colder months.Bridgnorth Aluminium, which employs 370 people at its plant in Shropshire in the UK’s industrial heartland, is already feeling the effects. Its combined gas and electricity bill is about £1.1m per month, 18% of its total costs, and rising.Its biggest contracts include a safety net – once gas prices cross a certain point, customers pay the difference. That threshold was crossed last month – but the question of whether clients will come back concerns Musgrave. “They have to pay because it’s in the contract, but they will obviously not like it,” he says. “When it comes up for renewal it will become an issue.”Musgrave says the company is not in a place where it would need to make layoffs or temporary shutdowns this winter. Others may not be so lucky – one forecast, by the Item Club, predicted earlier this year that Britain will lose 163,000 jobs in 2026 because of the war, concentrated in manufacturing-heavy regions such as south Wales and the Humber region.Bridgnorth Aluminium is considering taking a longer Christmas break, or doing planned maintenance – originally scheduled for April – earlier than expected in January, so the factory runs less during times of high prices. “And then the employees are obviously aware,” he says, “so then people begin to worry.”View image in fullscreenStorage tanks at the Grain liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal near Rochester, UK.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGas spikes and shortagesThe conflict has disrupted global energy supplies since Iran started attacking ships in the Gulf and choked off access through the strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes.British wholesale gas prices climbed to 205p per therm this week, the highest point since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and up 101% from 102p in June. That is compared with 78p per therm at the end of February. The UK imports about 70% of its gas, leaving it especially vulnerable to price swings.ChartA shortage of stored gas reserves compounds the issue. Europe is heading into winter with gas storesat their lowest level in over a decade, after the Hormuz disruption stopped countries topping up their reserves through the summer, when prices are normally lower. Storage is now about 67% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.Germany, which holds the largest storage capacity in Europe, is only about half full, and is on course to miss its official 70% storage target this year. The Netherlands is expected to miss its 80% target too.As one of Europe’s biggest gas consumers, the UK may be especially exposed, with some of the lowest levels of domestic storage capacity and relying instead on pipeline imports from Europe and tankers from the US and Middle East. Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of BritishGasowner Centrica, said last month that Britain had “almost no gas in storage” for the coming winter.View image in fullscreenA crane operator moves coils of steel at a steel plant in Duisburg, Germany.Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty ImagesStrife in the MittelstandAlexander Julius, managing partner of Macrometal Handelsgesellschaft, a steel distributor in Hamburg, says it is competing “against producers in regions where energy costs are often significantly lower and where governments provide direct or indirect industrial support”.For industries like his, part of Germany’s Mittelstand of medium-sized enterprises, he says energy is not just another item on the cost lines, but “a fundamental production input”. But instead of getting support they are being “hammered by green taxes while energy rises rocket”.Julius, who is also the president of trade body Eurometal, says companies will go to the wall and work will move to China or India unless something is done to reduce energy costs. Eurometal haswarned that manufacturing job losses across Europe could reach 300,000by the end of the year, driven partly by Chinese competition and compounded by energy costs.Natural gas price in the EU from December 2025 to September 2026Axel Eggert, director general of the European steel body Eurofer, adds that the high prices “will inevitably lead to production disruptions. Such additional costs cannot simply be absorbed by energy-intensive industries exposed to international competition.“The longer the crisis lasts, the greater the risk that temporary production cuts become structural, with consequences for investment, employment and, ultimately, the viability of industrial plants in Europe.”The car industry in Germany has also called for urgent action from Berlin and Brussels, saying “the high energy prices are among the biggest competitive disadvantages of Germany as a business location”, with electricity prices in some cases three times higher than the US.“Germany, just like the EU, urgently needs a jointly supported energy strategy with low electricity prices and future-proof grid infrastructure,” said a spokesperson for the trade association, the VDA. Building new industries will become “a decisive factor in determining” inward foreign investment in future, they added.‘It just keeps coming’The exposure is especially bad for the chemicals sector, where companies rely on gas to power their plants but also as feedstock – the raw material that many products are made from – meaning every spike in prices hits them twice.Francesco Buzzella, president of Italy’s chemicals trade body Federchimica, says it remains the “primary factor undermining the competitiveness of chemical companies” in the country. Energy now accounts for 18% of the value of everything Italy’s chemical industry produces, up from 14% in 2021 – and could reach 23% if gas and oil prices do not fall. This week oil hit $107 a barrel as the US and Iran continue to trade blows.Production output in the UK has fallen by 60% since 2021, according to the Chemicals Industry Association, with at least 25 sites closing.Peter Huntsman, chief executive of the chemicals group Huntsman Corporation, told the Guardian in March that continued high pricescould force the closure of the company’s last remaining UK plant, at Wilton on Teesside.Back in Shropshire, meanwhile, Musgrave says Bridgnorth Aluminium’s owner, the Belgian industrial group Viohalco, wants to invest further in the company’s operations, but the numbers are getting harder to justify.“They would like to make some significant investments – the UK market for aluminium is quite big, and we would like to be able to sell more at home,” he says.But energy and other pressures make it “a difficult picture for shareholders to get their head around … The business conditions for investment are really challenging, and changing quite rapidly.“I’ve been in this business just over 20 years. For the first 10, the macro environment was always pretty stable. But then we had Brexit, which changed things; the energy crisis with Ukraine; Covid; and now this.“You just think you’re going to get a year where maybe it won’t be too much change,” he adds. “But it just keeps coming.”Explore more on these topicsManufacturing sectorOilGasInflationUS-Israel war on IranEuropeSteel industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Self-driving cars should be taxed to offset job losses, thinktank urges | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Report says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Report says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk
Content: Report urges ministers to act early to mitigate the effects of robotaxis on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenReport urges ministers to act early to mitigate the effects of robotaxis on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersSelf-driving carsSelf-driving cars should be taxed to offset job losses, thinktank urgesReport says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at riskGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaxes on self-driving cars should be introduced now in the UK to offset the rise in congestion and threats to jobs they pose, a thinktank has urged.The first robotaxis on London’s streets onlystarted this month, but government projections are that up to 40% of cars sold could have self-driving capability by the middle of the next decade.The report says widespread autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk, while individual ownership is likely to increase car usage at the expense of public transport, and increase congestion.Introducing charges now on self-driving vehicles could ease the transition and provide a future revenue stream to replace dwindling fuel duty, according to the report from Centre for British Progress, a non-partisan thinktank focused on economic growth.Wayve, a British tech firm pioneering autonomous cars, said it would “penalise the UK’s most promising innovators”.About £27bn a year is brought in by fuel duty, which is projected to disappear with the transition to electric vehicles.While the report acknowledges potential benefits in safety and different skilled jobs in the sector, it said ministers should act early to mitigate the effects on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers, (121,000 in London), as “self-driving vehicles will eventually make much of this work obsolete”.It notes that almost half of the mileage covered byWaymo’s robotaxisin California occurs with no passenger on board, that the costs of an empty vehicle are minimal without a driver to pay – and that driving around is potentially cheaper than parking.According to the Department for Transport forecasts, highly automated driving will bring a 24% rise in road miles by 2050, with significant effects on congestion and road speeds.Taxes should be implemented now before AVs become commonplace, the report urges. It states: “There is not yet a substantial constituency of AV owners who will resist a charge; once there is, taxing them becomes far harder.”The thinktank calculates that by 2050, an AV charge set to match the social cost of congestion – about 88p per mile – would raise £47bn per year.David Lawrence, one of the authors of the report, said that the experience of fuel duty, introduced in 1909 before mass car adoption, showed it was best to build up before “a political fight later on – our view is that now is the time to do it”.He added: “In terms of the way that bond markets behave, even if tax revenue doesn’t peak until 2050, that’s still going to affect your 30-year bond yields today, which obviously is something the government is having to deal with. It can have an immediate impact on fiscal headroom, even if the actual revenue doesn’t come until much further down the line.”Ministers have backed the introduction of AVs as a “transformative opportunity” for UK, heralding the start of robotaxi services inLondonthis year as bringing “cutting-edge technology to British roads, creating thousands of jobs and unlocking billions for the economy by 2035”.Uber, partnering with Wayve, has started limited AV services in the capital, with Google’s Waymo and the Chinese firm Baiduvying to join. Robotaxis already operate in the US, China and the UAE, and Europe’s first fully driverless taxi trials started in Zagreb, Croatia, this week.Sarah Gates, VP global affairs and assurance at Wayve, said AVs were “a major growth opportunity for the UK – an industry in which we hold a genuine competitive advantage” and would bring high-value jobs and corporation tax revenues from a share of a £700bn global market.She added: “A sector-specific tax at this early stage would undermine the government’s growth agenda and send precisely the wrong signal: that the UK will penalise its most promising innovators, rather than give them the conditions to scale and succeed.”The GMB union, which represents taxi and private hire drivers, said a tax on AVs would not go far enough. Simon Rush, president of the GMB London region drivers branch, said: “Driverless cars threaten the livelihoods of private hire drivers and the businesses that depend on them. GMB has asked the government,TfL(Transport for London), and operators for a plan to reskill and redeploy drivers, but to date our questions have gone unanswered.“An AV charge could go some way to mitigating the economic disruption caused by the rollout of these vehicles, but we need more.”Uber declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsEnglandTfLUberRoad transportAI (artificial intelligence)LondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK chancellor urged to remove ‘hidden taxes’ from energy bills | Energy bills | The Guardian
description: Businesses, charities and other groups sign letter calling for levies to be paid by the government
Author: Mark Sweney
Headline: Businesses, charities and other groups sign letter calling for levies to be paid by the government
Content: The letter says the UK faces some of the highest energy costs of any developed nation.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe letter says the UK faces some of the highest energy costs of any developed nation.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianEnergy billsUK chancellor urged to remove ‘hidden taxes’ from energy billsBusinesses, charities and other groups sign letter calling for levies to be paid by the governmentMark SweneyFri 11 Sep 2026 08.37 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 120 organisations including big businesses and charities have called for the removal of “hidden taxes” added to energy bills to help reduce costs for consumers and prevent businesses closing.In a letter to the chancellor the signatories – including Energy UK, business trade body the CBI, End FuelPovertyand Age UK – called for levies amounting to 10% of energy bills that fund policies to be paid for by the government. John Healey is to present his first budget on 28 October.The signatories want the remainder of the levy funding the building of renewable energy projects to be scrapped. The former chancellor, Rachel Reeves,shifted 75%of the funding to government taxation last year.The organisations also called for an end to levies to help build nuclear power plants, the funding of the warm homes discount scheme and the feed-in tariff programme, which was closed in 2019 but continues to pay businesses and customers with ongoing contracts for generating their own energy and supplying excess back into the grid.The letter argues that moving levies off bills would lower the total average household bill by as much as £250 a year, including the £150 saving from Reeves’s moves to cut somelevies funding green energy schemes, and lower electricity prices for businesses by 20%.The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills | Nils PratleyRead more“The UK is actively sabotaging its own efforts to bring down energy costs by taxing electricity,” said Ed Matthew, director of UK programme at thinktank E3G, which co-authored the letter alongsideEnergyUK. “Any credible plan to tackle the cost of living and enable reindustrialisation needs to include removing these taxes from bills to the exchequer.”Last year, Britain’s biggest energy supplier, Octopus, said bills were on track to increase by20% over the next four years, even if wholesale prices were to drop, because of the increasing amount levied due to the rising cost of government policies.The outbreak of the Iran war has pushed gas and electricity prices up with households facing the highest energy charges in three years this winter. The energy consultant Cornwall Insight forecast that Ofgem, the UK regulator, will increase its quarterly price cap again in January, putting the average annual bill at £1,872.The government faces growing pressure to tackle the UK’s energy costs, which are some of the highest in the developed world, after its pre-election promise in 2024 to cut energy bills by £300 a year by 2030.Theletter, which has been backed by 123 organisations, including energy companies, business bodies, banks, retailers and campaigning groups, says UK energy bills are 70% higher now than they were in 2021.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn July, Andy Burnham announced acut to VAT on domestic energy bills from October, an average saving of £45, although this reduction is currently set to stay in place only until April.“High electricity prices hurt all of us,” said Dhara Vyas, chief executive of Energy UK. “By taking levies off the bill, the government can show it is serious about tackling fuel poverty and the cost-of-living crisis, growing the economy, and bringing down inflation. Cheaper electricity would have an outsized impact across the economy.”The letter also warned of the impact on companies, saying: “High energy costs are widely recognised as a significant constraint across the economy, driving business closures and job losses, while simultaneously deterring investment in the UK.”Explore more on these topicsEnergy billsHousehold billsFuel povertyRenewable energyConsumer affairsPovertyOctopus EnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for bills  | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: National Audit Office calls for greater transparency on £70bn programme that is running over budget and behind schedule
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: National Audit Office calls for greater transparency on £70bn programme that is running over budget and behind schedule
Content: Wind turbines at RWE's Gwynt y Mor, the world's second largest offshore wind farm, located off the coast of North Wales.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PAView image in fullscreenWind turbines at RWE's Gwynt y Mor, the world's second largest offshore wind farm, located off the coast of North Wales.Photograph: Ben Birchall/PANils Pratley on financeEnergy industryThe ‘great grid upgrade’ is off track – ministers should spell out the risks for billsNils PratleyNational Audit Office calls for greater transparency on £70bn programme that is running over budget and behind scheduleSpeed up electricity grid upgrade or else face higher bills, warns UK watchdogFri 11 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTShareIt’s an open secret in the energy industry that “the great grid upgrade” – the £70bn programme to rewire the nation’s electricity transmission network to enable clean power by 2030 – is running over budget and behind schedule, and may end up costing consumers and businesses more in their bills than advertised.How far behind? How much more? It is impossible to get straight answers from the bodies overseeing the massive spending programme, which may continue at an even greater scale into the 2030s. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (Desnz), its in-house body, the National Energy System Operator (Neso), andOfgem, the supposedly independent regulator, publish acres of information on narrow matters, but none provides a clear big-picture assessment: how is the grid upgrade really going?Thank goodness, then, for Friday’s National Audit Office (NAO) report. The watchdog has unearthed a few hard statistics and demanded far greater official transparency. Prime minister Andy Burnham, in cost-of-living mode, should take note: trouble is brewing.Of the 88 grid upgrade projects originally identified, 12 have already been completed (good news) and 12 have been subsumed into newer work (fair enough). But of the 56 deemed “essential” for meeting the government’s target of clean power by 2030, the NAO says 50 are “forecast to be delivered after their optimal date”. Of those, only 22 are forecast to be less than a year late; the rest are further behind schedule, with one put at between six and seven years behind.The “optimal” date, in this context, is the date required not only to fulfil the 2030 clean power deadline but also to keep a lid on the maddening “constraint costs” – payments to Scottish windfarms to turn off when the grid can’t handle their output, plus payments to southern gas-fired generators or interconnecters toFranceto start supplying electricity.On one windy day alone this week, such constraint payments reached £29m. The tally for the whole of 2026 is virtually guaranteed to top £2bn. The big worry is that the upper end of Neso’s forecast for 2030 – a colossal £7.8bn, all going on bills – might be realised if the delays worsen.Onshore windfarm applications hit 10-year high in EnglandRead moreTherein lies the reason why a grid upgrade is needed in the first place: the transmission network suffered from a lack of investment, even before the switch to renewables started. The transition makes the work more urgent. But what is also revealed is a state failure, going back decades, to expand the grid to keep pace with additional generating capacity. The suspicion now is that the same mistake is being repeated.Many construction delays can be explained, it should be said. The NAO report cites standard stuff such as acquiring land rights, obtaining planning consents and legal challenges. But then there are procurement headaches caused by the need to wait for project‑specific signoff from Ofgem. There is also global competition for equipment as other countries expand their electricity networks. According to the report, the government estimates that some kit has risen up to five times in price from 2022 levels, with delivery times becoming extended. In short, the whole thing is taking longer and costing more.But nailing down what it implies for that original £70bn figure, and thus bills, remains impossible. Nobody, it seems, is willing to put the numbers together. This passage from the NAO report is damning: “Publicly available information gives a partial and inconsistent view of progress towards upgrading the grid. Coverage is incomplete and key delivery risk metrics are missing. As a result, the available datasets cannot be reconciled with each other or the data we received from Ofgem, Neso and Desnz, and they do not give a clear view of overall portfolio delivery status.”The watchdog calls for Ofgem and Neso “to deliver critical projects on time and provide transparent reporting so parliament and the public can hold them to account”.More than half of clean energy schemes needed for Labour’s 2030 target offered grid connectionRead moreOn-time delivery may already be out of reach, but the demand for greater transparency is spot-on. Ofgem should publish medium-term forecasts for electricity bills, as this columnhas regularly argued, because the “network costs” element – what we’re talking about in this context – is capable of being forecast. Or it should take upthe excellent idea from EDF, one of the big generators and retail suppliers, for “a live, publicly accessible tracker” to “radically increase transparency on cost and ongoing construction progress” and allow a strategic review.The political danger for the government is that, sometime around 2028, the delays and cost inflation will become impossible to ignore. Even some pro-renewables enthusiasts, who fully back the government’s stance that the upgrade is the only way to bring down electricity bills eventually, warn of a backlash if £70bn becomes a much larger number. Ministers should do themselves a favour: be open.Explore more on these topicsEnergy industryNils Pratley on financeEnergy billsOfgemHousehold billsRenewable energyEnglandScotlandcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘The place lost its way. Now that’s changed’: can a Manchester art museum move beyond its troubled past? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Manchester’s Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new mission
Author: Lauren Kelly
Headline: Manchester’s Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new mission
Content: Art of the matter … esea contemporary.Photograph: Arthur SiukstraView image in fullscreenArt of the matter … esea contemporary.Photograph: Arthur SiukstraArt and design‘The place lost its way. Now that’s changed’: can a Manchester art museum move beyond its troubled past?The Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new missionLauren KellyFri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn March 2020, the visual artist JJ Chan was assembling video footage for a group exhibition scheduled at the Centre for Chinese Contemporary Art in Manchester. Centred on family VHS tapes, and titled A New Constellation: Chinese Diaspora Now, the artwork was an exploration of Chan’s emotionally complex relationship to Hong Kong, their parents’ birthplace. When Chan asked for guidance after the sudden departure of the initial curator, the artist discovered that the gallery did not employ anyone who was Chinese: 12 out of the 13 staff members were white, while most of the front-facing (unpaid) volunteers were of Chinese descent.Fearing their art would be shaped through a white lens, Chan withdrew and published an open letter to the centre, writing: “My experience, and my trauma, are being used as a leg-up into an industry for an already overrepresented demographic.” Later that year, the organisation recruited seven artists of Chinese heritage to address the lack of diversity before that initiative was cancelled when the artists raised issues surrounding institutional racism with the gallery. The artist-led working group subsequently petitioned for an international boycott of the institution resulting in the resignation of six board members and several employees. After closing due to Covid in 2020, the arts space never reopened.Two years on, Shanghai-born artist Xiaowen Zhu reattained public funding and relaunched the venue in 2023 under a new name,esea contemporary– incorporating the wider east and south-east Asian diaspora – alongside a new team primarily made up of first- and second-generation migrants. The director’s ethos, defined following a series of artist surveys and community focus groups, seeks connectedness in an increasingly polarised world.double quotation markOur role is not simply to provide visibility but to create the conditions for ambitious work on the artists’ own termsAs part of a year-long programme celebrating its 40th anniversary, the charity is hosting Two Improvisations, the first UK institutional solo exhibition by London-based, Wuhan-born Chris Zhongtian Yuan. There’s also an online interview series tracing the gallery’s shift from a community-oriented Chinese visual arts festival to its role today as the UK’s only non-profit gallery dedicated to local and global art informed by east and south-east Asian cultural backgrounds. In addition, Japanese film-maker Umi Ishihara’s experimental film Nocturnal Melody will preview on 9 October.Zhu believes the four-decade milestone presents an opportunity for reflection, as well as for clarity: who is esea contemporary accountable to, and why does it exist?“We want to demonstrate that an organisation rooted in Manchester can contribute meaningfully to global artistic conversations while remaining deeply accountable to its communities,” says Zhu, who is based between Manchester and Berlin. Explaining that east and south-east Asian perspectives are underrepresented in UK institutions, particularly within major galleries and permanent collections, she adds: “Our role is not simply to provide visibility but to create the conditions for artists to develop ambitious work on their own terms.”View image in fullscreenChris Zhongtian Yuan’s   Two Improvisations.Photograph: David LindsayYuan’s Two Improvisations – an original experimental film – bleeds punk. A pair of obscured musicians sing loudly. The band’s frontman, projected as a dark shadow, represents the “Yeren”, a lingering mythical Chinese misfit creature rumoured to roam the mountainous regions of Hubei. Adjoining the film, which shows musicians singing lyrics about deception and marginalisation, is an installation of Yuan’s architectural models of urban houses and skyscrapers (some built in China, and others handmade in the UK) which sit on an illuminated stage in the gallery foyer, mirroring Manchester’s Northern Quarter outside the window.For Zhu, the showcase – like much of the work exhibited at esea contemporary – illustrates the dual reality of living between cultures, and across borders, while challenging certain narratives. Typically punk is not associated with Chinese people in the west, who are often stereotyped as reserved, “or worse, powerful”, Yuan tells me. “And Wuhan is always the city people talk shit about,” he adds. By drawing cultural comparisons with Manchester, both past and present, Yuan encourages the viewer to question traditional narratives about rebellion in China, as well as in his home town. Yuan relates to the Yeren, he tells me: living in the diaspora, the artist is deemed an outsider.Alongside the gallery’s physical exhibitions, 40 Years, 40 Voices continues the celebrations online, inviting artists, stakeholders and longstanding collaborators to reflect on the organisation’s legacy and future. Art worker Kwong Lee, now director of London’s Deptford X festival, recalls participating in Beyond the Chinese Takeaway in 1992, marketed as “the first exhibition of its kind researching the innovative works of contemporary artists of Chinese origin living in Britain”. Meanwhile, trustee Xu Wenkai, a digital artist known as aaajiao, hopes “esea contemporary remains a space where Asian artists don’t have to justify themselves – where the work speaks first”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt remains a space where Asian artists don’t have to justify themselves – where the work speaks firstIt’s a marked change for a venue that – long before 2020 – had been embroiled in controversy. During the late 90s and 00s, the gallery changed dramatically due to China’s growing cultural and economic influence. In 2013, the Riba award-winning space launched Conservative MP George Osborne’s Manchester China Forum, playing host to global trade deals and geopolitics.According to Chan, the British government’s pro-China policy determined and ultimately restricted the artworks that were exhibited: “The gallery couldn’t be directly critical of the people the government were trying to do business with,” they say. “Galleries are shaped a lot by the political landscape, that’s where their money comes from. There’s often a manipulation of information.”Today, Zhu has re-rooted the institution within the community. Her popular Esea art outreach programme encourages east and south-east Asian residents over 50 to create art, combating loneliness and providing an opportunity for migrants to speak their native language. She also invests in local talent: the organisation’s events and visitor experience manager was initially hired as front of house while working as a cashier at Wing Yip, a nearby Chinese store. At the same time, Zhu intends for the gallery to appeal to a broader audience, and uses more “accessible” artforms – including video, music, food and games – to do so.It’s a marked change for an institution that had been embroiled in controversy. “The place lost its way for a while” says the artist Gayle Chong Kwan, who presented her first solo exhibition at the gallery in 2002 – and who facilitated the boycott in 2020. “Thankfully, that change happened.”Chris Zhongtian Yuan: Two Improvisations is at esea contemporary, Manchester, to13 September.Explore more on these topicsArt and designExhibitionsManchesterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A bee’s-eye view: art installation beside the Thames celebrates crucial pollinators | Installation | The Guardian
description: More than 100 lenses inside Luke Jerram’s Pollenarium let visitors see the outside world as insects would
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: More than 100 lenses inside Luke Jerram’s Pollenarium let visitors see the outside world as insects would
Content: Luke Jerram’s Pollenarium, containing more than 100 lenses, has its world premiere at Barking Riverside's Emerge East festival on SaturdayPhotograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLuke Jerram’s Pollenarium, containing more than 100 lenses, has its world premiere at Barking Riverside's Emerge East festival on SaturdayPhotograph: David Levene/The GuardianInstallationA bee’s-eye view: art installation beside the Thames celebrates crucial pollinatorsMore than 100 lenses inside Luke Jerram’s Pollenarium let visitors see the outside world as insects wouldSteven MorrisFri 11 Sep 2026 08.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the outside, it looks a little like something out of the Teletubbies.In fact, the new installation by the Bristol artistLuke Jerramrepresents a grain of pollen, and the inside represents an insect’s compound eye.Jerram wants the Pollenarium, which appeared on the banks of the Thames in eastLondonthis week, to entertain but also draw attention to the alarming rate pollinators at which are vanishing from the world.“I hope it will make people think about how we need to protect pollinators,” Jerram said. “There has been a massive drop in insect numbers.Flying insects in the UK have declined by 60% in 20 years,which is mad.”View image in fullscreenLuke Jerram’s Pollenarium, commissioned by Creative Barking and Dagenham, depicts a giant grain of pollen from the outside.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianHe said he was concerned that UK farmersstill used some neonicotinoid pesticides. “Aminuscule trace can disrupt a bee’s ability to navigate and reproduce, with long-lasting consequences for their survival.”Best known for touring large scale sculptures of the moon, the sun and Earth, for this new piece Jerram scaled up a microscopic grain of pollen to the size of a small building. It is made of brightly coloured nylon inflated into a 6m metre high dome.“When we had a test inflation in the car park atPaintworks[where his Bristol studio is based], people streamed out of offices to see what was going on,” Jerram said.View image in fullscreenEach lens acts as a camera obscura by focusing light from the surrounding landscape and projecting it on to the dome’s inner surface.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianInside the structure, there are more than 100 lenses, each acting as a camera obscura to create a “mosaic” of the world outside. The idea is to give an idea of how an insect might perceive the world through a compound eye. “I’ve created Pollenarium to be a bit like going inside a bee’s head,” he said.Pollenarium, which was commissioned byCreative Barking and Dagenham, can be seen on Saturday at theEmerge East festival at Barking Riverside. It is free to visit from 11am.It will be making an appearance at the University of Bristol after its east London debut, before embarking on a tour of the UK, accompanied by a programme of activities and workshops.Explore more on these topicsInstallationBeesArtInsectsLondonWildlifeAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy review – classical myth burns into modern England | Theatre | The Guardian
description: In Ava Pickett’s tense play, Michelle Dockery’s heroine returns to a Towie-styled world where the violence and misogyny are all too recognisable
Author: Emma John
Headline: In Ava Pickett’s tense play, Michelle Dockery’s heroine returns to a Towie-styled world where the violence and misogyny are all too recognisable
Content: Multiple gears … Michelle Dockery  in Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy  at Theatre Royal Stratford East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMultiple gears … Michelle Dockery  in Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy  at Theatre Royal Stratford East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewBloodsport: After Helen of Troy review – classical myth burns into modern EnglandTheatre Royal Stratford East, LondonIn Ava Pickett’s tense play, Michelle Dockery’s heroine returns to a Towie-styled world where the violence and misogyny are all too recognisableEmma JohnFri 11 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘And Zeus created … Essex.” PlaywrightAva Pickettset her award-winning debut,1536, in her home county during Tudor times: her latest has Helen of Troy returning home to a Towie-style living room at the end of an English civil war.An Adidas-clad Messenger functions as chorus, bringing us up to speed on this new England where angry men have rioted and petrol-bombed, wreaking havoc in Helen’s name after she left her husband, Marcus, for a so-called “foreigner”. The cream carpets and glass coffee tables belong to Cee – Helen’s best friend, married to Marcus’s big brother Mario – and it’s here that the men arrive with a shivering Helen to toast their victory with prosecco.View image in fullscreenDystopian dinner party … Laura Aikman (Cee) and Gerard Monaco (Mario) in Bloodsport: After Helen Of Troy.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWhat comes next is a truly tense two hours. Given real-life scenes of masked vigilantes in Dover and Portsmouth this month, Pickett’s dystopian vision feels uncomfortably close, albeit infused with a Martin McDonagh-esque black wit. At one point a guard looms with an automatic weapon as Laura Aikman’s tradwife Cee attempts to glide over the undercurrents of violence and misogyny with platters of mozzarella sticks and prawn picky bits.It’s a play that’s less about toxic masculinity and insidious racism than women’s response to it. Michelle Dockery’s Helen moves through multiple gears, from victim to rebel to a mother confronted with the daughter she abandoned. And on opening night,Maimuna Memon’s uncompromising Dani prompted a cheer in parts of the audience for her takedown of Cee’s complicity.Those versed in Greek myth – and the rest of us who’ve watched Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey – will have their ideas of where the plot is heading, correct or not. The abruptness of the play’s climax does leave us wondering what Pickett is really trying to say about free will – Ethan Moorhouse’s blisteringly poetic interludes as Messenger introduce a pantheon of external forces dressed as gods, while a naked tree reaches across Polly Sullivan’s set like a malevolent hand. But both comedy and drama are deftly paced and balanced in the production by Stratford East’s new artistic director Lisa Spirling, amplified by Nicola T Chang’s bone-shaking score and sound.AtTheatre Royal Stratford East, London, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMichelle DockeryTheatre Royal Stratford EastClassicsFolklore and mythologyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Housewife review – Naomi Watts is a secret suburban Nazi in an overcooked melodrama | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The chilling true story of a woman who tried to hide from her wartime crimes gets turned into a strangely inert misfire
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: The chilling true story of a woman who tried to hide from her wartime crimes gets turned into a strangely inert misfire
Content: Naomi Watts in The Housewife.Photograph: Toronto film festivalView image in fullscreenNaomi Watts in The Housewife.Photograph: Toronto film festivalFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewThe Housewife review – Naomi Watts is a secret suburban Nazi in an overcooked melodramaToronto film festival:the chilling true story of a woman who tried to hide from her wartime crimes gets turned into a strangely inert misfireBenjamin Leein TorontoFri 11 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first scene of the 60s-set drama The Housewife is a closeup of a whistling kettle, an early “wink, wink” sign that we’re watching a story where tensions are set to boil but also that we’re watching a film of minimal subtlety.Perhaps if it had been pitched closer to its adjacently named cousinThe Housemaid, as a silly, sensationalist thriller, such heavy-handed decision-making would feel more well-suited. But instead, while some scenes flirt with the idea of something juicier, this is a stuffy and stodgy slab of self-serious, old-school Oscar bait complete with all the shouting, crying, throwing and finger-pointing one would expect. Think overcooked rather than slow simmer.Being Heumann review – Coda director’s disability rights drama is well-intentioned but clunkyRead moreIt’s all awfully dry despite being based on a true story that is, at least on paper, anything but. The housewife is Austrian-born Hermine, played byNaomi Wattswith a decent enough accent, now living in Queens, New York, with an American husband (Luke Evans) and a tirelessly well-kept house. She’s the picture of suburban perfectionism even if her less-than-perfect dialogue starts to suggest there’s something else under the surface (“There are always things we don’t know about other people,” she purrs). When ambitious New York Times journalist Joseph (Tye Sheridan) receives a tip that a Nazi is living in the city, the road leads all the way to the Maspeth neighborhood and into Hermine’s house. Joseph is intent on speaking to her husband but she starts to entertain him instead, the two developing a strange, strained friendship.Strangely handled like a big first-act twist, by ensuring that we don’t hear the husband’s American accent for a convenient while and hoping we don’t spot the very clear signposting, we discover that Hermine is the Nazi and has been stringing Joseph along. She claims that her job was a mere nurse, saving rather than slaughtering, and that by associating her with misdeeds, Joseph is showing his ignorance of what the Holocaust was like to live through (“You do not know war in America,” she tells him). But a story is a story and, in Joseph’s mind, a Nazi is a Nazi especially when he finds new information on what really happened.After flirting with what might have been an interestingly perverse domestic psycho-thriller (Hermine’s interest in Joseph briefly veers between maternal and sexual), it becomes a plodding procedural involving Michael Imperioli’s aggrieved immigration officer and then an overheated courtroom drama. Watts, who gave one of her finest performances in years as another sleek, strong-willed woman in the 60s inFeud: Capote vs the Swans, is notably less convincing here, a little unsteady as she struggles to find her way through Hermine’s various masks and deceptions. There’s never the underlying chill there that I wanted; it’s all a little too artificial and self-aware to affect.
