The obvious comparison here is The Reader, a film I care very little for, but there, Kate Winslet nails an unshakable oddness that is sadly out of reach for Watts.First-time director Ben Shirinian has fun with some very effective period immersion (even if Montreal never quite works as a New York stand-in) but he’s lumbered with a dramatically inert and psychologically shallow script from Alyssa Hill. She lightly toys with interesting questions of complicity and forgiveness and citizenship (Hermine’s white friends tell her she’ll pass her test as she’s “the kind of people we want around here”) but she just can’t find a way to elevate any of it into something that isn’t just another Holocaust movie. Even in such an overpopulated subgenre, there are still so many new and impactful ways in (Lena Olin, who steals one of the film’s only mildly wrenching scenes as she gives grim testimony, evenstarred in one with Anthony Hopkins back at Toronto in 2023) but despite the spikier source material, there’s nothing new or noteworthy to see here. As explained in his introductory speech at the premiere, Shirinian clearly wanted to make something about how the very worst behaviour can often be found in the most familiar and unthreatening packaging but surely films about the banality of evil shouldn’t be quite this banal?The Housewife is premiering at theToronto film festivaland is seeking distributionExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewNaomi WattsDrama filmsToronto film festivalFestivalsLuke EvansreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Drawn Together review – preposterous romance with all the erotic charge of leaf mulch | Movies | The Guardian
description: The latest adaptation of Culpable trilogy author Mercedes Ron, about a ballet dancer and her security guard, has more holes than plot and chemistry that barely generates a spark
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The latest adaptation of Culpable trilogy author Mercedes Ron, about a ballet dancer and her security guard, has more holes than plot and chemistry that barely generates a spark
Content: Trash with pretensions … Ester Expósito and Hugo Diego Garcia in Drawn Together.Photograph: Amazon PrimeView image in fullscreenTrash with pretensions … Ester Expósito and Hugo Diego Garcia in Drawn Together.Photograph: Amazon PrimeMoviesReviewDrawn Together review – preposterous romance with all the erotic charge of leaf mulchThe latest adaptation of Culpable trilogy author Mercedes Ron, about a ballet dancer and her security guard, has more holes than plot and chemistry that barely generates a sparkCath ClarkeFri 11 Sep 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is Prime Video’s latest Mercedes Ron adaptation, following the massive ratings success of her Culpable trilogy (My Fault,Your Fault,Our Fault). Drawn Together tells the story of a ballet dancer falling in love with her bodyguard. It’s meant to be darker and sexier than the Culpable movies (which were derived from YA-aimed novels), but has all the erotic charge of leaf mulch. It’s the worst of all worlds – trash minus any froth or fun, trash with pretensions. Fans no doubt will be instantly at home in its glossy world of the ultra-wealthy, all the budget blown on cream-coloured furnishings and jodhpurs.Ester Expósito is Marfil, a 20-year-old student and ballet dancer from Spain living in New York. One night, she is abducted in Central Park and wakes up two days later in hospital with no memory of what happened. What Marfil doesn’t know is that her billionaire father Alejandro (Pablo Molinero) is an organised crime boss, and he hires bodyguard Sebastián (Hugo Diego Garcia) as 24/7 protection for Marfil. In a film with more holes than plot, this stands out as especially preposterous. No father alive would risk hiring smouldering Sebastián (think Tom Hardy’s hot young Spanish cousin) as security for his daughter.In truth, Alejandro’s ill-gotten gains would be better spent on therapy for Marfil to work through her deep-seated psychological issues. She wants to break free of her controlling father but throws herself into the arms of Sebastián, a man who won’t let her leave the house alone and secretly films her on CCTV. The chemistry between the two actors barely generates a spark – but stay alert at the 70-minute mark, because the sex, when it finally comes, is blink and you’ll miss it. There’s another book in the series, so the movie ends on an irritating cliffhanger, with a wait for the climax.Drawn Together is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsFilmRomance filmsThrillersFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Killer Story review – this tale of two relentless armchair detectives is prestige true crime | Television | The Guardian
description: Eileen and Keen Umbehr were convinced the wrong person was convicted for double-homicide. After sending Pulitzer-winning journalist Joe Sexton 2,714 emails about it, he agreed to investigate – and it led to a messy entanglement
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Eileen and Keen Umbehr were convinced the wrong person was convicted for double-homicide. After sending Pulitzer-winning journalist Joe Sexton 2,714 emails about it, he agreed to investigate – and it led to a messy entanglement
Content: Armchair detectives … Eileen Umbehr, left, and her husband Keen Umbehr in A Killer Story.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenArmchair detectives … Eileen Umbehr, left, and her husband Keen Umbehr in A Killer Story.Photograph: HBOTV reviewTelevisionReviewA Killer Story review – this tale of two relentless armchair detectives is prestige true crimeEileen and Keen Umbehr were convinced the wrong person was convicted for double-homicide. After sending Pulitzer-winning journalist Joe Sexton 2,714 emails about it, he agreed to investigate – and it led to a messy entanglementHannah J DaviesFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHBO is no stranger to true crime, though its offerings tend to be more prestige than your average, with documentaries such as the unrelenting sex cult nightmare The Vow andThe Yogurt Shop Murders, a measured reinvestigation into the deaths of four teenage girls in Texas in the 90s. They have form, too, in drily funny sagas, such asMcMillions, about a high-stakes conspiracy to fix the McDonald’s Monopoly promotion. Rarely are their documentaries both solemnandbizarro, with the exception perhaps of The Jinx. An unnerving tale of millionaire real estate heir turned convicted murderer Robert Durst, it occasionally lingered on the stranger points of his story, like the time he shoplifted a $6 sandwich for kicks.All this makes sense, really: it’s not like most homicides lend themselves to a deadpan retelling. A Killer Story is not laugh-out-loud funny, either. But this very meta three-parter manages to tell not one but two killer stories, one disturbing and the other absurd. The first concerns a woman, Dana Chandler, who is sentenced to life in prison for the murder of her ex-husband and his new girlfriend. The second is about a true crime-obsessed stranger, Eileen Umbehr, who becomes fixated on the case, spamming a journalist with tips. The emails from Umbehr were, says Joe Sexton – previously of the New York Times and investigative newsroom ProPublica – “a crazy assortment of shit … I [didn’t] know whether to call the cops on her or fucking hire her!”Sexton – an editor on multiple Pulitzer-winning projects – swears a lot, and his account of the email campaign from “pyjama lady in Kansas” overflows with profanity. Her 2,714th email changes his mind, however; Chandler has had her state conviction overturned, writes Umbehr. It was time for Sexton go to Kansas, to meet the couple he describes – with more than a hint of fatigue – as “the most earnest fucking people you [could] ever meet in your life”.We flash back to 2002, when Karen Harkness and Mike Sisco were found dead in their home. The couple had visited a casino that night, but there was no indication that this was a burglary gone wrong, with money and jewellery left untouched. Rather, says Ray Lundin, formerly of the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, “whoever did the killing was motivated by emotion” – in other words, somebody known to the couple. Chandler becomes the main suspect, but there isn’t enough evidence in the view of the district attorney to press charges. That is until a TV crime special about her airs on CBS, and a new prosecutor decides to proceed with a legal case. Her eventual arrest was also caught on television cameras.This is a story about a very public murder case, then, but it’s also about Umbehr and her husband, Keen, a former waste collector who moonlighted as a local newspaper columnist and later qualified as a lawyer (at one point, hysterically, Sexton refers to him as “fuckin’ Bob Woodward”). The Umbehrs’ preoccupation with the case is clear, with Chandler not only dominating conversation at home but also becoming the subject of their prayers. They don’t only believe that she is innocent, however – they also believe they know who killed Harkness and Sisco. Roll credits!View image in fullscreen‘Certainty is a dangerous notion’ … Dana Chandler, who was sentenced to life in prison.Photograph: HBO/APThis could, of course, be a regular documentary about a miscarriage of justice but of course it’s not. In episode two we meet the person the Umbehrs are convinced is the real killer – but is their apparent evidence enough to justify involving every single law enforcement body in Kansas? Do the Umbehrs worry, asks Sexton, that they’re doing to this new “person of interest”, as they call him, exactly what was done to Chandler?There are some serious flaws in that initial case put forward against Chandler. But A Killer Story isn’t about that, ultimately. Rather, it’s about the pull of true crime, and the power of armchair detectives – not just posting on Reddit, but reaching into a real-life murder case and deciding that they know what’s best for the accused. “Certainty is a dangerous notion,” says Sexton, who had expected to blow the case wide open, but instead ends up entangled in something far messier. A Killer Story is a sideways proposition, but it is rather compelling – a rare true crime story that’s as much about the viewers as it is the victims.A Killer Story is onHBO MaxnowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryHBOreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts: Second Song review – shaky album occasionally strikes gold | Neil Young | The Guardian
description: The 80-year-old continues his tireless output, delving into the past for inspiration to variable results – though two lengthy brand-new songs are real showstoppers
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The 80-year-old continues his tireless output, delving into the past for inspiration to variable results – though two lengthy brand-new songs are real showstoppers
Content: Spontaneity over finesse … Neil Young.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APView image in fullscreenSpontaneity over finesse … Neil Young.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APNeil YoungReviewNeil Young and the Chrome Hearts: Second Song review – shaky album occasionally strikes gold(Reprise)The 80-year-old continues his tireless output, delving into the past for inspiration to variable results – though two lengthy brand-new songs are real showstoppersAlexis PetridisFri 11 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 04.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can’t faultNeil Youngfor his industry. Second Song is his second new album of 2026: the first, a double live set called As Time Explodes, was released just over three months ago. Indeed, at 80, his work schedule seems mind-boggling. Since 2020, he’s released nine new albums, a 30-minute EP, five self-directed films and three more films directed by others, 10 archival live albums, six archival studio albums and two immense box sets. He has embarked on tours with his longstanding backing band Crazy Horse, his recently convened backing band the Chrome Hearts, and solo. He has gone to public war with Spotify, Amazon, Ticketmaster and – briefly – the BBC’s coverage of Glastonbury, and penned umpteen op-ed pieces about politics, the environment and corporate media for his online newspaper the Times-Contrarian. When he recently cancelled a European tour citing exhaustion, it was hard not to think: well, I’m not surprised.View image in fullscreenSecond Song album artwork.Photograph: PR HandoutYou do find yourself wondering if his workload is such a good thing: not just for an elderly gentleman’s health but also for the quality of his output. Young has always prized spontaneity over finesse, but some of his more recent releases have suggested that at least a soupçon of finesse might not go amiss. Last year’s Talkin to the Trees, however, seemed to cross the line that separates the instinctive from the dashed off. Young frequently sounded as if he was making the material up as he went along, with nugatory results: “When today has come and gone, I might be singing my new song,” he offered on Family Life. “Might be short, it might be long, but I’ll be singing my new song.” If some of the melodies sounded familiar, that’s because they were. Not one but two tracks echoed the tune of Woody Guthrie’s This Land Is Your Land; First Fire of Winter was essentially Young’s 1970 masterpiece Helpless with different lyrics; Thankful rewrote 1992’s Harvest Moon.Its follow-up leans more into Young’s gentle acoustic side than the gargantuan Crazy Horse-like din the Chrome Hearts are more than capable of creating. The music seems a little more honed than that on its predecessor. There are audible overdubs, including a backwards guitar solo on opener The Foggy Edge of Time. Like 1973’s Don’t Be Denied or 1979’s Thrasher, it’s one of those Neil Young songs in which he defends his right to follow his muse, regardless of the personal cost. But if you’re worried about declining inspiration, the omens augur ill. Two of Second Song’s seven tracks are re-recordings of tracks Young first performed with his early 60s band the Squires, which hardly suggests a surfeit of great new material.Casting Me Away From You and I’ll Love You Forever turn out to be pleasant enough, but slight. The former has already been plundered for its melody on The Emperor of Wyoming, from Young’s eponymous 1968 solo debut; I’ll Love You Forever, reworked as a paean to Young’s partner Daryl Hannah, is at least more charming than the tribute he offered up on Talkin to the Trees, which described Hannah as “my best wife ever” and “the best cook in the world”. Elsewhere, there’s another song cut from the same rambling cloth as the stuff on Second Song’s predecessor – Day After Day’s seven minutes feel like seven months – and an unexpected, but sweet diversion into pre-rock’n’roll pop on Earth Girl.That leaves two songs, although in fairness, they take up nearly half Second Song’s running time. From its title downwards, Soon I Might Be Going is thick with intimations of imminent mortality – “I miss you like tomorrow”, Young sings at one point – and feels like a weary, far older cousin of 1974’s Ambulance Blues: a long, ruminative sigh of a song whose subject matter ranges wildly about, from Donald Trump’s White House renovations to Young’s estrangement from his daughter Amber Jean. He also addressed the latter on Talkin to the Trees, but while the tone there was huffy and injured, here Young sounds plaintive and bereft: “Come back to me, my lovely girl, your memory is mine.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNeil Young – every album ranked!Read moreIt is genuinely gripping, but Second Song’s title track is something else entirely: a latter-day Neil Young song that you might compare to his best work without recourse to special pleading. Its melody is impossibly beautiful and – crucially – not markedly similar to any of the impossibly beautiful melodies Young has previously written: 11 minutes of it slip by without the listener checking their watch. Its lyrics capture a dying-of-the-light quality – “the leaves are falling, gathered in piles to burn outside / Somehow the smoke is calling, somehow the embers will decide” – but unlike Soon I Might Be Going, it reaches a comforting resolution: everything may be turning to shit, its final verses suggest, but you can always find solace in music.It would be nice if everything here was as good as those two songs, if you could justifiably claim Second Song as an autumn-years masterpiece along the lines of Dylan’s Rough and Rowdy Ways. Instead, the sublime shares space with the not bad and the insubstantial: a superior example of a late-period Neil Young album, but a late-period Neil Young album nonetheless.Second Song is released via Reprise on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsNeil YoungPop and rockAmericanareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: Grumpy’s weirded-up country celebration of trans joy and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: Sometime Zach Bryan backing vocalist Heaven Schmitt started Grumpy as a solo project. It’s now a six-piece band, blending alt-country with jubilant solidarity
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Sometime Zach Bryan backing vocalist Heaven Schmitt started Grumpy as a solo project. It’s now a six-piece band, blending alt-country with jubilant solidarity
Content: Painfully lovely … Grumpy.Photograph: Michael Tyrone DelaneyView image in fullscreenPainfully lovely … Grumpy.Photograph: Michael Tyrone DelaneyAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: Grumpy’s weirded-up country celebration of trans joy and the week’s best new tracksSometime Zach Bryan backing vocalist Heaven Schmitt started Grumpy as a solo project. It’s now a six-piece band, blending alt-country with jubilant solidaritySpencer Hughes,Ben Beaumont-ThomasandLaura SnapesFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromBrooklyn, USRecommended if you likeWednesday, This Is Lorelei, Alex GUp nextUnfindable Ring released 23 October“Found family” is something that queer people talk about a lot: finding your people and sticking with them is necessary in a world that often seems to want you quiet at best and dead at worst. Grumpy began as the solo project of frontman Heaven Schmitt, in between stints collaborating and touring withcountry-pop star Zach Bryanas a backing vocalist. It’s now a six-piece band with predominantly trans members; some of the group have dated or are dating, and they all work collaboratively on recording, producing, mixing, creating artwork and making music videos.The joy of this musical found family is tangible across Grumpy’s debut record, Unfindable Ring. They are gleefully dismissive of genre, tending towards warm alt-country and indie-folk but throwing in Auto-Tuned vocals alongside slowcore guitars and grunge choruses. One song, George Clanton – named in honour of the weirdo electronica cult hero – is a meta celebration of musical freedom: “I disobey balance, I’m writing epic ballads,” Schmitt affirms.But most of the celebrations are of trans joy and queer love. The painfully lovely OBL (One Beautiful Life) places jubilant, delirious romance directly alongside the experience of being intimidated for it at a petrol station – this kind of joy, it suggests, matters even more once you remember people hate you for it. This full-band phase of Grumpy brings to mind the old adage, “If you wanna get there fast, go alone; if you wanna go far, go together” – loving, laughing and flipping off the rest of the world.Spencer HughesThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenSeething … M(h)aol.Photograph: Ginny DaviesM(h)aol – Scam ManifestoThe Irish post-punks riff on Valerie Solanas’s Scum Manifesto to articulate the painful hypocrisy of railing against beauty norms while fixating on them, to seething, sludgy guitar and muttered self-recriminations.LS300SkullsAndCounting x Jenny Sparks – The Ballad of St Nick’s ParkAbsurdist screamo meets bassline house, lairy rap and seagull noises in order to honour a defunct skate park, and amusingly flex on how far (or not) 300SkullsAndCounting has come from that buzzing node of alt culture, Leamington Spa.BBTJunge Eko – SpanThe Swiss musician’s new album Pierced (June17th) is unfeasibly beautiful, mixing voice, pipe organ, guitar and more into ambient slowcore. Span adds strings, flute and a very far-off techno beat into a softly heaving mass.BBTDesire – Just Another Love SongWith synths that flutter like curtains on a sunset-facing window, Johnny Jewel’s band chase down the memory of an inescapable lost love, yearning to be Eternal Sunshine’d in order to forget.LSAmerican Motors – No Horses“This ain’t a one horse town / We wish we still had a horse around”: a bleak, droll, Protomartyr-esque anthem from the Pennsylvania rockers, in which a minimalist fuzz groove builds into a sumptuous epic.BBTChrystal x Rudimental – 321Over some liquid D’n’B throbbing from Rudimental, Chrystal continues to channel the wet-eyed, gritted-teeth melancholy of classic house vocalists, and her chorus has endless replay factor.BBTThe War on Drugs – Who’s ThatThis one-off loosie channels the unadulterated essence of WoD: horizon-tickling guitars, tentatively euphoric piano, hangdog Springsteenisms – though it’s newly emotionally exposing, detailing Adam Granduciel’s attempt to love himself through his demons.LSSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesExplore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 100 years after John Coltrane’s birth, secret tapes are emerging. What can they tell us about jazz’s great rulebreaker? | John Coltrane | The Guardian
description: The sax star turned his back on fame to embrace free jazz. Caught on a tape machine hidden in an overcoat, newly revealed recordings show how he did it
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: The sax star turned his back on fame to embrace free jazz. Caught on a tape machine hidden in an overcoat, newly revealed recordings show how he did it
Content: In an unsentimental mood … John Coltrane performs at Newport Jazz Festival in 1966.Photograph: Gai Terrell/RedfernsView image in fullscreenIn an unsentimental mood … John Coltrane performs at Newport Jazz Festival in 1966.Photograph: Gai Terrell/RedfernsJohn Coltrane100 years after John Coltrane’s birth, secret tapes are emerging. What can they tell us about jazz’s great rulebreaker?The sax star turned his back on fame to embrace free jazz. Caught on a tape machine hidden in an overcoat, newly revealed recordings show how he did itAmmar KaliaFri 11 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 1965, at the height of his fame, saxophonist John Coltrane headlined the DownBeat jazz festival in Chicago. Taking to the stage with a new member of his band, young experimentalist Archie Shepp on tenor, Coltrane’s quartet blew through a series of jagged and free improvisations, straying from structured compositions and, instead, hurling down sheets of sound so loud and aggressive that they reportedly caused widespread walk-outs. DownBeat’s own reviewerlater wrote: “They gave as tasteless a display of musicianship as I’ve ever heard … Shepp and Coltrane seemed to be more interested in trying to out-honk, out-squeal and out-bleat each other than in playing music.”That 1965 performance should have been a triumphant moment, after five years of Coltrane’s star ascending. Since leaving Miles Davis’s “first great quintet”, with whom he had recorded what would become the bestselling jazz album of all time – 1959’sKind of Blue– Coltrane founded an entirely new harmonic language in jazz with the 1960 release of his solo LPGiant Steps, had a radio hit with his 1961 version of The Sound of Music’s My Favourite Things and, in January 1965, formulated his own spiritual imagining of jazz music with the Grammy-nominated albumA Love Supreme. He was already a giant of the genre, contributing dozens of compositions to the standard repertoire, but two years later, in 1967, aged just 40, he would be dead of liver cancer.“He torched his commercial appeal by going avant garde,” says the writer and Coltrane biographerBen Ratliff. “He wasn’t interested in pissing people off but he wanted to absorb new influences, younger players and explore the unknown. He always wanted to keep moving forward and to keep listening to himself. He was questing and working towards a kind of endless music.”View image in fullscreen‘This was social music’ … John Coltrane.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesTo mark the centenary of Coltrane’s birth this month, that quest is being documented on a series of previously unreleased, holy grail recordings of his nightclub experiments. Regularly taking up four- to six-week residencies in spaces such as theJazzGallery in Manhattan, the Showboat in Washington DC or Pep’s Lounge in Philadelphia, Coltrane would play extended sets of new material that existed purely in the moment of their making: unplanned and unruly.View image in fullscreenThe Tiberi Tapes … holy grail recordings from the height of Coltrane’s live career.Dubbed The Tiberi Tapes after Frank Tiberi, the saxophonist who made the recordings, the reel-to-reel tapes initially existed as Tiberi’s private means of study. Taking a bulky Magnavox TR-100 to clubs, with its microphone hidden in the sleeve of his overcoat, Tiberi began recording concerts, managing to change the tapes in the dark every 30 minutes to capture as much of Coltrane’s virtuosity as possible. Following Coltrane’s quartet from 1960 to 1964, just before the recording of A Love Supreme, Tiberi amassed 80 reels of recordings and more than 60 hours of music that he began sharing with select peers and students: a map of Coltrane’s circuitous route to endless music.Sax legend Joe Lovano played with Tiberi as part of the Woody Herman Big Band in 1976 and remembers being astounded by the material. “Frank would come and put the headphones on me and press play on certain sections to illustrate the way Coltrane would work harmonic changes or melodies,” Lovano says. “It was inspiring because you could already hear how he was playing single tunes for 35 minutes or more; really stretching out to follow the music and let it take him where it wanted to go. That freedom of his later work was always present in the way he took his own melodic path and left space for others.” Lovano later played with McCoy Tyner, Coltrane’s pianist from 1960 to 1965, “and he told me they all knew Frank was recording but he had their blessing. The band knew it was for education and the music first.”double quotation markIt was legendary how much he practised and played, all day, every day and then performing until 4amTiberi, who is now 97 and was unavailable for interview, offered up the tapes recently to Coltrane’s final record label, Impulse!, as a means of preserving their history. Whittling down those 26 hours of music to 11 newly mastered compositions, the Tiberi Tapes compilation doesn’t shy away from the often poor audio quality of the haphazard recordings or the raucous environment of their making. Audience members can be heard chatting in the background or yelping in response to spirited passages, while Coltrane’s saxophone lines weave through the tape hiss to produce startlingly beautiful takes on a slower, more melodic version of Giant Steps, as well as a 33-minute extension of A Love Supreme’s Resolution. “The energy of these recordings is important because it captures the creative spark Coltrane was feeding off,” says jazz historianAshley Kahn. “This was social music, so people are chatting or making noise, but if you can work your way through, it gives as much back as you put in.”For Lovano, the Tapes serve as a testament to the relationships Coltrane had with each of the musicians in his band. “It was legendary how much he practised and played, all day, every day. And then performing until 4am before driving home to his babies. He’s just a young man striving in his 30s and he shares that inspirational energy,” he says. “You can hear how he digs new cats like Archie Shepp or [drummer] Rashied Ali or [saxophonist] Pharoah Sanders – they loved each other and he let everyone stand on their own two feet. You can always hear the seeds of where he will go next.”What came next was the most uncompromising album of Coltrane’s career. Recorded in June 1965 (a few weeks before the DownBeat festival show) and released the following year,Ascensionwas the first recorded taste of this unruly, alienating music. He expanded his quartet to include seven extra players from the experimental fringes of free jazz, including Sanders and John Tchicai who would go on to be pioneers in their own right. The 40-minute suite was recorded unrehearsed in two takes and plays like a big band spiralling through screeching solos that struggle to maintain their balance over the shifting tectonic plates of melody. At points, the cacophony is so overwhelming that it feels like listening to seven conversations at once.“Post-1965, it’s the line in the sand, and still the most challenging part of Coltrane’s career for many,” Kahn says. “It was so new and revolutionary they didn’t have names for it. Was it Energy Music? The New Thing? It was so radical that people had real issues understanding what was going on.”View image in fullscreenColtrane performing circa 1960.Photograph: Gai Terrell/RedfernsBy 1966, after Tiberi stopped recording and had embarked on his own career, Coltrane had absorbed several new, subversive players into his fold, including free music saxophonist Albert Ayler, who was famous for playing 40-minute elongated live versions of single, hard-blowing tunes. During a show with Ayler, two drummers and Coltrane’s wife, Alice, a pianist, at the Lincoln Center in New York in February of that year, even more of Coltrane’s audience reportedly left in droves after hearing the untethered, explosive direction in which his music was going. The writer Amiri Barakadescribedthe atonal experience as a sound “of an actual frightening nature ... it swallowed you!”, while saxophonist Dave Liebman estimated almost half of the 2,600-seat audience walked out over the hour-long performance.‘It’s the story of what happens when the music stops’: bringing tormented jazz legend Bill Evans to lifeRead more“In Coltrane’s later period, we have an artist who is at such a masterful level that his playing has moved beyond our immediate understanding,” saxophonist and Coltrane acolyte James Brandon Lewis says. “There was always intent and direction with his line but our ears might be too untrained to know what he was trying to solve. He was connecting improvisation to the tribal and spiritual history of music, seeing it all as one thing – the folklore and the future.”Continuing to perform and record until just months before his sudden death in July 1967, the question of where Coltrane would go next has haunted fans and listeners ever since. “He was always searching for his sound and he never stopped,” says saxophonist Melissa Aldana. “In the later years, it was like he was trying to find a divine vibration, free from any kind of preconceived limitations. He was deep into the sound and he was totally free. That’s what always brings me back to him and it means there will always be something new to find in his playing as we continue to listen.”While his audiences might have waned in his later years, it is that same, ceaseless searching that now seems to pull younger listeners in 100 years on from his birth. Ironically, Ascension – the album that heralded his “difficult” late phase – was reissued in June this year owing to demand. “Don’t analyse him, just hear,” Lewis says. “Open up your heart and receive the message. Whatever you think it might be.”The Tiberi Tapesare released on 6 November via Impulse! Melissa Aldana and Joe Lovano perform Coltrane 100 on 13 November at the Barbican, London, as part ofEFG London jazz festival. A new best-of compilation, Coltrane 100, is released on 2 October via RhinoExplore more on these topicsJohn ColtraneJazzMiles DavisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Haruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely review – slight songs with huge hearts from the Japanese pop pioneer | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Unpredictable and utterly beguiling, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songs
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: Unpredictable and utterly beguiling, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songs
Content: Playful … Haruomi Hosono.Photograph: Masahiro HandaView image in fullscreenPlayful … Haruomi Hosono.Photograph: Masahiro HandaPop and rockReviewHaruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely review – slight songs with huge hearts from the Japanese pop pioneer(Ghostly International)Unpredictable and utterly beguiling, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songsStevie ChickFri 11 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaruomi Hosono is one of the most influential figures in Japanese music. In 1969, his psych-folk groupHappy Endwere the first rock group to sing in Japanese; decades later, their songKaze wo Atsumetewas rediscovered for the Lost in Translation soundtrack. He was also an integral member of electronic pioneers Yellow Magic Orchestra, and scored movies and video games, while his solo albums swing from foundationalcity poptexts to experiments in ambient and arch exotica.View image in fullscreenHaruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely album artNow 79, with disciples including Van Dyke Parks and Harry Styles (who named 2022’sHarry’s Houseafter 1973 solo album Hosono House), he still makes whatever music he wants. His 23rd solo album is wilful, playful, unpredictable and utterly beguiling. Rooted in the Japanese concept ofomoiyari, roughly translated as compassion, these songs are big-hearted, focusing on warmth and positivity: opening reverieNote of Mothershipfeatures a chorus of overlapping voices murmur-singing “we are mothers”; the sweet Happy Holiday repeats its title over an enchantingly simple melody;Sincerelyis a sleepy, Leon Redbone-esque strum.But Yours Sincerely evades mawkishness with its mischievous invention. The Gallic waltz of Aayurveda is inverted exotica, with Europe cast as the mysterious “other”; the primitive electronica of Anemo Wheel channels the innocent charms of early synth innovators Isao Tomita and Wendy Carlos; Rojiura (Walking Vibration) is rooted in Japanese rhythms and percussion, but deliciously lost in time. Hosono’s themes of compassion and hope in humanity’s better side make this collection of miniatures and sketches something greater than its already bewitching parts.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockJapanElectronic musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup | Science fiction books | The Guardian
description: Massif by Garth Nix; Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan; An Immaculate Deception by Isabela Livino; Serenity Falls by CJ Tudor
Author: Lisa Tuttle
Headline: Massif by Garth Nix; Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan; An Immaculate Deception by Isabela Livino; Serenity Falls by CJ Tudor
Content: Ursula K Le Guin inspires a new collection of stories.Photograph: Beth GwinnView image in fullscreenUrsula K Le Guin inspires a new collection of stories.Photograph: Beth GwinnScience fiction roundupScience fiction booksReviewThe best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundupMassif by Garth Nix; Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan; An Immaculate Deception by Isabela Livino; Serenity Falls by CJ TudorLisa TuttleFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenMassifby Garth Nix (Gollancz, £25)The bestselling fantasy author’s first science fiction novel for adults is set three centuries from now, when humanity has spread out to the stars. The colonisation of other planets has been enabled by contact with mysterious aliens, and with much of the population split into competing economic spheres, war over territory is raging between the two biggest: United Earth Government and the Mars and Beyond Prosperity Sphere. This war in space is possible only because the godlike aliens continue to supply us with spaceships – but why? What do they want? Answers must await a sequel to this compelling, action-packed space opera with wonderfully weird aliens.View image in fullscreenRevolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guinedited by Jonathan Strahan (Titan, £22)The authors of these 15 original stories range from the well-established (Karen Joy Fowler, Kelly Link, Molly Gloss) to newer writers (Chana Porter, Ai Jiang, Vandana Singh). A few make direct reference to Le Guin, but most reveal her influence subtly, by shared interests in questioning established ideas and imagining other ways of living, whether among non-human beings, in the future, on other worlds, or in ours. My favourites include Sarah Pinsker’s Travelling, Home, about a young woman in present-day America seeking her place in the world, Ann Leckie’s Five-Eyed Jane, an ironic look at misunderstandings among aliens, and Karen Joy Fowler’s Blaumont, a dark fairytale that’s as disturbing and thought-provoking today as Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas. Probably the best original anthology of the year: a must-read.View image in fullscreenAn Immaculate Deceptionby Isabela Livino (Gollancz, £22)In 19th-century Brazil, the deeply religious Madalena knows she’s sinned with her beloved Leandro, but is sure that when she tells him she’s pregnant he will propose. She blurts out the truth before their carriage is wrecked in a storm: waking later in his house, weak and aching, she sees no love in his eyes, and he leaves her to the care of his friend, the strangely attractive Dr Lobo. The two men insist she must stay until she’s fully recovered, but she is determined to get home. Gothic elements glide into full Hammer horror mode as she learns that Dr Lobo belongs to an occult society given to performing dark magic rituals: there are more revelations to come before the end of this wildly entertaining debut.View image in fullscreenSerenity Fallsby CJ Tudor (Michael Joseph, £18.99)The latest creepy thriller from the author of The Burning Girls is set in a planned community in Florida, where everyone is comfortable and law-abiding. But when widower Dan and daughter Sadie arrive from England, having inherited a property, they find a dead body in the swimming pool. It turns out there have been a surprisingly large number of accidental deaths during the town’s 50-year history, while the few people who left were never heard from again. That there’s something sinister going on is perhaps a bit too obvious from the start, but the journey to figure out why is entertaining, with a jaw-dropping finale.View image in fullscreenScionby James Islington (Gollancz, £22)This fast-moving, violent thriller is narrated by Azure, a professional assassin. The world has become so overcrowded that, with increasingly limited resources, legislation has been passed making it legal to kill the rich “lifers” who take advantage of every longevity treatment available. Azure’s skills are always in demand, but his next job is different: he’s been hired to protect a very old lady from being killed. His own life is on the line, especially after her fortress is breached and they’re forced into the dangerous, overcrowded city, where he may find answers to a mystery from his own past. The inconclusive ending makes it clear there are more instalments to come of this gripping blend of neo-noir cyberpunk.Explore more on these topicsScience fiction booksScience fiction roundupFantasy booksHorror booksUrsula K Le GuinreviewsShareReuse this content

title: A Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan review – a brilliant interrogation of philosophy and wonder | Fiction | The Guardian
description: With a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditions
Author: Daisy Hildyard
Headline: With a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditions
Content: Meticulous precision … Adrian Duncan.Photograph: Steve PykeView image in fullscreenMeticulous precision … Adrian Duncan.Photograph: Steve PykeBook of the dayFictionReviewA Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan review – a brilliant interrogation of philosophy and wonderWith a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditionsDaisy HildyardFri 11 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor several years I ran community groups that involved reading books aloud with other adults. Sharing the experience of reading in that way made me notice how, when one or more of us was baffled by a story, this bafflement was rarely experienced without an accompanying sense of mild anger. It was so easy to make us, the readers, angry – at the characters; at the author; perhaps even at the nature of this reality on which we’d lost our grip. We were confronted with the fact that our capacity to understand the world was limited. We didn’t like that.Irish author Adrian Duncan’s fifth novel, A Thought Without Collision, takes risks with this bafflement: it relates and conveys an experience of being mystified by the universe. As it opens, in Ireland in 1923, it is becoming apparent that six-year-old Catherine has exceptional academic gifts, and that her father’s farm is failing. In the next chapter, set in 1951, Dr Josef Alois, a Tyrolean émigré academic in his mid-50s, is living in his self-built house on the east coast of Scotland. He is alone until Catherine reappears, “a handsome woman in her mid-thirties”, and now an Oxford professor. The second chapter ends starkly: Alois “is more unwell than he believes and will perish in one month and eleven days”.double quotation markIn Duncan's fiction, the Irish realist tradition converges with a cerebral European modeDetails of Alois’s biography, and aspects of his two books, are drawn from the life of Ludwig Wittgenstein. The novel references the philosopher’s near-contemporaries, GE Moore, Gottlob Frege and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. Like Alois and Catherine, these men laboured to establish a particular understanding of the world. Some pages of A Thought Without Collision present diagrams or passages of algebraic logic. Throughout, descriptions of small, mysterious places (“pockets” in Catherine’s mind, pits dug in the ground, golf holes, a swallow’s nest) are emblems of the other worlds that surround us, intimated but not available to human knowledge. As Catherine’s intelligence becomes increasingly polymathic, her interest ranges from complex mathematics to animal sentience. She pictures hidden worlds in the sky: a “plane of translucent and unconnected fragments above them all”.The narrative is related in short, alternating chapters that switch between the two time periods. This creates a sense of flickering movement, like chevrons on a motorway: we see Catherine’s life speed by, an effect intensified by Alois’s impending death. It’s a feat of engineering that the story can cut between these two temporalities and their respective revelations, as it plays with multiple philosophical traditions, while navigating the landscapes of the several distinct historical settings to which the novel takes us.Beyond these accomplishments, A Thought Without Collision does not feel abstruse or tricksy to read. Its mysteries, like the mysteries of the universe, are not here to infuriate reading groups. When Catherine’s father stakes his farm on American stock market investments, we see how floating abstractions are tethered to material realities.From his debut, Love Notes from a German Building Site, throughThe Gorgeous Inertia of the Earth, all Duncan’s novels share a meticulous, patient narrative voice. While some have leaned on a blurry psychological disintegration for their denouement, here the conclusions are more definite: with economic gestures, he offers glimpses of the characters’ new worlds. The novel often reads as a realist Irish rural story: hens underfoot, cold black tea on the table, drizzle. Catherine, so dignified, with a bone-deep sadness contracted via childhood tragedy, could almost be aWilliam Trevorcharacter. But in Duncan’s fiction that tradition converges with a cerebral European mode that is drawn to philosophy, architecture, madness and exile. I can’t think of another writer who draws from the same seams in any comparable way.The prose is exceptionally, perhaps deceptively, straightforward. When Alois makes dinner, he “sets a dark pot on his range to boil. He then lifts a skillet from the wall and begins to heat it up. He takes butter from his tiny pantry and carves a half-inch cube from it. Then he takes a delph pot from a cupboard and from it lifts two eggs, with which to prepare an omelette.”This physical attention is intense (there’s more detail here than in a cookbook) but not sustained (it isn’t Knausgård), and so the close descriptions, when they come, seem weighted with something other than themselves. What is the “tiny pantry” here to impart? Is it contextual detail, or a metaphor? We might consider the relation to Wittgensteinian language games; the differing positions played by words as they arise from, and become a part of, actions in the world.There is also a plainer effect of this superfluity of precision, which is that itfeelssuggestive – like a photorealistic still life, where the careful replication of detail is an occasion to meditate on something seen through it. In A Thought Without Collision, every half-inch cube of butter makes you wonder.A Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan is published by Tuskar Rock (£14.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionBook of the dayPhilosophy booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Raiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of Atlantis | Tomb Raider | The Guardian
description: We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?
Author: Tom Regan
Headline: We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?
Content: The leopards have changed their spots … Lara faces a familiar foe with new abilities in Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.Photograph: ATL GamescomView image in fullscreenThe leopards have changed their spots … Lara faces a familiar foe with new abilities in Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.Photograph: ATL GamescomTomb RaiderRaiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of AtlantisWe have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?Tom ReganFri 11 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe join Lara Croft in St Francis’ Folly – inspired by the Unesco-listed monasteries of Meteora in Greece – as the light shines through the cracked ceiling and a flock of bats glide across the vast ruins below. When Lara leaps down to the monastery’s crumbling pillared courtyard, it becomes clear that these screeching, leathery creatures aren’t just set dressing. As they lurch towards her with unpredictable movements, she dispatches the swarm with a flurry of gun fire and panicked punches.It’s a suitably cinematic reintroduction to our heroine and her very first adventure. Co-developed by longtime Lara custodians Crystal Dynamics and Polish studio Flying Wild Hog, Legacy of Atlantis is a reimagining of the classic 1996 gameTomb Raider, and this familiar cliffside location is now brimming with new life and believable detail. Yet while our reunion gets off to an auspicious start, I have my concerns. It feels like reconnecting with an old friend at the pub, only for them to begin spouting conspiracy theories two pints in.Where the ’96 original forced players to rely on their wits – or a pricey strategy guide – to figure out what to do, Lara can now straight-up cheat. She’s equipped with an environmental scanner, so a button tap reveals extra environmental lore or simply the solution to a puzzle. It’s a change that feels somewhat sacrilegious, and may detract from the eerily isolating atmosphere that made the original so beloved.View image in fullscreenLara v the bats is now suitably cinematic.Photograph: ATL Gamescom“If the devs from 1996 had the technology that we have today, what choices would they make?” asks Raul Siqueira, game director at Crystal Dynamics. “The sense of isolation in the original game was largely due to the technological limitations of that time,” says Arek Tomaszewski, art director at Flying Wild Hog, likening it to the fog in Silent Hill which was both an artistic decision and a way to cover up empty environments on the PlayStation 1. “The darkness and the feeling of being alone created an emotion that you remember. When I replayed Tomb Raider, my initial memory was the exact same. What we are trying to do now is build environments – like the spaces in Greece – where you feel as if you are the first person discovering them in centuries, entering places that have been left untouched.”Lara now crafts balms from a menu rather than finding anachronous first aid kits in centuries-old untouched tombs. Somewhat less believably, she can also pause her adventure to whip up stat-boosting stews,Breath of the Wild-style. These additions are among a slew of modern flourishes that I feel unsure about. Is the originalreallyimproved by giving Lara a grappling hook, RPG-esque stats, skill trees and quick time events?One area that Flying Wild Hog – the maker of Hard Reset and Shadow Warrior – knows well is combat. As Lara delves deeper into the dingy ruins of the Damocles chamber, she is ambushed by a familiar foe: a leopard. But this roaring beast now moves with convincing agility. As well as swiping at Lara, leopards now hide from her, retreating through holes in the walls before returning with an emboldened counterattack. Luckily Lara is fiercer too. As the beast lunges toward her, she draws her shotgun and blasts, causing the creature to crumple to the floor in Max Payne-esque slo-mo. The newly dynamic combat is the gameplay overhaul that looks most promising – a world away from the stationary shooting and “dog scooting across the carpet” backsteps of yesteryear.View image in fullscreenThe swords of Damocles puzzle area.Photograph: ATL GamescomNarratively, the remake promises a deeper story and some fan-pleasing easter eggs. For this iteration, Lara is played by Dragon Age: Inquisition and Cyberpunk 2077 actor Alix Wilton Regan. “Hearing her voice in the game now, sheisLara Croft,” says Tomaszewski. “The sheer amount of character and depth she brought to Lara is unbelievable.” The game’s publisher, Amazon, is also the custodian of a forthcoming Phoebe Waller-Bridge-producedTomb Raider TV show, and the developers suggest there will be some connective tissue between the two projects. After hopping across falling swords and solving Damocles’s puzzles, Lara emerges from the darkened tomb into a burst of sunshine, and my demo culminates with the tease of a vast, ancient civilisation.“I think this game changed our DNA as a studio,” says Tomaszewski. “In our previous games, like Shadow Warrior, every second was filled with nonstop action. Here we wanted to master pacing, and we learned a lot from Crystal Dynamics.”Gaming as a whole has undoubtedly transformed since Lara’s first adventure. Tomb Raider’s dodgy camera controls and questionable Playboy collaborations are thankfully now dusty historical relics themselves. Yet as visually impressive as Legacy of Atlantis looks, I can’t help but wonder if a touch of Lara’s brilliance lay in her original simplicity. By encumbering her with modern game mechanics, a bit of her soul may be lost. If Legacy of Atlantis offers the option to disable all of that for a purer Tomb-raiding experience, it could still be a winner.Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis is scheduled for release in FebruaryThis interview took place at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by Gamescom.Explore more on these topicsTomb RaiderGamesAction gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Liz Larner review – crystal comets crash to Earth yet fail to make much impact | Art and design | The Guardian
description: These portentous works, based on scans of a real asteroids, seem to warn of societal collapse, but this first UK exhibition of the US sculptor needed a simpler approach
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: These portentous works, based on scans of a real asteroids, seem to warn of societal collapse, but this first UK exhibition of the US sculptor needed a simpler approach
Content: Glittery, gritty ceramic … Liz Larner, Nyx, 2022.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsView image in fullscreenGlittery, gritty ceramic … Liz Larner, Nyx, 2022.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsArt and designReviewLiz Larner review – crystal comets crash to Earth yet fail to make much impactCamden Art Centre, LondonThese portentous works,based on scans of a real asteroids, seem to warn of societal collapse, but this first UK exhibition of the US sculptor needed a simpler approachEddy FrankelFri 11 Sep 2026 11.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCorporations are already selling off mining rights to asteroids. These massive balls of rock and ore and minerals and ice up in space, far out of the reach of humanity, and mostly named after ancient Greek or Roman goddesses, are being traded like real estate by greedy suits with telescopes.There are half a dozen asteroids in American sculptor Liz Larner’s exhibition at CamdenArtCentre, her first institutional exhibition in the UK, plonked on the floor like they’ve just burned through the atmosphere on their way in from space. Each one is based on a Nasa scan of a real asteroid and then re-formed out of glittery, gritty ceramic. They’re gleaming symbols of corporate greed, ecological collapse and sexism – comets of misery, sent from the future to crash land on Finchley Road.View image in fullscreenComplex bundle … Contrary Brunette, 2021.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsFeminism, ecology, post-humanism – you’re only beginning to scratch the surface of Larner’s complex, heavily referential, ultra-layered approach to sculpture, which she’s been honing since the 1980s in Los Angeles. Throughout the rest of this show you bump into references to art history, literature, music, grammar, mythology, Japanese kintsugi. It’s dizzying, confusing, a bit bewildering. It’s almost all new ceramic and plastic works, with a few older pieces dotted around the place.The exhibition functions as a sort of bleak hike across a scarred, arid landscape. Slabs of rock and mounds of plastic are pinned to the wall, boulders litter the ground, rubbish has been strung across the ceiling. As you meander through like an amateur geologist, you see cracks and crevices in stone, rocks split apart, shards of gold. The slab works on the wall – all made of ceramic – look like fossils of mesozoic fungal growths.The best slab works are pockmarked with agates and marble and crystal, or have cracked down the middle like broken fossils. Two have shattered into pieces, laying splintered across the floor.Some of the slabs are stunning: they feel heavy, earthy, ancient, primordial. Others look a bit like big decorative dinner plates. The little clusters of plastic detritus – discarded single-use spoons and cups tied together – form sculptural mini-galaxies out of rubbish. They’re great.Most of the newer plastic and ceramic works make aesthetic sense shown together like this, but the show starts to stumble when it widens the conceptual net. There are a handful of early sculptures: fractured metal tubes twisted into the shapes of smiles, and a network of ribbons, hair and measuring tapes stretched across the gallery. It’s hard to see what relationship these have to the ceramics. Worst of all is the newest piece, a sleek, gaudy, golden arch with a hand and a bird’s foot perched on top of it, all in reference to the mythological figure of Lilith. It’s not a good sculpture, and it makes no sense next to everything else on display. Whacking together works from different eras, in different materials, with different ideas, just hasn’t worked here.View image in fullscreenFractured … Smile (fangs), 1996-2010.Photograph: © Liz Larner. Courtesy Galerie Max Hetzler, Anton Kern Gallery, The Modern Institute, Regen ProjectsChoosing to focus on new ceramic works instead of properly introducing this relatively little-known American artist with a survey or retrospective is a strange choice that doesn’t service the audience. This result is a muddled, disparate, confusing mishmash of an introduction to an artist whose career deserved a simpler, easier way in.A lot of what Larner’s done here is great. There’s a sense of dismay to a lot of the work, like Larner has looked at the world around her – with its ecological collapse, its mounds of rubbish, its politics of greedy mining and extraction, its sexism and selfishness and injustice – and felt sheer panic, total distress. These newer sculptures are a way of processing that. It’s as if by creating her own asteroids, her own crystal forms and slabs of earth, she can make sense of what’s happening to the world. It doesn’t always work – but then the world doesn’t always make sense, either.AtCamden Art Centre, London, until 17 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designSculptureArtCeramicsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Playing With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworlds | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Wang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installation
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Wang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installation
Content: Potentially overwhelming … a VR still from Playing With Fire.Photograph: Vive Arts and Atlas VView image in fullscreenPotentially overwhelming … a VR still from Playing With Fire.Photograph: Vive Arts and Atlas VClassical musicReviewPlaying With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworldsSouthbank Centre, LondonWang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installationErica JealFri 11 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt might be the first time that a soloist at the Last Night of the Proms is simultaneously giving another performance in another London venue.Playing With Fireis an installation that lets the pianist Yuja Wang be in two places at once – or perhaps in two universes. Nine pieces of music conjure nine luminous dreamworlds for an audience wearing VR headsets: Disney’s Fantasia on steroids.A collaboration between the pianist, the director Pierre-Alain Giraud and artist Gabríela Friðriksdóttir, produced by Vive Arts and Atlas V, it has already been seen in Cannes, Paris and Shanghai, and now has a home in London until new year.Headsets on, we hear the click of Wang’s heels as her avatar emerges out of the pixels and walks to the piano stool. Then she begins to play. Or rather, the Steinway Spirio player piano in the middle of the room, programmed by Wang, plays – and we see digitised Wang play it. She begins with Ravel’s Jeux d’Eau, and after only a few seconds we are immersed, literally: water pools beneath the piano, then rises until we are submerged in a world of imaginary sea creatures. It’s enchanting, unnerving and in a way primal, all at once. After Debussy has led us to dry land again, Wang storms through the Danse Infernale from Stravinsky’s ballet The Firebird as the blazing bird swoops over our heads and creatures made of lava dance madly around us: a wild rumpus with Wang calm yet ferocious at its centre.View image in fullscreenThe future of performance? … Playing With Fire.Photograph: Pete WoodheadWorlds morph into each other with distant seismic rumbles. There’s an icy white land evoking a cathedral for Bach’s prelude Ich ruf zu dir, an inferno in Liszt’s Feux follets. The two dozen or so people sharing the experience are visible, up close, as vaguely humanoid shapes made of water vines, or blackened rock, or – more disturbingly – flames. If that’s not unsettling enough, the penultimate immersive episode is a terrifying realisation of the frenzied finale of Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No 7, one of his War Sonatas: villages burn on the horizon and drones skitter above.Yuja review – portrait of star pianist who is intellectually curious and deeply musically attunedRead moreIt’s powerful stuff, and it has the potential to be overwhelming, or indeed to induce motion sickness. But seats are available at the edge – or stand close enough to the piano and the dreamworld disappears, revealing fellow audience members inching around the room in their headsets, but with Wang’s avatar still at the piano.Finally we take the headsets off and listen to Chopin’s C sharp minor waltz, watching the piano keys and hammers move by themselves, readjusting ourselves to the mechanics of reality. It makes for an ending that’s slightly anticlimactic – but, given the weirdness and wonder of what’s gone before, it’s hard to think how it could be otherwise.At theSouthbank Centre, London, until 3 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsClassical musicSouthbank CentreYuja WangVirtual realityInstallationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tartuffe (Remixed) review – Mark Rylance sinks his false teeth into Molière’s trickster comedy | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Darren Raymond’s update drops Rylance’s impostor into a Jamaican-Nigerian wedding, with clever rhyming couplets but less political sting
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Darren Raymond’s update drops Rylance’s impostor into a Jamaican-Nigerian wedding, with clever rhyming couplets but less political sting
Content: Spiritual scheming … Usifu Jalloh and Mark Rylance in Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorView image in fullscreenSpiritual scheming … Usifu Jalloh and Mark Rylance in Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorTheatreReviewTartuffe (Remixed) review – Mark Rylance sinks his false teeth into Molière’s trickster comedyMarylebone theatre, LondonDarren Raymond’s update drops Rylance’s impostor into a Jamaican-Nigerian wedding, with clever rhyming couplets but less political stingMark LawsonFri 11 Sep 2026 08.09 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpitting posh platitudes through false teeth so bucked they might enforce a liquid diet, raking one hand across an oily comb-over while the other holds a Bible as tight as a manbag stuffed with gold,Mark Rylanceextends the long English tradition of comedy vicars to a French source: Molière’s 1664 comedy Tartuffe, about a trickster who fakes piety to defraud a devout family.The original targeted the Catholic church, the arrows sharp enough that the archbishop of Paris threatened excommunication to any Catholic who saw the play, forcingMolièreto write a new version, The Impostor, where the fakery was less directly sacred.View image in fullscreenOoh er … Mark Rylance and Suzette Llewellyn in Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Mark SeniorMore recently, the play has taken tweaks to the bogus holiness of the antagonist:at the RSC in 2018andBirmingham Rep four years later, Anil Gupta and Richard Pinto’s version turned the predatory priest into a fake imam who bamboozles a faithful Muslim family in the Midlands.Tartuffe (Remixed), writer-director Darren Raymond’s modern update, transplants the drama to a wedding bringing together Jamaican and Nigerian clans. Both families may well be Anglican, one character lamenting the transforming colonialism of Christian missionaries.Pastor Blake (as Tartuffe here becomes) is presumably Church of England – or pretending to be – rather than Roman Catholic, as a plot twist retained from the original requires him be offered as a husband. But it’s unclear – other than to allow Rylance to be cast – why these proud families would hire this creepy white guy to preside rather than someone from London’s Black clergy.This makes it hard to keep faith with Raymond’s spiritual scheme, although broader points are scored about public hypocrisy: the pastor backs charities for homeless people while investing in property companies and professes shame about slavery as a seduction tool.Some English adaptations prefer prose to approximate the tricky alexandrines of the original but Raymond retains rhyming couplets, alternating clever pairings – “immorality” / “normality”, “psalms” / “my arms” – with blunter runs: “heart” / “smart” / “fart” / “apart.”View image in fullscreenLikable performances … Sarah Mokonen, centre, in Tartuffe (Remixed).Photograph: Harriet CarterRylance, often playing directly to the audience, has enjoyable moments of excruciating Father-dancing at the wedding and, as the English farce tradition demands, is more than once reduced to his white Y-fronts and vest. Until stymied by an overlong second act, pushing the evening close to three hours, the cast achieves the speed farce needs.Engaging and likable performances include Usifu Jalloh as the bride’s father Oga and Nakeba Buchanan as stepmother Elmire, the characters who remain closest to Molière’s naming. As bride and groom, Sara Mokonen and Ivandro Da Cruz Leite sparkle together and apart.Molière satirised a society in which monarchy and church were superpowers, and as with another recent Anglicisation – the Sandra Oh-ledThe Misanthropeat the National – uprooting from that context can lose political sting and comic logic. “Remixed” risks being reduced.AtMarylebone theatre, London, until 24 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMolièreMark RylanceComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Don Giovanni review – reality recedes in visually dizzying Mozart tour de force | Opera | The Guardian
description: Kaspar Holten’s revival of his 2014 staging puts the focus on the Don’s psychology. Aigul Akhmetshina’s Elvira is a standout performance in a strong cast
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Kaspar Holten’s revival of his 2014 staging puts the focus on the Don’s psychology. Aigul Akhmetshina’s Elvira is a standout performance in a strong cast
Content: A jaded Lothario … Gordon Bintner (Don Giovanni) and Aigul Akhmetshina (Donna Elvira) in Mozart’s Don Giovanni at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA jaded Lothario … Gordon Bintner (Don Giovanni) and Aigul Akhmetshina (Donna Elvira) in Mozart’s Don Giovanni at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianOperaReviewDon Giovanni review – reality recedes in visually dizzying Mozart tour de forceRoyal Opera House, LondonThis revival of Kaspar Holten’s 2014 staging puts the focus on the Don’s psychology. Aigul Akhmetshina’s Elvira is a standout performance in a strong castClive PagetFri 11 Sep 2026 07.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePost #MeToo and #TimesUp, Mozart and Da Ponte’s tale of a predatory sex addict feels more pertinent than ever.Kaspar Holten’s 2014 staging, revived here with care and clarity by Greg Eldridge, may not be played in modern dress – Anja Vang Kragh’s semi-stylised costumes and Es Devlin’s Escher-inspired revolving set locate the action somewhere between 1850 and 1900 – but the contemporary resonances come over loud and clear. If only it wasn’t so frustratingly inconsistent.In Holten’s hands the overture becomes a visual as well as a musical tour de force. Luke Halls’ video design starts small, scrawling a single woman’s name on the grey stone facade. Soon, however, the trickle swells to a torrent as a catalogue of sexual conquests appear before our eyes. Projections are a constant throughout with scribbles, ink blots and splashes of blood spattering scenery and singers alike. In the famous Champagne Aria, images of buildings, rooms and staircases rotate at dizzying speed with the Don standing in the eye of the storm anticipating his latest binge. Remarkably, they rarely distract from the action, a testament to Bruno Poet’s dextrous lighting design.Holten places an appropriately intense focus on the title character as he spirals out of control. At first the upstairs rooms are haunted by a handful of ghostly exes. By the end, as the Don’s grasp on reality recedes, they’ve become legion. Even Leporello joins them, his face now white as a ghost. The Commendatore doesn’t drag Giovanni down to hell, he simply leaves him drained and alone, deprived of sexual gratification for eternity.View image in fullscreenRooms haunted by ghostly exes … Gordon Bintner (Don Giovanni) in Kaspar Holten’s staging of Don Giovanni at the Royal Opera House.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianLess successful is Holten’s handling of the opera’s women. Donna Anna is torn between desire for her seducer and guilt that she has caused her father’s murder. That weakens Donna Elvira, who now shares a similar character arc, while leaving Anna with no real connection to fiance Don Ottavio. Only Zerlina takes active steps to gain revenge, in this case by rending her clothes to suggest sexual assault before it’s actually happened.Gordon Bintnerplays Giovanni as a jaded Lothario, his bass-baritone at its ringing best when singing full out. He’s well paired with Roberto Tagliavini’s beefy-voiced, hangdog Leporello. As Donna Elvira, Aigul Akhmetshina offers power and passion in a standout performance. Rachel Willis-Sørensen delivers plenty of decibels as Donna Anna, though she could use a touch more flexibility at the very top. Bogdan Volkov is her sweet-toned Ottavio, especially effective in the two big arias. Giulia Semenzato sings extremely prettily as Zerlina, Dingle Yandell is a clarion, characterful Masetto and Andreas Bauer Kanabas a forceful Commendatore.Stefano Montanariconducts a punchy account of the score, his phrasing generally attentive to voices, though there were occasional coordination problems between pit and stage.Until 15 October.Explore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRoyal Opera HouseWolfgang Amadeus MozartreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’re fired!’ The TV shows you can’t stomach any more  | Television | The Guardian
description: Hating The Apprentice? Bored silly of House of the Dragon? Given up on your favourite soap opera after 50 years? Guardian readers share the shows they can’t bear to watch
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: Hating The Apprentice? Bored silly of House of the Dragon? Given up on your favourite soap opera after 50 years? Guardian readers share the shows they can’t bear to watch
Content: Chairman of the bored … Alan Sugar on The Apprentice.Photograph: N/A/BBC/FremantleMedia LtdView image in fullscreenChairman of the bored … Alan Sugar on The Apprentice.Photograph: N/A/BBC/FremantleMedia LtdTelevision‘You’re fired!’ The TV shows you can’t stomach any moreHating The Apprentice? Bored silly of House of the Dragon? Given up on your favourite soap opera after 50 years? Guardian readers share the shows they can’t bear to watchAlfie Packhamand Guardian readersFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ApprenticeWe loved this show for the first four or five seasons. It had a really good mix of candidates, different ages and walks of life. I think it was after season nine that we started to feel the programme was losing its authenticity. Contestants started to look like homogenous Love Islanders, all the same demographic – 20-30 age bracket, highly polished body image, eye on a post-show influencer career, etc. It lost its uniqueness and became just another reality show.Ngaire Vine, 56, DerbyshireWhen TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any moreRead moreLudwigThe first season was excellent but the new series is a massive disappointment. In the first, David Mitchell’s character was believably eccentric and Anna Maxwell Martin was amusingly quirky. In this series they have taken interesting and believable character traits too far and the whole thing is ridiculous. I had been eagerly awaiting a second series but have stopped watching. It’s a shame that two excellent actors have been given such ludicrous scripts.Margaret Ainsbury, 78, DenbighThe ChaseThe Chase feels well and truly past its sell-by date. It’s a real shame, because I love Bradley Walsh, and the Chasers themselves are all fantastic. However, the core concept of the show has grown tired. The player endures the initial cash builder, sweats through a head-to-head round and scrapes together money (usually a pitiful amount) just to pool it into a central pot. And what is the reward for surviving all of that? Watching it vanish in the final chase because the chaser rattles through a block of questions in a fraction of the allotted time. I want to keep loving it, but the magic has worn off.Jamie Jones, County DurhamGrey’s AnatomyView image in fullscreenRunning on EMT … Sandra Oh and Ellen Pompeo in Grey’s Anatomy.Photograph: Michael Desmond/fiveI was completely captivated when Grey’s Anatomy first aired in 2005. There were strong performances – notably Sandra Oh – and strong characters with interesting histories and gripping medical cases. Fast forward to the present day and only a handful of the original cast remain … and even they look bored with the proceedings. The younger doctors inspire little empathy and the storylines need oxygen. I could say urgently, but I think it best to let it rest in peace now.Ruth Muirhead, WalesPrison BreakSeries one felt like groundbreaking telly: stylish, gritty, twisty – I loved it. Series two followed the escapes so was a different show but still OK. But it really had nowhere else to go after that. Wrap it up? Nope, let’s stick them all back in another prison.Please.Matt, 43, ManchesterCoronation StreetA British friend and I have been watchingCoronation Streetfor more than 50 years. It was a mindless pleasure that I would end my stressful day with. In the last year or so, it has become a stressor. There are so many sinister, evil characters now. I had to fast forward through the scenes with the character Theo. My British friend bailed on the show completely because of that storyline. I miss the silliness of affairs and neighbourhood arguments in the pub.Jane, 72, Toronto, CanadaHouse of the DragonView image in fullscreenFalling flat … Steve Toussaint in House of the Dragon.Photograph: HBO/2026 Home Box Office, Inc. All rights reserved. HBO® and all related programs are the property of Home Box Office, Inc.I always liked the dragons in Game of Thrones, and I thought the prequel might be a fresh series that doesn’t have GoT’s later poor plotting baggage. Paddy Considine did such a superb turn in the first season as the troubled and sickly Viserys Targaryen. And I could even forgive the sudden cast changes in season one to account for elapsed time in the narrative. The soundtrack, by Ramin Djawadi, is lovely. Over three seasons, however, I’ve become increasingly apathetic about the characters. The show’s just fallen flat and hasn’t managed to reach the highs of the first few seasons of GoT. Perhaps it really is time that Warner Bros (and Disney etc) give up on legacy IP. Let’s have some new stuff, please.Reinhardt, 39, Pretoria, South AfricaFamily GuyView image in fullscreenFor Pete’s sake … Family Guy.Photograph: Fox/Getty ImagesFamily Guy was hilarious. The first 10 or so seasons were all great for different reasons. It’s just fun – turn your brain off and laugh. But the last few years have been tiresome. Not awful, just plain. The voices are beginning to fade – I understand why, it’s been 25 seasons – and the jokes feel stale and uninspired. Don’t get me wrong, there are good episodes and some have great political commentary. But it has just gotten sour, to the point where I, an avid viewer, slowly stopped watching. I’ve found comfort in Bob’s Burgers now, but hey, maybe that’s just growing up! I still remember when Family Guy started …Hunter, Glasgowskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLove for LydiaThis HE Bates drama was first shown in the late 70s when I was 14. I adored Lydia who was played by Mel Martin. She looked so sophisticated with a beautiful black bob hairstyle. Men fell in love with her left, right and centre. I wanted to be Lydia. Last year it was shown again on Talking Pictures TV. With age comes experience and I could see how terribly selfish and insensitive Lydia actually was. She was a beautiful monster and Richardson who was besotted with her was a complete drip!Julie Coan, 63, Heywood, Greater ManchesterThe Office (US)View image in fullscreenTaking the Michael … The Office US.Photograph: NBC Universal/Getty ImagesThe prime example would be the American Office. Carell departing was too much to overcome, despite the star power of Will Ferrell and Kathy Bates. No disrespect to those actors; I understand the dilemma. If a first season of a show is successful, they want to continue, and as viewers we want more. But it’s becoming increasingly rare that after the flush of initial quality, subsequent seasons can continue the magic.Charles David, Michigan, USAScrubsI can’t stand Dr Cox’s “tough love” any more. His character was heralded for his honesty, especially compared with the slimy Dr Kelso, but Cox was a manipulative, sexist bully.Sharon, 42, Vancouver, BC, CanadaGilmore GirlsView image in fullscreenSnow laughing matter … Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life.Photograph: THA/AlamyI am in a perpetual cycle of Gilmore Girls rewatch – it’s my cosy year-round comfort show.
