However, I don’t watch season seven, or God forbid, the Netflix revival. Season seven totally betrays the cute and cosy atmosphere of seasons one to six, and the lives of the main characters drastically change. I suppose that happens after six years, but the showrunner also changed and you can feel the pull in a new direction. Needless to say, elopement and sexting should never have been on the cards.Jazz, 38, WindsorRoseanneRoseanne was, for a long time, a wonderful sitcom and one which has given many, many happy memories. Razor-sharp dialogue and wit, extremely likable characters with terrific, emotional, relatable storylines all laced with a real bite. Then it just went completely off the rails towards the end with an utterly nonsensical plot. A real shame because it was one of the best TV shows ever made.Michael, BristolThe BoysView image in fullscreenSupe du jour … The Boys.Photograph: Panagiotis Pantazidis/APThe Boys began as a topical, biting commentary on modern superhero movies and our political landscape. Its final two seasons felt like a caricature of itself, with characters reduced to bizarre versions of themselves and lazy writing that completely failed to tackle the modern US.Aaron, LancashireExplore more on these topicsTelevisionThe ApprenticeStrictly Come DancingCoronation StreetHouse of the DragonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bruno Schrecker obituary | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Cellist and a member of the Allegri String Quartet in recordings of Schubert, Brahms, Elgar and Britten
Author: Stephen Venables
Headline: Cellist and a member of the Allegri String Quartet in recordings of Schubert, Brahms, Elgar and Britten
Content: Schrecker worked with the Netherlands Chamber Orchestra under the violinist Szymon GoldbergView image in fullscreenSchrecker worked with the Netherlands Chamber Orchestra under the violinist Szymon GoldbergClassical musicObituaryBruno Schrecker obituaryCellist and a member of the Allegri String Quartet in recordings of Schubert, Brahms, Elgar and BrittenStephen VenablesFri 11 Sep 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 14.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1967 the cellist Bruno Schrecker, who has died aged 97, was invited to join the Allegri String Quartet when William Pleeth left it. He was delighted to take up a place that he had declined in 1953, when it was founded with Eli Goren as leader;membership continued to change, and the ensemble remains active today.Bruno, above all a chamber musician and recitalist, remained with the quartet for the next three decades, until 1998. His convivial personality, irrepressible humour and determination always to get right to the truth of any piece enabled him to remain friends with his Allegri colleagues.He had a particularly close rapport with Hugh Maguire, the second of the three leaders he worked with. When Bruno joined, Goren was still the first violin, and Maguire was succeeded in 1976 by Peter Carter.As a friend and neighbour following the quartet, my own best memory was of a Beethoven series they gave at the Holywell Music Room, Oxford, in 1980. The many fine recordings from Bruno’s time include most of theSchubert quartets, theElgar Piano Quintetwith John Ogdon (1970),Britten’s Quartets Nos 1 and 2(1972), prepared with the composer, and theBrahms Clarinet Quintetwith James Campbell (1992).Born into a Jewish family in Frankfurt, Bruno was the youngest of three sons of Lisl (nee Bischitsky) and Robert Schrecker. The opera composerFranz Shrekerwas a cousin of Bruno’s grandfather, and the C missing from his name a registrar’s error.View image in fullscreenThe Allegri Quartet with, from left, Peter Carter (1st violin), David Roth (2nd violin), Bruno Schrecker and Prunella Pacey (viola), at a concert in Germany, 1979.Photograph: United Archives GmbH/AlamyIn 1933, the collapse of the family business making buttons from casein, a milk-based material, and the growing threat from Hitler prompted Robert to emigrate to Britain, where he had contacts. Lisl took the three boys to live temporarily in her home city of Prague, before joining him in 1935. Her own parents followed to Britain in 1938.The German language was forbidden in the Schreckers’ new home in Wimbledon, south London, and, aged seven, Bruno quickly learned English, later winning a speaking prize at Raynes Park high school. During the blitz he was evacuated toKelly House, in west Devon, where he enjoyed living with “impoverished gentry”.The servicemen billeted at the Palladian mansion included a cellist, and Bruno – whose father had encouraged him to seek a securer profession – started on the instrument only as a teenager and in secret. However, he won a place at the Royal College of Music in London, and for his graduating concerto with the college orchestra he chose Ernest Bloch’s Schelomo.He then played with the Peter Gibbs Quartet, but set aside the offer to join the new Allegri Quartet because of a French government scholarship to study twice a week with Pablo Casals inPrades, France, near the border with Spain. He admired not only the Catalan master’s playing, but also his “understanding of the world and deep feeling for people”.View image in fullscreenSchrecker’s photograph of the cellist Pablo Casals, with whom he studied on a French government grant.Photograph: Bruno SchreckerFor some years Bruno worked with the Netherlands Chamber Orchestra under the violinist Szymon Goldberg, sharing a desk with the idiosyncratic Dutch cellist Anner Bylsma, later a leading light of period instrument performance. A particular memory was of playing Bach’s Brandenburg Concertos on the Acropolis in Athens, andtheir recording of the workswas released in 1959.Back in London from the late 1950s, Bruno gave duo recitals with piano, often on the BBC Third Programme, did session work with the London Symphony Orchestra and appeared with his own chamber group. The violinist in the trio was Perry Hart, a student of Goldberg: stuck for a name, Bruno took up his father’s suggestion of Italianising Goldberg into Oromonte. The trio functioned both as a string trio with Margaret Major on viola, and as a piano trio with Nina Milkina, and was joined by other artists, such as the oboist Janet Craxton.In 1953 Bruno married the artistDoris Wilkinson, and they lived in the same house in Wimbledon that his parents had. That marriage ended in divorce,and in 1988 he married a fellow cellist, Shena Power. They moved to the village of Larkhall on the edge of Bath, where he spent his last four decades. After leaving the Allegri, he took on a few pupils, returned occasionally to play at the festival he had founded atLlanfyllin, Powys, in 1971, and was a guest coach at Chetham’s School of Music, Manchester.A keen photographer, he took portrait shots of several musicians. One ofMarisa Robleslooking through the strings of her harp is held at the National Portrait Gallery, London.He is survived by Shena and three sons: Marius and Jeremy from his first marriage, and Leo from his second.Bruno Schrecker, cellist, born 27 August 1928; died 23 August 2026Explore more on these topicsClassical musicobituariesShareReuse this content

title: A rollicking statue, Beryl’s buddies and a swimming pool in a roundabout – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A blue lady strides across the fourth plinth, Beryl Cook and friends gather in Bicester, and Spain repurposes a traffic junction
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: A blue lady strides across the fourth plinth, Beryl Cook and friends gather in Bicester, and Spain repurposes a traffic junction
Content: Tschabalala Self's sculpture Lady in Blue atop Trafalgar Square's fourth plinth in London.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersView image in fullscreenTschabalala Self's sculpture Lady in Blue atop Trafalgar Square's fourth plinth in London.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersArt Weekly newsletterArt and designA rollicking statue, Beryl’s buddies and a swimming pool in a roundabout – the week in artA blue lady strides across the fourth plinth, Beryl Cook and friends gather in Bicester, and Spain repurposes a traffic junction –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 11 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekTschabalala SelfA rollicking triumph of a statue that spreads good feelings and smiles in the heart of the capital. Saucy genius.Fourth plinth, Trafalgar Square, LondonAlso showingBeryl Cook and FriendsSome may see similarities between Tschabalala Self’s Trafalgar Square statue and Cook’s vibrant fun.House of Voltaire, Bicester Village, until 25 OctoberPeter HowsonGnarly, bloody, and bloody-minded paintings of Christ’s Passion.Flowers Gallery, London, until 10 OctoberLiz LarnerSculptures that meditate on myth, metamorphoses and our fragile earth.Camden Art Centre, London, until 17 JanuaryMonika SosnowskaThe sadness of Polish history haunts Sosnowska’s abstract sculptures and installations.South London Galleryuntil 22 NovemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Josema CutillasThe theme for this year’s biennial European Prize for Urban Public Space is architectural projects that repurpose infrastructure built for cars. Among the five finalists is Round About Baths, a true urban oasis for which Swiss architect Leopold Banchini has turned an obsolete roundabout in Logroño, northern Spain, into a public pool.Read more here.What we learnedStar Wars director George Lucas has opened a spaceship-sized art museumArgentina must return to the owner’s heir an 18th-century painting stolen by NazisVeteran Califiornia sculptor Liz Larner has been making ceramics based on asteroidsAlong with flowers and deserts, Georgia O’Keeffe also painted stunning urban scenesOur critic wondered why French thieves bothered stealing Renoir paintingsMasterpiece of the weekSaint Paul and a Donatrix by followers of Gerard David, 1515View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Vidimages/AlamyIn late medieval and Renaissance Europe, one of the most popular ways to spend money was on an altarpiece for a chapel in your local church. And if you were paying, why not have yourself painted into everyone’s grateful prayers? This is a wing of a folding multi-panelled painting on wood: the woman it shows is not known by name but she was one half of a well-off couple who probably lived in Bruges. We can feel close to her as she kneels piously with none other than Saint Paul himself behind her. For the painting’s first beholders, she may have been someone they often saw and spoke to in the street or at market, but here she’s enfolded in a holy, supernatural reality that’s one breath away from the visible. Paul is placing a supportive hand on her back – a direct contact between the donatrix – the donor – and the divine. Donor portraits come from a world that is very alien to our attitudes yet also very human: this woman’s confident portrayal as someone who communes with the saints in heaven seems narcissistic and naive yet it is a moving attempt to connect everyday experience with something beyond.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Danny Boyle, please make another film about drugs’: Venice film festival’s feedback wall takes no prisoners | Movies | The Guardian
description: The written forum allows members of the public to vent their fury at the movies they’ve seen – and the festival organisers
Author: Philip Oltermann
Headline: The written forum allows members of the public to vent their fury at the movies they’ve seen – and the festival organisers
Content: Poison pen … feedback on the public wall at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Philip OltermannView image in fullscreenPoison pen … feedback on the public wall at the Venice film festival.Photograph: Philip OltermannMovies‘Danny Boyle, please make another film about drugs’: Venice film festival’s feedback wall takes no prisonersThe written forum allows members of the public to vent their fury at the movies they’ve seen – and the festival organisersPhilip Oltermannin VeniceFri 11 Sep 2026 04.59 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn an industry that is reliant on the fickle vagaries of taste, film festivals exist to establish facts. The reason why film-makers still go through the rigmarole of ferrying their cast to the red carpets of Venice, Cannes or Sundance is the need for empirical evidence of unambiguous quality: a solid-gold prize, a top score on the critics’ grid, a record-timed standing ovation that will convince every doubter that this isa great film.View image in fullscreenThe wall also includes illustrations.Photograph: Philip OltermannFilm festivals, in turn, need beautiful A-listers to attract coverage and sponsorship, and hence there is a constant risk that these annual events become gigantic hype machines, in which every turkey is a classic and every half-hearted performance a masterclass.Which is why there may not be a more important institution in world cinema than the Venice film festival’sRidateci i soldi(“Give us our money back”): a makeshift chipboard wall erected next to the Palazzo del Cinema on which visitors are encouraged – with the blessing of the management – to scribble complaints and hatchet jobs in the most scathing terms possible.The wall’s 30-year tradition commands that the festival’s director Alberto Barbera has to personally hand out a prize to the meanest diatribe, making Venice’s wall of shame a barrier against hype, an institutionalised pricking of the film world’s own pomposity.On the Lido this year, there were complaints about the rising cost of entry badges, water taxis and local accommodation (“Maybe by 2030 we’ll have to pay for the oxygen we breathe”), queue lengths, uncomfortable seats and ceiling lights going on in the screening rooms.Most of the notes dealt with the films themselves, however. There were protests against the inclusion of epic “Russian Oppenheimer” biopicDAU, notorious forreportsof behind-the-scenes coercion and humiliation of cast and crew (“This is a disgusting, abusive (!!), pointless film!! Look it up!!!”), appeals to Trainspotting director Danny Boyle (“please make another movie about drugs”), insinuations about Paul Schrader’s child abuse dramaThe Basics of Philosophyso slanderous they cannot be repeated in print for risk of legal repercussions, and many a wordplay on the spoonerist title of Werner Herzog’sBucking Fastard.View image in fullscreenThe winner of this year’s cup for the best ad hoc review, Cristian Poletti.Photograph: Philip OltermannItalian titles in the lineup especially came in for drubbings, such as Andrea Pallaoro’s romantic drama The Echo Chamber, based on a script by Bernardo Bertolucci (“He will be turning in his grave”), Luca Guadagnino’s seven-hour documentary Joie de Vivre (“Arrest him!”), and Gerda Taro biopic The Girl with the Leica (“Insípido!”). It’s hard to imagine similarly buzz-killing language at Venice’s more po-faced competitors in Cannes or Berlin.“Italian audiences always interact a little more with films,” says John Bleasdale, an Italy-based British critic and novelist. Just as popular actors or directors are often applauded as soon as their names appear in the credits, boos are considered a legitimate expression of taste, he argues. “The boos are vociferous, as is ironic laughter and applause. Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin got booed at Venice, while other films split an audience and half of them boo while the others cheer.”Ridateci i soldiwas created in the late 90s by Gianni Ippoliti, a former football referee and TV presenter who acts as the prize’s one-man jury, in protest against reviews becoming overly enthusiastic. “If you read the reviews, you would believe that all 150 films shown at the festival this year are masterpieces,” he says as he stands guard at the festival’s wall of shame. “That’s not possible.”View image in fullscreen‘Arrest him!’ … a response on the wall to the Luca Guadagnino’s seven-hour long Joie de Vivre.Photograph: Courtesy Venice Film FestivalThe rules are flexible, he explains: “Of course people are also allowed to write something positive, but we find most of the time people who come out of the cinema want to vent their negative feelings.”The Golden Lion, awarded to the winner of the 21 films in competition, is one of the most sought-after accolades in world cinema. But the Coppa Codacons – a wooden sculpture sponsored by Italy’s consumer watchdog and carved by artist Ferdinando Codognotto that is awarded to the most scathing comment – is the more beautiful object to put on your mantlepiece.Festival visitor Cristian Poletti won the cup this year for a review in which he suggested a more suitable title for The Echo Chamber might have been “The Echo Bathroom” given how many scenes featured characters bathing. If Bertolucci really wrote the script for this movie, it said, perhaps it was intended to be a shampoo advert instead.View image in fullscreenA festivalgoer takes inspiration from Herzog’s Bucking Fastard.Photograph: Philip OltermannIn spite of everything, Poletti says he remains a passionate fan of film festivals. In recent years there have been signs that Hollywood’s big studios are retreating from the festival circuit, aware that social-media campaigns can serve as more effective hype machines and that critical drubbings at Venice or Cannes can establish the wrong kind of irrefutable facts.“I’ve been coming to Venice since 2015, and I always see 30 to 40 films,” says Poletti. “Even watching a bad movie is better than not watching a movie at all.”Explore more on these topicsFilmVenice film festivalFestivalsFilm criticismnewsShareReuse this content

title: It’s a slam dunk for Tommy Hilfiger as stars turn out for Plaza homecoming | New York fashion week | The Guardian
description: Preppy is back in the zeitgeist, says designer blending sportswear codes and collegiate chic at New York show
Author: Jess Cartner-Morley
Headline: Preppy is back in the zeitgeist, says designer blending sportswear codes and collegiate chic at New York show
Content: Looks from the Tommy Hilfiger show at the Plaza in New York.Composite: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLooks from the Tommy Hilfiger show at the Plaza in New York.Composite: ShutterstockNew York fashion weekIt’s a slam dunk for Tommy Hilfiger as stars turn out for Plaza homecomingPreppy is back in the zeitgeist, says designer, blending sportswear codes and collegiate chic at New York showJess Cartner-Morleyin New YorkFri 11 Sep 2026 10.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTommy Hilfiger’s front row was a slam dunk. The Knicks are the kings ofNew Yorkright now, so scoring Josh Hart, Karl-Anthony Towns and Miles McBride, three of the team’s stars, for the guest list of his New York catwalk show was a victory. Travis Kelce, who is co-designing another upcoming collection with Hilfiger and had been rumoured to attend this event with his new bride, was a no show, but you can’t win them all.View image in fullscreenBasketball player Karl-Anthony Towns in the front row.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPATommy Hilfiger is all about sport. The design vocabulary of oversized jerseys, team stripes, rugby shirts and letterman jackets draws heavily on the visual language of the stadium. Kelce, whose NFL tunnel walks have become a catwalk of their own, is the latest in a line of sporting ambassadors that includes Thierry Henry, Rafael Nadal and Lewis Hamilton. Hilfiger has long stood for a certain glossy stars-and-stripes Americana – its graphic red, white and blue logo is a riff on the flag – but American identity is delicate cultural territory right now. Sport, which unites audiences across all backgrounds and political allegiances, gives the brand a wholesome place to congregate. “People really like him,” Hilfiger said backstage, explaining why he chose to collaborate with Kelce. “He’s really humble, down to earth, sweet, fun, and funny. And a superstar athlete.”View image in fullscreenTwo models on the catwalk.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPABackstage before the show, Hilfiger said: “Preppy is back in the zeitgeist.” And on the catwalk, sportswear codes and collegiate chic were blended together. A bright, boxy rugby shirt was worn loose over a neatly pleated skirt, a slick quarterzip layered under a neat blazer. Hotdog-stand colours of mustard and ketchup were splashed over civilised tones of Oxford blue and chino beige. There was a deep-cut nod to Hilfiger’s history in the form of a silk dress, which re-printed the audacious Times Square billboard that launched his career. The advert listed the four greatest American menswear designers as Ralph Lauren, Perry Ellis, Calvin Klein and the then almost unknown Tommy Hilfiger. It was a provocative stunt from a rookie which, 41 years later, stands the test of time.View image in fullscreen‘I loved the idea of a show in my former home,’ Hilfiger said.Photograph: Sarah Yenesel/EPAThe show was one in a long line of pop culture cameos for the Plaza hotel. This is where Cary Grant was kidnapped from the Oak Room in Hitchcock’s North by Northwest, and where Macaulay Culkin ran into its then owner, Donald Trump, in the lobby in Home Alone 2. For Hilfiger, the venue was a homecoming: the designer lived in the hotel with his family for a decade. “I loved the idea of a show in my former home,” Hilfiger said beforehand, “and I am inspired by all the different types of people who come through these doors every day.” His personal favourite moment in the hotel’s history, he said, was Truman Capote’s Black and White Ball of 1966.Explore more on these topicsNew York fashion weekFashion weeksNew YorkBasketballnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘She changed the beauty industry’: how Charlotte Mensah brought black hair into the spotlight | Women's hair | The Guardian
description: A new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith. She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair types
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: A new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith. She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair types
Content: ‘I can do all hair types. So everyone else should be able to’ … Charlotte Mensah.Photograph: PRView image in fullscreen‘I can do all hair types. So everyone else should be able to’ … Charlotte Mensah.Photograph: PRWomen's hair‘She changed the beauty industry’: how Charlotte Mensah brought black hair into the spotlightA new exhibition in London celebrates the influential hairstylist whose clients include Janelle Monáe and Zadie Smith. She explains her story – and why she’s on a mission to ensure stylists are trained to work with all hair typesSinéad CampbellFri 11 Sep 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Charlotte Mensah was a young child growing up in Accra, Ghana in the 1970s, she would spend hours watching her aunties having their hair intricately threaded, an ancient African technique where hair is wrapped tightly using yarn or thread. She didn’t know then that she would go on to become one of the most influential hairdressers in the UK. Renowned for championing natural black hair textures, she has worked as hairstylist to singers Janelle Monáe and Erykah Badu, and the writer Zadie Smith.According to Smith, in anessayshe penned about Mensah’s magic earlier this year: “Charlotte can make a great mane of braids appear where previously there were only split ends and hair loss.”A three-time winner of afro hairdresser of the year and the first black woman to be inducted into the British Hairdressing Awards Hall of Fame in 2018: the extraordinary course of her 40-year-long career is now the subject of an exhibition,Charlotte Mensah: Community Mattersin west London. It charts her rise from growing up in the Ghanaian capital, through her early days as a junior hairdresser in London’s West End in the 80s, to styling celebrities for magazine covers.The dynamics of black hair and the beauty industry have changed dramatically in this time. According to Madeleine Haddon, senior curator of the V&A East, who has worked with Mensah on the exhibition: “This is a story of Black British creativity and many of the prejudices and hurdles that she [Charlotte] had to overcome in the 80s and 90s, but also how she changed the beauty industry and transformed perceptions of black beauty.”View image in fullscreen‘Transforming perceptions of black beauty’: the exhibition Charlotte Mensah: Community Matters in west London.Photograph: Dave Benett/Jahnay Tennai/Getty ImagesWhen Mensah moved from Ghana to Stonebridge, north-west London, aged 11, she first became conscious of her hair – and was bullied for it. Whereas the black children at her school wore their hair relaxed, in braids or in cornrows, Mensah had what she calls a “TWA” – a tiny weeny afro. “I turned up with this short hair and they all started laughing at me,” she says. “I used to cry … they just thought my hair was so funny and I looked like an alien.”When she left school at 16 in the mid 80s, Mensah landed an apprenticeship at the first luxury black hair salon in the UK, Splinters in Mayfair, which opened in 1970. At that time, Mensah had only practised at home, styling her younger sister’s hair in “simple little braids, twists, cornrows”.Splinters was worlds away from her bedroom in north London. The teenage Mensah was sweeping the floors at a salon where clients such as Diana Ross, and Flori Roberts – the eponymous owner of the first cosmetics brand developed specifically for women of colour – passed through the door. She then worked her way up through some of London’s top black hair salons, such as Terry Jacques in Knightsbridge, which was frequented by Luther Vandross and Brandy. “It opened my eyes to a bigger world that I didn’t think existed,” she says. “I saw those women that came into the salon, they were very independent, they had their own businesses, and I thought, ‘I want to be like one of these women’.”In 1999, at the age of 29, Mensah opened her first salon, Hair Lounge in Kilburn. The location later moved to Portobello Road, in London’s Notting Hill, where, 25 years and countless awards later, Mensah can still be found braiding hair and chatting to customers every day. As Smith has written: “Charlotte Tilburyis unlikely to do your makeup at the Selfridges counter, but Charlotte Mensah will definitely braid your hair in Ladbroke Grove. She’ll also weave it, cut it, blow it out, colour it, treat it, whatever you need. Her craft is her passion, and she applies it to everyone equally, from the pop star prepping for a show to the auntie getting ready for church.”View image in fullscreenNick Laird, Zadie Smith and Charlotte Mensah.Photograph: Hannah Young/ShutterstockFor the last 10 years, Mensah has also had an eponymous product line, a high-end range of hair oils and finishing mists. It grew out of a need – growing up in the 70s and 80s, relaxed hair and curly perms were the fashion, but the products necessary for them weren’t widely sold. Mensah had to travel out-of-borough to buy brands such as Dax and Sofnfree, that were imported from the US.Now the landscape has changed. Boots and Superdrug have designated afro hair sections stocked with brands such as Camille Rose and SheaMoisture, for different black hair types. The celebrity-owned beauty business wave has ushered in brands such as Pattern by Tracee Ellis Ross, Cecred by Beyoncé and UK-based afro hair care lines, such as Afrocenchix. “There’s more access,” says Mensah. “So if I’m a young black girl living in Sheffield, I can go into my local high street or online and find something for my hair, which never used to happen.”View image in fullscreenMensah was the first black woman to be inducted into the British Hairdressing Awards Hall of Fame.Photograph: courtesy of Charlotte MensahMensah has also pushed the creative potential of black hair styling. One of the pictures in the exhibition is a photograph of the British boxer Nicola Adams in a Grace Jones-style boxed afro on the cover of Vanity Fair UK, styled by Mensah. Others of her covers include model Jourdan Dunn with spiralling braids for Heroine magazine, the singer Celeste with cornrows on Found And Vision, and writer-actor Michaela Coel bare-faced with Bantu knots for New York Magazine.Her aim now is to address the remaining social prejudices surrounding black hair types, the notion that natural, kinkier hair textures need to be “tamed” or straightened to look “beautiful”. In particular, the lack of access to hairdressersoutside big cities trained to style black hair types is a significant barrier.Last year, the BBCreportedthat out of 259 colleges in England, only 82 said they taught a curriculum inclusive of afro hair care, and women are still travelling across the UK to get their afro hair cared for. Mensah suggests that education on treatment and styling of different hair textures outside the European standard is needed to tackle the issue. She has set up her own academy, based in London and Accra, which offers a training and mentorship programme for hair stylists.“You should be able to walk into any hair salon on your high street and have your hair done, [an experience] which doesn’t exist,” she says, referring to the fact that many stylists still do not have the expertise to work with hair of all textures. “That comes from the education system … I can do all hair types. So everyone else should be able to.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's hairBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Want Mr Whippy on tap? I put the viral Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl ice-cream maker to the test | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Whether it’s soft serve or sorbet, gelato or fro-yo, the Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl is a faff-free way of making all your favourite frozen treats
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: Whether it’s soft serve or sorbet, gelato or fro-yo, the Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl is a faff-free way of making all your favourite frozen treats
Content: Twist and shout: the Scoop and Swirl puts a new spin on the classic Creami.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTwist and shout: the Scoop and Swirl puts a new spin on the classic Creami.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterIce-cream and sorbetReviewWant Mr Whippy on tap? I put the viral Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl ice-cream maker to the testWhether it’s soft serve or sorbet, gelato or fro-yo, the Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl is a faff-free way of making all your favourite frozen treatsThe best ice-cream makers for your homeDanielle AmatoFri 11 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor me, ice-cream isn’t only for summer. It’s my dessert of choice all year round, and a goodice-cream makerensures it’s always readily available. When I put more than a dozen modelsthrough their pacesearlier this year, one thing became clear: the most important feature in any machine is ease of use.On that front, the Ninja Creami really scored highly for me. I’ve used the originalNC300 modelfor a few years, and I like its simplicity and that it’s easy to clean. Nowadays, though, we expect our appliances to do a little more – and when it comes to ice-cream, the current craze is soft serve.Homemade Mr Whippy has become hugely popular over the past year or so, both on social media and in restaurants, and it’s now a feature on several slushie machines (another appliance having a moment). The Ninja Scoop and Swirl ice-cream maker takes a slightly different approach. Rather than using a compressor to chill the mixture in real time, it combines the classic freeze-first method of the original Creami with a mechanism that transforms the frozen mixture into soft serve.Easier to clean than a slushie machine and packed with impressive functionality, the Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl promises the best of both worlds when it comes to homemade ice-cream. If you’re a regular social media user, you may well have come across one of the many thousands of videos posted about it this summer. But is it any good?View at SharkNinjaView at John LewisHow I testedView image in fullscreenChurn test: seeing how the Scoop and Swirl handles different frozen treats.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianThe Scoop and Swirl is a little more feature-rich than your average ice-cream maker, so alongside my usual tests, I also gave the machine’s more unusual features a (s)whirl.My standard tests include making a batch of Felicity Cloake’s perfectvanilla ice-creamandlemon sorbet. I also made Ninja’s own soft-serve recipe, a lower-calorie ice-cream from the booklet and a dairy-free option, putting its claim to do it all to the test. I assessed each recipe as soon as it came out of the machine, and returned to them after a couple of days in the freezerto see how well they held up.I also considered ease of use and cleaning – after all, too much post-churn faff, and you might as well just buy premade ice-cream. As well as noting whether it was easy to disassemble and the parts were dishwasher-safe, I measured noise levels with a decibel meter – this style of ice-cream maker is notoriously noisy.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenAll in: the Scoop and Swirl is aimed at those who’d rather experiment than settle for traditional ice-cream.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianView at SharkNinjaView at John LewisThe Ninja Scoop and Swirl is a clear response to an ever-growing appetite for homemade soft serve, but to call it simply a soft-serve model would be a disservice to this weird and wacky machine. It’s very much aimed at those of us who’d rather experiment than settle for traditional ice-cream – although, of course, you can still make that if you want to.Think “healthier” frozen treats using semi-skimmed milk, protein-packed fro-yo or sugar alternatives, alongside all the classics. This is evident in the included recipe book, which offers plenty of ways to customise your ice-cream to better suit a healthier lifestyle. To some, that might sound a little boring, but I think it gives people the freedom to enjoy a dessert without worrying quite so much about the fat or sugar.View image in fullscreenMode shift: the Scoop and Swirl offers a wide range of programmes, from soft serve to sorbet.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianThe Scoop and Swirl works in two distinct stages. First, a classic blade-churning mechanism takes your frozen mixture and processes it into smooth ice-cream – if you’ve used Ninja’s Creami machines before, this will be familiar to you. Then there’s the new soft-serve attachment, which pushes the churned mixture through a silicone nozzle, via the rather fun dispensing handle on the side. This means you can enjoy it straight from the bowl or take it one step further for that classic soft, swirly texture.Ten functions create different frozen desserts, including classics such as gelato, ice-cream and sorbet, alongside some rather Ninja-esque additions such as CreamiFit, for protein-based recipes, and Lite Ice Cream for lower-fat and lower-sugar options. You can even make milkshakes, which is a fun addition. Each setting churns at varying speeds and times – between three and five minutes –to give you the right texture for each style of ice-cream.In addition to those main ice-cream functions, there is an option to re-spin your ice-cream if it has lost its creamy texture from being in the freezer a while. Plus, there’s a Mix-In button that gives your mixture a slower, secondary pass to add extras such as chocolate chips.Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl specificationsDimensions:25.5 x 48.5 x 44.5cm (WDH)Maximum capacity:480ml to max fill lineModes:Ice Cream, Gelato, Soft-serve Gelato, Sorbet, Lite Ice Cream, Fruiti, CreamiFit, Frozen Yoghurt, Milkshake, Mix-InMachine type:freeze-firstSpare parts:available fromSharkNinja’s websiteWeight:9.45kgWhat we loveView image in fullscreenThe Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl creates a super-impressive soft serve ice-cream.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianLike all new kitchen tech, ice-cream makers – particularly those that offer soft serve – come with a bit of a learning curve. Yet the Ninja Scoop and Swirl makes the whole process almost suspiciously easy.Having used the original Ninja Creami for years, I wasn’t too concerned about getting to grips with the Scoop and Swirl. But unboxing it and seeing the new design and containers did trigger what I call “overcomplication concern” – that tendency for kitchen tech to make simple things unnecessarily complex with features nobody asked for. Thankfully, I needn’t have worried:the instructions areclear, and I quickly felt at ease with the machine.The Scoop and Swirl comes with two 480ml tubs, so my initial tests focused on making Felicity Cloake’s classic vanilla ice-cream and sorbet. Each setting adjusts the churn speed and time to suit the consistency of the type of frozen treat. Using the respective settings yieldedfairly good results, but it’s worth keeping expectations realistic: this machine uses a different method from traditional churners, so its results won’t be identical to, say, a compressor model.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHaving said that, the vanilla ice-cream came out very creamy. I felt the sorbet needed a bit of manual mixing to finesse the texture, although achieving perfectly smooth results with any machine is tricky, so I wouldn’t consider this a huge red flag. The sorbet was still perfectly good to serve – and I can’t imagine you’d get many complaints around the table.I was also super impressed by the soft serve the Scoop and Swirl produced. Since the mixture is already frozen when you process it, the texture is much firmer than the softer consistency of a slushie-style compressor machine.What’s more, Ninja’s provided recipe uses a 1/4 teaspoon of xanthan gum, which significantly improves the stability and shape of the soft serve. This was certainly true of both the dairy and vegan versions I made. Most dairy-free milks and creams already contain thickeners, so there’s no need to add extra xanthan gum. You can also make the dairy version without it; just don’t expect it to hold its shape for long in a wafer cone.I reallyliked the lighter ice-cream optionsin the recipe booklet, too. The texture is a little icier than traditional ice-cream, as fat and sugar help prevent the formation of ice crystals. But it still tasted like ice-cream and scratched the same itch, just with fewer calories.The Scoop and Swirl is also surprisinglyeasy to clean,despite appearing to have lots of nooks and crannies in which ice-cream could hide. It’s clear Ninja has thought about this because I found it easy to flush through the containers and soft-serve chambers with soapy water. Dried-on ice-cream may need a bit of a soak first, though. The tubs can be popped in the dishwasher, while the rest of the machine stays relatively ice-cream-free and can simply be wiped over with a damp cloth.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreen‘Stingy’: each 480ml tub produces just enough soft serve to fill only three small ice-cream cones.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianAs much as I enjoyed using this machine, it’s not perfect. I think the biggest and most obvious concern for many people will bethe price. At its full price of £369.99, it’s one of the priciest ice-cream makers I’ve tested. It’s also one of the best in terms of functionality and ease of use, but that’s still a sizeable investment. And if you already own the original Ninja Creami or similar and are happy with it, I’m not sure that the soft-serve function will add all that much to your life.Another thing that struck me was thetub size. At 480ml, the Scoop and Swirl’s tubs are a similar size as those of the original Creami, but that feels stingy for a machine designed to serve soft ice-cream.I think of soft serve as something to wheel out at larger gatherings, and when I did, the two tubs were able to fill just six small ice-cream cones. Both tubs also left a small amount of unprocessed soft serve in the bottom that I had to laboriously scoop out with a spoon. Much like theCreami XL, which comes with 710ml tubs as standard, I’d have liked to see an XL option for the Scoop and Swirl.As a final note, I can’t ignorehow noisy this machine is. In my tests, it measured between 80 and 90dB (the top end of which is similar to a power tool) depending on the setting, and that’s at a consistent level for about three to five minutes. Unfortunately, it’s an unavoidable side-effect of this type of blade-based machine– one you’ll have to stomach for the sake of your ice-cream.Warranty and repairabilityNinja offers a two-year warranty on the Scoop and Swirl if you register, which covers free repairs or replacements. This doesn’t include expected wear and tear, misuse of parts or breakages caused by third-party repairs. You can also buy additional tubs and accessories viathe SharkNinja website.Ninja Creami Scoop and Swirl:should I buy it?View image in fullscreenWorth the swirl? A versatile machine, if you can justify the cost.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianIf you like the idea of an ice-cream maker that does more than produce traditional ice-cream, the Ninja Scoop and Swirl is a worthwhile investment. Most good-quality compressor models cost well over £200 and aren’t as generous in terms of features. The thought and time that have gone into making the Creami machines are clear, and they’re particularly beginner-friendly, with plenty of tried-and-tested recipes to get you started. The Scoop and Swirl is also a great choice for those of us who love a regular sweet treat but want their indulgences to be lighter, lower-sugar or dairy-free.I wouldn’t say this is a necessary upgrade if you already have an ice-cream machine – unless it’s on its last legs. It’s too expensive for that. But if you’re in the market for your first ice-cream maker and love soft serve, then the Scoop and Swirl is a very competent, well-thought-out and easy-to-use machine.View at SharkNinjaView at John LewisFor more, read thebest (and worst) chef’s knivesand thebest blenders for smoothies, soups and frozen dessertsDanielle Amato is a consumer reviews journalist with almost a decade of experience covering kitchen and home appliances. She’s an avid ice-cream and pasta enthusiast (not at the same time, though she wouldn’t judge) and loves nothing more than getting stuck into a new recipe or appliance in her unofficial test kitchenExplore more on these topicsIce-cream and sorbetThe FilterDessertFoodGadgetsHomesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The age of tiramisu: a runaway dessert trend – and what it reveals about nostalgia and decadence | Food | The Guardian
description: The coffee and cream pudding has always been popular. But now it’s inspired a dedicated cafe and countless products, from drinks to ice-creams to buns. What’s behind this big cultural craving?
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: The coffee and cream pudding has always been popular. But now it’s inspired a dedicated cafe and countless products, from drinks to ice-creams to buns. What’s behind this big cultural craving?
Content: Just tiramisu … Lucy Knight tucks in at Marrone, London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJust tiramisu … Lucy Knight tucks in at Marrone, London.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianFoodThe age of tiramisu: a runaway dessert trend – and what it reveals about nostalgia and decadenceThe coffee and cream pudding has always been popular. But now it’s inspired a dedicated cafe and countless products, from drinks to ice-creams to buns. What’s behind this big cultural craving?Lucy KnightFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Giancarlo Fanigliulo opened Marrone, a cafe dedicated to tiramisu in London’s Soho in August, he hadn’t anticipated he would sell out within two and a half hours. “I was expecting a buzz, but I wasn’t expecting queues around the corner,” he tells me. “It was insane.”This kind of excitement about the Italian dessert is not a one-off – we are, it seems, living in an age of tiramisu-mania. Nearly all of the high street coffee chains have offered some kind of tiramisu coffee as a seasonal special (in the US, Dunkin’ currently has four different tiramisu-flavoured drinks on its menu). Meanwhile, Haagen-Dazs and Carte D’or now sell tiramisu ice-cream, London chain Buns from Home offers a tiramisu-flavoured croissant-dough bun and social media is awash with tiramisu recipes and videos of “tiramisu drawers” – trays of the dessert ready to serve out of drawers in chefs’ kitchens – as popularised bythe viral one at Manchester pasta restaurantOnda.View image in fullscreenMarrone tiramisu.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMarrone is not the first “just tiramisu” vendor to pop up in recent years: Sheffield’sParadiso– which, along with classic tiramisu, will sell you a “latte-misù” (an iced coffee topped with a slab of tiramisu) – opened in 2023; while theTikTok viral Secret Layers, where you can buy the dessert from a tiny hatch in a wall, opened in Paddington, London, last year. In March, the Guinness World Record for the world’s longest tiramisu was broken when chefs assembled a440.6 metre portion of the pudding(although there was some discussion, among my friends at least, about whether it should actually count as the longest, since it appeared to be a series of smaller portions of tiramisu joined together).Supermarkets are also noticing an uptick in tiramisu purchases. “Sales of our own brand tiramisu range have grown by 5% over the last year, with our Tesco Finest Coffee & Amaretto TiramisuDessert, proving particularly popular, selling nearly 10% more,” says Peter Wood, Tesco’s category buying manager for desserts. M&S, which is currently stocking “creamy tiramisu brownies” and, at Easter, sold tiramisu hot cross buns, says tiramisu sales are up 27% compared with last year.View image in fullscreenThe ‘world’s longest’ tiramisu, at Chelsea Old Town Hall, London.Photograph: Getty ImagesThe tiramisu trend has reached weddings, too, sometimes as a replacement for a wedding cake. The dessert “is probably one of the main trends of 2026,” says Cotswolds-based wedding planner Oliver Stanton – when we speak, he has just finished working on a wedding where tiramisu featured. “A lot of couples are having tiramisu served in coupe glasses and arranged in a tower like you would with a champagne tower. It serves as an extra photo opportunity as well as dessert for the guests.”Tiramisu has always been a beloved pudding, but Lisa Harris, co-founder of Harris and Hayesfood and drink consultancy, can see why it is enjoying a spike in popularity at the moment: social media algorithms reward nostalgia and anything that symbolises decadence – and tiramisu does both: “A good tiramisu is actually an exercise of this balance of the coffee, the cream and the sponge. There’s sort of not that much to it,” says Harris. “And yet it’s also this shorthand for indulgence.”The proliferation of tiramisu-flavoured products, she adds, is probably in part due to the word “tiramisu” itself: “It sort of says elegance without really needing to try too hard.” It’s also an easy way to describe a specific flavour profile: “I could say tiramisu latte, tiramisu cookie, tiramisu doughnut, and you would know that I mean it has got cream and coffee in it.”The emergence of“Little Treat Culture”– the concept of giving yourself small rewards amid trying political and economic times – has also aided the success of tiramisu and tiramisu-flavoured products. At a time “when people are perhaps eating out less, in the current economic climate,” indulgence becomes more coveted. Someone “just thinking about what dessert they’re going to have” is a bigger deal, Harris says.View image in fullscreenGiancarlo Fanigliulo at work in the Marrone kitchen.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianIt was partly because tiramisu has become “such a culture” that Fanigliulo decided to open Marrone. The 30-year-old doesn’t have a background in hospitality – he previously worked in tech sales – but he was struck that “when you think of tiramisu, there’s never been a brand associated with it”. His family is Italian on his father’s side, and his tiramisu is inspired by his grandmother’s recipe. All three of the tiramisus on Marrone’s menu (original classic, dark chocolate and sea salt, and pistachio, each sold for £10 a pot) are light and glossy in style – as opposed to a block that retains its shape when cut into – which is how Fanigliulo prefers his tiramisu. He is hoping that Marrone will become a go-to spot for people after this style of tiramisu (which, I can confirm, is absolutely delicious).Fanigliulo’s enthusiasm for good tiramisu is infectious, and reminds me that I do actually really love this beautiful, creamy, caffeine-and-booze-filled pudding. And I’m all for there being more places to get great tiramisu. But whenever I see a new modification of this beautiful dessert into yet another drink or snack, I can’t help but think we might be overdoing it a little. Perhaps it’s time to make it tirami-stop?Explore more on these topicsFoodDessertChocolateCoffeeWinefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas | Brazil | The Guardian
description: ‘The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,’ Maria Cristina de Sales says
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: ‘The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,’ Maria Cristina de Sales says
Content: Maria Cristiane de Sales, from Herói's Burger, opened her burger restaurant, inside Maré, a complex of 16 favelas home to 140,000 people.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMaria Cristiane de Sales, from Herói's Burger, opened her burger restaurant, inside Maré, a complex of 16 favelas home to 140,000 people.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianBrazilHow a month-long competitive food tour is rewriting the story of Rio’s favelas‘The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,’ Maria Cristina de Sales saysTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven at the age of nine, Maria Cristina de Sales knew exactly when to ask her mother’s colleagues at the slaughterhouse for a piece of the pig they were butchering: when they got close to the pork leg, her favourite part.When she grew up, Sales followed the path of many others fromBrazil’s deprivednorth-east and moved south in search of better work opportunities. She arrived in Rio de Janeiro and, unable to afford a home in tourist-heavy south zone, moved to a favela further north.She crossed the city every day to work as a receptionist and secretary, but only really found her footing 15 years laterwhen she and her husband opened a burger restaurant, inside the favela.“The doors that aren’t open to us in the rest of the city, we open for ourselves here,” said Sales, 39, inside her restaurant in Maré, a favela complex that emerged in the 1940s in a vast mangrove area, settled by workers who could not afford to live in – or had been evicted by the state from – the wealthier parts of the city.What usually dominates the headlines about Maré, a complex of 16 favelas home to 140,000 people, are problems such as poverty, armed drug traffickers and bloody police operations, but Sales’s restaurant has joined an effort to change that perception.From 1 October, local bars and restaurants will take part in a month-long competitive food trail made up entirely of Maré establishments, hoping to attract visitors from across the city who are often afraid to visit a favela.View image in fullscreen‘Violence exists here just as it does in other parts of the city, but it does not define Maré entirely,’ chef Mariana Aleixo says.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“We face prejudice simply for saying that we live in a favela, but there are a lot of good things here,” she said.Were it not for the surrounding alleys so narrow that sometimes only one person can pass at a time, the tangled web of electrical wires crowding the utility poles and the occasional young man riding a motorcycle with a rifle, Sales’s restaurant could be anywhere else in the city – a family-friendly, air-conditioned burger joint. The superhero-themed decor was a request by Sales’s sons, and includes a life-size Spider-Man.Her entry for the food trail will be, of course, a pork leg, made into burger named Peppa Pig. “It’s a reference to my story: a girl who came from the north-east, went through hell and is now here, proud and still fighting – just like many other people here in Maré,” she added.One sweet-and-slightly-spicy element of the dish – a pineapple jam with chilli and ginger – she learned to make at Casa das Mulheres da Maré, a centre set up by alocal NGO, Redes da Maré, to support women and which organises the food trail, calledComida de Favela, or Favela Food.“When we improve the quality of life of a woman in Maré, we’re improving the whole community,” said Mariana Aleixo, 38, the centre’s coordinator, herself a chef who was born and raised in Maré and has worked in the kitchens of Rio’s luxury hotels, including the Copacabana Palace.The food trail is now in its fourth edition – the first was held in 2015 – and is one of four finalists in the Best Culinary Festival in Latin America category at the 2026 World Culinary Awards, which will announce the winners in October.The 16 restaurants – selected from more than 150 applicants, most of themBlack-owned– receive management and marketing training and, starting this year, guidance on how to support customers who report sexual harassment. The winners, chosen by customer vote, receive cash prizes.Reflecting the origins of many residents or their ancestors, many of the dishes feature other references to north-eastern cuisine, such as the “North-eastern Explosion”, a pizza topped with cassava cream,coalhocheese – similar to halloumi – andcarne de sol, a lightly salted cured beef usually fried in a clarified butter similar to ghee.“Gastronomy is the biggest economic sector in the community,” said Aleixo, noting that of the roughly 3,200 businesses in the area, about 1,200 are restaurants and bars.Aleixo said she had approached sponsors of other food festivals across the city and had never succeeded in securing their support. “I believe it’s because of prejudice against favelas,” she said.Although the aim is for visitors to experience the favela from a “perspective other than violence”, Aleixo acknowledges that some may witness something that the thousands of people who live there have to contend with: the occasional presence ofarmed drug traffickers. Police generally do not patrol favelas unless carrying out operations.The food trail has no connection to the criminals, who also do not interfere with its activities because they seem to understand that it benefits the community.“Some of the experiences we live through here are very violent, and we want the city to have access to that. Understanding that sense of indignation that residents often have is important so that people can build a different repertoire for thinking about public security in Rio,” she said.View image in fullscreenAleixo is coordinator of Casa das Mulheres da Maré, a centre to support women that organises the Comida de Favela food trail,Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian“Violence exists here just as it does in other parts of the city, but it does not define Maré entirely,” added Aleixo.Despite the invitation to outsiders – Favela Food’ssocial media pagesoften advertise shuttle vans to bring visitors from other parts of the city and take them back again – another aim is to encourage the circulation of people and money between the complex’s own favelas.While Sales’s burger restaurant is in the Parque União favela, the snack bar run by Beatriz Santos Antônio, 39, is in the Nova Holanda favela, a 15-minute walk away.Born in another city inRio de Janeirostate, Antônio arrived in Maré 16 years ago because she could not afford to live elsewhere. She and her children went through periods of hunger, but neighbours helped them, and she drew on cooking skills learned from her mother to start selling cassava fritters.Her entry for the food trail consists of four elliptical fritters, a classic Brazilian bar snack that Antônio has taken to new heights: crisp on the outside and moist inside, filled with either roast beef or prawns with cream cheese.“I’ve come a long way,” said Antônio, smiling as she wiped away tears and made the final preparations for her first time taking part in FavelaFood.“Today, these tears are no longer because of hunger. Today it’s a story of happiness and of being able to encourage other women to start their own businesses too. There is also a lot of happiness in the favela.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilFoodRio de JaneirofeaturesShareReuse this content

Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Cometa’s carajillo – recipeThe classic Mexican combo of espresso and Licor 43 gets a shot in the arm with a decent hit of cold-brew coffee liqueurTom KingFri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe carajillo is a ubiquitous drink found across Mexico, and it comes in many forms. Some bars simply pour espresso over ice and add a shot ofLicor 43, while others shake coffee with the liqueur and serve it straight up. Whatever the variation, the non-negotiables are coffee and Licor 43. Our version takes those two core ingredients and lengthens the drink with a light, delicious cold-brew coffee liqueur. title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for ricotta, blackberry and lemon cake | Food | The Guardian
description: Make the most of the early-autumn glut of fruit with this quick, squidgy-crumbed bake that’s bursting with berries
Author: Benjamina Ebuehi
Headline: Make the most of the early-autumn glut of fruit with this quick, squidgy-crumbed bake that’s bursting with berries
Content: Benjamina Ebuehi’s ricotta, blackberry and lemon cake.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenBenjamina Ebuehi’s ricotta, blackberry and lemon cake.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotFoodBenjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for ricotta, blackberry and lemon cakeMake the most of the early-autumn glut of fruit with this quick, squidgy-crumbed bake that’s bursting with berriesBenjamina EbuehiFri 11 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEvery year, I get annoyed with myself for not making the most of blackberry season, and then it’s gone before I’ve had a chance really to enjoy them. They’re such great berries to bake with, and here I’ve scattered them in a simple ricotta cake. It’s a quick, one-bowl bake with a perfectly squidgy crumb that’s bursting with fruit.Ricotta, blackberry and lemon cakePrep10 minCook45 minServes8-10170g caster sugarFinely grated zest of 2 unwaxed lemons2 large eggs70g olive oil125g ricotta130g plain flour1 tsp baking powder¼ tsp salt150g blackberriesTo finish125g ricotta1 tbsp lemon juice½ tbsp icing sugar,plus extra for dustingHeat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4, and grease and line a 23cm loose-bottomed cake tin.Put the sugar and lemon zest in a bowl and use your fingertips to rub together until fragrant. Add the eggs and oil, whisk until frothy, then mix in the ricotta. Finally, sift in the flour, baking powder and salt, and stir gently to combine.Pour the batter into the lined tin, scatter the blackberries on top, and bake for 28-32 minutes, until a skewer inserted into the middle comes out clean. Leave the cake to cool completely in its tin, then turn out and dust with icing sugar.For the whipped ricotta, whisk all the ingredients in a bowl until smooth and creamy; alternatively, for a super-smooth result, blitz it in a food processor.Serve slices of the cake with a dollop of the whipped ricotta.Explore more on these topicsFoodThe sweet spotCakeFruitCheeseBakingEggsSummer food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine’: readers’ favourite foodie experiences in Europe | Food and drink | The Guardian
description: Your top culinary discoveries, from Bled cake in Slovenia to sardines in Portugal and seafood soup in Spain
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: Your top culinary discoveries, from Bled cake in Slovenia to sardines in Portugal and seafood soup in Spain
Content: Sardines, bread and wine in the Algarve, Portugal.Photograph: Paul Thompson Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenSardines, bread and wine in the Algarve, Portugal.Photograph: Paul Thompson Images/AlamyReaders' travel tipsFood and drink‘I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine’: readers’ favourite foodie experiences in EuropeYour top culinary discoveries, from Bled cake in Slovenia to sardines in Portugal and seafood soup in SpainTell us aboutautumn days out in the UK– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 11 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSimple sardines in the AlgarveLast August, the smoky aroma of grilled sardines drifting over the beach in Portimão woke me up from my sunbathing on the beach. Attracted by the aroma of barbecued fish, we found ourselves in the old port where, for €12, I was served two delicious sandwiches on rustic bread of sardines in garlic and olive oil, with a small cold beer. I sat down, ate and chatted with locals on benches at simple communal tables. The important thing seemed to be to enjoy food together. The next morning, a reenactment of the fishing boats arriving loaded with fish, as they once were, was a real spectacle – complete with guitar playing, drum-banging and excited seagulls whirling and wailing above in the hope of a feast. Later, concerts and dancing animated the town as the party forthe sardine festivalwent on well into the night. Cooking demos and dishes including sardine-based soup and salads, added to the enjoyment. I never imagined such pleasure could be had from the simple sardine.JoeA family dinner in the Faroe IslandsView image in fullscreenFaroe Islands salmon.Photograph: Roberto Moiola/Sysaworld/Getty ImagesMy wife and I visited the Faroe Islands a few years ago, where we took part inheimablídni, a concept where traditional Faroese food is served in a home. We found it to be one of the best ways to experience the Faroes and a unique experience to share a meal with a local family. Homecooked dishes showcase ingredients from the surrounding sea and mountains. We were served smoked salmon from the host’s own smoker, lamb, potatoes and traditional specialities, all accompanied with great conversation about Faroese life and traditions. Sitting around a family table makes the experience feel personal and authentic.MikeA vegan feast in SicilyView image in fullscreenChickpea fritters in Palermo.Photograph: Randolph Images/AlamyAs a vegan who loves trying local cuisine, the combination of warm hospitality and a high proportion of locals with a lactose intolerance makes Sicily the ideal foodie getaway. Having hiked to the top of Monte Pellegrino in 35C heat, we popped into a small nondescript street-food shop (the only place that was open) and were delighted to findpanelle– delicious crispy chickpea-flour fritters served in sesame bread. We ate them overlooking Palermo harbour. That evening, we triedHaiku, a vegan restaurant with reimagined classics based on dishes such as carbonara and tiramisu. It was so good we kept ordering more and more courses until we could barely move.EstherProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Strong spirits and small plates in GreeceView image in fullscreenTsipouro and meze in Volos.Photograph: Wirestock/AlamyThe city of Volos is famous for its Tsipouradika – tavernas that servetsipouro, a strong spirit made from pomace, the stems, skins and seeds that are left over from wine making. It comes plain or infused with botanicals and anise, and is served with ice and water. Each glass you order arrives with a different small plate or meze. It could be grilled peppers, sundried octopus, a spicy cheese spread or smoked mackerel. You take pot luck as to what the patron fancies dishing up that day.BarbaraThe perfect snack to pair with Lithuanian beerView image in fullscreenEvery bar in Vilnius has its own version of kepta duona.Photograph: Ana del Castillo/Getty ImagesIn Vilnius, we came across the ultimate food pairing for the fantastic beers available there in the form ofkepta duona– deep-fried rye bread with garlic and cheese. Every bar has a slightly different version – raw, roast or confit garlic with cream, melted or simply grated cheese. A heavenly snack that could easily become your main meal.NatalieVegan delights in the patisseries of ParisView image in fullscreenLand & Monkeys patisserie.Photograph: Hemis/AlamyBeing an unfortunate combination of a foodie and a vegan, I was prepared for a weekend of staring longingly into patisserie windows when heading to Paris earlier this summer. I was not prepared for the unbridled joy awaiting me at theLand & Monkeysboulangeries/patisseries scattered across the capital. It began with an outrageously creamy raspberry petit gateaux from its Montmartre branch, followed by the unbelievable fluff and flake of a croissant aux champignons in the Marais the next day. A parting madeleine for the Eurostar on our last day was the pièce de résistance.Elinorskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPasta with pears in BolognaView image in fullscreenTortellini with gorgonzola cheese and caramelised pears.Photograph: Caitlin McGrawIt was in Bologna, Italy’s self-proclaimed food capital, where I sampled the city’s signature dish of tortellini. We stumbled acrossRosarose Bistrot, enticed by tables with red-checked cloths set in the middle of a cobblestone road. I enjoyed shells stuffed with tangy gorgonzola cheese and chunks of caramelised pears, a fruit I would usually avoid, but I placed trust in the regional delicacy. The fruit’s sweetness blended harmoniously with the strong cheese flavour; crispy and soft fried bread known ascrescentine, was used to soak up the remaining sauce. It was only right to mark this culinary experience with a small tortellini keyring from a nearby gift shop, filled with various merchandise emblazoned with the pasta shell.CaitlinCatalonia’s ultimate slow-food festivalView image in fullscreenCatalan snails being cooked on a wood fire.Photograph: Nito 100/Getty Images/iStockphotoLast year, I discovered the ultimate slow-food festival – the Snail Feast of Lleida (L’Aplec del Caragol), 100 miles west of Barcelona. Over a long weekend, there was music, dancing, cooking and feasting, all in celebration of the tiny mollusc. Entrance to the festival is free, and visitors can enjoy traditional snail dishes in tents, local restaurants or simply in the town squares. I had two helpings of snailsa la gormanda, cooked in a sauce of spicy paprika and herbs. Since attending the festival, I have been treading carefully in my garden in case I harm what I discovered are delicate and delicious creatures.HelenHeavenly cakes in SloveniaView image in fullscreenBled cake is like a custard slice, but much better.Photograph: Varvara Kurakina/AlamyHaving travelled by train from Bristol down through the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland and Italy, we reached our penultimate stop, Lake Bled. We’d been awed by the beautiful Swiss alpine scenery, but Bled took it up a notch. After a day of cycling from Bled to Lake Bohinj and back, we refuelled on the local delicacy, Bled cake, a sumptuously smooth set custard encased in the lightest of mille-feuille pastry and topped with whipped cream. Imagine an English custard slice, only a million times better. It was so welcome after a day in the Slovenian mountain air, we made it a holiday habit. A Bled cake a day until we had to come home!SaraWinning tip: delicious seafood soup in SpainView image in fullscreenSopa de pescado y marisco.Photograph: Gary Conner/Getty ImagesFew meals linger in the memory like a proper Asturiansopa de pescado y marisco(seafood soup). After kayaking 10 miles down the Sella River, my reward in the town of Arriondas wasn’t a humble bowl of soup – it was a whole pan! Every flavour shone through in a broth packed with white fish, prawns and sweet crab claws, so extraordinarily rich it almost brought me to tears. I devoured it all, skipping the rest of the courses without regret. Years later in Gijón, history repeated itself. Even my soup-sceptical husband declared it the best he had ever tasted. In Asturias, fish soup isn’t a starter. It’s an obsession in a pot.OksanaView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsFood and drinkReaders' travel tipsEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I’ve visited every motorway service station in Britain | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Some people don’t understand my lifelong enthusiasm for roadside stop-offs – now visiting and cataloguing them is what I do for a living
Author: Heather Main
Headline: Some people don’t understand my lifelong enthusiasm for roadside stop-offs – now visiting and cataloguing them is what I do for a living
Content: ‘I think of them as one of life’s great levellers’: Rich Cross, at Leigh Delamere service station in Wiltshire.Photograph: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I think of them as one of life’s great levellers’: Rich Cross, at Leigh Delamere service station in Wiltshire.Photograph: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianExperienceLife and styleExperience: I’ve visited every motorway service station in BritainSome people don’t understand my lifelong enthusiasm for roadside stop-offs – now visiting and cataloguing them is what I do for a livingRich CrossFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I was 10 years old, the highlight of my summer holidays was going to work with my dad, whois a lorry driver. For a couple of years in the mid-2000s, I’d excitedly climb into the cab next to him and we’d set off on a 10-hour trip. My job was to follow the AA Road Atlas, and I’d joyfully track the services marked on the map as we thundered along.My dad thought stopping was a waste of time, but his designated rest stops were my favourite part of the trip. Depending on the journey, we might stop for two or three meals. I always hoped at least one would be at a Little Chef. I loved their Olympic Breakfast, a massive full English, and every meal was rounded off with a lollipop – what more could a 10-year-old want?As I got older, motorway services retained their air of magic. In 2012, when I was 14, I found the websitemotorwayservices.uk, which reviewed lots of major service stations. Any time my family visited one, I’d take pictures and contribute to the site.I learned to drive as soon as I turned 17 and bought myself a two-door Smart car, which I still drive today. After I passed my test, I’d drive out to services near my home in Bristol.double quotation markIn my view, the services are the destination, not just part of the journeyAfter leaving school, I got a job as a bus driver, but I soon realised that, while I loved the driving, there wasn’t enough time for stopping. I carried on visiting as many services as I could on my days off, just as a hobby, but soon I decided to try to make this my job.I left the bus company and started posting more reviews to the site and my own social media channels under the nameThe Services King. Now it’s my full-time job. Alongside reviews, I write articles for industry publications and do sponsored posts on social media.I love the history connected to service stations, how they chart the growth of Britain’s road network and our changing tastes in food. In my view, the services are the destination, not just part of the journey. There’s an underlying sense of occasion connected to them.I hit the milestone of visiting every one of the UK’s 97 motorway service stations in 2019. I revisit them all periodically to review and post updates on their facilities, as well as visiting smaller rest stops on A roads. I work away from home four days a week and can visit up to five service stations a day, although I don’t always stop for something to eat and drink. I see what’s new since my last visit and photograph the facilities so drivers can plan their stops.View image in fullscreen‘I can visit up to five service stations a day.’Photograph: Gareth Iwan Jones/The GuardianI like to include a bit of history or trivia about each service station. My most popular posts are usually new site openings, and my followers come from all walks of life, but lots are industry professionals.My dad struggles to understand my obsession. Sometimes people don’t believe me when I tell them what I do for a living, but it’s always a conversation starter. Everyone has something to say about services. I think of them as one of life’s great levellers; no matter who you are, or where you’re from, everybody has the shared experience of visiting one.There are a few key factors that make an exemplary service station; bonus points if it has a notable landmark and looks unusual – for instance, the Pennine Tower at Lancaster services on the M6, or a bridge where you can sit and have a coffee watching the cars go by underneath you. Some stations now have lovely outdoor features; Rugby services has gardens and a fountain. Most people prefer it if they’re easy to get to – straight off the motorway is better than having to come off at a junction and navigate roundabouts.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: I brought a bear back to lifeRead moreI’m always asked what my favourite station is. I don’t have one, but I do favour those that have a proper sit-down area to eat a meal and relax. As so many of them are full of chains these days, independently owned Tebay, on the M6, and Gloucester, on the M5, which have farm shops and a proper restaurant, are high on my list.I really enjoy my job, but it’s a lot of travel. I can easily cover 25,000 miles in a year. When I take time off, I like to holiday in the UK, so wherever I go, I can’t escape the services. Not that I’d want to. To me, they will always be the best part of any holiday.As told to Heather MainDo you have an experience to share?
