title: I heard it through the grapevine: everything you need to know about growing grapes | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: Vines are a beautiful addition to an edible garden, yet will only thrive with plenty of light and shelter
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: Vines are a beautiful addition to an edible garden, yet will only thrive with plenty of light and shelter
Content: Removing some of the grapes from the bunch encourages the others to swell and ripen.Photograph: coldsnowstorm/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRemoving some of the grapes from the bunch encourages the others to swell and ripen.Photograph: coldsnowstorm/Getty ImagesGardening adviceI heard it through the grapevine: everything you need to know about growing grapesVines are a beautiful addition to an edible garden, yet will only thrive with plenty of light and shelterClaire RatinonFri 11 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy garden faces east-ish and gets a decent amount of sunlight, but it’s fairly exposed and can be cool, so plants that need really warm weather don’t like to grow here. Yet, there’s a corner by the back door that’s a pocket of sun and shelter, and a wise former occupant decided to plant a grapevine there. If I hadn’t inherited this mature grapevine, I can’t imagine I would have thought to plant one, but if you’ve got the right conditions they’re a lovely addition to an edible garden.First you have to choose whether you want to grow wine grapes or dessert grapes. Wine grapes are smaller and less palatable – but hardier – than dessert grapes, which generally need to be grown in a sturdy greenhouse in order to fully ripen. Grapevines can be sourced from plant sellers and garden centres, and most will have been grafted – so make sure to choose a vine that is best suited to your soil type and local climate.double quotation markGrapevines need free-draining soil with a decent level of fertility, so choose your location wiselyLike other perennial fruit plants, grapevines are best planted when dormant, though young plants can be vulnerable to cold temperatures, so aim for early spring to give them the best chance. Grapevines need free-draining soil with a decent level of fertility, so choose your location wisely and incorporate organic matter into the planting hole. My grapevine grows against a fence furnished with wires, which gives it the shelter and structure it needs.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFancy fresh cabbages next spring? Then it’s time to get sowingRead moreA newly planted grapevine will need regular watering in its first season in order to establish well, but from then on it should be happy being watered by the rain (aside from when there’s a drought, of course). Mulching in winter will improve soil structure and water retention; just be sure not to let the organic matter touch the vine itself.Some people are put off growing grapevines by the precise training and pruning they need. While this is true, if – like me – you’re happy to see a thriving plant bearing a decent (but perhaps not optimal) amount of fruit, then the following less rigorous approach should do. I regularly trim the leaves and vines on mine to ensure there’s good airflow to keep the plant healthy. Just as when thinning apples, remove some bunches of grapes (or even some grapes from the bunches) to encourage the remaining fruit to swell and ripen. If you’re up for the challenge, do look up the different ways to train a vine and give it a go.Grapes are ready to harvest from late summer into autumn, depending on the variety, and the best way to know whether they’re ready is to give them a taste. While cultivating grapevines can be exacting, they are a beautiful plant if you’ve got a spot with the right conditions for them to flourish.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations album review – freshness and flair | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songs
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songs
Content: Not to be pigeonholed … Lucas Debargue.Photograph: Andreas FleckView image in fullscreenNot to be pigeonholed … Lucas Debargue.Photograph: Andreas FleckClassical musicReviewLucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations album review – freshness and flair(Sony)Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songsClive PagetFri 11 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 02.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver since Lucas Debargue took fourth prize at the 2015 international Tchaikovsky competition, he’s refused to be pigeonholed. His distinctive journey brings him now to George Gershwin, complementing the piano concerto and preludes with beguiling original explorations of the composer’s songs in the form of a dozen études. His supple account of Rhapsody in Blue is based on Gershwin’s solo piano arrangement, to which he adds his own partly improvised cadenzas. Like everything here, it comes up fresh as a daisy.View image in fullscreenLucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations album art.Photograph: Sony ClassicalThe Piano Concerto in F brings Debargue’s jazz credentials to the fore (he cut his teeth on the club circuit). The Orchestre de Paris under Elim Chan provides an admirably clear and concise accompaniment. The edge-of-your-seat stakes are reminiscent of André Previn.In his programme note, Debargue admires Gershwin as a maverick whose music transcends time and place. His 12 virtuoso études on Gershwin songs, impeccable compositions in their own right, view familiar tunes through unfamiliar lenses. Embraceable You, for example, is reinvented as a sultry rumba, while Fascinating Rhythm is a cheeky Parisian waltz. It Ain’t Necessarily So barnstorms as a Bach-flavoured Fantasie, Chaconne and Fugue. The colossal 12th étude comprises 20 whirlwind variations on Summertime. Performances are rhythmically alert and full of imaginative flair.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: ‘We can’t stop for a second’: the centre tracking South Korea’s stalkers in real time | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Since June, an app has allowed survivors, who are overwhelmingly women, to see exactly where their stalker is
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Since June, an app has allowed survivors, who are overwhelmingly women, to see exactly where their stalker is
Content: Stalker APP VideoSouth Korea‘We can’t stop for a second’: the centre tracking South Korea’s stalkers in real timeSince June, an app has allowed survivors, who are overwhelmingly women, to see exactly where their stalker isRaphael Rashidin SeoulThu 10 Sep 2026 22.51 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTShareOn a large screen in a control centre in eastern Seoul, a dot representing a man closes in on a woman. The dot changes direction, and the distance reading between them falls from 845 metres to 792.On the woman’s phone, the same map is loading. A probation officer rings her: the stalker is approaching, don’t panic, officers have been dispatched. The man is a stand-in and the scenario is staged, but the system is real.Since late June, a stalking survivor in South Koreacan open an appand watch a tagged perpetrator move in real time once they come within a 2km radius. If they come within a kilometre, an alert is passed to police and probation authorities, who call the victim. Previously, survivors received only a text message stating a distance, with no indication of location. About 400 people are now enrolled in the new scheme.“Waiting with no idea what’s happening is deeply distressing,” says Yoon Hyun-bong, who directs the control centre. “A distance alone doesn’t tell you which direction he’s coming from, but seeing it on a map, you know where to hide.”Stalking cases are on the rise in South Korea. Reports have tripled in the four years since a dedicated stalking law was introduced in 2021, reaching 44,687 in 2025. Around 80% of stalking victimsare women. In South Korea, police can apply to the courts to make a suspected stalker wear an ankle tag that tracks them.View image in fullscreenThe Central Electronic Monitoring Centre, Seoul, Korea.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianThe introduction of the app follows astring of stalking killingsthat shocked the country. In March, prosecutors allege a man wearing an ankle tag blocked his former partner’s car as she left work in Namyangju, north-east of Seoul, broke the window with a drill and stabbed her. A court had already barred him from approaching her after she reported him for stalking. He is on trial for murder, which he denies, claiming diminished responsibility.The justice ministry, which runs the tagging system, could see where he was at all times, but the police handling her stalking case did not know he was being tracked.Can this app help combat stalking? – video19,000 alerts a dayTwo control centres, in Seoul and Daejeon, handle around 19,000 alerts a day between them, covering the more than 5,000 people who are under electronic monitoring for offences ranging from sexual violence to murder. Most are filtered out by staff at the centres but about 300 a day are serious enough to send out a probation officer.In Seoul, probation officers sit calmly at three banks of screens showing a live list of danger and caution alerts, and beside each, the subject’s description and even the battery level of their tag.Each officer handles more than 20 monitored people, a figure the ministry says it is trying to halve as the numbers grow.View image in fullscreenThe centre in Seoul handles thousands of alerts every day.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The Guardian“We’d have liked to suspend monitoring while you were here, but we can’t stop for a minute, not for a second,” an official says.Opinions about the new app, which is still in its early days and on a limited scale, are mixed. Anna*, a woman who fled a violent former partner, says knowing where he was would have made a difference. She spent two weeks moving between state-run shelters for survivors of domestic violence before being given a panic-button watch which alerts police and sends officers her location. The app was not available at the time for her, but she says she would have welcomed it.“Even with the watch on, it still never gave me the peace of mind, because I didn’t know where he was at any time,” she said. “What if I took it off for a shower, and that just happened to be the time he broke into my house?”View image in fullscreenAn example of an ankle tag used to track the location of stalkers in South Korea.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianSujeong Kim, the director of the women’s human rights counselling centre at the Korea Women’s Hotline says knowing a perpetrator’s whereabouts can be more helpful than not knowing. But she questions whether giving survivors that information also risks shifting responsibility for their safety on to them.“If the authorities did their job properly, who would want to check it themselves?” she says, adding that victims may end up checking wherever they go to see whether the perpetrator has entered the radius, adding to the psychological burden of living with the threat and feeling they must be ready to flee.Then there is the issue of tagging. The app works only if a court has ordered tagging, and in stalking cases that is rarely sought.Police apprehended 29,404 people on stalking charges across 2024 and 2025. Over the same period they made 1,187 applications to tag suspects, of which courts only granted 427. Whether the new app changes how often tagging is sought or granted is not yet clear.South Korea’s police agency said they apply for a tag where there is a risk of reoffending, and that in practice they escalate measures to separate a perpetrator from a victim in stages, according to the risk and the seriousness of the case.Kang Shin-won, who heads the justice ministry’s electronic monitoring division, says the tag serves as a minimum safety measure, because not every suspect can realistically be removed from society.View image in fullscreenPolice apprehended nearly 30,000 people on stalking charges across 2024 and 2025.Photograph: Raphael Rashid/The GuardianYoon Hyun-bong, who directs the Seoul centre, says that having something concrete to watch is less distressing than waiting blind, and an improvement on the distance figure that was previously given via text.For Kim, none of this addresses the wider issue.“The cause of this problem, and the reason it doesn’t get solved, is gender discrimination”, she says. “Treating it as unimportant, as a private matter, as something the victim can sort out on her own, that all comes from gender discrimination, too.”*Name has been changed.In the UK, theNational Stalking Helplineis on 0808 802 0300 or email via theirinquiry form. In the US, resources are available atstalkingawareness.org.

title: ‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on Pulp | Movies | The Guardian
description: Before the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another record
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: Before the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another record
Content: Composite: Guardian design; Courtesy of MubiView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design; Courtesy of MubiMoviesInterview‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on PulpRebecca NicholsonBefore the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another recordFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the director Garth Jennings first moved to Paris,Jarvis Cocker, who was living there, dropped in on his old friend. “And I nearly got you arrested,” the Pulp frontman recalls. It was bonfire night, and Cocker had taken some welcoming fireworks over to Jennings’ place. “It turned out Garth’s apartment was quite near to the – not an army base, but what’s it called?”“TheÉcole Militaire,” says Jennings.“So obviously they didn’t like explosives,” says Cocker. “We got told off for that. The best welcome to Paris.”“It was lovely,” adds Jennings, fondly. “I remember it very well.”The men had first met in the late 1990s, when Jennings directed two gorgeous music videos for Pulp, for the singlesHelp the AgedandA Little Soul. Now, almost 30 years later, they are working together again, on Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? This joyful, funny, celebratory film is a hybrid beast: part concert movie and part documentary on the long history of the band. The live show was filmed at London’s O2 Arena in the summer of 2025, on the night that Pulp were told thatMore, their eighth studio albumand first album in 24 years, had gone to No 1 in the British album charts. You can see Cocker waving around the trophy on stage.Jennings, director ofSon of RambowandThe Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, has lived in Paris for the past 13 years, where the animation for Sing, his wildly successful kids’ musical film franchise, is made. He is working on a short Christmas special, and the third and final film in the series. “It’s a slow process,” he says, from the studio, “but we’re getting there.” Cocker moved back to London a few years ago, and today he is at home, getting ready toheadline the End of the Road festival. It will be Pulp’s last show for a while.You can blame Instagram and Abba Voyage for the existence of What Do You Do for an Encore? Pulp, formed by Cocker in Sheffield in 1978, split up in 2002. They got back together for a reunion tour between 2011 and 2013, the final date of which was captured for another idiosyncratic documentary, Florian Habicht’sPulp: A Film About Life, Death & Supermarkets. Cocker had considered those shows to be a fitting – and final – farewell.“WhenPulpgot together that time, I had this idea that things had ended in a not-nice way, and I wanted it to have a happy ending,” Cocker says. “I thought the way to do that would be to play concerts, and we invited Russell Senior back” – the violinist and guitarist had quit in 1997 – “and I just thought it would be like: we’re all friends, everything’s good, and then we’d all retire,” says Cocker. “And to be honest, that tour did seem to do that.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t go to shows any more. I’m an old bloke’ ... Jarvis Cocker.Photograph: Tom JacksonSo when a promoter got in touch years later, to ask if Pulp would be interested in playing again, Cocker had to think about it. “Because the worst thing to do would have been to spoil the happy ending.” How did he decide to say yes? “I confessed my fear that people wouldn’t come, or that people weren’t that bothered, and why would they be?” The promoter assured him that people would most definitely be bothered. “He told me about a few times when he’d been to shows and a Pulp song had come on before a band went on, and everybody sang along. You know, I don’t go to shows any more. I’m an old bloke.” (Cocker is about to turn 63.) “I just said: ‘All right, I hope you’re right, let’s do it.’ But I wanted to make sure that it would be a good thing for us to do as well.”Cocker teased the news of a second Pulp reunion on Instagram in 2022. Jennings messaged him to tell him how excited he was, and to offer his help. It is obvious, when chatting to Jennings, that as well as being Cocker’s friend, he is a huge Pulp fan. As they started to work on the creative direction of the live show together, Jennings remembers, “I’d be in some other room working on a graphics thing, and then I’d suddenly hear you lot playing, and I’d have to just drop it and come outside. Especially a song like Razzmatazz, which was my first Pulp song. I found you through that. You started playing that at one point, and it was just the best thing ever. I had this wonderful little secret window into this world.”When it became obvious that the live show was going to be a spectacle, they started to wonder about turning it into a film. “Some of my favourite films are concert films, and they don’t need to be anything more. But this felt like an opportunity to go a bit further,” says Jennings.View image in fullscreenCelebratory ... Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Which is whereAbba Voyagecomes in. Both Jennings and Cocker had seen – and loved – the theatrical experience, which blends live music with giant holograms of Abba in their prime. “That was something that was very inspiring. Just the sheer joy of it,” says Jennings, who has seen it three times. As well as performing the hits, Abba Voyage tells the story of Abba, just as What Do You Do for an Encore? tells the story of Pulp, giving each song context.“I was so glad when Garth got in touch, because it felt as if he could help make it something that people hadn’t seen before,” Cocker says. “I am very familiar with Pulp’s backstory because I’ve lived through it. But I’m always flabbergasted at how long the band has gone on.” It is clear from the footage of the crowd, showing people losing their minds and singing every word, that some of the audience were not even born when Pulp split up for the first time. “That’s something amazing, really. And something I can’t explain – why young people have latched on to it.” They played in Manchester recently. “A lot of young people,” Cocker laughs. “But I’m happy about it.”View image in fullscreen‘It felt as if he could make it something that people hadn’t seen before’ ... Garth Jennings.Photograph: Ezra PetronioThe film uses animation, old TV clips and grainy VHS footage, as well as documents and objects that fans may recognise from Cocker’s2023 book Good Pop Bad Pop. It was a “huge job” to pull it together, says Jennings, who credits the archivist Tess McNally-Watson with some serious hard work. “Because it’s not all in one place. It’s in people’s bedrooms and attics, and someone’s friend’s brother’s still got a cassette, so it’s a lot of Raiders of the Lost Ark-style gathering and then transferring.” At one point, there is a funny, fond interview with Cocker’s mother and grandmother, who crack jokes about his newfound fame. “That’s a bit embarrassing for me,” says Cocker. “My grandma’s been dead ages, and my mum died only three or four years ago, so it was quite a thing.”During the live show, Pulp pay a moving tribute to Steve Mackey, who joined the band as bassist in 1989, and whodied in 2023aged 56. Mackey was not going to play on this tour, though he had wished his old bandmates luck. It was important that he was included in the film, and Cocker says that they were able to show it to Mackey’s family before it was signed off. “Just to make sure that they were happy with it. But I think you did a very good job there, Garth. It’s a hard thing to express in the right way.”What Do You Do for an Encore? does not shy away from the more complicated times in Pulp’s story. Around the release of their then-divisive album This Is Hardcore in 1998, Cocker describes “going down a dark tunnel”. Jennings was making videos for the band back then. Had he noticed that things seemed off?“I didn’t notice Jarvis going down a dark tunnel, and maybe you were, Jarvis, and I apologise if I wasn’t there to help you,” he says, sincerely. “But no, because the actual act of making these things was always lovely. I never noticed you being tricky, or anything.”View image in fullscreen‘I’d decided to be in a band when I was seven’ … Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Photograph: Courtesy of Mubi“It was probably because I’d decided to be in a band when I was seven,” Cocker reflects. “Like a lot of people, you think that if you achieve fame, that will be the magic wand that makes everything in your life work, and obviously that’s not the case. You still have to make an effort in your life. You can’t just lie in a bed and say: ‘Right, OK, that’s it, job done.’ But I didn’t realise that, so that’s why I had issues with it.” Over time, he says, “I went back into real life and appreciated it. That was probably another reason why it took me a while to decide to do Pulp again. I was thinking: ‘Well, what’s the motivation? What will you get from it?’”In the film, Cocker describes Pulp as “scaling Mount Pop”, but it sounds as if he didn’t much like what he found at the summit. “It’s like seeing videos of your wedding. Your wedding is a magical thing, but then somebody shows you a video, and you think: ‘Oh God, what’sthat?’” He prefers fantasy to reality, he says, “but sometimes you have to look at reality. And that’s what happened.” Fame, he says, “is an exciting thing, but you just have to keep your wits about you, and make sure you’re doing things for the right reason, and try not to get too up your own arse.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s a lot of Raiders of the Lost Ark-style gathering’ … Cocker in his younger years.When he was still at school, in one of his exercise books, Cocker wrote out a “Pulp master plan”. It makes an appearance in the film. But really, he says, they’ve never had one. “I’m glad things that things didn’t go according to a plan. That’s the great thing about groups. You know that you have to work with other people, and everybody adds something to it, and then you get something that you can’t really say exactly where it came from.”Pulp’s End of the Road set last week marked the end of a tour that started in 2023, though the band are planning to meet up again in October, to celebrate it all. They’re going to see Abba Voyage together. Will there be another encore? “You know, it’s like a tree,” says Cocker, philosophically. “A tree doesn’t decide it’s going to grow. If the weather’s right, it’ll grow a branch. And if the intellectual weather is right in the next couple of years, maybe we’ll sprout another record.” He said it himself: there has never been a master plan.Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? is on Mubi from 25 September, with special one night only preview screenings at UK and Irish cinemas on 18 September and in US cinemas on 24 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmJarvis CockerDocumentary filmsPulpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: $15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwide | Women's rights and gender equality | The Guardian
description: Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally
Author: Karen McVeigh
Headline: Her Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globally
Content: Gambian activists celebrate the overturning of a bill to end a ban on female genital mutilation in 2024. But progress remains fragile, advocates say.Photograph: Malick Njie/ReutersView image in fullscreenGambian activists celebrate the overturning of a bill to end a ban on female genital mutilation in 2024. But progress remains fragile, advocates say.Photograph: Malick Njie/ReutersWomen's rights and gender equality$15m fund launched to create ‘unstoppable momentum’ to end FGM worldwideHer Horizon Fund seeks $100m to stop practice harming 230m women and girls globallySupported byAbout this contentKaren McVeighFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrontline activists and leaders in the fight against female genital mutilation, which has affected more than230 million women and girls worldwide, have welcomed an unprecedented $15.5m (£11.4m) fund aimed at creating “unstoppable momentum” to finally end the practice.The launch of the fund comes aswomen’s rights are increasingly under attackand donor funding is in sharp decline, particularly for work led by FGM survivors in local communities. It is thought to be the largest single philanthropic contribution to ending the practice of FGM.The United Nations has set a goal ofelimination by by 2030, but progress is not on track as funding declines and legal protections are challenged.Funding received by the largest initiative to end the practice – a joint programme operated in 18 countries by the UN’s sexual and reproductive health agency, UNFPA, and the UN humanitarian organisation for children, Unicef – fell by 45% last year, from $29.6m to $16.3m.The Her Horizon Fund has been seeded with $14m from the Wallace Global Fund, plus an additional $1.5m contribution from an anonymous donor, making $15.5m in total.The aim of Her Horizon Fund, set up by the US-based Wallace Global Fund, is to pool $100m from donors to reach a “tipping point” towards ending FGM within a generation.Ifrah Ahmed, a Somali-Irish activist and survivor of FGM who set up theIfrah Foundationto end practice in Somalia, where it is nearly universal, said: “By giving $14m, the global fund will ensure activists can continue their work in this area.”UN funding worth $300,000 to her organisation was cut by UNFPA last year, but Ahmed managed to raise money from elsewhere. The Ifrah Foundation has helped push for anti-FGM legislation in Somalia, she said.Three of Somalia’s seven federal member states have enacted anti-FGM laws, while in two other states bills banning the practice have been endorsed by cabinet and are awaiting parliamentary approval, albeit with opposition by religious leaders in some areas.“If we don’t continue to raise money, the dream where this practice will end will have died for young girls,” she added.Advocates warn that while international recognition of FGM as a human rights violation has grown, and countries such as Burkina Faso, the Gambia and Kenya have criminalised the practice, progress remains fragile.In recent years, survivors and frontline groups have been trying to protect gains made over several decades.The Gambia’s supreme court, for instance, is considering aconstitutional challengeto the country’s 2015 ban on female genital mutilation and cutting. The case follows a 2024 parliamentary effort to repeal the ban, which lawmakers rejected after months of debate, amid strong resistance from women’s rights groups. In Sierra Leone, the newChild Rights Act does not prohibit FGM, despite sustained campaigning from rights groups.Susan Gibbs, the Wallace Global Fund’s senior adviser on women’s rights and FGM, said: “Female genital mutilation is a global crisis, an extreme manifestation of gender-based violence and violence against children, and a public health emergency.“There has been decades of progress, and UN data indicates declines in prevalence in a number of countries. But there have also been anti-rights pushback and political crises. Obviously, donor funding is in decline. So it’s a mixed picture.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe added: “We’re at this critical inflection point. Most frontline organisations have been absolutely starved for resources, and so more direct funding would allow them to sustain and scale [up] their work.”Sierra Leone’s first lady refuses to condemn FGM without ‘reliable data’ on harmsRead moreGibbs, who attended aJustice for Girlsglobal gathering in Kenya earlier this month, where the fund was officially launched, said the momentum at the meeting was “incredible”.“Lasting change must be led by the frontline – it cannot be imposed from the outside. Frontline survivors, activists, they know their communities and they know what it will take. They must have the resources and power to lead.“I’m convinced the impact [of the fund] will be catalytic,” she said. “There’s no doubt in my mind that with adequate funding, these frontline activists have what it takes to get this done.”FGM is thepartial or total removal of female genitalia for non-medical reasons. It has been endured by more than 144 million women and girls in Africa, 80 million in Asia and 6 million in the Middle East. The practice can cause immediate health complications such as severe pain, excessive bleeding and infection, as well as long-term consequences that include complications during childbirth, chronic pain and lasting psychological trauma.A 2025 study estimated that FGM causes approximately44,000 deaths each yearin the 15 countries examined, making it one of the leading causes of death for women and girls in those countries.Explore more on these topicsWomen's rights and gender equalityGlobal healthFemale genital mutilation (FGM)HealthWomenViolence against women and girlsAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Buddhist monk arrested in Thailand on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m | Thailand | The Guardian
description: Phra Wachirayan Wi arrested alongside woman he was filmed having sex with in latest scandal to hit country’s clergy
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Phra Wachirayan Wi arrested alongside woman he was filmed having sex with in latest scandal to hit country’s clergy
Content: Police officers escort Phra Wachirayan Wi outside the Central Investigation Bureau in Bangkok on Thursday.Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice officers escort Phra Wachirayan Wi outside the Central Investigation Bureau in Bangkok on Thursday.Photograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/AFP/Getty ImagesThailandBuddhist monk arrested in Thailand on suspicion of embezzling $2.8mPhra Wachirayan Wi arrested alongside woman he was filmed having sex with in latest scandal to hit country’s clergyAgence France-Press in BangkokFri 11 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice inThailandhave arrested a senior Buddhist monk on suspicion of embezzling $2.8m intended for his monastery, alongside a suspected female accomplice he was filmed having sex with.The case is the latest scandal to hit the clergy in the Buddhist-majority country, after a sex and extortion case involving senior monks last year prompted public outrage and calls for greater scrutiny of temple finances.Phra Wachirayan Wi, the 66-year-old abbot of the 14th-century temple Wat Phutthaisawan in the ancient capital of Ayutthaya, was arrested on Thursday on charges including embezzlement and money laundering, according to the lead police investigator Pattanasak Bupphasuwan.A 47-year-old woman accused of helping convert and conceal the money was also arrested.Leaked CCTV footage of the pair having sex on a table in the monk’s residence was widely broadcast on Thai media.In Thailand, Buddhist monks take a vow of celibacy and also renounce material possessions.Police began investigating Phra Wachirayan in mid-July after receiving an anonymous tip alleging him of misconduct and misuse of temple funds.Pattanasak, a commander of the police crime suppression division, said investigators identified two streams of money linked to donation receipts issued in the temple’s name.About 89m baht ($2.7m or £2m) was donated for temple renovations, with another 2.8m baht in payments for Buddhist amulets and other sacred objects, he said.“But the money from both streams did not enter the temple’s account – not a single baht,” Pattanasak told a news conference on Friday.View image in fullscreenPolice say authorities seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg of gold bars, jewellery, watches and land title deedsPhotograph: Panumas Sanguanwong/Thai News Pix/AFP/Getty ImagesHe said authorities had seized assets worth about 215m baht, including 16kg (35lb) of gold bars and jewellery and 28 land title deeds.Police are investigating which are personal property and which belong to the temple.“We will expand the investigation to identify other people involved and restore public confidence inBuddhism,” said Nattasak Chaowanasai, the commissioner of Thailand’s Central Investigation Bureau.Wat Phutthaisawan is a prominent royal monastery with a large following that includes government officials, businesspeople, police and military personnel.The former abbot, also known as Luang Pho Atichot, was well known for making amulets, with the Thai prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, reported to be among those who wore his creations.The abbot was defrocked shortly after his arrest.Last year,police arrested a woman accused of blackmailing at least 11 monks she had sex with, extorting nearly $12m of monastery funds from them, in a case that shook Thailand.Explore more on these topicsThailandAsia PacificReligionBuddhismnewsShareReuse this content

care in case Australia’s aged care algorithm cuts fundingExclusive:FoI documents show senior health officials were warned of concerns about assessment tool weeks after it launchedGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMelissa DaveyMedical editorFri 11 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople with dementia were warned not to apply for home support because of fears their care would be downgraded by the government’s aged care algorithm.Documents released to Guardian Australia under freedom of information (FoI) laws reveal the warnings came within weeks of the November rollout of the algorithm, which is used to determine funding packages and priority of need for older Australians requiring home support.Home support packages are critical to help prevent avoidable hospital admissions, deterioration and early entry into residential care.‘Catastrophic’ fears: health staff made lists of concerning cases days after Australia’s aged care funding tool launchRead moreDays before the algorithm was rolled out, the government barred aged care assessors from overriding the Integrated Assessment Tool’s (IAT) decisions, even if the level of funding and priority allocated were wrong or inadequate.Dementia Australia wrote to senior health department staff on 8 December to say that since the addition of the algorithm, “We remain very concerned about the feedback we are receiving”.The organisation cited the example of a man caring for his wife with dementia who was on a level three home care package, entitling her to around eight hours of support each week.But her dementia had progressed and she needed to be reassessed so she could access additional care.The woman’s husband was “advised by his local assessment service not to pursue a reassessment as they have seen a number of people with dementia receiving less or no support following IAT assessment, even if their care needs are increasing”.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe Older Persons Advocacy Network (Opan) sent a paper to department officials in February warning of deaths occurring due to the failing assessment system, and people with “extreme needs” being left without adequate support before their deaths.“The inability of clinicians to intervene” and “over-reliance on automated decision-making is contributing to preventable deterioration and in some cases, death,” the document said.In one example given by Opan, the algorithm refused a funding upgrade for a rapidly deteriorating person, forcing them to pay for private care despite the assessor’s view their existing package was grossly inadequate.A senior health department staff member shared concerns ahead of a meeting between the department and advocacy groups in late December, the FoI documents show.“Assessment orgs are telling [people] not to get an assessment as there is no guarantee they will get more funding,” the internal email read, adding that assessors were telling advocacy groups they had not been properly trained on the IAT.Prof Tanya Buchanan, the CEO of Dementia Australia, told Guardian Australia: “We remain concerned about the IAT and the aged care assessment process being able to meet the needs of Australians living with dementia, their families and carers.”She said she wants the system to include a return of clinical oversight.A spokesperson from the health department said rather than human override being returned, the government will legislate a new “assessment escalation pathway”, giving assessors the option to raise cases to a system governor – in this case, the secretary of the Department ofHealth, Disability and Ageing.“It will sit alongside the existing review provision where an older person can request a review by contacting the department,” the spokesperson said. “Assessment organisations themselves will initiate a referral based on the clinical judgement of the assessment delegate.”Carers and advocates have repeatedly shared concerns that review processes for wrong algorithm decisions are lengthy, and that older people are at risk of deteriorating or dying while they wait.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOpan’s director of policy, Samantha Edmonds, said that without further details of the government’s new escalation pathway “it is difficult to determine the effectiveness of the process”.“We look forward to clarification and consultation on the proposed changes, and to continuing to engage with government as those details develop,” she said.“The IAT algorithm has been an ongoing challenge and concern for older people.These assessments have a real impact on an older person’s life, so it is crucial that human oversight remains part of the decision-making and outcomes.”The FoI documents show that Ageing Australia, the national peak body for aged care, in February sent senior department officials a comprehensive discussion paper outlining issues with assessments including examples of people being under-assessed, especially those with dementia.“Participants being assessed are being approved for less than or the same level that they are currently receiving,” the paper said.Among many examples provided were two separate cases of people living with Parkinson’s disease, both with complex care needs, no friend or family supports, and requiring intensive medication, diabetes management and personal care including wound care.Both were reassessed under the algorithm as requiring no additional support or care despite declining health.A fifth of older Australians who contested automated decision on home support funding got more after human reviewRead more“The assessors advised that the algorithm did not support a higher level and one assessor suggested seeking a new diagnosis … to potentially change the outcome instead of applying for reconsideration,” Ageing Australia wrote.The organisation included feedback from assessors that the IAT could not understand the nuance of functional changes in people living with dementia.The warnings from the advocacy groupscame alongside concerns and alarm raised by state and territory health department staffincluding the head of the Western Australian health department, Dr Shirley Bowen. Department staff logged hundreds of cases, provided to their federal counterparts, of the algorithm systemically under-assessing older Australians, whileBowen warned of “catastrophic” outcomes.The Commonwealth Ombudsmanis investigating.Do you know more? melissa.davey@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsHealthAged careLabor partyAustralian politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Labor ditches new packaging laws to cut plastic waste, sparking unprecedented ‘scale and breadth of outrage’ | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Federal environment department tells industry representatives the government does not want to ‘exacerbate cost of living pressures’
Author: Lisa Cox
Headline: Federal environment department tells industry representatives the government does not want to ‘exacerbate cost of living pressures’
Content: Environment minister Murray Watt (left) and prime minster Anthony Albanese. Labor says it will balance ‘environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy’ in the next term of government.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenEnvironment minister Murray Watt (left) and prime minster Anthony Albanese. Labor says it will balance ‘environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy’ in the next term of government.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian politicsLabor ditches new packaging laws to cut plastic waste, sparking unprecedented ‘scale and breadth of outrage’Federal environment department tells industry representatives the government does not want to ‘exacerbate cost of living pressures’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastLisa CoxEnvironment and climate correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Albanese government has been accused of breaking a promise after it shelveda longstanding commitmentto bring in packaging standards intended to force manufacturers and retailers to cut plastic waste.The federal environment department told industry representatives via email last week that the promise would not be kept before the next election because the government did not want to “exacerbate cost of living pressures”.The director of the Boomerang Alliance, Jeff Angel, warned “ongoing inaction and token measures won’t be tolerated”.“The Albanese government’s failure to act on packaging reform as promised is a repudiation of the public’s support of recycling and concerns about the health and environmental impacts of plastic pollution,” he said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“The scale and breadth of outrage across a broad set of stakeholders from green groups to industry to state governments is something I have not seen before.”The packaging laws had been under developmentsince a 2023 agreementbetween the federal and state governments that the then environment minister, Tanya Plibersek, described as “historic”. They would have required producers to cut waste and boost plastics recycling.Clean Up Australia’sannual litter reportshighlight the persistent problem of packaging in the environment, with packaging accounting for 59.5% of all litter reported.A suite of potential rules would have set design standards for packaging, for example by prohibiting use of certain chemicals, restricting unnecessary or excessive layers of packaging, or limiting the amount of empty space permitted within packaging.Other potential changes could have required producers to be responsible for the packaging across its full life cycle – from the design stage to how the packaging is used and then disposed of.The government’s decision to shelve its plans were due to its concern that any costs arising from changes could be passed on to consumers when they bought products such as groceries.Death trap: what to do about the everyday items catching and killing Australian wildlifeRead moreThe department email said the environment minister, Murray Watt, wanted to pursue reforms “in a way that balances environmental outcomes with the broader needs of the economy, with the government looking closely at its policies to ensure it does not exacerbate cost of living pressures”.The email said “a new Commonwealth scheme for packaging will not be introduced in this term of government” and the government would instead work with the states and territories “on opportunities to improve Australia’s packaging regulations and policies in the nearer term”.The plastics campaign manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, Cip Hamilton, said the decision was “deeply disappointing”.“Recyclers want action, businesses want certainty, and environmental organisations want an end to plastic pollution,” she said.“Almost everyone was at the table, and the government has walked away.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHamilton said the laws would have “put the cost and the responsibility back where they belong – on the businesses using the packaging, not the households stuck with it”.“Plastic pollution is having very real consequences. Little penguins are choking, seabirds are starving, and corals are suffocating,” she said.Australian Packaging Covenant Organisation chief executive, Chris Foley, said producers wanted certainty. He said a national packaging regime with clear rules would “unlock investment in recycling, and replace fragmented approaches with a more consistent system”.The chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, Suzanne Toumbourou, said the sector was calling for a “nationally consistent scheme with real targets”.“We are already seeing recycling facilities close, with others under growing pressure, and the investment that built them go to waste, because there is no policy certainty to keep them viable,” she said.Watt said the government understood that waste and recycling firms faced a range of challenges.“The Albanese government is working closely with industry, and state and territory governments to strengthen the systems that support recycling, and improve the circularity, of Australia’s packaging,” he said.“We’re committed to delivering stronger environmental outcomes while keeping costs to consumers and wider industry in check.”He said the government’s immediate focus was to work with the states and territories to “reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia”.Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsPollutionConsumer affairsAnthony AlbaneseWastenewsShareReuse this content

title: One flight cancelled every three days due to staff shortages – as it happened | Australia news | The Guardian
description: This blog is now closed
Author: Achol Arok
Headline: This blog is now closed
Content: 00.10 EDTOne flight cancelled every three days across Australia due to staff shortagesLuca IttimaniWorker shortages have cancelled one flight every three days on average in the last year,Airservices Australiahas told a Senate hearing.The government agency’s deputy CEO,Peter Curran, said Australia’s airports recorded 2,536 cancellations over the year to 31 August, of which 121 were attributed to Airservices. Sydney accounted for 103 of those.Just this morning,the troubled airportrecorded 14 inbound cancellations and more outbound cancellations, after some overnight staff were unavailable, Curran said. Airservices and airlines manage the shortage by delaying or cancelling flights.Curran said Sydney had grown and now needed a team of 41 air traffic controllers, spread across the roster. It has 49 employed but eight are unavailable at the moment. Curran said:double quotation markWhen we have a bit of short-term sickness or unavailability, like we had last night, it makes it very difficult to recover.Curran said retired staff had been asked to come back to work but some of them were “simply not interested”. He said there were about 1,100 air traffic controllers working across Australia and 91 would join in the coming year.With more recruitment, Curran said Airservices would be able to enough on-call staff to cover two absences a day by March 2027.double quotation markIt’s not an ironclad model, but it certainly reduces the likelihood of the sorts of issues that we’re having today.Planes on the tarmac at Sydney international airport.Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAPShareUpdated at01.27 EDT

title: Australian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’ | Business | The Guardian
description: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promise
Content: Australian fuel prices are on track to climb 30 cents in coming weeks as the Middle East conflict pushes the global oil price to its highest since mid-May.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralian fuel prices are on track to climb 30 cents in coming weeks as the Middle East conflict pushes the global oil price to its highest since mid-May.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesBusinessAustralian fuel prices set to rise by 30c as global markets react to ‘deadly cocktail’Global oil price at its highest since May while investors dump stocks and bonds after Donald Trump’s $5,000 ‘dividend’ promiseFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPatrick ComminsEconomics editorFri 11 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 02.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFuel prices are on track to climb a further 20-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, after the escalating Middle East conflict pushed the global oil price to its highest since mid-May.As investors dumped stocks and bonds in an increasingly febrile environment, Donald Trump’s promise to give everyUS adult citizen a US$5,000 “dividend”after the November midterms if Republicans win added to alarm around the parlous state of the country’s finances.Investors pushed US bond yields towards 5% for the first time since 2007 as the prospect of higher energy costs firmed up expectations that the US Federal Reserve would need to hike rates again.That dragged Australia’s 10-year rate up to 5.38% and to fresh 15-year highs.The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, pushed towards US$110 a barrel, before settling at above US$108 in late Friday trade.Global oil benchmark has jumpedSteve Miller, an investment strategist at fund manager GSFM, said bonds were reacting to a “deadly cocktail” of high oil prices, American fiscal irresponsibility, and worries around the independence of the Fed.“The $5,000 promise is a great example of Trump’s unwillingness to tackle the deficit, and even to make it worse for short-term political expediency. No wonder bond markets are sketchy,” Miller said.Tai Hui, chief market strategist for Asia-Pacific at JP Morgan Asset Management, said rising long-term borrowing rates would normally undermine stock valuations, as investors rethink the relative trade-off between the riskier sharemarket and climbing yields on safe bonds.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailEvidence of this was clear on the ASX this week, where the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 index was on track to end the week down 3% and below the level it was this time last year.But Hui said ongoing optimism about the state of the global economy and, especially, the titanic boom in artificial intelligence investment was providing a tailwind for sharemarkets around the world, and especially on Wall Street.Since the start of theUS-Israel war on Iranat the end of February, the US benchmark S&P 500 sharemarket index is up about 10%, against a 5% fall for the ASX 200.But the Hong Kong-based Hui said the increasingly debated question among investors was at what point the steady march higher in yields begins to drive a broader and deeper switch out of stocks and into bonds.“We are approaching a crossroad,” he said.Bond rates are at 15-year highsAs economists warned of a new post-Covid era of structurally higher interest rates, financial markets upped their bets that the Reserve Bank of Australia would deliver a fourth rate hike on 29 September, pricing in an 80% chance.Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said the RBA would have to respond to recent evidence that inflationary pressures were not easing as hoped, even as the economy proved resilient.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I think they [the RBA] will go in September,” Kearns said.The former top RBA official said the central bank’s inflation-fighting credentials were increasingly at stake.“They need to get inflation to 2.5%, and that’s not forecast to happen until early 2028; that then becomes almost a seven-year inflationary episode.”The prospect of higher mortgage costs comes as Vivek Dhar, CBA’s head of commodities research, warned that diesel prices could climb by 10-30 cents per litre over the coming weeks, from over $2.50 per litre today.Woolworths increased prices of at least four ‘family staples’ during ‘Price Freeze’ promotionRead moreUnleaded petrol prices could push from about $2.10 a litre in major east coast cities to about $2.30 over the next couple of weeks, according to a rough rule of thumb that says every US$1 increase in the crude oil benchmark translates to a 10c increase at the pump.Dhar, who is based in Singapore, said meetings with energy producers and traders on the sidelines of a major energy conference over recent days revealed a deep sense of uncertainty about how the next six to 12 months will play out.Dhar said he expected Brent crude to swing between US$70 and US$100 a barrel for the foreseeable future, until eventually the world becomes comfortable with the supply workarounds to a restricted strait of Hormuz.But the more pressing worries were around the supply of refined products, particularly diesel.“Everyone pays attention to oil, but it’s the refined product that hits the economy and feeds through to inflation. And that is what everyone is worried about, because there isn’t any workaround; we just need disruptions to stop.”Explore more on these topicsBusinessPetrol pricesUS-Israel war on IrannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policy | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Sweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU country
Content: Questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration.Photograph: Wdnet Studio/AlamyView image in fullscreenQuestions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement over migration.Photograph: Wdnet Studio/AlamySweden‘Absurd, hardline calls’: questions over Sweden’s post-Brexit migration policySweden has ordered more Britons, including vulnerable people, to leave post-Brexit than any other EU countryLisa O’Carrollin StockholmFri 11 Sep 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe arrived with nothing other than the clothes he wore that morning. Hours later he was banged up in a detention centre close to a Stockholm airport to await deportation.Charles, a former business director from Cambridge, who did not want his full name published, moved to Sweden in 2017 to be with his Swedish wife, Lily, and applied to remain afterBrexit, before the deadline of December 2021.But the migration agency rejected his application, and he and his wife have been fighting with the Swedish authorities ever since.In a message passed on by Lily, he said he was the only Briton in the detention centre, where he described being hemmed in by three lines of fences separated by a “no man’s land”.“I arrived here with nothing apart from the clothes I had on,” Charles said. “We were told the meeting … with the border police was to discuss my case. They then said they thought I would abscond, which is why they were going to detain me.”Lily, a lawyer, questioned whether Sweden,considered a global leader in human rights and progressive politics, was now like Afghanistan. “They have hunted us for five years,” she said.Charles could be deported in the next week unless his latest legal challenge delivers a reprieve.He joins a list of 2,490 Britons – of an estimated 14,000 inSweden– deported from the country between 2020 and 2025, as questions are mounting as to why Sweden appears to have taken such a hardline approach to the Brexit withdrawal agreement (WA) over migration.In total, Sweden is responsible for 33% of all British nationals deported from the EU between 2021 and 2025, compared with France, which accounted for 6% of all British deportees, Spain at 3% and Germany at 2%. France deported 450, Spain 250 and Germany 160, while Italy deported just 15 Britons in that period.Different countries collate data in different ways, but Eurostat data suggests the Netherlands is another outlier, with 2,270 Britons deported in the same period.Data shows 2,100 removal orders were also issued in Sweden, though it is not clear how many of these resulted in voluntary departures or progressed to deportations.View image in fullscreenJoyce Thomas, 78, walks her dog just hours before she is due to be ‘removed’ from Sweden after 22 years.Photograph: Lisa O’CarrollPeople served with removal orders includeJoyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who has been in Sweden for 22 years, andGeorge Mason, a 74-year-old with dementia who has been in Sweden for 25 years, both of whose applications missed the deadline to apply to remain in Sweden post-Brexit.John Sellers, a 34-year-old Briton who has lived in Sweden since he was 10, was deported in January.The cases also raise the question of whether the WA delivers the political promise made by the Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier and others promising citizens should not be collateral damage of Brexit.“The level of protection afforded under EU law must not be watered down. Brexit should not alter the nature of people’s daily lives,” Barnier said in 2017.Nine years on, some have asked if Sweden’s approach has been infected byits apparent lurch to the rightmore broadly, servingdeportations on childrenand evena 95-year-old Iraqi womanwho had lived in Sweden for 20 years.“The number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up,” the Swedish author and journalist Martin Gelinwrote this weekahead of the general election on Sunday.British citizens who lived in the country before Brexit have unique protection under the WA, but activists have noted that they appear to be subject to the same treatment as other foreign nationals.View image in fullscreenGeorge Mason, 74, seen here with his daughter Michelle, has been served with a removal notice.Photograph: The Mason family“The question is, has national migration policy affected the way in which they apply the withdrawal agreement in edge cases? And has it affected the culture in Migrationsverket [the migration agency] and perhaps in the courts as they apply the withdrawal agreement?” asked James Savage, the editor of the Local, whichrecently revealed the pressure applied to Swedenby the European Commission.Family members acting on behalf of Mason turned to the general migration route for residency after the migration agency rejected the withdrawal agreement request for him to remain in the country. The judge’s ruling was clear: “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace[George]Mason’s interest in continuing to reside [in Sweden].”Since the surge in publicity surrounding deportations of British citizens in Sweden, all three opposition parties have pledged new laws to reopen the application process for Britons, and the incumbent government has said it would look at doing the same.Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party,has promised new lawsif his party retains power. “Some of these cases are just stupid,” he told the Guardian. “They [the migration agency] should not be lenient, but the present decision-making leans towards deportation.”The Swedish migration agency insists it has only deported 458 British people in strict Brexit-related cases but activists – who have been trying to get granular detail on the remaining cases – say that data may not include Britons who upon rejection from the agency then applied to stay under different routes and ended up with deportation orders.The agency also says there is “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other [EU] member states” and that it has “applied applicable law” with appeal processes.Savage notes that promises to change the law were made three years ago after other cases emerged.David Milstead,who runs the activist group Brits in Sweden, has welcomed promises of action but is concerned that politicians might provide a fix for future British applicants without giving a second chance to those already deported or who have left voluntarily.A spokesperson for theEuropean Commissionsaid: “Correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement is very important to us,” but added: “Reasonable grounds that may justify a late application for beneficiary status are not defined in the withdrawal agreement.”This means “host states have a certain margin of discretion in deciding what they accept as reasonable grounds”.View image in fullscreen‘Some of these cases are just stupid,’ said Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party.Photograph: Centerpartie, SwedenIn other words, Sweden has not breached the withdrawal agreement but rather is exercising allowable discretion.Catherine Barnard, a professor of EU law at Cambridge University, says the withdrawal agreement is “unique”, as no other member state has ever left the EU, and will take time to test. But decisions by migration authorities have to be proven to be “proportionate”.While Swedish courts have not referred their decision-making upwards to the European court of justice, Barnard says a case in the UK may provide precedent for EU citizens affected by the WA.Inthe case of “CG”,the European court of justice ruled that the UK breached the EU charter of fundamental rights in denying benefits to an EU citizen in Northern Ireland.“In a 2021 case … the court ruled that the charter would apply to those who had moved to another member state before Brexit and lived there,” Barnard said.“While the facts of the case were somewhat different, the principle should remain: the state’s interest in protecting its immigration must be balanced against the rights to family life of vulnerable individuals.”The Swedish migration authorities and police have been approached for comment on the detention of Charles.Explore more on these topicsSwedenBrexitEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionMigrationImmigration and asylumEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Ireland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet Trump | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Many are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds back
Content: Ireland’s government is said to be anxious about Donald Trump’s meeting with Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence.Composite: ReutersView image in fullscreenIreland’s government is said to be anxious about Donald Trump’s meeting with Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence.Composite: ReutersIrelandIreland holds its breath as its leftwing president prepares to meet TrumpMany are rooting for vocal critic Catherine Connolly to let rip in Dublin meeting, but others hope she holds backRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCatherine Connolly, Ireland’s president, once said she abhorred Donald Trump’s policies. In his sole previous comment on Connolly, the US president seemed to think she was a man. Now that they are about to meet, Ireland is holding its breath.Trump is to fly into Dublin on Saturday morning for a two-day visit centred on golf. But before making it to his beloved greens, protocol obliges him to meet a woman who has given every impression of loathing him.A courtesy call to Áras an Uachtaráin, the Irish president’s official residence and workplace in the city’s Phoenix Park, has left the government anxious and the media reaching for popcorn. “What could possibly go wrong?” headlines ask.Many inIrelandare rooting for Connolly to let rip at Trump for his policies and rhetoric on immigrants and the Middle East. Others hope she will stifle any criticisms to avoid provoking a visitor who could upend Ireland’s economy.The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he had no concerns “at all” about the encounter, but one senior official said the government was on tenterhooks. “We need to get him [Trump] in the Áras, then out of the Áras. We’ll breathe easier after,” they said.View image in fullscreenAs MP, Connolly protested Trump’s 2019 visit to Ireland and more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues.Photograph: Niall Carson/PABeforewinning the Irish presidency– a ceremonial post – last year, Connolly was an independent leftwing member of parliament for Galway who protested against Trump’s2019 visitand more recently assailed him over his positions and policies on Gaza, Iran and other issues. “If we are going to act as an independent sovereign state, a neutral republic, we must use our voice to speak to power and the abuse of power by president Trump,” she said.Asked in March about the criticism, Trump replied: “He’s lucky I exist.”Trump is now to meet Connolly – and Martin in a separate meeting – before heading to his golf resort in Doonbeg, County Clare, which is hosting the Irish Open.Heavy security around the Phoenix Park and Doonbeg will insulate the US president from protests, including a “No welcome for Trump” demonstration that is expected to draw thousands to central Dublin on Saturday afternoon.View image in fullscreenGarda officers patrol the beach at the Irish Open in Doonbeg before Donald Trump’s expected arrival at the weekend.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PASome hope Connolly will speak for them when she meets Trump behind closed doors. “She should speak truth to power,”Rosie O’Donnell, the US comedian who moved to Ireland after Trump won a second term, told the Irish Independent. “I don’t think she should drop what she believes in to be polite to a madman. He is like a mad king that has destroyed the country.”Leftwing parties that supported Connolly’s presidential run urged the former barrister to “find a way” to convey criticism without causing a diplomatic storm. Trump has expressed affection for the emerald isle but also wants American tech and pharmaceutical firms to move jobs and taxes from Ireland to the US, a scenario that could devastate Irish state finances.During her election campaign, Connolly promised to heed constraints of the office, which is largely symbolic and has no responsibility for foreign policy. She also said that if asked, she would meet Trump.“That implies that it’s not to meet him in order to berate him,” saidBobby McDonagh, an former Irish ambassador to the UK and EU. “She’ll have an opportunity to have a chat with President Trump and make some gentle points reflective of Irish values. I expect it to go smoothly.”Connolly could emulate Martin, who discreetly rebutted some of Trump’s opinions during a visit to the White House, said McDonagh. “He had the emotional intelligence and experience to do it in a way that didn’t provoke any reaction.”The six-time major champion golferRory McIlroysaid he and other competitors at Doonbeg would focus on the game, not politics. “It’s going to be different with him being here but we’re here to play a golf tournament and it’s a good golf course so we’ll keep our heads down and play,” McIlroy said.Explore more on these topicsIrelandDonald TrumpEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-Nazis | Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) | The Guardian
description: Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt
Author: Kate Connolly
Headline: Far-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-Anhalt
Content: The AfD’s parliamentary group leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, referred to the MPs under criminal investigation as ‘the bad guys’.Photograph: Karina Hessland/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe AfD’s parliamentary group leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, referred to the MPs under criminal investigation as ‘the bad guys’.Photograph: Karina Hessland/ReutersAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)AfD’s new state MPs include ex-Stasi officer, former porn actor, neopagans and neo-NazisFar-right German party’s newly elected representatives face fresh scrutiny as it tries to form government in Saxony-AnhaltWhy is the AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next?Kate Connollyin BerlinFri 11 Sep 2026 11.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 20.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Alternative für Deutschland is facing scrutiny over the suitability of some of its prospective new MPs – including a former Stasi officer and a former pornography actor – just days after its historicwin in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.Presented by the AfD’s lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, for a photocall in the state capital of Magdeburg on Thursday, some of the members-elect were revealed to have a range of questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks.View image in fullscreenThe AfD’s newly elected members of the Saxony-Anhalt parliament.Photograph: Karina Hessland/ReutersGerman media has revealed that among the 39 parliamentarians who will represent constituencies across Saxony-Anhalt in the state parliament, is a man alleged to have participated in pornography films and falsified academic qualifications; a former officer for the East German secret police, the Stasi; and several members under criminal investigation for their involvement in neo-Nazi organisations.Two MPs are facing investigations into allegations they sought to continue the activities of the banned rightwing extremist organisation Artgemeinschaft, a neopagan group that has embraced nationalist and antisemitic ideas. The younger of the two is also alleged to have violated the law in relation to weapons, according to the public prosecutor’s office. Both reject the allegations.The erstwhile pornography actor was convicted for stealing bedding in bulk from a hotel. A court confirmed he had been a pornography actor after he contested a local newspaper’s claims. He was expelled from a university after being found to have falsified his school leaving certificate, Die Zeit reported. The MP says he was readmitted after a legal challenge.An ex-Stasi officer, aged 78, who won a direct mandate in his constituency, has admitted to having worked for the ministry for state security in the communist GDR, focused on East German citizens who wanted to permanently emigrate.His role as an MP-elect has been criticised by campaign groups on behalf of victims of the former East German dictatorship.Also, an investigation by the broadcaster ZDF revealed that some AfD ministers-elect who were also members of the previous parliamentary group, had ties to rightwing extremist groups. This included some having been members of the subsequently outlawed Homeland-Loyal German Youth group, HDJ. At one stage one of them had led the organisation, while an adviser to the AfD’s parliamentary group wrote a biography described as an “homage to national socialism”.Among the prospective MPs are a number with pro-Kremlin links, as well as some who visited members of the Maga movement in Washington.Russian president Vladimir Putin initially said he would not comment on the AfD victory, but speaking to reporters during a visit to India for the BRICS summit later blamed “western globalists”.“I think that everything happening inEuroperight now is basically ‌the result of system errors by the so-called West … the western globalists in politics, security, and economics,” Putin said.The AfD has promised to curb migration and restore ties with Moscow.Asked to respond to the questionable biographies, in particular of the two MPs under criminal investigation, Siegmund, a former fragrance salesman who was unanimously re-elected as the AfD’s parliamentary group leader on Thursday, referred to the men in jest as “the bad guys” and said “we will await the results of the investigations and then discuss them”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund at the AfD election party after polls closed last Sunday.Photograph: Fabrizio Bensch/ReutersSiegmund himself triggered fierce criticism during the presentation of his new parliamentary group after linking the production of arms inGermanyto the party’s planned deportation offensive.In response to a journalist’s question about the planned opening of an Israeli arms company in the state, Siegmund said: “We do not categorically condemn the production of arms, because we will of course need equivalent resources for the future remigration and deportation offensive. This is also in the interest of internal security, our own instability and national defence.”The statement was seized on by the party’s opponents. Katja Pähle, the chair of the Social Democrats (SPD) parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, said Siegmund had issued a “political threat” by suggesting the use of “violence as a political tool”.“This reveals the ugly face of a political system whose language and ideas are once again reminiscent of totalitarian models,” she said.Whether the AfD, which secured 44% of the seats, forms a state government, which would make it the first far-right party to gain power in Germany since the second world war, will depend on whether it can find other like-minded MPs who might defect, or a single party willing to support the AfD. So far, the mainstream parties have refused to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has just under half of the 83 seats in the state, three short of an absolute majority.Protests against the AfD are planned in more than 20 cities across Germany this weekend in response to the party’s win last Sunday, and ahead of two crucial state elections on 20 September, in Berlin and in Mecklenburg Vorpommen, where the AfD are predicted to do well.Explore more on these topicsAlternative für Deutschland (AfD)GermanyEuropeThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweden’s PM channels Trump saying he wants to ‘make Sweden great again’ ahead of election – as it happened | Europe | The Guardian
description: Ulf Kristersson’s comments come ahead of the parliamentary election taking place this Sunday
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Ulf Kristersson’s comments come ahead of the parliamentary election taking place this Sunday
Content: 08.23 EDTSweden's PM channels Trump as he wants to 'make Sweden great again'Channeling his Donald Trump spirit,Sweden’s prime minister Ulf Kristersson told AFP that he hoped to secure a second term in this Sunday’s parliamentary election to “makeSwedengreat again.”Prime minister Ulf Kristersson talks to members of the media after a Moderate Party rally ahead of the general election in Stockholm, Sweden.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersKristersson has led a three-party centre-right coalition since 2022, which relies on outside support from the far-right Sweden Democrats. If the right bloc wins, the party is expected to join the government for the first time in history.Butpolls suggest that a centre-left opposition bloc of former PM Magdalena Andersson is slightly ahead, with a combined 50.8% of vote share, compared to 47.6% for the centre-right and far-right parties.The vote on Sunday is expected to beveryclose,and it may take weeks before we know who will form the next government as political talks are likely to be fraught and take time.Share

title: Russia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered drones | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Three facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensity
