Content: The aftermath of a Russian drone strike on one of two petrol stations targeted on Friday.Photograph: Alina Smutko/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a Russian drone strike on one of two petrol stations targeted on Friday.Photograph: Alina Smutko/ReutersUkraineRussia targets Kyiv petrol stations for first time with jet-powered dronesThree facilities in two days struck as bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters new phase of intensityEurope live – latest updatesAmy Hawkinsin KyivFri 11 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePetrol stations in Kyiv have been hit by jet-powered drones in a wave of targeted Russian attacks as the bombardment of Ukraine’s capital enters a new phase of intensity.At least two people were killed and 12 injured in strikes on two petrol stations on Friday morning, according to the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.The rush-hour strikes follow a similar attack on a petrol station on Thursday, the first of its kind in the capital.At the Ukrnafta petrol station in the Pochaina neighbourhood in northernKyiv, bystanders said three people had been injured in Friday’s blast – the manager of a nearby car wash, his wife and the driver of a passing car. The blown-out vehicle was stranded by the side of the road, its windows shattered and seats spattered in blood.Witnesses said they had heard two explosions, and local authorities later saidRussiahad carried out a double-tap attack on the facility.View image in fullscreenPochaina petrol station. All three strikes targeted sites operated by UkrnaftaPhotograph: Amy Hawkins“This is probably one of the most difficult periods of the war because life is just like on a rollercoaster,” said Anastasiia Demchenko, 30, who works at a delivery company opposite the petrol station. “It feels like life is on the edge.”All three strikes targeted petrol stations operated by Ukrnafta, a state-owned oil and natural gas extraction company.Sergiy Fedorenko, the acting head of Naftogaz, Ukrnafta’s parent company, said: “There is, and can be, no military objective behind such attacks. This is terror directed at the civilian population, at peaceful people.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered dronesRead moreA list of 18 petrol stations in Kyiv expected to be hit by Russian drones started circulating on Telegram on Wednesday. The three struck so far were on the list.At the other station hit on Friday, in Desnianskyi district, one of the most densely populated parts of the capital, the manager of a nearby car wash said it had been a miracle that no one had died in the blast.Fedir Lesovin said the air-raid siren had given the petrol station workers time to run to a nearby shelter, and that a customer waiting outside his business saw the incoming drone and also ran to safety.View image in fullscreenDesnianskyi district petrol station was also hit, in one of the most densely populated areas of Kyiv.Photograph: Amy HawkinsRussia has increased its attacks on Ukrainian petrol stations in recent months. Facilities in the east and south of the country have been repeatedly targeted, but this week’s attacks mark the first time that strikes against a vital part of daily life have been brought to the capital.Ukraine has also targeted Russian oil infrastructure. Its special forces said this week that they had struck facilities at the Caspian Sea port of Makhachkala.Kyiv has been pounded bydaily drone and missile strikessince late August, at a time when Ukraine isrunning low on Patriot interceptors. A brief reprieve for the visit of theUS envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoffover the weekend ended on Monday.The petrol station attacks happened as Volodymyr Zelenskyy was on an overseas trip intended to drum up international support and aid before what is expected to be a difficult winter. On Thursday the Ukrainian presidentmet Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, who offered support to help boost Ukraine’s drone stocks.Additional reporting by Illia DyadikExplore more on these topicsUkraineKyivRussiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump and Hegseth use 9/11 memorial remarks at Pentagon to defend war on Iran | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: President and defense secretary try to link worst terrorist attack in US history to current unpopular war
Author: Shrai Popat
Headline: President and defense secretary try to link worst terrorist attack in US history to current unpopular war
Content: Donald Trump and Pete Hegseth during a 9/11 observance ceremony on the 25th anniversary of the attack on the Pentagon in Washington DC.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and Pete Hegseth during a 9/11 observance ceremony on the 25th anniversary of the attack on the Pentagon in Washington DC.Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/ReutersSeptember 11 2001Trump and Hegseth use 9/11 memorial remarks at Pentagon to defend war on IranPresident and defense secretary try to link worst terrorist attack in US history to current unpopular warUS politics live – latest updatesShrai PopatandJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald TrumpandPete Hegsethused remarks at the memorial ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of 9/11 to defend theUS-Israel war on Iran– and suggest the controversial conflict was part of the legacy of the worst terrorist attack in US history.While such ceremonies on September 11 typically focus on the victims of the 2001 attacks, the US president and his defense secretary each pointed to the war they launched onIranmore than six months ago, with no end in sight.“We salute every member of the United States military who served in the ‘war on terror’,” Trump said at the Pentagon, which was struck by a hijacked airliner, killing all 64 people onboard and 125 inside the building. “And we salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamic Republic of Iran, will never ever have a nuclear weapon.”‘I think of him every year’: remembering those lost in 9/11, 25 years laterRead moreThe US president’s decision to stay in Washington has drawn criticism, while his vice‑president, JD Vance, traveled to New York for a memorial at Ground Zero, the site of the World Trade Center’s destruction on 9/11.Closing out his speech, Trump also tried to draw a direct link between his war on Iran – which is vastly unpopular in the US, according to opinion polls – and the 9/11 terror attacks.“Today we renew the sacred oath that we first swore in their names a quarter of a century ago. We will never, ever forget,” he said. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory. We fight hard. We fight to win.”Earlier, Hegseth, the US defense secretary, delivered a bellicose speech at the somber memorial. Noting that the Iran war was part of the fight against an “Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century”, he claimed that Iran’s defenses “are gone”, despite evidence to the contrary.13:36How 9/11 changed the world - The Latest“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong – to hell,” declared Hegseth. “And tankers to the bottom of the ocean where they belong, and we are ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. The economic pressure tightens every day.”Hegseth said at the ceremony: “The struggle against evil continued, and it continues now. It will continue until judgment day. Our only answer here on Earth is eternal vigilance.”He also claimed the threat extended into US borders, warning that “enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home”.Hegseth went on to credit Trump with dismantling Iran’s military capabilities, and closed by calling for a new generation of “strong, brave warriors who will say when it matters most, ‘send me’”.Separately, during the New York City ceremony, the leader of one group of 9/11 victims’ families pleaded with theTrump administrationto hold Saudi Arabia accountable for its alleged support of the terrorists who carried out the attacks.“It has been one betrayal after another. President Trump can still change that,” said Terry Strada, a widow of one of the victims. “Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this – all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through.”Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001Donald TrumpPete HegsethIranUS-Israel war on IranTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Iran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping route | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Rampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exports
Content: Houthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters on a march to mobilise more fighters against Saudi-backed government troops, in Sana'a on Thursday.Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPAYemenIran’s Houthi allies capture strategic island on vital oil shipping routeRampant Yemeni fighters take control of island in narrow point of Bab al-Mandab strait, which Saudi is relying on for oil exportsWhy the rapid Houthi advance matters and what’s at stakePatrick WintourDiplomatic editorFri 11 Sep 2026 11.55 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s rampant Houthi forces have captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait, expanding their control of the narrow waterway, one of the ​world’s vital shipping routes.The Iran-aligned Houthis took control of the volcanic island after forces allied to the UN-backed, Aden-based government left in the latest of a dramatic series of reverses along Yemen’s west coast in recent days, includingthe loss of the port city of Mochaon Thursday.Saudi Arabia, which supports and bankrolls the official Yemen government, mounted air raids on Houthi positions in Mocha on Friday.The Bab al-Mandab strait links Asia to Europe via the Red Sea and Suez canal. Perim island, also known as Mayun, divides the waterway in two, close to its narrowest point. The United Arab Emirates, a former Saudi ally in the anti-Houthi coalition, had been building an airbase on the island before ending its active involvement in the conflict in January.Houthi advance mapSaudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab to export its crude sinceIranhas been targeting vessels in the strait of Hormuz. About 12% of the world’s goods are typically shipped through the strait.Full Houthi control of shipping in the strait, alongside Iranian control of the strait of Hormuz, would strengthen the chokeholds of anti-western forces over global energy shipments.Oilprices have risen to more than $100 a barrel as the fighting in Yemen has escalated.Iran hailed the Houthi advances in an official statement on Friday, its first extended comment on the renewed fighting inside Yemen. Iran and theHouthishave been allied since the Houthis rose to power inside Yemen in 2014.View image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis march during a rally to recruit more fighters, in Sana’a on Thursday.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIn a statement the Houthis hailed the expulsion of “Saudi enemy” troops from six districts in the Taiz and Hodeidah regions, the capture of 4,500 sq miles, the targeting of “seven military divisions of the Saudi enemy’s forces” and the “killing, capture, and wounding” of hundreds of soldiers. It also claimed to have released hundreds of prisoners “held by the Saudi enemy’s mercenaries for years”.British diplomatic sources said they did not at present expect Donald Trump to sanction any US bombing of Houthi positions in Yemen, despite requests to do so from Saudi Arabia. The pace of the Houthi advance, and political divisions in the Yemen governorates not controlled by the Houthis, have left western capitals fearful that even the Yemen government capital, Aden, could fall to the Houthis. The UK effectively treated Yemen as a British protectorate until 1967.The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.View image in fullscreenPerim island seen in a 2021 satellite photograph.Photograph: Planet Labs Inc./APThe Houthi progress down the Red Sea coast from the port of Hodeidah also strengthens Iran’s hand in trying to reach an agreement with other Gulf states on future control of the strait of Hormuz, the central dispute between the US and Iran. Iran has reached an agreement on temporary approved routes with Oman, the country sharing the southern coast of the Hormuz strait. The proposed deal is supposed to be discussed at a meeting of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) foreign ministers in the Omani coastal city of Salalah on Monday.The deal, including a temporary approved route for shipping largely under Iranian control, would – if agreed by the GCC – put pressure on the US to lift its highly effective blockade of Iranian oil ports, which is severely damaging the Iranian economy.Map of Houthi-controlled areas of YemenThe US struck a surprise ceasefire deal with the Houthis in May 2025after the cost of a bombing campaign escalated, and Houthis gave private assurances that they would not attack US shipping in the Red Sea. The Houthi leadership this week continued to give similar assurances to all shipping except Saudi Arabian oil tankers.On 14 August Saudi Arabia assembled a 14-country international maritime naval coalition to protect freedom of navigation in the Bab al-Mandab strait and the Gulf of Aden. The coalition, including Bahrain, Pakistan, Somalia, Djibouti, Turkey and Egypt, has so far been invisible, though Riyadh would argue that such a coalition of the willing takes time to assemble.Recriminations are under way over the fall of Mocha, with the role of Maj Gen Tareq Saleh, the leader of the National Resistance Forces that retreated from the city, under scrutiny. He said the retreat was necessary to regroup his forces.View image in fullscreenA view of the Bab al-Mandab strait from the Yemeni coast.Photograph: Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty ImagesOn her Facebook page, the Yemeni 2011 Nobel peace prize winner, Tawakkol Karman, called on Yemen’s president, Rashad al-Alimi, to dismiss Saleh and to refer him for investigation and trial on charges of conspiracy and high treason.Amr al-Bidh, the foreign affairs representative of the separatist political organisation the Southern Transitional Council (STC), said he had warned western diplomats repeatedly of the need for a comprehensive national regional and international strategy to defeat the Houthis, adding occasional airstrikes were not enough.He accused the Saudis of strategic incompetence and of alienating the southern forces most needed to combat the Houthis.“The position is now very serious,” he said. “The Houthis’ presence in the strait means they will be able to control the waterways without needing to use sophisticated weapons that as a result they can now use elsewhere. The advance is also likely to give them a new income through control of ports along the west coast of the Red Sea.” The Houthis are already offering concessionary rates to draw traffic from ports controlled by the Yemeni government in the Gulf of Aden.The STC was the dominant political and military force in southern Yemen until this January, when Saudi Arabia bombed its troops, closed its political organisation down and detained as many as 20 of its leaders in Riyadh.A Saudi promise of a dialogue about the southern question made in January has never been kept, al-Bidh said, adding that Human Rights Watch warned in a March report that some pro-STC protests in Aden were being repressed with undue violence.“The betrayal of promises had left the southern population unwilling to leave their home territories to fight the Houthis in the north,” he said. “The Saudis for 10 years have been dependent on the people of the south to deter the Houthis, and the STC with as many as 80,000 troops at its disposal, has been the backbone of that force.”Saudi Arabia is facing a familiar dilemma: whether to reach a negotiated settlement with the Houthis on the future of Yemen or to try to push the highly stretched Houthi forces back.Although the Houthis operate independently of Tehran’s instructions, it is hugely to Iran’s advantage for them to be fighting Saudi Arabia, as the Saudis are more likely in turn to put pressure on Washington to relent over Iran.There is also concern in western capitals about the use of western weaponry by the Saudis in Yemen, and whether their activity complies with international humanitarian law, including whether the Saudi strikes can truly be seen as acts of self-defence.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisUS-Israel war on IranIranOilSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: CIA releases dozens of presidential daily briefs on Bin Laden and al-Qaida from before 9/11 | September 11 2001 | The Guardian
description: The presidential briefing documents were declassified on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The presidential briefing documents were declassified on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks
Content: The CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs.Photograph: Larry Downing/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe CIA director, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs.Photograph: Larry Downing/ReutersSeptember 11 2001CIA releases dozens of presidential daily briefs on Bin Laden and al-Qaida from before 9/11The presidential briefing documents were declassified on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacksAssociated PressFri 11 Sep 2026 18.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSeveral dozen presidential briefing documents declassified on Friday, the 25th anniversary of theSeptember 11 attacks, detail intelligence that government officials had gathered aboutOsama bin Ladenandal-Qaidaleading up to the hijackings that killed nearly 3,000 people and upended Americannational security.The documents illustrate security analysts’ tracking of Bin Laden’s movements and support system, as well as concerns about possible threats to US targets. They also detail officials’ understanding of his network in the United States and other countries, including how his operations were financed.Proclaiming it “an act of exceptional transparency”, theCIAdirector, John Ratcliffe, said the documents were the agency’s single largest release of declassified presidential daily briefs – the highly classified briefings prepared by the nation’s intelligence community for the government’s most senior leaders.Trump and Hegseth use 9/11 memorial remarks at Pentagon to defend war on IranRead moreThe documents range from a February 1998 file – prepared for then president Bill Clinton – titled “Terrorists seeking WMD capability” and mentioning Bin Laden and other Islamic extremists – to a 12 September 2001 report in which a source indicated the attacks had been planned for two years and had also targeted the US Capitol.An April 1998 document described the Taliban’s unwillingness to hand over Bin Laden, at the time seen as their “guest” inAfghanistan, noting their “gratitude for his assistance during the Soviet occupation” was making them “reluctant to alienate him by monitoring or controlling his activities”.Briefers in July 1998 called it “plausible that Bin Ladin places a high priority on conducting attacks in the United States” and noted his “interest in conducting attacks with chemical and biological agents”.Two months later, a briefer wrote that Bin Laden’s “preferred option is to strike the US on its own soil in Washington”, and that al-Qaida “may fly an explosive-packed airplane into a US city”.Potential hijackings were also discussed in December 1998, when a briefer described how conspirators “had evaded security checks during a recent trial run at an unidentified New York airport”, and “some members of the Bin Ladin network have received hijack training”.Other documents detail Bin Laden’s pursuit of materials for making “dirty bombs”, conventional weapons infused with radioactive material. By June 1999, according to intelligence officials, his operatives had conducted such experiments with explosives to “increase their energy output”.About two years before the attacks, intelligence officials were aware that Bin Laden appeared to be misleading theTalibanabout his reluctance to launch an unprovoked attack on the US. Briefs prepared for George W Bush in early 2001 focused in part on Bin Laden’s “experimentation by crude means to make and deploy biological agents”.A report a month before the attacks indicated Bin Laden’s commitment “to conduct terrorist attacks in the US”, noting that the 1998 al-Qaida attacks on US embassies “demonstrate that he prepares operations years in advance and is not deterred by setbacks”.At that time – August 2001 – officials wrote of “suspicious activity in this country consistent with preparations for hijackings or other types of attacks, including recent surveillance of federal buildings in New York”, adding that theFBIwas “conducting approximately 70 full field investigations throughout the US that it considers Bin Ladin-related”.Many of the documents were redacted to conceal sources’ names and other identifying information. They didn’t appear to break any new ground on the planning of the attacks or on US officials’ understanding of how they had unfolded.In the years immediately after the attacks, a bipartisan commission highlighted a lack of information-sharing among agencies such as the CIA and FBI, and issued recommendations that yielded new positions, including a centralized director of national intelligence, as well as the National Counterterrorism Center, which analyzes domestic and foreign terrorism information across different government branches.Asked for comment on the release, the White House noted the release of another batch of documents by the National Archives, also on Friday. That batch, including interviews with national security officials in the Clinton and Bush administrations, was a product of the commission that investigated the attacks from 2002 to 2004.Explore more on these topicsSeptember 11 2001Osama bin LadenAl-QaidaTalibanUS national securityTrump administrationCIAnewsShareReuse this content

title: Military aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outage  | Air transport | The Guardian
description: Meltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report says
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Meltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report says
Content: Passengers at Heathrow airport in west London during the disruption on Tuesday.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAView image in fullscreenPassengers at Heathrow airport in west London during the disruption on Tuesday.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PAAir transportMilitary aircraft reportedly blamed for UK air traffic control outageMeltdown that grounded thousands of flights caused by ‘spurious’ flight data being entered into system, report saysRaphael BoydFri 11 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe air traffic control outage that caused thousands of flights to be grounded across the UK earlier in the week was caused by a military aircraft entering “spurious” flight data into the system, according to a report.Hundreds of thousands of passengers were affected after more than 2,000 flights were cancelled on Tuesday when the system used by the National Air Traffic Services (Nats) shut down for four hours.According to the Financial Times, four people briefed on the incident claimed that the shutdown was caused by a flight plan submitted by a UK military aircraft, which caused a meltdown in air traffic control systems used by Nats which remained unfixed for several hours.The paper also reported that Nats operations officer Kathryn Leahy called the operations managers of numerous airports and airlines, and “tensions boiled over” after Leahy informed them their flight processing system did not have a dedicated backup due to Nats being in the midst of a “complete overhaul of its systems” and because the amount of data it keeps meant duplicating it would cost “vast amounts”.The crisis has put pressure on Martin Rolfe, the chief executive of Nats, who was summoned to a meeting by transport secretary Heidi Alexander on Wednesday.Alexander, who said she did “not believe the issue was unavoidable”, was understood to have given Rolfe a week to report on the causes of the shutdown, while also commissioning an independent review by the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) into the incident.The outage is the most serious to affect British commercial airspace since August 2023, when a technical problem led to almost 1,600 flights being delayed. Nats came under fire after that episode, with the CAA setting out 34 recommendations to improve its systems to avoid similar incidents, all of which were said to have been fully implemented.Rolfe ruled out a cyber-attack, which was initially suspected, saying he “believes we’ve never seen an incident happen more than once, so this will be something different that we’ve never seen in 50 years of operation”.Numerous airlines have already called for Rolfe to resign or be fired over the outage. Ryanair’s chief executive, Michael O’Leary, accused Rolfe of “telling lies to save his own skin” and said his position was “untenable”.O’Leary added: “We don’t need more investigations, we don’t need more reports and we don’t need another parliamentary committee hearing where Martin Rolfe will promise change, will promise resilience and will promise an effective backup system.”The delays led to someaircraft full of passengers being stuck waiting for information for more than four hours, while flights due to arrive in the UK were diverted to different airports, with some forced to land in Germany.Despite the far-reaching effect of the outage, it was understood that passengers affected were unlikely to be able to claim compensation, as delays were due to “extraordinary circumstances”.The Ministry of Defence has said there was no wrongdoing on the part of the military.A spokesperson from the MoD said: “We do not believe there’s any indication of an error on the part of the military. This is subject to the live Nats investigation, so it’d be inappropriate for us to comment further while that’s ongoing.”Explore more on these topicsAir transportAirline industryTransportFlightsMilitarynewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK given record £36m donation by British crypto billionaire | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Ben Delo was convicted in US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls but pardoned by Trump
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Ben Delo was convicted in US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls but pardoned by Trump
Content: Ben Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationView image in fullscreenBen Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum.Photograph: The Ben Delo FoundationReform UKReform UK given record £36m donation by British crypto billionaireBen Delo was convicted in US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls but pardoned by TrumpRowena MasonWhitehall editorFri 11 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK has been given a record £36m donation by Ben Delo, a British cryptocurrency billionaire convicted in the US for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls.The businessman, who has moved back to the UK from Hong Kong, is now the biggest UK political donor by far, dwarfing the £15m contribution to Reform UK from Thailand-based Christopher Harborne.The huge donation will be a boost for party leader Nigel Farage at a time when he is facing a police investigation into overseas funding for Reform, plus a standards inquiry into a £5m undeclared personal gift from Harborne.It had been thought Delo could be caught by the overseas cap requiring donors to have been resident in the UK for 12 months before giving more than £100,000 butReform insisted earlier this month that they were confident Delo would not have to take back any cash.Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his trillion-dollar cryptocurrency business BitMEX, before being pardoned byDonald Trump. He has previously given Reform £8m since the start of the year.His gifts show the rise of Reform’s mega-donors, which Labour has been considering clamping down on.Keir Starmer shied away from the idea of a cap on all donations and Andy Burnham also recently backed away from supporting a cap. However, more recently the government said it was looking at ways of dealing with mega-donations to make sure a few figures are not having an excessive influence in politics.On Friday night, Stella Creasy, the Labour MP pushing for a cap, said: “The government has admitted UK mega-donors are a problem – donations like this show why we must act and the good news is it’s not too late to do something about them.“We can still stop these people from distorting the next election by confirming what the cap should be on UK donations in the representation of the people bill in the Lords.Met police launch inquiry into alleged overseas donations to Reform UKRead more“This donation tonight – more for Reform on one day than the entire amount spent by Labour in the general election – shows that cannot come too soon to protect British democracy.”Many more Labour MPs were also horrified by the prospect of such a huge cash injection for Reform ahead of the next election.Delo’s donation was revealed in the Telegraph, which was given the information by Reform after the party was approached by the Sunday Times earlier on Friday.Farage said: “I am honoured and humbled that Ben Delo has shown such confidence in Reform. Ben knows that we are the only party that can turn the country around and reverse Britain’s decline.”In a Telegraph article in April, Delo explained his motivation for turning to Reform, saying England was his home and that “the biggest obstacle to national recovery is the entrenched self-deception of our elites”.“Their regime of nonsense now poses such a grave threat to the UK that, for the first time in my life, I’ve become politically active,” he wrote.He said that as a person on the autism spectrum, he did not like it that “the official culture of government now forces everyone to be chronically dishonest”, citing expression of views on transgender people.In his Telegraph article, he wrote: “I helped build one of the world’s first major crypto trading platforms, fell foul of US regulators, accepted a plea bargain and a civil fine for a regulatory failing that isn’t even a crime in the UK, but then ended up being pardoned by Donald Trump, the US president, anyway.”Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum and public life, as well as non-affiliated groups and individuals, from a political base near Westminster Abbey.AGuardian investigationinto Delo’s political base found he had given support in kind to Rupert Lowe, the anti-migration MPchallenging Farage from the right, while also connecting with more mainstream figures including the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, and the former Tory cabinet minister Michael Gove.Delo’s lawyers previously told the Guardian that he provided space for those with diverse views to express them, and financial support to a broad range of organisations, many of which had conflicting views. This did not mean he endorsed the opinions of each, they said.Explore more on these topicsReform UKParty fundingThe super-richCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’  | Employment tribunals | The Guardian
description: UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activity
Content: Dayne Oram takes part in a rally outside the Rockstar Games tribunal in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenDayne Oram takes part in a rally outside the Rockstar Games tribunal in Glasgow.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAEmployment tribunalsMan sacked by Grand Theft Auto maker believes employees were put on ‘watch list’UK employment tribunal examines whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 staff for trade union activityPatrick GreenfieldFri 11 Sep 2026 14.13 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA worker fired by the makers ofGrand Theft Autohas said he believed employees were put on a “watch list” after signing a petition about remote working.Dayne Oram told an employment tribunal inGlasgowexamining whether Rockstar Games unlawfully fired 31 employees for trade union activity on Friday that he thought the company started keeping an eye on a group of workers after the petition was sent to leadership in 2023.Rockstar, which disputes the claims, says Oram and his colleagues were dismissed for gross misconduct after confidential company information was shared, not because of trade union membership or activity.The workers had been helping to make Grand Theft Auto VI, which is set for release on 19 November and will probably be among the biggest launches in gaming history. The production for the game, which has reportedly generated more than $3bn (£2.27bn) in preorders, is led from the company’s Edinburgh office Rockstar North.View image in fullscreenGrand Theft Auto 6 is set for release in November.Illustration: Rockstar GamesMuch of the case relies on what was shared in a Discord forum, used by about 300 Rockstar employees to discuss the company. Oram was involved in setting up the forum and helped moderate it, which is where Rockstar says sensitive information was shared and discussed.Oram told the tribunal that discussions on the forum could “get a bit out of hand”. Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar at the tribunal, read Oram the forum rules requiring workers to remain “professional and constructive” when posting. Cordrey suggested that the rules had been “routinely broken”.Cordrey read out a number of Discord posts where he suggested employees were making disparaging remarks about the company and management, including messages in which one was called “cowardly corporate fucks” and another was called a “cunt”.Oram told the tribunal that he would probably “remake” some of the moderation decisions if he had the chance to do so again, but said moderators did not want to “over-police” the channel.Oram also said he believed there was a connection between the list of names who signed the 2023 petition about remote working and the eventual firings in 2025. But Cordrey questioned whether this was really the case when 141 of 154 people who signed it were not fired.View image in fullscreenRockstar Games’ Edinburgh office.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA“It was maybe the start of them keeping an eye on things,” Oram told the tribunal.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe case is expected to last about six weeks, with testimony from Rockstar Games witnesses set for October. Thecompany remains in talks with current workers, who hope official union recognition can be secured before the release of GTA VI.In total, 34 Rockstar workers were fired last year, including three in Canada who are not taking part in the tribunal. Of the 31 who were based inScotland, 23 are involved in the case and are being represented by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain.A spokesperson for Rockstar Games said: “Rockstar Games’ position has been clear and consistent throughout.“Individuals across the UK and Canada were dismissed for gross misconduct following the sharing of confidential company information, not because of alleged trade union membership or activity. We reject the claims and will defend them vigorously before the tribunal,” the said.The tribunal in Glasgow continues before the judge Lucy Wiseman.Explore more on these topicsEmployment tribunalsGrand Theft AutoGlasgowScotlandWork & careersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Northern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next year | Northern Ireland | The Guardian
description: DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: DUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniform
Content: A law passed last year aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers, but campaigners said it did not got far enough.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyView image in fullscreenA law passed last year aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers, but campaigners said it did not got far enough.Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/AlamyNorthern IrelandNorthern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next yearDUP education minister accused of dragging feet before revising guidelines on uniformRory CarrollIreland correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSchools inNorthern Irelandmust give girls the choice to wear trousers as part of their uniforms as well as for PE and games, according to revised guidelines.From next year schools would no longer be able to prohibit female pupils from wearing trousers, Paul Givan, the country’s education minister, said on Friday. “Today, I am taking that decision, that will be formally communicated, schools will be hearing from me,” hetold the BBC.A law passed last year that was aimed at reducing the cost of uniforms gave girls the legal right to challenge schools that banned them from wearing trousers.However, campaigners said the change did not go far enough and put pressure on Givan, a Democratic Unionist party member of the Northern Ireland assembly (MLA) whosaid his own daughters wore skirts to school, to revise the guidelines.Givan said he had to strike a balance between schools’ autonomy and the level of prescription in departmental guidelines. “I have listened carefully over recent months to young people and the message is clear: girls want the choice to wear trousers as part of their school uniform.”The revised guidelines would not go into immediate effect to give schools time to update their policies, said Givan.Other parties welcomed the change but accused the education minister of dragging his feet.“I’m glad that it appears the minister has seen fit to U-turn on his decision not to ensure that all girls have the right to wear trousers as part of their school uniform,” said Nick Mathison, an Alliance MLA and chair of the Stormont assembly education committee.“I want to thank all of the young campaigners who have been bravely raising their voices about this, and whose dedication will lead to seeing this wrong righted. The fact that in 2026 young girls and women had to campaign for this at all will not be forgotten.”Substantial sums of public money were spent on drafting legislation to fix the minister’s error of judgment, Mathison added.A girl’s right to wear trousers should not have been controversial, said Cathy Mason, a Sinn Féin MLA. “It should not have required further legislation from the education committee to force movement on something so basic.”Cara Hunter, a Social Democratic and Labour party MLA, said young people who challenged the existing rules and refused to let the issue disappear deserved credit for the change. “The department must now deliver. This cannot be a right that exists on paper but becomes an argument at the school gate,” she said.Explore more on these topicsNorthern IrelandSchoolsEducation policyPrimary schoolsSecondary schoolsChildrenNorthern Irish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why did the assisted dying bill fail in the Commons? | Assisted dying | The Guardian
description: MPs quietly withdrew support when it became clear it was not a priority of Andy Burnham’s government
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: MPs quietly withdrew support when it became clear it was not a priority of Andy Burnham’s government
Content: Labour MP Lauren Edwards, proposer of the bill, speaks in the Commons.Photograph: Parliament TV/PALabour MP Lauren Edwards, proposer of the bill, speaks in the Commons.Photograph: Parliament TV/PAAssisted dyingAnalysisWhy did the assisted dying bill fail in the Commons?Rowena MasonWhitehall editorMPs quietly withdrew support when it became clear it was not a priority of Andy Burnham’s governmentMPs vote against legalising assisted dying in England and WalesFri 11 Sep 2026 13.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.52 EDTShareAfter two years of impassioned arguments, tearful personal testimonies, noisy protests and ethical dilemmas,the assisted dying bill for England and Wales failedon a knife edge.Campaigners on the pro side largely blame the House of Lords for making it seem an impossible struggle to get the bill through parliament, afterblocking itthe first time by putting through more than 1,000 amendments so that it ran out of time.The opponents are more inclined to think that they ended up picking so many holes in the legislation that it was bound to fail, as they raised more and more objections on safety grounds.But the truth was that many MPs felt momentum was lost when it became clear it was not a priority of Andy Burnham’s government.Although as Greater Manchester mayor he had said he would probably vote in favour of the initial private member’s bill, in July Burnham said he now thought the bigger issue should beto improve end-of-life support.How did your MP vote on the reintroduced assisted dying bill?Read moreIt suddenly became very unlikely that the government would throw its weight behind giving the bill its full backing or expending energy on policy development to help it succeed.Burnham’s change of position was a blow to the pro campaigners after Keir Starmer had long given his tacit support to the first bill proposed by Kim Leadbeater, even though it was a conscience vote.In private, many MPs also admit that another factor in losing support for the bill was that backing it did not do Starmer’s administration many favours.The bill caused bitter division among its MPs and diverted attention from the many pressing issues that might be more electorally important toLabour, such as the cost of living and healthcare.As it took up more and more parliamentary bandwidth and media airtime, former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney was among the advisers who thought the legislation was a bad idea.There were also some reservations about the sponsors of the bill hoping to use the Parliament Act to force it through if blocked a second time by the Lords, with a rule that states if the same bill is approved twice by the Commons in two consecutive sessions and opposed by peers, then it can be passed anyway.‘A tragic day’: campaigners react as MPs say no to legalising assisted dyingRead moreHowever, this would have meant it being unchanged from the bill presented last year – which worried some MPs who voted for the bill in principle but wanted to see it amended with further protections against coercion.One of the many with a complicated personal position on the issue was Labour MP David Burton-Sampson, who voted in favour of it progressing to give people individual choice, even though he was personally against assisted dying because of his Christian faith; however, he said he would be uncomfortable with it passing into law without further safeguards.When it became clear that Burnham lacked enthusiasm for the bill, it ultimately gave some of those MPs who supported it in theory – but had misgivings about it in practice – permission to absent themselves from the vote.The quiet withdrawal of support is evident in the numbers: the last time MPs voted, 291 voted against it, versus 314 in favour. This time, 286 voted against, while just 270 were in favour, a fall of 45.Campaigners in favour of assisted dying say it is not the end of the road for their efforts to secure a change in the law – and the public still seems to be in favour of the policy in essence.But MPs are likely to be wary of devoting much more time in this parliament to a debate when the arguments have been rehearsed near exhaustively and opinion in parliament is still so evenly split.Explore more on these topicsAssisted dyingHouse of CommonsEnglandWalesAndy BurnhamLabouranalysisShareReuse this content

title: Republican senator fires aide who used Nazi soldiers as Facebook profile picture | Republicans | The Guardian
description: Washington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on Spotify
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: Washington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on Spotify
Content: Jon Husted, whose Senate race is on a knife-edge, in Dallas on Wednesday. The Husted campaign did not say whether Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his hiring.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJon Husted, whose Senate race is on a knife-edge, in Dallas on Wednesday. The Husted campaign did not say whether Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his hiring.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesRepublicansRepublican senator fires aide who used Nazi soldiers as Facebook profile pictureWashington Post report also reveals Jon Husted staffer Stephen Woytek created pro-Rhodesia playlist on SpotifyRobert Taitin WashingtonFri 11 Sep 2026 19.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Republican senator forOhio, Jon Husted, has fired an aide who was discovered to have used a photo of Nazi SS soldiers as his Facebook profile photo.Stephen Woytek was appointed as Husted’s political director last month in the senator’s knife-edge re-election contest against former Democrat senator Sherrod Brown.According to the Washington Post, Husted had decided to “part ways” with Woytek, 25, after learning that his Facebook profile showed he followed a military re-enactment group called LAH Living History Unit, which portrays the 1st SS Panzer division.The group’s website says its members dress up as the Leibstandarte, a Waffen-SS armored division that began as Adolf Hitler’s bodyguards. LAH says the Leibstandarte “came to symbolize the highest dedication to duty and individual as well as collective loyalty”. The group claims to be “non-political” and insists is disavows “political and religious persecution” that happened the second world war.A Spotify playlist recently created by an account bearing Woytek’s name hailed the former racist white-minority regime of Rhodesia, now Zimbabwe, seen as a symbol of white supremacy by some racist groups.In a statement, a spokesperson for Husted said the campaign had ended its relationship with Woytek.“While he denies negative intent, his social media activity displays a complete lack of judgement and disregard for its impact on others,” the spokesperson said. “Senator Husted demands better of those who represent him. Upon learning about the social media posts today, Senator Husted made the immediate decision to part ways.”The campaign did not respond to the Post’s questions about whether and how Woytek’s social media activity had been vetted before his appointment, the newspaper reported.Woytek’s departure follows a series of damaging episodes in which young Republicans groups have been discovered expressing pro-Nazi sympathies in group chats and internet forums. And in Georgia, Republican congressman Mike Collins’s campaign for Senate has been shaken by controversies involving his staff’s online activity. This summer, Collins replaced top aide, Kip Talley, after Slaterevealedhe had been part of a group chat with white supremacists.Woytek, who serves in the national guard and was a graduate of the Citadel, a military academy based in Charleston, South Carolina, issued a statement of regret, saying he wished he had “exercised better judgment when posting about my activities online”.“I want to be unequivocal: I reject the racist and antisemitic ideology the SS and Nazi Germany represented. I believe it is important to educate our younger generations, which is why I participate in historical reenactments,” he said.LAH shared a photo on a Flickr account that showed Woytek in 2018 – when he was 16 – wearing an SS uniform and marching in an area adorned with Nazi flags. Woytek follows several suppliers of SS uniforms on his Facebook page.On a Quora account bearing his name, Woytek also answered a question on whether anything good had occurred under Hitler, writing in 2017 “that Hitler started an anti-smoking campaign”.More recently, he created a public playlist of pro-Rhodesia songs on Spotify called “Tales from Rhodesia”, which is captioned: “Homesick for a place that no longer exists.” One of the songs uses a slur to refer to African troops.The former British colony’s white minority government fought a long war against guerrilla groups after issuing a unilateral declaration of independence in 1965. The country was officially recognized as Zimbabwe under black majority rule in 1980, a year after the minority government accepted its rule was unsustainable and entered peace negotiations.Rhodesia has been used by white supremacists as a symbol of the supposed superiority of white rule.Explore more on these topicsRepublicansUS politicsOhionewsShareReuse this content

title: US consumers faced more high prices in August as Iran war raised energy costs | Inflation | The Guardian
description: Annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, same as July, and core inflation, which omits energy and food prices, rose to 2.4%
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Annualized inflation rate was 3.4%, same as July, and core inflation, which omits energy and food prices, rose to 2.4%
Content: Consumer sentiment dropped to record lows earlier this summer as Americans said they were struggling to afford gas and groceries.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenConsumer sentiment dropped to record lows earlier this summer as Americans said they were struggling to afford gas and groceries.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesInflationUS consumers faced more high prices in August as Iran war raised energy costsAnnualized inflation rate was 3.4%, same as July, and core inflation, which omits energy and food prices, rose to 2.4%Gaya GuptaFri 11 Sep 2026 08.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS consumer prices remained stubbornly high in August as the end of the ceasefire between the US andIranpushed energy prices up, according to data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics released on Friday.The annualizedinflationrate was 3.4%, the same as it was in July. The most recent peak was seen in May, when the inflation rate hit a three-year high at 4.2%. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, increased 0.3% from the month before and 2.4% annually.Gasoline increased 27.4% compared with the year before, accounting for more than one-third of the overall monthly increase in prices. Fuel , which is used to power and heat homes, increased annually at a staggering 52%.Prices of common grocery store essentials, such as meat, poultry, eggs and dairy, increased slightly, from 0.1% to 0.3%. Lettuce prices continued to fall, probably continued fallout from thecyclosporiasis outbreak.Despite dipping from its most recent peak, inflation remained above levels that were seen before thewar in Iran, largely because of higher energy prices. On Friday, the cost of diesel, used for trucks, buses and trains, rose past $6 a gallon for the first time ever. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, also surpassed $108 on Friday, its highest level since May. Meanwhile, gas prices at the pump sat at an average of $4.29 a gallon, $1.10 higher than the average a year ago, according toAAA.A line chart showing latest US inflation figuresIt’s a worrying sign for Republicans, who are on the ballot at a time when consumer sentiment has hit record lows and Americanssaythey are struggling to afford gas and groceries. Concerns over inflation have also bled into the US bond market, where the yields on some US treasurys have reached their highest points since the 2008 recession. Yet it’s unclear when relief will come.Global bond sell-off resumes as surging oil prices stoke fears about inflationRead moreThe White House is aware of what this could mean for the upcoming elections. On Wednesday night, Trump said Americans would get a $5,000 “dividend” if Republicans win a majority in the midterms, which criticssaidwas akin to bribery.One of the most direct ways the federal government can affect prices comes from the power of the USFederal Reserve, which sets the interest rates that have an effect on the price of loans, including mortgages, car payments and student debt.With prices remaining stubbornly high and core inflation rising, Friday’s report bolsters the likelihood that the Fed will vote to increase rates at its board meeting next week.. Either move could have heavy implications for theUS economy.In a social media post last week, Trump said the central bank “must get smart” and lower rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE,” he declared.But pressure to increase rates has been growing. At the Fed’s last board meeting in July, it voted 9-3 to maintain rates – the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHistorically, raising interest rates helps to lower inflation – making investments more expensive slows the economy.Inflationreached 9.1%, a 40-year high, in 2022. After the Fed spent the next few years increasing interest rates, up to a range of 5.25%-5.5%, inflation went down to 2.3% in April 2025.Interest rates now sit at a range of 3.5%-3.75%, two percentage points lower than where they were two years ago. With inflation back up, some Fed economists have said it might be time for higher interest rates.Last week, the Fed governor Christopher Waller said there was “considerable uncertainty about how military conflicts, trade policy, and artificial intelligence will affect prices and economic activity” and it might be appropriate to raise rates if inflation showed no signs of easing.“If there is continued progress toward our 2% goal, then I am willing to support holding the policy rate at its current level,” he said at a Reuters event. “But if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike.”The Fed’s new chair, Kevin Warsh, has made it clear the central bank will combat inflation during his tenure and achieve price stability. During a closely watched speech in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, last month, Warsh said that underlying inflation trends had not “meaningfully improved” over the summer.“We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do,” Warsh said.Explore more on these topicsInflationUS interest ratesFederal ReserveUS economynewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Just worry upon worry’: Europe faces a bleak winter as supply shock pushes factories to the brink | Manufacturing sector | The Guardian
description: From Shropshire to Hamburg, depleting reserves and spiralling costs are spawning a continent-wide energy crisis
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: From Shropshire to Hamburg, depleting reserves and spiralling costs are spawning a continent-wide energy crisis
Content: Soaring energy bills are a grim prospect for many industrial businesses across Europe already stretched as a result of global unrest and earlier energy shocks.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSoaring energy bills are a grim prospect for many industrial businesses across Europe already stretched as a result of global unrest and earlier energy shocks.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesManufacturing sector‘Just worry upon worry’: Europe faces a bleak winter as supply shock pushes factories to the brinkFrom Shropshire to Hamburg, depleting reserves and spiralling costs are spawning a continent-wide energy crisisAlex DanielandLisa O’CarrollFri 11 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBridgnorth Aluminium has faced down Brexit, Covid and repeated energy shocks in recent years. But this winter is bringing extra “stress and pressure”, says its head of sales, Adrian Musgrave.Musgrave’s company makes rolled aluminium, used in packaging, construction and the manufacture of items such as cars and batteries. Like many stretched industrial businesses acrossEurope, Bridgnorth Aluminium faces a looming threat of soaring energy bills, which Musgrave describes as “just worry upon worry”.The cost of natural gas has doubled in the past two months, caused by renewed fighting between the US and Iran, reaching a three-year high in the UK and the EU this week. More price rises are likely in the colder months.Bridgnorth Aluminium, which employs 370 people at its plant in Shropshire in the UK’s industrial heartland, is already feeling the effects. Its combined gas and electricity bill is about £1.1m per month, 18% of its total costs, and rising.Its biggest contracts include a safety net – once gas prices cross a certain point, customers pay the difference. That threshold was crossed last month – but the question of whether clients will come back concerns Musgrave. “They have to pay because it’s in the contract, but they will obviously not like it,” he says. “When it comes up for renewal it will become an issue.”Musgrave says the company is not in a place where it would need to make layoffs or temporary shutdowns this winter. Others may not be so lucky – one forecast, by the Item Club, predicted earlier this year that Britain will lose 163,000 jobs in 2026 because of the war, concentrated in manufacturing-heavy regions such as south Wales and the Humber region.Bridgnorth Aluminium is considering taking a longer Christmas break, or doing planned maintenance – originally scheduled for April – earlier than expected in January, so the factory runs less during times of high prices. “And then the employees are obviously aware,” he says, “so then people begin to worry.”View image in fullscreenStorage tanks at the Grain liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal near Rochester, UK.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesGas spikes and shortagesThe conflict has disrupted global energy supplies since Iran started attacking ships in the Gulf and choked off access through the strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil and gas passes.British wholesale gas prices climbed to 205p per therm this week, the highest point since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and up 101% from 102p in June. That is compared with 78p per therm at the end of February. The UK imports about 70% of its gas, leaving it especially vulnerable to price swings.ChartA shortage of stored gas reserves compounds the issue. Europe is heading into winter with gas storesat their lowest level in over a decade, after the Hormuz disruption stopped countries topping up their reserves through the summer, when prices are normally lower. Storage is now about 67% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.Germany, which holds the largest storage capacity in Europe, is only about half full, and is on course to miss its official 70% storage target this year. The Netherlands is expected to miss its 80% target too.As one of Europe’s biggest gas consumers, the UK may be especially exposed, with some of the lowest levels of domestic storage capacity and relying instead on pipeline imports from Europe and tankers from the US and Middle East. Chris O’Shea, the chief executive of BritishGasowner Centrica, said last month that Britain had “almost no gas in storage” for the coming winter.View image in fullscreenA crane operator moves coils of steel at a steel plant in Duisburg, Germany.Photograph: Sean Gallup/Getty ImagesStrife in the MittelstandAlexander Julius, managing partner of Macrometal Handelsgesellschaft, a steel distributor in Hamburg, says it is competing “against producers in regions where energy costs are often significantly lower and where governments provide direct or indirect industrial support”.For industries like his, part of Germany’s Mittelstand of medium-sized enterprises, he says energy is not just another item on the cost lines, but “a fundamental production input”. But instead of getting support they are being “hammered by green taxes while energy rises rocket”.Julius, who is also the president of trade body Eurometal, says companies will go to the wall and work will move to China or India unless something is done to reduce energy costs. Eurometal haswarned that manufacturing job losses across Europe could reach 300,000by the end of the year, driven partly by Chinese competition and compounded by energy costs.Natural gas price in the EU from December 2025 to September 2026Axel Eggert, director general of the European steel body Eurofer, adds that the high prices “will inevitably lead to production disruptions. Such additional costs cannot simply be absorbed by energy-intensive industries exposed to international competition.“The longer the crisis lasts, the greater the risk that temporary production cuts become structural, with consequences for investment, employment and, ultimately, the viability of industrial plants in Europe.”The car industry in Germany has also called for urgent action from Berlin and Brussels, saying “the high energy prices are among the biggest competitive disadvantages of Germany as a business location”, with electricity prices in some cases three times higher than the US.“Germany, just like the EU, urgently needs a jointly supported energy strategy with low electricity prices and future-proof grid infrastructure,” said a spokesperson for the trade association, the VDA. Building new industries will become “a decisive factor in determining” inward foreign investment in future, they added.‘It just keeps coming’The exposure is especially bad for the chemicals sector, where companies rely on gas to power their plants but also as feedstock – the raw material that many products are made from – meaning every spike in prices hits them twice.Francesco Buzzella, president of Italy’s chemicals trade body Federchimica, says it remains the “primary factor undermining the competitiveness of chemical companies” in the country. Energy now accounts for 18% of the value of everything Italy’s chemical industry produces, up from 14% in 2021 – and could reach 23% if gas and oil prices do not fall. This week oil hit $107 a barrel as the US and Iran continue to trade blows.Production output in the UK has fallen by 60% since 2021, according to the Chemicals Industry Association, with at least 25 sites closing.Peter Huntsman, chief executive of the chemicals group Huntsman Corporation, told the Guardian in March that continued high pricescould force the closure of the company’s last remaining UK plant, at Wilton on Teesside.Back in Shropshire, meanwhile, Musgrave says Bridgnorth Aluminium’s owner, the Belgian industrial group Viohalco, wants to invest further in the company’s operations, but the numbers are getting harder to justify.“They would like to make some significant investments – the UK market for aluminium is quite big, and we would like to be able to sell more at home,” he says.But energy and other pressures make it “a difficult picture for shareholders to get their head around … The business conditions for investment are really challenging, and changing quite rapidly.“I’ve been in this business just over 20 years. For the first 10, the macro environment was always pretty stable. But then we had Brexit, which changed things; the energy crisis with Ukraine; Covid; and now this.“You just think you’re going to get a year where maybe it won’t be too much change,” he adds. “But it just keeps coming.”Explore more on these topicsManufacturing sectorOilGasInflationUS-Israel war on IranEuropeSteel industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Solheim Cup: USA fightback sparks hope of away win after Europe’s fast start | Solheim Cup | The Guardian
description: After a morning session that ended 2-2 in the Solheim Cup, USA clawed Europe back to 4-4 after sinking early on in the fourballs
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: After a morning session that ended 2-2 in the Solheim Cup, USA clawed Europe back to 4-4 after sinking early on in the fourballs
Content: Carlota Ciganda gives it the celebration her all after holing a putt on the 18th to earn a half point for Europe.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenCarlota Ciganda gives it the celebration her all after holing a putt on the 18th to earn a half point for Europe.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APSolheim CupSolheim Cup: USA fightback sparks hope of away win after Europe’s fast startScores level at 4-4 after day oneEurope fail to make advantage pay in fourballsEwan Murrayat Bernardus GolfFri 11 Sep 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 16.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rain poured and the United States roared. Hope had cascaded through the European contingent at thisSolheim Cupduring Friday afternoon until the sort of fightback that endorsed the sense that, come Sunday evening, the US will have won this trophy in a foreign land for the first time since 2015. This compelling day concluded with the scores level at 4-4. For Europe, it had promised to be so much better.Solheim Cup golf 2026: Europe 4-4 USA after day one drama in fourballs – as it happenedRead moreAfter a morning session that closed all square at 2-2, Europe surged ahead in three fourball matches. This felt like validation for Anna Nordqvist, the home captain. She had opted not to deploy any of the four players who returned two foursomes points – Maja Stark, Linn Grant, Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit – after lunch.Heads turned, especially in respect of Maguire. She was controversially lightly raced as Europe lost in the 2024 Solheim Cup. Victory for Maguire and Henseleit over Andrea Lee and Lindy Duncan meant the Irishwoman became statistically the most successful European Solheim Cup player of all time. Maguire had cause to wonder why she was left on the sidelines; especially as Céline Boutier and Nanna Koerstz Madsen, who visibly toiled in the foursomes, slumped to a second defeat out of two. Megan Khang and Alison Lee cantered to a 5&3 fourball success in the one straightforward clash of the afternoon.As the heavens opened and competitors turned for home, the US discovered pulses elsewhere. Blue started to be wiped from scoreboards. The sun was out again by the time Yealimi Noh produced the shot of the day, from a fairway bunker on the 17th. Noh could not even see the green from the sand trap yet played a glorious iron to five feet. As Noh converted from there, a three-up lead for Charley Hull and Lottie Woad after 11 holes had been cancelled out. Noh had made birdie at four holes from a run of six.On the final green, Noh stood over a putt to complete the turnaround and win the match. Woad had been visibly distracted by music coming from the spectator village while over her attempt at a three. Noh, in fairness, had the same backdrop. The American’s attempt was tame yet a halved match represented a blow to Europe given early dominance. Noh’s partner Angel Yin was in floods of tears afterwards; her Solheim Cup involvement had been in serious doubt due to illness.View image in fullscreenUSA’s Nelly Korda (left) and Lauren Coughlin beat Charley Hull and Lottie Woad 4&3.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APCarlota Ciganda and Julia López Ramírez were two holes to the good over Nelly Korda and Lauren Coughlin at the turn. Korda looked horrendously out of sorts. By the 16th tee, the US were one up. Europe won that hole in what suddenly looked such a crucial match. Mind games applied on the 17th, where Europe opted not to concede either one of two tap‑in American putts for a half. López found sand at the last, with Ciganda even more wayward. Ciganda struck lucky not only there but with a wild second. And still, she rescued half a point with the day’s last act. Korda and company were rightly irked.Europe’s star turns in the afternoon were debutants. Chemistry was obvious between Mimi Rhodes and the huge-hitting Nastasia Nadaud, who closed out their success over Allisen Corpuz and Auston Kim on the penultimate green.Hull and Woad were comfortably beaten by Korda and Corpuz in the morning. Alison Lee and Coughlin took match two over Boutier and Koerstz Madsen. Henseleit and Maguire defeated Andrea Lee and Duncan for Europe’s first point of the event. Stark and Grant ended the morning session by swatting aside Rose Zhang and Jennifer Kupcho.The Solheim Cup involves a more sedate backdrop than its male equivalent and is all the better for that. The last Ryder Cup staging at Bethpage regressed into a moronic mess. In this rural corner of the Netherlands, nobody missed the yobbish element.Nordqvist revealed team Europe had sought out a group of colourfully dressed fans who typically appear front and centre at Ryder Cups. The self-proclaimed “guardians of the cup” were invited to the Netherlands but, according to a Solheim Cup official, still had to pay for their tickets.“I don’t think I’ve ever seen as many European supporters,” said Nordqvist. “I know it’s just so amazing to play in an atmosphere like that. We have recruited the team from the Ryder Cup and they have been teaching everyone all these amazing songs. So it has been really cool to be on the first tee today.”Explore more on these topicsSolheim CupGolfUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Leading athletes still waiting on large sums owed by ill-fated Grand Slam Track  | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Agents for many Grand Slam Track stars say they are yet to receive 50% of earnings nearly 15 months on from the collapse of Michael Johnson’s venture
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Agents for many Grand Slam Track stars say they are yet to receive 50% of earnings nearly 15 months on from the collapse of Michael Johnson’s venture
Content: Michael Johnson, the four-time Olympic champion, who launched Grand Slam Track’s first event in April 2025 only for it to collapse after three meets.Photograph: Kirby Lee/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters ConnectView image in fullscreenMichael Johnson, the four-time Olympic champion, who launched Grand Slam Track’s first event in April 2025 only for it to collapse after three meets.Photograph: Kirby Lee/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters ConnectAthleticsLeading athletes still waiting on large sums owed by ill-fated Grand Slam TrackGST founder Michael Johnson said he ‘got the athletes paid’Money stuck in escrow account after bankruptcy filingSean Inglein BudapestFri 11 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 18.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGrand Slam Track athletes have still only received 50% of their earnings nearly 15 months on from the collapse of Michael Johnson’s ill-fated venture.Many of the Grand Slam stars are atthe Ultimate Championships in ­Budapest, where they are competing for a $10m (£7.4m) prize fund, the richest in the sport’s history, with first prizes of $150,000 (£111,000) for individual events.Four leading agents have told the Guardian that their athletes are still waiting on large sums of money from GST, despite Johnson claiming last month that he had “got the athletes paid”.Johnson, a four-time Olympic champion and BBC pundit, launched GST in April last year, with the promise to revolutionise the sport with huge prizes and salaries. But it ­collapsed after only three events, before ­organisers voluntarily filed for bankruptcy in the US in December.Athletes ended up receiving half their earnings last October, but have not had anything since. Their agents are hopeful that they will receive another sum in the region of 25% from an escrow account in the next month or two.Vendors, meanwhile, have so far only received 14% of what they are owed.A spokesperson for Johnson said: “Over the last year Michael has worked to ensure athletes who competed in GST were paid what they were owed. Against all odds, he secured funding to do just that. Athletes received half of what they were owed in October 2025.“In May of this year GST paid the remaining funds owed to athletes into an escrow account to guarantee they would be received by athletes. GST, as per the bankruptcy plan voted on by the creditors [including the athletes], is not involved in ­distributing the funds to athletes. Our understanding is that distribution of payments is in process.“A process controlled by Force10 partners under the guidelines and supervision of the bankruptcy court. Michael understands the significant interest in this situation and chose the bankruptcy process specifically for its transparency.”Several high-profile athletes are understood to still be owed payments in excess of £100,000, including ­British former world 1500m champion Josh Kerr and world 400m champion Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone.Meanwhile WorldAthleticspresident, Sebastian Coe, recently pointed out the differences between the Ultimate Championship and GST. “Where would you like me to start?” said Coe. “We have a business. We have a fully funded business plan. And I can guarantee you the athletes will be paid on time.”Josh Kerr: ‘What has running taught me about life? If you are determined enough, you can 100% do it’Read moreExplore more on these topicsAthleticsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Benn and Garcia turn past scandals into a $30m Las Vegas world title payday | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Fight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championship
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: Fight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championship
Content: Ryan Garcia (left) and Conor Benn fight for the WBC welterweight world championship on Saturday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Ian Maule/APView image in fullscreenRyan Garcia (left) and Conor Benn fight for the WBC welterweight world championship on Saturday in Las Vegas.Photograph: Ian Maule/APBoxingBenn and Garcia turn past scandals into a $30m Las Vegas world title paydayFight offers revealing snapshot of boxers once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests now vying for a welterweight world championshipBryan Armen GrahamFri 11 Sep 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFour years ago Conor Benn’s career was thrown into limbo after two positive drug tests scuppered his blockbuster fight with Chris Eubank Jr. Two years ago Ryan Garcia was serving a one-year suspension after testing positive for ostarine at the time of his greatest victory.On Saturday night they will each be rewarded with an eight-figure payday when they meet at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas for Garcia’s WBC welterweight championship. The purses have not been disclosed, although reports have put the combined pot at around $30m (£22m) with each fighter expected to haul in roughly $15m.Their routes to one of boxing’s biggest stages on Mexican Independence Day weekend have been different, as were the cases against them and their eventual outcomes. Both men insist they are not drug cheats, with Bennhaving ultimately been clearedby the National Anti-Doping Panel. But their collision course offers a striking reminder of a sport in which scandal can derail a career without necessarily compromising the value of the fighter involved in it.Garcia (25-2, 20 KOs), the 28-year-old from Victorville, California, one of boxing’s first Gen-Z superstars, tested positive for the performance-enhancing anabolic agent ostarineon the day beforeand theday afterhis surprise win over Devin Haney in April 2024. His majority-decision victory wasoverturned to a no-contest, he was suspended for a year and his team blamed contaminated supplements.Benn (25-1, 14 KOs) went through a longer and considerably more complicated ordeal. Two positive tests for the female fertility drug clomifene, a banned substance that can boost testosterone by 50%, emerged before the Londoner’s proposed fight with Eubank in October 2022, launching a regulatory battle that prevented him from fighting in Britain for two years. Benn maintained his innocence throughout.Three years later, here they are. Garcia will make the first defense of the WBC title he won by dropping and outpointing Mario Barrios in February. For the 29-year-old Benn, it is a first world title shot and a chance to follow in the footsteps of his father, Nigel, who captured the WBC super-middleweight title more than three decades ago.View image in fullscreenConor Benn’s most recent fight was at a 150lb limit in April rather than the 147lb welterweight limit he has to make now.Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PAThat Saturday’s fight was made at all speaks volumes about professional boxing’s peculiar moral ecosystem, where there is no single governing authority, universal anti-doping system or commissioner capable of imposing consistent sanctions across jurisdictions.
