Much of the power instead rests with promoters, broadcasters and sanctioning bodies whose financial interests are rarely served by keeping valuable fighters out of the ring.Dismissed by critics for his good looks, luxury-brand endorsements and huge social-media reach – upwards of 13.1m Instagram followers with 9m more on TikTok – Garcia has amassed a massive following while oscillating between elite performances and episodes of extraordinary self-sabotage. His return from suspension brought an immediate world title shot – and a flatunanimous-decision loss to Rolando Romeroin May 2025 – only for him to rebound against Barrios nine months later and win his first recognized world championship.Benn’s journey has been different but hardly quieter. After eventually returning to fight in Britain, he lost to Eubank in April 2025before avenging the defeatseven months later. Those fights restored his commercial momentum but did considerably less to establish him as a leading welterweight challenger.Benn has not fought at the division’s 147lb limit for four‑and‑a‑half years, having recently campaigned at middleweight before coming down to 150lb to face Regis Prograis in April. Getting back down to welterweight may be the biggest gamble of all. “People say: ‘Oh, you can’t go up to this weight and then go back down.’ All right, cool. Well, just watch me do it,” Benn said at Thursday’s final press conference. “Discipline prevails, and I will make the weight.”Garcia remains skeptical, suggesting the effects of the cut could leave Benn vulnerable once the punches start landing. “Even if he makes the weight, your brain can’t rehydrate fast enough,” Garcia said. “Them punches going to do some real damage.”There is, beneath all the uncomfortable baggage, an intriguing fight between two men who certainly talk a good game. Garcia expects Benn to come forward and “try to resort to some dirty tactics”. Benn’s description of his approach sounded remarkably similar: “Tenacity, ferocity, spite, experience. I’m here to come and really set the tone from the first round.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTherein lies the danger for the challenger. Garcia is the more naturally gifted boxer, with exceptional hand speed and a vicious left hook that is most dangerous against opponents coming forward. Benn’s best route to victory may require him to walk directly toward Garcia’s best weapon.Garcia has shown he can be vulnerable when forced backwards, but Benn does not possess the timing or precision of Gervonta Davis, who handed Garcia his first professional setback with awithering seventh-round body shot in 2023. Benn, meanwhile, insists that virtually every apparent disadvantage works in his favor because it leaves Garcia carrying the expectations.View image in fullscreenRyan Garcia has argued this week that Conor Benn is not in the title fight on merit but because of his famous boxing father.Photograph: Ringo HW Chiu/AP“The pressure’s on Ryan completely,” Benn said. “No one’s given me a chance in this fight. Twenty amateur fights, just not made 147 for four-and-a-half years, the weight problem, the this, the that. No one’s given me a chance.”There is also something more personal at stake for Benn, who has spent years carrying the advantages and burdens of his surname, including Garcia’s repeated contention this week that he would never have reached this position without it. There is a certain irony in Garcia attacking Benn as a nepo baby: Garcia has been a child of boxing privilege in his own right, enjoying nearly every advantage the industry can confer, never more than during his microwaved redemption. “It’s just a blessing to be in this position, to be headlining in Vegas, to be fighting on a mega show and put the Benn name back up in bright lights,” Benn said.For all the talk of legacy, Saturday also offers a revealing snapshot of boxing in 2026. Two men once facing uncertain futures after positive drug tests will instead fight for a world championship and another handsome payday. Few sports are better at turning yesterday’s scandal into tomorrow’s main event.Explore more on these topicsBoxingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Crowd of 100,000 laps up relentless sensory experience as NFL woos Melbourne | NFL | The Guardian
description: The morning kick-off provided ‘incredible’ vibes for a sell-out crowd clearly different to that for AFL and cricket games at the venue
Author: Jack Snape
Headline: The morning kick-off provided ‘incredible’ vibes for a sell-out crowd clearly different to that for AFL and cricket games at the venue
Content: The Royal Australian Air Force Roulettes perform a flyover at the NFL match between Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers at the MCG.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Royal Australian Air Force Roulettes perform a flyover at the NFL match between Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers at the MCG.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesNFLCrowd of 100,000 laps up relentless sensory experience as NFL woos MelbourneThe morning kick-off provided ‘incredible’ vibes for a sell-out crowd clearly different to that which attends AFL and cricket games at the venueJack Snapeat the MCGFri 11 Sep 2026 00.35 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 03.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 9am on a Friday, Melbourne’s tongues would usually be tinged with toothpaste. Beer, however, was the flavour craved by this throng of bros brought together by the visit of one of the United States’ great institutions.Dressed inSan Francisco 49ersred, LA Rams blue and every other colour of the 32-team NFL rainbow, the 100,021 fans had come to the competition’s first regular season match in Australia. They were there in droves, and 90 minutes from kick-off their thirst had already forced the closure of the pop-up pub adjacent to the MCG.NFL stars, cheerleaders and the Jonas Brothers: American football comes to Melbourne – in picturesRead moreThe horde had paid hundreds of dollars, some even thousands, for the privilege of seeing athletes in the storied American pastime run out into Melbourne’s sporting cathedral. They had come from more than 30 countries, with almost one in 10 making the trip from the US. They had waited patiently in snaking lines that peaked around 7.30am, but even then it took only 20 minutes to get past security.These Americophiles had spent years following the sport through ESPN and the Madden series of video games, via US podcasters and fantasy football. Here they were now, living their American sporting dream, celebrating a passion that had survived in the shadows of the Australian mainstream.It is a hobby that reflects a reverence for the nation across the Pacific, one that is based on defensive lines, rather than defence bases. Aukus, in this context, appeared a natural fit.One man, holding four large beers, was one of few in the crowd wearing a Jacksonville Jaguars jersey, even if he admitted he was a San Diego Chargers fan. His spirits were high, and sentiment genuine, when saying the vibes were “incredible”.View image in fullscreenFans arrive ahead of the NFL match in Melbourne.Photograph: Josh Chadwick/Getty Images“I took the train here this morning and the amount of jerseys I saw was crazy,” he said, saying his name was Jarrod Wilson, who also happens to be a former Jaguars player. Alongside him was John Stockton, coincidentally one of the NBA’s greatest point guards. “We’ve counted every team jersey that we’ve seen and we’ve hit all 32,” Wilson said.Apart from the cornucopia of licensed merchandise, the MCG turnout was clearly different to those that attend AFL and cricket games, the traditional sporting attractions in this corner of the country. There were very few children – it was a school day after all – and if there were roughly 10,000 Americans in the crowd, there appeared to be fewer women.More than a game: NFL hopes Melbourne visit will advance case for Olympic flag footballRead moreAlexandra Augustinus, who was there with her husband and brother and curious to see the spectacle first hand, was the only woman in her row. She said it felt “so different” to the AFL, but was impressed by an experience heavy on entertainment and a stadium full of enthusiasm. “I’ve been really shocked by how many Americans have come over, that’s really fun because they’re all dressed up, and they are massive fans. Everyone’s excited.”In hotels, restaurants, pubs and retailers around Melbourne’s CBD, NAB predicted there would be $300m of economic activity this weekend. No one doubts this match has delivered an economic uplift – as well as showcasing Melbourne to millions of viewers overseas – but the bank would not clarify how much of that was over and above what would usually be spent. And the cost to host the match, reported to be at least $10m, is one borne by Victorian taxpayers.View image in fullscreenThe Jonas Brothers perform at half-time.Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty ImagesFriday was the start of a four-year deal to have the NFL in Melbourne, although there may not be a match in Australia every season. Thetiming for next yearalready looks complicated given the start of the NFL season falls during the AFL finals. But few in attendance on Friday were concerned about next year.Famous faces included AFL player Patrick Cripps and Jai Arrow, the NRL back rowerforced into retirement due to motor neurone disease. Rugby league powerbroker Peter V’landys had also ventured into enemy territory, his own sport having gone the other way with their Las Vegas season opener.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA mellow US anthem before kick-off was appropriate for a match that marked 25 years since the September 11 terrorist attacks. That tragedy was acknowledged by the prominence of US Marines and the Australian Defence Force, who provided a fly-over. Advance Australia Fair was sung by pop star-slash-swimmer Cody Simpson, before Eddie McGuire and G-Flip came out to toss the coin as the boos – presumably for the former Collingwood president – rained down.Organisers had imported the clear-bag policy, which barred patrons from bringing backpacks into the ground. Instead only small transparent plastic containers were allowed, roughly the size of an A4 piece of paper. It meant fans were expected to spend almost as long at the MCG as they might in a day of Test cricket, but without the thermos of tea. Instead, the bars and food vendors – concession stands in American parlance – were jammed throughout the morning.View image in fullscreenChristian McCaffrey of the 49ers runs with the ball.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPThe narrow rectangular field meant fans were roughly 50m from the action at the halfway line, and the entire lower level spent much of the afternoon on their feet, straining on tip toes to see the action on the field. Booming through the stadium’s speakers was the American announcer, who would walk through the play situation and the athletes involved; which cornerback broke up a play, or giving a reminder of the downs and yardage. Together with short music clips, the presentation delivered a relentless sensory experience, even if the contest –won easily by the 49ers 27-7– was unmemorable.Circus or spectacular? Either way, NFL’s exercise in cultural exchange has gripped Melbourne | Jack SnapeRead moreDisney products The Jonas Brothers, one of whom missed a flight and only just arrived in time to perform, delivered a muted half-time performance. Kylie Minogue – scheduled for the AFL grand final later this month – promises a far more dazzling experience.With the 49ers leading 10-7 at the break, the American pop trio performed a brief medley of hits. They were accompanied by the Rams cheerleaders, their three men among two dozen woman roughly the reciprocal of the crowd’s gender split.Despite their global fandom and pop success, a cover of John Farnham’s 30-year-old hit You’re the Voice resonated with the crowd most. It was a reminder that not everything is better in America.Explore more on these topicsNFLLos Angeles RamsSan Francisco 49ersAustralia sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mas closes on first Vuelta after Dunbar reels in Buitrago to win stage 19 summit finish  | Vuelta a España | The Guardian
description: Pinarello Q36.5 rider Eddie Dunbar won stage 19 by 14 seconds while Enric Mas maintained his 1:37 cushion in the race for the red jersey
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pinarello Q36.5 rider Eddie Dunbar won stage 19 by 14 seconds while Enric Mas maintained his 1:37 cushion in the race for the red jersey
Content: Eddie Dunbar roars with delight after passing Santiago Buitrago with 300m of the stage left to take the win.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAView image in fullscreenEddie Dunbar roars with delight after passing Santiago Buitrago with 300m of the stage left to take the win.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAVuelta a EspañaMas closes on first Vuelta after Dunbar reels in Buitrago to win stage 19 summit finishPinarello Q36.5 rider Dunbar wins stage by 14 secondsMas maintains his 1min 37sec cushion in red jersey raceAgence France-PresseFri 11 Sep 2026 12.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIrishman Eddie Dunbar secured a stunning last-ditch victory on stage 19 of theVuelta a Españaas Spaniard Enric Mas maintained his overall lead with only one mountain stage remaining before Sunday’s finale.The 30-year-old caught and passed Colombian Santiago Buitrago with just 300 metres left of the mountainous 210km slog from Vélez-Málaga to Peñas Blancas.Bahrain Victorious rider Buitrago struck out for home inside the final 2km to distance his three breakaway companions, including Dunbar, who initially did not react. However, the Pinarello Q36.5 rider launched his counterattack in the final kilometre and wasted little time in reeling in Buitrago, who is the leader of the mountains classification. Dunbar finished 14sec ahead of Buitrago, with his British teammate, Thomas Gloag, coming home in third 23sec back.“It’s incredible, I really didn’t expect this today,” said Dunbar. “I even said in the team radio after about 50 or 60km that today wasn’t my day. I wasn’t feeling good. Then I ended up in the break and my legs came around a bit.”View image in fullscreenEnric Mas salutes the crowd after negotiating stage 19 unscathed.Photograph: Javier Lizón/EPAMovistar’s Mas comfortably held on to his 1min 37sec lead over four-time former champion Primoz Roglic as the overall contenders crossed the line together.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRoglic’s Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team and the EF Education-Easypost outfit of former Giro d’Italia winner Richard Carapaz tried to increase the pace on the 18km final climb to the finish. However, they were unable to exert any pressure on Mas, who followed comfortably as he bids for a first Vuelta title after three previous second-place finishes.Explore more on these topicsVuelta a EspañaCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Welcome to the Madring, a new, brutal and unforgiving F1 challenge for Spanish Grand Prix | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: New hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunities
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: New hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunities
Content: Spectators watch on opposite La Monumental corner at the Madring circuit.Photograph: David Davies/PAView image in fullscreenSpectators watch on opposite La Monumental corner at the Madring circuit.Photograph: David Davies/PAFormula One 2026Welcome to the Madring, a new, brutal and unforgiving F1 challenge for Spanish Grand PrixNew hybrid street circuit has fast corners and virtually no margin for error – but limited overtaking opportunitiesGiles Richardsat the MadringFri 11 Sep 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn Madrid’s Puerta del Sol this week,Formula Onefans were not shy in calling on the gods to look kindly on their favoured drivers on a newly built circuit that appears punishingly unforgiving.Legend has it that rubbing the paws or backside of the bear in the famous El Oso y el Madroño statue at the square’s heart confers good luck. The drivers may well need it. Day one of action at the Madring track began with F2’s Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak careening into the barriers and his car catching fire, leaving the onlookingGeorge Russellshocked before the F1 drivers took to the wheel.View image in fullscreenThe Art Racing car of Tasanapol Inthraphuvasak is removed on a lorry.Photograph: Kym Illman/Getty ImagesDespite fears the Madring would not be ready, it is done and dusted. What sort of racing it will present for the Spanish Grand Prix is now the question. Billed as a street circuit, it is in fact a hybrid of roads and purpose-built track; narrow, with fast corners and walls looming for much of the lap, there is going to be virtually no margin for error.Hamilton confirms no rules of engagement at Ferrari despite Monza clash with LeclercRead moreThis was demonstrated in F2 practice on Friday. Russell, who had previously described the Madring as the “most risky” on the calendar was watching F2 practice with some members of the media in the Mercedes motorhome when the Art Grand Prix driver’s crash happened.“Oh wow,” he said. “This circuit is mental.” Inthraphuvasak, who leapt out in short order after his car burst into flames, had crashed rearward at high speed into the barriers after spinning at turn 19, and Russell observed the Madring was set to be an even sterner test than Monaco.“I would put this as a circuit that has less margin, purely because of the speed,” he said. “In Monaco the walls are closer but because you’re going slower – if you make a mistake you’re not into the wall as quickly, and you can recover it sometimes. It’s more lock-up. Here, there’s less margin.”The issue, explained Russell, was that the fast corners were combined with the angles of the barriers on exit. “You see at this barrier, it’s kind of like coming back on to the track,” he said, indicating where the smoking wreckage of Inthraphuvasak’s car was sitting. “So if you are to go wide and hit the wall, you’re not hitting it at the same angle as the car is going. The car is going towards the wall but the wall is sort of coming in.”When F3 held a test here recently, there were 19 red flags and three cars suffered broken chassis. “They’re Formula 3 drivers, but it’s a track that kills cars,” was the assessment of Williams’ team principal, James Vowles. Russell said he was surprised it was only 19 red flags.View image in fullscreenMercedes driver George Russell during free practice.Photograph: David Davies/PAHe was not alone in his concern, with Lewis Hamilton echoing his sentiments. “It’s a massively challenging circuit,” he said. “Of all the new tracks I’ve gone to, this one, maybe Saudi, are the two closest in terms of how difficult it was to get on top of the car and find the right lines.”There was at least cause for optimism after first practice with the hour-long session proceeding without a stoppage and the walls receiving only some delicate glances at best. The drivers were up to speed with alacrity and no little composure, with Russell topping the timesheets for Mercedes, from his teammate, Kimi Antonelli, who leads Russell by 66 points in the world championship. In the second session, however, Britain’s Arvid Lindblad came a cropper, losing the rear of his Racing Bulls car in turn 13 and slewing sideways into the barriers in another heavy impact, but from which he emerged unhurt. The session was halted by a red flag but resumed, and completed with Antonelli on top from Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc and Hamilton.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCertainly the sense of spectacle was delivered, as was surely the aim, with high speeds on a narrow track flanked by walls, and illustrated in its signature corner La Monumental, a 550m stretch of 13.5-degree banking, through which the cars are accelerating to great effect, compressing into the track amid an amphitheatre of grandstands before heading over a blind crest and barrelling downwards out of the corner. There is even a little history here too, with turn eight – “El Bunker” – named forLa Mata Espesa, two bunkers built in 1936 by the Republican forces to protect Madrid from attack during the Spanish civil war. Their preservation was a condition of the track being built.The circuit lacks the backdrop of Monaco of course, flanked only by the large, grey square boxes so beloved of convention centres situated in industrial estates. Some areas are still somewhat building site-esque too, but the bits that matter are in place and for the fans it is but a 20-minute subway ride from the city. Indeed, it is an achievement that might be considered no little feat given there were objections to it happening at all, relating to costs, the construction and complaints about sound levels exceeding legal levels.View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell (centre) cycles round the Madring as teams and drivers get accustomed to the new circuit.Photograph: David Davies/PAThe circuit, which sits around the Institución Ferial de Madrid convention centre area between the city centre and the airport, is perhaps exactly what F1 had in mind with its pursuit of “destination races” in cities. This means events that would be entertainment weekends, to rival the Superbowl and draw fans and finance to the host city. But it also faces a further acid test to come. There remains concern, though, as to quite what sort of racing will be possible come Sunday. The drivers were largely in agreement that it would be a thrilling technical challenge of inch-perfect execution, but equally sceptical about whether overtaking would be possible. As the four-time world champion Max Verstappen noted, the main braking zones such as turns five, eight and 17 are angled, making passing all but impossible with drivers simply putting their car in the middle of the track.“You can’t really go for an overtake because you’re braking but you’re steering either right or left, which is the worst thing you can do for creating an overtaking opportunity,” he said. This will put huge emphasis on qualifying but also raises the spectre of a procession on Sunday, potentially only interrupted by what many still consider will be inevitable red-flag stoppages. A long, hot train of cars circling in unchanging order is certainly not the hoped-for debut at F1’s newest circuit and a threat for which the promoters might too be hoping for some ursine intervention.Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneGeorge RussellMotor sportfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning | Premier League | The Guardian
description: English top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighter
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: English top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighter
Content: Chelsea's Cole Palmer, Liverpool's Bradley Barcola, Arsenal's Kai Havertz.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChelsea's Cole Palmer, Liverpool's Bradley Barcola, Arsenal's Kai Havertz.Composite: Getty ImagesPremier LeagueBallon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turningEnglish top flight’s forwards are not well represented on the list, reflecting a season of set-piece grapple, but 2026-27 already looks brighterJacob SteinbergFri 11 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePremier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players onthis year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.The trio givingArsenala presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.Men’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years?Read moreIt was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.View image in fullscreenAnthony Gordon has said Spanish football demands a ‘different level of tactical and technical intelligence’.Photograph: Newhouse Media/MB Media/Getty ImagesNow comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.Graphic showing Premier League games have been more end-to-end early in 2026‑27There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up.Manchester Citymay soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals –Arsenal taking on Chelseaat the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHavertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard,Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.View image in fullscreenFlorian Wirtz has struggled to adapt to the pace of the Premier League.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoThis matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenalbut stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool afterhis arrival from PSG.Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beatChelsea. It felt refreshing.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBallon d'OrArsenalChelseaLiverpoolManchester CityLa LigafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurt | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: England reached the World Cup semi-finals although the midfielder did not play a minute but he is key to Manchester United’s hopes in the derby
Author: David Hytner
Headline: England reached the World Cup semi-finals although the midfielder did not play a minute but he is key to Manchester United’s hopes in the derby
Content: Kobbie Mainoo’s statistics this season show a player just as adept on the ball as off.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo’s statistics this season show a player just as adept on the ball as off.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoManchester UnitedKobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurtEngland reached World Cup semis yet midfielder did not play a minute. But he is key to Manchester United in derbyDavid HytnerFri 11 Sep 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a sight the England press pack became increasingly used to seeing after the team’s World Cup matches over the summer. Kobbie Mainoo was invariably the first to leave the dressing room, walk through the mixed zone – eyes dead ahead, features impassive – and board the bus.It was as if he could not get out of the stadiums quick enough andthe further England progressedthe more pronounced it started to feel. There was a real gap between Mainoo and the next England player to depart the stadiumin the knockout rounds. The Manchester United midfielder is inscrutable, even in the heat of battle. It is part of his enviably unflappable temperament. It was no great leap to imagine what lay behind the mask – tremendous frustration as Thomas Tuchel kept on leaving him out.Sesko soars as Manchester United surge past Sabah on Champions League returnRead moreMainoo did not play a single minute at the tournament. He was an unused substitute all the way to the semi-final exit against Argentina, and when everyone expected to see him in thethird-place playoff against Francehe did not make the bench. The Football Association said before the game he had picked up an unspecified injury.For Mainoo it was a lost summer and yet it was physically and mentally draining all the same, what with the training and travel; the demand to stay focused as he waited and waited. Like every player who was part of a squad that reached the final weekend of the World Cup, he reported late for pre-season training with his club. Mainoo played the last half hour of United’s final friendly against Milan and that was it. On the opening weekend of the season, he was fit enough only to be a substitute at Hull, coming on with 23 minutes to goand United 2-0 down, en route to a damaging defeat.There has been a spotlight on Mainoo, with some fans wondering how he would react to the suffocation of his World Cup dream; his treatment by Tuchel, who preferred Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice in the deeper midfield positions and, also, at various times, Reece James, Jude Bellingham, Jordan Henderson, Morgan Rogers and Nico O’Reilly. Nobody should have worried. Mainoo is made of stern stuff. United regeared their midfield to the tune of £155m during the transfer window, adding Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. Baleba has not yet played because of injury, but as United prepare for Sunday’s derby at Old Trafford, it is Mainoo who has reasserted himself.The 21-year-old has been outstanding in each of United’s matches since the opener at Hull – against Ipswich, Everton and then Sabah in the Champions League on Thursday night. The question for Michael Carrick in the derby will be Mainoo and who in front of the back four.View image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo in action against Sabah in United’s 4-0 Champions League win.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/SportsphotoThere is a reason why the United support have adapted the lyrics to Billy Ocean’s Love Really Hurts Without You to declare that their team cannot play without Mainoo. A couple of statistics. In the past three games, he has attempted 211 passes and completed 201, which represents extraordinary security on the ball – particularly given the frequency with which he has it. Also, the degree of risk inherent to so much of what he does.Then there is the number that shows he made a game‑high 15 defensive contributions against Ipswich and Everton. He is improving out of possession. As much as anything, though, it is the quickness of the feet, the hip-shaking feints and changes of direction; how he simultaneously keeps his opponents on their heels and recalibrates United’s angles of attack.Mainoo, of course, has already made his big comeback this year. Ruben Amorim could not fit him into his 3-4-2-1 system; the Portuguese did not trust him defensively. But even so, it continues to feel absurd that Amorim did not give him a single start in the Premier League last season. Mainoo’s first in the competition camein January against Cityat Old Trafford after Carrick had taken over.It was the first match of Carrick’s second spell as the club’s manager and nobody really knew how it would go. “The players … maybe myself [as well], the coaches, obviously you guys in the media,” Carrick says. Everything came together in spectacular fashion, United winning 2-0, Mainoo straight back into the groove that had helped him win over Amorim’s predecessor, Erik ten Hag.If it was an ignition point for Carrick, it was the same for Mainoo, whose form for the remainder of the season helped to drive United to a third-place finish and convince Tuchel to take him to the World Cup. As an aside, Mainoo v Anderson, who completed a £116m move from Nottingham Forest to City in July, will be box office. Anderson was a target for United before City blew them away with their offer. He called City “the kings of Manchester” on the day he signed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUnited’s dominance of the derby in January was almost total and a key takeaway was the slick first-time football they played. Remember the passing sequence when Rayan Cherki was triangulated by Matheus Cunha, Luke Shaw and Bruno Fernandes? The click was immediate for Carrick. This is the type of stuff that he wants; what he needs to see more of against City as he hopes to locate a bit of early-season momentum.View image in fullscreenKobbie Mainoo had a delayed start to the league season because of his involvement with England at the World Cup.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPACarrick knows a deep-sitting tempo-setter when he sees one, the player of the pass before the pass, and he doubled down on this sort of technician with his summer reboot, especially in Tielemans. It was also noticeable that when the luckless Mason Mount, who is back from his latest injury, came on for Tielemans against Sabah, he did so in a deeper midfield role. Carrick’s idea is to play through the middle. It is about balls to feet, timing, distances.“It was nice to get Mason on in the second half and Andrey Santos [for Mainoo] and keep seeing the same things,” Carrick says. “It’s the combinations and connections. Taking the ball and playing close together at times. We have the technical ability for the boys to take the ball in the middle of the pitch. A lot of it is on wavelength and understanding … where each of them want the ball, which we are developing. It’s probably something that we’ve done a bit more of this season.”Carrick is expected to start Tielemans alongside Mainoo with Fernandes as the third midfielder. They will be up against Anderson, Enzo Fernández and Cherki. It is a mouthwatering showdown. It will be where the derby is won or lost.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: West Ham cut loose to hit Wrexham for six and go top of Championship | Championship | The Guardian
description: West Ham returned to the top of the Championship with a 6-0 demolition of Wrexham
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: West Ham returned to the top of the Championship with a 6-0 demolition of Wrexham
Content: Manor Solomon completes Wrexham’s humiliation with West Ham’s sixth goal.Photograph: John Walton/PAView image in fullscreenManor Solomon completes Wrexham’s humiliation with West Ham’s sixth goal.Photograph: John Walton/PAChampionshipWest Ham cut loose to hit Wrexham for six and go top of ChampionshipPress AssociationFri 11 Sep 2026 17.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWest Ham secured their fourth league win in a row as they returned to the top of theChampionshipwith a thumping 6-0 win over Wrexham at the London Stadium. It was a marvellous display of attacking football from Nuno Espírito Santo’s side, who swept to victory with room to spare and six different scorers.Jarrod Bowen got the ball rolling after 28 minutes, Joël Piroe made it two before the break, then Konstantinos Mavropanos, Taty Castellanos, Mohamadou Kanté and Manor Solomon all scored in the second half as the Welsh side were dealt a hiding. The performance was further evidence the Hammers are finding their feet in the second tier after failing to win any of their first three games following Premier League relegation.Daniel Kretinsky to become biggest West Ham shareholder in blow to Amanda StaveleyRead moreThey should have led inside seven minutes, Castellanos sending a free header from Solomon’s cross over from six yards. Bowen then got clear in the box from a quick throw, but his shot was turned against the crossbar by a reflex save from Anthony Patterson. From the corner that resulted, Mavropanos headed a foot wide at the far post.Piroe was guilty of an awful miss midway through the half, leaning back and blasting high into theWrexhamfans behind Patterson’s goal. Bowen showed him how it was done a minute later. Morato’s cross from the right was timed perfectly into the six-yard box, where the home side’s captain was arriving ahead of Jacques Ekomié to guide it into the far corner.Mavropanos cleared off the line from George Dobson with Mads Hermansen beaten, which proved to be the closest Wrexham would come to a goal. Castellanos stayed onside and strode on to a through pass before unselfishly squaring the ball for Piroe to make it 2-0 before the break.Patterson prevented Solomon from putting the game beyond Wrexham in the first two minutes of the second half, racing from his goal to smother the forward’s low shot. It would be a momentary reprieve and under a minute later it was 3-0. From Bowen’s corner, Mavropanos was left free inside the six-yard box to head home.Bowen flashed a shot inches wide after cutting inside as the besieged visitors teetered on the edge of an all-out collapse in east London. West Ham’s fourth came from a Wrexham corner. A poor ball into the box was collected by Kyle Walker-Peters, who dashed away on the counter, exchanging passes before teeing up Castellanos to slot the ball into the corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKanté came off the bench and made it 5-0, a lovely rising finish after being sent clear by Solomon, then the Israel international completed the rout with a deflected shot via a post.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWest Ham UnitedWrexhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League news: Iraola values Wirtz’s work ethic; Moyes backs ‘senior citizen’ Grealish | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Liverpool manager insists midfielder should be judged by his influence rather than numbers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Liverpool manager insists midfielder should be judged by his influence rather than numbers
Content: Florian Wirtz has face criticism as £116m Germany international has one assist and no goals in the Premier League so far.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Allstar Picture Library/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenFlorian Wirtz has face criticism as £116m Germany international has one assist and no goals in the Premier League so far.Photograph: Richard Sellers/Allstar Picture Library/SportsphotoThe talkPremier LeaguePremier League news: Iraola values Wirtz’s work ethic; Moyes backs ‘senior citizen’ GrealishLiverpool manager insists midfielder should be judged by his influence rather than numbersGuardian sport writers and agenciesFri 11 Sep 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 17.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1.Wirtz’s worth ‘not all about statistics’Andoni Iraola has insisted Florian Wirtz should be judged by his influence on Liverpool rather than statistics and believes the player’s impact will increase as his rapport with a new-look attack develops.Wirtz impressed inLiverpool’s defeat of Atlético Madridon Wednesday, having also produced some of his best performances last season in the Champions League. But he has also come in for criticism this season for the amount of times he has conceded possession. The £116m Germany international has one assist and no goals in the Premier League so far.“Flo played very well against Atlético Madrid and I also think he has been unlucky,” said Iraola. “I remember the ‘goal’ he scored against Nottingham Forest; they gave it live and then VAR disallowed it. He could have had very good assists but we haven’t finished them. That is why you cannot just play because of the numbers.“Whether a striker scores a lot of goals or he doesn’t, you have to look at the performances. Does he help us to play well? Yes. Well, someone will score the goals and someone will give the assists. I am not too focused on numbers. Nowadays everything is about numbers, everyone tells players you have to assist, you have to score goals. For me, you have to help us play well. Someone will score the goals and I don’t care if it is the midfielders like it was the other day. Someone will score the goals if we are doing well collectively.”Wirtz created an excellent chance for Bradley Barcola against Atlético and Iraola believes the 23-year-old will exert a greater influence as his understanding with the France international and fellow new signing Victor Muñoz improves.“There is an argument to make that the wingers have changed more than anywhere else,” Iraola said. “Now we have new weapons we can use with Bradley and Victor. With Florian, he is key for us. I am not worried because he will quickly learn where Victor prefers the ball or where Bradley prefers the ball. And, also, Bradley in just his second game you could see they already had a good association. I am not very worried.”Andy Hunter2.Grealish ‘can be a wingers’ role model’David Moyes has told Jack Grealish he wants him to become a role model at Everton for fellow wingers Tyrique George and Tyler Dibling.Grealish made an immediate impact from the bench againstManchester United last Sundayin his first outing since rejoining Everton on loan from Manchester City. Despite a lack of minutes in pre-season, as he recovered from the fractured foot that curtailed his first campaign with Everton, the 31-year-old could start for Moyes’s side at Tottenham on Saturday. The Everton manager wants Grealish to take on more responsibility this season.“Jack knows when he comes here there is an opportunity for him to play and to show what he can do,” Moyes said. “But I also want him to be a senior professional and a role model. We’ve got Tyrique and Tyler and if ever you are looking at somebody for how to play as a wide player, Jack Grealish would certainly be one of them.“I think both of them could learn an awful lot from Jack and I want him to become that senior citizen among them, somebody who teaches them. We’ve got a mature Jack Grealish now as well in terms of understanding the game and being a team player – not that he is an individual but he plays with an individual style.”Moyes believes there is greater expectation on Grealish given it is his second season at the club and there is a need to fill the creative gap created by Iliman Ndiaye’s departure. “If there is one person who would be able to carry that it would be Jack, just because of the way he is,” he added.View image in fullscreenJack Grealish made an immediate impact from the bench against Manchester United last Sunday in his first outing since rejoining Everton on loan.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA“He will find it easy to carry expectation and he’ll be happy to do so. That’s his character. Everybody wants Jack to get back to where he was. His first three months for us last season was hugely important in getting us wins so now it is about getting him right to perform at that level again.“He’s had six and a half months out. He’s had no pre-season games, he came on for 15 minutes in the Community Shield, so he’s had no real football and Jack is someone who thrives on the football. He gets himself fit through the games more so than the training. We need to be careful and see how he goes but he’s looking good.”Andy Hunter3.João Pedro ‘as good as Haaland’, says AlonsoXabi Alonso has claimed João Pedro is at Erling Haaland’s level and similar in style to Karim Benzema. The Chelsea striker has reacted to missing out on Brazil’s World Cup squad by making an excellent start to the season and was named the Premier League’s player of the month on Friday.João Pedro has scored twice in his first three league appearances and has formed an exciting attacking trio with Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers. Chelsea have scored 16 goals in all competitions and Alonso did not hold back when asked if the 24-year-old is as good as Haaland. “I would say yes,” Chelsea’s manager said. “If you count how many top strikers we have in the Premier League, I’m sure that João is there. Haaland for sure is there. So I would rate him that way.”The range of João Pedro’s game has added to his threat. Alonso played with Benzema at Real Madrid and sees similarities between the pair. “In many things he reminds me of Benzema,” he said. “He is good in the box, he is good out of the box, he is good coming to his left side, he is good with the head, he is very complete, he is intelligent. Still young, still things to develop, but many, many absolutely outstanding qualities.”Chelsea host Hull on Saturday afternoon and will be looking for a strong home performances afterfighting back from 2-0 down to beat Leeds 6-3in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday.View image in fullscreenJoão Pedro has scored twice in his first three league appearances for Chelsea.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersPalmer was key to the comeback and revealed that Alonso, who had rotated heavily, ripped into his players at half-time against Leeds. “I was angry with myself that I didn’t help the players to play better or have a better feeling,” Alonso said. “There is a moment that you try to explain what is not working well, try to make preparations and then there is a moment that you need to kick their arse a little bit, in a nice way. It worked – not for me but the players who came on with a better quality and better everything in the second half.”Chelsea will again be without Moisés Caicedo. The midfielder is yet to start this season and Alonso does not want to risk him.Jacob Steinberg4.De Zerbi wants exile Richarlison to stayRoberto De Zerbi insists he does not regret the handling ofRicharlison’s situation at Tottenhamafter the forward was omitted from his Premier League squad, even though Spurs are yet to score in the competition.De Zerbi said Richarlison had in effect exiled himself by refusing to sign a new contract and repeatedly saying he wanted to leave. The 29-year-old’s absence looks increasingly unfortunate for Spurs after three league matches. They have never gone four league games without scoring at the start of a season.De Zerbi described Richarlison’s omission as a “consequence” of the Brazilian’s actions over the past month and a half. A deadline-day move to Everton, who visit the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday, collapsed after Spurs had signed replacements. Richarlison continues to train with the first team. “If I had decided myself to leave him outside of the squad, I would have regrets,” De Zerbi said. “But the decision has not even been taken by the club.”The Italian said it would be “much better” if Richarlison were in his squad, happy to stay and “maybe to extend his contract, because he is still an important player, he was important last season, we can’t forget. But we can’t forget also the last 45 days.”De Zerbi is missing last season’s three top scorers: Richarlison, João Palhinha, who left for Benfica, and Cristian Romero, who joined Atlético Madrid. Mykhailo Mudryk signed on loan from Chelsea, picked up an injury in training. An ankle scan revealed ligament damage that will keep the winger out for about six weeks. De Zerbi feels the “silly injury”, caused by playing too much after being out for so long, could have been avoided.View image in fullscreenRoberto De Zerbi believes Sávio ‘can score more goals – even if he isn’t Harry Kane.’Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersSávio arrived from Manchester City for £75m, closely followed by Omar Marmoush on loan. Marmoush scored only 10 league goals in a season and a half at Manchester City, but was more prolific in the Bundesliga at Eintracht Frankfurt. “In terms of goals he’s not Harry Kane but he can score more goals than he has done in the last two seasons,” De Zerbi said.“If you analyse his qualities, he can score more goals and he has to demand more goals from himself. Even the stupid goals, he has to change his habits after being used to scoring the great goals.”De Zerbi says his players have lacked confidence and freedom on the pitch this season and challenged them to take more risks and show personality “like a big team” and “like big players”.Meanwhile, Lucas Bergvall has signed a new long-term contract. The 20-year-old wanted to leave in the summer but was convinced to stay by De Zerbi.Sam Cunningham5.Manchester United take action against ticket toutsManchester United believe they have disrupted organised ticketing networks having removed 685 season tickets as part of a contentious ticket touting investigation. The club’s summer crackdown resulted in widespread condemnations from fans and supporter groups after many innocent people faced the threat of sanction.The 1958 this week called for fans to “stand united” against the “season ticket ban fiasco” in a protest before Sunday’s derby against Manchester City as a “line has been crossed”.United released an outcome update on their investigation before this weekend’s action, revealing that 685 accounts have been subject to a ban while 464 supporters received a reduced sanction or final warning.A club statement read: “Bans were issued where there was significant misuse of the ticketing system for financial gain. This included the operation of organised ticketing networks, which were controlling, selling and distributing tickets from hundreds of accounts.“These actions undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United. Our focus now turns to ensuring these tickets are returned to our supporters. All season tickets released through this process will be offered to supporters on the season ticket waiting list.”United say the investigation identified 1,617 accounts that required further review due to what it calls “unusual activity”. Of those stripped of season tickets, 113 failed to respond to requests for further information, 73 did not appeal and 499 received bans upheld by an independent appeals panel.Press Association6.Jaissle hopes Fernandez-Pardo can face LeedsMatthias Jaissle revealed that summer signing Matias Fernandez-Pardo is edging closer to starting for Newcastle. The 21-year-old forward arrived on Tyneside from Lille on deadline day and has featured as a substitute in Newcastle’s last two matches.Speaking before Monday’s fixture with Leeds, Jaissle said: “Yeah, he’s getting closer. I said that we need to be smart with his load management. Now he’s getting more and more minutes. He has now almost a full training week to Leeds, that helps him a lot. I think it’s the first time now since he arrived, and then we can make the decision on Sunday, maybe even on Monday.”Jaissle was also pleased to see Tino Livramento continue his return from injury as the full-back got 45 minutes of football under his belt with an appearance from the bench during the second half ofTuesday’s Carabao Cup win over Millwall.“I’m happy for him that he got 45 minutes on a high level against a strong opponent in difficult circumstances playing there in Millwall,” the Newcastle manager said. “That makes us proud to see him already on a high level.”Press Association7.Rose needs a win before things get RealMarco Rose says Bournemouth must stick together to end his winless start in the Premier League before the club’s maiden European campaign begins. The south coast club have taken only two points from a possible nine under their new head coach after surrendering late leads to lose 2-1 at Manchester City and draw 1-1 with Everton and 2-2 against Newcastle.Bournemouth, who thumped Championship club Lincoln City 4-0 in the Carabao Cup in midweek, host Brentford on Saturday before a landmark Europa League fixture away to Spanish side Real Sociedad on Thursday.“It’s important and I would love to have it done already but it’s not the case,” Rose said of securing a first top-flight victory. “We need to work for it. We have to stick together, we have to believe in it. I think a home game with our fans is a big chance to do it and always the next game is a chance to change things, to change situations. We are quite confident.”View image in fullscreenMarco Rose is desperate for a first win at Bournemouth, starting with Brentford before facing Real  Sociedad on Thursday.Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PABournemouth have never beaten Brentford in the Premier League, losing five and drawing three of the previous eight meetings between the clubs. “We just have to continue, so it means finding the right balance in everything,” said Rose. “We didn’t get nervous after the first results, we played quite confident, and that’s what we have to now do in the next game: believe in our qualities and our abilities.”Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueThe talkEvertonLiverpoolChelseaManchester UnitedTottenham HotspurBournemouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall: ‘I’ve seen all of the meltdowns and it annoyed me’ | Everton | The Guardian
description: Midfielder on rising above the negativity after Everton’s struggles in the transfer window, becoming a leader in the dressing room and a possible England call-up
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Midfielder on rising above the negativity after Everton’s struggles in the transfer window, becoming a leader in the dressing room and a possible England call-up
Content: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall believes Everton’s squad is good enough to play in Europe.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenKiernan Dewsbury-Hall believes Everton’s squad is good enough to play in Europe.Photograph: Robbie Hoad/Every Second Media/ShutterstockEvertonInterviewKiernan Dewsbury-Hall: ‘I’ve seen all of the meltdowns and it annoyed me’Andy HunterMidfielder on rising above the negativity after Everton’s struggles in the transfer window, becoming a leader in the dressing room and a possible England call-upFri 11 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTransfer deadline day may be “exciting for everyone”, as Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall puts it, but his experience ofthattransfer deadline day atEvertonhauled him through the same gamut of emotions as every Evertonian. Excitement turned to bewilderment before the conclusion of the window left the midfielder exasperated, but for entirely different reasons to a fanbase left questioning the club’s direction under The Friedkin Group.How, now, is the mood in the squad? It is the obvious place to start after a deadline day that left David Moyes with fewer players than he had at the beginning, one striker and no cover for either full-back position. It also featured the US international strikerFolarin Balogun walking out on a £40m transferminutes after submitting a deal sheet. “Really good to be honest,” Dewsbury-Hall insists. “Definitely not the same mood as what I’ve seen on the outside. There’s a good mentality this year of: ‘We’ll show everyone.’” Everton’s performances so far this season support that view.“I’ve seen all of the reactions, all of the meltdowns, and in all honestly it annoyed me a bit,” Dewsbury-Hall says in forthright and insightful fashion. “I get where people are coming from; everyone wants to sign everyone and have the perfect squad. But there are still 19 lads in this building who are going to hopefully take this club to good things this year. That was getting disregarded.“I saw people saying: ‘We’ll be lucky to stay up this year.’ What message is that sending to the lads who are already here? I’m not blaming anyone. We get it. It didn’t work. But let’s all be positive – right, it’s done, bang, let’s go – and that’s what we’ve been trying to say in the dressing room. Of course we would have wanted to sign a couple more, but we’re happy with what we’ve got and it’s given us more impetus now to move on.”Moyes has expressed concern over the signals Everton’s transfer business could send to the dressing room at a time when he is trying to push the team on. So has it had a detrimental impact? “Not really, no,” Dewsbury-Hall insists. “I know we’ve got a smaller squad but we’ve got some really good players. Our starting XI is top, a European starting XI.View image in fullscreenKiernan Dewsbury-Hall says he needed his move to Everton to avoid his career stagnating.Photograph: Tony McArdle/Everton FC/Getty Images“I get it, you need a whole squad, but we’ve got 17, 18 players at a really, really good level. I don’t think a couple of years ago it was at that level. Actually I know it wasn’t. Things can be out of your hands in football and that’s what happened for us. But we quickly realised: ‘Hang on a minute, look around the dressing room – top player, top player, top player.’ If we’re doing the right things we can still be successful.”Dewsbury-Hall will be crucial to those prospects. The midfielder has flourished since his £28m arrival from Chelsea last summer, his game-time and growing influence vindicating the decision to leave Stamford Bridge behind. “I’m in the prime years of my career,” he says. “I couldn’t afford to spend more years stagnating.” The 28-year-old’s influence extends behind the scenes. This summer, following Séamus Coleman’s departure, he was nominated for a new leadership group that was established to compensate for the loss of the long-serving Everton captain.“Because Séamus has left such a big hole we need a group of experienced lads to crack on together and keep the standards high and to drive things,” Dewsbury-Hall explains. “It’s just the more experienced lads – [Jordan] Pickford, Tarky [James Tarkowski, the new club captain], Jimmy [James] Garner, myself. The ones that have been playing in the Premier League for years or feel like they are settled at the club.View image in fullscreenKiernan Dewsbury Hall lets fly in Everton’s impressive 2-2 draw with Manchester United.Photograph: Tony McArdle/Everton FC/Getty Images“It’s nice [to be voted in after just one season] but it’s definitely an impact I wanted to have. I’m really pleased that the lads look at me as someone that can be important for the dressing room.”That sense of responsibility is evident in Dewsbury-Hall’s mentoring of fellow midfielder Harrison Armstrong, the 19-year-old who almost joined Nottingham Forest before deadline day only for the furious response of Evertonians at Bournemouth to prompt a U-turn from the club’s owners. “They definitely made their feelings known and obviously it worked,” says Dewsbury-Hall. “Big credit to them for that, they were amazing that day. And I know for a fact it made Harrison feel very good and it helped him. He is a very confident lad and well respected in the dressing room for such a young age.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“If there is anything I can help him with then I will. Shooting’s definitely one because his shooting is sometimes not the best, and I’ve told him that many times. But he’s got pretty much everything else. He always likes to say he’s got a better strike than me so I just tell him to look at the [Crystal] Palace goal [that Dewsbury-Hall scored on the opening day] or the Wolves goal last season. We have good banter.”The Nottingham-born midfielder is clear in his targets for this season: European qualification, which he contends can be achieved despite the smaller squad, a strong cup run, improvement in his all-round game and a first England call-up. His rising performance levels have not gone unnoticed by Thomas Tuchel, who names his squad next Friday.Dewsbury-Hall says: “I know I’m the closest I have ever been now. You get a message two weeks before the squad is announced. I got one for the long list for the World Cup and I’ve had one for these next games. It’s nice. It means you are doing OK. It’s a long, long message. It tells you that it’s a legal requirement for us [the Football Association] to tell you in advance that you are in contention and to be available for these dates. It’s a good feeling because you think: ‘OK, I am close,’ but you know you have to keep pushing it to the last minute. It’s up to me. It’s got to be me that forces his hand to choose me. It’s not going to be given to me.”Nor will anything be given to Everton, but Dewsbury-Hall and company will push on regardless.Explore more on these topicsEvertoninterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Delay the meals’: Mikel Arteta reveals latest maverick Arsenal methods | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Mikel Arteta likes to set players challenges, such as making the dressing room hotter or arriving late, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Mikel Arteta likes to set players challenges, such as making the dressing room hotter or arriving late, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality
Content: Mikel Arteta speaks to his Arsenal players during Wednesday’s 1-0 win over Napoli, a game they took part in following a five-hour flight postponement.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta speaks to his Arsenal players during Wednesday’s 1-0 win over Napoli, a game they took part in following a five-hour flight postponement.Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty ImagesArsenal‘Delay the meals’: Mikel Arteta reveals latest maverick Arsenal methodsManager wants players to cope with things going wrongOther tactics include making dressing room even hotterEd AaronsFri 11 Sep 2026 06.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has revealed that he likes to set players challenges, such as delaying their meals before matches and making the dressing room hotter, to ensure they are fully prepared for any eventuality.Arsenal’s flight to Italy on Tuesday for their Champions League opener against Napoli wasdelayed for more than five hours, with Arteta forced to cancel his pre-match press conference after the squad arrived in Naples just before 10pm local time.The disruption proved no handicap as they made it 13 successive league-stage victories in Europe,thanks to Martin Ødegaard’s second-half winner.Declan Rice shrugs off Arsenal concerns and says 60 games a season is sustainableRead moreArteta has a reputation for his innovative methods having previouslyemployed pickpockets during pre-season training campsand preparing for a trip to Anfield by pumping crowd noises through a speaker.TheArsenalmanager has now explained how his players have been trained to expect things to go wrong. “I love those challenges. I try to create them in pre-season,” he said. “So when they happen, we already experience them and we already know. So, get to the stadium very late, change the routine as soon as the players have to do something else.“Because when it happens, and it can happen, you can miss the flight, the train can be delayed, there’s so much traffic, and I don’t want the players, the staff as well, panicking.“So, when that happens, adapt to it. ‘OK, we have another two or three hours on the plane, how can we use them?’ Play together, spend some time together, sleep, use it, but ­certainly don’t complain and then use it as an excuse because that’s not helpful at all.”Asked what other methods he has employed, Arteta added: “Just delay the meals, delay the transport, take a different route. We have done many things: make the dressing room hotter, more difficult, more challenging, less [massage] beds. Those kind of things. Because we are going to have to adapt to different contexts and we will try to anticipate it and create the best possible conditions. But when there is that element of stress or ­surprise on matchday, it’s important [to be prepared].”Arsenal travel to Sunderland on Saturday night looking to extend their 100% start to the new campaign after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last year. Leandro Trossard scored Arsenal’s second goal beforeBrian Brobbey’s late equaliserand Arteta contrasted the Belgium forward’s reaction to leaving in the summer with that of Gabriel Jesus, whohas complained that he was kept in the dark over his future before being sold to Barcelona. “No one told me nothing,” said the Brazilian, who was made to train separately from the rest of Arsenal’s squad before moving to Barcelona. Trossard, meanwhile, was at the Emirates forlast week’s win over Chelseahaving joined Beskitas in July.“Very surprised, to be fair, especially because with Gabriel I had an individual talk in the dressing room,” said Arteta. “And the words that we used for each other, it was all about gratitude. So, I don’t know. It’s OK. Sometimes I understand when you have to deliver bad news or news that people don’t expect. Those things are reactive. Somebody has to be the bad cop; if I have to be, I have to be.“What is important is normally what happens three months later, six months later. When Trossard comes in, he’s in the dressing room with all of us, the atmosphere and the relation you have with all the players that they left, at some point their relationship has been really good. I hope that’s the same case.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea hand Pedro Neto new deal in wake of his rejecting Manchester City | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Chelsea have rewarded Pedro Neto’s strong start to the season and commitment to the club by giving him a new five-year deal
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Chelsea have rewarded Pedro Neto’s strong start to the season and commitment to the club by giving him a new five-year deal
Content: Pedro Neto has scored twice in five appearances this season under Xabi Alonso.Photograph: Visionhaus/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPedro Neto has scored twice in five appearances this season under Xabi Alonso.Photograph: Visionhaus/Getty ImagesChelseaChelsea hand Pedro Neto new deal in wake of his rejecting Manchester CityWinger shining after summer pursuit by several clubsChelsea felt selling Fernández to City was right moveJacob SteinbergFri 11 Sep 2026 08.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChelsea have rewarded Pedro Neto’s strong start to the season and commitment to the club by handing the winger a new contract. The Portugal international had summer interest from several Premier League clubs includingManchester City, but indicated a desire to stay and play for Xabi Alonso. He has signed a five-year deal with the option of an extra year and is to receive a pay rise.Alonso has used Neto as an attacking wingback and the 26-year-old has scored twice in five appearances. Neto, who has registered 40 goal involvements since joining from Wolves for £54m in 2024, follows other leading players at Chelsea in signing new deals. João Pedro, Reece James and Moisés Caicedo have received improved terms this year, and Cole Palmer signed a new deal in 2024 and committed his future to the club inan interview with the Guardianlast season.Clearlake Capital close on buying out Chelsea co-owners Todd Boehly and Mark WalterRead moreChelsea’s owners have a strategy of giving lengthy incentivised contracts. However, the club have demonstrated that being on those multi-year deals will not stop players from receiving pay increases as reward for good performances. Further contract renewals are expected to be announced soon.Neto’s determination to stay contrasted with the stance of Enzo Fernández, who wassold to City for £125mduring the closing hours of the transfer window.He was not handed a new contract after initial discussions were held. The Argentina midfielder raised questions over his future in March, criticising January’s departure of Enzo Maresca as head coach and sparking talk of a move to Real Madrid by expressing a desire to live in the Spanish capital. Chelsea responded bybanning Fernándezfor two games.Madrid downplayed their interest in Fernández but the 25-year-old continued to push for a new challenge. City, who appointed Maresca as Pep Guardiola’s replacement, emerged as Fernández’s strongest suitors. Chelsea were prepared to hold on to him if their valuation were not met but concluded that selling was the right long-term move. There was disappointment that one of the team’s senior players did not show better leadership when Chelsea were struggling. They missed out on European qualification after finishing 10th.View image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca and Enzo Fernandez during their time at Chelsea. They have been reunited at Manchester City.Photograph: Mark Pain/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Chelsea sacked Liam Rosenior in April and announced Alonso’s appointment in mid-May. They were willing to reintegrate Fernández but he is understood to have submitted a written transfer request. It is understood he also informed Chelsea he had been in contact with a former coach, believed to be Maresca, at the end of last season and during the transfer window.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Stamford Bridge hierarchy concluded that Fernández’s relationship with his teammates was broken after his public comments. Fernández’s representatives have been approached for comment.Sources have dismissed the idea that Chelsea were bullied into selling Fernández. Neto’s renewal is viewed as the latest evidence that key players have bought into the project and will be rewarded.Explore more on these topicsChelseaManchester CityTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Olid’s United on back foot due to late business and unforgiving WSL start | Manchester United Women | The Guardian
description: The new head coach has a harsh spotlight on her as she prepares for Chelsea’s visit on Sunday, but she deserves time, patience and investment in the squad
Author: Suzanne Wrack
Headline: The new head coach has a harsh spotlight on her as she prepares for Chelsea’s visit on Sunday, but she deserves time, patience and investment in the squad
Content: Eva Olid watches her side labour ineffectively against London City Lionesses in their WSL opener.Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEva Olid watches her side labour ineffectively against London City Lionesses in their WSL opener.Photograph: Katie Chan/Action Plus/ShutterstockManchester United WomenOlid’s United on back foot due to late business and unforgiving WSL startHead coach has harsh spotlight on her as she prepares for Chelsea on Sunday, but she deserves time and investmentSuzanne WrackFri 11 Sep 2026 07.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was tough watching Manchester United’s playerslabour ineffectivelyagainst the hungry and aggressive press of London City Lionesses in the Women’s Super League’s opening match. Simi Awujo’s late consolation goal did little to ease the mounting concern for a side that have several teams nipping at their heels.Don’t panic; that has to be United’s message. To an extent, it is very early to be writing the team’s obituary.The new head coach, Eva Olid, had only three weeks to try to implement her ideas about the way the team should play before that match in Bromley on Friday 4 September. That is not long enough for her to peel away Marc Skinner’s imprint on the team.Saloons, school and specialty coffee: NWSL players enjoy new era of side hustlesRead moreThe forward Monica Jusu Bah did not arrive from the Swedish side Häcken until 28 August and Rebeca Bernal signed from Washington Spirit on 2 September. United’s late business, in regards to their managerial change and transfer activity, has put the team and coaching staff on the back foot, playing catch-up with clubs who got most of their business done early in the window, the better to capitalise on the opportunity for a full pre-season presented by the lack of a major international tournament.The problem is the spotlight is harsh on the red side of Manchester. The minority owner Jim Ratcliffe’sdismissive commentsrelating to the women’s team and the lack of serious investment in the squad provide reasons to be somewhat forgiving of the head coach and her charges, their struggles an indictment of a club that seemingly do not fully care.The focus is said to be on a sustainable investment model recruitment-wise and on developing younger players. In isolation they are admirable goals, but in the context of investment gathering pace at other WSL teams and the relative pocket change required at a club of United’s stature to have a transformatory effect on the women’s side, these goals become shackles.There is some irony in Olid leaving Hearts and coming to United. She arrived in Scotland to take charge of an amateur team that had avoided relegation only owing to the expansion of the top division and within five years had taken them to professionalism and a Scottish Women’s Premier League title.
