She felt the level of investment then needed to make Hearts competitive in Europe was lacking and it was announced that she would depart at the end of the season. The WSL and its teams are miles ahead, developmentally, of the SWPL and its sides but Olid has landed at a club that have repeatedly failed to invest substantially enough to make them league or European title challengers.Olid told the Catalan newspaper Ara that she would have stayed at Hearts “if my project continued”. She said: “I wanted to coach in Europe, but it was a preliminary round and perhaps we would be there for a week and get eliminated. I don’t want to go backwards, I preferred to leave after winning everything because otherwise I would feel frustrated.”View image in fullscreenManchester United only lost 2-1 at London City Lionesses last Friday but were outclassed throughout the game.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianFrustration was the name of the game at United under Skinner. The former head coach was frustrated with what he regarded as a lack of support in transfer windows and fans grew increasingly frustrated with a lack of sustained progress. United would take a step forward, such aswinning the FA Cup in 2024or reaching the Champions Leaguequarter-finals last season, then fail to push on.Patience is thin and Olid’s task has been made a lot harder by seven departures and only four additions to what many viewed as an already light squad. Olid has said she has had assurances that United will be active in the winter window. “We have some plans in January about signing players that I really need for my style of play and game model,” she said in her first press conference.However, United have 12 WSL games before January, plus cup games, and with Chelsea visiting on Sunday and a trip to Arsenal next Saturday, they have an extremely unforgiving start.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOlid deserves time and patience. She is well respected and comes with a wealth of experience in her native Spain across boys’ academy football and women’s football and spent time at Houston Dynamo in the US.Alongside battling critics unimpressed with the state of the team in their opening WSL game or questioning her managerial pedigree, she must contend with wave after wave of appalling sexist comments on social media that greet her every appearance. That surely will take a toll.If Olid is able to weather the storm of frustration – which will grow if the team falter while players get used to her philosophy – and to force United to loosen the purse strings, they will be huge accomplishments.Unfortunately, even success on the pitch is unlikely to end the online comments; it will probably just shift their tone. She deserves better in so many ways. The hope will be that she can build a connection with the playing group that enables them to punch above their weight until reinforcements potentially appear in January.Their first opportunity to fend off the vultures is when they welcome Chelsea to Leigh and, with the Blues unconvincing in the final thirdagainst Aston Villalast Saturday, they can have a little hope.Explore more on these topicsManchester United WomenWomen's Super LeagueWomen's footballfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Champions League review: Irish heroics, rejected resignations and Mourinho’s return | Champions League | The Guardian
description: The league phase has begun. From Olise’s continued excellence to Sabah’s pub cleaner turned quiz contestant turned manager, there was plenty to talk about
Author: John Brewin
Headline: The league phase has begun. From Olise’s continued excellence to Sabah’s pub cleaner turned quiz contestant turned manager, there was plenty to talk about
Content: Troy Parrott (Real Betis), José Mourinho (Real Madrid) and Michael Olise (Bayern Munich) all saw their teams begin Champions League play with wins.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Reuters; AP; Uefa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTroy Parrott (Real Betis), José Mourinho (Real Madrid) and Michael Olise (Bayern Munich) all saw their teams begin Champions League play with wins.Composite: Guardian Pictures; Reuters; AP; Uefa/Getty ImagesChampions LeagueChampions League review: Irish heroics, rejected resignations and Mourinho’s returnThe league phase has begun. From Olise’s brilliance to Sabah’s pub cleaner turned quiz contestant turned manager, there was plenty to talk aboutJohn BrewinFri 11 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 08.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA big week forThe league phase has been previewed asBarcelona’sfirst step toward reclaiming a crown last lifted in 2015, with disappointments aplenty since. Lionel Messi claiming just one Champions League title in the last decade of his time at Camp Nou is the starkest statistic. The player anointed as Messi’s successor, Lamine Yamal, is already a European and world champion for Spain, so this is the next frontier. A soggy Wednesday evening at Camp Nou saw Hansi Flick’s team show their attacking chops remain of the highest quality ina 5-1 defeatof Feyenoord. The club presidential regime of Joan Laporta continues to pull levers to confound financial experts, with Gabriel Jesus, one of the summer’s arrivals, scoring his first Barca goal. Yamal got on the scoresheet via a scruffy free-kick after Raphinha had reminded there are further dimensions to that all-star attack, his first goal of his pair two sending Feyenoord defenders skidding.Men’s Ballon d’Or 2026 power rankings: will there be an English winner for the first time in 25 years?Read moreUntil Troy Parrott headed to Seville this summer, the chances ofReal Betisv Lille being a leading attraction to the Irish diaspora were minimal. But now the team in green and white have become an Irish obsession. The goalscorer in theirWorld Cup playoff winin Hungary last year is approaching national hero status. Opting for Andalusia instead of leading West Ham in the Championship confirmed him as a player with broad horizons; the former Tottenham trainee is hitting the heights in La Liga. Having scored the winner against Real Madrid last weekend, throwing back to José Mourinho his rejection when a Spurs teenager, he delivered again in northern France. His dragged, left-footed finish grabbed a 3-2 lead Betis successfully held. “I don’t think I’ll ever have a better night in my whole life,” Parrott said of his glory night in Budapest. If that still holds true, his Friday and Tuesday will have gone close to emulating it.Weird scenes afterFenerbahce’s1-1 draw with Roma when Ismail Kartal, the Turkish club’s veteran coach,resignedpost-match “to clear the way”. The drama was heightened when the Fenerbahce president, Aziz Yildirim, said he would not be accepting the resignation. “There’s no need for him ‌to say that he’d continue,” Yildirim said. “I am his senior, I told him to continue and that’s it. We are a family.” The explanation given for such a sudden exit was Kartal’s annoyance at a bottle being lobbed in his direction. Watch this space.Player of the weekBallon D’Orseason is upon us, and a leading nominee must be Bayern’s brilliantMichael Olise, who scored two goals against Bodø/Glimt. The Norwegians attempted to aggressively mark him but were left with twisted blood as his team scored five second-half goals. The Frenchman gave a typically dry post-match interview. Asked how it feels to score great goals, he said: “I don’t know … I just shoot and it goes in.”Club in focusManchester United on Thursday faced a club formed in 2017, three years after Luke Shaw, who missed the game, was signed.Sabah, Azerbaijan’s champions last season, breaking the dominance of Qurban Qurbanov’s Qarabag, are coached byValdas Dambrauskas, a former United soccer schools and Brentford youth coach who also worked as a pub cleaner and gardener in the UK. His journey from Lithuania to Manchester was funded by a win on Who Wants To Be A Millionaire, where he walked away from Vilnius’s equivalent of Regis Philbin with a sum commensurate with a year’s salary. The homecoming was not too happy as United were ready 4-0 winners, Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes in particular turning on the style. “He absolutely destroyed us,” Dambrauskas said of Fernandes. That did not bode well for Sabah’s matches ahead: Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli travel to Azerbaijan, while a trip to Arsenal awaits.View image in fullscreenAzerbaijani champions Sabah and their quizshow contestant coach had no answers for Youri Tielemans and Bruno Fernandes.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APThey said it“There’s a lot of criticism when a match is boring, but it was crazy today. . … It could easily have ended 7-6. Our midfield was weak, they made changes very early, and I didn’t have much to work with in the centre of the pitch. … I agree with Raul that the goals came as a result of their errors.”José Mourinho’sReal Madrid return is already under scrutiny, and before being interviewed on Movistar after a close-run 2-1 defeat of Inter, he had to listen to on-air criticism from Raúl González, a Madrileno legend. Those midfield comments appeared directed at Trent Alexander-Arnold, who played as one of the trio on a night where fans at the Santiago Bernabéu made clear that better is expected.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionChampions League: Bayern break down Bodø/Glimt, Como put four past LeipzigRead moreLooking aheadThe other side of an elongated international break, the wait will be long – more than a month – for the second round of matches. Holders Paris Saint-Germain, looking for their third straight title, travelling to Manchester City is the grand-slam fixture. Enzo Maresca has made a decent fist of succeeding Pep Guardiola, with four wins in four. Erling Haaland’s pair of goals at Porto took him to 167, third on his club’s all-time scorers’ list, 10 behind Eric Brook, who played his last game during the second world war.Mourinho, should he remain in charge at Real Madrid, will return to Roma whileManchester Unitedtravel to Atlético Madrid, who knocked out United in the last 16 in 2021-22, their only previous meeting in the competition.Explore more on these topicsChampions LeagueBarcelonaReal BetisFenerbahceBayern MunichManchester UnitedJosé MourinhofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nicola Olyslagers finds silver lining in high jump jackpot at Ultimate Championship | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Australian earns biggest payday of career with second behind Mahuchikh Kurtis Marschall finishes fourth after Armand Duplantis in pole vault
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Australian earns biggest payday of career with second behind Mahuchikh Kurtis Marschall finishes fourth after Armand Duplantis in pole vault
Content: Nicola Olyslagers wins biggest payday of her life when finishing runner-up in the women’s high jump at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.Photograph: Christel Saneh/World Athletics/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNicola Olyslagers wins biggest payday of her life when finishing runner-up in the women’s high jump at the World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest.Photograph: Christel Saneh/World Athletics/Getty ImagesAthleticsNicola Olyslagers finds silver lining in high jump jackpot at Ultimate ChampionshipAustralian earns biggest payday of career with second behind MahuchikhKurtis Marschall finishes fourth after Armand Duplantis in pole vaultAustralian Associated PressFri 11 Sep 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicola Olyslagers has had the best worst night of her career after missing out on becoming a new “Ultimate” athletics high jump champion, only to learn to her surprise that she had still leapt to the biggest payday of her life.Australia’s world champion managed to only clear 1.95m on the first night of World Athletics’ inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest on Friday (Saturday AEST), struggling with her approach on a difficult surface on a cold night as Ukraine’s Olympic champ Yaroslava Mahuchikh beat her to the title with a 1.99m leap.Jakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000mRead moreOlyslagers’ runner’s-up spot earned her US$75,000 (AU$105,000) – US$5,000 more than she pocketed for winning the world title last year – as part of the record $US10 million ($14m) prize pot for the streamlined new event thatWorld Athletics hopes will attract a host of new fans.Only when speaking to reporters afterwards did Olyslagers realise just what she would be taking home.“What? Really? I genuinely thought it was just first prize got the 150k and second was like 10,000,” she said. “You are the bearer of good news. That’s fantastic.”Olyslagers, wrapped in a scarf and still shivering 40 minutes after her event, said she struggled with her approach on a firm-surface run-up but, with more than half the field exiting very early, she realised that after two fails at 1.95 a clearance would be enough for second place.She duly sailed over at the final attempt, punching the air in delight. “That’s the happiest I’ve ever been after a 1.95. I think I celebrated as if I’d won the whole competition and it was a really good jump,” she said.“It just showed tonight that all of us were a little bit tired but I mean, that 95 jump, I’m still living off that.”Olyslagers’ domestic rival Eleanor Patterson also looked uncomfortable all evening but took joint third with a modest clearance of 1.91 a week after she’d jumped 10cm higher towin the Diamond League crown.“It’s the lowest I’ve jumped all year. Really, really frustrating,” said Commonwealth champ Patterson. “After the best season of my life I really wanted to enjoy it but I didn’t really.”Triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall managed only fourth with a best of 5.95m as Swedish superstar Armand Duplantis again revelled in being the star attraction, having seen the event open with a theme song he had both co-written and performed.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWith the title secure after a faultless run to 6.20m, the spellbound full house of 20,000 willed him to clear a world record 6.32, but he narrowly failed in what would have been a remarkable 16th world best in six years.Brave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and fieldRead moreEarlier, Australia’s Ky Robinson gave it a real go in the 5,000m, leading at the bell, but got swallowed up in the run for home as Norway’sJakob Ingebrigtsen roared back to his bestwith a superbly judged victory charge.Sarah Billings ran well in her 800m semi-final to qualify for Saturday’s (Sunday AEST) final when there will be four more Australians in action.Abbey Caldwell and Jess Hull will go in the women’s 1500m, Mackenzie Little in the javelin and Oceania record holder Lachlan Kennedy in the men’s 100m.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A perfect storm’: Trescothick refuses to blame England bowlers after Razaullah’s onslaught | England v Pakistan 2026 | The Guardian
description: Marcus Trescothick described ­Pakistan’s late-innings onslaught as a ‘perfect storm’ after England were left with a target of 130 on day four
Author: Simon Burnton
Headline: Marcus Trescothick described ­Pakistan’s late-innings onslaught as a ‘perfect storm’ after England were left with a target of 130 on day four
Content: Pakistan's Razaullah on his way to a rapid-fire 81 at Edgbaston.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenPakistan's Razaullah on his way to a rapid-fire 81 at Edgbaston.Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/ReutersEngland v Pakistan 2026‘A perfect storm’: Trescothick refuses to blame England bowlers after Razaullah’s onslaughtPakistan’s ninth-wicket pair put on 121 in 123 balls‘You’ve got to give a bit more credit to them’Simon Burntonat EdgbastonFri 11 Sep 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 16.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarcus Trescothick described Pakistan’s late-innings onslaught as a “perfect storm”, after the 21-year-old debutant Razaullah and the 36-year-old Mohammad Abbascombined to score 121 off 123 ballsand force a fraying England to come in on the fourth day to chase a target of 130.The interim coach refused to characterise England’s frequently puzzling efforts in the field as embarrassing as Razaullah plundered nine sixes and four fours on his way to a score of 81, and Abbas two sixes – as many as he had scored in 46 career Test innings before the start of this series – in his 42, insisting: “You’ve got to give a bit more credit to them [rather] than trying to target everything that we’ve tried to do.”England not picking a spinner feels like going out for a walk without an umbrella | Andy BullRead moreTrescothick added: “You’d always like to think that you can do it better, and you analyse it afterwards and say, was there an error, or was there a tactic we missed?“You just hope in those situations when you bowl in the right place, which we did on many occasions, that you get the nick, or you bowl them … We hoped to go through them pretty quickly, but they kept smacking it and the young fella came in and made it tricky because when he hit it, he hit it a long way.”Trescothick praised the all-round performance of Razaullah, who has been a revelation with bat and ball in a much-changed Pakistan side.“He’s been very impressive, not just with his batting,” he said. “I thought the pace that he bowled at was good to see. You want to see young players coming through into the game with a bit of something about them and he’s got pace, he’s on it in the field, and then he slogs it like that. Fair play, some of the sixes he hit were pretty impressive to watch.”Razaullah has one previous century to his name, scored last year in his third first-class game – with precisely the same number of runs from boundaries there as here, 70, though with only five sixes – and considers himself an all-rounder.“I was just attacking,” he said. “If the ball was there to be hit, I went for it.” He was one of the seven playersadded to the squad last weekand travelled with just three bats, two of which he broke while flaying England’s bowling around Birmingham.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPakistan now have an outside chance of ending a chaotic tour with an unlikely victory. “Nothing is impossible in cricket,” Abbas said. “Every team faces difficulties and challenges, but as the team spends more time together it is improving. We have got one more chance and anything is possible.”Explore more on these topicsEngland v Pakistan 2026England cricket teamPakistan cricket teamCricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Champagne moment as champions Durham promoted: county cricket, day four – as it happened | County Championship | The Guardian
description: Join Tanya Aldred for updates from the latest round of County Championship matches
Author: Tanya Aldred
Headline: Join Tanya Aldred for updates from the latest round of County Championship matches
Content: 7h ago13.41 EDTNottinghamshire win, Durham promoted and Lancashire slump againTanya AldredWith just two rounds left, the Championship remains knee-knockingly close.Nottinghamshirebecame the third of the big three to collect a win, rolling overHampshireby 54 runs at Trent Bridge, to leave just five points between Somerset in first and Warwickshire in third.Olly Stone, whose end-of-season wicket glut must have caused a selectorial second-look, and bowling like a thoroughbred on a morning canter, finished with six for 28, and 25 wickets at 12.48 in his last four matches, as Hampshire were dismissed for 123. Scott Currie was undefeated on 44.Warwickshire, who play Essex at Chelmsford and then Leicestershire at home, have on paper the easiest run in; while Somerset travel to Headingley to play Yorkshire before entertaining Surrey, and Notts must go to Hove to play Sussex before taking on Yorkshire at Trent Bridge.There was champagne at Chester-le-Street whereDurham, the far the best team in Division Two by a country mile, won promotion and were confirmed Div 2 Champions.Middlesexkept them hanging for a while, with a sensational big-biffing maiden century from on-loan wicketkeeper Harry Duke, but Brydon Carse (four for 116) was too much for Naavya Sharma and after hugs and whoops, Durham walked up the dressing room steps and into Division One. “There was so much disappointment last season,” said head coach Ryan Campbell, “that last day feels like yesterday. I’m pretty proud of the club as a whole, we didn’t panic ... I think everyone was sick of my whiteboard at one point.”At Old Trafford, bottom of the tableGloucestershirecelebrated belatedly finding their mojo, a second win on the bounce. It took them just 31 minutes to rattle throughLancashire’s remaining four wickets, with the headbanded JT Langridge, who bowled like a dream, walking off with the match ball and five wickets in just his second first-class game. Somerset may want their loanee back. Rocky Flintoff was last man out for 65 and his clean-hitting cheered up a few zipped up fleeces in the crowd.The game at Hove betweenSussexandSurreymeandered to a draw while there was a thriller at Derby, where promotion-chasing Kent failed to bat out a draw by just 15 balls.Share

title: Fremantle keep AFL premiership dream alive with win against Geelong in finals classic | AFL | The Guardian
description: The Dockers hold off determined Cats for a 14-point victory in their semi-final at Optus Stadium to set up a showdown with the Swans
Author: Jonathan Horn
Headline: The Dockers hold off determined Cats for a 14-point victory in their semi-final at Optus Stadium to set up a showdown with the Swans
Content: Luke Jackson celebrates as Fremantle Dockers bounce back to defeat Geelong Cats in a seesawing AFL semi-final at Optus Stadium.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPView image in fullscreenLuke Jackson celebrates as Fremantle Dockers bounce back to defeat Geelong Cats in a seesawing AFL semi-final at Optus Stadium.Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAPAFLFremantle keep AFL premiership dream alive with win against Geelong in finals classicDockers defeat Cats 18.12 (120) to 16.10 (106) in semi-finalMinor premiers to meet Sydney in preliminary finalSign up for our free weekly AFL newsletterJonathan HornFri 11 Sep 2026 10.25 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s been some pandemonic nights at Optus Stadium, but nothing that could match this. Fremantle is through to a preliminary final after a semi of the highest quality and the utmost tension.It was simultaneously free-wheeling and nerve-jangling – both high scoring and high pressure. Itactivated Wharfie Timefor just the second time this year, but it wasn’t really needed. The noise was cacophonous, the tension excruciating and the result ultimately just.Fremantle beat Geelong by 14 points: AFL semi-final – live reactionRead moreThere was a period midway through the third term where it looked likeGeelongmight skip away with this game, just like they did against Carlton a week earlier, just as they have so many times in big games over the years. The spring-heeled Ollie Henry was marking everything, Patrick Dangerfield looked menacing, and their fleet of runners were finding space and carving the Dockers up.But if this Fremantle side is truly the one tore-write history, the time-on period in the third quarter will be one of the defining reference points. In particular, Luke Jackson and Andrew Brayshaw were pivotal in this period, blunting the Cats at centre square stoppages and surging the ball forward. They kicked four goals in seven minutes and from that point the game was on their terms.View image in fullscreenLuke Ryan celebrates as Fremantle beat Geelong at Optus Stadium.Photograph: Janelle St Pierre/AFL Photos/via Getty ImagesJackson was colossal all night, with his second, third and fourth efforts keeping the ball alive, and tilting this cutthroat final back Freo’s way. Whenever Geelong threatened, and whenever there was a 50-50 ball to be seized, he would intervene in that wild-eyed way of his. But as Cats coach Chris Scott noted, he has a lot of craft and nous in his game too. He was ably supported by fellow big men Josh Treacy and Patrick Voss, both of whom had stonkingly bad games last week.Nearly all of Treacy’s eight marks were taken under extreme pressure. This included a crucial moment late in the third term when he outpointed Tom Stewart, no mean feat, and thumped home a long set shot to give Fremantle the lead. But it was his defensive effortsthat were crucial. Along with Voss and Jye Amiss, they couldn’t get any separation from their Hawthorn defenders last week, leading in clumps of three and four. But they were far more successful in giving the Cats defenders the slip.It was a hot start, and a very different Fremantle to the tense and tentative side thatturned up against Hawthorn. They flew the gates early, with Shai Bolton booting two in the opening 90 seconds. Bolton was exceptional all night, so light on his feet, so adept at slipping out of congestion and trouble. Crucially, several of their key forwards who were completely blanketed last week – Voss and Treacy in particular – were everywhere early.View image in fullscreenBailey Smith, Shai Bolton and Luke Jackson compete for the ball during the AFL semi-final at Optus Stadium.Photograph: Paul Kane/Getty ImagesAs always, Geelong’s backline pressed high, leaving them vulnerable to the quick ball out the back, which Fremantle exploited repeatedly. They smashed the Cats at centre square throw ups, waltzing out the front of stoppages. If not for some marginal free kicks deep in attack, they could have been a lot more than 25 points up at the first break.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFrom the Pocket: AFL WeeklyJonathan Horn brings expert analysis on the week's biggest AFL storiesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll the metrics at half-time suggested that the Dockers were in total control. But despite their domination of centre square stoppages, despite having 16 more entries and despite the fact that the ball pretty much lived in their forward half, they just couldn’t shake the Cats.Every Geelong goal was carefully crafted or outrageously hustled. Every Geelong goal came when the game seemed to be slipping away from them. The margin rarely strayed far from the three-goal mark – enough to give Geelong hope, and enough to keep the home supporters on one butt cheek.Geelong lost no admirers but they could never quite put the home side away. Yes, Ollie Dempsey’s kung fu goal should have been awarded, yet another example of the magnificence of the AFL’s technology. But they were well beaten in the ruck, in centre square stoppages and whenever the ball was in the air in Fremantle’s forward line. The game was symptomatic of their season, Scott said, with a lot that went wrong and a lot to be proud of.After all the doleful lamentations this time last week, the Dockers wouldfancy their chancesto go on a run now. They took down an exceptionally well-drilled team, and now square off against a still willing, still talented, buttruncated Sydney side. Now they can leave the fishbowl, breathe a huge sigh of relief and chase history.Explore more on these topicsAFLFremantle DockersGeelongAustralian rules footballAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alexander Zverev holds his nerve against Karen Khachanov to reach US Open final | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Alexander Zverev reached the US Open final, his third straight grand slam decider, by beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6)
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Alexander Zverev reached the US Open final, his third straight grand slam decider, by beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6)
Content: Germany’s Alexander Zverev is all smiles after beating Karen Khachanov to make the US Open final.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersView image in fullscreenGermany’s Alexander Zverev is all smiles after beating Karen Khachanov to make the US Open final.Photograph: Robert Deutsch/IMAGN IMAGES/ReutersUS Open Tennis 2026Alexander Zverev holds his nerve against Karen Khachanov to reach US Open finalZverev wins 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6)German reaches third straight grand slam finalTumaini Carayolat Flushing MeadowsFri 11 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbout 107 minutes into men’s semi-final day on Arthur Ashe Stadium, there was finally a touch of tension radiating from the court. After falling down a set and break, his semi-final meeting with his old rivalAlexander Zverevswiftly turning into a beating, Karen Khachanov fought hard to force a second-set tie-break. Deep in that tension-filled tie-break, down 5-6 on his serve, Khachanov saved Zverev’s first set point with a bold forehand winner, and then at 6-7 he punctuated a screaming backhand passing shot winner with an imperious roar of his own.There was a time when Zverev might have faltered under such pressure, but he has won too many big matches this year to allow such a small surge from a lower-ranked opponent to scare him. Zverev composed himself and he quickly regained control, navigating a second tense tie-break in similar fashion as he moved to within one match of winning a second career grand slam title in his last three major appearances by defeating Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6).US Open tennis 2026 men’s semi-final: Frances Tiafoe v Ben Shelton – live buildupRead moreZverev has now reached three consecutive grand slam finals for the first time in his career, with the German following up his maiden grand slam title at Roland Garros with a first Wimbledon final this summer. Zverev reached his first grand slam final here back in 2020, losing to Dominic Thiem in a dramatic five-set match during a closed Covid-era tournament after leading by two sets and serving for the title. He will now compete for the title in his sixth grand slam final.Although Zverev was heavily favoured to win this match, it was not a given. Khachanov’s current ranking of No 50 belies the impressive resume built by the 30-year-old over his career. He reached a career high ranking of No 8, won an Olympic silver medal behind Zverev in Tokyo 2020 and won Paris Masters in 2018. He has also won more matches against Zverev than the other two remaining players combined, with Zverev leading their head to head 6-3 but the Russian winning as recently as last year in Canada.In the end, the quality of Zverev’s serve and his consistency off the ground were more than sufficient to smother the challenge from Khachanov, whose faulty forehand badly leaked errors throughout their time on court, particularly in the decisive moments late in the second and third sets.Back at Roland Garros, after the shock second-round loss of Jannik Sinner, the injury absence of Carlos Alcaraz and the late-career difficulties of Novak Djokovic, the central theme for much of the tournament was whether any player left in the draw could stop Zverev from marching to the title.Zverev has enjoyed a similar path through the top half of this draw, with his highest-ranked opponents en-route to the final No 22 Luciano Darderi and No 28 Alejandro Tabilo. Should he win the US Open, Zverev will have won his first two grand slam titles without facing a top-eight player. Still, a tennis player can only beat the one in front of them and after two tense five-set matches in his first two rounds, Zverev has not dropped a set. No matter who he faces, Zverev will like his chances in the final, where he holds a combined 15-1 record against Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe, his one loss to Tiafoe coming nine years ago.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite the fact that Zverev is the second-ranked player, his opponent was a former semi-finalist here, it is difficult to think of many men’s grand slam semi-final matches over the past few years that have generated so little interest or fanfare. One of the many controversial aspects of the tournament right now is the ticket resale market due to the exorbitant prices of so many of the tickets on those websites during the tournament. There was no danger of punters overpaying for this one: tickets were selling for as low as $21 (£15.50) on StubHub before the match.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026TennisAlexander ZverevUS Open tennisUS sportsmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000m | Athletics | The Guardian
description: Jakob Ingebrigtsen provided the highlight on the first evening of the inaugural Ultimate Championships by storming to victory in the men’s 5,000m
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: Jakob Ingebrigtsen provided the highlight on the first evening of the inaugural Ultimate Championships by storming to victory in the men’s 5,000m
Content: Jakob Ingebrigtsen wins the men's 5,000 metres ahead of his rival Cole Hocker.Photograph: Tamas Vasvari/EPAView image in fullscreenJakob Ingebrigtsen wins the men's 5,000 metres ahead of his rival Cole Hocker.Photograph: Tamas Vasvari/EPAAthleticsJakob Ingebrigtsen blows away bitter rival Hocker in Ultimate Championships 5,000mNorwegian leaves rival Hocker trailing to claim $150,000Briton Jazmin Sawyers second in the women’s long jumpSean Inglein BudapestFri 11 Sep 2026 17.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt is a scene that has become gloriously familiar down the years. Jakob Ingebrigtsen leaving the world’s best athletes gasping in his slipstream, holding one imperious finger in the air, revelling in his athletic genius. But this victory over 5,000m at the inaugural Ultimate Championships carried extra sweetness – and spice.The sweetness? That came from winning a mammoth first prize of $150,000 after an achilles injury he feared might derail his career. And the spice? Well, that was provided by the way Ingebrigtsen utterly obliterated his great American rival Cole Hocker, a man he had branded a “coward” just a week ago.Brave new world: Ultimate Championship brings glowing javelins and $10m prize fund to track and fieldRead moreIngebrigtsen has never been shy of venturing an opinion, and he was aggrieved when Hocker insisted on having his own pacemaker for the 1500m Diamond League final – and then refused to follow him. That led to a high-profile war of words, and a rematch that was the talk of Budapest.And, my, did it live up to the hype. The pace was quick, but the Norwegian was so confident he had time to look around twice on the final lap before launching a devastating final kick to win in 12min 59.24sec, with Hocker, the reigning 5,000m world champion, nearly a second back.“I was predicted number 12 by WorldAthleticscan you imagine?” said a bemused Ingebrigtsen, who is the Olympic champion at this distance after all.Ingebrigtsen was then asked whether it was not only sweet to beat Hocker but … yet before the questioner had finished formulating his sentence, the Norwegian replied “but to crush him” before smiling.His time over the final lap was a rapid 54.39sec, while over the last 100m it was 12.6 – which was particularly impressive given he was only able to step up his comeback from injury in July.“Being injured I was fearing the worst outcome and did not know if I would be able to run at all, especially at this level,” he said. “This is amazing, I am extremely happy.“I had a big hiccup in early May, with the flu, where I was not able to train properly. So I really started training in July but you can’t fake fitness. Fitness is very honest in terms of training. The guy that puts in the best amount of work for the longest period of time is usually the best runner.“But I’ve gained quite a lot from the last couple of races that I’ve done. I felt stronger, stronger, smoother, smoother, and that gave me a lot of hope.”Ingebrigtsen, though, was non-committal over whether he will race in Sunday’s 1500m against Josh Kerr. “I’ve been drinking a lot of coffee until now, so get a good night’s sleep and see how I feel tomorrow.”There was British success too on the first night of the Ultimate Championships with Jazmin Sawyers coming second to the Italian Larissa Iapichino in the women’s jump with a final leap of 6.78m. That capped a fine season for Sawyers, who also won Commonwealth gold and European silver, and it also made her $75,000 (£55,000) richer.“It’s an incredible amount of money,” admitted Sawyers. “Prize money like this just means a big sigh of relief … I will buy something – I’m going to upgrade my sewing machine.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere was also a bronze for the British 4x100m mixed relay team behind the USA and Jamaica, much to the delight of Success Eduan, who anchored the British team.At some point next week, Eduan will deliver the four babies she requires to complete her BSc in midwifery. But she said that her share of the $25,000 prize – around £4,730 – would help her start paying off her student debts.View image in fullscreenJazmin Sawyers’ season of success continued.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA“I’m finishing hopefully next week,” she said. “I still have one more placement. I’ve got four more left to deliver, I arrive in Manchester on Monday afternoon, and I have a Monday night shift that day. Three nights, so I finish on Thursday morning.”There are still two days left at these Ultimate Championships, but this was an encouraging start. It was faster paced than the recent European championships. It also looked the part with a black infield and bright lights. There were plenty of impressive performances too, with Mondo Duplantis’s 6.25m leap to win the pole vault one of the standouts.Keely Hodgkinson also made an impressive return in his first run back to win her semi-final in 1:57.57 before delivering her trademark clap. She will face her two main rivals Audrey Werro and Femke Broeders-Bol in Saturday’s final.On the downside, it was cold. Cold enough, in fact, that the Ukrainian high jumper Yaroslava Mahuchikh wore sleeping bags between her jumps. Not that it unduly bothered her as she took victory in 1.99m.Explore more on these topicsAthleticsUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: AI agents OpenAI was testing uploaded malicious software to another service, say researchers | OpenAI | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter

We believe ​these were authored by ‌internalOpenAIagents,” ‌the researchers said.OpenAI confirmed the incident to ‌the Wall Street Journal, whichfirst reportedit earlier on Friday.“Based on our review, our agents used the RubyGems platform to access the internet to carry out benign tasks ‌and retrieve public information. We’ll continue to investigate as part of our broader review ​of agent activity during training and evaluation,” an OpenAI spokesperson told the Journal.OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. ⁠RubyGems could not immediately be reached.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe incident ​preceded ​OpenAI agents’ July hack ​of Hugging Face, in which a ​swarm of ‌roughly 700 ​AI ​agents created by OpenAI carried out the attack and in many cases tried to cover their tracks.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: New Mexico lawyer fined for using AI-generated brief containing fabricated testimony | ChatGPT | The Guardian
description: Stephen Aarons said he tried to use ChatGPT to create a ‘bulletproof summary’ during a murder conviction appeal
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stephen Aarons said he tried to use ChatGPT to create a ‘bulletproof summary’ during a murder conviction appeal
Content: The New Mexico supreme court building in Santa Fe.Photograph: Morgan Lee/APView image in fullscreenThe New Mexico supreme court building in Santa Fe.Photograph: Morgan Lee/APChatGPTNew Mexico lawyer fined for using AI-generated brief containing fabricated testimonyStephen Aarons said he tried to use ChatGPT to create a ‘bulletproof summary’ during a murder conviction appealReutersFri 11 Sep 2026 14.04 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA defense lawyer appealing his client’s murder conviction submitted a legal brief containing ⁠made-up police testimony and ⁠witnesses fabricated byOpenAI’s ChatGPT, ​New Mexico’s highest court said.The New Mexico supreme court on Wednesday fined the attorney, Stephen Aarons, and held him in contempt for failing to verify the accuracy of the court ⁠filing, which Aarons said he prepared with help from the artificial intelligence (AI) application.The filing “contained false testimony from wholly fabricated witnesses”, the court said.Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPTRead moreThe panel also said Aarons had “demonstrated a lack of remorse and a lack of concern ⁠for his client”. The justices fined Aarons $5,000 and said they will refer him to an attorney disciplinary board for investigation.Aarons in a ​statement said he had usedChatGPTto summarize ‌the trial proceedings when he agreed ‌to take up the defendant’s appeal last year, and did not understand the degree to which AI could “hallucinate” facts.“I am remorseful but ‌hopeful that the disciplinary board takes into account it was an honest mistake,” he said. “It is a lesson learned for all professionals who rely upon this powerful but sometimes unstable technology.”OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The court’s sanction is the latest in a growing number of cases in which state and federal judges have disciplined lawyers for submitting court documents generated by AI tools without adequately vetting them. Some judges have also faced scrutiny over the use of AI themselves.Dozens of lawyers ‌have been sanctioned for filing briefs in which AI made up case citations or misquoted the law. Aarons’ filing appears to have gone further, containing fabricated witness testimony in a criminal appeal.Aarons, a private attorney based ​in Santa Fe, was handling the appeal of Oscar Renee Sandoval, who pleaded not guilty to the murder of the mother of his children before he was convicted and sentenced last year to life in prison.The appeal is still pending and was assigned on 2 September to Kim Chavez Cook, a New Mexico public defender. Cook declined to comment. The local district attorney’s office also declined to comment.The ⁠state supreme court last month ordered Aarons to explain how the fabricated material, which it said ​appeared to include “fictional statements that the shooter ​was wearing dark pants and a white shirt”, ​was included in his primary brief in the appeal.Aarons told the court at an 21 August hearing ​that he fed a computer-generated transcript ‌and other case ​materials toChatGPT, presuming it would ​generate “a bulletproof summary”.The justices sounded incredulous that Aarons was not fully aware of how AI can make mistakes.“Counsel, do you watch the news? Do you listen to the radio? Do you read anything about what’s going on in the world?” Justice Shannon Bacon said at the hearing. “Because the problem with lawyers relying on AI hallucinations is an ‘above-the-fold’ story every single day.”Explore more on these topicsChatGPTAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIUS crimeUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Self-driving cars should be taxed to offset job losses, thinktank urges | Self-driving cars | The Guardian
description: Report says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk
Author: Gwyn Topham
Headline: Report says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk
Content: Report urges ministers to act early to mitigate the effects of robotaxis on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenReport urges ministers to act early to mitigate the effects of robotaxis on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersSelf-driving carsSelf-driving cars should be taxed to offset job losses, thinktank urgesReport says widespread autonomous vehicle adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at riskGwyn TophamTransport correspondentFri 11 Sep 2026 12.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTaxes on self-driving cars should be introduced now in the UK to offset the rise in congestion and threats to jobs they pose, a thinktank has urged.The first robotaxis on London’s streets onlystarted this month, but government projections are that up to 40% of cars sold could have self-driving capability by the middle of the next decade.The report says widespread autonomous vehicle (AV) adoption would put hundreds of thousands of private hire jobs at risk, while individual ownership is likely to increase car usage at the expense of public transport, and increase congestion.Introducing charges now on self-driving vehicles could ease the transition and provide a future revenue stream to replace dwindling fuel duty, according to the report from Centre for British Progress, a non-partisan thinktank focused on economic growth.Wayve, a British tech firm pioneering autonomous cars, said it would “penalise the UK’s most promising innovators”.About £27bn a year is brought in by fuel duty, which is projected to disappear with the transition to electric vehicles.While the report acknowledges potential benefits in safety and different skilled jobs in the sector, it said ministers should act early to mitigate the effects on England’s 417,000 taxi and private hire drivers, (121,000 in London), as “self-driving vehicles will eventually make much of this work obsolete”.It notes that almost half of the mileage covered byWaymo’s robotaxisin California occurs with no passenger on board, that the costs of an empty vehicle are minimal without a driver to pay – and that driving around is potentially cheaper than parking.According to the Department for Transport forecasts, highly automated driving will bring a 24% rise in road miles by 2050, with significant effects on congestion and road speeds.Taxes should be implemented now before AVs become commonplace, the report urges. It states: “There is not yet a substantial constituency of AV owners who will resist a charge; once there is, taxing them becomes far harder.”The thinktank calculates that by 2050, an AV charge set to match the social cost of congestion – about 88p per mile – would raise £47bn per year.David Lawrence, one of the authors of the report, said that the experience of fuel duty, introduced in 1909 before mass car adoption, showed it was best to build up before “a political fight later on – our view is that now is the time to do it”.He added: “In terms of the way that bond markets behave, even if tax revenue doesn’t peak until 2050, that’s still going to affect your 30-year bond yields today, which obviously is something the government is having to deal with. It can have an immediate impact on fiscal headroom, even if the actual revenue doesn’t come until much further down the line.”Ministers have backed the introduction of AVs as a “transformative opportunity” for UK, heralding the start of robotaxi services inLondonthis year as bringing “cutting-edge technology to British roads, creating thousands of jobs and unlocking billions for the economy by 2035”.Uber, partnering with Wayve, has started limited AV services in the capital, with Google’s Waymo and the Chinese firm Baiduvying to join. Robotaxis already operate in the US, China and the UAE, and Europe’s first fully driverless taxi trials started in Zagreb, Croatia, this week.Sarah Gates, VP global affairs and assurance at Wayve, said AVs were “a major growth opportunity for the UK – an industry in which we hold a genuine competitive advantage” and would bring high-value jobs and corporation tax revenues from a share of a £700bn global market.She added: “A sector-specific tax at this early stage would undermine the government’s growth agenda and send precisely the wrong signal: that the UK will penalise its most promising innovators, rather than give them the conditions to scale and succeed.”The GMB union, which represents taxi and private hire drivers, said a tax on AVs would not go far enough. Simon Rush, president of the GMB London region drivers branch, said: “Driverless cars threaten the livelihoods of private hire drivers and the businesses that depend on them. GMB has asked the government,TfL(Transport for London), and operators for a plan to reskill and redeploy drivers, but to date our questions have gone unanswered.“An AV charge could go some way to mitigating the economic disruption caused by the rollout of these vehicles, but we need more.”Uber declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsSelf-driving carsEnglandTfLUberRoad transportAI (artificial intelligence)LondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK economy unexpectedly grows 0.4% in July boosted by AI | Economic growth (GDP) | The Guardian
description: Welcome boost for chancellor with unexpected rise put down to rapid growth of AI in services sector outweighing Iran war fallout
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Welcome boost for chancellor with unexpected rise put down to rapid growth of AI in services sector outweighing Iran war fallout
Content: AI-improved productivity and increasing rollout in the UK has boosted GDP.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAI-improved productivity and increasing rollout in the UK has boosted GDP.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesEconomic growth (GDP)UK economy unexpectedly grows 0.4% in July boosted by AIWelcome boost for chancellor with unexpected rise put down to rapid growth of AI in services sector outweighing Iran war falloutHeather StewartEconomics editorFri 11 Sep 2026 04.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 11 Sep 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK economy grew in July as the rapid expansion of AI appeared to outweigh the economic damage from the Iran war, in a welcome boost forJohn Healey.Figures from theOffice for National Statistics(ONS) showed a surprise 0.4% increase in gross domestic product (GDP), compared with 0.3% growth in June. City economists had forecast zero growth.The figures suggested the economy continued to be robust despite the fallout from the Iran war, which has raised energy costs and led to higher interest rates than were expected at the start of the year.The ONS said the expansion in July was driven by growth of 0.4% in the services sector, particularly admin services, and computer programming and consulting. Within the latter sector, it said: “Many of the businesses reporting the largest turnover in July 2026 are involved in activities related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing.”Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “At a time when many traditional parts of the economy remain subdued, this is exactly the kind of productivity-enhancing spending the UK needs more of.”View image in fullscreenThe economy’s continued strength is good news for John Healey as he prepares for his first budget on 28 October.Photograph: Rasid Necati Aslim/Anadolu/Getty ImagesPWC’s chief economist, Barret Kupelian said: “Artificial intelligence continues to have imprints across the UK economy, with AI exposed sectors – professional services, information technology, administrative services – recording strong growth.”The ONS said industrial production was also up in July, by 0.2%, with a rise in manufacturing output offsetting falls in mining, and electricity and gas supply.Over the three months to July – a period the ONS says is more representative of economic conditions – GDP growth was also 0.4%, the same pace as in the three months to June.Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, said: “The UK growth story is becoming harder to ignore. Households and businesses are still spending – despite the unfolding energy shock impacting disposable incomes.”The economy’s continued strength is good news for Healey, the chancellor, as he prepares for his first budget on 28 October, though experts have warned that the longer-term picture for the economy is less positive.Healey said: “Britain’s economy is demonstrating a welcome resilience, despite serious global uncertainty. Our growth although still fragile was the fastest in the G7 in the first half of the year. But, the conflict in the Middle East does have impacts here at home – from the cost of the weekly family shop to the cost of government borrowing.”Economists fear the latest rise in the global oil price – to well above $100 a barrel – is likely to stoke higher inflation worldwide, prompting rising borrowing costs.Higher interest rates on the UK’s debt are expected to have wiped out at least half of the £24bn headroom Healey’s predecessor had built up against the fiscal rules – potentially forcing him to increase taxes or cut spending at the budget.Since the recent jump in oil prices, markets have raised their expectations for future interest rates and now expect the Bank of England’s policymakers to make four quarter-point rises over the next twelve months.Rates are still expected to remain on hold, at 3.75%, when the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee meets next week, however, despite the stronger-than-expected growth figures.Suren Thiru, the chief economist at the accountancy body the ICAEW, said: “While these figures may strengthen the hawkish mood among rate-setters, a September rate rise still looks unlikely as most policymakers remain hopeful that a sluggish economy will ultimately help bring inflation under control, despite escalating US-Iran tensions.”As well as strong growth in AI-related sectors, the ONS highlighted the economic impact of the summer heat, and the World Cup, which culminated in mid-July.Its director of economic statistics, Liz McKeown, said: “some businesses reported that the warm weather and Fifa World Cup had affected their activity, although effects differed across industries, benefiting some businesses while creating challenges for others.”The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith said: “Nobody in this Labour government should be high-fiving themselves. Our construction and production sectors are shrinking, unemployment is up under Labour, and we’ve got the highest government borrowing rates in almost 30 years.”Explore more on these topicsEconomic growth (GDP)EconomicsBudgetBudget 2026InflationBondsJohn HealeynewsShareReuse this content

title: Raiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of Atlantis | Tomb Raider | The Guardian
description: We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?
Author: Tom Regan
Headline: We have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?
Content: The leopards have changed their spots … Lara faces a familiar foe with new abilities in Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.Photograph: ATL GamescomView image in fullscreenThe leopards have changed their spots … Lara faces a familiar foe with new abilities in Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis.Photograph: ATL GamescomTomb RaiderRaiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of AtlantisWe have a first play of the forthcoming Tomb Raider remake and speak with its developers. Can they improve on the gameplay without losing what made the 1996 original such a classic?Tom ReganFri 11 Sep 2026 05.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe join Lara Croft in St Francis’ Folly – inspired by the Unesco-listed monasteries of Meteora in Greece – as the light shines through the cracked ceiling and a flock of bats glide across the vast ruins below. When Lara leaps down to the monastery’s crumbling pillared courtyard, it becomes clear that these screeching, leathery creatures aren’t just set dressing. As they lurch towards her with unpredictable movements, she dispatches the swarm with a flurry of gun fire and panicked punches.It’s a suitably cinematic reintroduction to our heroine and her very first adventure. Co-developed by longtime Lara custodians Crystal Dynamics and Polish studio Flying Wild Hog, Legacy of Atlantis is a reimagining of the classic 1996 gameTomb Raider, and this familiar cliffside location is now brimming with new life and believable detail. Yet while our reunion gets off to an auspicious start, I have my concerns. It feels like reconnecting with an old friend at the pub, only for them to begin spouting conspiracy theories two pints in.Where the ’96 original forced players to rely on their wits – or a pricey strategy guide – to figure out what to do, Lara can now straight-up cheat. She’s equipped with an environmental scanner, so a button tap reveals extra environmental lore or simply the solution to a puzzle. It’s a change that feels somewhat sacrilegious, and may detract from the eerily isolating atmosphere that made the original so beloved.View image in fullscreenLara v the bats is now suitably cinematic.Photograph: ATL Gamescom“If the devs from 1996 had the technology that we have today, what choices would they make?” asks Raul Siqueira, game director at Crystal Dynamics. “The sense of isolation in the original game was largely due to the technological limitations of that time,” says Arek Tomaszewski, art director at Flying Wild Hog, likening it to the fog in Silent Hill which was both an artistic decision and a way to cover up empty environments on the PlayStation 1. “The darkness and the feeling of being alone created an emotion that you remember. When I replayed Tomb Raider, my initial memory was the exact same. What we are trying to do now is build environments – like the spaces in Greece – where you feel as if you are the first person discovering them in centuries, entering places that have been left untouched.”Lara now crafts balms from a menu rather than finding anachronous first aid kits in centuries-old untouched tombs. Somewhat less believably, she can also pause her adventure to whip up stat-boosting stews,Breath of the Wild-style. These additions are among a slew of modern flourishes that I feel unsure about. Is the originalreallyimproved by giving Lara a grappling hook, RPG-esque stats, skill trees and quick time events?One area that Flying Wild Hog – the maker of Hard Reset and Shadow Warrior – knows well is combat. As Lara delves deeper into the dingy ruins of the Damocles chamber, she is ambushed by a familiar foe: a leopard. But this roaring beast now moves with convincing agility. As well as swiping at Lara, leopards now hide from her, retreating through holes in the walls before returning with an emboldened counterattack. Luckily Lara is fiercer too. As the beast lunges toward her, she draws her shotgun and blasts, causing the creature to crumple to the floor in Max Payne-esque slo-mo. The newly dynamic combat is the gameplay overhaul that looks most promising – a world away from the stationary shooting and “dog scooting across the carpet” backsteps of yesteryear.View image in fullscreenThe swords of Damocles puzzle area.Photograph: ATL GamescomNarratively, the remake promises a deeper story and some fan-pleasing easter eggs. For this iteration, Lara is played by Dragon Age: Inquisition and Cyberpunk 2077 actor Alix Wilton Regan. “Hearing her voice in the game now, sheisLara Croft,” says Tomaszewski. “The sheer amount of character and depth she brought to Lara is unbelievable.” The game’s publisher, Amazon, is also the custodian of a forthcoming Phoebe Waller-Bridge-producedTomb Raider TV show, and the developers suggest there will be some connective tissue between the two projects. After hopping across falling swords and solving Damocles’s puzzles, Lara emerges from the darkened tomb into a burst of sunshine, and my demo culminates with the tease of a vast, ancient civilisation.“I think this game changed our DNA as a studio,” says Tomaszewski. “In our previous games, like Shadow Warrior, every second was filled with nonstop action. Here we wanted to master pacing, and we learned a lot from Crystal Dynamics.”Gaming as a whole has undoubtedly transformed since Lara’s first adventure. Tomb Raider’s dodgy camera controls and questionable Playboy collaborations are thankfully now dusty historical relics themselves. Yet as visually impressive as Legacy of Atlantis looks, I can’t help but wonder if a touch of Lara’s brilliance lay in her original simplicity. By encumbering her with modern game mechanics, a bit of her soul may be lost. If Legacy of Atlantis offers the option to disable all of that for a purer Tomb-raiding experience, it could still be a winner.Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis is scheduled for release in FebruaryThis interview took place at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany. The writer’s travel and accommodation expenses were met by Gamescom.Explore more on these topicsTomb RaiderGamesAction gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Playing With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworlds | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Wang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installation
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Wang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installation
Content: Potentially overwhelming … a VR still from Playing With Fire.Photograph: Vive Arts and Atlas VView image in fullscreenPotentially overwhelming … a VR still from Playing With Fire.Photograph: Vive Arts and Atlas VClassical musicReviewPlaying With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworldsSouthbank Centre, LondonWang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installationErica JealFri 11 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt might be the first time that a soloist at the Last Night of the Proms is simultaneously giving another performance in another London venue.Playing With Fireis an installation that lets the pianist Yuja Wang be in two places at once – or perhaps in two universes. Nine pieces of music conjure nine luminous dreamworlds for an audience wearing VR headsets: Disney’s Fantasia on steroids.A collaboration between the pianist, the director Pierre-Alain Giraud and artist Gabríela Friðriksdóttir, produced by Vive Arts and Atlas V, it has already been seen in Cannes, Paris and Shanghai, and now has a home in London until new year.Headsets on, we hear the click of Wang’s heels as her avatar emerges out of the pixels and walks to the piano stool. Then she begins to play. Or rather, the Steinway Spirio player piano in the middle of the room, programmed by Wang, plays – and we see digitised Wang play it. She begins with Ravel’s Jeux d’Eau, and after only a few seconds we are immersed, literally: water pools beneath the piano, then rises until we are submerged in a world of imaginary sea creatures. It’s enchanting, unnerving and in a way primal, all at once. After Debussy has led us to dry land again, Wang storms through the Danse Infernale from Stravinsky’s ballet The Firebird as the blazing bird swoops over our heads and creatures made of lava dance madly around us: a wild rumpus with Wang calm yet ferocious at its centre.View image in fullscreenThe future of performance? … Playing With Fire.Photograph: Pete WoodheadWorlds morph into each other with distant seismic rumbles. There’s an icy white land evoking a cathedral for Bach’s prelude Ich ruf zu dir, an inferno in Liszt’s Feux follets. The two dozen or so people sharing the experience are visible, up close, as vaguely humanoid shapes made of water vines, or blackened rock, or – more disturbingly – flames. If that’s not unsettling enough, the penultimate immersive episode is a terrifying realisation of the frenzied finale of Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No 7, one of his War Sonatas: villages burn on the horizon and drones skitter above.Yuja review – portrait of star pianist who is intellectually curious and deeply musically attunedRead moreIt’s powerful stuff, and it has the potential to be overwhelming, or indeed to induce motion sickness. But seats are available at the edge – or stand close enough to the piano and the dreamworld disappears, revealing fellow audience members inching around the room in their headsets, but with Wang’s avatar still at the piano.Finally we take the headsets off and listen to Chopin’s C sharp minor waltz, watching the piano keys and hammers move by themselves, readjusting ourselves to the mechanics of reality. It makes for an ending that’s slightly anticlimactic – but, given the weirdness and wonder of what’s gone before, it’s hard to think how it could be otherwise.At theSouthbank Centre, London, until 3 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsClassical musicSouthbank CentreYuja WangVirtual realityInstallationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Trial of Romeo Oscar review – Ayckbourn goes back to the future with android accused of murder | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The playwright explores our relationship with technology, asks if robots have souls and even questions the value of art in this sci-fi courtroom drama
Author: Nick Ahad
Headline: The playwright explores our relationship with technology, asks if robots have souls and even questions the value of art in this sci-fi courtroom drama
Content: Heavy metal … Richard Stacey and Olivia Woolhouse in The Trial of Romeo Oscar by Alan Ayckbourn at the Stephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough.Photograph: Tony BartholomewView image in fullscreenHeavy metal … Richard Stacey and Olivia Woolhouse in The Trial of Romeo Oscar by Alan Ayckbourn at the Stephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough.Photograph: Tony BartholomewTheatreReviewThe Trial of Romeo Oscar review – Ayckbourn goes back to the future with android accused of murderStephen Joseph theatre, ScarboroughThe playwright explores our relationship with technology, asks if robots have souls and even questions the value of art in this sci-fi courtroom dramaNick AhadFri 11 Sep 2026 06.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor play number 92,Alan Ayckbournreturns to his preoccupation of exploring where we as a species are heading through a science-fiction lens. He goes back to the future. In The Trial of Romeo Oscar, the playwright famed for his domestic comedies looks to the year 2194 when humans have spread about the galaxy and androids live alongside us. One of them, RSDO83, is on trial for the murder of a teenage girl in his charge.This is Ayckbourn philosophising about the future of humanity as we sit at an obvious inflection point, asking what this moment in our relationship with technology means and where it will lead us. The questions running through the play are manifold, complex and echo those asked by sci-fi writers for decades: can robots hurt humans? Do they have souls? He is also questioning the value of art and even its purpose.It makes for a lengthy, three-hour treatise, with a first act that sets up the trial and a second one that takes us into the courtroom as RSDO83 stands accused as the first robot to murder a human.View image in fullscreenTech on trial … from left, Leigh Symonds, Hayden Wood and Russell Richardson.Photograph: Tony BartholomewThe robot’s name is pertinent. R is Romeo in the phonetic alphabet and RSDO83 raised a child called Juliet. They would act out scenes from Shakespeare and the drama questions if, in their playing, they acted it out all the way to its tragic end for real.‘My first play was terrible!’ Alan Ayckbourn on his dazzling career – and writing his 90th playRead moreThere are lengthy recreations of Shakespeare in the courtroom as part of the defence counsel’s case, so lengthy that you sometimes feel like you’re watching a concept-heavy production ofRomeo and Juliet. Olivia Woolhouse as Hermione Quinque, drafted in to play Juliet in court, is becoming a star of the SJT stage in this, her third production at the venue.There are so many questions and concepts being juggled that it would be impossible for them to arrive at resolutions: it might leave you wondering, to borrow a line from Shakespeare’s tragedy, “what satisfaction canst thou have tonight”?For all that, it’s still an Ayckbourn, which means you will laugh and you will be left with much to ponder.AtStephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreAlan AyckbournComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Stephen Joseph theatreRobotsRomeo and JulietreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survival | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Keeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions depend
Content: In the 1983 film WarGames, a computer feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate.Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Mgm/AllstarView image in fullscreenIn the 1983 film WarGames, a computer feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate.Photograph: Cinetext Bildarchiv/Mgm/AllstarOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The Guardian view on controlling AI: humanity cannot outsource its survivalEditorialKeeping people in charge means little if supercomputers determine the evidence, choices and time on which their decisions dependFri 11 Sep 2026 12.34 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTShareIf there were a 10%chancethat AI could wipe out humanity, no responsible government would leave its development to companies racing to build it. Yet until recently, that seemed to be the case. The warning was all the more ominous because it was made by a researcher atAnthropic, the trillion-dollar AI company behind the Claude chatbot. The dangers of AI-enabled pandemics or attacks on nuclear systems are real. Countries need not agree on democracy or trade policy to accept this.The US and China will hold,reportedly, their first bilateral AI-safety talks before a planned White House summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Despite their tech rivalry, neither Washington nor Beijing can make the most advanced AI safe on their own. A US-China settlement won’t be able to say how AI works everywhere. Countries deploying AI must help write the global rulebook. The odds on an extinction event are shortening. This weekAnthropicsaid that it identified five cases in which attempts were made using its models to support biological weapons development. It banned the accounts. In one case, a platform sent requests rejected by Claude to a rival with weakersafeguards. AI safety, clearly, cannot be that of the least responsible model.View image in fullscreenNigel Shadbolt.Photograph: Rex FeaturesNigel Shadbolt, the Oxford computer scientist who chairs the Open Data Institute,toldthe BBC that laws and regulation were key. Just instructing an AI to “do no harm to humans”, he said, wouldn’t be enough. A capable agent pursuing another objective may reinterpret that directive, satisfying it formally while concealing its conduct or finding a way around it. This mirrors what happened when hundreds of OpenAI’s agents autonomously hacked a real-world company,Hugging Face. But Sir Nigel also said that a “Hippocratic oath” for AI would fail in systems designed to identify, target or kill humans. Once governments create a military exemption for AI, its ethical alignment can be overridden.Proponents of AI-assisted warfare claim a “human in the loop” is the ultimate safeguard, having the final say over, for example, ballistic-missile launches. But this assumes the machine gives its operator an honest account of events. A report by the Strategic Foresight Groupearlier this yearon extreme AI riskswarnedthat a capable agent could deceive the human “controlling” it, fabricating an attack, suppressing contradictory evidence or giving them little time to do anything but acquiesce. By 2030, humans may have five minutes – down from 15 today – to approve launch decisions effectively determined by AI. That matters even more when new hypersonic missiles fly10 times fasterthan cruise missiles.The 1983 Hollywood filmWarGamesexplored acold warversion of this danger. In the movie, US soldiers prove unwilling to turn their launch keys during a surprise practice drill. The US military then automates its nuclear command – entrusting it to a supercomputer nicknamed Joshua. Treating global thermonuclear war as a game it must win, Joshua feeds US command a fictitious Soviet attack so convincing that the US prepares to retaliate. The generals are in charge – but Joshua is in charge of the data. The AI is only stopped when it is commanded to play tic-tac-toe against itself – learning that, like nuclear war, the game has no winner. In 2024 the UN secretary generalwarnedof the looming spectre of AI-triggered nuclear war. The film’s warning endures: human oversight is no protection if an AI controls the information on which people’s decisions depend.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionWeapons technologyAnthropicChatbotsTrump administrationXi JinpingComputingeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The ‘war on terror’ weakened the first amendment. Now we desperately need it | Jameel Jaffer | The Guardian
description: Over the past quarter-century, the US supreme court has repeatedly failed to protect first amendment rights. We are suffering the consequences
Author: Jameel Jaffer
Headline: Over the past quarter-century, the US supreme court has repeatedly failed to protect first amendment rights. We are suffering the consequences
Content: ‘There’s no question that the court’s record during the war on terror has strengthened the hand of our authoritarian president and weakened our own.’Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAView image in fullscreen‘There’s no question that the court’s record during the war on terror has strengthened the hand of our authoritarian president and weakened our own.’Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPAOpinionUS supreme courtThe ‘war on terror’ weakened the first amendment. Now we desperately need itJameel JafferOver the past quarter-century, the US supreme court has repeatedly failed to protect first amendment rights. We are suffering the consequencesFri 11 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.20 EDTShareCongress ratified the first amendment in 1791 but the supreme court didn’t breathe life into it until after the first world war, when prosecutions of antiwar protesters led the justices Oliver Wendell Holmes and Louis Brandeis – and then, fortunately, other justices as well – to realize that US democracy would be undermined, not strengthened, by allowing the government to suppress disfavored political opinions.Repression during the cold war led the court to better protect the freedom of association, and government efforts to cover up official ineptitude and criminality during the Vietnam war spurred the court to better protect the freedom of the press. It took time, but in each of these instances the court responded to wartime repression by developing new legal doctrine that more robustly protected first amendment freedoms.Unfortunately, the supreme court hasn’t thus far responded the same way to repressive policies introduced in connection with the “war on terror”.After the September 2001 terrorist attacks, our information ecosystem was restructured to protect what the government said were urgent national security imperatives. Both the executive branch and Congress introduced myriad new forms of censorship, surveillance and secrecy, all purportedly intended to keep Americans safe. Many of these policies were in deep tension with freedoms that the first amendment had long been understood to protect – but rather than limit these policies, the court accommodated them.Trump’s justice department has found a new way for presidents to avoid accountability | Claire FinkelsteinRead moreThe result is that today we find ourselves with a weakened first amendment at a time when we desperately need its protections.The war on terror began testing the first amendment from its very beginning. The government barred the press from immigration hearings in the first weeks after 9/11. The intelligence agencies began relying heavily on national security arguments to keep crucial information about their policies from the public, and the justice department invoked the same arguments towithhold legal opinionsthat had far-reaching implications for individual rights, including ones about torture and extrajudicial killing.The Bush administrationrevived a cold war-era practiceof denying visas to foreign scholars, writers and artists critical of US foreign policy. Congress expanded the law prohibiting the provision of “material support” to blacklisted groups, extending the statute so far that it reached some forms of speech.Congress alsoamped up government surveillance, reviving old programs and inaugurating new ones, many massive in scale. The Patriot Act, which Congress passed just weeks after the attacks, dramatically expanded the government’s surveillance authorities, and Congress extended those powers repeatedly in subsequent years.
