The FBI exploited new communications technologies to track journalists’ emails and phone calls, and the justice department beganusing the Espionage Actto prosecute journalists’ sources.Not all of these issues were presented to the supreme court, but the court batted away almost all of the ones that were. It declined multiple opportunities to consider the constitutionality of national security surveillance. It refused multiple chances to consider the constitutionality of gag orders imposed on the recipients of national security letters – administrative subpoenas issued in foreign-intelligence investigations.It also declined an opportunity to consider whether the first amendment guarantees the public a right of access to opinions issued by the foreign intelligence surveillance court – a question that the Knight First Amendment Institute (which I lead), the ACLU, the former solicitor general Ted Olson, and many former intelligence officials allurged the court to take up. (The justices Neil Gorsuch and Sonia Sotomayordissentedfrom the denial of certiorari, asking: “If these matters are not worthy of our time, what is?”)Over the course of the quarter century that followed 9/11 – a period during which the court heard about a dozen cases involving the second amendment and about 70 involving intellectual property law – the court agreed to hear only three cases involving conflicts between the government’s counter-terrorism policies and free speech. In each of those cases, it narrowed or weakened first amendment rights.In Humanitarian Law Project v Holder, a challenge to the material support law, the court held that the government could make it a crime for a human rights organization to provide training in human rights law to groups that the government had designated as terrorist organizations. In Clapper v Amnesty, which I argued, the court decided that human rights groups lacked standing to challenge a mass surveillance law because they couldn’t prove that their own communications would be collected; the decision had the effect of shielding most national security surveillance from ordinary constitutional review.Trump has embraced a disturbing strategy to silence free speech | David BralowRead moreMore recently, in TikTok v Garland, the court rejected a first amendment challenge to a law that banned Americans from accessing the short-form video app, crediting national security arguments thateven the NSA’s general counselhad rejected. That decision purported to be a narrow one but itsignificantly underminedAmericans’ right to access information and media from abroad.The supreme court’s failure to defend the first amendment against the considerable encroachments of the war on terror has handed the Trump administration a broad set of tools it can use in its assault on democratic institutions and freedoms. Government whistleblowers who inform the public about abuse or criminality in the military or intelligence agencies – andjournalists and publisherswho report on those abuses – risk prosecution under the Espionage Act. Those who participate inanti-ICEorpro-Palestiniandemonstrations do so under the shadow of the expanded material support laws. Government secrecy about matters relating to war and foreign policy, such as government surveillance in the national security sphere, has become all but unchallengeable.It’s not surprising that 9/11 and the war on terror would test the protections of the first amendment, as they were tested repeatedly by crises and conflicts in the last century. What is surprising and noteworthy is the extent to which the supreme court has failed to rise to the challenge, as its predecessors did, to ensure that the freedoms of speech and the press emerged from these stresses not just intact but fortified against future pressures.We’re suffering the consequences of the court’s failure now. We’ll preserve our democracy against Trump’s assault – but there’s no question that the court’s record during the war on terror has strengthened the hand of our authoritarian president and weakened our own.Jameel Jaffer directs the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia UniversityExplore more on these topicsUS supreme courtOpinionTrump administrationSeptember 11 2001US CongressUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: George W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessness | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: The reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violence
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: The reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violence
Content: ‘Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side.’Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side.’Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesOpinionGuantánamo BayGeorge W Bush’s impunity led to Trump’s lawlessnessKenneth RothThe reluctance of later administrations to repudiate Bush-era torture and endless detention laid the groundwork for recent violenceFri 11 Sep 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.05 EDTShareIf George W Bush’s abusive response to the September 11 attacks had been prosecuted rather than swept under the rug,Donald Trumpwould be less able to pursue his lawless policies. We can’t rewind history, but we can learn from our historic failure.Twenty-five years ago, on a clear and crisp morning, I was sitting in the Human Rights Watch office in the Empire State Building with an unobstructed view of the World Trade Center towers as al-Qaida operatives flew two commercial jets into them. The horror of the attack required a response, but Bush and his vice-president, Dick Cheney, chose to react by throwing out the rulebook. They deployed torture and endless detention without trial in Guantánamo.At first, Americans were so fearful of another al-Qaida attack that many accepted the Bush administration’s argument that extraordinary measures were required. But as the utter brutality of the response became apparent, dissenting voices grew more pronounced. Yet the reluctance of later administrations to repudiate these measures laid the foundation for Trump’s misconduct.A May 2009meetingI had with Barack Obama epitomized the problem. He had recently assumed office and invited me and several colleagues to the White House to discuss his counter-terrorism program. The meeting wasdisappointing.Trump admin spends billions to deport Black and brown people while doubling dollars for white ‘refugees’ | Heba GowayedRead moreOur top priority was securing prosecution of the senior Bush administration officials who had ordered the systematic torture of terrorist suspects. Obamadeclined, wanting tolookforward, not back. His priority was working with Congress to secure healthcare reform (ultimately the Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare) as well as on issues such as education and climate change. He felt that prosecuting senior Bush officials would be too contentious.Other steps had already been taken to end the torture. Public outrage, hastened by the leaked Abu Ghraibphotographsof US servicemembers mistreating detainees in Iraq, led even the Bush administration to stop. TheDetainee Treatment Actof 2005, sponsored by the senator John McCain, himself a torture victim, closed some of the legal loopholes used by the Bush administration to justify the unjustifiable. But no senior officialwas ever prosecutedfor the torture.That left a legacy of impunity that haunts us. Later presidents have not revived the torture, although the administrations of Joe Biden as well as Trump have continued the flow of military aid to Israel despite itssystematictortureof Palestinian detainees.Yet the deliberate use of excessive force by Trump’s deportation agents suggests confidence in a similar impunity for today’s declared crisis du jour: immigration. The Trump justice department hasclosedits eyes even when immigration officials gratuitouslyshoot, and sometimes kill, people.Bush’s lengthy detention of suspects without trial at Guantánamo has had even greater lethal consequences. Ordinarily, a criminal suspect must be charged and tried within areasonabletime or released. But the Bush administration often had no evidence to justify charges beyond confessions secured by torture. The military commissions designed to allow prosecution despite the torture proved to be travesties that to this day have not evenbegunthe trial of the principal 9/11 suspects.The legal device that the Bush administration used to justify endless detention without trial was to call the suspects “enemy combatants”. Inwar, it is possible to hold opposing combatants without trial until the end of the armed conflict, but there was no armed conflict with al-Qaida, only a series of horrible terrorist attacks.Bush concocted the “war on terror”, but it wasn’t a real war because there was no organized military force on the other side to justify invoking the rules of war. Rather, the rhetoric was a contrivance to sidestep the requirements of criminal prosecution.At the time, Iarguedthat allowing this legal subterfuge could have dangerous consequences. If a declared but fake enemy combatant could be held indefinitely without charge, why could he not also be shot? After all, in war, there is no duty to capture combatants from the other side. So long as they are not in custody, they can be killed.I made the argument in the meeting with Obama as a reason to close Guantánamo – to charge or release all its detainees. I couldn’t imagine that the US government would really start to shoot suspects whom it could detain. But that is what Trump is now doing, not with alleged al-Qaida terrorists but with drug suspects, using a similar theory.Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro | Ken RothRead moreLike Bush, Trump has concocted a war, this time with drug traffickers, even though there is no organized military force on the other side fighting the United States. He then declared suspected traffickers in boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific to be “narcoterrorists”. His aim is to justify summarily killing them by drone rather than capturing and prosecuting them. Trump has taken the Bush theory, modified it for the new enemy, and intensified the consequences.Precursors to thesemurderscan be found in the actions of the Obama and Biden administrations. They summarily killed people in Yemen and north-western Pakistan but at least maintained the pretense, though untenable, that these terrorist suspects posed an imminent threat to the United States because arrest was impossible in the relatively lawless terrain of these distant lands. That is, they invoked anexceptionin policing rules that allows lethal force rather than the fiction that these people were enemy combatants.But that misuse of policing rules isn’t available for the drug suspects whom Trump is targeting because the US Coast Guard has a long tradition of successfullyinterdictingthem at sea. Trump thus relies on his fake war to order them murdered instead.The lesson I take is that when past abuses are glossed over rather than prosecuted, they set precedents that can come back to haunt us. It is never easy to establish the rule of law when the perpetrators are powerful officials. An administration rarely prosecutes itself, and later administrations have their own priorities. Addressing the past is often believed to require too much political capital.But the rule of law is important. It is a value worth upholding even at a price. It is too late to address the Bush-era atrocities, but it is not too late to address Trump’s. He won’t do it, but we should insist that the next administration does. Meanwhile, state and international prosecutors should start now.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsGuantánamo BayOpinionSeptember 11 2001George BushTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS immigrationcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Smithsonian chief’s exit is a blow to democracy | Kimberlé Crenshaw and Jason Stanley | The Guardian
description: The Trump administration wants a feel-good version of American history. That is not a feature of a democratic system
Author: Kimberlé Crenshaw
Headline: The Trump administration wants a feel-good version of American history. That is not a feature of a democratic system
Content: ‘Bunch’s retirement comes as the Trump administration has pressured the Smithsonian to adopt its agenda of “patriotic” education.’Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APView image in fullscreen‘Bunch’s retirement comes as the Trump administration has pressured the Smithsonian to adopt its agenda of “patriotic” education.’Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APOpinionTrump administrationThe Smithsonian chief’s exit is a blow to democracyKimberlé CrenshawandJason StanleyThe Trump administration wants a feel-good version of American history. That is not a feature of a democratic systemFri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 13.14 EDTShareOn Tuesday, Lonnie G Bunch III announced he would step down as the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian.Bunch was the first historian to lead the august institution, as well as the first African American. His retirement comes as theTrump administrationhas pressured the Smithsonian to adopt its agenda of “patriotic” education.On 28 August, the Department of Interior issued a threatening letter to the Smithsonian, declaring that “action must be taken” against “a radical institutional ideology” that threatens “to permeate … the operations” of the National Museum of American History (NMAH). The letter challenges NMAH’s longstanding commitment to demonstrating history’s relevance by tying the presentation of American history to “the core issues of our time”.The administration’s attack on the Smithsonian is far more than a conflict over imbalance. It is an effort to weaponize history to undercut the very terms of our democratic existence. According to the 24 July executive order “Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian Institution”, its role should be to “present American history as a shared national inheritance to be taught and celebrated”. In the language of an earlier executive order (on K-12 education), the administration declared that the purpose of American history in museums and schools should be to create a shared American identity, one grounded in “a patriotic admiration for our incredible nation” and praise for the great men who founded it.American democracy depends on the census. Trump is undermining it | danah boydRead moreBy this measure, the Smithsonian – and Bunch in particular – exist in a state of non-compliance. The historical record that one encounters in its collections – ranging from acknowledging the fact thatfounders such as Benjamin Franklin enslaved African Americansto the fact that Europeans originally moved to the United States asa colonizing force– doesn’t feel good enough to inspire patriotic admiration either for the great men who created the nation, or its current ideology.But the belief that history and the institutions responsible for curating it must be beholden to a feelgood narrative is not a feature of a democratic system but its opposite. Historically, it is democracy’senemieswho have called for a “patriotic education” that focuses on lauding the great leaders and founders of the country. For example, in Mein Kampf, Hitler criticizes the historical education of Weimar democracy as failing to provide “a real national enthusiasm”. In its place, Hitler calls for history to be replaced by a system of education that makes “the really significant men of our people appear as outstanding heroes in the eyes of the present, to concentrate the general attention upon them, and thus create a unified mood” The education under Weimar, Hitler complains, was “not able to raise what was glorious for the nation … above the level of objective presentation, and fire the national pride by such gleaming examples”.It should worry us all that the educational goals of fascism so clearly overlap with the agenda of the Trump administration. It should worry us all that the accusation of “indoctrination” is so readily deployed against a more inclusive American story, and that this is not immediately seen for what it is: a force-fed and blinkered vision of how we’ve come to be, the only terms available to be a true American.It is of course also hard to take seriously even the demand for “patriotic education” from an administration thatis aggressively restoringdecidedly traitorous white supremacists (Confederates) to places of honor. What exactly is the American identity to which such an education is asking us to be beholden?Underlying the muted response to the alarming rewriting of the historical record is an ill-defined understanding of the role of government-supported institutions such as the Smithsonian in safeguarding democracy. Democracy is based onpolitical equality. Political equality means everyone’s perspectives are given equal recognition. Central to this essential democratic ideal is a system of education that exposes all citizens to the perspectives, experiences and histories of the different groups who make up the polity. The purpose of democratic institutions such as the museums and universities is to defend history inallof its difficult complexity. In the case of NMAH, as well as the different historical museums of the Smithsonian, the goal should be to present anaccurateversion of the histories ofallthe peoples of the United States, without erasure. Without such an education, there is no hope for the political equality that is the basis of democracy. Citizens will fear each other, rather than understand each other, and their votes will be based on this fear.Trump’s justice department has found a new way for presidents to avoid accountability | Claire FinkelsteinRead moreIt is of course not a coincidence that the administration that is stoking this fear is also attacking democracy head-on with some of the very practices that it seeks to diminish and even erase from its version of patriotic education. The rich pro-democracy history of the battle over voting rights, for example, is a history worthy of celebratory reflection, but not so if the record of disenfranchisement and the racial tyranny it unleashed is sanitized out of historical memory, with thehelp of the supreme court.The consequences of this erasure are far greater than hobbling our democracy with inaccurate or partial understandings of the past. As WEB DuBois notes in the final chapter of Black Reconstruction, “The Propaganda of History”, the rewriting of history in a way that made for “pleasant reading for Americans” was part and parcel of a counterrevolution against democracy – one that dismantled Reconstruction and restored white supremacy in the south with the acquiescence of the federal government. DuBois’s point was that so-called patriotic education that erased and distorted Black history was central to the justification of the transition from freedom “back towards slavery”.Central to the point of education for both countries and individuals is to carry forward the lessons of the past to help us better navigate challenges in the present and future. An educated citizenry is essential to a fully functioning democracy, which is precisely why the Trump administration’s attack on history and our democracy are different fronts of the same war.It is often said that those who do not learn their history are doomed to repeat it. But for those who refuse to teach that history accurately, repetition is precisely the point.Kimberlé Crenshaw is a professor of law at Columbia Law School and UCLA School of Law. She is the author of Backtalker: An American MemoirJason Stanley is a professor of Philosophy at the Munk School at the University of Toronto and author of Erasing History: How Fascists Rewrite the Past to Control the FutureExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionMuseums (Education)Museums (Culture)commentShareReuse this content

title: Wake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the world  | Simon Jenkins | The Guardian
description: The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Author: Simon Jenkins
Headline: The US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t wait, says Guardian columnist Simon Jenkins
Content: Donald Trump and King Charles inspecting a guard of honour at Windsor Castle, September 2025.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and King Charles inspecting a guard of honour at Windsor Castle, September 2025.Photograph: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpWake up, Britain: Donald Trump’s US is no friend of ours. We must secure our own place in the worldSimon JenkinsThe US president is ever more wayward – and has little interest in defending Europe. The constitution may hold him to account, but we can’t waitFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTShareIf Americans vote for a Republican majority in both houses of Congress in November, “I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000.” But they must not spend it in Canada or China or anywhere else outside the US.So said Donald Trumpin Texas on Wednesday in advance of the forthcoming midterm elections. He further told voters to “Pretend that I’m on the ballot”. It was a climactic moment in an almost two-hour rant.Trump does not have the requiredtrillion dollarsin his pocket, and it would be illegal to disperse such a sum without congressional approval. In any case, JD Vance now appears to haverowed backon the promise.Observers from abroad must beware: it is unwise to subject Trump’s populism to the discipline of truth. Trump also said Americans should thank him for attacking Iran since that country was “two, maybe three weeks away from having a nuclear weapon”, which it intended to use against them. It was the old Saddam Hussein gambit.The problem is that almost every one ofTrump’s speechesrefers back to himself, as if he and the United States were synonymous. He claimed to have won the presidency three times. He says: “If we hadn’t won the last election, I’m not sure that our country right now would even exist.” He added that the arena where he was speaking was packed, with crowds outside clamouring to get in. Pictures show ithalf empty.Anyone watching can see why there has been much medical debate over whether Trump is exhibiting signs ofnarcissism disorder. Key symptoms are mendacity and inconsistency. In 2021 members of the House of Representatives called for the constitution’s25th amendment, by which a president can be declared unfit for office, to be invoked over the Capitol Hill riot. But that has a high constitutional threshold, requiring a majority of his sycophantic cabinet to declare him unfit.As for more conventional checks on a wayward president, they have proved extraordinarily weak. A Congress over which Trump exerts a populist terrorism has been reluctant to use its powers to call him to account. He has flagrantly declared wars without congressional authority, abusedexecutive ordersas “emergencies” and frozen federal spending to halt the “advance [of] Marxist equity”. He has even tried toredefine US citizenship, which is unconstitutional.Very gradually some institutions supposed to hold the White House in check are finding muscle. Judges haveblockedattempts to limit birthright citizenship. Trump’s blanket firing of public officials is beinglegally challenged, although the supreme court has often sided with him. Even the Senate Republican leader,John Thune, has balked at Trump’s proposedSave America Act– which would require anyone voting to show documentary proof of US citizenship. Its outrageous gerrymandering would shrink Democrat votes and aid Republicans. It is an echo of the Jim Crow laws of the post-civil war south.Where this president leaves the US’s longstanding allies overseas is less clear. Visitors to the British embassy in Washington are traditionally warned that “we disagree with America about almost everything, but remain the closest of friends”. Britain distanced itself from war in Vietnam but joined the US, inexplicably, in Iraq. But nothing has come near Trump’s sustained abuse of Britain in the past year on everything from defence spending to wind turbines. He sees the UK as “weak” and “on the edge of disaster”. It was “once” the US’s greatest ally. But by implication, is no more.This opens the central weakness in Anglo-American relations that Trump has made explicit. This is the assumption that the US would honour the principle of collective defence and go to war with Russia, in the event that Russia declared war on Europe. This held during the cold war, with the US’s guarantee of Europe’s security taken as axiomatic.Since the end of the cold war, that guarantee has become ever more flimsy. Despite events in Ukraine, it has longseemed implausible that Russia would declare nuclear waron the west, let alone on America itself. It is therefore equally implausible that the US could threaten Russia with nuclear retaliation.At which point a central essence of the Nato alliance starts to crumble. European governments have seen a president ready to annex foreign countries, invade others, disrupt world trade with aggressive tariffsand defy international law. Can such a wayward and egocentric man, devoid of domestic constraints, really be relied on to exercise extreme caution and dependability in circumstances where nuclear weapons are at issue – whether or not the end of the cold war has diminished the threat of east-west confrontation?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn other words, nations should start looking realistically at the defence of their own continent and their own borders. There is no new world order any longer. That balloon has been punctured.Friends of the US have always relied on its constitution to hold autocratic presidents to the straight and narrow. But not since Andrew Jackson in the 1830s has there been one who flouts law and convention as brazenly as Trump. Over the next two years his nation’s political institutions are to be sorely tested. But then he will be gone. Perhaps only then will Britain learn his legacy.Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsUS foreign policyDefence policyUS national securityUS midterm elections 2026commentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassment | Sidney Blumenthal | The Guardian
description: The president’s chaotic schemes of aggrandizement, from Venezuela to Iran, have no larger rationale
Author: Sidney Blumenthal
Headline: The president’s chaotic schemes of aggrandizement, from Venezuela to Iran, have no larger rationale
Content: ‘Trump’s outlandish exhibitions of triumphalism in the face of rejection and defeat echo the Marx Brothers more than Marx and Lenin.’Photograph: Jim Watson,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Trump’s outlandish exhibitions of triumphalism in the face of rejection and defeat echo the Marx Brothers more than Marx and Lenin.’Photograph: Jim Watson,dave Chan/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s clash with Canada is his latest imperialistic embarrassmentSidney BlumenthalThe president’s chaotic schemes of aggrandizement, from Venezuela to Iran, have no larger rationaleFri 11 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.15 EDTShareTrumpism is the lowest stage of imperialism. “We’re not going to invade Greenland. We’re going to buy it,” Donald Trump reportedlytoldthe annual black-tie dinner on 1 February of the private Alfalfa Club, an assemblage of prominent Washington figures, a number of whom he had publicly humiliated, and others he was investigating or suing. “It’s never been my intention to make Greenland the 51st state. I want to make Canada the 51st state. Greenland will be the 52nd state. Venezuela can be 53rd.” The room greeted several of his remarks with dead silence. His cosplay as thePirate Kingwas not received as a good-humored takeoff from a Gilbert and Sullivan opera. He went on. “So many people in the room I hate,” he said in a display of honesty. “Most of you I like,” he claimed. Then, at his peak euphoria, he flew off to Mar-a-Lago to plan his attack on Iran, which took place 27 days later.Trump’s imperialism of piracy and plunder is less of a system even than that of the earliest imperialism of 17th-century privateers raiding the Spanish Main, the divine right of kings, and monarchs dividing up the spoils as favors to create their lords and earls. His schemes of aggrandizement operating by threat and force are justified by no larger rationale, nothing as exalted as “the white man’s burden”, marauding wherever and however he can to seize resources.How Mark Carney’s speeches have become political earthquakes | Ted WidmerRead moreDescribing his actions as some version of colonialism grants him a more orderly and coherent method than he possesses. His pillaging bears not the slightest resemblance to the highly organized administration of Queen Victoria’s British empire. Trump’s predation is calculated to wreck the long-established arrangements of international trade, law and cooperation created after the second world war and the fall of colonial empires, whose guidelines he sees as obstructing his own profit and power. Obsessed with his fortune hunting, he couldn’t care less about the political consequences for ill-fated Republican candidates in the midterm elections who must face the music for the harm he is doing to their states. They are the least of his collateral damage.Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, offered the most succinct critique of Trump’s intent to usurp the sovereignty of countries in order to make them turn over their wealth to him. Carneysaid: “Canada is a sovereign, independent nation. We are not a target to be bullied, nor are we a client state to be subordinated … We will not sign an agreement that sacrifices our basic sovereignty, undermines our legal system, or cedes control over our foreign trade to Washington.” HecalledTrump’s demands a “last-minute power play intended to reduce Canada to an economic subsidiary”.Trump’s ultimatum abrogated the legal foundation of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, which he himself had signed in 2020. He had previouslydemeaned Carneyas the “governor” of Canada. Now, adopting his characteristic pose as victim, TrumpclaimedCanada had been “ripping off the United States for years” and were among “worst” nations to “deal with”.. “They feel entitledand will be entitled no longer … It’stime to teachCanada you can’t do this anymore….Someone shouldget these clowns to fall in line.”Carney replied that Canada was “at war” and would adopt “counter-measures”, tariffs of its own. “America,” hesaid, “has changed … If Washington wants to trade, they must come to the table as equals.”Trump’s answer was to issue anexecutive orderrenaming Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, the reflexive branding of the real estate operator. The White House put out AI-generatedvideosof Trumpkicking overa sign reading “Lake Ontario” and replacing it with a new one, “Lake America”, andanotherwith a squadron of ducks all with Trump’s hairdo and armed with machine guns patrolling the shore of “Lake America” to the theme music of Hawaii Five-O. The implied invocation of the Marx brothers’ farce of the ludicrous country of Freedonia nonsensically going to war, Duck Soup, seems lost on the busy beavers of Trump’s slop.Trump’s method has been consistent since he leveraged a mineral resource deal out of Ukraine in April 2025 at a weak point in its conflict with Russia. Rather than pressure Putin, Trump’s agents disguised as diplomats, his son-in-law Jared Kushner and real estate pal Steve Witkoff, the Rosencrantz and Guildenstern of Trump’s imperialism, stand by to negotiate post-sanctions deals on his behalf.Trump’s ridiculous bullying of Canada is backfiring | Robert ReichRead moreVenezuela became Trump’s template for his piratical adventures. After swooping in on 3 January to capture its strongman, Nicolás Maduro, Trump promised a transition to democratic elections and that the US would play a custodial role over Venezuelan oil for the benefit of its people.Not long after Trump grabbed Maduro, he declared he needed to acquire Greenland andthreatened a tariff waragainst Denmark and European allies to “get Greenland, including right, title and ownership”. “We probably won’t get anything unless I decide to use excessive strength and force, where we would be frankly unstoppable. But I won’t do that,”Trump said, adding, “I don’t have to use force,” and “I don’t want to use force.” He relented momentarily on 21 January after heclaimedhe had reached a “framework” agreement to negotiate over natural resources, though he subsequently sent preposterous agents into Greenland to stir up a quixotic annexation movement to no avail.A month later, he bombed Iran. Trump stated that his true inspiration for the Iran war was the Venezuelan model in aposton 11 June: “At some point in the not too distant future, we will … assume total control of their Oil and Gas Markets, much like we have with Venezuela, which is working out brilliantly for both Venezuela and the United States of America.”On 31 August, Trump announced that the US would take a stake in17 oilfieldsin partnership with North American Blue Energy Partners, controlled by a Venezuelan oilman,Alejandro Betancourt. Betancourt was briefly detained in Britain, which was reportedly linked to a Swiss warrant on suspicion of money laundering. Betancourt has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with any offenses. The Swiss warrant was withdrawn in May and he became a Trump associate.The Trump administration has already claimed tohave received proceeds of $500mfrom oil sales, initially deposited in an account in Qatar. When the congressman Sean Casten of Illinois and the senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland wrote aletterrequesting information, the administrationshifted the moneyto an opaque account managed by the treasury department. In anarticlepublished in June by the Council on Foreign Relations, “The U.S. Took Over Venezuela’s Oil Industry. Where Has All the Money Gone?”, Roxana Vigil, a former treasury department expert, observed that in dealing with the “same corrupt regime, different leader … the Trump administration has provided almost no information on the system it has established to sell Venezuelan oil, collect the revenue, and use the funds”.The countries whose sovereignty, self-interest and rule of law Trump has struck include the United States. His assault on Canada has sent a shock through the whole US economy. The statemost affectedeconomically, Michigan, shares with Canada one of the most integrated industrial relationships in the world. More than 38% ofMichigan’s exportsgo to Canada, theDetroit-Windsor corridorhandles 25% of all US-Canada trade, and Trump’s tariffs immediately threaten260,000 jobswith an immensely damaging multiplier effect. As of March, his tariffs had already caused estimated losses of$35bnto automakers. Theaverage costper Michigan household is estimated to be $5,619 in added expenses due to tariff-induced price increases.Trump’s tariffs have effectively hamstrung the Republican candidate for the Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, leaving him with the Hobson’s choice of either inciting Trump’s rage or submitting to his whim. Rogers has decided to take the latter course. He hascalledTrump’s economic policies “masterful”. When JD Vance came to the state, Rogers praised the administration. “The impact you have had on our state is phenomenal,” hesaid. Rogers hurls language about “extremism” against the Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed that substitutes for discussing Trump’s economic fiasco. Rogers is performing the kind of self-abasing fealty to Trump that Trump wishes he would receive from Carney. If only Rogers were the prime minister of Canada, there would be no trouble about “independence”.With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael BehrRead moreVladimir Lenin, in his 1917 tract, Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism, argued in his dogmatic and overdetermined style that imperialism at the turn of the 20th century represented the integration of monopoly, finance and industrial capital, with the great powers dividing the world into colonies, and their conflict precipitating the first world war.In Trump’s imaginarium, he views himself as omnipotent and omniscient. When the world isn’t pliable, he must resort to greater force to reassure himself that the world acknowledges his self-image. The more he meets resistance to his fixed idea, the more pressure he must exert. He finds himself in a vicious cycle. His power hemorrhages, US power dissipates and he spins in a whirlpool.Trump’s Venezuelan paradigm, whose conditions cannot be replicated, have quickly descended into questionable business deals. Failed from the start of his Iran war, his pursuit of “total control” recedes over the horizon. His clash withCanadahas been confronted with Carney’s fierce defiance. Trump’s quest for a new field to conquer has landed him in yet another quagmire.“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,”saidCarney. In the meantime, Trump’s outlandish exhibitions of triumphalism in the face of rejection and defeat echo the Marx Brothers more than they echo Marx and Lenin: “Hail Freedonia!”Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln:A Self-Made Man,Wrestling With His AngelandAll the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of theCourt of History podcastExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionCanadaMark CarneyAmericasUS foreign policycommentShareReuse this content

title: 9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you think | Moustafa Bayoumi | The Guardian
description: Anti-Muslim sentiment is used as a political weapon. Meanwhile, Muslim American leaders are making a difference for all
Author: Moustafa Bayoumi
Headline: Anti-Muslim sentiment is used as a political weapon. Meanwhile, Muslim American leaders are making a difference for all
Content: ‘What makes Mamdani and El-Sayed noteworthy is not just their obvious communication skills but their deliberate attention to policies that enhance the public good for all.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘What makes Mamdani and El-Sayed noteworthy is not just their obvious communication skills but their deliberate attention to policies that enhance the public good for all.’Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesOpinionIslamophobia9/11 entrenched Islamophobia in US politics. But it doesn’t work the way you thinkMoustafa BayoumiAnti-Muslim sentiment is used as a political weapon. Meanwhile, Muslim American leaders are making a difference for allFri 11 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.53 EDTShareIt’s been 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11, and during this time Muslim Americans have learned how to live in that dangerous space between other Americans’ fears and their ignorance.The fear was clear from the beginning. Immediately following 9/11, Muslim Americans faced what Human Rights Watchcalled“a severe wave of backlash violence”. A tide of hate rose up against ordinary Muslims and those who appeared to be Muslim, includingat least three murdersin the immediate backlash after the attacks. The federal government, for its part, began targeting Muslim immigrants in a massive surge of repression that legal experts sooncomparedto the Palmer Raids of the 1920s.The ignorance was just as evident. Even Oprah Winfrey did her part to allay it, dedicating anepisodeof her show in October 2001 to “Islam 101”. The Qur’anleapton to the New York Times bestseller list that fall. Yet despite these early efforts at education, most Americans still learned little about Islam and Muslims. One 2006studyfound that only a third of those polled realized that Muslims worship the same God as Christians and Jews do. Close to 10% of respondents thought Muslims worship a “moon god”.Much of this fear and ignorance has continued unevenly over the last quarter century, with negative attitudes towards Muslim Americans softening at times and hardening, sometimes intodeadly violence, at other times. What’s interesting is when expressions of these attitudes happen. It turns out that predicting when animosity to Muslims will rise and fall may not be quite what you think.Researchers who study Islamophobia discovered several years ago that anti-Muslim outbreaks in the United States don’t follow highly publicized acts of terrorism. Rather, Islamophobic incidents tend to cluster more routinely around our election cycles. That’s what the New American Foundationfoundin 2018. That’s what the researcher Dalia Mogaheddiscoveredearlier. And that’s partly what the Brookings Institution’s Shibley Telhami was referencing when hewrote, in 2024, that there was “strong suggestive evidence” that presidential messaging and crisis rhetoric can considerably sway American public attitudes toward Muslims.Anti-Muslim hate and antisemitism are twin crises. We must confront them together | Binairfer NowrojeeRead moreIslamophobia, in other words, is better understood not as an irrational fear of a religious other but rather as an increasingly instrumentalized part of our politics, one that is most often activated around our elections. (Needless to say, whenIslamophobiais deployed, it’s at the expense of the American Muslim community’s wellbeing.) And since we’re also closing in on a fiercely contested midterm election season, we should take note of the sky-high levels of Islamophobic rhetoric we’re witnessing today from the (mostly Republican) politician class.Consider Laura Loomer, the far-right activist and Donald Trump’sclose confidante. “Ban Muslims from holding office in America,” shepostedon Twitter/X in July. Then there’s the South Carolina representative Nancy Mace, whowrote: “Every single Muslim holding public office in America is a trojan horse, and a threat to both national security and our republic. We refuse to be silent.” The Florida representative Randy Fine, who has called for thedeportationof the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani,believes: “We need more Islamophobia, not less. Fear of Islam is rational.” And the senator Tommy Tubervillerecently stated: “Michigan Democrats just voted to send a TERRORIST to the Senate. Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed is a RADICAL ISLAMIST who will do everything he can to destroy America.” In a thinly veiled Islamophobic comment, JD Vancerecently said: “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil. And on the rise in the United States of America today.”In Texas, the levels of Islamophobia are now stratospheric. Lone Star politicians loudly trumpet anti-Muslim messages and repeatedly introduce versions of anti-Muslim legislation, seeking to forbid everything from sharia courts, whichdon’t actually existin Texas, toreal estate developments by Muslims. Must be election season.The Texas governor Greg Abbott, who is up forre-election, hasdesignatedthe country’s largest Muslim civil rights organization, the Council on American Islamic Relations (Cair), a foreign terrorist organization. This is ludicrous, of course, but as a Muslim organization, Cair’s an easy mark. As the Knight First Amendment Institutepoints out, “the domestic targeting of dissent starts with groups that those in power deem to be attractive political targets, but it never ends there. Without further opposition to these orders, CAIR is likely only the first of many groups to be in the crosshairs of politically motivated governors.”And that’s the larger point. Muslim Americans have been weathering these kinds of attacks for decades now, but what we also know is that attacks on Muslims won’t end as attacks on Muslims. For 25 years, we have known what it means to live under a national security state. We have known whatwarrantless surveillancefeels like. We have known whatpoliticized immigrationenforcement looks like (remember theMuslim ban?). We have known what it means when our dissenting voices are silenced, especially whenadvocating for Palestine.And so, we recognize when thosesame toolsare used by the National Security Agency to spy on ordinary Americans (as revealed by the whistleblowerEdward Snowden) or when today’smass deportationscarried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcementresembletheimmigration crackdownon Muslim immigrants decades earlier. Republicans worry loudly about their made-up fantasy of “creeping sharia”, but what all of us should really be concerned about is the reality of this creeping authoritarianism.Muslim Americans have hardly been silent when facing this repression. Instead, we’veorganizedourselves to oppose it. If the political culture of the United States is poised to deny us our legitimate rights, then the response must be preserving those rights for everybody, not just for Muslim Americans.The Guardian view on Islamophobia: political rhetoric is fuelling hate crime | EditorialRead moreThat’s exactly what we’re witnessing today. Muslim Americans are more present in the American political scene than ever before. According to arecent study, a record 255 Muslims now serve in elected positions across the country, including 11 mayors, 18 judges and four members of the US House of Representatives. Muslim women account for more than 43% of the total.Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed are probably today’s most visible Muslim American politicians. What makes them noteworthy is not just their obvious communication skills, but their deliberate attention to policies that enhance the public good for all.El-Sayed, for example, prioritizes universal access tohealthcareandclean water, eliminatingmedical debtand banningcorporate moneyin politics. Mamdani, for his part, hasdelivereda pilot program delivering taxpayer-funded childcare for two-year-olds, arent freezeon rent-stabilized apartments, and aparents’ night outprogram, where children spend supervised time at city recreation centers so parents can have time for themselves. These Muslim politicians have discovered a simple, timeless truth: Democracy’s best defense is ensuring that everyone lives well.For the last 25 years, a bevy of political forces have routinely mobilized fear and ignorance against Muslim Americans to peddle the fiction that Muslims will take over the country. Their message has always been that Muslim Americans don’t belong in the United States.But you know what? We’re paying less attention to them by the hour. Muslim Americans have too much work to do preserving our democracy. The truth is that, while the Islamophobes waste everyone’s time with the ludicrous charge that Muslims and Americans are irreconcilably different, Muslim Americans are just too busy making a difference. For everyone’s sake.Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel to Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnistExplore more on these topicsIslamophobiaOpinionSeptember 11 2001Zohran MamdaniIslamReligioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Five-set tennis is under attack. Killing it would be a colossal unforced error | US Open Tennis 2026 | The Guardian
description: Shelton and Alcaraz’s 3.33am finish has renewed the debate over best-of-five tennis. Scrapping one of the sport’s great traditions would be the wrong fix
Author: Andrew Lawrence
Headline: Shelton and Alcaraz’s 3.33am finish has renewed the debate over best-of-five tennis. Scrapping one of the sport’s great traditions would be the wrong fix
Content: The clock inside Arthur Ashe Stadium shows 3.33am as Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz contest the latest-finishing match in US Open history.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe clock inside Arthur Ashe Stadium shows 3.33am as Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz contest the latest-finishing match in US Open history.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesUS Open Tennis 2026Five-set tennis is under attack. Killing it would be a colossal unforced errorAndrew Lawrenceat Flushing MeadowsFive-set matches are physically punishing, occasionally absurd and increasingly under threat. They also produce much of what makes grand slam tennis greatFri 11 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.40 EDTShareTuesday night’s quarter-final matchbetween Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcarazhad everything a US Open spectacle could ask for: huge stakes, knife-edge drama, top-shelf competition and an American hero who comes through in the end. The only fault to find was really the matter of time. The first ball wasn’t struck until 11.05 in the evening, and Shelton’s clinching ace didn’t come until 3.33 in the morning – marking, after a total of 4hr 28min on court, the latest-ending US Open match by a whopping 43 minutes.Somewhat predictably, the discourse among media and fans following the late-night match has swiftly moved on from the USTA’s misadventures in scheduling to a referendum on the five-set match and whether it should be put out to pasture. For the record: that would be a colossal unforced error.Tiafoe v Shelton US Open semi-final a legacy of the departing Gaël MonfilsRead moreFive-setters aren’t just intrinsic to the grand slam canon. They are a badge of honor in the men’s game, confirmation that a player can and did indeed hack it in the big leagues. John Isner may not have won a major during his time on tour. But his capacity for grinding out marathon matches – not leastthe three-day, 11-hour epiche played against Nicholas Mahut at Wimbledon in 2010 – is why he remains highly respected by peers and fans alike.Best-of-five is the exclusive framing device for the best matches in history and an imprimatur of the sport’s most revered champions. (See,The Greatest Match Ever Playedorlast year’s French Open final.) Even the losers are celebrated merely for having survived and played on to become part of the tale. “People still remember this match but he didn’t know if I was the winner,” Mahutsaidin 2015. “So, maybe, in 10 years people will think I won the match.”Five-setters are the mother of sporting crucibles – a test of will, nerve and focus. That holds true as much for the men who play as their spectators. Much of what makes the experience of following tennis so affirming is the global group-watch sessions that take over social media anytime an Australian Open match goes the distance.Viewers who can’t babysit the full marathon into the night – lest they risk sleeping through their morning alarms or, worse, cheering the exciting points too boisterously and rousing their house and neighbors – get to wake up and find the fifth set still raging as they’re getting ready for work the next day. A skeptic might point to the Australian Open, perhaps more so than any other slam, as a prime reason to abolish the five-setter. But true tennis nerds see the Happy Slam for what it is: a rite of passage. In fact, if they don’t seem surprised by the US Open’s Melbourne hours, it’s because Craig Tiley, formerly the CEO ofTennisAustralia, is now running the USTA.View image in fullscreenJohn Isner and Nicolas Mahut during their record-breaking 11-hour, five-minute match at Wimbledon in 2010, which Isner won 70-68 in the fifth set after three days of play.Photograph: Leo Mason/Corbis/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesStill, for all the honor and valor there is to be extracted from five-setters, especially as they pile up, there’s no denying the matches exact a physical toll from players that has become harder to ignore as the pressure to maintain a hectic touring calendar puts them at increasing risk of missing tournaments from wear and tear. That tension between tradition and evolution has animated an existential debate around five-setters that has been simmering for years.Last month, incoming Tennis Australia CEO Andrew Abdo tossed out ideas for a shorter-form game. “Maybe we’re not playing best of five all the way through,” Abdosaidat a Melbourne sports conference. “Maybe the point scoring system changes. Maybe there are different permutations to how we engage and entertain audiences without losing the fabric, and what really makes the sport special.”Abdo’s remarks – which come after Tiley, his predecessor, suggestedwomenplay five-set matches – might not have resonated if Novak Djokovic, the slam king who built his reputation on five-set matches, hadn’t first proposed changes to the scoring system that would keep the five sets but dilute the number of games to “keep the matches within a two-hour window”. And even though the 24-time major champion was being somewhat facetious – he was specifically asked for an opinion that would inflame fans – it didn’t stop John McEnroe, tennis’ self-righteous conscience, from breaking out his gas canister. “People’s attention spans are shorter than ever,” said McEnroe – famously, the five-set loser of an epic 1980 Wimbledon final canonized asthe War of 18-16.View image in fullscreenRafael Nadal lies on Centre Court after defeating Roger Federer in their epic five-set Wimbledon final in 2008.Photograph: Simon Bruty/Sports Illustrated/Getty ImagesBut those voices, however prominent, have yet to reach a volume that drowns out five-set traditionalists. “Do I love five setters? Absolutely not,” Frances Tiafoe said after hanging on to beat fellow American Alex Michelsenin a five-set quarterfinal he surely would’ve lostif the scoring revolutionists had their way. “When I’m up two sets to love I would love to shake hands and go home. But it’s tennis, man. I grew up watching incredible tennis, incredible five setters. Novak vs Rafa, Federer vs Rafa. Incredible five setters which go on for hours and hours. That is the history of the game.”The quarter-final between Shelton and Alcaraz wrote another chapter, one that gave Arthur Ashe Stadium the feel of a Queens dive after last call. Shelton, still woozy from outlasting the US Open’s defending champion, beseeched his sister’s employer, Morgan Stanley, to give her the day off from work. (She was due back by 6am.) As he and Alcaraz contested the final points, with Tuesday having turned into Wednesday, custodial workers could be seen and heard tidying up the stadium and grounds for the horde to come after sunrise. On social media, US Open patrons who hung on til the bitter end shared the outrageous surge pricing they encountered for rideshares back home (“I could get a hotel, bro”) and posted videos of exhausted ballkids hustling back into the city before school starts “in three hours”.No one’s suggesting the US Open needs a curfew. (That’s Wimbledon’s turf, after all.) There’s a simple fix to the late-night match problem that doesn’t involve fundamentally restructuring the way the men’s game is played. The USTA could just move one of its primetime features to the world’s 13th-largest tennis show court – Louis Armstrong Stadium, right next door to Ashe – and move the start times up to ensure play didn’t extend much past midnight. The start of Shelton-Alcaraz was delayed by Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro taking three sets to wrap up their quarter-final, which was itself delayed by the afternoon matches ahead ofthemgoing long. But that might mean missing out on the filthy lucre that Ashe generates from its doubled capacity and extravagant suites – and god forbid the USTA make slightly less money.View image in fullscreenCarlos Alcaraz in action during his five-set quarter-final defeat by Ben Shelton at the US Open.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesThe funny thing about all this panting to change tennis for its own good is that tennis has changed so much already. Electronic line calls, 10-point tiebreaks, on-court coaching, the serve clock – the hidebound sport has proven it can be tweaked for pace and entertainment without a cost to its core integrity.But what truly makes the talk about abolishing the five-setter so hard to hear, particularly from veterans of those wars, is the fundamental misunderstanding. In other sports, time has a negative correlation. Who among us hasn’t been held hostage by the football game that lumbers on because the coach can’t be bothered to take their timeouts home? Who among us hasn’t been prisoner to a basketball game that would have ended in 30 seconds if it hadn’t been for all the fouling?In tennis, a match that stretches on for hours and hours isn’t a drag. It’s an obvious marker of quality, an implied reason to tune in. And if engagement is the name of the game, the drama of a fifth act that holds the potential to maintain an audience, capture a new one and – in the case of the Shelton-Alcaraz quarter – extend the primetime viewing window on the West Coast – should be an incentive for those committed to growing the game to embrace the five-setter even tighter, not abolish it.One can just imagine the lines that would be drawn if the five-set format ever changed: the players who come after having to put up with cranky veterans of those five-set marathons of yesteryear prattling on about how thereallegends were forgedin my day. That’s no kind of ending for a sport that has a great ending already.Explore more on these topicsUS Open Tennis 2026Carlos AlcarazTennisUS Open tennisUS sportsNovak DjokovicJohn McEnroecommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia and Canada can learn from each other on climate if we separate action from declaration | Rosa Galvez | The Guardian
description: Climate integrity means being honest about the gap between emissions reduced on paper and emissions reduced in the atmosphere
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Climate integrity means being honest about the gap between emissions reduced on paper and emissions reduced in the atmosphere
Content: ‘Climate cannot be separated from biodiversity loss, inequality or reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. Tackled together, these challenges produce more resilient, equitable solutions.’Photograph: Brett Monroe Garner/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Climate cannot be separated from biodiversity loss, inequality or reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. Tackled together, these challenges produce more resilient, equitable solutions.’Photograph: Brett Monroe Garner/Getty ImagesOpinionClimate crisisAustralia and Canada can learn from each other on climate if we separate action from declarationRosa GalvezClimate integrity means being honest about the gap between emissions reduced on paper and emissions reduced in the atmosphereFri 11 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 19.58 EDTShareCanada and Australia are both democracies built on abundant resources, extraordinary biodiversity and world-class science, with prosperity built substantially on mining,oil and gas. We are major fossil fuel exporters running an economic model incompatible with a stable climate, and living the consequences through worseningbushfires, floods and drought.As I prepare for the Climate Integrity Summit in Sydney, I am struck less by the distance between our countries than by how much we have in common. We face the same defining question: how do we move beyond fossil fuels without sacrificing prosperity or nature?Our political systems differ, but Australians are asking the same questions Canadians are: young people wanting action to match promises, Indigenous communities wanting real recognition of their rights, scientists warning about tipping points, businesses recognising that tomorrow’s economy will reward innovation over dependence on yesterday’s technology.BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influenceRead moreThe challenge facing our countries is not technological. It is governance.Canada and Australia have focused on reducing emissions from fossil fuels while avoiding the harder conversation about reducing our dependence on them. That distinction matters. It determines whether we are managing decline or genuinely transforming our economies. The world is already moving to renewable energy. Australia has started that shift,Canadais late to it. Expanding renewables while continuing to expand fossil fuels is not a transition, it is addition. Every extra tonne of greenhouse gas warms the planet, no matter how sophisticated our accounting becomes.This debate is especially live in Australia now. Parliament is reviewing reforms to the Safeguard Mechanism, the country’s main industrial emissions framework. The central question: should major emitters meet their obligations by buying carbon offsets instead of cutting emissions on-site?1:31Train crew in Canada 'encased' by intense flames amid wildfires - videoCanada has wrestled with near-identical debates over carbon capture and offset markets. My own view, shaped by science rather than ideology, is that offsets and carbon capture have a limited role, for genuinely hard-to-abate emissions only. They should never excuse delaying the transformation science tells us is unavoidable.Climate integrity means being honest about the gap between emissions reduced on paper and emissions reduced in the atmosphere. Research increasingly questions whether offset credits are truly additional, or whether buyers decarbonise any faster than those who don’t. If offsets stay cheaper than innovation, we reward the status quo. Canada’s own wildfires have shown, starkly, that forests are not permanent carbon stores.Finance is another area of convergence. Australia has introduced a science-based Sustainable Finance Taxonomy directing investment toward net zero activities. Canada has pursued mandatory climate disclosures, and through my proposed Climate-Aligned Finance Act, I am seeking to align financial markets with our climate commitments. The question is no longer whether finance should support the transition, but whether policy keeps favouring yesterday’s industries. Canada’s own taxonomy debate shows how hard these choices remain: sustainable finance only works when it reflects science, not political compromise.Climate cannot be separated from biodiversity loss, inequality or reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. Tackled together, these challenges produce more resilient, equitable solutions. Australia’s integration of Indigenous safeguards into its finance framework offers Canada real lessons. Canada’s parliamentary oversight and accountability legislation may offer something back.Cities sweltering and the smell of the middle ages: has the climate crisis killed Instagram’s Euro summer? | Brigid DelaneyRead moreNeither country has the perfect model, and legislation on both sides remains fragmented. That is why dialogue between democracies matters, and why Parliamentarians for a Fossil-Free Future exists: legislators cannot solve global problems in national silos. As the talks inColombiashowed, sharing our successes is valuable, and sharing our mistakes may be more valuable still.Canada and Australia should see this transition as an opportunity, not a sacrifice. The countries that lead will be those that channel investment into innovation, protect nature and build economies generating long-term wellbeing within planetary limits.We have the capacity to lead. What remains to be seen is whether we have the political courage to make our climate commitments more than declarations. Climate integrity is ultimately a question of trust: whether citizens believe governments and industries will align decisions with the science they publicly accept. Trust may be our most valuable national resource.Together, as two middle powers with complementary experience, we can help show that prosperity, biodiversity, Indigenous reconciliation and climate leadership are not competing ambitions. They are the foundations of the same future.Rosa Galvez is an Independent Senator for Québec (Bedford). title: In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for elsewhere?  | Ahdaf Soueif | The Guardian
description: For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all, says author Ahdaf Soueif
Author: Ahdaf Soueif
Headline: For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all, says author Ahdaf Soueif
Content: Israeli rightwing activists overlooking Gaza during a rally calling for the re-establishment of Israeli settlements in Gaza, 30 July 2025.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APView image in fullscreenIsraeli rightwing activists overlooking Gaza during a rally calling for the re-establishment of Israeli settlements in Gaza, 30 July 2025.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APOpinionIsraelIn Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for elsewhere?Ahdaf SoueifFor now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us allFri 11 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 10.58 EDTShareLast week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put outan AI-generated videothat showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building anexecution sitefor Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel andtaunted female prisonerswho complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning tointroduce crocodilesto patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while thelaw that he championedmandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks isbuilt on public support.Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand itsillegal settlements in theWest Bank.It had been a widely held tenet that if enough people in the democratic western world knew the reality of whatIsraelwas doing to the Palestinians, they would pressure their governments, and Israel would be made to observe the norms of international law. Eventually, a reality would be born in which Jews, Muslims and Christians would live as equals within some political system that would be as good – and as flawed – as others. South Africa was always cited as the example, where rising international pressure over the decades was decisive.But what looked like the winning of the moral, rational argument was offset by an acceleration of the processes of occupation, an increase in the frequency and blatancy of settler attacks in the West Bank, and of Israel Defense Forces (IDF) attacks on Gaza. The past three years have been the logical development of this. In the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 attacks, Israel escalated its killing, maiming and displacement of the Palestinians to the level ofcertifiable genocide. The defence minister, Israel Katz, says he iscommitted to the ethnic cleansingof Gaza, while a West Bank settlerproudly tellsthe BBC that one Jewish life is worth 10 million Palestinian lives. Social media is awash with Israelis – from pundits on TV news debates to IDF soldiers – stating and performing the outrages necessary to achieve the objective of a Palestinian-free Palestine.Israeli ministers keep telling everyone their brutal plans – so why doesn’t the world take them seriously? | Nesrine MalikRead moreAnd while people across the world now know the truth of what is happening in Palestine and repeatedly and full-heartedly reject it, many democracies across the west continue to send arms and provide intelligence to Israel – even in a time of genocide. The US president’sBoard of Peacemakes a mockery of Palestinians, while hundreds of Israeli trucksclear the rubble from Gaza– and, with it, evidence of war crimes. The US attacks international institutions, such as theinternational criminal court, that seek to offer some semblance of justice for Palestinians. And to repress the constant protests of hundreds of thousands of their citizens, western democracies compromise their justice systems, attack their educational institutions and undermine their own democratic freedoms. Some have belatedly announced sanctions limited to Israeli settlements – illegal settlements that have should have been sanctioned years ago.In 2014, I served on the jury of the Russell Tribunal onPalestine. In the preface to the report, which came after Israel’s third war on Gaza in six years, I wrote: “If not genocide, then genocide is not far behind.”Today I wonder if the genocide is not also a trailer for something more to come.If the genocide was not a surprise, neither is the fact that the old colonial masters have no particular aversion to it. In a line of continuity with their own history, western countries have for decades partnered with Israel on weapons production and intelligence and surveillance technology. The west has sought Israeli advice and training in counter-terrorism, interrogation and civilian population-control techniques. A selling point for Israeli weapons has always beenthat they have been tried and tested.And now, as Israel’s genocide is livestreamed, the establishment watches, enables, protects and helps tidy up. We may be watching a research and development exercise, a blueprint, a template, an example being created. We are already in a world where – it has been argued – some populations are surplus to requirements. Some of them live in areas that are a property developer’s dream.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis war is not only about Palestinians and Israelis, but about ideologies of supremacy and domination that threaten the people of the world, its civil societies and what is left of its international organisations. For the moment, it is the Palestinians who are on the frontline, the Palestinians who are being killed and maimed and tortured and displaced. But the Palestinians are also standing between all of us and a world remade in Israel’s image.Ahdaf Soueif is the author of Mezzaterra: Fragments from the Common GroundDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Memo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the script  | Marina Hyde | The Guardian
description: If the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world works, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Author: Marina Hyde
Headline: If the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world works, says Guardian columnist Marina Hyde
Content: Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex,  during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, 17 April  2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/APView image in fullscreenHarry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex,  during a visit to Bondi Beach, Australia, 17 April  2026.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/Pool PA/APOpinionPrince HarryMemo to King Charles: you can’t stop the Sussexes’ reality show bandwagon. You only spice up the scriptMarina HydeIf the monarch thought his sniffy letter would put Harry and Meghan at a disadvantage, he doesn’t understand how the celebrity world worksFri 11 Sep 2026 08.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.56 EDTShareOnce again, it has been a lively week for the Real Housewives of Windsor franchise, with Harry and Meghan back in the UK for precisely 12 days before the kingfired out a lettervia the lord chamberlain on Monday, reminding viewers that the Sussexes are “private citizens” and not to treat them as working royals. You have to say the producers on this unscripted reality show are truly at the top of their game with these targeted provocations. Harry and Meghan duly took the bait and issued an intemperately hurt rejoinder – but we’ll get to that in a bit.First, let’s deal with King Charles’s missive to “relevant senior stakeholders across government, the military and Lord Lieutenancies”. Ugh. Not to be too aesthetically sensitive, but I think we can all live without the sovereign being reduced to the ghastly language of “relevant senior stakeholders”. What next? Seeking “buy-in” for ribbon-cutting events and referring to posies as “high levels of audience engagement”? It does all rather reinforce the idea that the Windsors’ cringe-makingly self-styled “the firm” really is some dreary mid-range company with a wan Meet Our Team page on its website, in which Prince William – carefully photographed without a tie – explains that he “enjoys long walks with the dog and is a passionate Aston Villa supporter”.Either way, the letter sent on Charles’s behalf was guaranteed to send the plot into overdrive, much as it does in any Real Housewives franchise when one of the cast sends a cease-and-desist letter to one of the others. (An event that basically feels like it can occur weekly.) Typically these letters then become dramatic drivers. Far from suppressing stories as supposedly intended, they always end up sparking whole new public debates and plotlines in themselves. This is what happened with the Windsors this week – and, indeed, was always going to happen, given the appearance of a pre-emptive slapdown.The royal household must be able to see that the key thing about the Sussexes is that they are forever desperate to be taken seriously, like a music act that was put together on a TV talent show but now wants you to think they’re up there with Patti Smith and Nick Cave.And so it was that Meghan and Harry’s spokespersonimmediately hit backin public, announcing that the couple “were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance”. Ouch. Never show weakness, guys! A briefinggiven to the Telegraphadded that: “The Sussexes prefer the term ‘public figures’, and would have liked an acknowledgment that, on a personal level, they remained members of the royal family, despite no longer receiving public funding.”As indicated, this all hints at a season of endlessly messy dramas to come, given it took less than a fortnight of the pair being back in the country before a public blow-up occurred. In terms of the kind of bizarro unintended consequences you might see on a Housewives episode when someone’s kicked off at a girls’ spa day, the military chief of Ugandapromptly announcedhis country was pulling out of Prince Harry’s Invictus Games because they didn’t want to participate in something “that does not have His Majesty’s approval”. What can you say? Other than: deploy the reaction gifs.You don’t have to be a reality TV obsessive to spot the faultlines here that should guarantee that the Sussexes’ unexpected return to the UK will result in endless drink tosses. It’s all there in their immediate reaction. Harry and Meghan are really wholly formed reality TV stars now. Not only do they do the tit-for-tat media release to move the plot along, but they also let you know what they were feeling when they read the original press-released letter from the king. In reality TV, moments like these are gleaned from “master interviews” (MIVs), filmed at the end of a season to provide useful retrospective commentary that the producers can cut the main action with. So you’ll see Hell’s Kitchen contestants helpfully reflecting on the scene you’ve just watched, and going: “And I’m standing there thinking – Chef Ramsay is going to go crazy when he sees this.” Or, in this case, “I was a little surprised not to have been told by Chef Ramsay about this in advance.”This is precisely how the Sussexes now conduct public life, and it remains incompatible with the way the royal household does it. For all their supposed desire for a quiet life, Harry and Meghan have done that thing that the Beckhams – and indeed the secessionist Beckham-Peltzes – seemingly cannot help but do, where they claim to enjoy privacy but in fact live life out loud in a way that has come to feel normal to them but is really anything but.Which brings us back to the burning question of why on earth you’d move back somewhere you are on the record – multiple times – as absolutely loathing in all its aspects. Increasingly, and faster than predicted, it feels like the answer to that is “for content” – scripted or otherwise. It’s fairly difficult to see the Sussexes’ relocation as anything other than laying the groundwork for a sequel to the only story of theirs that has ever rated with audiences: their own struggle with the forces of the British establishment/media/enemies within the royal household. Or as Real Housewives of Beverly Hills star Lisa Rinna once put it – and her head would be right up there on the franchise’s Mount Rushmore – “you better believe I’m gonna talk about it”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarina Hyde is a Guardian columnistWhat a Time to be Alive! by Marina Hyde (Guardian Faber, £20). title: Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriously | Gaby Hinsliff | The Guardian
description: AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
Author: Gaby Hinsliff
Headline: AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late, says Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff
