Content: ‘AI agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life.’Photograph: MattLphotography/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘AI agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life.’Photograph: MattLphotography/AlamyOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriouslyGaby HinsliffAI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too lateFri 11 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.02 EDTShareAnother day, another horseman of the apocalypse galloping over the horizon. Lately we have heard from so many AI doomers – tech whistleblowers popping up to warn that their work isprobably going to kill us– that we’re becoming almost blase about it. Humanity wiped out within a decade? Well, only if another world war or the climate crisis doesn’t get us first. Since it’s never clear whether the tech threat is real, or just a twisted form of hype from an industry that drums up investment by making their products sound more powerful than they really are, most of us settle for trying not to think about it too hard.But something about the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’svery public resignationfrom the cutting-edge American lab Anthropic, via a post on X arguing that he can’t keep working for companies “gambling with our lives”, has cut through where bigger names have not. Most chillingly, he claimed that colleagues still at Anthropic aren’t staying because they think he’s wrong about the dangers of pursuing self-improving super intelligence – the holy grail of machines that are not just smarter than humans but capable of building their own even more powerful successors, evolving independently of humans – but because they’re afraid of ceding the field to people with fewer scruples. His colleagues, Coxon said, talk routinely about the “endgame” or the “crunch time”, meaning that what they do in the next year or two will decide the fate of humanity. Whether that’s true or simply self-aggrandising techbro delusion, what he describes is an industry now practically begging to be saved from itself.Thefrisson of alarmover AI running through Westminster this week was real, sharpened by news of Anthropic – which pitches itself as being more safety-conscious than its rivals OpenAI – declining for the first time to submita new model for scrutiny by Britain’s AIsafety watchdog. We are now entering a far more disruptive era of AI, dominated not by relatively basic chatbots but by agents designed to undertake tasks on humans’ behalf, making their own decisions about how to complete them. Unfortunately, it turns out even basic life admin requires the kind of fine judgments that come instinctively to humans but seem remarkably hard to codify for machines.Take the over-zealous agent tasked recently by its Australian client with bookinghim into a pilates class, which responded to finding the class full byhacking the gym’s websiteand booting other people off the waiting list.Now imagine it blundering into something more life-threatening than a gym class. WhenCoxon says his industry hasn’t fixed problems with alignment, and when OpenAI’s chief scientistwarned last weekthat no lab had solved them well enough to carry on scaling this fast much longer, what they’re talking about is this failure to replicate in machines the values and assumptions humans apply to decisions without even really knowing they’re doing it – including the sense of how far it’s justifiable to go in getting what you want.A series of reportedescapes by agentssupposedly confined to OpenAI’s lab for testing, some of which contrived to access the internet behind their human supervisors’ backs and conduct real-world cyber-attacks, has meanwhile raised serious questions over the industry’s ability even to experiment safely. (Unnervingly, Coxon says newer models seem to know when they’re being tested, making it easier for them to deceive researchers.)And agents don’t have to acquire anything like super intelligence to threaten human life: think how easily a cyber-attack on air traffic control, or NHS data systems, or even water purification systems could cause mass fatalities.What’s happening in some frontier AI labs now is arguably the equivalent of the Manhattan Project that built the atomic bomb, but this time led by private companies in a mad dash for wealth and market dominance, not scientists under an elected government’s command. Britons meanwhile got more say in sugar taxes on junk food than we’re getting over regulating something theoretically capable of rendering us extinct.Given time, of course, it might prove possible to replicate in machines the vast ecosystem of social ties, moral codes, intensive parenting and state policing that humans have developed to stop us behaving like sociopaths. (Only this week, Google’sDeepMindreported an experiment where 100 agents were given a maths problem and told not to cheat: though a minority promptly did cheat, a larger group either snitched on them to the humans or helped devise technical fixes.) But time is the one thing nobody dares to give themselves in the middle of an arms race, which is why it’s high time for governments to act. We need an international agreement topress pause, not on AI research as a whole, but on the riskiest projects, until we better understand whether it will ever be possible to mitigate the dangers or control the results. Since it’s hard to imagine Donald Trump voluntarily sacrificing US geopolitical or commercial advantage over China for the good of humanity, leadership may have to come for now not from above but below, where industry insiders spooked by their own work are making common cause with the rest of us.More Americans are nowconcerned than excitedabout AI, according to polling this summer from the Pew Research Center – and unusually it’s the young who are most hostile, afraid it will not only take their jobs but make it harder to form relationships or think creatively. (That’s what growing up on social media seemingly does for trust in tech.) Even big business seems increasingly sceptical, with almost two-thirds of international executives surveyed by the consultantsMcKinseythis summer reportingno measurable impact on earningsfrom using the admittedly basic AI tools now available to them.Warnings about an AI bubble triggering another 2008-style globalfinancial crashhaven’t helped, while plans to build giant, energy-guzzling datacentres are meetingangry local resistanceon both sides of the Atlantic from people who can’t see what’s in it for them. Pressing pause on potential Armageddon looks in the circumstances less like the luddite option, and more like a smart way for tech companies to avoid a full-on backlash that will sweep away the good with the bad.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut if the AI doomers are right, then the window to do so may not always be open. It’s time for humans to stop and think about what we’re doing to ourselves – while we alone still have the power to do so.Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionComputingTechnology policyEthicsAnthropicOpenAIcommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s time for a Gardeners’ World that reflects Britain’s gardens in all their messy, realistic chaos | Claire Ratinon | The Guardian
description: I’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-up, says organic food grower and writer Claire Ratinon
Author: Claire Ratinon
Headline: I’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-up, says organic food grower and writer Claire Ratinon
Content: Monty Don in the Paradise Garden at Longmeadow, his space in Herefordshire.Photograph: BBC StudiosView image in fullscreenMonty Don in the Paradise Garden at Longmeadow, his space in Herefordshire.Photograph: BBC StudiosOpinionGardensIt’s time for a Gardeners’ World that reflects Britain’s gardens in all their messy, realistic chaosClaire RatinonI’ll miss Monty Don, and I know I’m not alone in finding the show a balm for the soul. But this is the perfect opportunity for a shake-upFri 11 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTShareIt’s finally happened. National treasure Monty Don is hanging up his TV garden shearsand saying goodbyeto Gardeners’ World after more than 20 years as the BBC show’s lead presenter. I’ve been a grower for more than a decade myself, and Monty has been a steady and wise omnipresence throughout my journey – especially as he’s been on the right side of contemporary gardening debates over the environment and wildlife, and the use of chemicals and peat in horticulture.That is where the overlap between our worlds of growing end, though. My modest patch of a few veg beds at the end of a small, chaotic and mostly gravelled garden is a universe away from the two-acre dreamscape that is Longmeadow, Don’s garden at his home in Herefordshire. I suspect I’m one of millions who’ve looked longingly at Monty’s remarkable space and the impressive infrastructure (not to mention hired hands!) that make it so special, and cursed the fact that such an ideal garden will never be within reach of us ordinary folk. That’s not to say that it hasn’t been a glorious setting for Monty to share his abundance of plant wisdom from, but now that the search for his replacement is presumably on, perhaps this is an opportunity for a little reimagining.A handful of times over the years, television production companies have asked whether I’d present a new show they were trying to get commissioned, which they hoped would capture the attention of the next generation of gardeners. Unfortunately, not one of them had an idea that wasn’t just a rehash of a makeover show, and that approach is the antithesis of my growing ethos. I’d want to persuade more gardeners to nurture their plots intentionally – so you wouldn’t catch me encouraging anyone to bring that unhinged (and mostly unsustainable) Changing Rooms-style energy to their outside spaces. As a format that honours the true nature of gardening – embracing the steady process of cultivation and not looking for quick results – Gardeners’ World has got the market cornered, and I hope it keeps going for many years to come.And while I’m notnotsaying the next Gardeners’ World presenter should be me (wink-wink), I do have some thoughts on who it could be. There are clearly potential successors waiting in the wings, all of whom have proved themselves worthy. The favourite appears to be Frances Tophill, who would be my first choice from the shortlist too. But what I’dreallylike to see are dispatches and insights from different gardeners in different regions.View image in fullscreenFrances Tophill, one of the main contenders to take over as the lead presenter of Gardeners’ World.Photograph: BBC StudiosThe UK might not be the largest country, but its weather and climate vary massively. A gardener in Cornwall is going to encounter a very different set of conditions to a gardener in Cumbria. And as we face a future in which the seasons become less predictable, tried-and-tested gardening advice may well become moot. Wouldn’t it be wonderful and highly informative to instead see what is possible – and impossible – in different parts of the country, following a consortium of gardeners and their outdoor spaces throughout the growing season?While I’m dreaming up my perfect show, let’s say that some – perhaps all – of those spaces should be ordinary gardens tended by ordinary gardeners. People who are time-poor, resource-light and chaotic in their execution, due to their many other responsibilities. I’m thinking of it being similar to Top Gear flinging family-friendly hatchbacks around its test track as well as luxury sports cars.This may well be a pipe dream, and perhaps it’s only me who is interested in truly realistic gardens. But I think I’ve reached my personal saturation point with aspirational, unobtainable spaces wholly detached from my own growing reality. There’s so much to be learned from the ingenuity and scrappiness of those who succeed – as well as fail – at creating gardens filled with flourishing crops and blooms, when their space and wallets have limits and their lives are full.The one thing that I wouldn’t want to change, though, is how soothing Gardeners’ World can be. I know I’m not alone in finding the tone and the pace – even the ambient sound of bees buzzing past – to be a balm for the soul, and plenty of that can be attributed to Monty’s gentle screen presence. I’d wager that the upcoming generation of gardeners also have jangled nervous systems that could do with some calm – so let’s hope that whoever comes next understands the assignment and keeps the show sailing on a steady and serene trajectory.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionClaire Ratinon is an organic food grower and writerExplore more on these topicsGardensOpinionTelevisionFactual TVGardening advicecommentShareReuse this content

title: How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden | Martin Gelin | The Guardian
description: In 2022 my country entered a new era of cruelty. It will take more than one election to get the old, tolerant Sweden back, writes Swedish journalist Martin Gelin
Author: Martin Gelin
Headline: In 2022 my country entered a new era of cruelty. It will take more than one election to get the old, tolerant Sweden back, writes Swedish journalist Martin Gelin
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesOpinionSwedenHow Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being SwedenMartin GelinIn 2022, my country entered a new era of cruelty. It will take more than one election to get the old, tolerant Sweden backFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.39 EDTShareLast year, a baby named Emanuel was born in Sweden. Before his first birthday, his parents were told that Emanuel could no longer stay in the country. The department of migrationordered his removal, alone, to Iran– despite the ongoing war.Emanuel’s parents were legally in the country. They had Swedish residency permits, but the laws that allowed them to stay were tightened after the baby’s birth, and the family got sucked into a Kafkaesque maze of official hurdles, designed to limit migration toSweden.Raif is a four-year-old boy with autism,who still wears nappies and is unable to talk. This spring, he was informed that he would be deported alone. Raif’s case attracted significantmedia coverageand the authorities eventually reversed the decision.But the number of absurd, hardline calls from the migration department just keeps piling up. A74-year-old British man with dementiawas told to leave the country after 25 years.Another British man, on a generous World Bank retirement pension, was also told he was not welcome to reside permanently in Sweden because retirement money does not count as salary for the purposes of new income thresholds for migrants.The young, the old, vulnerable people, the wealthy: all are the target of harsh and often aggressive immigration policies. And Sweden’s leaders remain unyielding. “We cannot adjust the law based on each and every personal fate,” Ulf Kristersson, the prime minister, said, commenting on a series of hardline immigration decisions involving children.View image in fullscreenElection posters of Swedish Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson in StockholmPhotograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty ImagesSwedes vote in a general election on Sunday 13 September and, according to opinion polls, the centre-left opposition has a slight lead. But even if there is a change of government, many previously unthinkable far-right ideas are now comfortably embedded in the mainstream of Swedish politics. The past four years have been characterised by an astonishing acceptance of ethnonationalist views, xenophobic rhetoric and authoritarian policies, increasingly targeting children. And many of these ideas have been absorbed and appropriated by the centre-left opposition Social Democrats.Not even the deportation of toddlers or the alarming new shift in judicial policy to build prisons for teenagers as young as 14, are too much of a moral red line, it seems.The story of the transformation that now blights Sweden goes back to 2022, when the conservative bloc won that year’s Swedish general election, but only with a tiny margin. TheTidö agreementstruck that December, between the three conservative parties (Moderates, Christian Democrats and Liberals) and the far-right Sweden Democrats meant a minority government could be formed. But this formal pact breached the mainstream’scordon sanitaireagainst cooperating with the radical right. It also launched an attempt to redefine modern Sweden, marking profound policy shifts on immigration, crime, climate and energy, schools and healthcare.Establishment conservatives defended the accord on the grounds that it would blunt the impact of the Sweden Democrats, whose support had been growing since 2015. Instead, it in effect passed the torch of conservative leadership to the far right, giving the Sweden Democrats no ministerial jobs but extraordinary power to shape policy.As a Swede who lived in the US for two decades, I was reluctant to admit that my birth country had changed. I brushed away alarming anecdotes as isolated cases, or a brief departure from the status quo. Surely, Sweden would remain itself, guided by the progressive, egalitarian and humanitarian ideals that defined the country and its public life – at least on the surface – when I was growing up.But in the last four years the Overton window of acceptable debate has shifted radically to the right.A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants, including highly skilled employees of research institutions, universities, tech and medical companies – who have been stunned to learn that they are no longer welcome to work in a country where they have lived for years, sometimes decades.Only15% of Swedes approve of Donald Trump. And yet ideas quite similar to Trump’s ethnonationalism now define much of contemporary Swedish politics, and are challenging our democratic foundations. The Swedish Institute for Human Rights, an independent government agency, claims that Sweden is increasingly shaped by growing acceptance of xenophobic views, hate crimes and by punitive policies directed at children. In its 2026annual reportit expresses “serious concern” over anerosion of human rightsin Sweden.The legal watchdogCivil Rights Defenders also claimsthat a shift has taken place, where the government no longer talks about rights, but about control. Ministers have entwined migration with crime, and increasingly depict citizens, even children, as problems, risks and costs.If this authoritarian turn can be widely accepted so quickly in Sweden, where the democratic and humanitarian foundations were until recently solid, it can happen anywhere.Astring of scandals in the final sprint of the election campaign has not been kind to the far right. Expo, a Swedish magazine that monitors far-right extremism,reportedthat one of the most influential ideologues in the Sweden Democrats, Gustav Gellerbrant, lives with a partner – who also works for the party – and is alleged to have deep ties to Russian influence operations. Gellerbrant was one of the architects of the Tidö agreement and sits in the Sweden Democrats’ coordinating office within the government. He has been placed on paid leave following the reports but Peter Hultqvist, a Social Democrat former defence minister, called the matter a “security crisis” for Sweden that “goes right into the prime minister’s own office”.Gellerbrant himself was unapologetic, denouncing what he called a media “witch-hunt” – a Trumpian strategy that has also become the new default whenever scandals envelop the Swedish far right.If the rightwing coalition loses the election, it is also prepared to find a scapegoat: Muslim voters. Over the past few months, influential rightwing pundits have lined up to suggestthat the left is mobilising Muslims to vote them out. A writer for the newspaper Svenska Dagbladet recently referred elsewhere to a reported increase in early voting in immigrant-majority suburbs as “the cattle” being herded by leftwing parties.In just a few years, conservatives have distanced themselves from their two most recent prime ministers, Fredrik Reinfeldt and Carl Bildt, who advocated a more inclusive, centre-right liberalism. In the government’s“cultural canon” – originally a strange nationalist initiative promoted by the far right – the authors mock Reinfeldt for his pro-immigration views and blame his “internationalist” agenda for most of Sweden’s contemporary problems. The cultural canon, a list of the references and ideas that supposedly define Swedishness excludes all works from the multicultural Sweden that has emerged since 1975 – meaning we get Ingmar Bergman, Ikea, Pippi Longstocking and the Viggen fighter jet, but nothing made by my generation, the most diverse in Swedish history.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenBibi Andersson and Liv Ullmann in Ingmar Bergman’s 1966 film Persona. Bergman features on the government’s ‘cultural canon’Photograph: United Artists/AllstarThe conservatives have imported the most toxic tropes of the US culture wars in a populist performance of such intensity that it has become internalised on the right, and normalised by the media. Now when a conservative politician in Lidingö, the wealthiest suburb of Stockholm,calls for a banon “strange Peruvian fish stews” in the school cafeterias, it barely makes the headlines.This embrace of rightwing populism has also led to a departure from Sweden’s ambitious climate politics and a general turn away from scientific consensus. Johan Rockström, a climate scientist, last year told me that he had been invited by every government in Sweden in the past few decades, left or right, to sharehis research on planetary boundaries, but the current government was the exception – they have not reached out a single time.The government increasingly ignores advisory bodies that are supposed to weigh in on any legislation or proposals. This is most evident when it comes to authoritarian crime policies. New bills have repeatedly been passed against the advice of experts, criminologists and social scientists, who warn against imposing ever-harsher punishments on children.What we are seeing is a fundamental challenge to the Swedish tradition of pragmatism.The small but persistent lead for the opposition in election polls may suggest that the tide is turning, and that there is still an underpinning of humanitarian ideals grounding Swedish voters. Recently, the billionaire Roger Akelius, who used to vote conservative,said he would not vote for the rightwing coalitionin this election. “Sweden can’t build a future on isolation and prisons,” he said.View image in fullscreenA row of posters for the Social Democrats, featuring party leader Magdalena Andersson, in Stockholm, September 6, 2026.Photograph: Tom Little/ReutersBut the opposition struggles to articulate a clear ideological alternative, preferring a painfully cautious campaign similar to Denmark’s Social Democrats or the UK Labour party as it was under Keir Starmer. There is a clear risk in taking no risks. Relying only on carefully poll-tested centrist positions has not worked for European progressives as the political landscape shifts towards anti-establishment ideas and fury at the status quo. The tight polls suggest that millions of Swedes still consider prisons and isolation the future.Eight years ago, the conservative prime minister Ulf Kristerssonpromised a Holocaust survivorhe would never form a government with the far right.“My values are not those of the Sweden Democrats,” he said in aninterview. “I will not cooperate, engage in dialogue, collaborate, or form a coalition government with the Sweden Democrats.”Now Kristersson is promising the far right cabinet positions.The Sweden Democrats have not changed in those years. But Sweden certainly has.Martin Gelin writes for the Swedish newspaper Dagens NyheterDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsSwedenOpinionThe far rightEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligence | Movies | The Guardian
description: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killing
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killing
Content: ‘It’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen’ … Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen’ … Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianMoviesInterview‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceXan Brooksin VeniceRachel Szor and Yuval Abraham collected the testimony of 24 insiders who helped remotely target Gazans’ homes. They explain how they got these self-professed ‘small cogs’ to talk about the killingFri 11 Sep 2026 11.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a darkened rooftop in Tel Aviv, Israeli intelligence officers outline the details of their work. These men tell us how they helped develop an AI mapping tool that trawled for phone signals and recommended apartment buildings inGazato bomb. Indirectly, they admit, they are responsible for thousands of deaths, but they never spoke up because that wasn’t their place. “My role is technical,” says one. “I’m just a small cog,” says another.Secret systems used by Israel in mass killings of Gaza civilians revealed in new filmRead moreNAZA – directed by the Israeli film-makers Rachel Szor and Yuval Abraham and produced by the Guardian – is a chilling documentary about a mass slaughter that was authorised at the highest levels of government. But it is also, primarily, about the process, the system, the little links in the killing chain. Szor and Abraham build their film around the accounts of 24 anonymised military and intelligence insiders.NAZA, we learn, is an acronym used by the intelligence service to indicate how many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike on Gaza. The Israel Defense Forces prefer to target Hamas terrorists in their homes at night – and if they live with their family, or in heavily populated neighbourhoods, too bad. At one point, a source claims, approval was given to kill 500 NAZA for one Hamas member.I meet Szor and Abraham at the Venice film festival, where NAZA is competing for the Golden Lion award. The pair won an Oscar for their previous documentary, 2024’sNo Other Land(co-directed with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal), which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank. “No Other Land documented horrible crimes,” Abraham says. “But at the same time it gave people … I don’t want to say hope, but some light to latch on to. It’s not a coincidence that this film is all in the dark. We are in a very dark place right now.”double quotation markSome people talk because they feel the opposite of shame. They feel pride in their accomplishment and expertiseYuval AbrahamThe Gaza health ministry has reported more than 73,000 deaths in three years of Israeli bombardment, the vast majority of which have been civilian casualties. NAZA briefly shows us the rubble, grieving parents, dead children on the ground. Its main backdrop, though, is placid, normal Tel Aviv, just 44 miles to the north, where rush-hour traffic drifts dreamily on the street and the cinematheque is showing a Claude Lanzmann retrospective. Tellingly, the film was executive produced by Jonathan Glazer, the director ofThe Zone of Interest. Glazer, says Szor, supported the structure and creative approach she and Abraham had adopted, that fostered the sense of a home that sits next door to hell.NAZA deliberately concerns itself with the system – the policy of mass surveillance, the industrial business of murder – more than the individual psychology of those involved. But presumably its sources must feel guilt and shame, otherwise they’d never have agreed to put their careers and liberty at risk.View image in fullscreen‘We are in a very dark place right now’ … a scene from NAZA.Photograph: The GuardianAbraham is unconvinced. “Well, it depends which one,” he says. “There are many motivations for an individual to speak. Some people talk because they feel the opposite of shame. They feel pride in their accomplishment and expertise. Remember that these people serve in sensitive units. They are not often asked what they do. So there is an attraction to [our] curiosity that drives them to speak up.”The film uncovers a system that is fiendishly efficient. Its series of disconnects appears designed to distance the perpetrators from the crime. Many of these men work remotely from Tel Aviv. AI selects the target and a drone drops the bomb. Even the language feels purposely euphemistic and obfuscatory. NAZA translates as collateral damage, which in turn translates to human beings.“Sure, it’s easier to kill people when you’re doing it on a screen,” Abraham says. “There is some truth in that, I guess. But equally it should be said that intelligence officers know the most. They listen to the cellphones. They know the house they are bombing is full of children. They can hear babies crying. They still order another strike.”What is the status of these men now? Some discuss their work in the past tense. Others don’t, which suggests that they might still be at work, overseeing airstrikes each night. Abraham won’t say; he’s mindful of protecting his sources. “But you can imagine. We are dealing with 24 people, so there is a whole variety of statuses.”Documentary NAZA gets 25-minute standing ovation at Venice film festival premiere – videoNAZA prompts obvious questions about the creatures of darkness we see on screen. But it prompts intriguing ones, too, about Szor and Abraham, a pair of dissident investigative journalists from the country’s middle class. In the furious, febrile climate of post-7 October Israel, their work is liable to make them pariahs, if not enemies of the state.Szor jokes that she just wields the camera and therefore keeps out of sight. “Nobody knows who I am, and I’m very happy about that. But some of my family – and some people I’m close to – don’t accept what I do. After the Oscars [last year] they were very ashamed, very angry. But this is a small price to pay.”Abraham, by contrast, is more vocal and visible. After No Other Land’s premiere at the 2024 Berlin film festival, his family home wastargetedby a rightwing mob. “For me, that was the worst moment of all,” he says. “My mum is hoping it doesn’t happen again.”double quotation markWhen we say we have to learn from the Holocaust, the way to do that is to think about patterns that can be seen in the presentYuval AbrahamEven so, he adds quickly, let’s keep things in perspective. “We’re taking risks in a system that privileges us, that has Jewish-Israeli supremacy as its founding characteristic. So yeah, it was scary for my mum. But she went and slept at my sister’s and her house is still there. For so many Palestinians, it’s not a rightwing mob that’s coming to their home: it’s US-funded bulldozers and weapons. Imagine if a Palestinian journalist in Gaza tried to do what we did and called up senior Israeli officials. There is no comparison. They would most likely be murdered.”Rooftops at night are a good location, says Szor. They lend themselves to contemplation and help people speak more freely. One soldier recalls the “insane fun” of planning airstrikes. Another remembers visiting Holocaust sites as a boy and wondering how the German people could have acted as they did. “I still see the Nazis as evil,” he says. “But what does that mean I am?”After its Venice premiere, NAZA is greeted with a 25-minute ovation. Varietycallsit a “devastating exposé” of systematic mass slaughter. The Hollywood Reporterclaimsthat its “bombshell” revelations are likely to provoke outrage and disgust “on a profound level, for the current Israeli regime and its prime minister, Bibi Netanyahu”(The Israeli military on Friday said it “categorically rejects” the allegations made in the documentary, and criticised the film’s use of anonymous testimonies, which it said “cannot be verified”. In its statement to the Guardian, the IDF said that it “makes unprecedented efforts to minimise harm to civilians” during its offensive in Gaza.)NAZA review – Israeli intelligence officers cast chilling light on civilian deathsRead moreAt the official press conference, the film-makers are asked about parallels between the Holocaust and the killing in Gaza. Abraham points out that this connection was made by one of the soldiers in the film. But he takes the man’s point. “When we say ‘never again’ and that we have to learn from what happened in the Holocaust, the way to do that is to think about patterns that can be seen and observed in the present. I’m not saying [the situation is Gaza] is the same or identical. I don’t think it is. But what we should be doing is recognising these similar patterns of dehumanisation and killing.”Who are these men who we can barely see on the screen? The polite data analysts. The soft-spoken officers. Almost all, it turns out, are products of Tel Aviv’s middle class: intelligent, educated and liberal, at least up to a point. Or to put it more bluntly, these are Szor and Abraham’s people. They come from the same neighbourhoods, share similar interests and probably have friends in common. It’s the ultimate paranoid horror trope: the call that comes from inside the house. It shows the extent of the rot and the film-makers’ own proximity to it.NAZA asks how these men helped kill tens of thousands of civilians. That’s somehow simpler and less frightening than asking why. Abraham shakes his head. “And I have to say I don’t have a clear answer as to why so many people took part in this. And why so few people – in fact, I don’t know of any – refused in real time to do it. It’s scary what that says about the state of Israel. When people talk about genocide, they often speak about it as something that spreads across society, this general atmosphere that normalises death. When everyone else is doing it, it’s easier not to ask questions.”Additional reporting by Lorenzo Tondo in JerusalemExplore more on these topicsFilmNAZAVenice film festivalFestivalsGazaPalestineNo Other LandinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on Pulp | Movies | The Guardian
description: Before the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another record
Author: Rebecca Nicholson
Headline: Before the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another record
Content: Composite: Guardian design; Courtesy of MubiView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design; Courtesy of MubiMoviesInterview‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on PulpRebecca NicholsonBefore the release of a joyful film on the history of the Sheffield band, frontman Cocker and director Garth Jennings talk dark times, taking inspiration from Abba – and why there could yet be another recordFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen the director Garth Jennings first moved to Paris,Jarvis Cocker, who was living there, dropped in on his old friend. “And I nearly got you arrested,” the Pulp frontman recalls. It was bonfire night, and Cocker had taken some welcoming fireworks over to Jennings’ place. “It turned out Garth’s apartment was quite near to the – not an army base, but what’s it called?”“TheÉcole Militaire,” says Jennings.“So obviously they didn’t like explosives,” says Cocker. “We got told off for that. The best welcome to Paris.”“It was lovely,” adds Jennings, fondly. “I remember it very well.”The men had first met in the late 1990s, when Jennings directed two gorgeous music videos for Pulp, for the singlesHelp the AgedandA Little Soul. Now, almost 30 years later, they are working together again, on Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? This joyful, funny, celebratory film is a hybrid beast: part concert movie and part documentary on the long history of the band. The live show was filmed at London’s O2 Arena in the summer of 2025, on the night that Pulp were told thatMore, their eighth studio albumand first album in 24 years, had gone to No 1 in the British album charts. You can see Cocker waving around the trophy on stage.Jennings, director ofSon of RambowandThe Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, has lived in Paris for the past 13 years, where the animation for Sing, his wildly successful kids’ musical film franchise, is made. He is working on a short Christmas special, and the third and final film in the series. “It’s a slow process,” he says, from the studio, “but we’re getting there.” Cocker moved back to London a few years ago, and today he is at home, getting ready toheadline the End of the Road festival. It will be Pulp’s last show for a while.You can blame Instagram and Abba Voyage for the existence of What Do You Do for an Encore? Pulp, formed by Cocker in Sheffield in 1978, split up in 2002. They got back together for a reunion tour between 2011 and 2013, the final date of which was captured for another idiosyncratic documentary, Florian Habicht’sPulp: A Film About Life, Death & Supermarkets. Cocker had considered those shows to be a fitting – and final – farewell.“WhenPulpgot together that time, I had this idea that things had ended in a not-nice way, and I wanted it to have a happy ending,” Cocker says. “I thought the way to do that would be to play concerts, and we invited Russell Senior back” – the violinist and guitarist had quit in 1997 – “and I just thought it would be like: we’re all friends, everything’s good, and then we’d all retire,” says Cocker. “And to be honest, that tour did seem to do that.”View image in fullscreen‘I don’t go to shows any more. I’m an old bloke’ ... Jarvis Cocker.Photograph: Tom JacksonSo when a promoter got in touch years later, to ask if Pulp would be interested in playing again, Cocker had to think about it. “Because the worst thing to do would have been to spoil the happy ending.” How did he decide to say yes? “I confessed my fear that people wouldn’t come, or that people weren’t that bothered, and why would they be?” The promoter assured him that people would most definitely be bothered. “He told me about a few times when he’d been to shows and a Pulp song had come on before a band went on, and everybody sang along. You know, I don’t go to shows any more. I’m an old bloke.” (Cocker is about to turn 63.) “I just said: ‘All right, I hope you’re right, let’s do it.’ But I wanted to make sure that it would be a good thing for us to do as well.”Cocker teased the news of a second Pulp reunion on Instagram in 2022. Jennings messaged him to tell him how excited he was, and to offer his help. It is obvious, when chatting to Jennings, that as well as being Cocker’s friend, he is a huge Pulp fan. As they started to work on the creative direction of the live show together, Jennings remembers, “I’d be in some other room working on a graphics thing, and then I’d suddenly hear you lot playing, and I’d have to just drop it and come outside. Especially a song like Razzmatazz, which was my first Pulp song. I found you through that. You started playing that at one point, and it was just the best thing ever. I had this wonderful little secret window into this world.”When it became obvious that the live show was going to be a spectacle, they started to wonder about turning it into a film. “Some of my favourite films are concert films, and they don’t need to be anything more. But this felt like an opportunity to go a bit further,” says Jennings.View image in fullscreenCelebratory ... Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Which is whereAbba Voyagecomes in. Both Jennings and Cocker had seen – and loved – the theatrical experience, which blends live music with giant holograms of Abba in their prime. “That was something that was very inspiring. Just the sheer joy of it,” says Jennings, who has seen it three times. As well as performing the hits, Abba Voyage tells the story of Abba, just as What Do You Do for an Encore? tells the story of Pulp, giving each song context.“I was so glad when Garth got in touch, because it felt as if he could help make it something that people hadn’t seen before,” Cocker says. “I am very familiar with Pulp’s backstory because I’ve lived through it. But I’m always flabbergasted at how long the band has gone on.” It is clear from the footage of the crowd, showing people losing their minds and singing every word, that some of the audience were not even born when Pulp split up for the first time. “That’s something amazing, really. And something I can’t explain – why young people have latched on to it.” They played in Manchester recently. “A lot of young people,” Cocker laughs. “But I’m happy about it.”View image in fullscreen‘It felt as if he could make it something that people hadn’t seen before’ ... Garth Jennings.Photograph: Ezra PetronioThe film uses animation, old TV clips and grainy VHS footage, as well as documents and objects that fans may recognise from Cocker’s2023 book Good Pop Bad Pop. It was a “huge job” to pull it together, says Jennings, who credits the archivist Tess McNally-Watson with some serious hard work. “Because it’s not all in one place. It’s in people’s bedrooms and attics, and someone’s friend’s brother’s still got a cassette, so it’s a lot of Raiders of the Lost Ark-style gathering and then transferring.” At one point, there is a funny, fond interview with Cocker’s mother and grandmother, who crack jokes about his newfound fame. “That’s a bit embarrassing for me,” says Cocker. “My grandma’s been dead ages, and my mum died only three or four years ago, so it was quite a thing.”During the live show, Pulp pay a moving tribute to Steve Mackey, who joined the band as bassist in 1989, and whodied in 2023aged 56. Mackey was not going to play on this tour, though he had wished his old bandmates luck. It was important that he was included in the film, and Cocker says that they were able to show it to Mackey’s family before it was signed off. “Just to make sure that they were happy with it. But I think you did a very good job there, Garth. It’s a hard thing to express in the right way.”What Do You Do for an Encore? does not shy away from the more complicated times in Pulp’s story. Around the release of their then-divisive album This Is Hardcore in 1998, Cocker describes “going down a dark tunnel”. Jennings was making videos for the band back then. Had he noticed that things seemed off?“I didn’t notice Jarvis going down a dark tunnel, and maybe you were, Jarvis, and I apologise if I wasn’t there to help you,” he says, sincerely. “But no, because the actual act of making these things was always lovely. I never noticed you being tricky, or anything.”View image in fullscreen‘I’d decided to be in a band when I was seven’ … Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Photograph: Courtesy of Mubi“It was probably because I’d decided to be in a band when I was seven,” Cocker reflects. “Like a lot of people, you think that if you achieve fame, that will be the magic wand that makes everything in your life work, and obviously that’s not the case. You still have to make an effort in your life. You can’t just lie in a bed and say: ‘Right, OK, that’s it, job done.’ But I didn’t realise that, so that’s why I had issues with it.” Over time, he says, “I went back into real life and appreciated it. That was probably another reason why it took me a while to decide to do Pulp again. I was thinking: ‘Well, what’s the motivation? What will you get from it?’”In the film, Cocker describes Pulp as “scaling Mount Pop”, but it sounds as if he didn’t much like what he found at the summit. “It’s like seeing videos of your wedding. Your wedding is a magical thing, but then somebody shows you a video, and you think: ‘Oh God, what’sthat?’” He prefers fantasy to reality, he says, “but sometimes you have to look at reality. And that’s what happened.” Fame, he says, “is an exciting thing, but you just have to keep your wits about you, and make sure you’re doing things for the right reason, and try not to get too up your own arse.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s a lot of Raiders of the Lost Ark-style gathering’ … Cocker in his younger years.When he was still at school, in one of his exercise books, Cocker wrote out a “Pulp master plan”. It makes an appearance in the film. But really, he says, they’ve never had one. “I’m glad things that things didn’t go according to a plan. That’s the great thing about groups. You know that you have to work with other people, and everybody adds something to it, and then you get something that you can’t really say exactly where it came from.”Pulp’s End of the Road set last week marked the end of a tour that started in 2023, though the band are planning to meet up again in October, to celebrate it all. They’re going to see Abba Voyage together. Will there be another encore? “You know, it’s like a tree,” says Cocker, philosophically. “A tree doesn’t decide it’s going to grow. If the weather’s right, it’ll grow a branch. And if the intellectual weather is right in the next couple of years, maybe we’ll sprout another record.” He said it himself: there has never been a master plan.Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore? is on Mubi from 25 September, with special one night only preview screenings at UK and Irish cinemas on 18 September and in US cinemas on 24 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmJarvis CockerDocumentary filmsPulpfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 100 years after John Coltrane’s birth, secret tapes are emerging. What can they tell us about jazz’s great rulebreaker? | John Coltrane | The Guardian
description: The sax star turned his back on fame to embrace free jazz. Caught on a tape machine hidden in an overcoat, newly revealed recordings show how he did it
Author: Ammar Kalia
Headline: The sax star turned his back on fame to embrace free jazz. Caught on a tape machine hidden in an overcoat, newly revealed recordings show how he did it
Content: In an unsentimental mood … John Coltrane performs at Newport Jazz Festival in 1966.Photograph: Gai Terrell/RedfernsView image in fullscreenIn an unsentimental mood … John Coltrane performs at Newport Jazz Festival in 1966.Photograph: Gai Terrell/RedfernsJohn Coltrane100 years after John Coltrane’s birth, secret tapes are emerging. What can they tell us about jazz’s great rulebreaker?The sax star turned his back on fame to embrace free jazz. Caught on a tape machine hidden in an overcoat, newly revealed recordings show how he did itAmmar KaliaFri 11 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 05.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn August 1965, at the height of his fame, saxophonist John Coltrane headlined the DownBeat jazz festival in Chicago. Taking to the stage with a new member of his band, young experimentalist Archie Shepp on tenor, Coltrane’s quartet blew through a series of jagged and free improvisations, straying from structured compositions and, instead, hurling down sheets of sound so loud and aggressive that they reportedly caused widespread walk-outs. DownBeat’s own reviewerlater wrote: “They gave as tasteless a display of musicianship as I’ve ever heard … Shepp and Coltrane seemed to be more interested in trying to out-honk, out-squeal and out-bleat each other than in playing music.”That 1965 performance should have been a triumphant moment, after five years of Coltrane’s star ascending. Since leaving Miles Davis’s “first great quintet”, with whom he had recorded what would become the bestselling jazz album of all time – 1959’sKind of Blue– Coltrane founded an entirely new harmonic language in jazz with the 1960 release of his solo LPGiant Steps, had a radio hit with his 1961 version of The Sound of Music’s My Favourite Things and, in January 1965, formulated his own spiritual imagining of jazz music with the Grammy-nominated albumA Love Supreme. He was already a giant of the genre, contributing dozens of compositions to the standard repertoire, but two years later, in 1967, aged just 40, he would be dead of liver cancer.“He torched his commercial appeal by going avant garde,” says the writer and Coltrane biographerBen Ratliff. “He wasn’t interested in pissing people off but he wanted to absorb new influences, younger players and explore the unknown. He always wanted to keep moving forward and to keep listening to himself. He was questing and working towards a kind of endless music.”View image in fullscreen‘This was social music’ … John Coltrane.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesTo mark the centenary of Coltrane’s birth this month, that quest is being documented on a series of previously unreleased, holy grail recordings of his nightclub experiments. Regularly taking up four- to six-week residencies in spaces such as theJazzGallery in Manhattan, the Showboat in Washington DC or Pep’s Lounge in Philadelphia, Coltrane would play extended sets of new material that existed purely in the moment of their making: unplanned and unruly.View image in fullscreenThe Tiberi Tapes … holy grail recordings from the height of Coltrane’s live career.Dubbed The Tiberi Tapes after Frank Tiberi, the saxophonist who made the recordings, the reel-to-reel tapes initially existed as Tiberi’s private means of study. Taking a bulky Magnavox TR-100 to clubs, with its microphone hidden in the sleeve of his overcoat, Tiberi began recording concerts, managing to change the tapes in the dark every 30 minutes to capture as much of Coltrane’s virtuosity as possible. Following Coltrane’s quartet from 1960 to 1964, just before the recording of A Love Supreme, Tiberi amassed 80 reels of recordings and more than 60 hours of music that he began sharing with select peers and students: a map of Coltrane’s circuitous route to endless music.Sax legend Joe Lovano played with Tiberi as part of the Woody Herman Big Band in 1976 and remembers being astounded by the material. “Frank would come and put the headphones on me and press play on certain sections to illustrate the way Coltrane would work harmonic changes or melodies,” Lovano says. “It was inspiring because you could already hear how he was playing single tunes for 35 minutes or more; really stretching out to follow the music and let it take him where it wanted to go. That freedom of his later work was always present in the way he took his own melodic path and left space for others.” Lovano later played with McCoy Tyner, Coltrane’s pianist from 1960 to 1965, “and he told me they all knew Frank was recording but he had their blessing. The band knew it was for education and the music first.”double quotation markIt was legendary how much he practised and played, all day, every day and then performing until 4amTiberi, who is now 97 and was unavailable for interview, offered up the tapes recently to Coltrane’s final record label, Impulse!, as a means of preserving their history. Whittling down those 26 hours of music to 11 newly mastered compositions, the Tiberi Tapes compilation doesn’t shy away from the often poor audio quality of the haphazard recordings or the raucous environment of their making. Audience members can be heard chatting in the background or yelping in response to spirited passages, while Coltrane’s saxophone lines weave through the tape hiss to produce startlingly beautiful takes on a slower, more melodic version of Giant Steps, as well as a 33-minute extension of A Love Supreme’s Resolution. “The energy of these recordings is important because it captures the creative spark Coltrane was feeding off,” says jazz historianAshley Kahn. “This was social music, so people are chatting or making noise, but if you can work your way through, it gives as much back as you put in.”For Lovano, the Tapes serve as a testament to the relationships Coltrane had with each of the musicians in his band. “It was legendary how much he practised and played, all day, every day. And then performing until 4am before driving home to his babies. He’s just a young man striving in his 30s and he shares that inspirational energy,” he says. “You can hear how he digs new cats like Archie Shepp or [drummer] Rashied Ali or [saxophonist] Pharoah Sanders – they loved each other and he let everyone stand on their own two feet. You can always hear the seeds of where he will go next.”What came next was the most uncompromising album of Coltrane’s career. Recorded in June 1965 (a few weeks before the DownBeat festival show) and released the following year,Ascensionwas the first recorded taste of this unruly, alienating music. He expanded his quartet to include seven extra players from the experimental fringes of free jazz, including Sanders and John Tchicai who would go on to be pioneers in their own right. The 40-minute suite was recorded unrehearsed in two takes and plays like a big band spiralling through screeching solos that struggle to maintain their balance over the shifting tectonic plates of melody. At points, the cacophony is so overwhelming that it feels like listening to seven conversations at once.“Post-1965, it’s the line in the sand, and still the most challenging part of Coltrane’s career for many,” Kahn says. “It was so new and revolutionary they didn’t have names for it. Was it Energy Music? The New Thing? It was so radical that people had real issues understanding what was going on.”View image in fullscreenColtrane performing circa 1960.Photograph: Gai Terrell/RedfernsBy 1966, after Tiberi stopped recording and had embarked on his own career, Coltrane had absorbed several new, subversive players into his fold, including free music saxophonist Albert Ayler, who was famous for playing 40-minute elongated live versions of single, hard-blowing tunes. During a show with Ayler, two drummers and Coltrane’s wife, Alice, a pianist, at the Lincoln Center in New York in February of that year, even more of Coltrane’s audience reportedly left in droves after hearing the untethered, explosive direction in which his music was going. The writer Amiri Barakadescribedthe atonal experience as a sound “of an actual frightening nature ... it swallowed you!”, while saxophonist Dave Liebman estimated almost half of the 2,600-seat audience walked out over the hour-long performance.‘It’s the story of what happens when the music stops’: bringing tormented jazz legend Bill Evans to lifeRead more“In Coltrane’s later period, we have an artist who is at such a masterful level that his playing has moved beyond our immediate understanding,” saxophonist and Coltrane acolyte James Brandon Lewis says. “There was always intent and direction with his line but our ears might be too untrained to know what he was trying to solve. He was connecting improvisation to the tribal and spiritual history of music, seeing it all as one thing – the folklore and the future.”Continuing to perform and record until just months before his sudden death in July 1967, the question of where Coltrane would go next has haunted fans and listeners ever since. “He was always searching for his sound and he never stopped,” says saxophonist Melissa Aldana. “In the later years, it was like he was trying to find a divine vibration, free from any kind of preconceived limitations. He was deep into the sound and he was totally free. That’s what always brings me back to him and it means there will always be something new to find in his playing as we continue to listen.”While his audiences might have waned in his later years, it is that same, ceaseless searching that now seems to pull younger listeners in 100 years on from his birth. Ironically, Ascension – the album that heralded his “difficult” late phase – was reissued in June this year owing to demand. “Don’t analyse him, just hear,” Lewis says. “Open up your heart and receive the message. Whatever you think it might be.”The Tiberi Tapesare released on 6 November via Impulse! Melissa Aldana and Joe Lovano perform Coltrane 100 on 13 November at the Barbican, London, as part ofEFG London jazz festival. A new best-of compilation, Coltrane 100, is released on 2 October via RhinoExplore more on these topicsJohn ColtraneJazzMiles DavisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy review – classical myth burns into modern England | Theatre | The Guardian
description: In Ava Pickett’s tense play, Michelle Dockery’s heroine returns to a Towie-styled world where the violence and misogyny are all too recognisable
Author: Emma John
Headline: In Ava Pickett’s tense play, Michelle Dockery’s heroine returns to a Towie-styled world where the violence and misogyny are all too recognisable
Content: Multiple gears … Michelle Dockery  in Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy  at Theatre Royal Stratford East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMultiple gears … Michelle Dockery  in Bloodsport: After Helen of Troy  at Theatre Royal Stratford East, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreReviewBloodsport: After Helen of Troy review – classical myth burns into modern EnglandTheatre Royal Stratford East, LondonIn Ava Pickett’s tense play, Michelle Dockery’s heroine returns to a Towie-styled world where the violence and misogyny are all too recognisableEmma JohnFri 11 Sep 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘And Zeus created … Essex.” PlaywrightAva Pickettset her award-winning debut,1536, in her home county during Tudor times: her latest has Helen of Troy returning home to a Towie-style living room at the end of an English civil war.An Adidas-clad Messenger functions as chorus, bringing us up to speed on this new England where angry men have rioted and petrol-bombed, wreaking havoc in Helen’s name after she left her husband, Marcus, for a so-called “foreigner”. The cream carpets and glass coffee tables belong to Cee – Helen’s best friend, married to Marcus’s big brother Mario – and it’s here that the men arrive with a shivering Helen to toast their victory with prosecco.View image in fullscreenDystopian dinner party … Laura Aikman (Cee) and Gerard Monaco (Mario) in Bloodsport: After Helen Of Troy.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianWhat comes next is a truly tense two hours. Given real-life scenes of masked vigilantes in Dover and Portsmouth this month, Pickett’s dystopian vision feels uncomfortably close, albeit infused with a Martin McDonagh-esque black wit. At one point a guard looms with an automatic weapon as Laura Aikman’s tradwife Cee attempts to glide over the undercurrents of violence and misogyny with platters of mozzarella sticks and prawn picky bits.It’s a play that’s less about toxic masculinity and insidious racism than women’s response to it. Michelle Dockery’s Helen moves through multiple gears, from victim to rebel to a mother confronted with the daughter she abandoned. And on opening night,Maimuna Memon’s uncompromising Dani prompted a cheer in parts of the audience for her takedown of Cee’s complicity.Those versed in Greek myth – and the rest of us who’ve watched Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey – will have their ideas of where the plot is heading, correct or not. The abruptness of the play’s climax does leave us wondering what Pickett is really trying to say about free will – Ethan Moorhouse’s blisteringly poetic interludes as Messenger introduce a pantheon of external forces dressed as gods, while a naked tree reaches across Polly Sullivan’s set like a malevolent hand. But both comedy and drama are deftly paced and balanced in the production by Stratford East’s new artistic director Lisa Spirling, amplified by Nicola T Chang’s bone-shaking score and sound.AtTheatre Royal Stratford East, London, until 10 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMichelle DockeryTheatre Royal Stratford EastClassicsFolklore and mythologyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘The place lost its way. Now that’s changed’: can a Manchester art museum move beyond its troubled past? | Art and design | The Guardian
description: Manchester’s Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new mission
Author: Lauren Kelly
Headline: Manchester’s Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new mission
Content: Art of the matter … esea contemporary.Photograph: Arthur SiukstraView image in fullscreenArt of the matter … esea contemporary.Photograph: Arthur SiukstraArt and design‘The place lost its way. Now that’s changed’: can a Manchester art museum move beyond its troubled past?The Centre of Chinese Contemporary Art closed in 2021 after a series of controversies. Now it’s been relaunched under a new name – and with a new missionLauren KellyFri 11 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 09.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn March 2020, the visual artist JJ Chan was assembling video footage for a group exhibition scheduled at the Centre for Chinese Contemporary Art in Manchester. Centred on family VHS tapes, and titled A New Constellation: Chinese Diaspora Now, the artwork was an exploration of Chan’s emotionally complex relationship to Hong Kong, their parents’ birthplace. When Chan asked for guidance after the sudden departure of the initial curator, the artist discovered that the gallery did not employ anyone who was Chinese: 12 out of the 13 staff members were white, while most of the front-facing (unpaid) volunteers were of Chinese descent.Fearing their art would be shaped through a white lens, Chan withdrew and published an open letter to the centre, writing: “My experience, and my trauma, are being used as a leg-up into an industry for an already overrepresented demographic.” Later that year, the organisation recruited seven artists of Chinese heritage to address the lack of diversity before that initiative was cancelled when the artists raised issues surrounding institutional racism with the gallery. The artist-led working group subsequently petitioned for an international boycott of the institution resulting in the resignation of six board members and several employees. After closing due to Covid in 2020, the arts space never reopened.Two years on, Shanghai-born artist Xiaowen Zhu reattained public funding and relaunched the venue in 2023 under a new name,esea contemporary– incorporating the wider east and south-east Asian diaspora – alongside a new team primarily made up of first- and second-generation migrants. The director’s ethos, defined following a series of artist surveys and community focus groups, seeks connectedness in an increasingly polarised world.double quotation markOur role is not simply to provide visibility but to create the conditions for ambitious work on the artists’ own termsAs part of a year-long programme celebrating its 40th anniversary, the charity is hosting Two Improvisations, the first UK institutional solo exhibition by London-based, Wuhan-born Chris Zhongtian Yuan. There’s also an online interview series tracing the gallery’s shift from a community-oriented Chinese visual arts festival to its role today as the UK’s only non-profit gallery dedicated to local and global art informed by east and south-east Asian cultural backgrounds. In addition, Japanese film-maker Umi Ishihara’s experimental film Nocturnal Melody will preview on 9 October.Zhu believes the four-decade milestone presents an opportunity for reflection, as well as for clarity: who is esea contemporary accountable to, and why does it exist?“We want to demonstrate that an organisation rooted in Manchester can contribute meaningfully to global artistic conversations while remaining deeply accountable to its communities,” says Zhu, who is based between Manchester and Berlin. Explaining that east and south-east Asian perspectives are underrepresented in UK institutions, particularly within major galleries and permanent collections, she adds: “Our role is not simply to provide visibility but to create the conditions for artists to develop ambitious work on their own terms.”View image in fullscreenChris Zhongtian Yuan’s   Two Improvisations.Photograph: David LindsayYuan’s Two Improvisations – an original experimental film – bleeds punk. A pair of obscured musicians sing loudly. The band’s frontman, projected as a dark shadow, represents the “Yeren”, a lingering mythical Chinese misfit creature rumoured to roam the mountainous regions of Hubei. Adjoining the film, which shows musicians singing lyrics about deception and marginalisation, is an installation of Yuan’s architectural models of urban houses and skyscrapers (some built in China, and others handmade in the UK) which sit on an illuminated stage in the gallery foyer, mirroring Manchester’s Northern Quarter outside the window.For Zhu, the showcase – like much of the work exhibited at esea contemporary – illustrates the dual reality of living between cultures, and across borders, while challenging certain narratives. Typically punk is not associated with Chinese people in the west, who are often stereotyped as reserved, “or worse, powerful”, Yuan tells me. “And Wuhan is always the city people talk shit about,” he adds. By drawing cultural comparisons with Manchester, both past and present, Yuan encourages the viewer to question traditional narratives about rebellion in China, as well as in his home town. Yuan relates to the Yeren, he tells me: living in the diaspora, the artist is deemed an outsider.Alongside the gallery’s physical exhibitions, 40 Years, 40 Voices continues the celebrations online, inviting artists, stakeholders and longstanding collaborators to reflect on the organisation’s legacy and future. Art worker Kwong Lee, now director of London’s Deptford X festival, recalls participating in Beyond the Chinese Takeaway in 1992, marketed as “the first exhibition of its kind researching the innovative works of contemporary artists of Chinese origin living in Britain”. Meanwhile, trustee Xu Wenkai, a digital artist known as aaajiao, hopes “esea contemporary remains a space where Asian artists don’t have to justify themselves – where the work speaks first”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt remains a space where Asian artists don’t have to justify themselves – where the work speaks firstIt’s a marked change for a venue that – long before 2020 – had been embroiled in controversy. During the late 90s and 00s, the gallery changed dramatically due to China’s growing cultural and economic influence. In 2013, the Riba award-winning space launched Conservative MP George Osborne’s Manchester China Forum, playing host to global trade deals and geopolitics.According to Chan, the British government’s pro-China policy determined and ultimately restricted the artworks that were exhibited: “The gallery couldn’t be directly critical of the people the government were trying to do business with,” they say. “Galleries are shaped a lot by the political landscape, that’s where their money comes from. There’s often a manipulation of information.”Today, Zhu has re-rooted the institution within the community. Her popular Esea art outreach programme encourages east and south-east Asian residents over 50 to create art, combating loneliness and providing an opportunity for migrants to speak their native language. She also invests in local talent: the organisation’s events and visitor experience manager was initially hired as front of house while working as a cashier at Wing Yip, a nearby Chinese store. At the same time, Zhu intends for the gallery to appeal to a broader audience, and uses more “accessible” artforms – including video, music, food and games – to do so.It’s a marked change for an institution that had been embroiled in controversy. “The place lost its way for a while” says the artist Gayle Chong Kwan, who presented her first solo exhibition at the gallery in 2002 – and who facilitated the boycott in 2020. “Thankfully, that change happened.”Chris Zhongtian Yuan: Two Improvisations is at esea contemporary, Manchester, to13 September.Explore more on these topicsArt and designExhibitionsManchesterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Céline Dion sparks mass karaoke and power-ballad fever with return to stage in Paris | Céline Dion | The Guardian
description: Fans from around the world gather for star’s long-awaited performances after break because of neurological condition
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Fans from around the world gather for star’s long-awaited performances after break because of neurological condition
Content: The singer told fans outside her hotel she was being careful to protect her health.Photograph: Cyril Pecquenard/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe singer told fans outside her hotel she was being careful to protect her health.Photograph: Cyril Pecquenard/SIPA/ShutterstockCéline DionCéline Dion sparks mass karaoke and power-ballad fever with return to stage in ParisFans from around the world gather for star’s long-awaited performances after break because of neurological conditionAngelique Chrisafisin ParisFri 11 Sep 2026 06.56 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 30,000 Céline Dion fans have gathered in Paris for the Canadian singer’s long-awaited return to performing on Saturday night, four years after sherevealed her diagnosisof stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition.Thousands more people without tickets have flocked to a series of giant karaoke events acrossFranceto belt out Dion’s famous power ballads, in celebration of the star’s health stabilising enough for her to return to the stage.‘She’ll outdo herself’: Céline Dion fans camp out for glimpse of star before sold-out Paris comebackRead moreParis city hallorganised a free outdoor karaoke for 10,000 people on Friday night in the north of the cityas a giant sing-along to hits such as Dion’sMy Heart Will Go On, which featured in the Oscar-winning film Titanic and became one of the bestselling singles by a woman in music history.Emmanuel Grégoire, the mayor ofParis, said the capital’s giant street karaoke would honour Dion as “an artist of the people” and a great unifier in France. “Music has that singular power to bring together and build a society,” he said.Dion, who grew up the youngest of 14 children in a small town near Montréal in French-speaking Quebec, has a massive fanbase in France. Her French-language ballads are regularly the most requested songs at karaoke venues.View image in fullscreenDion performing in Quebec in 2019.Photograph: Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press/APDion’s popularity also stems from her life story: from an upbringing in a poor Quebec family, singing as a child at her father’s piano bar, to her massive stadium gigs.Dion, 58, announced in 2022 that she had been diagnosed with the incurable autoimmune disorder stiff person syndrome. She took a break from performing, later describing how the condition meant she had suffered muscle spasms so strong that her ribs were broken. She told journalists there were times she could not walk. In the 2024 documentaryI Am: Céline Dionshe provided insight into the severity of her pain from the condition, including having a seizure.View image in fullscreenDion with the director Irene Taylor at a special event screening  of I Am: Céline Dion in New York in 2024.Photograph: Andrew Kelly/ReutersThe content of Dion’s series of concerts at the Plenitude arena in La Défense, west of Paris – the biggest indoor concert venue in Europe – has been kept secret. The singer toldfans outside her hotelthat she was being careful to protect her health, travelling to and from her hotel only to rehearse and greeting waiting fans from a safe distance.View image in fullscreenDion greeting fans outside her hotel in Paris last week.Photograph: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty ImagesDion told the crowd that the concerts would be longer than her usual performances and advised them to wear comfortable shoes.Usually in France, Dion would sing a set mostly made up of her French-language hits – her 1995 album D’eux became the biggest-selling Francophone album of all time. But with Paris currently her only venue, many fans are coming from North America and across the world, so English-language hits will also feature.In April, about 9 million people had registered for the pre-sale ticket lottery. The concerts swiftly sold out.The Paris region expects the 16-date residency in September and October as well as further sold-out dates in May to boost the local economy by up to €800m (£690m). TheCéline Dionfrenzy could eclipse the profits local hotels, restaurants and tourist sites enjoyed around previous concerts by Taylor Swift and Beyoncé.At the Galeries Lafayette department store, a Céline Dion merchandise corner had seen a steady trade, with some fans arriving before opening hours.View image in fullscreenThe Eiffel Tower illuminated for Celine Dion in March 2026, when the comeback concerts were announced.Photograph: Pierre Suu/Getty ImagesAlexandra, 36, a civil servant from the Paris region, had bought a T-shirt and signature Céline Dion macarons. “It’s important to me because I grew up with her music,” she said. “My mother was huge a fan so I listened to Céline Dion songs on the way to school.“Whenever we went on holiday, Céline Dion would be playing in the car. Her music is part of some of my best memories of childhood. She is humble and she has managed to stay very close to the people.”She added: “I’ve followed her health challenges. I thought she might not be able to perform again. But she has clearly set herself an incredible challenge and I hope she can manage these concerts without impacting her health. I think she’ll be so lifted up by the fans’ love for her that she will find strength in it.”Explore more on these topicsCéline DionParisFranceEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: A rollicking statue, Beryl’s buddies and a swimming pool in a roundabout – the week in art | Art and design | The Guardian
description: A blue lady strides across the fourth plinth, Beryl Cook and friends gather in Bicester, and Spain repurposes a traffic junction
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: A blue lady strides across the fourth plinth, Beryl Cook and friends gather in Bicester, and Spain repurposes a traffic junction
Content: Tschabalala Self's sculpture Lady in Blue atop Trafalgar Square's fourth plinth in London.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersView image in fullscreenTschabalala Self's sculpture Lady in Blue atop Trafalgar Square's fourth plinth in London.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersArt Weekly newsletterArt and designA rollicking statue, Beryl’s buddies and a swimming pool in a roundabout – the week in artA blue lady strides across the fourth plinth, Beryl Cook and friends gather in Bicester, and Spain repurposes a traffic junction –all in your weekly dispatchJonathan JonesFri 11 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExhibition of the weekTschabalala SelfA rollicking triumph of a statue that spreads good feelings and smiles in the heart of the capital. Saucy genius.Fourth plinth, Trafalgar Square, LondonAlso showingBeryl Cook and FriendsSome may see similarities between Tschabalala Self’s Trafalgar Square statue and Cook’s vibrant fun.House of Voltaire, Bicester Village, until 25 OctoberPeter HowsonGnarly, bloody, and bloody-minded paintings of Christ’s Passion.Flowers Gallery, London, until 10 OctoberLiz LarnerSculptures that meditate on myth, metamorphoses and our fragile earth.Camden Art Centre, London, until 17 JanuaryMonika SosnowskaThe sadness of Polish history haunts Sosnowska’s abstract sculptures and installations.South London Galleryuntil 22 NovemberImage of the weekView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Josema CutillasThe theme for this year’s biennial European Prize for Urban Public Space is architectural projects that repurpose infrastructure built for cars. Among the five finalists is Round About Baths, a true urban oasis for which Swiss architect Leopold Banchini has turned an obsolete roundabout in Logroño, northern Spain, into a public pool.Read more here.What we learnedStar Wars director George Lucas has opened a spaceship-sized art museumArgentina must return to the owner’s heir an 18th-century painting stolen by NazisVeteran Califiornia sculptor Liz Larner has been making ceramics based on asteroidsAlong with flowers and deserts, Georgia O’Keeffe also painted stunning urban scenesOur critic wondered why French thieves bothered stealing Renoir paintingsMasterpiece of the weekSaint Paul and a Donatrix by followers of Gerard David, 1515View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Vidimages/AlamyIn late medieval and Renaissance Europe, one of the most popular ways to spend money was on an altarpiece for a chapel in your local church. And if you were paying, why not have yourself painted into everyone’s grateful prayers? This is a wing of a folding multi-panelled painting on wood: the woman it shows is not known by name but she was one half of a well-off couple who probably lived in Bruges. We can feel close to her as she kneels piously with none other than Saint Paul himself behind her. For the painting’s first beholders, she may have been someone they often saw and spoke to in the street or at market, but here she’s enfolded in a holy, supernatural reality that’s one breath away from the visible.
