Paul is placing a supportive hand on her back – a direct contact between the donatrix – the donor – and the divine. Donor portraits come from a world that is very alien to our attitudes yet also very human: this woman’s confident portrayal as someone who communes with the saints in heaven seems narcissistic and naive yet it is a moving attempt to connect everyday experience with something beyond.National Gallery, LondonSign up to the Art Weekly newsletterIf you don’t already receive our regular roundup of art and design news via email,please sign up here.Get in TouchIf you have any questions or comments about any of our newsletters please emailnewsletters@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsArt and designArt Weekly newsletterPaintingPhotographyArtExhibitionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You’re fired!’ The TV shows you can’t stomach any more  | Television | The Guardian
description: Hating The Apprentice? Bored silly of House of the Dragon? Given up on your favourite soap opera after 50 years? Guardian readers share the shows they can’t bear to watch
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: Hating The Apprentice? Bored silly of House of the Dragon? Given up on your favourite soap opera after 50 years? Guardian readers share the shows they can’t bear to watch
Content: Chairman of the bored … Alan Sugar on The Apprentice.Photograph: N/A/BBC/FremantleMedia LtdView image in fullscreenChairman of the bored … Alan Sugar on The Apprentice.Photograph: N/A/BBC/FremantleMedia LtdTelevision‘You’re fired!’ The TV shows you can’t stomach any moreHating The Apprentice? Bored silly of House of the Dragon? Given up on your favourite soap opera after 50 years? Guardian readers share the shows they can’t bear to watchAlfie Packhamand Guardian readersFri 11 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ApprenticeWe loved this show for the first four or five seasons. It had a really good mix of candidates, different ages and walks of life. I think it was after season nine that we started to feel the programme was losing its authenticity. Contestants started to look like homogenous Love Islanders, all the same demographic – 20-30 age bracket, highly polished body image, eye on a post-show influencer career, etc. It lost its uniqueness and became just another reality show.Ngaire Vine, 56, DerbyshireWhen TV turns sour: the shows we simply can’t stomach any moreRead moreLudwigThe first season was excellent but the new series is a massive disappointment. In the first, David Mitchell’s character was believably eccentric and Anna Maxwell Martin was amusingly quirky. In this series they have taken interesting and believable character traits too far and the whole thing is ridiculous. I had been eagerly awaiting a second series but have stopped watching. It’s a shame that two excellent actors have been given such ludicrous scripts.Margaret Ainsbury, 78, DenbighThe ChaseThe Chase feels well and truly past its sell-by date. It’s a real shame, because I love Bradley Walsh, and the Chasers themselves are all fantastic. However, the core concept of the show has grown tired. The player endures the initial cash builder, sweats through a head-to-head round and scrapes together money (usually a pitiful amount) just to pool it into a central pot. And what is the reward for surviving all of that? Watching it vanish in the final chase because the chaser rattles through a block of questions in a fraction of the allotted time. I want to keep loving it, but the magic has worn off.Jamie Jones, County DurhamGrey’s AnatomyView image in fullscreenRunning on EMT … Sandra Oh and Ellen Pompeo in Grey’s Anatomy.Photograph: Michael Desmond/fiveI was completely captivated when Grey’s Anatomy first aired in 2005. There were strong performances – notably Sandra Oh – and strong characters with interesting histories and gripping medical cases. Fast forward to the present day and only a handful of the original cast remain … and even they look bored with the proceedings. The younger doctors inspire little empathy and the storylines need oxygen. I could say urgently, but I think it best to let it rest in peace now.Ruth Muirhead, WalesPrison BreakSeries one felt like groundbreaking telly: stylish, gritty, twisty – I loved it. Series two followed the escapes so was a different show but still OK. But it really had nowhere else to go after that. Wrap it up? Nope, let’s stick them all back in another prison.Please.Matt, 43, ManchesterCoronation StreetA British friend and I have been watchingCoronation Streetfor more than 50 years. It was a mindless pleasure that I would end my stressful day with. In the last year or so, it has become a stressor. There are so many sinister, evil characters now. I had to fast forward through the scenes with the character Theo. My British friend bailed on the show completely because of that storyline. I miss the silliness of affairs and neighbourhood arguments in the pub.Jane, 72, Toronto, CanadaHouse of the DragonView image in fullscreenFalling flat … Steve Toussaint in House of the Dragon.Photograph: HBO/2026 Home Box Office, Inc. All rights reserved. HBO® and all related programs are the property of Home Box Office, Inc.I always liked the dragons in Game of Thrones, and I thought the prequel might be a fresh series that doesn’t have GoT’s later poor plotting baggage. Paddy Considine did such a superb turn in the first season as the troubled and sickly Viserys Targaryen. And I could even forgive the sudden cast changes in season one to account for elapsed time in the narrative. The soundtrack, by Ramin Djawadi, is lovely. Over three seasons, however, I’ve become increasingly apathetic about the characters. The show’s just fallen flat and hasn’t managed to reach the highs of the first few seasons of GoT. Perhaps it really is time that Warner Bros (and Disney etc) give up on legacy IP. Let’s have some new stuff, please.Reinhardt, 39, Pretoria, South AfricaFamily GuyView image in fullscreenFor Pete’s sake … Family Guy.Photograph: Fox/Getty ImagesFamily Guy was hilarious. The first 10 or so seasons were all great for different reasons. It’s just fun – turn your brain off and laugh. But the last few years have been tiresome. Not awful, just plain. The voices are beginning to fade – I understand why, it’s been 25 seasons – and the jokes feel stale and uninspired. Don’t get me wrong, there are good episodes and some have great political commentary. But it has just gotten sour, to the point where I, an avid viewer, slowly stopped watching. I’ve found comfort in Bob’s Burgers now, but hey, maybe that’s just growing up! I still remember when Family Guy started …Hunter, Glasgowskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLove for LydiaThis HE Bates drama was first shown in the late 70s when I was 14. I adored Lydia who was played by Mel Martin. She looked so sophisticated with a beautiful black bob hairstyle. Men fell in love with her left, right and centre. I wanted to be Lydia. Last year it was shown again on Talking Pictures TV. With age comes experience and I could see how terribly selfish and insensitive Lydia actually was. She was a beautiful monster and Richardson who was besotted with her was a complete drip!Julie Coan, 63, Heywood, Greater ManchesterThe Office (US)View image in fullscreenTaking the Michael … The Office US.Photograph: NBC Universal/Getty ImagesThe prime example would be the American Office. Carell departing was too much to overcome, despite the star power of Will Ferrell and Kathy Bates. No disrespect to those actors; I understand the dilemma. If a first season of a show is successful, they want to continue, and as viewers we want more. But it’s becoming increasingly rare that after the flush of initial quality, subsequent seasons can continue the magic.Charles David, Michigan, USAScrubsI can’t stand Dr Cox’s “tough love” any more. His character was heralded for his honesty, especially compared with the slimy Dr Kelso, but Cox was a manipulative, sexist bully.Sharon, 42, Vancouver, BC, CanadaGilmore GirlsView image in fullscreenSnow laughing matter … Gilmore Girls: A Year in the Life.Photograph: THA/AlamyI am in a perpetual cycle of Gilmore Girls rewatch – it’s my cosy year-round comfort show. However, I don’t watch season seven, or God forbid, the Netflix revival. Season seven totally betrays the cute and cosy atmosphere of seasons one to six, and the lives of the main characters drastically change. I suppose that happens after six years, but the showrunner also changed and you can feel the pull in a new direction. Needless to say, elopement and sexting should never have been on the cards.Jazz, 38, WindsorRoseanneRoseanne was, for a long time, a wonderful sitcom and one which has given many, many happy memories. Razor-sharp dialogue and wit, extremely likable characters with terrific, emotional, relatable storylines all laced with a real bite. Then it just went completely off the rails towards the end with an utterly nonsensical plot. A real shame because it was one of the best TV shows ever made.Michael, BristolThe BoysView image in fullscreenSupe du jour … The Boys.Photograph: Panagiotis Pantazidis/APThe Boys began as a topical, biting commentary on modern superhero movies and our political landscape. Its final two seasons felt like a caricature of itself, with characters reduced to bizarre versions of themselves and lazy writing that completely failed to tackle the modern US.Aaron, LancashireExplore more on these topicsTelevisionThe ApprenticeStrictly Come DancingCoronation StreetHouse of the DragonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Killer Story review – this tale of two relentless armchair detectives is prestige true crime | Television | The Guardian
description: Eileen and Keen Umbehr were convinced the wrong person was convicted for double-homicide. After sending Pulitzer-winning journalist Joe Sexton 2,714 emails about it, he agreed to investigate – and it led to a messy entanglement
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Eileen and Keen Umbehr were convinced the wrong person was convicted for double-homicide. After sending Pulitzer-winning journalist Joe Sexton 2,714 emails about it, he agreed to investigate – and it led to a messy entanglement
Content: Armchair detectives … Eileen Umbehr, left, and her husband Keen Umbehr in A Killer Story.Photograph: HBOView image in fullscreenArmchair detectives … Eileen Umbehr, left, and her husband Keen Umbehr in A Killer Story.Photograph: HBOTV reviewTelevisionReviewA Killer Story review – this tale of two relentless armchair detectives is prestige true crimeEileen and Keen Umbehr were convinced the wrong person was convicted for double-homicide. After sending Pulitzer-winning journalist Joe Sexton 2,714 emails about it, he agreed to investigate – and it led to a messy entanglementHannah J DaviesFri 11 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 00.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHBO is no stranger to true crime, though its offerings tend to be more prestige than your average, with documentaries such as the unrelenting sex cult nightmare The Vow andThe Yogurt Shop Murders, a measured reinvestigation into the deaths of four teenage girls in Texas in the 90s. They have form, too, in drily funny sagas, such asMcMillions, about a high-stakes conspiracy to fix the McDonald’s Monopoly promotion. Rarely are their documentaries both solemnandbizarro, with the exception perhaps of The Jinx. An unnerving tale of millionaire real estate heir turned convicted murderer Robert Durst, it occasionally lingered on the stranger points of his story, like the time he shoplifted a $6 sandwich for kicks.All this makes sense, really: it’s not like most homicides lend themselves to a deadpan retelling. A Killer Story is not laugh-out-loud funny, either. But this very meta three-parter manages to tell not one but two killer stories, one disturbing and the other absurd. The first concerns a woman, Dana Chandler, who is sentenced to life in prison for the murder of her ex-husband and his new girlfriend. The second is about a true crime-obsessed stranger, Eileen Umbehr, who becomes fixated on the case, spamming a journalist with tips. The emails from Umbehr were, says Joe Sexton – previously of the New York Times and investigative newsroom ProPublica – “a crazy assortment of shit … I [didn’t] know whether to call the cops on her or fucking hire her!”Sexton – an editor on multiple Pulitzer-winning projects – swears a lot, and his account of the email campaign from “pyjama lady in Kansas” overflows with profanity. Her 2,714th email changes his mind, however; Chandler has had her state conviction overturned, writes Umbehr. It was time for Sexton go to Kansas, to meet the couple he describes – with more than a hint of fatigue – as “the most earnest fucking people you [could] ever meet in your life”.We flash back to 2002, when Karen Harkness and Mike Sisco were found dead in their home. The couple had visited a casino that night, but there was no indication that this was a burglary gone wrong, with money and jewellery left untouched. Rather, says Ray Lundin, formerly of the Kansas Bureau of Investigation, “whoever did the killing was motivated by emotion” – in other words, somebody known to the couple. Chandler becomes the main suspect, but there isn’t enough evidence in the view of the district attorney to press charges. That is until a TV crime special about her airs on CBS, and a new prosecutor decides to proceed with a legal case. Her eventual arrest was also caught on television cameras.This is a story about a very public murder case, then, but it’s also about Umbehr and her husband, Keen, a former waste collector who moonlighted as a local newspaper columnist and later qualified as a lawyer (at one point, hysterically, Sexton refers to him as “fuckin’ Bob Woodward”). The Umbehrs’ preoccupation with the case is clear, with Chandler not only dominating conversation at home but also becoming the subject of their prayers. They don’t only believe that she is innocent, however – they also believe they know who killed Harkness and Sisco. Roll credits!View image in fullscreen‘Certainty is a dangerous notion’ … Dana Chandler, who was sentenced to life in prison.Photograph: HBO/APThis could, of course, be a regular documentary about a miscarriage of justice but of course it’s not. In episode two we meet the person the Umbehrs are convinced is the real killer – but is their apparent evidence enough to justify involving every single law enforcement body in Kansas? Do the Umbehrs worry, asks Sexton, that they’re doing to this new “person of interest”, as they call him, exactly what was done to Chandler?There are some serious flaws in that initial case put forward against Chandler. But A Killer Story isn’t about that, ultimately. Rather, it’s about the pull of true crime, and the power of armchair detectives – not just posting on Reddit, but reaching into a real-life murder case and deciding that they know what’s best for the accused. “Certainty is a dangerous notion,” says Sexton, who had expected to blow the case wide open, but instead ends up entangled in something far messier. A Killer Story is a sideways proposition, but it is rather compelling – a rare true crime story that’s as much about the viewers as it is the victims.A Killer Story is onHBO MaxnowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryHBOreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Lenny Henry and Joanne McNally pop into the Lycett Arms | Television | The Guardian
description: They join pub landlord Joe for more a night of more convivial chaos. Plus: cosy crime in Brooke Shields’ You’re Killing Me. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: They join pub landlord Joe for more a night of more convivial chaos. Plus: cosy crime in Brooke Shields’ You’re Killing Me. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: The snacks are on me … Joe Lycett in Live From the Lycett Arms.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PAView image in fullscreenThe snacks are on me … Joe Lycett in Live From the Lycett Arms.Photograph: Matt Crockett/Channel 4/PATV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Lenny Henry and Joanne McNally pop into the Lycett ArmsThey join pub landlord Joe for more a night of more convivial chaos. Plus: cosy crime in Brooke Shields’ You’re Killing Me. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Ali Catterall,Hannah J DaviesandGraeme VirtueFri 11 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLive From the Lycett Arms10pm, Channel 4It’s opening time once again at Joe Lycett’s paisley-carpeted boozer, and even though the pub is only open for an hour a week, Lycett isn’t a man to do things by halves. Accordingly, the premises are legit, the bevvies are real and hopefully so is the atmosphere of convivial chaos. This week, Joe welcomes Lenny Henry, who offers Brum solidarity as temporary bar manager, and comic Joanne McNally, who proves a lively punter.Phil HarrisonNew World Symphony at the Proms8pm, BBC FourIt often takes an outsider to truly tap into another nation’s DNA, as this piece demonstrates. It was penned by Dvořák, a homesick Bohemian in New York, who took his musical cues from the “tender and passionate” African American spirituals (“all that is needed for a great and noble school of music”, he enthused). Sakari Oramo conducts the BBC Symphony Orchestra.Ali CatterallOur Great Yorkshire Life8pm, Channel 5Another series of a show that strays dangerously close to being an extended advert for the Yorkshire tourist board but offers gentle escapism all the same. Gaynor Faye enlists the help of a horse called Toffee as she overcomes a lifelong fear of the animals, while country pile Castle Howard undergoes a restoration. Bucolic.PHView image in fullscreenNow you see it … Brooke Shields and Amelia Williamson in You’re Killing Me.Photograph: Mike Tompkins/AcornTVYou’re Killing Me8pm, U&DramaIf you’re in the market for a cosy crime show that definitely won’t require your full attention, this Brooke Shields vehicle is the epitome of a double-screen delight. This week’s episode – titled The Front Window – is a thoroughly silly, poison-infused take on Hitchcock’s classic tale of voyeurism and murder.Hannah J DaviesThe Rainmaker9pm, ITV1More of the bingeable – if rather far-fetched – legal drama based on John Grisham’s novel. Rudy (Milo Callaghan) is drawn further into the dangerous home life of his neighbours, and there are revelations about the excellently named litigator Jocelyn “Bruiser” Stone (Lana Parrilla) and her scandal-hit dad.HJDGrimsburg11.40pm, Sky OneJon Hamm voices old-school detective Marvin Flute in this animated sitcom that delights in sending up cop show cliches. A ribald triple bill kicks off with Flute causing chaos at Grimsburg’s annual true-crime convention when he realises that the fans are more interested in notorious killers than him and his paunch.Graeme VirtueLive sportGolf: Solheim Cup. title: A Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan review – a brilliant interrogation of philosophy and wonder | Fiction | The Guardian
description: With a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditions
Author: Daisy Hildyard
Headline: With a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditions
Content: Meticulous precision … Adrian Duncan.Photograph: Steve PykeView image in fullscreenMeticulous precision … Adrian Duncan.Photograph: Steve PykeBook of the dayFictionReviewA Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan review – a brilliant interrogation of philosophy and wonderWith a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditionsDaisy HildyardFri 11 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor several years I ran community groups that involved reading books aloud with other adults. Sharing the experience of reading in that way made me notice how, when one or more of us was baffled by a story, this bafflement was rarely experienced without an accompanying sense of mild anger. It was so easy to make us, the readers, angry – at the characters; at the author; perhaps even at the nature of this reality on which we’d lost our grip. We were confronted with the fact that our capacity to understand the world was limited. We didn’t like that.Irish author Adrian Duncan’s fifth novel, A Thought Without Collision, takes risks with this bafflement: it relates and conveys an experience of being mystified by the universe. As it opens, in Ireland in 1923, it is becoming apparent that six-year-old Catherine has exceptional academic gifts, and that her father’s farm is failing. In the next chapter, set in 1951, Dr Josef Alois, a Tyrolean émigré academic in his mid-50s, is living in his self-built house on the east coast of Scotland. He is alone until Catherine reappears, “a handsome woman in her mid-thirties”, and now an Oxford professor. The second chapter ends starkly: Alois “is more unwell than he believes and will perish in one month and eleven days”.double quotation markIn Duncan's fiction, the Irish realist tradition converges with a cerebral European modeDetails of Alois’s biography, and aspects of his two books, are drawn from the life of Ludwig Wittgenstein. The novel references the philosopher’s near-contemporaries, GE Moore, Gottlob Frege and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. Like Alois and Catherine, these men laboured to establish a particular understanding of the world. Some pages of A Thought Without Collision present diagrams or passages of algebraic logic. Throughout, descriptions of small, mysterious places (“pockets” in Catherine’s mind, pits dug in the ground, golf holes, a swallow’s nest) are emblems of the other worlds that surround us, intimated but not available to human knowledge. As Catherine’s intelligence becomes increasingly polymathic, her interest ranges from complex mathematics to animal sentience. She pictures hidden worlds in the sky: a “plane of translucent and unconnected fragments above them all”.The narrative is related in short, alternating chapters that switch between the two time periods. This creates a sense of flickering movement, like chevrons on a motorway: we see Catherine’s life speed by, an effect intensified by Alois’s impending death. It’s a feat of engineering that the story can cut between these two temporalities and their respective revelations, as it plays with multiple philosophical traditions, while navigating the landscapes of the several distinct historical settings to which the novel takes us.Beyond these accomplishments, A Thought Without Collision does not feel abstruse or tricksy to read. Its mysteries, like the mysteries of the universe, are not here to infuriate reading groups. When Catherine’s father stakes his farm on American stock market investments, we see how floating abstractions are tethered to material realities.From his debut, Love Notes from a German Building Site, throughThe Gorgeous Inertia of the Earth, all Duncan’s novels share a meticulous, patient narrative voice. While some have leaned on a blurry psychological disintegration for their denouement, here the conclusions are more definite: with economic gestures, he offers glimpses of the characters’ new worlds. The novel often reads as a realist Irish rural story: hens underfoot, cold black tea on the table, drizzle. Catherine, so dignified, with a bone-deep sadness contracted via childhood tragedy, could almost be aWilliam Trevorcharacter. But in Duncan’s fiction that tradition converges with a cerebral European mode that is drawn to philosophy, architecture, madness and exile. I can’t think of another writer who draws from the same seams in any comparable way.The prose is exceptionally, perhaps deceptively, straightforward. When Alois makes dinner, he “sets a dark pot on his range to boil. He then lifts a skillet from the wall and begins to heat it up. He takes butter from his tiny pantry and carves a half-inch cube from it. Then he takes a delph pot from a cupboard and from it lifts two eggs, with which to prepare an omelette.”This physical attention is intense (there’s more detail here than in a cookbook) but not sustained (it isn’t Knausgård), and so the close descriptions, when they come, seem weighted with something other than themselves. What is the “tiny pantry” here to impart? Is it contextual detail, or a metaphor? We might consider the relation to Wittgensteinian language games; the differing positions played by words as they arise from, and become a part of, actions in the world.There is also a plainer effect of this superfluity of precision, which is that itfeelssuggestive – like a photorealistic still life, where the careful replication of detail is an occasion to meditate on something seen through it. In A Thought Without Collision, every half-inch cube of butter makes you wonder.A Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan is published by Tuskar Rock (£14.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsFictionBook of the dayPhilosophy booksreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Drawn Together review – preposterous romance with all the erotic charge of leaf mulch | Movies | The Guardian
description: The latest adaptation of Culpable trilogy author Mercedes Ron, about a ballet dancer and her security guard, has more holes than plot and chemistry that barely generates a spark
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The latest adaptation of Culpable trilogy author Mercedes Ron, about a ballet dancer and her security guard, has more holes than plot and chemistry that barely generates a spark
Content: Trash with pretensions … Ester Expósito and Hugo Diego Garcia in Drawn Together.Photograph: Amazon PrimeView image in fullscreenTrash with pretensions … Ester Expósito and Hugo Diego Garcia in Drawn Together.Photograph: Amazon PrimeMoviesReviewDrawn Together review – preposterous romance with all the erotic charge of leaf mulchThe latest adaptation of Culpable trilogy author Mercedes Ron, about a ballet dancer and her security guard, has more holes than plot and chemistry that barely generates a sparkCath ClarkeFri 11 Sep 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is Prime Video’s latest Mercedes Ron adaptation, following the massive ratings success of her Culpable trilogy (My Fault,Your Fault,Our Fault). Drawn Together tells the story of a ballet dancer falling in love with her bodyguard. It’s meant to be darker and sexier than the Culpable movies (which were derived from YA-aimed novels), but has all the erotic charge of leaf mulch. It’s the worst of all worlds – trash minus any froth or fun, trash with pretensions. Fans no doubt will be instantly at home in its glossy world of the ultra-wealthy, all the budget blown on cream-coloured furnishings and jodhpurs.Ester Expósito is Marfil, a 20-year-old student and ballet dancer from Spain living in New York. One night, she is abducted in Central Park and wakes up two days later in hospital with no memory of what happened. What Marfil doesn’t know is that her billionaire father Alejandro (Pablo Molinero) is an organised crime boss, and he hires bodyguard Sebastián (Hugo Diego Garcia) as 24/7 protection for Marfil. In a film with more holes than plot, this stands out as especially preposterous. No father alive would risk hiring smouldering Sebastián (think Tom Hardy’s hot young Spanish cousin) as security for his daughter.In truth, Alejandro’s ill-gotten gains would be better spent on therapy for Marfil to work through her deep-seated psychological issues. She wants to break free of her controlling father but throws herself into the arms of Sebastián, a man who won’t let her leave the house alone and secretly films her on CCTV. The chemistry between the two actors barely generates a spark – but stay alert at the 70-minute mark, because the sex, when it finally comes, is blink and you’ll miss it. There’s another book in the series, so the movie ends on an irritating cliffhanger, with a wait for the climax.Drawn Together is on Prime VideoExplore more on these topicsFilmRomance filmsThrillersFilm adaptationsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Trial of Romeo Oscar review – Ayckbourn goes back to the future with android accused of murder | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The playwright explores our relationship with technology, asks if robots have souls and even questions the value of art in this sci-fi courtroom drama
Author: Nick Ahad
Headline: The playwright explores our relationship with technology, asks if robots have souls and even questions the value of art in this sci-fi courtroom drama
Content: Heavy metal … Richard Stacey and Olivia Woolhouse in The Trial of Romeo Oscar by Alan Ayckbourn at the Stephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough.Photograph: Tony BartholomewView image in fullscreenHeavy metal … Richard Stacey and Olivia Woolhouse in The Trial of Romeo Oscar by Alan Ayckbourn at the Stephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough.Photograph: Tony BartholomewTheatreReviewThe Trial of Romeo Oscar review – Ayckbourn goes back to the future with android accused of murderStephen Joseph theatre, ScarboroughThe playwright explores our relationship with technology, asks if robots have souls and even questions the value of art in this sci-fi courtroom dramaNick AhadFri 11 Sep 2026 06.15 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 06.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor play number 92,Alan Ayckbournreturns to his preoccupation of exploring where we as a species are heading through a science-fiction lens. He goes back to the future. In The Trial of Romeo Oscar, the playwright famed for his domestic comedies looks to the year 2194 when humans have spread about the galaxy and androids live alongside us. One of them, RSDO83, is on trial for the murder of a teenage girl in his charge.This is Ayckbourn philosophising about the future of humanity as we sit at an obvious inflection point, asking what this moment in our relationship with technology means and where it will lead us. The questions running through the play are manifold, complex and echo those asked by sci-fi writers for decades: can robots hurt humans? Do they have souls? He is also questioning the value of art and even its purpose.It makes for a lengthy, three-hour treatise, with a first act that sets up the trial and a second one that takes us into the courtroom as RSDO83 stands accused as the first robot to murder a human.View image in fullscreenTech on trial … from left, Leigh Symonds, Hayden Wood and Russell Richardson.Photograph: Tony BartholomewThe robot’s name is pertinent. R is Romeo in the phonetic alphabet and RSDO83 raised a child called Juliet. They would act out scenes from Shakespeare and the drama questions if, in their playing, they acted it out all the way to its tragic end for real.‘My first play was terrible!’ Alan Ayckbourn on his dazzling career – and writing his 90th playRead moreThere are lengthy recreations of Shakespeare in the courtroom as part of the defence counsel’s case, so lengthy that you sometimes feel like you’re watching a concept-heavy production ofRomeo and Juliet. Olivia Woolhouse as Hermione Quinque, drafted in to play Juliet in court, is becoming a star of the SJT stage in this, her third production at the venue.There are so many questions and concepts being juggled that it would be impossible for them to arrive at resolutions: it might leave you wondering, to borrow a line from Shakespeare’s tragedy, “what satisfaction canst thou have tonight”?For all that, it’s still an Ayckbourn, which means you will laugh and you will be left with much to ponder.AtStephen Joseph theatre, Scarborough, until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreAlan AyckbournComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Stephen Joseph theatreRobotsRomeo and JulietreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Gretchen Parlato: The Wise Ones review – snappy grooves and languid covers from always-arresting jazz singer | Music | The Guardian
description: With guests including Robert Glasper, Parlato turns her immaculate phrasing to soft funk, dancefloor numbers and interpretations of Stevie Wonder and Tears for Fears
Author: John Fordham
Headline: With guests including Robert Glasper, Parlato turns her immaculate phrasing to soft funk, dancefloor numbers and interpretations of Stevie Wonder and Tears for Fears
Content: Eloquent … Gretchen Parlato.Photograph: Lauren DesbergView image in fullscreenEloquent … Gretchen Parlato.Photograph: Lauren DesbergJazz album of the monthMusicReviewGretchen Parlato: The Wise Ones review – snappy grooves and languid covers from always-arresting jazz singer(Edition)With guests including Robert Glasper, Parlato turns her immaculate phrasing to soft funk, dancefloor numbers and interpretations of Stevie Wonder and Tears for FearsJohn FordhamFri 11 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 12.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHearing Gretchen Parlato’sspellbinding versionof the Herbie Hancock song Butterfly was unforgettable when the eloquent LA-born singer’s star glimmered into view in the 2000s. The unique qualities she revealed soon brought her worldwide acclaim. Butterfly would open in an onstage silence only broken by Parlato’s soft handclap on a Brazilian groove, eventually turned into a wordless vocal hook, and then the awestruck natural-world homage of the lyrics written by Hancock’s sister Jean. She would time phrases between deliberately emphatic in-breaths like cymbal hits, and arrestingly morph words in and out of abstract sound.View image in fullscreenGretchen Parlato: The Wise Ones album art.Photograph: Edition RecordsThe Wise Ones arrives as her third album since 2021, when she returned from six years of parenting. Here, she’s backed by longtime partners including folk-rockish and jazz-influenced multi-instrumentalist Alan Hampton and Parlato’s percussionist husband Mark Guiliana, plus guests including Robert Glasper, Meshell Ndegeocello and Becca Stevens.Parlato’s Never Come Down is a snappy groover for Giuliana’s hustling drums and Ndegeocello’s vocals and bass – full of fast, anthemic rephrasing of a catchy hook that wouldn’t be out of place on a dancefloor. The smooth-jazziness of Glasper’s soft-funky Rainbow is gently resisted by Parlato’s immaculate phrasing, canny timing and clever pacing of the backing vocals, while singer/producer Amber Navran guides her expressively close to neo-soul on the title track. Stevie Wonder’s If It’s Magic is a big highlight, as are Parlato’s languid account of Tears for Fears’ Mad World over a contrasting punchy vamp; her quietly intense chant of the typically pop-seductive Hampton ballad It’s You; and Glasper’s moving paean to creative receptivity Block the Sun. Perhaps aimed at a wider marketplace than its more improvisational and intimate predecessors Flor andLean In, and not without a humdrum moment or two, The Wise Ones nonetheless confirms that Parlato’s inimitable character never lets her slip into the generic.Also out this monthPeace and Justice (Flexatronic) is an enthralling session led by an overlooked multi-generic maestro, New York original and longtime Meredith Monk collaboratorJohn Hollenbeck. A Ukraine-themed repertoire originally scheduled for a 2022 Kyiv premiere, it’s a gripping mix of Ukrainian traditional and resistance music, Christmas carols and Hollenbeck originals, played by Portugal’s superb Hot ClubJazzOrchestra and powered by the composer’s creative momentum at the drum kit. Young UK pianistNoah Stonemancontinues to develop the spontaneous fluency and freedom from cliche that has already marked him out on Like Yours, a set of freewheeling post-bop variations on lyrical and quietly striking originals, featuring young Danish bass star Felix Moseholm and drummer Jacob Patrone. And Tomorrow’s Warriors-mentored saxophonist/composerMali Sheard, with A-listers Huw Warren (piano) and Rob Luft (guitar) augmenting her empathic quintet, releases an atmospheric mix of rural tranquillity, urban-jazzy edginess and distinctively talkative alto and soprano sax phrasing on her sophisticated debut Hayfever (ECN Music).Explore more on these topicsMusicJazz album of the monthJazzreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Haruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely review – slight songs with huge hearts from the Japanese pop pioneer | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Unpredictable and utterly beguiling, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songs
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: Unpredictable and utterly beguiling, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songs
Content: Playful … Haruomi Hosono.Photograph: Masahiro HandaView image in fullscreenPlayful … Haruomi Hosono.Photograph: Masahiro HandaPop and rockReviewHaruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely review – slight songs with huge hearts from the Japanese pop pioneer(Ghostly International)Unpredictable and utterly beguiling, the septuagenarian beloved by Harry Styles brings a hint of mischief to his innocently charming songsStevie ChickFri 11 Sep 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHaruomi Hosono is one of the most influential figures in Japanese music. In 1969, his psych-folk groupHappy Endwere the first rock group to sing in Japanese; decades later, their songKaze wo Atsumetewas rediscovered for the Lost in Translation soundtrack. He was also an integral member of electronic pioneers Yellow Magic Orchestra, and scored movies and video games, while his solo albums swing from foundationalcity poptexts to experiments in ambient and arch exotica.View image in fullscreenHaruomi Hosono: Yours Sincerely album artNow 79, with disciples including Van Dyke Parks and Harry Styles (who named 2022’sHarry’s Houseafter 1973 solo album Hosono House), he still makes whatever music he wants. His 23rd solo album is wilful, playful, unpredictable and utterly beguiling. Rooted in the Japanese concept ofomoiyari, roughly translated as compassion, these songs are big-hearted, focusing on warmth and positivity: opening reverieNote of Mothershipfeatures a chorus of overlapping voices murmur-singing “we are mothers”; the sweet Happy Holiday repeats its title over an enchantingly simple melody;Sincerelyis a sleepy, Leon Redbone-esque strum.But Yours Sincerely evades mawkishness with its mischievous invention. The Gallic waltz of Aayurveda is inverted exotica, with Europe cast as the mysterious “other”; the primitive electronica of Anemo Wheel channels the innocent charms of early synth innovators Isao Tomita and Wendy Carlos; Rojiura (Walking Vibration) is rooted in Japanese rhythms and percussion, but deliciously lost in time. Hosono’s themes of compassion and hope in humanity’s better side make this collection of miniatures and sketches something greater than its already bewitching parts.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockJapanElectronic musicalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts: Second Song review – shaky album occasionally strikes gold | Neil Young | The Guardian
description: The 80-year-old continues his tireless output, delving into the past for inspiration to variable results – though two lengthy brand-new songs are real showstoppers
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: The 80-year-old continues his tireless output, delving into the past for inspiration to variable results – though two lengthy brand-new songs are real showstoppers
Content: Spontaneity over finesse … Neil Young.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APView image in fullscreenSpontaneity over finesse … Neil Young.Photograph: Rebecca Cabage/Invision/APNeil YoungReviewNeil Young and the Chrome Hearts: Second Song review – shaky album occasionally strikes gold(Reprise)The 80-year-old continues his tireless output, delving into the past for inspiration to variable results – though two lengthy brand-new songs are real showstoppersAlexis PetridisFri 11 Sep 2026 04.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 04.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou can’t faultNeil Youngfor his industry. Second Song is his second new album of 2026: the first, a double live set called As Time Explodes, was released just over three months ago. Indeed, at 80, his work schedule seems mind-boggling. Since 2020, he’s released nine new albums, a 30-minute EP, five self-directed films and three more films directed by others, 10 archival live albums, six archival studio albums and two immense box sets. He has embarked on tours with his longstanding backing band Crazy Horse, his recently convened backing band the Chrome Hearts, and solo. He has gone to public war with Spotify, Amazon, Ticketmaster and – briefly – the BBC’s coverage of Glastonbury, and penned umpteen op-ed pieces about politics, the environment and corporate media for his online newspaper the Times-Contrarian. When he recently cancelled a European tour citing exhaustion, it was hard not to think: well, I’m not surprised.View image in fullscreenSecond Song album artwork.Photograph: PR HandoutYou do find yourself wondering if his workload is such a good thing: not just for an elderly gentleman’s health but also for the quality of his output. Young has always prized spontaneity over finesse, but some of his more recent releases have suggested that at least a soupçon of finesse might not go amiss. Last year’s Talkin to the Trees, however, seemed to cross the line that separates the instinctive from the dashed off. Young frequently sounded as if he was making the material up as he went along, with nugatory results: “When today has come and gone, I might be singing my new song,” he offered on Family Life. “Might be short, it might be long, but I’ll be singing my new song.” If some of the melodies sounded familiar, that’s because they were. Not one but two tracks echoed the tune of Woody Guthrie’s This Land Is Your Land; First Fire of Winter was essentially Young’s 1970 masterpiece Helpless with different lyrics; Thankful rewrote 1992’s Harvest Moon.Its follow-up leans more into Young’s gentle acoustic side than the gargantuan Crazy Horse-like din the Chrome Hearts are more than capable of creating. The music seems a little more honed than that on its predecessor. There are audible overdubs, including a backwards guitar solo on opener The Foggy Edge of Time. Like 1973’s Don’t Be Denied or 1979’s Thrasher, it’s one of those Neil Young songs in which he defends his right to follow his muse, regardless of the personal cost. But if you’re worried about declining inspiration, the omens augur ill. Two of Second Song’s seven tracks are re-recordings of tracks Young first performed with his early 60s band the Squires, which hardly suggests a surfeit of great new material.Casting Me Away From You and I’ll Love You Forever turn out to be pleasant enough, but slight. The former has already been plundered for its melody on The Emperor of Wyoming, from Young’s eponymous 1968 solo debut; I’ll Love You Forever, reworked as a paean to Young’s partner Daryl Hannah, is at least more charming than the tribute he offered up on Talkin to the Trees, which described Hannah as “my best wife ever” and “the best cook in the world”. Elsewhere, there’s another song cut from the same rambling cloth as the stuff on Second Song’s predecessor – Day After Day’s seven minutes feel like seven months – and an unexpected, but sweet diversion into pre-rock’n’roll pop on Earth Girl.That leaves two songs, although in fairness, they take up nearly half Second Song’s running time. From its title downwards, Soon I Might Be Going is thick with intimations of imminent mortality – “I miss you like tomorrow”, Young sings at one point – and feels like a weary, far older cousin of 1974’s Ambulance Blues: a long, ruminative sigh of a song whose subject matter ranges wildly about, from Donald Trump’s White House renovations to Young’s estrangement from his daughter Amber Jean. He also addressed the latter on Talkin to the Trees, but while the tone there was huffy and injured, here Young sounds plaintive and bereft: “Come back to me, my lovely girl, your memory is mine.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNeil Young – every album ranked!Read moreIt is genuinely gripping, but Second Song’s title track is something else entirely: a latter-day Neil Young song that you might compare to his best work without recourse to special pleading. Its melody is impossibly beautiful and – crucially – not markedly similar to any of the impossibly beautiful melodies Young has previously written: 11 minutes of it slip by without the listener checking their watch. Its lyrics capture a dying-of-the-light quality – “the leaves are falling, gathered in piles to burn outside / Somehow the smoke is calling, somehow the embers will decide” – but unlike Soon I Might Be Going, it reaches a comforting resolution: everything may be turning to shit, its final verses suggest, but you can always find solace in music.It would be nice if everything here was as good as those two songs, if you could justifiably claim Second Song as an autumn-years masterpiece along the lines of Dylan’s Rough and Rowdy Ways. Instead, the sublime shares space with the not bad and the insubstantial: a superior example of a late-period Neil Young album, but a late-period Neil Young album nonetheless.Second Song is released via Reprise on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsNeil YoungPop and rockAmericanareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Playing With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworlds | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Wang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installation
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: Wang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installation
Content: Potentially overwhelming … a VR still from Playing With Fire.Photograph: Vive Arts and Atlas VView image in fullscreenPotentially overwhelming … a VR still from Playing With Fire.Photograph: Vive Arts and Atlas VClassical musicReviewPlaying With Fire review – like Disney’s Fantasia on steroids as a virtual Yuja Wang plays amid luminous dreamworldsSouthbank Centre, LondonWang’s avatar performs music from Ravel and Debussy to Prokofiev and Liszt while dizzying virtual worlds take shape around her in this virtual reality installationErica JealFri 11 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 11.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt might be the first time that a soloist at the Last Night of the Proms is simultaneously giving another performance in another London venue.Playing With Fireis an installation that lets the pianist Yuja Wang be in two places at once – or perhaps in two universes. Nine pieces of music conjure nine luminous dreamworlds for an audience wearing VR headsets: Disney’s Fantasia on steroids.A collaboration between the pianist, the director Pierre-Alain Giraud and artist Gabríela Friðriksdóttir, produced by Vive Arts and Atlas V, it has already been seen in Cannes, Paris and Shanghai, and now has a home in London until new year.Headsets on, we hear the click of Wang’s heels as her avatar emerges out of the pixels and walks to the piano stool. Then she begins to play. Or rather, the Steinway Spirio player piano in the middle of the room, programmed by Wang, plays – and we see digitised Wang play it. She begins with Ravel’s Jeux d’Eau, and after only a few seconds we are immersed, literally: water pools beneath the piano, then rises until we are submerged in a world of imaginary sea creatures. It’s enchanting, unnerving and in a way primal, all at once. After Debussy has led us to dry land again, Wang storms through the Danse Infernale from Stravinsky’s ballet The Firebird as the blazing bird swoops over our heads and creatures made of lava dance madly around us: a wild rumpus with Wang calm yet ferocious at its centre.View image in fullscreenThe future of performance? … Playing With Fire.Photograph: Pete WoodheadWorlds morph into each other with distant seismic rumbles. There’s an icy white land evoking a cathedral for Bach’s prelude Ich ruf zu dir, an inferno in Liszt’s Feux follets. The two dozen or so people sharing the experience are visible, up close, as vaguely humanoid shapes made of water vines, or blackened rock, or – more disturbingly – flames. If that’s not unsettling enough, the penultimate immersive episode is a terrifying realisation of the frenzied finale of Prokofiev’s Piano Sonata No 7, one of his War Sonatas: villages burn on the horizon and drones skitter above.Yuja review – portrait of star pianist who is intellectually curious and deeply musically attunedRead moreIt’s powerful stuff, and it has the potential to be overwhelming, or indeed to induce motion sickness. But seats are available at the edge – or stand close enough to the piano and the dreamworld disappears, revealing fellow audience members inching around the room in their headsets, but with Wang’s avatar still at the piano.Finally we take the headsets off and listen to Chopin’s C sharp minor waltz, watching the piano keys and hammers move by themselves, readjusting ourselves to the mechanics of reality. It makes for an ending that’s slightly anticlimactic – but, given the weirdness and wonder of what’s gone before, it’s hard to think how it could be otherwise.At theSouthbank Centre, London, until 3 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsClassical musicSouthbank CentreYuja WangVirtual realityInstallationreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Lucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations album review – freshness and flair | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songs
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songs
Content: Not to be pigeonholed … Lucas Debargue.Photograph: Andreas FleckView image in fullscreenNot to be pigeonholed … Lucas Debargue.Photograph: Andreas FleckClassical musicReviewLucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations album review – freshness and flair(Sony)Alongside supple and distinctive accounts of Rhapsody in Blue and the Piano Concerto and Preludes, the French pianist showcases his jazz chops in reinterpretations of Gershwin’s timeless songsClive PagetFri 11 Sep 2026 02.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 11 Sep 2026 02.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEver since Lucas Debargue took fourth prize at the 2015 international Tchaikovsky competition, he’s refused to be pigeonholed. His distinctive journey brings him now to George Gershwin, complementing the piano concerto and preludes with beguiling original explorations of the composer’s songs in the form of a dozen études. His supple account of Rhapsody in Blue is based on Gershwin’s solo piano arrangement, to which he adds his own partly improvised cadenzas. Like everything here, it comes up fresh as a daisy.View image in fullscreenLucas Debargue: Gershwin Variations album art.Photograph: Sony ClassicalThe Piano Concerto in F brings Debargue’s jazz credentials to the fore (he cut his teeth on the club circuit). The Orchestre de Paris under Elim Chan provides an admirably clear and concise accompaniment. The edge-of-your-seat stakes are reminiscent of André Previn.In his programme note, Debargue admires Gershwin as a maverick whose music transcends time and place. His 12 virtuoso études on Gershwin songs, impeccable compositions in their own right, view familiar tunes through unfamiliar lenses. Embraceable You, for example, is reinvented as a sultry rumba, while Fascinating Rhythm is a cheeky Parisian waltz. It Ain’t Necessarily So barnstorms as a Bach-flavoured Fantasie, Chaconne and Fugue. The colossal 12th étude comprises 20 whirlwind variations on Summertime. Performances are rhythmically alert and full of imaginative flair.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
